title: Tabula Smaragdina
title_english: The Emerald Tablet
author: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.)
date: c. 1150 CE (Hugo of Santalla, Latin trans.)
representative_sentence: Quod est inferius est sicut quod est superius, et quod est superius est sicut quod est inferius, ad perpetranda miracula rei unius.
latin_text: Verum, sine mendacio, certum et verissimum: quod est inferius est sicut quod est superius, et quod est superius est sicut quod est inferius, ad perpetranda miracula rei unius. Et sicut omnes res fuerunt ab uno, meditatione unius, sic omnes res natae fuerunt ab hac una re, adaptatione. Pater eius est Sol, mater eius est Luna. Portavit illud ventus in ventre suo. Nutrix eius terra est. Pater omnis telesmi totius mundi est hic. Virtus eius integra est si versa fuerit in terram. Separabis terram ab igne, subtile a spisso, suaviter cum magno ingenio.
english_gloss: True, without falsehood, certain and most true: that which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracle of one thing. And as all things were made from one, by the contemplation of one, so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation. Its father is the Sun, its mother is the Moon. The wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the Earth. The father of all perfection in the whole world is here. Its power is integral if it is turned into earth. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, gently, with great skill.

vocabulary.definition: lower, that which is below
upper, that which is above
to accomplish, perform, bring about
miracle, wonder, marvel
contemplation, meditation, thought
adaptation, fitting, adjustment
talisman, perfection, consecrated object (from Greek)
whole, untouched, complete
you shall separate, divide
fine, subtle, delicate
dense, thick, compressed
natural capacity, skill, cleverness

source_notes: The most influential alchemical text in the Western tradition. The Latin derives from Hugo of Santalla's 12th-century translation from an Arabic intermediary.
bibliography: Ruska, Julius. Tabula Smaragdina. Heidelberg: Carl Winter, 1926. // Holmyard, E.J. Alchemy. Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1957.

title: Asclepius, §2
title_english: The Asclepius — On God and World
author: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.); Latin attributed to Apuleius
representative_sentence: Deus enim, o Asclepi, et omnia quae sunt in mundo vel per nos vel per aliud quodcumque spiritale officium moderantur.
latin_text: Deus enim, o Asclepi, et omnia quae sunt in mundo vel per nos vel per aliud quodcumque spiritale officium moderantur. Nihil enim in mundo quod non sit plenum Deo. Ipse enim Deus omnia continet, nec est aliquid quod non sit in Deo. Mens enim Dei esse non cessavit. Hoc enim modo Deus omnium pater atque dominus est: omnia ex se ipse facit, omnia in se ipse retinet. Sensus eius ac ratio, id est intellectus et anima, vehicula sunt ad eius officium ferenda. Ipsa igitur anima mundi tam grandi ornata est virtute, ut omnia plena sint.
english_gloss: For God, O Asclepius, and all things that are in the world are governed either through us or through some other spiritual ministry. For there is nothing in the world that is not full of God. For God himself contains all things, and there is nothing that is not in God. The Mind of God did not cease to exist. For in this way God is the father and lord of all: he makes all things from himself, he holds all things in himself. His sense and reason, that is, intellect and soul, are vehicles for carrying out his ministry. Therefore the soul of the world is endowed with such great power that all things are full.

vocabulary.definition: govern, manage, control (passive/deponent)
ministry, duty, service, function
contains, holds together
vehicles, carriers, conveyances
intellect, understanding, intelligence
soul, breath of life
power, virtue, excellence, strength

source_notes: The Asclepius is one of two Hermetic texts available in Latin throughout the Middle Ages. It was central to Ficino's synthesis of Platonism and Hermetism.
bibliography: Copenhaver, Brian P., trans. Hermetica: The Greek Corpus Hermeticum and the Latin Asclepius. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1992.

title: Asclepius, §38
title_english: The Asclepius — On Animated Statues
author: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.)
representative_sentence: Ita deorum cultus hominesque se miscent, sic numina et homines inter se miscentur.
latin_text: Quoniam de cognatione et consortio hominum deorumque dicere incepimus, potestatem hominis accipe, o Asclepi. Ut dominus et pater, vel, ut ipse se superans, Deus fecit deos qui sunt aeterni: ita humanitas finxit deos suos ex sui vultus similitudine. Sic enim hi dei qui ex utraque natura mixti sunt amant sua instituta, utpote qui ex natura propria humana sint initiati. Statuas, Asclepi, illas dicimus animatas, sensu et spiritu plenas, tantas res efficiunt, praesciunt futura, easque per sortes, per vates, per somnia multaque alia praedicunt.
english_gloss: Since we have begun to speak of the kinship and companionship of men and gods, receive, O Asclepius, the power of man. Just as the Lord and Father, or God himself surpassing himself, made gods who are eternal: so humanity fashioned its own gods in the likeness of its own face. For those gods who are mixed from both natures love their own institutions, being initiated, as it were, from their own human nature. We speak of those statues, Asclepius, animated, full of sense and spirit, which accomplish such great things, foreknow future events, and predict them through lots, through prophets, through dreams and many other means.

vocabulary.definition: kinship, relationship, connection
partnership, fellowship, companionship
fashioned, shaped, formed, invented
likeness, resemblance, similarity
animated, enlivened, ensouled
foreknow, know in advance
lots, oracles, divination, fate
prophet, seer, bard, poet

source_notes: This passage on animated divine statues was profoundly influential on Renaissance magicians, especially Ficino and Bruno, who saw it as a model for drawing spirits into material objects.
bibliography: Copenhaver, Brian P., trans. Hermetica: The Greek Corpus Hermeticum and the Latin Asclepius. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1992.

title: De Radiis Stellarum, §1
title_english: On Stellar Rays — The Foundation
author: Al-Kindi (Yaqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi)
representative_sentence: Stellarum radii, qui per naturam in omnia diffunduntur, naturam rerum sub caelo positarum immutant.
latin_text: Stellarum radii, qui per naturam in omnia diffunduntur, naturam rerum sub caelo positarum immutant, nec sola corpora, sed etiam spiritus et mentes humanas. Ex harmonia enim motuum caelestium mundus est gubernatus, et quicquid hic inferius agitur a superiorum virtute dependet. Omnis res in mundo posita est quasi chorda in citharae: si una tangitur, omnes resonant secundum proprietatem suam. Sic radii planetarum, cum in materiam incidunt, proprietates suas materiae imprimunt. Qui igitur hanc harmoniam intelligit, potest et rerum naturas cognoscere et futura praedicere et per artem vim stellarum in usum suum convertere.
english_gloss: The rays of the stars, which are diffused through nature into all things, change the nature of things placed beneath the sky, and not bodies alone, but also the spirits and minds of men. For the world is governed by the harmony of celestial motions, and whatever is done here below depends on the power of the superior things. Every thing placed in the world is like a string on a lyre: if one is touched, all resonate according to their own property. Thus the rays of the planets, when they fall upon matter, imprint their properties upon it. He who understands this harmony can both know the natures of things and predict future events and convert the power of the stars to his own use through art.

vocabulary.definition: rays, beams, spokes (of light/influence)
are diffused, spread out, poured through
change, alter, transform
harmony, agreement, consonance (from Greek)
governed, steered, directed
string (of instrument), cord
lyre, cithara (stringed instrument)
resound, echo back, vibrate in response
fall upon, strike, come across
turn, convert, direct toward

source_notes: Al-Kindi's De Radiis provided the theoretical basis for talismanic and astrological magic in the Latin West. Its theory of rays influenced Agrippa, Ficino, and the entire tradition of natural magic.
bibliography: d'Alverny, Marie-Thérèse, and Françoise Hudry, eds. "Al-Kindi: De Radiis." Archives d'histoire doctrinale et littéraire du Moyen Âge 41 (1974): 139–260.

title: Picatrix, I.2
title_english: Picatrix — On the Foundation of Magic
author: Pseudo-Maslama al-Majriti (attrib.)
date: c. 10th cent. Arabic; 13th cent. Latin trans.
representative_sentence: Intelligere debes, o fili, quod fundamentum et radix totius huius scientiae est scientia figurarum caelestium et planetarum.
latin_text: Intelligere debes, o fili, quod fundamentum et radix totius huius scientiae est scientia figurarum caelestium et planetarum. Scire enim debes quod omnes planetae habent proprietates suas, virtutes suas, et naturas suas, et quod operationes et effectus qui fiunt in mundo inferiori fiunt per virtutem et potestatem superiorum corporum. Qui vult ergo in hac scientia proficere, oportet ut primo sciat naturas planetarum et signorum, et postea sciat quando planetae sunt in virtute sua et quando in detrimento. Tunc enim potest operator elicere earum virtutes et operationes ad effectum perducere.
english_gloss: You must understand, O son, that the foundation and root of this entire science is the knowledge of the figures of the heavens and the planets. For you must know that all planets have their properties, their powers, and their natures, and that the operations and effects that occur in the lower world come about through the power and authority of the superior bodies. Whoever therefore wishes to advance in this science must first know the natures of the planets and signs, and afterward know when the planets are in their power and when in their detriment. For then the operator can draw forth their powers and bring operations to their effect.

vocabulary.definition: foundation, base, groundwork
figures, shapes, forms (here: astronomical configurations)
properties, characteristics, special qualities
effects, results, accomplishments
to advance, make progress, profit
detriment, harm, loss (astrological term)
operator, worker, practitioner
to draw out, elicit, call forth

source_notes: The Picatrix (Arabic: Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm, 'The Goal of the Wise') is the most comprehensive manual of astrological magic from the medieval period. Translated into Castilian in 1256, then into Latin.
bibliography: Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: Speculum Astronomiae, Ch. 11
title_english: Mirror of Astronomy — On Books of Images
author: Albertus Magnus (attrib.)
representative_sentence: Sunt autem libri qui pertinent ad nigromantiam sub nomine astronomiae, qui execrabiles sunt et anathematizati.
latin_text: Sunt autem libri qui pertinent ad nigromantiam sub nomine astronomiae, qui execrabiles sunt et anathematizati. In his autem libris inveniuntur imagines de metallis, et earum nomina, et confectiones, et suffumigationes, et imprecationes, et characteres, et nomina daemonum, et alia multa quae pertinent ad idololatriam et ad invocationem daemonum. Sunt etiam alii libri de imaginibus astronomicis qui non sunt anathematizati, qui virtutes habent ex stellis, non ex daemonibus: inter quos est liber de imaginibus Ptolemaei et Thebith et similium. Haec autem imago ex virtute caelestis figurae suam habet operationem naturalem.
english_gloss: There are, moreover, books which belong to necromancy under the name of astronomy, which are execrable and anathematized. In these books are found images of metals, and their names, and preparations, and fumigations, and imprecations, and characters, and names of demons, and many other things which pertain to idolatry and to the invocation of demons. There are also other books of astronomical images that are not anathematized, which have their powers from the stars, not from demons: among which is the book of images of Ptolemy and Thabit and similar authors. This image, however, has its natural operation from the power of the celestial figure.

vocabulary.definition: necromancy, divination through the dead
execrable, accursed, detestable
anathematized, cursed by Church decree
fumigations, incense offerings
imprecations, curses, invocations
magical characters, sigils, inscribed signs
idolatry, worship of false gods
images, likenesses, representations
astronomical, of astronomy
celestial, heavenly, of the sky

source_notes: The Speculum Astronomiae (c. 1260) is a famous bibliographic survey of astrological and magical texts, drawing a crucial distinction between lawful astronomical image-magic and illicit necromancy.
bibliography: Zambelli, Paola. The Speculum Astronomiae and Its Enigma: Astrology, Theology and Science in Albertus Magnus and His Contemporaries. Dordrecht: Kluwer, 1992.

title: De Mineralibus, II.3
title_english: On Minerals — The Philosopher's Stone
author: Albertus Magnus
representative_sentence: Lapis philosophorum est lapis pretiosus qui omnia metalla imperfecta in aurum vel argentum perfectum transmutare dicitur.
latin_text: Lapis philosophorum est lapis pretiosus qui omnia metalla imperfecta in aurum vel argentum perfectum transmutare dicitur. Hunc lapidem antiqui philosophi multiplici nomine appellaverunt: vocaverunt enim eum tinctura, elixir, aurum potabile, quintam essentiam, et aliis nominibus. Natura eius est ex sulphure et argento vivo composita, sed sulphur et argentum vivum philosophorum non sunt sulphur et argentum vivum vulgare, sed sunt spiritus quos natura in metallis operatur. Qui igitur hanc naturam intelligit, potest per artem accelerare quod natura per saecula longissima perficit.
english_gloss: The philosopher's stone is a precious stone which is said to transmute all imperfect metals into perfect gold or silver. The ancient philosophers called this stone by many names: for they called it tincture, elixir, potable gold, the fifth essence, and other names. Its nature is composed of sulfur and quicksilver, but the sulfur and quicksilver of the philosophers are not common sulfur and quicksilver, but are spirits which nature works in metals. Whoever understands this nature can by art accelerate what nature perfects over very long ages.

vocabulary.definition: to transmute, transform, change completely
tincture, dye, coloring agent (alchemical)
elixir (from Arabic al-iksir), the transforming agent
drinkable, potable
fifth (as in fifth essence or quintessence)
essence, being, substance
sulfur (one of the two alchemical principles)
silver; mercury (argentum vivum = quicksilver)
to accelerate, hasten, speed up
brings to completion, perfects, finishes

source_notes: Albertus Magnus wrote the most systematic medieval treatment of minerals and alchemy, distinguishing natural processes from fraud while leaving open the theoretical possibility of transmutation.
bibliography: Wyckoff, Dorothy, trans. Albertus Magnus: Book of Minerals. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1967.

title: Opus Majus, Part VI
title_english: The Great Work — On Experimental Science
author: Roger Bacon
representative_sentence: Experimentalis scientia tribus modis cognoscit occulta naturae et miranda artis quae non possunt alio modo sciri.
latin_text: Experimentalis scientia tribus modis cognoscit occulta naturae et miranda artis quae non possunt alio modo sciri. Primus modus est ut per experimenta sciat verba philosophorum: unum enim experimentum plus valet quam mille rationes. Secundus modus est ut per experientiam addat nova aliqua ad ea quae iam sciuntur. Tertius modus est nobilis et mirabilis: ut per experimenta indagine sana penetret secreta naturae et aperiat ea. Haec scientia maestra est omnium scientiarum praecedentium, quia omnes alias certificat.
english_gloss: Experimental science comes to know the secrets of nature and the wonders of art by three modes, which cannot be known in any other way. The first mode is to know by experiments the words of the philosophers: for one experiment is worth more than a thousand arguments. The second mode is to add through experience certain new things to those already known. The third mode is noble and wonderful: to penetrate by sound experimental inquiry the secrets of nature and reveal them. This science is the mistress of all preceding sciences, because it certifies all the others.

vocabulary.definition: experimental, based on experience/testing
hidden things, secrets, occult matters
wonderful things, marvels, wonders
experiments, tests, proofs by trial
reasons, arguments, logical proofs
investigation, tracking, inquiry
penetrate, pierce, enter deeply
certifies, makes certain, verifies

source_notes: Roger Bacon's Opus Majus argued that mathematical and experimental science must undergird all knowledge, anticipating the later scientific revolution. His concept of 'experimental science' influenced Renaissance natural magic.
bibliography: Burke, Robert Belle, trans. The Opus Majus of Roger Bacon. 2 vols. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1928.

title: Ars Notoria, Prologue
title_english: The Notory Art — Opening Prayer
author: Solomon (attrib.); compiled c. 12th-13th cent.
representative_sentence: O Deus munde et immense, qui ab initio omnia creasti et in bonitate tua omnia ordinasti, exaudi preces servi tui.
latin_text: O Deus munde et immense, qui ab initio omnia creasti et in bonitate tua omnia ordinasti, exaudi preces servi tui. Haec ars notoria a Salomone rege sapientissimo per angelum Dei sibi revelata esse dicitur, qui per hanc scientiam omnem sapientiam et omnes scientias in una nocte percepit. Per eam enim omnes artes et scientiae liberales, tam philosophicae quam theologicae, infunduntur menti studenti sine labore et studio diuturno. Verba autem huius artis sunt sancta et arcana et a nullo impuro vel infideli tractanda. Quisquis autem haec verba pure et devote pronuntiarit, gratiam divinam et illuminationem mentis obtinebit.
english_gloss: O God, pure and immense, who created all things from the beginning and ordered all things in your goodness, hear the prayers of your servant. This Notory Art is said to have been revealed to King Solomon the Wisest by an angel of God, by which he perceived all wisdom and all sciences in a single night. Through it all the liberal arts and sciences, both philosophical and theological, are infused into the mind of the student without labor and prolonged study. The words of this art are holy and arcane and must not be handled by anyone impure or faithless. Whoever pronounces these words purely and devoutly will obtain divine grace and illumination of the mind.

vocabulary.definition: pure, clean (here used as address to God: 'O pure God')
immeasurable, boundless, vast
hear (imperative), hearken to, attend to
notory (from 'nota'), related to signs/marks; hence the art of sacred marks
revealed, uncovered, disclosed
perceived, grasped, received
are infused, poured into, instilled
lasting, prolonged, long-continued
secret, arcane, hidden mysteries
illumination, enlightenment, lighting up of the mind

source_notes: The Ars Notoria claims to be a revelation to Solomon granting instant mastery of all knowledge through sacred prayers and geometric figures. It was widely copied in medieval monasteries despite ecclesiastical condemnation.
bibliography: Véronèse, Julien, ed. L'Ars notoria au Moyen Âge: Introduction et édition critique. Florence: SISMEL/Edizioni del Galluzzo, 2007.

title: Liber Juratus, Prologue
title_english: The Sworn Book of Honorius — Prologue
author: Honorius of Thebes (attrib.)
representative_sentence: Incipit liber sacratus sive iuratus magistri Honorii, qui est fundamentum omnium artium magicarum.
latin_text: Incipit liber sacratus sive iuratus magistri Honorii, qui est fundamentum omnium artium magicarum et secretorum. Honorius filius Euclidis, magister Thebis, congregavit magos de diversis partibus mundi et de communi consilio fecerunt hunc librum qui dicitur liber iuratus, quia nullus debet eum revelare nisi filio vel discipulo fideli, sub iuramento. In hoc libro continetur visio Dei beatifica et nomina angelorum et daemonum, et virtutes eorum, et modi invocandi eos. Haec scientia est arcana et a paucis intellecta et a nullo impuro tractanda.
english_gloss: Here begins the sacred or sworn book of Master Honorius, which is the foundation of all magical arts and secrets. Honorius, son of Euclid, master of Thebes, gathered magicians from diverse parts of the world and by common counsel made this book which is called the sworn book, because no one should reveal it except to a son or faithful disciple, under oath. In this book is contained the beatific vision of God and the names of angels and demons, and their powers, and the modes of invoking them. This science is arcane and understood by few and must not be handled by any impure person.

vocabulary.definition: sacred, consecrated, holy
sworn, having taken an oath
foundation, base, groundwork
gathered, assembled, collected together
disciple, student, pupil
oath, sworn promise
beatific, making blessed, of heavenly bliss
of invoking, calling upon, summoning

source_notes: The Sworn Book (c. 13th cent.) claims to be a distillation of a vast magical library destroyed by Church authorities. Its hundred-day operation for the beatific vision of God is one of the most elaborate ritual sequences in medieval magic.
bibliography: Hedegård, Gösta, ed. Liber Iuratus Honorii: A Critical Edition of the Latin Version of the Sworn Book of Honorius. Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 2002.

title: Clavicula Salomonis, Book I
title_english: The Key of Solomon — The Great Conjuration
author: Solomon (attrib.)
representative_sentence: In nomine Dei fortis et excelsi exorcizo et coniuro vos, omnes spiritus, per Deum qui caelum et terram creavit.
latin_text: In nomine Dei fortis et excelsi exorcizo et coniuro vos, omnes spiritus, per Deum qui caelum et terram creavit, per Deum Adonai, per Deum El, per Deum Elohim, per Deum Tetragrammaton, per Deum Sadai, per Deum vivum et verum. Coniuro etiam vos per sanctissima nomina quae Moyses in tabulis lapideis scripta vidit, et per omnia quae scripta sunt in libro vitae, et per nomen summum ineffabile quod nemo pronuntiare valet nisi qui terram et caelum creavit. Advenite ergo et pareatis iussioni meae, et nolite nocere mihi neque sociis meis.
english_gloss: In the name of the strong and most high God I exorcize and conjure you, all spirits, by God who created heaven and earth, by God Adonai, by God El, by God Elohim, by God Tetragrammaton, by God Sadai, by the living and true God. I also conjure you by the most holy names which Moses saw written on stone tablets, and by all things written in the book of life, and by the supreme ineffable name which no one is able to pronounce except he who created earth and heaven. Come therefore and obey my command, and do not harm me or my companions.

vocabulary.definition: most high, exalted, lofty
I exorcize, adjure, charge with authority
I conjure, swear together, bind by oath
Lord (Hebrew divine name, 'my Lord')
The four-letter divine name YHWH
ineffable, unspeakable, that cannot be uttered
to pronounce, declare, speak aloud
obey (subjunctive), comply with, appear
command, order, injunction
companions, associates, allies

source_notes: The Key of Solomon (Clavicula Salomonis) is the foundational text of the Solomonic tradition of ceremonial magic. Its divine names draw on Hebrew Kabbalah, Christian liturgy, and Neoplatonic angelology.
bibliography: Skinner, Stephen, and David Rankine. The Veritable Key of Solomon. Singapore: Golden Hoard Press, 2008. // Mathers, S.L. MacGregor, trans. The Key of Solomon the King. London: George Redway, 1888.

title: De Occulta Philosophia, I.1
title_english: Three Books of Occult Philosophy — On Magic
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
representative_sentence: Magicam antiqui sapientes, propter vim rerum mirabilem et infinitam, Regiam Scientiam vocaverunt.
latin_text: Magicam antiqui sapientes, propter vim rerum mirabilem et infinitam, Regiam Scientiam vocaverunt. Haec autem partim naturalis est, partim caelestis, partim ceremonialis. Naturalis enim philosophia agit de rerum naturalium proprietatibus et virtutibus occultis; caelestis autem de influentiis et impressionibus caelestibus; ceremonialis vero de officiis et ministeriis spiritalibus. His tribus partibus veluti tribus mundi regionibus respondentibus: mundo elementali, caelesti et intellectuali, perfecta philosophia continetur. Nec potest vir aliquis magus esse nisi his tribus partibus doctissimus.
english_gloss: The ancient wise men called Magic the Royal Science, on account of the wonderful and infinite power of things. This, moreover, is partly natural, partly celestial, and partly ceremonial. Natural philosophy deals with the hidden properties and powers of natural things; celestial with celestial influences and impressions; ceremonial truly with spiritual offices and ministries. In these three parts, corresponding as it were to the three regions of the world—elemental, celestial, and intellectual—perfect philosophy is contained. Nor can any man be a magus unless he is most learned in all three parts.

vocabulary.definition: the wise (men), sages, philosophers
royal, kingly, of a king
natural, of nature
celestial, heavenly
ceremonial, of ritual observance
influences, flows of power (from Latin influere, 'to flow into')
intellectual, of the intellect, mental
ministries, services, offices
spiritual, of the spirit
most learned, most skilled (superlative)

source_notes: Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia (1531) is the greatest Renaissance synthesis of magical theory, weaving together Neoplatonism, Hermetism, Kabbalah, and astrology into a comprehensive philosophical system.
bibliography: Tyson, Donald, ed. Three Books of Occult Philosophy Written by Henry Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim. St. Paul: Llewellyn, 1993.

title: De Occulta Philosophia, I.14
title_english: Three Books of Occult Philosophy — On Fascination
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
representative_sentence: Fascinatio est quaedam ligatio per aspectum, emissione spiritus procedente ab oculis fascinantis.
latin_text: Fascinatio est quaedam ligatio per aspectum, emissione spiritus procedente ab oculis fascinantis, qui spiritus quidam est vapor subtilissimus, genitus ex sanguine purissimo corde concoctus, et in oculis relucens, ferensque secum vim animae ex qua emittitur. Spiritus enim hic radius oculorum similis est, per quem etiam visus ipse perficitur. Hunc spiritum aliquid attractum ex oculis fascinantis, intrans per oculos fascinati, usque ad cor penetrat, et hoc pacto cor fascinati corrumpit. Qui igitur fortes et integros spiritus habent, et puros, ipsi solum fascinant, non fascinantur.
english_gloss: Fascination is a certain binding through the gaze, proceeding from an emission of spirit from the eyes of the one who fascinates, which spirit is a certain most subtle vapor, generated from the purest blood digested in the heart, and shining in the eyes, and bearing with it the power of the soul from which it is emitted. For this spirit is similar to the ray of the eyes, through which also vision itself is accomplished. This spirit, drawn somewhat from the eyes of the one who fascinates, entering through the eyes of the one fascinated, penetrates all the way to the heart, and in this way corrupts the heart of the fascinated. Those therefore who have strong and whole spirits, and pure ones, themselves fascinate only, and are not fascinated.

vocabulary.definition: fascination, the evil eye, a binding spell
binding, tying, a magical bond
gaze, look, sight, appearance
emission, sending forth, discharge
vapor, steam, subtle emanation
most subtle, most fine, most delicate
digested, cooked through, prepared
shining forth, gleaming, reflecting light
penetrates, pierces through to
corrupts, ruins, destroys

source_notes: Agrippa's theory of fascination draws on ancient medical theories of visual spirits, combining them with Ficino's pneumatic psychology. The 'evil eye' (fascinatio) was a serious concern in Renaissance medicine and magic.
bibliography: Tyson, Donald, ed. Three Books of Occult Philosophy Written by Henry Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim. St. Paul: Llewellyn, 1993.

title: De Vita, III.1
title_english: Three Books on Life — Drawing Celestial Gifts
author: Marsilio Ficino
representative_sentence: Coelum undique afflat in nos, sed afflatus eius non percipitur nisi spiritu nostro coelesti congruente.
latin_text: Coelum undique afflat in nos, sed afflatus eius non percipitur nisi spiritu nostro coelesti congruente. Spiritum autem nostrum conformem coelo facere possumus per ea quae coelestia similiter sunt: per lumen, per calorem, per odorem, per harmoniam musicam. Sol enim, qui anima mundi vicarius est, afflat in nos per lumen suum aureum: qui igitur aurum gestat, et chrysolithum, et solem respicit, et thus odorat, et aurea musica utitur, is spiritum suum solarem facit et donis solis repletur. Similiter singuli planetae singulos spiritus nostros movent et trahunt, si eorum symbola tractamus.
english_gloss: Heaven breathes into us from all sides, but its breath is not perceived unless our spirit agrees with the celestial spirit. But we can make our spirit conform to heaven through those things which are similarly celestial: through light, through heat, through fragrance, through musical harmony. For the Sun, who is the vicar of the world-soul, breathes into us through his golden light: whoever therefore wears gold, and chrysolite, and gazes at the sun, and smells frankincense, and uses golden music, makes his spirit solar and is filled with the gifts of the sun. Similarly the individual planets move and draw our individual spirits, if we handle their symbols.

title: De Vita, III.21
title_english: Three Books on Life — On Fashioning Talismans
author: Marsilio Ficino
representative_sentence: Imagines ex metallis planetis attributis, opportuno tempore formatae, vim caelitem in se recipiunt et hanc in corpus eas gestantis transfundunt.
latin_text: Imagines ex metallis planetis attributis, opportuno tempore formatae, vim caelitem in se recipiunt et hanc in corpus eas gestantis transfundunt. Hoc autem non fit per artem daemonicam aut illicitam, sed per conformitatem naturalem quam imago cum stella sua habet. Sicut enim speculum sole obiectum radios solares colligit, sic imago Solis ex auro facta et sub favore Solis fabricata, radios eius in se colligit et per contactum in nos transfundit. Medicus ergo prudens non spernit hanc artem, modo ea in usum sanitatis et non in superstitionem vel daemonum cultum convertat.
english_gloss: Images formed from metals attributed to the planets, at the opportune time, receive celestial power into themselves and transfuse this into the body of the one who wears them. This, however, does not happen through demonic or illicit art, but through the natural conformity which the image has with its star. For just as a mirror held against the sun collects the solar rays, so an image of the Sun made from gold and fabricated under the favor of the Sun, collects its rays into itself and transfuses them into us through contact. The prudent physician therefore does not scorn this art, provided he converts it to the use of health and not to superstition or the cult of demons.

title: Oratio de Hominis Dignitate, §5
title_english: Oration on the Dignity of Man — On Human Freedom
author: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
representative_sentence: Nec certam sedem, nec propriam faciem, nec munus ullum peculiare tibi dedimus, o Adam, ut quam sedem, quam faciem, quae munera tute optaveris, ea pro voto, pro tua sententia, habeas et possideas.
latin_text: Nec certam sedem, nec propriam faciem, nec munus ullum peculiare tibi dedimus, o Adam, ut quam sedem, quam faciem, quae munera tute optaveris, ea pro voto, pro tua sententia, habeas et possideas. Definita caeteris natura intra praescriptas a nobis leges coercetur. Tu, nullis angustiis coercitus, tuo arbitrio, in cuius manu te posui, tibi illam praefinies. Medium te mundi posui, ut circumspiceres inde commodius quidquid est in mundo. Nec te caelestem neque terrenum, neque mortalem neque immortalem fecimus, ut tui ipsius quasi arbitrarius honorariusque plastes et fictor, in quam malueris tute formam effingas.
english_gloss: We have given you, O Adam, no fixed abode, no form of your own, no gift peculiarly your own, so that whatever seat, whatever form, whatever gifts you may, with premeditation, select, these same you may have and possess through your own judgment and decision. The nature of all other creatures is defined and restricted within laws which We have laid down; you, by contrast, unconfined by any such restrictions, may, by your own free will, to whose custody We have assigned you, trace for yourself the lineaments of your own nature. I have placed you at the very center of the world, so that from that vantage point you could with greater ease glance round about you on all that the world contains. We have made you neither of heavenly nor of earthly stuff, neither mortal nor immortal, so that with free choice and dignity, you yourself may craft your being into whatever form you prefer.

source_notes: Pico's Oration (1486) was written as the preface for the Roman disputation of his 900 Theses. The address by God to Adam describing man's unique freedom became the classic statement of Renaissance humanism — and underpins the mage's power of self-transformation.

title: Arbatel de Magia Veterum, Aphorism I
title_english: Arbatel of Magic — The First Aphorism
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: In omnibus tuis operationibus ante omnia habenda est cura, ut tibi Deus sit propitius, ut sine ipso nihil facias.
latin_text: In omnibus tuis operationibus ante omnia habenda est cura, ut tibi Deus sit propitius, ut sine ipso nihil facias. Hoc enim est primum et praecipuum arcanum totius philosophiae occultae. Qui enim Deum non colit et non timet, is neque in naturalibus rebus neque in spiritualibus proficere potest, quia fundamentum omnis sapientiae est timor Domini. Haec scientia est donum Dei, non inventio hominis, et ei soli datur qui puro corde et mundo spiritu ad eam accedit. Omnia enim Deus sua bonitate et providentia administrat, et per angelos suos hominibus puris secreta naturae revelat.
english_gloss: In all your operations, before all else, care must be taken that God be favorable to you, so that without him you do nothing. For this is the first and chief secret of all occult philosophy. For whoever does not worship and fear God can advance neither in natural things nor in spiritual things, because the foundation of all wisdom is the fear of the Lord. This science is a gift of God, not an invention of man, and it is given only to him who approaches it with pure heart and clean spirit. For God administers all things through his goodness and providence, and through his angels reveals the secrets of nature to pure men.

title: Arbatel de Magia Veterum, Aphorism XVII
title_english: Arbatel of Magic — The Seven Olympian Spirits
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Septem sunt spiritus Olympici qui toti mundo praesunt, quibus Deus mundum in principio creavit et adhuc gubernat.
latin_text: Septem sunt spiritus Olympici qui toti mundo praesunt, quibus Deus mundum in principio creavit et adhuc gubernat. Eorum nomina sunt haec: Aratron, Bethor, Phaleg, Och, Hagith, Ophiel, Phul. Aratron dominatur in iis quae pertinent ad Saturnum: dat longam vitam, datque vetus corpus in herbam transmutare et e converso. Bethor dominatur iis quae pertinent ad Iovem: dat thesauros et amicos inter magnates. Och dominatur in rebus solaribus: dat sapientiam, medicinam perfectam, aurum et gemmas pretiosas. Phul dominatur in rebus lunaribus: dat vitam longam et convertit quodlibet metallum in argentum.
english_gloss: There are seven Olympian spirits who preside over the whole world, by whom God created the world in the beginning and still governs it. Their names are these: Aratron, Bethor, Phaleg, Och, Hagith, Ophiel, Phul. Aratron rules in those things that pertain to Saturn: he gives long life, and can transmute an old body into a plant and conversely. Bethor rules in those things that pertain to Jupiter: he gives treasures and friends among magnates. Och rules in solar matters: he gives wisdom, perfect medicine, gold and precious gems. Phul rules in lunar matters: he gives long life and converts any metal into silver.

title: Steganographia, Preface
title_english: Hidden Writing — To His Friend Arnoldus
author: Johannes Trithemius
representative_sentence: Multos et varios usus habet hic liber, qui in occulta philosophia versantur, et per spirituum ministerium ad longinquos transmittere possunt nuntios.
latin_text: Multos et varios usus habet hic liber, qui in occulta philosophia versantur, et per spirituum ministerium ad longinquos transmittere possunt nuntios. Haec autem scientia per angelos et spiritus aërios operatur, qui hominis voluntati parent et per longas distantias nuntios celerrime deferunt. Sed haec non dico ut quis credat me per daemones aut malignos spiritus operari: nam longe abest a me ista suspicio. Per bonos enim angelos, qui administrando mundo a Deo positi sunt, haec fiunt. Oportet autem operatorem esse mundum, castum et Deum timentem, quia angeli sancti immundis non comunicant.
english_gloss: This book has many and various uses for those who are versed in occult philosophy, and through the ministry of spirits can transmit messages to distant persons. This science, however, operates through angels and aerial spirits who obey the will of man and carry messages with the greatest speed over long distances. But I do not say this so that anyone should believe I operate through demons or malign spirits: for that suspicion is far from me. For these things happen through good angels, who are set by God to administer the world. The operator must, however, be pure, chaste, and fearing God, because holy angels do not communicate with the impure.

title: Heptameron, General Conjuration
title_english: Heptameron — The General Conjuration of Spirits
author: Pietro d'Abano (attrib.)
representative_sentence: Coniuro vos, omnes spiritus, per Deum patrem omnipotentem, per Iesum Christum filium eius, per Spiritum Sanctum.
latin_text: Coniuro vos, omnes spiritus, per Deum patrem omnipotentem, per Iesum Christum filium eius, per Spiritum Sanctum, et per sanctam et individuam Trinitatem, et per memoriam passionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, et per praeciossissimum sanguinem eius, et per virtutem omnium sacramentorum, et per nomen et sigillum angelorum quibus vos ligatos tenere dixit Deus. Et per terram et caelum et mare et omnia quae in eis sunt. Advenite igitur, advenite, in nomine Domini, ut paretis voluntati meae et omnibus mandatis meis.
english_gloss: I conjure you, all spirits, by God the Father Almighty, by Jesus Christ his Son, by the Holy Spirit, and by the holy and undivided Trinity, and by the memory of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by his most precious blood, and by the power of all the sacraments, and by the name and seal of the angels by which God said he keeps you bound. And by earth and heaven and sea and all things that are in them. Come therefore, come, in the name of the Lord, that you may obey my will and all my commands.

title: De Umbris Idearum, Prologue
title_english: On the Shadows of Ideas — Opening
author: Giordano Bruno
representative_sentence: Umbrae idearum sunt vestigia quaedam in animis nostris relicta ab ipsis ideis divinis, per quas mundus factus est.
latin_text: Umbrae idearum sunt vestigia quaedam in animis nostris relicta ab ipsis ideis divinis, per quas mundus factus est. Mens divina omnia simul et semel videt et intelligit; mens humana autem per umbras, per imagines, per vestigia ad illam lucem ascendit. Ars igitur memoriae non est ars parva: est via qua mens humana ad intellectum divinum accedit, per ordinem imaginum in locis dispositas. Qui hanc artem perfecte novit, is potest omnes res cognitas in memoriam revocare et nova ex veteribus componere. Hoc autem Hermes ipse primus docuit, et Pythagoras, et Plato, et omnes philosophi veteres.
english_gloss: The shadows of ideas are certain vestiges left in our souls by the divine ideas themselves, through which the world was made. The divine mind sees and understands all things simultaneously and at once; the human mind, however, ascends to that light through shadows, through images, through vestiges. The art of memory therefore is no small art: it is the way by which the human mind approaches the divine intellect, through the order of images disposed in places. Whoever perfectly knows this art can recall all known things into memory and compose new things from old. But this Hermes himself first taught, and Pythagoras, and Plato, and all the ancient philosophers.

title: Monas Hieroglyphica, Theorem I
title_english: The Hieroglyphic Monad — First Theorem
author: John Dee
representative_sentence: Punctus centrum est omnium in natura existentium, ab hoc enim omnia procedunt et ad hunc omnia redeunt.
latin_text: Punctus centrum est omnium in natura existentium, ab hoc enim omnia procedunt et ad hunc omnia redeunt. Circulus autem qui a puncto centrali formatur, ipsius puncti perfectissimam expressionem constituit. Sol, signorum principium, in centro figurae nostrae ponitur: circa eum vero Luna, ceteraque planetarum signa, ordine suo disponuntur. Monas haec est signum universale, in quo omnia signa continentur, et per quod omnia intelliguntur. Qui hanc hieroglyphicam monetam intelligit, is clavis philosophorum potitus est.
english_gloss: The point is the center of all things existing in nature, for from this all things proceed and to this all things return. The circle, moreover, which is formed from the central point, constitutes the most perfect expression of the point itself. The Sun, the beginning of signs, is placed at the center of our figure: around it truly the Moon and the other signs of the planets are disposed in their order. This Monad is a universal sign, in which all signs are contained, and through which all things are understood. Whoever understands this hieroglyphic monad has obtained the key of the philosophers.

title: Etymologiae, VIII.9
title_english: Etymologies — On Magicians
author: Isidore of Seville
representative_sentence: Magi sunt qui vulgo malefici ob facinorum magnitudinem nuncupantur: hi et elementa concutiunt, turbant mentes hominum, ac sine ullo veneni haustu violentia tantum carminum interimunt.
latin_text: Magi sunt qui vulgo malefici ob facinorum magnitudinem nuncupantur: hi et elementa concutiunt, turbant mentes hominum, ac sine ullo veneni haustu violentia tantum carminum interimunt. Daemones enim evocant, audent commovere, ut quisque inimicos suos diabolica fraude perdat. Hi etiam sanguine utuntur et victimis, et saepe contingunt corpora occisorum. Harioli autem a diis inferis nomen sumpsere: haruspicina a speculatione viscerum animalium dicta. Augures ab avium garritu et volatu futura praedicunt. Astrologi qui ante tempus id agebant quod nunc mathematici ab astrorum contemplatione nomen acceperunt.
english_gloss: Magicians are those who are commonly called evildoers on account of the magnitude of their crimes: these also shake the elements, disturb the minds of men, and without any intake of poison destroy by the power of incantations alone. For they call up demons, and dare to stir them up, so that each person may destroy his enemies through diabolical fraud. These also use blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the slain. Soothsayers, however, took their name from the infernal gods: divination from entrails takes its name from the inspection of the viscera of animals. Augurs predict future things from the chatter and flight of birds. Astrologers, who previously did what mathematicians now do, took their name from contemplation of the stars.

title: Liber Lunae, §1
title_english: The Book of the Moon — The Twenty-Eight Mansions
author: Anonymous (Arabic source, Latin trans. c. 13th cent.)
representative_sentence: Luna per viginti octo mansiones in mense suo currit, et in qualibet mansione virtutem habet specialem ad diversa opera magica.
latin_text: Luna per viginti octo mansiones in mense suo currit, et in qualibet mansione virtutem habet specialem ad diversa opera magica. Prima mansio vocatur Alnath, et est in capite Arietis: qui vult iter facere, incipiat in hac mansione, et erit tutus a periculis viae. Secunda mansio vocatur Albotain: valet ad amicitiam et concordiam inter homines. Tertia est Azoraya: valet ad thesauros inveniendos et res perditas recuperandas. Quarta, Aldebaran, est mansio fortitudinis: valet ad victoriam in bellis. Qui haec scit et opportuno tempore operatur, is plus potest in magicis quam qui per annos multos laboravit ignorans electionem.
english_gloss: The moon runs through twenty-eight mansions in its month, and in each mansion it has a special power for various magical operations. The first mansion is called Alnath, and it is in the head of Aries: whoever wishes to make a journey, let him begin in this mansion, and he will be safe from the dangers of the road. The second mansion is called Albotain: it avails for friendship and concord between men. The third is Azoraya: it avails for finding treasures and recovering lost things. The fourth, Aldebaran, is the mansion of strength: it avails for victory in wars. Whoever knows this and operates at the opportune time can accomplish more in magical arts than one who has labored many years without knowing the election.

title: De Magia, §1
title_english: On Magic — The Definition of Magic
author: Giordano Bruno
representative_sentence: Magus dicitur sapiens cum virtute agendi: magia est potestas agendi mirabilia per cognitionem naturae, vel per invocationem spiritibus mediantibus.
latin_text: Magus dicitur sapiens cum virtute agendi: magia est potestas agendi mirabilia per cognitionem naturae, vel per invocationem spiritibus mediantibus. Primus modus magiae est per naturalem philosophiam: is qui intelligit nexum rerum et sympathiam et antipatiam omnium in mundo, is potest uti una re ad aliam movendam. Secundus modus est per mathematicam: per figuras et numeros et caracteres et sigilla quae vim naturalem continent. Tertius est per invocationem et preces et verborum efficaciam, qui modus est ceremonialis. Nec sunt hi modi adeo distincti ut non saepe misceantur: perfectus magus omnes tres novit.
english_gloss: A magus is called a wise man with the power of acting: magic is the power of working wonders through knowledge of nature, or through invocation with spirits as intermediaries. The first mode of magic is through natural philosophy: he who understands the connection of things and the sympathy and antipathy of all things in the world can use one thing to move another. The second mode is through mathematics: through figures and numbers and characters and seals which contain natural power. The third is through invocation and prayers and the efficacy of words, which mode is ceremonial. Nor are these modes so distinct that they are not often mixed: the perfect magus knows all three.

title: Utriusque Cosmi Historia, Vol. I
title_english: History of Both Worlds — The Macrocosm
source: Utriusque Cosmi Maioris scilicet et Minoris Historia
author: Robert Fludd
representative_sentence: Macrocosmus est magnus mundus, microcosmus autem homo: utrique unam et eandem animam communem esse dicit Hermes.
latin_text: Macrocosmus est magnus mundus, microcosmus autem homo: utrique unam et eandem animam communem esse dicit Hermes. Sicut enim mundus habet animam suam quae est spiritus universalis, sic homo habet spiritum suum qui est anima rationalis. Et sicut mundus in tribus regionibus consistit, elementali scilicet, aetherea, et empyrea, sic homo in corpore, anima, et mente. Mundi corpus est terra et aqua et aer et ignis: hominis corpus est caro et sanguis et spiritus et intellectus. Qui igitur naturam hominis perfecte novit, is naturam mundi novit; et qui mundi naturam intelligit, is se ipsum intelligit. Haec est scientia admirabilis quam antiqui philosophi sub velamine symbolicarum figurarum tradiderunt.
english_gloss: The macrocosm is the great world, and the microcosm is man: Hermes says that both share one and the same common soul. For just as the world has its soul which is the universal spirit, so man has his spirit which is the rational soul. And just as the world consists in three regions, namely elemental, ethereal, and empyrean, so man in body, soul, and mind. The body of the world is earth and water and air and fire: the body of man is flesh and blood and spirit and intellect. Whoever therefore perfectly knows the nature of man, knows the nature of the world; and whoever understands the nature of the world, understands himself. This is the admirable science which the ancient philosophers handed down under the veil of symbolic figures.

vocabulary.definition: macrocosm, the great world (from Greek makros + kosmos)
microcosm, the small world, man (from Greek mikros + kosmos)
both, each of two
common, shared, belonging to all
universal, pertaining to the whole
elemental, of the elements
ethereal, of the aether, heavenly
empyrean, of the highest heaven of fire
rational, of reason
veil, covering, garment (symbolic concealment)
symbolic, of symbols
handed down, transmitted, taught (perfect tense)

source_notes: Fludd's Utriusque Cosmi Historia (1617–21) is one of the most visually spectacular works of Renaissance Hermetism, containing dozens of elaborate engravings depicting the macrocosm-microcosm relationship. It was published by Johann Theodor de Bry in Oppenheim.
bibliography: Fludd, Robert. Utriusque Cosmi Maioris scilicet et Minoris Metaphysica, Physica atque Technica Historia. Oppenheim: Johann Theodor de Bry, 1617. // Godwin, Joscelyn. Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher and Surveyor of Two Worlds. London: Thames and Hudson, 1979.

title: De Arte Cabalistica, Book I
title_english: On the Kabbalistic Art — The Threefold Wisdom
author: Johannes Reuchlin
representative_sentence: Cabala est symbolica receptio divinae revelationis, tradita in utilitatem contemplantium et ad salutem animarum.
latin_text: Cabala est symbolica receptio divinae revelationis, tradita in utilitatem contemplantium et ad salutem animarum. Haec enim sapientia non inventa est ab hominibus per rationem aut per experientiam, sed revelata est a Deo primo patribus, deinde prophetis, et per eorum manus tradita posteris. Tria sunt instrumenta huius sapientiae: primo nomina divina, quae sunt claves omnium mysticorum; secundo, sefirot, id est emanationes Dei quibus mundus gubernatur; tertio, litterae et numeri, per quos Deus mundum creavit. Qui haec tria perfecte novit, is potest et divina contemplari et humana ad ordinem redigere.
english_gloss: Kabbalah is the symbolic reception of divine revelation, handed down for the benefit of those who contemplate and for the salvation of souls. For this wisdom was not discovered by men through reason or experience, but was revealed by God first to the patriarchs, then to the prophets, and handed down through their hands to posterity. There are three instruments of this wisdom: first, the divine names, which are the keys of all mysteries; second, the Sephiroth, that is, the emanations of God by which the world is governed; third, the letters and numbers, through which God created the world. Whoever perfectly knows these three can both contemplate divine things and reduce human things to order.

vocabulary.definition: Kabbalah (from Hebrew qabbalah, 'reception, tradition')
symbolic, using symbols
reception, receiving, taking back
revelation, uncovering, divine disclosure
of those contemplating, meditating
prophets, seers (from Hebrew/Greek)
posterity, descendants, future generations
Sephiroth (Hebrew: the ten divine emanations in Kabbalistic cosmology)
emanations, outflowings, divine radiances
of mysteries, mystical secrets
reduce, bring back, restore to order

source_notes: Reuchlin's De Arte Cabalistica (1517) is the foundational text of Christian Kabbalah, presenting Jewish mystical tradition as the key to understanding Christianity. Written as a dialogue set in the home of Pythagoras, it deeply influenced Agrippa and the entire Renaissance magical tradition.
bibliography: Goodman, Martin, and Sarah Goodman, trans. Johann Reuchlin: On the Art of the Kabbalah (De Arte Cabalistica). New York: Abaris Books, 1983.

title: Mundus Subterraneus, X.1
title_english: The Subterranean World — On the Central Fire
author: Athanasius Kircher
representative_sentence: Ignis centralis est anima terrae, per cuius calorem et virtutem omnia metalla et lapides et herbae in visceribus terrae producuntur.
latin_text: Ignis centralis est anima terrae, per cuius calorem et virtutem omnia metalla et lapides et herbae in visceribus terrae producuntur. Hic ignis non est ignis vulgaris qui comburit et destruit, sed ignis philosophicus qui generat et nutrit et perficit. Ex hoc igne procedunt sulphurosi vapores et mercuriales qui per terrae venas ascendentes metalla in suis cuniculis formant. Ubi vapor sulphureus mercuriali miscetur et per calorem centralem coquitur, metallum producitur: quo purior est haec mixtio et diuturnior coctio, eo nobilius metallum. Aurum ergo est quod perfectissimam passus est coctionem in utero terrae matris.
english_gloss: The central fire is the soul of the earth, through whose heat and power all metals and stones and plants are produced in the bowels of the earth. This fire is not common fire which burns and destroys, but philosophical fire which generates and nourishes and perfects. From this fire proceed sulphurous and mercurial vapors which, ascending through the veins of the earth, form metals in their channels. Where the sulphurous vapor is mixed with the mercurial and is cooked by the central heat, a metal is produced: the purer this mixture and the longer the cooking, the nobler the metal. Gold therefore is that which has undergone the most perfect cooking in the womb of the earth mother.

vocabulary.definition: central, of the center
bowels, entrails, inner parts (of earth or body)
burns up, consumes with fire
nourishes, feeds, sustains
sulphurous, containing sulfur
mercurial, of mercury, quick and volatile
vapors, steams, exhalations
veins (of earth or body), channels, streams
passages, channels, underground tunnels
is cooked, digested, prepared by heat
longer, more lasting (comparative)
nobler, more excellent (comparative)

source_notes: Kircher's Mundus Subterraneus (1665) is an encyclopedic account of geology, volcanology, and subterranean phenomena interpreted through Hermetic and alchemical lenses. The central fire theory integrates Aristotelian natural philosophy with Paracelsian alchemy.
bibliography: Kircher, Athanasius. Mundus Subterraneus. Amsterdam: Joannem Janssonium, 1665. // Godwin, Joscelyn. Athanasius Kircher's Theatre of the World. Rochester: Inner Traditions, 2009.

title: Liber de Angelis, §7
title_english: The Book of Angels — Invocation of the Angel of Venus
author: Anonymous (Bodleian MS Rawlinson D. 252)
representative_sentence: Coniuro te, Hanael, angele Veneris, per nomen quod Deus imposuit stellae Veneris, ut mihi apparias in forma pulchra et placida.
latin_text: Coniuro te, Hanael, angele Veneris, per nomen quod Deus imposuit stellae Veneris, ut mihi apparias in forma pulchra et placida et mihi obedias in omnibus quae a te petiero. Per Adonai Sabaoth et per omnia nomina Dei et per virtutem caeli et terrae et maris, exaudi me. Da mihi gratiam et amorem apud omnes homines et mulieres, et da mihi in rebus amoris et concordiae perfectum effectum. Tu enim es qui praesides diei Veneris et horae eius, et qui materiam amoris in cordibus hominum movet et ordinat. Veni ergo et appare et praesta quod peto.
english_gloss: I conjure you, Hanael, angel of Venus, by the name which God imposed upon the star of Venus, that you appear to me in a beautiful and peaceful form and obey me in all things that I ask of you. By Adonai Sabaoth and by all the names of God and by the power of heaven and earth and sea, hear me. Give me grace and love with all men and women, and give me in matters of love and concord perfect effect. For you are the one who presides over the day of Venus and its hour, and who moves and orders the matter of love in the hearts of men. Come therefore and appear and grant what I ask.

vocabulary.definition: Hanael, the angel of Venus (from Hebrew Hana'el, 'grace of God')
imposed, placed upon, assigned
appear, become visible (subjunctive of purpose)
peaceful, calm, gentle, pleasing
I shall ask, seek, request (future perfect)
Sabaoth (Hebrew tseva'ot, 'hosts, armies') — divine title
concord, harmony, agreement between people
preside over, be in charge of, govern
orders, arranges, governs, puts in order
furnish, provide, perform, excel (imperative)

source_notes: The Liber de Angelis (c. 14th-15th cent.) is an Anglo-Latin magical compilation preserved in several manuscripts, including Bodleian MS Rawlinson D. 252. It contains operations for each of the seven planets, using their angelic governors for practical magical ends.
bibliography: Véronèse, Julien. "Magic, Theurgy, and Spirituality in the Medieval Ritual of the Ars Notoria." In Fanger, Claire, ed. Invoking Angels: Theurgic Ideas and Practices, Thirteenth to Sixteenth Centuries. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2012.

title: De Amore, II.2
title_english: On Love — Love as the Bond of the World
author: Marsilio Ficino
representative_sentence: Amor est vincula quoddam mundi et rerum omnium nexus perpetuus et copula mundi.
latin_text: Amor est vincula quoddam mundi et rerum omnium nexus perpetuus et copula mundi. Nam ipse Deus, cum sit summa pulchritudo, amat pulchritudinem suam: et amor Dei in pulchritudine rerum sese reflectit et in mundum diffunditur. Hic amor, a Deo incipiens, per angelos et caelum in naturam et in homines descendit, et ex hominibus rursus in Deum ascendit per animam. Est ergo amor circulus quidam ab bono in bonum continuus. Mens enim humana, cum pulchritudinem in rebus sensibilibus videt, reminiscitur pulchritudinis divinae quam ante corpus vidit, et desiderio illius ardet. Hoc desiderium est amor: id est, appetitus pulchritudinis divinae.
english_gloss: Love is a certain bond of the world and the perpetual link of all things and the clasp of the world. For God himself, since he is the highest beauty, loves his beauty: and the love of God reflects itself in the beauty of things and is diffused into the world. This love, beginning from God, descends through angels and heaven into nature and into men, and from men ascends again to God through the soul. Love therefore is a certain circle continuous from the good to the good. For the human mind, when it sees beauty in sensible things, recalls the divine beauty which it saw before the body, and burns with desire for it. This desire is love: that is, the appetite for divine beauty.

vocabulary.definition: bonds, chains, ties (neuter plural)
link, connection, binding together
bond, coupling, clasp that holds together
beauty, loveliness, excellence
reflects, turns back, bends back
again, back, in turn
continuous, unbroken, extending without gap
sensible, perceptible by the senses
recalls, remembers (deponent verb)
burns, blazes, is aflame with desire
appetite, desire, yearning

source_notes: Ficino's De Amore (1469) is a commentary on Plato's Symposium, the founding text of Renaissance Neoplatonic love theory. Its concept of love as a circular motion from God through creation and back shaped Renaissance poetry, art, and magic for two centuries.
bibliography: Jayne, Sears, trans. Marsilio Ficino's Commentary on Plato's Symposium on Love. Dallas: Spring Publications, 1985.

title: De Occulta Philosophia, III.36
title_english: Three Books of Occult Philosophy — On the Threefold Soul
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
representative_sentence: Anima humana triplicem virtutem habet: vegetativam, sensitivam, et intellectivam; et secundum has tres partes triplici mundo respondet.
latin_text: Anima humana triplicem virtutem habet: vegetativam, sensitivam, et intellectivam; et secundum has tres partes triplici mundo respondet. Virtus vegetativa mundo elementali convenit, sensativa mundo siderali, intellectiva mundo intellectuali. Hinc homo, cum in his tribus mundi regionibus conversetur, a tribus mundi his regionibus influentias in se recipit: a mundo elementali per corpus, a mundo siderali per spiritum animalem, a mundo intellectuali per mentem. Magus ergo qui haec tria in se ordinaverit et ad superiora direxerit, potest per has tres vias in mundum agere et in mundo mirabilia efficere. Hoc est secretum totius artis magicae.
english_gloss: The human soul has threefold power: vegetative, sensitive, and intellective; and according to these three parts it corresponds to the threefold world. The vegetative power agrees with the elemental world, the sensitive with the sidereal world, the intellective with the intellectual world. Hence man, since he moves in these three regions of the world, receives influences into himself from these three regions: from the elemental world through the body, from the sidereal world through the animal spirit, from the intellectual world through the mind. The magus therefore who has ordered these three in himself and directed them toward the higher, can through these three ways act upon the world and accomplish wonders in the world. This is the secret of the entire magical art.

vocabulary.definition: threefold, triple
vegetative, relating to growth and nourishment
sensitive, relating to sense and perception
intellective, relating to intellect and reason
sidereal, of the stars, astral
moves in, inhabits, dwells in (deponent)
influences, inflowings, astral forces
animal (spirit) — the spirit connecting body and soul
has ordered, arranged, put in right sequence
has directed, aimed, guided upward
accomplish, bring about, produce as an effect

source_notes: Agrippa's threefold soul doctrine (drawn from Neoplatonism and Scholastic psychology) underpins his entire theory of magical causation: the magus acts on the world through the same threefold structure through which the world acts on him.
bibliography: Tyson, Donald, ed. Three Books of Occult Philosophy Written by Henry Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim. St. Paul: Llewellyn, 1993.

title: Ecloga VIII
title_english: Eclogue VIII — The Binding Spell
author: Publius Vergilius Maro
representative_sentence: Ducite ab urbe domum, mea carmina, ducite Daphnin.
latin_text: Ducite ab urbe domum, mea carmina, ducite Daphnin. Carmina vel caelo possunt deducere lunam; carminibus Circe socios mutavit Ulixi; frigidus in pratis cantando rumpitur anguis. Limus ut hic durescit, et haec ut cera liquescit uno eodemque igni, sic nostro Daphnis amore.
english_gloss: Lead Daphnis home from the city, my spells, lead him home. Spells can draw the moon down from the sky; by spells Circe transformed the companions of Ulysses; the cold snake in the meadows bursts asunder by singing. As this clay hardens and as this wax melts in one and the same fire, so may Daphnis melt with our love.

vocabulary.definition: songs, spells, incantations
lead, draw, bring
clay, mud — used in wax-image sympathetic magic
wax — the wax effigy melted in binding rites
hardens, grows hard
melts, dissolves, liquefies

source_notes: Virgil's Eighth Eclogue contains the most complete literary description of Roman binding magic: sung carmina, a wax effigy, and knotted wool. The refrain 'ducite domum' mirrors actual defixio tablet formulae. Foundational for understanding Roman sympathetic magic and its continuity through medieval and Renaissance practice.
bibliography: Clausen, Wendell. A Commentary on Virgil, Eclogues. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994. // Coleman, Robert, ed. Vergil: Eclogues. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1977.

title: Aeneis VI.124–129
title_english: Aeneid VI — The Descent to the Underworld
author: Publius Vergilius Maro
representative_sentence: Facilis descensus Averno: noctes atque dies patet atri ianua Ditis; sed revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras, hoc opus, hic labor est.
latin_text: Facilis descensus Averno: noctes atque dies patet atri ianua Ditis; sed revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras, hoc opus, hic labor est. Pauci, quos aequus amavit Iuppiter aut ardens evexit ad aethera virtus, dis geniti potuere. Tenent media omnia silvae, Cocytusque sinu labens circumvenit atro.
english_gloss: Easy is the descent to Avernus: night and day the door of dark Dis stands open; but to retrace one's steps and escape to the upper air — this is the task, this the toil. A few, whom just Jupiter loved or blazing valor carried to the sky, born of gods, have been able. The woods hold all the middle way, and Cocytus glides winding round with its black curve.

vocabulary.definition: descent, going down
Avernus — volcanic lake near Cumae, entrance to the underworld
Dis (Pluto), king of the underworld
to call back, retrace — the necromantic challenge
Cocytus — river of wailing in the underworld

source_notes: The Cumaean Sibyl's warning in Aeneid VI frames the underworld journey as the supreme magical-religious challenge. Foundational for medieval conceptions of the katabasis, cited from Augustine to Dante to Agrippa. The phrase 'facilis descensus Averno' became the standard warning about the ease of descending into forbidden knowledge.
bibliography: Horsfall, Nicholas. Virgil, Aeneid 6: A Commentary. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2013.

title: Epodi V
title_english: Epode V — Canidia's Rite
author: Quintus Horatius Flaccus
representative_sentence: Nefas videre: puer nefandis ignibus cinctus, inpuberber adhuc, nefandis ignibus.
latin_text: Nefas videre: puer nefandis ignibus cinctus, inpuberber adhuc. Canidia brevibus implicata viperis crines et incomptum caput iubet sepulcris caprificos erutas et iubet cupressos funebris et uncta turpis ova ranae sanguine plumamque nocturnae strigis.
english_gloss: Dreadful to see: a boy encircled by unspeakable fires, still beardless. Canidia, with short vipers twisted through her hair and her head disheveled, commands wild fig-trees torn from graves, and commands funeral cypresses, and eggs smeared with the blood of a foul toad, and a feather of the night screech-owl.

vocabulary.definition: Canidia — Horace's archetypal witch, appears across multiple poems
vipers, adders — entwined in the witch's hair
graves — graveyard plants used in the rite
wild fig-trees growing from graves
screech-owl, vampire-bird — the classic Roman witch-creature

source_notes: Horace's Epode V depicts Canidia and her companions preparing a love-magic ritual using graveyard plants, owl feathers, and toad blood. Together with Epodes III and XVII it provides the fullest portrait of Roman literary witchcraft. Canidia was the primary classical model for the witch figure through the medieval period.
bibliography: Watson, Lindsay. A Commentary on Horace's Epodes. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003.

title: Pharsalia VI.507–569
title_english: Pharsalia VI — Erichtho the Necromancer
author: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus
representative_sentence: Sola Thessaliam caelo permittente tenebat maestos secessus et dirae silentia famae Erichtho.
latin_text: Sola Thessaliam caelo permittente tenebat maestos secessus et dirae silentia famae Erichtho. Non illa in tecta vocari numina, non pluviis voluit contexere amictus. Pallentes habitabat agros atque invia busta, cara deis Stygiis, non indignantibus umbris. Revocare animas donis impendit opacis.
english_gloss: Erichtho alone, with heaven's permission, inhabited the mournful retreats and dread silences of Thessaly. She would not call divinities into rooftops nor wished to weave offerings in the rain. She inhabited pale fields and trackless burial grounds, dear to the Stygian gods, with the shades not resenting her. She spent dark gifts to recall souls.

vocabulary.definition: Erichtho — Lucan's supreme necromancer, most powerful witch in Latin literature
Thessaly — the region proverbially associated with witchcraft in antiquity
Stygian — of the Styx, pertaining to the underworld
funeral pyres, burial grounds — the witch's dwelling
recall, call back — raising the dead for prophecy

source_notes: Lucan's Pharsalia Book VI presents the most elaborate necromancy scene in classical literature: the witch Erichtho reanimates a corpse for Sextus Pompeius to learn the battle's outcome. The passage was the primary classical source on necromantic technique for medieval and Renaissance theorists — Richard Kieckhefer calls it the necromancer's Aeneid.
bibliography: Braund, Susan H., trans. Lucan: Civil War. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992.

title: Metamorphoses VII.192–219
title_english: Metamorphoses VII — Medea's Nocturnal Invocation
author: Publius Ovidius Naso
representative_sentence: Nox, arcanis fidissima rebus, aurea cum luna succeditis, oraque vestra huc adhibete, meis.
latin_text: Nox, arcanis fidissima rebus, aurea cum luna succeditis, oraque vestra huc adhibete, meis. Ter se convertit, ter sumptis flumine crines inroravit aquis, ternisque ululatibus ora solvit et in dura submisit genua tellure, atque ita 'Nox' inquit 'arcanis fidissima rebus, precor.'
english_gloss: Night, most faithful to secret things, and you, golden moon, who succeed, lend your faces here to my rites. She turned around three times, three times sprinkled her hair with water taken from the stream, and three times opened her mouth in howling, and bent her knees to the hard earth, and thus she said: 'Night, most faithful to secret things, I pray.'

vocabulary.definition: secrets, mysteries, hidden rites
the moon — witness and power-source in magical rites
howlings, ululations — the ritual cry in magical operations
three times — the sacred number in magical ritual
moistened, sprinkled with water — ritual purification

source_notes: Ovid's Medea episode in Metamorphoses VII contains the most detailed magical ritual in classical Latin epic: nocturnal invocation to Night and the Moon, threefold action, and a catalogue of magical herbs. The passage directly influenced the grimoire tradition's format for planetary invocations and the structure of nocturnal magical operations.
bibliography: Anderson, W.S., ed. Ovidi Nasonis Metamorphoses. Leipzig: Teubner, 1977. // Galinsky, G. Karl. Ovid's Metamorphoses: An Introduction to the Basic Aspects. Oxford: Blackwell, 1975.

title: Elegiae I.2.43–52
title_english: Elegies I.2 — The Witch Who Commands the Moon
author: Albius Tibullus
representative_sentence: Hanc ego de caelo ducentem sidera vidi, fluminis haec rapidi carmine vertit iter.
latin_text: Hanc ego de caelo ducentem sidera vidi, fluminis haec rapidi carmine vertit iter. Haec cantu finditque solum Manisque sepulchris elicit et tepido devocat ossa rogo; iam tenet infernas magico stridore catervas, iam iubet aspersas lacte redire domum.
english_gloss: I saw this woman drawing down the stars from heaven; by her spell she turns the course of the rapid stream. She splits the ground with her song and calls up the Manes from their tombs and summons bones from the warm pyre; now she holds the infernal companies with a magical shriek, now she bids them go home sprinkled with milk.

vocabulary.definition: stars — drawn down from heaven by the witch's power
song, incantation, spell
the spirits of the dead, shades of the underworld
shriek, screech — the magical utterance commanding spirits
milk — libation offered to the spirits of the dead

source_notes: Tibullus's elegies I.2 and I.5 describe a Roman witch commanding stars, reversing rivers, and raising the dead — the full repertoire of ancient witch-powers. This passage precedes the speaker's request for a love charm, illustrating how literary witchcraft was always entangled with erotic magic in the Roman elegiac tradition.
bibliography: Maltby, Robert, ed. Tibullus: Elegies. Cambridge: Francis Cairns, 2002.

title: Naturalis Historia XXX.1–2
title_english: Natural History XXX — On the Origin of Magic
author: Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder)
representative_sentence: Magia, ut arbitror, orta est a Zoroastre, ut inter omnes in ea re convenire videtur.
latin_text: Magia, ut arbitror, orta est a Zoroastre, ut inter omnes in ea re convenire videtur. Nemo dubitat quin mixtura quaedam trium artium sit — ex medicina, religione et mathematica — ars magica. Ortu ab Oriente in nos pervenit, primo in Persas, deinde in Graecos, postremo in Romanos transmissa.
english_gloss: Magic, as I believe, originated with Zoroaster, as all appear to agree on this matter. No one doubts that it is a certain mixture of three arts — medicine, religion, and mathematics — the magical art. It came to us from its origin in the East; first transmitted to the Persians, then to the Greeks, and finally to the Romans.

vocabulary.definition: Zoroaster (Zarathustra) — Persian sage, credited as founder of magic
mathematics — here in the ancient sense of astrology
mixture — magic as a combination of medicine, religion, astrology
the East — origin of magical wisdom in the ancient worldview
transmitted, passed on through traditions

source_notes: Pliny's Naturalis Historia Book XXX opens with the most authoritative ancient account of magic's origins, tracing it to Zoroaster and the Persian magi. Books XXV–XXX form the most comprehensive ancient pharmacopoeia of magical plants and animal parts. An essential reference for natural magic theory and the history of the magical tradition.
bibliography: Rackham, H., trans. Pliny: Natural History, Vol. 8 (Books XXVIII–XXXII). Loeb Classical Library. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1963.

title: Apologia sive De Magia §26
title_english: Apology — In Defense of Philosophical Magic
author: Lucius Apuleius of Madauros
representative_sentence: Magi apud Persas sunt qui apud nos philosophi: eorum philosophia utraque pars est, et intelligentia divina et rerum humanarum scientia.
latin_text: Magi apud Persas sunt qui apud nos philosophi: eorum philosophia utraque pars est, et intelligentia divina et rerum humanarum scientia. Quod si magus est qui, ut Plato interpretatur, divinarum rerum interpres et minister est, quid hoc pertinebit ad crimen? Ego vero fateor me esse curiosum, fateor philosophum, fateor magun quem Plato laudat.
english_gloss: Magi among the Persians are what philosophers are among us: their philosophy has two parts, divine understanding and knowledge of human affairs. But if a magus is, as Plato interprets, an interpreter and minister of divine things, how does this relate to a crime? Indeed I confess I am curious, I confess a philosopher, I confess a magus such as Plato praises.

vocabulary.definition: philosophers — Apuleius equates Persian magi with Greek philosophers
interpreter, mediator between human and divine
curious, inquisitive — charged against Apuleius as a fault
crime, accusation — Apuleius faces legal charges of magic
I confess, admit — rhetorical admission used as defense

source_notes: Apuleius was tried for magic at Oea c. 158–159 CE, accused of bewitching a rich widow. His Apologia is the most detailed ancient discussion of the distinction between legitimate philosophical magic (Persian magi = philosophers) and criminal maleficia. The text was a major source for Renaissance defenses of natural magic by Ficino, Agrippa, and della Porta.
bibliography: Harrison, S.J., J. Hilton, and V. Hunink, eds. Apuleius: Rhetorical Works. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001.

title: De Divinatione II.1
title_english: On Divination II — The Skeptical Case
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
representative_sentence: Divinatio est earum rerum quae fortuitae putantur praedictio atque praesensio.
latin_text: Divinatio est earum rerum quae fortuitae putantur praedictio atque praesensio. Vetus opinio est iam usque ab heroicis ducta temporibus eaque et populi Romani et omnium gentium firmata consensu, versari quandam inter homines divinationem, quam Graeci mantiken appellant. Superstitione sublata religio non tollitur.
english_gloss: Divination is the foreknowledge and foresight of those things which are considered to be matters of chance. There is an ancient opinion traced from the age of heroes and confirmed by the consensus of the Roman people and all nations, that there exists among men a certain divination, which the Greeks call mantike. By removing superstition, religion is not removed.

vocabulary.definition: divination, prophecy, foreknowledge of future events
foresensing, premonition
superstition — Cicero distinguishes this from legitimate religio
Greek μαντική — the divinatory art, prophetic skill
consensus, agreement — Cicero cites universal agreement as evidence

source_notes: Cicero's De Divinatione (44 BCE) is the most systematic ancient treatment of divination. Book I presents the Stoic defense; Book II (here) systematically refutes each form: augury, haruspicy, astrology, dreams, oracles. The distinction between religio (acceptable) and superstitio (condemnable) became the standard framework for all subsequent Christian and scholastic treatment of divination.
bibliography: Falconer, W.A., trans. Cicero: De Senectute, De Amicitia, De Divinatione. Loeb Classical Library. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1923.

title: De Civitate Dei X.9–10
title_english: City of God X — On Theurgy and Demons
author: Aurelius Augustinus Hipponensis
representative_sentence: Theurgici, vel potius daemones qui per artem theurgicam invocari solent, non ad beatitudinem perducunt sed in erroribus detinent.
latin_text: Theurgici, vel potius daemones qui per artem theurgicam invocari solent, non ad beatitudinem perducunt sed in erroribus detinent. Angeli veri non sinunt sibi exhiberi cultum qui deo debetur; contrarium faciunt daemones qui per theurgiam invitantur. Haec est differentia: angeli deum ostendunt, daemones se ipsos quasi deos praebent.
english_gloss: Theurgists, or rather the demons who are customarily invoked through the theurgic art, do not lead to blessedness but hold souls in their errors. True angels do not allow themselves to be given the worship owed to God; the demons invited through theurgy do the opposite. This is the difference: angels show God, demons present themselves as if they were gods.

vocabulary.definition: theurgists — practitioners of ritual invocation of divine powers
blessedness, happiness — the true goal of religious life
worship, veneration — due to God alone
demons — Neoplatonic daimones reinterpreted as evil spirits by Augustine
show, display, point toward — angels point to God rather than themselves

source_notes: City of God Book X is the most influential patristic critique of theurgy, written against Porphyry's defense of theurgic practice. Augustine's framework — all magic involves demonic deception, true angels never accept worship — shaped Christian demonology for a millennium, and was the starting point for every scholastic treatment of magic from Hugh of Saint Victor through Aquinas.
bibliography: Dyson, R.W., trans. Augustine: The City of God against the Pagans. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

title: Mathesis I.1–4
title_english: Mathesis I — On the Celestial Science and Fate
author: Julius Firmicus Maternus
