representative_sentence: Fatum sive necessitas, deo sic disponente, per stellarum motus ac numeros indefessis cursibus humano generi imperatur.
latin_text: Fatum sive necessitas, deo sic disponente, per stellarum motus ac numeros indefessis cursibus humano generi imperatur. Stellas autem has, id est planetas septem, summus ille deus quasi instrumenta suae providentiae per totum mundum diffudit. Per haec quasi per artus totius corporis mundi temperamenta describuntur.
english_gloss: Fate or necessity, thus ordained by God, is imposed upon the human race through the motions and numbers of the stars in their unceasing courses. These stars — the seven planets — the supreme God diffused through the whole world as instruments of his providence. Through these, as if through the limbs of the whole body of the world, its conditions are described.

vocabulary.definition: fate, destiny — that which is spoken by divine decree
necessity — the unavoidable order of events
planets (Greek: πλανήτης, wanderers) — the seven traditional planets
instruments — the planets as God's tools for governing the world
providence — divine foresight and governance of the cosmos

source_notes: Julius Firmicus Maternus wrote the Mathesis (c. 335–37 CE), the most comprehensive Latin astrological manual to survive from antiquity. His theological framing — astrology as God's instrument — was crucial for later Christian defenses of judicial astrology against accusations of fatalism. The Mathesis was the standard Latin horoscopic manual through the 12th century.
bibliography: Monat, Pierre, ed. Firmicus Maternus: Mathesis. 3 vols. Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 1992–1994.

title: Commentarius in Somnium Scipionis I.12
title_english: Commentary on the Dream of Scipio — The Soul's Descent Through the Spheres
source: Commentarii in Somnium Scipionis, Liber I
author: Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius
representative_sentence: Anima in descensu per sphaerarum orbitas transit, et in singulis mansionibus nonnulla induit ac sumit.
latin_text: Anima in descensu per sphaerarum orbitas transit, et in singulis mansionibus nonnulla induit ac sumit. In Saturni sphaera rationem et intelligentiam, in Iovis vim agendi, in Martis animositatem, in Solis sensum et imaginationem, in Veneris desiderium, in Mercurii nuntiantem interpretandique facultatem, in Lunae augendi et minuendi corpus.
english_gloss: The soul in its descent passes through the orbits of the spheres, and in the individual dwellings it dons and assumes certain things. In the sphere of Saturn: reason and intelligence; in Jupiter's: the power of acting; in Mars's: boldness; in the Sun's: sense and imagination; in Venus's: desire; in Mercury's: the faculty for messages and interpretation; in the Moon's: the power of growing and diminishing the body.

vocabulary.definition: descent — the soul's downward journey from the Milky Way
spheres — the concentric celestial spheres of planetary motion
dwellings, stations — resting-places on the soul's journey
puts on, dons — the soul 'dresses' in planetary qualities
boldness, high-spiritedness — Mars's gift to the soul

source_notes: Macrobius's Commentary on the Somnium Scipionis was the primary vehicle for Neoplatonic cosmology in the Latin Middle Ages. The soul's descent through seven planetary spheres, acquiring a faculty from each, directly underlies astrological psychology, Ficino's planetary magic, and the entire theory of celestial influence in the grimoire tradition.
bibliography: Stahl, William Harris, trans. Macrobius: Commentary on the Dream of Scipio. New York: Columbia University Press, 1952.

title: Didascalicon II.29
title_english: Didascalicon — The Magical Arts as False Learning
author: Hugo de Sancto Victore (Hugh of Saint Victor)
representative_sentence: Magice non est in philosophiae genere sed, omnium errorum mater et magistra, quam philosophia repudiat.
latin_text: Magice non est in philosophiae genere sed, omnium errorum mater et magistra, quam philosophia repudiat. Adhibet se tamen philosophiae, quasi de eius numero, et sic doctrinas adulterinas et inutiles miscet. Partes eius sunt: mantice id est divinatio, mathesis id est fati positio ex nativitate, sortilegia, maleficia.
english_gloss: Magic is not among the kinds of philosophy, but is the mother and teacher of all errors, which philosophy repudiates. It nonetheless presents itself alongside philosophy as if of that number, and mixes adulterated and useless teachings. Its parts are: mantice, divination; mathesis, the imposition of fate from birth; sortilege; and maleficia.

vocabulary.definition: mantike — divination, prophecy (from Greek)
here: judicial astrology, calculation of fate from birth
sortilege, lot-casting, divination by lots
harmful magic, sorcery, evil-working
adulterated, spurious — magic as counterfeit philosophy

source_notes: Hugh of Saint Victor's Didascalicon (c. 1127) is the most influential medieval guide to learning. His taxonomy of the magical arts — mantice, mathesis, sortilegia, maleficia — became the standard medieval classification, reproduced from John of Salisbury to Albertus Magnus. Hugh rejects magic as false philosophy while inadvertently preserving the most systematic ancient account of its varieties.
bibliography: Taylor, Jerome, trans. The Didascalicon of Hugh of Saint Victor. New York: Columbia University Press, 1961.

title: Policraticus I.9–11
title_english: Policraticus I — Against Diviners and Augurs
source: Policraticus sive De Nugis Curialium, Liber I
author: Ioannes de Saresberiae (John of Salisbury)
representative_sentence: Aruspices, augures, hariolorum confessiones, genethliaci et cetera huiusmodi superstitio iure damnata est et a philosophis reprobata.
latin_text: Aruspices, augures, hariolorum confessiones, genethliaci et cetera huiusmodi superstitio iure damnata est et a philosophis reprobata. Haec enim non naturae scrutationi sed daemonum commercio student. Illi errantes et in tenebris versantes, futura praenuntiantes aut fallunt aut raro verum dicunt, et tunc vel casu vel daemone suggerente.
english_gloss: Haruspices, augurs, the confessions of soothsayers, genethliacists, and the rest of such superstition are justly condemned and reprobated by philosophers. For these do not pursue investigation of nature but commerce with demons. Those wandering spirits, moving in shadows, either deceive those who foretell the future, or rarely speak truly — and then either by chance or a demon's suggestion.

vocabulary.definition: haruspices — diviners who read the entrails of sacrificed animals
augurs — diviners who read bird-omens
soothsayers, fortune-tellers
genethliacists — astrologers who cast birth horoscopes
commerce, dealings — commerce with demons

source_notes: John of Salisbury's Policraticus (1159) contains one of the most thorough medieval critiques of divinatory practices. Books I–II survey and condemn augury, astrology, sortilege, and dream interpretation as demonic deception. The work drew heavily on patristic sources and in turn influenced Aquinas and the scholastic treatment of divination in the Summa Theologiae.
bibliography: Pike, Joseph B., trans. Frivolities of Courtiers and Footprints of Philosophers: Being a Translation of the First, Second, and Third Books and Selections from the Seventh and Eighth Books of the Policraticus. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 1938.

title: De Universo II.3
title_english: On the Universe — On Demonic Operations
author: Guillelmus Alvernus (William of Auvergne)
representative_sentence: Daemones operantur per figuras, imagines, characteres et per incantationum verba, non ex vi propria sed per occultam scientiam naturalium.
latin_text: Daemones operantur per figuras, imagines, characteres et per incantationum verba, non ex vi propria sed per occultam scientiam naturalium. Virtutem occultam naturalem quam sensus hominum non capit, daemones norunt et ad effectus suos utuntur. Ideoque opera daemonum a miraculis differunt: miracula supra naturam sunt, daemonum opera intra naturam latent.
english_gloss: Demons operate through figures, images, characters, and the words of incantations, not by their own power but through their hidden knowledge of natural things. The hidden natural power which does not fall within human senses, demons know and use for their effects. Therefore the works of demons differ from miracles: miracles are above nature, but demonic works lie concealed within nature.

vocabulary.definition: figures — magical diagrams, drawn shapes
characters, magical signs (Greek: χαρακτήρ)
incantations, spoken spells
miracles — supernatural acts proper to God alone
hidden — demonic knowledge of natural occult virtues

source_notes: William of Auvergne's De Universo (c. 1231–36) is the most systematic early scholastic demonology, arguing that demons operate exclusively through hidden natural causes — not supernatural power. This framework explained real magical effects without granting demons divine-level power, influencing Aquinas, Bacon, and Albertus Magnus.
bibliography: Teske, Roland J., trans. William of Auvergne: The Universe of Creatures. Milwaukee: Marquette University Press, 1998.

title: Summa Contra Gentiles III.104–106
title_english: Summa Contra Gentiles III — On Divination and Demonic Pacts
author: Thomas de Aquino (Thomas Aquinas)
representative_sentence: Divinatio ex pacto cum daemonibus semper illicita est: quia vel expresse vel tacite cultum his exhibet qui non sunt dii.
latin_text: Divinatio ex pacto cum daemonibus semper illicita est: quia vel expresse vel tacite cultum his exhibet qui non sunt dii. Daemones autem libenter huiusmodi commercia ineunt, quia per hoc homines in suam societatem trahunt. Ideo Augustinus dicit daemonum commercium esse perniciosissimum: vacant enim curiositati perniciosis et subdunt errori.
english_gloss: Divination arising from a pact with demons is always illicit: because it exhibits worship, either expressly or tacitly, to those who are not gods. Demons readily enter into dealings of this kind, because through this they draw humans into their company. Therefore Augustine says commerce with demons is most pernicious: they occupy us with ruinous curiosity and subject us to error.

vocabulary.definition: pact, compact — the demonic pact at the heart of illicit magic
unlawful, illicit, forbidden
dealings, intercourse — with demons
curiosity — disordered desire for forbidden knowledge
most destructive, most pernicious, most ruinous

source_notes: Thomas Aquinas treats magic systematically in Summa Contra Gentiles III and Summa Theologiae II-II. His definition of the demonic pact as the basis of all illicit magic became the standard scholastic framework. The SCG passage distinguishes natural magic (which may be acceptable) from any operation involving demonic pact (always forbidden). This directly influenced the witch-trial tradition.
bibliography: Pegis, Anton C., et al., trans. Saint Thomas Aquinas: Summa Contra Gentiles. Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press, 1975.

title: Opus Majus, De Scientia Experimentali
title_english: Opus Majus — Experimental Science and Natural Wonders
author: Rogerus Baco (Roger Bacon)
representative_sentence: Mirabilia naturae quae a magicis et sortilegiis putantur fieri, revera ex arte et natura fiunt; nec est magia sed philosophia naturalis.
latin_text: Mirabilia naturae quae a magicis et sortilegiis putantur fieri, revera ex arte et natura fiunt; nec est magia sed philosophia naturalis. Haec scientia certificat omnes alias et sola potest certificare de potente naturae et artis; et ad hoc deservit scientia experimentalis quam nemo potest ignorare.
english_gloss: The wonders of nature which are supposed to be accomplished by magicians and sorcerers are in truth accomplished through art and nature; nor is this magic but natural philosophy. This science certifies all others and alone can certify what is powerful in nature and art; and to this end experimental science serves, which no one can afford to ignore.

vocabulary.definition: wonders, marvels — natural effects wrongly attributed to magic
sorcery — what Bacon seeks to reframe as natural science
experimental — based on direct experience and testing
certifies, gives certainty, proves
natural philosophy — the disciplined investigation of nature

source_notes: Roger Bacon's Opus Majus (c. 1267), submitted to Pope Clement IV, argues that experimental science explains apparent magical wonders through natural causes. Bacon's work — bridging optics, mathematics, alchemy, and natural magic — was foundational for the Renaissance program of naturalizing magical operations as applied natural philosophy.
bibliography: Burke, Robert Belle, trans. The Opus Majus of Roger Bacon. 2 vols. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1928.

title: De Mineralibus II.3
title_english: On Minerals — The Hidden Virtues of Stones
source: De Mineralibus et Rebus Metallicis, Liber II
author: Albertus Magnus
representative_sentence: Virtutes lapidum occultae non sunt ex elementis sed a formis specificis et proprietate caelesti quam habent.
latin_text: Virtutes lapidum occultae non sunt ex elementis sed a formis specificis et proprietate caelesti quam habent. Non enim causa efficiens est aqua vel ignis, sed virtus stellarum quae est in eis forma et proprietas. Magi et philosophi haec noverunt qui tradiderunt quomodo per lapidum applicationem mirabilia fieri possint.
english_gloss: The hidden virtues of stones are not from the elements but from the specific forms and the celestial property which they have. For the efficient cause in such stones is not water or fire, but the virtue of the stars which is in them as form and property. Magi and philosophers have known this, who have handed down how wonders can be accomplished through the application of stones.

vocabulary.definition: hidden, concealed — occult virtues not perceivable by the senses
forms — the Aristotelian principle determining a thing's nature
property, characteristic — the specific occult quality
application, placing in contact — use of stones in proximity to the patient
celestial — stones receive virtue from their celestial archetype

source_notes: Albertus Magnus's De Mineralibus contains his account of occult virtues in gems and stones, explaining hidden properties through Aristotelian form rather than elemental qualities. This was the major medieval source for lapidaries and amulet theory. Albertus drew on Arabic sources including the Pseudo-Aristotelian Secretum Secretorum and wrote a companion volume on the occult properties of plants.
bibliography: Wyckoff, Dorothy, trans. Albertus Magnus: Book of Minerals. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1967.

title: Liber Introductorius
title_english: Liber Introductorius — On Astrological Images
author: Michael Scotus
representative_sentence: Imagines sub constellationibus fabricatae virtutem stellarum in materiam inferiorem trahunt et per eam mirabiles effectus edunt.
latin_text: Imagines sub constellationibus fabricatae virtutem stellarum in materiam inferiorem trahunt et per eam mirabiles effectus edunt. Oportet artificem electam horam observare et planetam dominantem in ascendente habere. Sic imago sigillum caeleste accipit et in terra stellae vim exercere potest.
english_gloss: Images made under constellations draw the virtue of the stars into lower matter and produce marvellous effects through it. The craftsman must observe the elected hour and have the dominating planet in the ascendant. In this way the image receives a celestial seal and can exercise the star's power on earth.

vocabulary.definition: images, talismans — figures made under astrological conditions
constellations — the astrological configuration at the time of making
the ascendant — the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon
seal, sigil — the celestial mark impressed on the image
elected — the astrologically chosen moment for the operation

source_notes: Michael Scot served as court astrologer to Frederick II and produced several astrological works. The Liber Introductorius systematizes astrological image-making (talismanic magic), drawing heavily on Arabic sources including Picatrix. Scot was a major channel for transmitting Arabic astrological magic into Latin Europe, alongside his translations of Aristotle and Averroes.
bibliography: Haskins, Charles Homer. Studies in the History of Mediaeval Science. 2nd ed. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1927.

title: Liber Razielis Angeli
title_english: The Book of Raziel the Angel
author: Anonymous (Hebrew original attrib. to Adam; Latin trans. 13th cent.)
representative_sentence: Haec est sapientia quam Adam accepit de manu Razielis angeli in paradiso, per quam omnes naturae secretas et caeli mysteria cognovit.
latin_text: Haec est sapientia quam Adam accepit de manu Razielis angeli in paradiso, per quam omnes naturae secretas et caeli mysteria cognovit. Continet nomen dei et nomina angelorum et virtutes herbarum et lapidum et stellarum, et per haec omnia vir sapiens potest in mundo mirabilia facere et a malis spiritibus se defendere.
english_gloss: This is the wisdom which Adam received from the hand of the angel Raziel in paradise, through which he knew all the secrets of nature and the mysteries of heaven. It contains the name of God and the names of angels and the virtues of herbs, stones, and stars, and through all these things a wise man can work wonders in the world and defend himself from evil spirits.

vocabulary.definition: Raziel — the angel of secrets, keeper of divine mysteries
paradise — the Garden of Eden where Adam received the book
angels — their names and powers contained in the book
virtues, powers — the occult properties of herbs, stones, and stars
defend, protect — against malicious spirits

source_notes: The Liber Razielis Angeli is a Latin translation (c. 1240–50, possibly made for Alfonso X of Castile) of a Hebrew compilation attributed to Adam and the angel Raziel. It synthesizes astral magic, angelology, and practical ritual in a format that directly influenced the Key of Solomon and subsequent Solomonic grimoires. Studied by Pablo Torijano (2002).
bibliography: Véronèse, Julien. "God's Names and Their Uses in the Books of Magic Attributed to King Solomon." Magic, Ritual, and Witchcraft 5 (2010): 30–50.

title: Heptameron seu Elementa Magica
title_english: Heptameron — Magical Elements for Each Day
author: Pseudo-Petrus de Abano
representative_sentence: In unaquaque hora, tam diei quam noctis, regnant angeli qui a mago vocari et compelli possunt ad effectus mirabiles.
latin_text: In unaquaque hora, tam diei quam noctis, regnant angeli qui a mago vocari et compelli possunt ad effectus mirabiles. Prima hora diei Dominicae regitur a Michaele; secunda ab Anael; tertia a Raphaele. Per septem planetas omnes horae septem angelis distribuuntur, et sub hac distributione omnis ars magica ordinatur.
english_gloss: In each hour, both of the day and night, angels reign who can be called and compelled by the magician to marvellous effects. The first hour of Sunday is ruled by Michael; the second by Anael; the third by Raphael. Through the seven planets all hours are distributed to seven angels, and under this distribution all the magical art is ordered.

vocabulary.definition: planetary hour — each hour governed by a different planet and angel
reign, rule — angels rule specific hours
to be compelled, summoned by force — the art of compelling spirits
of Sunday — dies Dominica, ruled by the Sun and Michael
are distributed, apportioned — the Chaldean order of planetary hours

source_notes: The Heptameron (Seven Days) attributed to Peter of Abano provides a complete system of angelic conjuration organized by the seven days and planetary hours. One of the most widely circulated practical magic manuals of the 15th–17th centuries, it provided the template of circle, fumigation, and hour-selection that the Key of Solomon systematized. Printed with Agrippa's works from the 16th century.
bibliography: Rankine, David, and Paul Harry Barron, trans. The Heptameron. London: Avalonia, 2010.

title: Codex Latinus Monacensis 849
title_english: The Munich Necromantic Handbook
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Ad invocandum spiritum mortui: eligas noctem obscuram et vadas ad sepulchrum hominis nuper mortui et circumscribas circulum.
latin_text: Ad invocandum spiritum mortui: eligas noctem obscuram et vadas ad sepulchrum hominis nuper mortui et circumscribas circulum et scribas nomina angelorum custodientium. Tunc dices ter: 'Ego te invoco, spiritus N., per virtutem dei omnipotentis.' Et apparebit in forma humana respondens ad quaestiones tuas.
english_gloss: To invoke the spirit of a dead person: choose a dark night and go to the grave of a recently dead man and describe a circle and write the names of the guardian angels. Then say three times: 'I invoke you, spirit N., by the power of almighty God.' And he will appear in human form, answering your questions.

vocabulary.definition: to invoke, call upon, summon
tomb, grave — site of necromantic operations
describe a circle around — the protective magical circle
guarding — the guardian angels of the grave
will appear — the spirit's visible manifestation

source_notes: The Munich Handbook (Clm 849, c. 1440s) is the most complete surviving Latin necromantic manual, containing ~45 experiments for spirit summoning, love magic, and illusion. Studied by Richard Kieckhefer (Forbidden Rites, 1997), it exemplifies the learned necromantic tradition that combined ritual magic with academic demonology in late medieval European universities.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. Stroud: Sutton Publishing, 1997.

title: Summa Perfectionis Magisterii II
title_english: The Sum of Perfection — Sulphur and Mercury as Metallic Principles
author: Geber (attrib.; prob. Paul of Taranto)
representative_sentence: Sulphur et Mercurius sunt duo prima principia metallorum, ex quorum variatione et mixtione diversa metalla sub terra nascuntur.
latin_text: Sulphur et Mercurius sunt duo prima principia metallorum, ex quorum variatione et mixtione diversa metalla sub terra nascuntur. Aurum est perfectissimum metallum, quia Sulphur et Mercurius eius in perfecta mixtione et puritate combinati sunt. Opus artis est imitari naturam: quod natura in millenis annis perficit, ars in brevi accelerare potest.
english_gloss: Sulphur and Mercury are the two primary principles of metals, from whose variation and mixture different metals are born beneath the earth. Gold is the most perfect metal, because its Sulphur and Mercury are combined in perfect mixture and purity. The work of art is to imitate nature: what nature perfects in thousands of years, art can accelerate in a short time.

vocabulary.definition: sulphur — the active, fiery, masculine principle of metals
mercury — the passive, fluid, feminine principle of metals
metals — gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, tin, mercury
most perfect — gold as the perfect balance of sulphur and mercury
to imitate — alchemical art imitates and accelerates natural processes

source_notes: The Summa Perfectionis attributed to 'Geber' (almost certainly Paul of Taranto, late 13th century) is the most influential Latin alchemical theory text of the Middle Ages. It establishes the sulphur-mercury theory of metallic composition that dominated Western alchemy until the 17th century, providing the theoretical basis for all subsequent transmutation claims.
bibliography: Newman, William R. The Summa Perfectionis of Pseudo-Geber: A Critical Edition, Translation and Study. Leiden: Brill, 1991.

title: Ars Almadel — Constructio Almadel
title_english: The Art of the Almadel — Construction of the Wax Tablet
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Fac Almadel ex cera alba et pura, latitudinis quatuor digitorum, in qua scribantur nomina angelorum chori primi in quatuor angulis.
latin_text: Fac Almadel ex cera alba et pura, latitudinis quatuor digitorum, in qua scribantur nomina angelorum chori primi in quatuor angulis. Pone quatuor virgulas de ligno myrrhae sub Almadel, et accende candelam de cera alba et pura. Invoca angelos per nomina eorum, et apparebit tibi spiritus in forma parvuli, qui respondebit ad omnia quaesita tua.
english_gloss: Make an Almadel of pure white wax, four fingers in width, on which shall be written the names of the angels of the first choir in four corners. Place four rods of myrrh wood under the Almadel, and light a candle of pure white wax. Invoke the angels by their names, and a spirit will appear to you in the form of a small child, who will answer all your questions.

vocabulary.definition: almadel — a wax tablet used in angelic invocation, from Arabic al-mandal
wax — ritual material; white wax symbolizes purity
of the angels — from Greek angelos, messenger; heavenly beings of specific choirs
of the choir — the nine orders of angels (seraphim, cherubim, thrones, etc.)
invoke — to call upon by name; formal ritual address to a spirit or angel

source_notes: The Ars Almadel forms Part IV of the Lemegeton (Lesser Key of Solomon), a grimoire compiled c. 17th century but drawing on medieval Latin sources. The Almadel is a wax tablet divided into four sections corresponding to the four altitudes (heavenly regions), each with its own angelic hierarchy. Manuscript traditions trace it to at least the 13th–14th centuries.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Lesser Key of Solomon: Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis. York Beach: Weiser Books, 2001.

title: De Secretis Operibus Artis et Naturae
title_english: On the Secret Works of Art and Nature — Hidden Powers of Science
source: De Secretis Operibus Artis et Naturae et de Nullitate Magiae
author: Roger Bacon
representative_sentence: Possibile est fieri instrumenta navigandi sine hominibus remigantibus, ut naves maximae, fluviales et marinae, ferantur unico homine regente maiori velocitate quam si plenae essent hominibus.
latin_text: Possibile est fieri instrumenta navigandi sine hominibus remigantibus, ut naves maximae, fluviales et marinae, ferantur unico homine regente maiori velocitate quam si plenae essent hominibus. Item instrumenta volandi fieri possunt, ut homo sedeat in medio instrumenti revolvens aliquod ingenium, per quod alae artificiales aerem verberent. Haec non sunt figmenta poetarum sed opera sapientum antiquorum, et multa alia mirabilia per scientiam naturalem fieri possunt.
english_gloss: It is possible to make instruments of navigation without men rowing, so that the greatest ships, river and sea vessels, may be driven by a single man steering at greater speed than if they were full of men. Likewise instruments for flying can be made, so that a man may sit in the middle of the instrument turning a certain device by which artificial wings beat the air. These are not the fictions of poets but the works of wise men of antiquity, and many other marvels can be brought about through natural science.

vocabulary.definition: instruments, devices — mechanisms produced by art and science
of sailing — navigation; the art of guiding ships across water
of flying — flight; aerial locomotion through artificial means
artificial — made by art and skill, not occurring naturally
science, knowledge — systematic understanding of natural causes

source_notes: Roger Bacon's De Secretis (c. 1248–1257) is a letter addressed to a friend, distinguishing genuine natural science from demonic magic. It contains famous predictions of flying machines, self-propelled boats, and explosive powder — all attributed to ancient wisdom rather than supernatural art. Bacon argues that true marvels come from mastery of natural forces, anticipating the Renaissance concept of magia naturalis.
bibliography: Brewer, J.S., ed. Fr. Rogeri Bacon Opera Quaedam Hactenus Inedita. London: Longman, Green, Longman, and Roberts, 1859.

title: Conclusiones de Magia — Theses on Natural Magic
title_english: Conclusions on Magic — Natural Magic as Instrument of Knowledge
author: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
representative_sentence: Magia naturalis est pars practica scientiae naturalis, cuius altissima et sanctissima pars est philosophia Cabalistica.
latin_text: Magia naturalis est pars practica scientiae naturalis, cuius altissima et sanctissima pars est philosophia Cabalistica. Nulla est scientia quae nos magis certificet de divinitate Christi quam Magia et Cabala. Mago enim non licet uti opera daemonum, sed sola virtute naturae et caeli, quam philosophi occultam nominant.
english_gloss: Natural magic is the practical part of natural science, whose highest and most holy part is Kabbalistic philosophy. There is no science that certifies us more about the divinity of Christ than Magic and Kabbalah. For the magician is not permitted to use the work of demons, but only the virtue of nature and of heaven, which philosophers call occult.

vocabulary.definition: magic — from Greek mageia; here the practical application of natural philosophy
natural — pertaining to nature; natural magic operates through natural causes
Kabbalistic — relating to the Jewish mystical tradition; Pico's synthesis of Kabbalah and Christianity
of demons — evil spirits; legitimate magic explicitly excludes demonic agency
occult, hidden — virtues not perceptible to ordinary senses but real in nature

source_notes: Pico's 900 Theses (1486), proposed for a public disputation in Rome, include 26 conclusions on magic and 47 on Kabbalah. The Church found 13 theses heretical, triggering a crisis. These passages define natural magic as the operative arm of natural philosophy — entirely separate from demonic conjuration — and mark the definitive Renaissance rehabilitation of magia as a respectable discipline.
bibliography: Farmer, S.A. Syncretism in the West: Pico's 900 Theses (1486). Tempe: Medieval & Renaissance Texts & Studies, 1998.

title: De Verbo Mirifico — The Miraculous Word
title_english: On the Wonder-Working Word — The Name of God as Magical Force
author: Johannes Reuchlin
representative_sentence: Verbum Dei mirificum et ineffabile est Tetragrammaton, quod est nomen proprium Dei, virtute cuius omnia in caelo et terra continentur.
latin_text: Verbum Dei mirificum et ineffabile est Tetragrammaton, quod est nomen proprium Dei, virtute cuius omnia in caelo et terra continentur. Ad hoc nomen Hebraicum additur litera schin, et fit pentagrammaton Iesus, per quod miracula et opera mira in mundo fiunt. Nomina divina non sunt signa arbitraria, sed virtutes reales quibus Deus mundum gubernat.
english_gloss: The miraculous and ineffable Word of God is the Tetragrammaton, which is the proper name of God, by whose virtue all things in heaven and earth are contained. To this Hebrew name the letter shin is added, and the Pentagrammaton Jesus is formed, through which miracles and wondrous works are done in the world. Divine names are not arbitrary signs, but real powers by which God governs the world.

vocabulary.definition: Tetragrammaton — the four Hebrew letters YHWH, the unpronounceable name of God
ineffable, unspeakable — too sacred or too great to be expressed in words
Pentagrammaton — YHSWH, the divine name with shin added, equated with Jesus
miracles — wondrous deeds that transcend ordinary nature
governs, steers — the divine names as active forces directing creation

source_notes: Reuchlin's De Verbo Mirifico (1494) is the first major work of Christian Kabbalah, presenting a dialogue in which a Jew, a Pythagorean, and a Christian philosopher discuss the divine name. Reuchlin's equation of YHWH with YHSWH (Jesus) through insertion of the letter shin became foundational for all subsequent Christian Kabbalah and influenced Agrippa, Dee, and the entire Renaissance magical tradition.
bibliography: Reuchlin, Johann. De Verbo Mirifico. Tübingen: Thomas Anshelm, 1514 (rev. ed.). // Hirsch, Wili, ed. De Verbo Mirifico. Stuttgart: Frommann-Holzboog, 1964.

title: De Harmonia Mundi — The Great Chain of Names
title_english: On the Harmony of the World — Kabbalah as Universal Harmony
source: De Harmonia Mundi Totius Cantica Tria
author: Francesco Giorgio (Zorzi)
representative_sentence: Omnia quae in mundo sunt per numerum, mensuram et pondus disposita sunt, et haec tria ad Cabalae mysteria referuntur.
latin_text: Omnia quae in mundo sunt per numerum, mensuram et pondus disposita sunt, et haec tria ad Cabalae mysteria referuntur. Sephiroth sunt virtutes et potentiae divinae per quas Deus mundum creavit et gubernat; earum cognitio est fundamentum omnis magiae naturalis et divinae. Harmonia mundi non est aliud quam consensus omnium rerum in Uno principio.
english_gloss: All things in the world are arranged by number, measure, and weight, and these three are referred to the mysteries of Kabbalah. The Sephiroth are the divine powers and virtues through which God created and governs the world; knowledge of them is the foundation of all natural and divine magic. The harmony of the world is nothing other than the agreement of all things in One principle.

vocabulary.definition: harmony — from Greek; the coherent order of all things in the universe
Sephiroth — Hebrew; the ten divine emanations of the Kabbalistic Tree of Life
number — the mathematical basis of creation; Pythagorean and Kabbalistic numerology
powers, potencies — the active divine forces through which creation is sustained
agreement, harmony — all things sharing a common nature or origin

source_notes: Francesco Giorgio's De Harmonia Mundi (Venice, 1525) is an encyclopedic synthesis of Neoplatonism, Christian theology, and Kabbalah in three books ('canticles'). Written by a Venetian Franciscan friar, it was widely read across Europe and placed on the Index in 1558. It represents the mature form of Renaissance Christian Kabbalah, treating the Sephiroth as compatible with Christian trinitarian theology.
bibliography: Secret, François. Les Kabbalistes Chrétiens de la Renaissance. Paris: Dunod, 1964. // Zorzi, Francesco. De Harmonia Mundi Totius Cantica Tria. Venice: Bernardinus de Vitalibus, 1525 [facsimile, Frankfurt: Minerva, 1962].

title: Antipalus Maleficiorum — Against Witchcraft and Maleficia
title_english: Enemy of Evil Magic — On Combating Witchcraft by Angelic Names
author: Johannes Trithemius
representative_sentence: Maleficia et veneficia per invocationem sanctorum angelorum et per virtutem nominum Dei dissolvi et destrui possunt.
latin_text: Maleficia et veneficia per invocationem sanctorum angelorum et per virtutem nominum Dei dissolvi et destrui possunt. Magus malus potestatem suam a daemonibus accipit, cui resistendum est non per eandem viam, sed per contrarios spiritus et nomina divina. Qui scit naturam angelorum et daemonum, ille potest utrumque ligare et solvere.
english_gloss: Maleficia and veneficia can be dissolved and destroyed through invocation of the holy angels and through the power of the names of God. The evil magician receives his power from demons, which must be resisted not by the same path, but through contrary spirits and divine names. He who knows the nature of angels and demons can bind and loose either.

vocabulary.definition: maleficia — harmful magic, evil deeds; the legal and theological category of injurious sorcery
veneficia — poisoning, potion magic; harmful magic through substances
invocation — the ritual calling-upon of angelic or divine names
from demons — evil spirits who empower malevolent practitioners
to bind — magically restrain or neutralize a spirit or curse

source_notes: Trithemius (1462–1516), abbot of Sponheim and later Würzburg, was the most influential German occultist before Agrippa (his student). The Antipalus Maleficiorum addresses the counter-magical use of angelic invocations to break harmful magic. Trithemius occupied a precarious position — deeply interested in magic and steganography (the Steganographia), yet orthodox enough to be respected by church authorities.
bibliography: Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology: A Chapter in the Controversy over Occult Studies in Early Modern Europe. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999.

title: Propaedeumata Aphoristica — Astral Virtues and Natural Magic
title_english: Propaedeutic Aphorisms — On the First Principles of Celestial Influence
author: John Dee
representative_sentence: Omnis res creata in hac mundi machina a caelestibus virtutibus influentiis subiicitur, nec ulla est tam humilis quae non aliquam stellarum vim participet.
latin_text: Omnis res creata in hac mundi machina a caelestibus virtutibus influentiis subiicitur, nec ulla est tam humilis quae non aliquam stellarum vim participet. Virtus radio toto ex fonte primario progrediendum est per media quaeque ad ultima usque, et in omnibus rebus quaedam est sympathia et consensus universalis. Per haec fundamenta, philosophus naturalis mundum legere potest ut librum a Deo scriptum.
english_gloss: Every created thing in this machine of the world is subject to celestial powers and influences, nor is there anything so humble that it does not share in some power of the stars. Virtue must proceed by its whole ray from the primary source through all intermediaries to the very last things, and in all things there is a certain sympathy and universal agreement. Through these foundations, the natural philosopher can read the world as a book written by God.

vocabulary.definition: celestial — of the heavens; the stars as sources of influence over sublunary things
influences — literally 'inflowings'; the continuous effect of stellar radiation on lower creation
sympathy — from Greek; the hidden resonance between things sharing a common nature
ray, beam — the medium by which celestial virtue travels through space
machine — the ordered mechanism of the cosmos; a common Renaissance metaphor

source_notes: John Dee's Propaedeumata Aphoristica (1558, revised 1568) is his first published work, presenting 120 aphorisms on astral magic and natural philosophy. Written before his angelic conversations, it shows Dee as a rigorous mathematical natural philosopher attempting to provide quantitative foundations for astrological influence. The work draws on Roger Bacon, Ficino, and Agrippa while aspiring toward a mathematical physics of celestial force.
bibliography: Debus, Allen G., ed. John Dee: Propaedeumata Aphoristica (1558 and 1568). London: Science History Publications, 1975.

title: De Subtilitate — Hidden Causes and Occult Virtues
title_english: On Subtlety — The Finest Operations of Nature and Art
author: Girolamo Cardano
representative_sentence: Subtilitas est ratio quaedam qua sensibilia a sensibus, intelligibilia ab intellectu, difficile comprehenduntur.
latin_text: Subtilitas est ratio quaedam qua sensibilia a sensibus, intelligibilia ab intellectu, difficile comprehenduntur. Multae res in natura sunt quarum causas neque sensus neque ratio vulgaris assequitur; haec vocamus occulta, non quia natura eas celat, sed quia ingenium nostrum ad eas penetrandum non sufficit. Talis est sympathia magnetis, talis virtus gemmae, talis influentia stellarum in corpora inferiora.
english_gloss: Subtlety is a certain principle by which sensible things are grasped with difficulty by the senses, and intelligible things by the intellect. There are many things in nature whose causes neither the senses nor ordinary reason can attain; these we call occult, not because nature hides them, but because our intellect is insufficient to penetrate them. Such is the sympathy of the magnet, such the virtue of the gem, such the influence of the stars on lower bodies.

vocabulary.definition: subtlety — fineness of operation; the power of hidden causes in nature
occult things — hidden from ordinary perception but accessible to trained investigation
of the magnet — the magnet as paradigm case of occult sympathy
of the gem — precious stones as repositories of astral and elemental virtue
are grasped, comprehended — the act of intellectual or sensory apprehension

source_notes: Cardano's De Subtilitate (1550) is a vast encyclopedic work covering all natural phenomena from first principles to gems, metals, plants, animals, souls, demons, and angels. It defines 'subtlety' as the investigation of hidden natural causes — occupying the borderland between natural science and natural magic. Cardano treats occult virtues as genuine natural phenomena awaiting explanation, not supernatural interventions.
bibliography: Forrester, John M., trans. The De Subtilitate of Girolamo Cardano. 2 vols. Tempe: ACMRS, 2013.

title: De Sensu Rerum et Magia — Universal Sense and Magical Action
title_english: On the Sense of Things and Magic — The World as Living, Sensing Being
author: Tommaso Campanella
representative_sentence: Mundus est animal magnum et perfectum, omnia sentiens et vivens, cuius membra et partes omnia alia animalia et res sensibiles sunt.
latin_text: Mundus est animal magnum et perfectum, omnia sentiens et vivens, cuius membra et partes omnia alia animalia et res sensibiles sunt. Magia est ars qua per rerum naturalium virtutes, quae in earum sensu fundatae sunt, miranda operantur. Non potest esse magia sine sympathia universali, quae est consensus omnium rerum per sensus communes fundatus.
english_gloss: The world is a great and perfect animal, sensing and living all things, of which all other animals and sensible things are members and parts. Magic is the art by which, through the virtues of natural things grounded in their sense, wonders are worked. There can be no magic without universal sympathy, which is the agreement of all things grounded in common senses.

vocabulary.definition: animal, living being — Campanella's world-soul doctrine makes the cosmos itself a living creature
sensing, perceiving — all things in nature possess some degree of sensation
wonderful things, marvels — the products of magical operation through natural virtue
sympathy — the universal resonance between things sharing common sensory natures
agreement, consonance — the harmony of all parts of the living cosmos

source_notes: Campanella's De Sensu Rerum et Magia (written c. 1590, published 1620) presents a panpsychist natural philosophy in which all things possess sensation (sensus). Magic operates by exploiting the universal sympathy arising from this shared sensory life. Campanella was imprisoned by the Inquisition for 27 years partly for views expressed in this work. He represents the late Renaissance tradition of naturalistic magic at its most radical.
bibliography: Ernst, Germana, ed. Tommaso Campanella: De Sensu Rerum et Magia. Pisa: Fabrizio Serra, 2007.

title: De Incertitudine Scientiarum — On the Vanity of Magic
title_english: On the Uncertainty and Vanity of Sciences — The Limits of Magical Knowledge
source: De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum et Artium
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
representative_sentence: Magia nihil aliud est quam summa et perfectissima scientia, quam tamen ego postquam multos annos colui tandem incertam, vanam et fallacissimam esse comperi.
latin_text: Magia nihil aliud est quam summa et perfectissima scientia, quam tamen ego postquam multos annos colui tandem incertam, vanam et fallacissimam esse comperi. Non enim ars ulla nos ad veritatem ducere potest quam sola fides et gratia divina. Omnes philosophi, magi, et sapientes mundi nihil sciunt, nisi Deum solum, qui solus sapit et intelligit.
english_gloss: Magic is nothing other than the highest and most perfect science, which nevertheless, after I cultivated it for many years, I at last found to be uncertain, vain, and most deceptive. For no art can lead us to truth except faith alone and divine grace. All philosophers, magicians, and wise men of the world know nothing, except God alone, who alone is wise and understands.

vocabulary.definition: uncertainty, unreliability — the epistemological limits of all human knowledge including magic
vanity, emptiness — Ecclesiastes' theme: all human endeavors are vanity
most deceptive, most fallacious — magic as an ultimately unreliable system
faith — in the Christian sense; the only reliable path to truth
I cultivated — Agrippa's autobiographical confession of his magical studies

source_notes: Agrippa's De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum (1530), published a year before the De Occulta Philosophia, appears to recant his magical studies and embrace Christian fideism. Scholars debate whether this is sincere recantation, protective self-distancing, Erasmian satire, or a dialectical companion to De Occulta. The tension between these two works defines the ambivalence at the heart of Renaissance magical philosophy.
bibliography: Nauert, Charles G. Agrippa and the Crisis of Renaissance Thought. Urbana: University of Illinois Press, 1965. // Agrippa. Of the Vanity and Uncertainty of Arts and Sciences. Trans. James Sanford. London: Henry Binneman, 1569.

title: Philosophia Sagax — The Astral Body and Magical Sympathy
title_english: Wise Philosophy — On the Sidereal Body and Its Operations
source: Astronomia Magna seu Philosophia Sagax Astronomiae et Astrologiae
author: Paracelsus (Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim)
representative_sentence: Homo duplex est: unus visibilis ex elementis compositus, alter invisibilis et sidereus, qui ex firma mundi stella ad formam hominis coagulatus est.
latin_text: Homo duplex est: unus visibilis ex elementis compositus, alter invisibilis et sidereus, qui ex firma mundi stella ad formam hominis coagulatus est. Corpus sidereum est vehiculum animae et medium inter spiritum et corpus elementale; per ipsum homo cum stellis et spiritibus communicat. Magus qui corpus suum sidereum novit, potest per spatia longa operari et in somniis verum videre.
english_gloss: Man is twofold: one visible, composed of elements, the other invisible and sidereal, who has been coagulated from the firm star of the world into human form. The sidereal body is the vehicle of the soul and the medium between the spirit and the elemental body; through it man communicates with the stars and spirits. The magician who knows his sidereal body can work across great distances and see truth in dreams.

vocabulary.definition: twofold, double — man as elemental and sidereal being simultaneously
sidereal, astral — of the stars; the subtle body composed of stellar substance
coagulated, congealed — the alchemical term for solidification from a subtle to a denser state
vehicle, vessel — the astral body as carrier of the soul through different planes
communicates, shares — the sidereal body as medium of connection between man and cosmos

source_notes: Paracelsus's Astronomia Magna (Philosophia Sagax, c. 1537–38, pub. 1571) is his most comprehensive account of the relationship between macrocosm and microcosm. The doctrine of the 'sidereal body' (corpus sidereum or Astralleib) — a subtle vehicle of the soul composed of stellar substance — became foundational for later concepts of the astral body in Western esotericism. Written in German vernacular and Latin, it synthesizes alchemy, astrology, and medicine into a unified magical cosmology.
bibliography: Sudhoff, Karl, ed. Theophrast von Hohenheim gen. Paracelsus: Sämtliche Werke, I. Abt., Vol. 12. Munich/Berlin: Oldenbourg, 1929. // Weeks, Andrew. Paracelsus: Speculative Theory and the Crisis of the Early Reformation. Albany: SUNY Press, 1997.

title: Oedipus Aegyptiacus — Egyptian Magic and the Hermetic Chain
title_english: Egyptian Oedipus — On Hieroglyphics, Magic, and Universal Wisdom
author: Athanasius Kircher
representative_sentence: Magia Aegyptiorum antiquissima omnem sapientiam humanam praecessit, et in hieroglyphicis Mercurii Trismegisti omnis philosophia naturalis et divina comprehensa est.
latin_text: Magia Aegyptiorum antiquissima omnem sapientiam humanam praecessit, et in hieroglyphicis Mercurii Trismegisti omnis philosophia naturalis et divina comprehensa est. Catena aurea sapientiae a Deo per angelos et daemons ad Hermetem, ab Hermete ad Orpheum, ab Orpheo ad Pythagoram, a Pythagora ad Platonem et sic usque ad nostram aetatem descendit. Qui hanc catenam intelligit, intelligit omnia.
english_gloss: The most ancient magic of the Egyptians preceded all human wisdom, and in the hieroglyphics of Mercury Trismegistus all natural and divine philosophy is comprehended. The golden chain of wisdom descends from God through angels and daemons to Hermes, from Hermes to Orpheus, from Orpheus to Pythagoras, from Pythagoras to Plato, and so to our own age. He who understands this chain understands all things.

vocabulary.definition: hieroglyphics — Egyptian sacred writing; Kircher (wrongly) believed he had decoded them
Thrice-Greatest — the epithet of Hermes Trismegistus, legendary founder of Hermeticism
chain — the prisca theologia, the golden chain of ancient wisdom transmitted through the ages
ancient, primordial — the prisca theologia: primeval theology common to all cultures
descends — wisdom flowing downward through time from its divine source

source_notes: Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus (3 vols., 1652–54) is the most ambitious attempt of the 17th century to decode Egyptian hieroglyphics and reconstruct the prisca theologia — the primeval universal wisdom. Though his hieroglyphic 'translations' were entirely fanciful (the real decipherment came with Champollion in 1822), the work synthesizes the entire Western esoteric tradition and influenced occultists until the 19th century. Kircher represents the last great Renaissance synthesis before the Scientific Revolution fully separated natural science from natural magic.
bibliography: Kircher, Athanasius. Oedipus Aegyptiacus. 3 vols. Rome: Vitalis Mascardi, 1652–1654. // Godwin, Joscelyn. Athanasius Kircher: A Renaissance Man and the Quest for Lost Knowledge. London: Thames and Hudson, 1979.

title: De Mysteriis Aegyptiorum — On Theurgy and Divine Invocation
title_english: On the Mysteries of the Egyptians — Why Theurgy Surpasses Philosophy
author: Iamblichus of Chalcis
representative_sentence: Non cognitio enim nos coniungit diis, sed actio sacra et perfecta et supra omnem humanum intellectum.
latin_text: Non cognitio enim nos coniungit diis, sed actio sacra et perfecta et supra omnem humanum intellectum. Theurgia est ars divinius operandi per signa sacra, symbola et res mysteriis plenas. Dii non movuntur precibus humanis quasi persuasi, sed propter ipsa sacra symbola quae eis cognata sunt, ad nos descendunt et in nobis operantur.
english_gloss: For it is not knowledge that unites us to the gods, but the sacred and perfect action that is beyond all human intellect. Theurgy is the art of operating divinely through sacred signs, symbols, and things full of mysteries. The gods are not moved by human prayers as if persuaded, but because of the very sacred symbols that are akin to them, they descend to us and operate within us.

vocabulary.definition: theurgy — from Greek theos + ergon; divine work; ritual operations that unite the practitioner with the gods
knowledge, cognition — Iamblichus argues knowledge alone cannot achieve divine union
symbols — sacred tokens or objects that share the divine nature they represent
signs — ritual markers with inherent divine power, not arbitrary codes
they descend — the gods condescending to manifest in lower matter through proper ritual

source_notes: Iamblichus's De Mysteriis (c. 280–305 CE), written as a response to Porphyry's skeptical 'Letter to Anebo,' is the foundational text of theurgical Neoplatonism. Against Porphyry and Plotinus, Iamblichus argues that philosophical contemplation alone cannot unite the soul with the divine — only ritual action (theurgy) using divinely-charged symbols (synthemata) can accomplish this. The work defined the ritual-magical dimension of Neoplatonism and profoundly influenced Renaissance magic through Ficino and Pico.
bibliography: Clarke, Emma C., John M. Dillon, and Jackson P. Hershbell, trans. Iamblichus: De Mysteriis. Leiden: Brill / Society of Biblical Literature, 2003.

title: De Sacrificio et Magia — Sympathies Between Worlds
title_english: On Sacrifice and Magic — How the Chain of Being Enables Ritual
author: Proclus Diadochus
representative_sentence: Sapientes antiqui per hanc sympathiam quae vincit caelestia cum terrenis, substantias caelestes ad terras attraxerunt et terras ad caelum elevaverunt.
latin_text: Sapientes antiqui per hanc sympathiam quae vincit caelestia cum terrenis, substantias caelestes ad terras attraxerunt et terras ad caelum elevaverunt. Non enim per intellectum solum divina contingimus, sed per ea quae diis cognata sunt in mundo materiali: lapides, herbae, animalia, odores. Tota mundana hierarchia simul communicat, et qui hanc communicationem intelligit, magia utitur.
english_gloss: The ancient wise men, through this sympathy that connects celestial things with earthly ones, drew celestial substances down to earth and raised earthly things up to heaven. For we do not touch the divine through intellect alone, but through those things in the material world that are akin to the gods: stones, herbs, animals, fragrances. The entire worldly hierarchy communicates simultaneously, and he who understands this communication uses magic.

vocabulary.definition: sympathy — the hidden affinity linking different levels of reality in the Neoplatonic chain of being
they drew down — the magical operation of attracting divine virtue into material objects
akin, kindred — things sharing the same divine source as a particular god
hierarchy — the graded chain of being from the One through intellect, soul, and matter
communicates — participates in a common nature; the basis of magical sympathy

source_notes: Proclus's short treatise De Sacrificio et Magia (preserved only in a Latin translation by Ficino) articulates the theoretical basis for theurgical ritual: because all things in the material world participate in the divine through the chain of being (henads), certain material objects are genuinely 'akin' to specific gods and can be used in ritual to attract divine presence. Ficino's translation was enormously influential; this text directly underpins his theory of talismans in De Vita III.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio, trans. In Iamblichus de mysteriis Aegyptiorum. Venice: Aldus Manutius, 1497. // Lewy, Hans. Chaldaean Oracles and Theurgy. Rev. ed. Paris: Études augustiniennes, 1978.

title: Epistola ad Anebonem — Skeptical Questions on Divination
title_english: Letter to Anebo — On the Philosophical Difficulties of Divination and Oracles
author: Porphyry of Tyre
representative_sentence: Si dii voluntate nostra flecti possunt, non sunt dii sed daemones; si non flecti possunt, quid prodest eos invocare?
latin_text: Si dii voluntate nostra flecti possunt, non sunt dii sed daemones; si non flecti possunt, quid prodest eos invocare? Haec est prima dubitatio de divinatione et sacrificio. Cur dii materiales res desiderant — fumum, sanguinem, unguentum — si incorporei sunt et nihil materiale egent? Cur per aquam et specula veritatem ostendunt potius quam per intellectum purum?
english_gloss: If the gods can be bent by our will, they are not gods but demons; if they cannot be bent, what profit is there in invoking them? This is the first doubt concerning divination and sacrifice. Why do the gods desire material things — smoke, blood, ointment — if they are incorporeal and need nothing material? Why do they show truth through water and mirrors rather than through pure intellect?

vocabulary.definition: divination — the art of gaining knowledge of hidden or future things through divine contact
incorporeal — without body; the philosophical puzzle of immaterial gods requiring material sacrifice
mirrors — used in catoptromancy; divination by gazing into reflective surfaces
daemons — intermediate beings between gods and humans; Porphyry uses them to explain magical manipulation
doubt, skeptical question — Porphyry's philosophical critique of traditional theurgical practice

source_notes: Porphyry's Letter to Anebo (a fictional Egyptian priest, c. 268–270 CE) poses probing philosophical questions about divination, theurgy, and sacrifice from a Neoplatonic perspective. Porphyry doubts that the gods of popular religion are truly divine if they respond to ritual manipulation. The letter prompted Iamblichus's De Mysteriis as its direct rebuttal. Preserved only in fragments cited by Eusebius and Iamblichus, it represents the rationalist pole of Late Antique debate about magic.
bibliography: Sodano, Angelo R., ed. Porfirio: Lettera ad Anebo. Naples: L'Arte Tipografica, 1958. // Clarke, Emma C., et al., trans. Iamblichus: De Mysteriis (includes Porphyry's letter as preface). Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Divinis Nominibus — The Hierarchy of Divine Names
title_english: On the Divine Names — How God Is Named Through What He Causes
author: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
representative_sentence: Omnia nomina divina sunt sacra et efficacia, per quae anima ad Deum ascendit, et per quae Deus ad animam descendit in scala luminis perpetui.
latin_text: Omnia nomina divina sunt sacra et efficacia, per quae anima ad Deum ascendit, et per quae Deus ad animam descendit in scala luminis perpetui. Bonum, Ens, Vita, Sapientia, Virtus — haec sunt nomina realia, non arbitraria signa, quia ex ipsa natura divina manant. Qui haec nomina intelligit et recitat, particeps fit lucis increatae.
english_gloss: All divine names are sacred and efficacious, through which the soul ascends to God, and through which God descends to the soul on the ladder of perpetual light. Good, Being, Life, Wisdom, Virtue — these are real names, not arbitrary signs, because they flow from the very divine nature. He who understands and recites these names becomes a participant in uncreated light.

vocabulary.definition: names — divine names as real powers flowing from the divine nature itself
efficacious, effective — the names produce real effects, not merely describe
ascends — the soul's movement upward toward divine union through contemplation
participant, sharer — participation in divine nature as the goal of mystical/magical practice
uncreated — the divine light that has no beginning, as distinct from created light

source_notes: The Dionysian corpus (c. 480–520 CE), attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite mentioned in Acts 17:34, is almost certainly by a late Neoplatonist heavily influenced by Proclus. De Divinis Nominibus explores how God can be named at all, given divine transcendence. Its doctrine that divine names are efficacious because they flow from divine nature directly influenced medieval Christian magic, Kabbalistic theories of divine names, and Renaissance magic of every kind. Thomas Aquinas wrote a commentary on it.
bibliography: Luibheid, Colm, trans. Pseudo-Dionysius: The Complete Works. Mahwah: Paulist Press, 1987. // Suchla, Beate Regina, ed. Corpus Dionysiacum I: De Divinis Nominibus. Berlin: De Gruyter, 1990.

title: Physica — Virtutes Gemmarum
title_english: Physica — The Hidden Powers of Precious Stones
source: Physica (Liber Subtilitatum Diversarum Naturarum Creaturarum), Book IV
author: Hildegard of Bingen
representative_sentence: Smaragdus de sole et de aere nascitur, et ideo plus virtutis habet quam alii lapides, et contra omnes infirmitates valet.
latin_text: Smaragdus de sole et de aere nascitur, et ideo plus virtutis habet quam alii lapides, et contra omnes infirmitates valet. Omnis lapis vim et virtutem ex oriente habet, quia lux prima ibi oritur et in eo residet. Qui smaragdum secum portat, cor eius non turbatur, nec mens eius in phantasmate aliquo vexatur.
english_gloss: The emerald is born from the sun and from air, and therefore has more virtue than other stones, and is effective against all infirmities. Every stone has its power and virtue from the east, because the first light rises there and resides in it. He who carries an emerald with him, his heart is not disturbed, nor is his mind troubled by any phantom.

vocabulary.definition: emerald — the most powerful stone in Hildegard's system, born of sun and air
virtue, power — the inherent occult force of natural objects, especially gems
infirmities, illnesses — physical and spiritual ailments that gems can combat
phantom, apparition — demonic or mental disturbances that gems protect against
carries — the gem must be worn or carried to transmit its virtue to the person

source_notes: Hildegard of Bingen's Physica (c. 1150–60) is a vast catalogue of plants, animals, stones, metals, and their medical and magical properties. Book IV on stones lists the hidden virtues (virtutes) of gems and their uses in healing and protection. Hildegard integrates natural magic seamlessly with Christian theology, attributing gem-virtues to their origin in the primal light of creation. A Benedictine abbess, mystic, and composer, she represents the most prominent female voice in medieval natural philosophy.
bibliography: Throop, Priscilla, trans. Hildegard von Bingen's Physica. Rochester: Healing Arts Press, 1998. // Reuss, Michael, ed. Hildegardis Bingensis Physica. Corpus Christianorum Continuatio Mediaevalis 260. Turnhout: Brepols, 2010.

title: Ars Magna — Principia Fundamentalia
title_english: The Great Art — The Fundamental Principles of Universal Knowledge
author: Ramon Lull
representative_sentence: Per revolutionem figurarum et combinationem principiorum, omnes quaestiones de Deo, mundo et anima solvi possunt et demonstrari.
latin_text: Per revolutionem figurarum et combinationem principiorum, omnes quaestiones de Deo, mundo et anima solvi possunt et demonstrari. Principia nostra sunt: Bonitas, Magnitudo, Aeternitas, Potestas, Sapientia, Voluntas, Virtus, Veritas, Gloria — haec novem sunt nomina Dei et radices totius scientiae. Ars ista non est magia, sed methodus naturalis qua intellectus ad veritatem pervenit.
english_gloss: Through the revolution of figures and the combination of principles, all questions about God, the world, and the soul can be solved and demonstrated. Our principles are: Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, Power, Wisdom, Will, Virtue, Truth, Glory — these nine are names of God and roots of all knowledge. This art is not magic, but a natural method by which the intellect arrives at truth.

vocabulary.definition: revolution — the rotation of Lull's combinatorial wheels to generate combinations of principles
of principles — the absolute divine attributes that underlie all reality
combination — the systematic pairing of divine attributes to generate knowledge
to be demonstrated — Lull's claim that divine truths can be rationally demonstrated, not just believed
method — systematic procedure; Lull insists the Ars is science, not sorcery

source_notes: Ramon Lull's Ars Magna (final version: Ars Generalis Ultima, 1305–08) is a combinatorial system using rotating wheels (figurae) to combine divine attributes and generate all possible knowledge. Though Lull insisted it was rational theology, not magic, the Ars was enormously influential on Renaissance magic: Bruno used it as a memory-magical system, and it influenced Leibniz's dreams of a universal calculus. Lull's nine divine dignities echo Kabbalistic Sephiroth and became part of the Christian Kabbalah tradition.
bibliography: Bonner, Anthony, ed. Selected Works of Ramon Llull (1232–1316). 2 vols. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1985.

title: Secretum Secretorum — De Proprietatibus Lapidum
title_english: The Secret of Secrets — On the Properties of Stones and Talismans
author: Anonymous (attrib. Aristotle; trans. Philip of Tripoli)
date: Arabic original c. 10th c.; Latin trans. c. 1230
representative_sentence: Aristoteles dixit Alexandro: Cum vis aliquam rem magnam et secretam facere, accipe lapidem Iovis et sculpe in eo imaginem regis sedentem in throno.
latin_text: Aristoteles dixit Alexandro: Cum vis aliquam rem magnam et secretam facere, accipe lapidem Iovis et sculpe in eo imaginem regis sedentem in throno. Haec est sapientia antiqua de virtutibus lapidum et signorum caelestium. Omnis figura sculpta in lapide proprio planeta dominante vim caelestem in se tenet et eam ad hominem portatorem transigit.
english_gloss: Aristotle said to Alexander: When you wish to do something great and secret, take the stone of Jupiter and carve upon it the image of a king seated on a throne. This is the ancient wisdom concerning the virtues of stones and celestial signs. Every figure carved in a stone while its proper planet dominates retains celestial power within itself and transmits it to the person who carries it.

vocabulary.definition: secret — hidden knowledge reserved for rulers and initiates; the Arabic sirr al-asrar
carve — the talismanic operation of engraving images under planetary influence
image — the figure engraved on the talisman that concentrates planetary virtue
dominating — when a planet is in its strongest astrological position during talismanic engraving
transmits, conveys — the talisman passing its stored virtue to the wearer

source_notes: The Secretum Secretorum (Arabic: Sirr al-Asrar, c. 10th century) purports to be Aristotle's private letter of advice to Alexander the Great, covering rulership, medicine, astrology, and talismanic magic. Translated into Latin by Philip of Tripoli (c. 1230), it became one of the most widely copied texts of the Middle Ages (over 600 manuscripts). Its practical talismanic instructions were influential on the broader tradition of carved stone amulets.
bibliography: Steele, Robert, ed. Secretum Secretorum. In Opera hactenus inedita Rogeri Baconi, Fasc. V. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920. // Ryan, W.F., and Charles B. Schmitt, eds. Pseudo-Aristotle: The Secret of Secrets. London: Warburg Institute, 1982.

title: Liber Florum Caelestis Doctrinae — The Flower of Heavenly Doctrine
title_english: The Book of the Flowers of Heavenly Teaching — Vision, Prayer, and Magical Art
author: John of Morigny
representative_sentence: Per has orationes et figuras sacras, scientia omnium artium liberalium infunditur a Deo in animam puram et devotam.
latin_text: Per has orationes et figuras sacras, scientia omnium artium liberalium infunditur a Deo in animam puram et devotam. Non est haec ars magica neque daemonica, sed pura oratio et sancta contemplatio per quam Virgo Maria et angeli scientiam tradunt. Prius quam hoc opus incipiatur, confessio et ieiunium et oratio per multos dies sunt necessaria.
english_gloss: Through these prayers and sacred figures, knowledge of all the liberal arts is poured by God into the pure and devout soul. This is not magical nor demonic art, but pure prayer and holy contemplation through which the Virgin Mary and the angels transmit knowledge. Before this work is begun, confession and fasting and prayer for many days are necessary.

vocabulary.definition: is poured in, infused — divine knowledge as a liquid poured into the receptive soul
of the liberal arts — grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy
devoted, pious — the required moral state of the practitioner before working the art
confession — sacramental preparation; the Liber Florum integrates Christian practice with magical art
fasting — ritual abstinence as preparation for the infusion of heavenly knowledge

source_notes: John of Morigny was a Benedictine monk who composed the Liber Florum (c. 1304–17) as a reformed alternative to the Ars Notoria — a grimoire for acquiring knowledge of all arts through prayer and sacred figures. John claimed to have received the book through visions of the Virgin Mary. He was accused of necromancy and his book was burned. Studied by Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson (Liber Florum, PIMS, 2015), it represents the fraught boundary between medieval piety and ritual magic.
bibliography: Fanger, Claire, and Nicholas Watson, eds. and trans. Liber Florum Celestis Doctrine / The Flowers of Heavenly Teaching. Toronto: Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 2015.

title: Magia Naturalis — De Sympathia et Antipathia Rerum
title_english: Natural Magic — On the Sympathy and Antipathy of Things
source: Magia Naturalis sive de Miraculis Rerum Naturalium
author: Giambattista della Porta
representative_sentence: Magus est homo sapiens qui naturam novit, et per cognitionem naturae admiranda opera producit quae vulgo miracula vocantur.
latin_text: Magus est homo sapiens qui naturam novit, et per cognitionem naturae admiranda opera producit quae vulgo miracula vocantur. Sympathia est occulta rerum cognatio quae diversas res iungit; antipathia est inimicitia naturalis quae eas separat. Has virtutes qui perscrutatur et in usus convertit, hic est verus naturalis magus, non qui daemones invocat.
english_gloss: The magician is the wise man who knows nature, and through knowledge of nature produces wondrous works which the common people call miracles. Sympathy is the hidden kinship of things that joins diverse things together; antipathy is the natural enmity that separates them. He who investigates these virtues and turns them to use — this is the true natural magician, not one who invokes demons.

vocabulary.definition: sympathy — occult affinity between things; the basis of all natural magic
antipathy — natural enmity between things; the negative pole of occult relations
kinship — the hidden family resemblance between apparently unrelated things
investigates thoroughly — the naturalist's empirical investigation of occult virtues
wondrous things — marvels produced by deep knowledge of nature, not supernatural intervention

source_notes: Giambattista della Porta's Magia Naturalis (1558, expanded to 20 books in 1589) is the most widely read popular account of natural magic in the Renaissance, translated into every major European language. Written by a Neapolitan nobleman and founder of the Accademia dei Segreti, it covers sympathy/antipathy, optics, magnetism, cosmetics, cookery, distillation, and much more. The Inquisition investigated della Porta and he was briefly ordered to cease his philosophical society, but the book circulated freely.
bibliography: Eamon, William. Science and the Secrets of Nature: Books of Secrets in Medieval and Early Modern Culture. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1994. // Della Porta, Giambattista. Natural Magick. London: Thomas Young and Samuel Speed, 1658 (English trans.).

title: De Vinculis in Genere — The Art of Binding
title_english: On Bonds in General — How All Things Are Bound and Loosed
author: Giordano Bruno
representative_sentence: Vinculum est omne illud quo aliquid aliud ad se allicit, tenet et constringit; amor est vinculum vinculorum, et qui amat omnium est dominus.
latin_text: Vinculum est omne illud quo aliquid aliud ad se allicit, tenet et constringit; amor est vinculum vinculorum, et qui amat omnium est dominus. Qui vult ligare alium, prius debet nosse quid amet ille, quid timeat, quid speret; per haec tria omnes homines et daemones ligantur. Magus ergo debet esse philosophus, psychologus et amator, non incantator verborum vacuorum.
english_gloss: A bond is everything by which something attracts, holds, and constrains another thing; love is the bond of bonds, and he who loves is master of all things. He who wishes to bind another must first know what that person loves, fears, and hopes for; through these three all men and demons are bound. The magician therefore must be philosopher, psychologist, and lover — not a chanter of empty words.

vocabulary.definition: bond, chain — the operative concept: every magical relationship is a binding
attracts, allures — the first phase of binding: drawing the target toward the magician
constrains, binds tight — the final phase: the target cannot act contrary to the binding
love — the supreme magical bond; all other bonds are derivatives of love's attractive power
psychologist — Bruno's term for one who understands the soul's desires, fears, and hopes

source_notes: Bruno's De Vinculis in Genere (c. 1591, written in Rome shortly before his arrest) is his most explicitly magical work, providing a general theory of magical binding. Bruno argues that the magician operates through psychological understanding of desire, fear, and hope — the three bonds that constrain all rational creatures. Love (eros/amor) is identified as the supreme binding force underlying all other magic. The text was unpublished in Bruno's lifetime and circulated in manuscript; he was arrested by the Inquisition in 1592 and burned in 1600.
bibliography: Gatti, Hilary. Giordano Bruno and Renaissance Science. Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1999. // Bruno, Giordano. De Vinculis in Genere. In Opera Latine Conscripta, Vol. 3. Naples: Morano, 1891.

title: Medulla Alchimiae — The Heart of the Alchemical Work
title_english: Marrow of Alchemy — On the One Medicine and Its Preparation
author: George Ripley
representative_sentence: Una est medicina, unum vas, unum regimen, et una dispositio a principio ad finem; qui hoc ignorat, nihil in arte scit.
latin_text: Una est medicina, unum vas, unum regimen, et una dispositio a principio ad finem; qui hoc ignorat, nihil in arte scit. Lapis noster non est lapis pretiosus, non est sulphur, non est sal, non est mercurius vulgaris — est tamen in his omnibus virtualiter. Solvatur autem fixum, et figatur solutum, et habebis arcanum artis.
english_gloss: There is one medicine, one vessel, one regimen, and one disposition from beginning to end; he who does not know this knows nothing in the art. Our Stone is not a precious stone, is not sulphur, is not salt, is not common mercury — yet it is virtually in all of these. Let the fixed be dissolved, and let the dissolved be fixed, and you will have the secret of the art.

vocabulary.definition: medicine — the philosopher's stone as universal medicine for metals and for human bodies
regimen, direction — the single correct procedure of the alchemical work from start to finish
fixed — the stable, solid phase of matter; solve et coagula: dissolve the fixed
dissolved, liquid — the fluid phase; coagulate the dissolved into the permanent Stone
secret, arcanum — the hidden truth of alchemical art; from arcanus, locked away

source_notes: George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), an Augustinian canon of Bridlington, Yorkshire, was the most important English alchemist of the 15th century. His Medulla Alchimiae and the Compound of Alchymy (1471) became foundational texts for English alchemy. Ripley's works were published by Elias Ashmole in the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum (1652) and greatly influenced John Dee, Edward Kelley, and Newton, who annotated Ripley's texts heavily.
bibliography: Ashmole, Elias, ed. Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum. London: J. Grismond, 1652. // Linden, Stanton J., ed. The Alchemist in English Literature and Culture, 1471–1700. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996.

title: Libri Mysteriorum — The First Spirit Conversation
title_english: Books of Mysteries — The Angel Uriel Appears in the Shewstone
source: Libri Mysteriorum (British Library MS Cotton Appendix XLVI)
author: John Dee
representative_sentence: Anno 1581, Novembris 21, hora noctis 9a, angelus Uriel in speculo crystallino apparuit et loquebatur nobiscum de secretis caelestibus.
latin_text: Anno 1581, Novembris 21, hora noctis 9a, angelus Uriel in speculo crystallino apparuit et loquebatur nobiscum de secretis caelestibus. Dixit: Ecce, ego sum servus Dei Altissimi, et mitto vos ad gentium reformationem. Lingua angelica non est humana lingua, sed prior omnibus linguis, et in ea creata est prima lux.
english_gloss: In the year 1581, November 21, at the 9th hour of the night, the angel Uriel appeared in the crystal mirror and spoke with us about celestial secrets. He said: Behold, I am a servant of God Most High, and I send you to the reformation of the nations. The angelic language is not human language, but prior to all languages, and in it the first light was created.

vocabulary.definition: mirror, speculum — the crystal shewstone used as a focus for scrying and angelic contact
of crystal — Dee used an obsidian mirror and crystal ball for his angelic operations
angelic — pertaining to the angels; the Enochian language as the original tongue of creation
reformation — the angels charged Dee with a mission of universal religious reform
of the nations, peoples — the angels' universal mission across all of humanity

source_notes: John Dee's spirit diaries (1581–1589, British Library MS Cotton Appendix XLVI) record his scryer Edward Kelley's visions in the shewstone, through which the angels dictated the Enochian language, tables, and system of ceremonial magic. The first recorded session (Nov. 21, 1581) features Uriel. The diaries were first published by Meric Casaubon as A True and Faithful Relation (1659). Dee's Enochian system — complete with its own alphabet, language, and magical calls — became one of the most influential magical systems in Western history, adopted by the Golden Dawn and Aleister Crowley.
bibliography: Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999. // Casaubon, Meric, ed. A True and Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Yeers Between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits. London: T.G., 1659.

title: Enneades IV.4 — De Magia et Fascinatione
title_english: Enneads IV.4 — Why Magic Works: Sympathy in the World-Soul
author: Plotinus
representative_sentence: Magus autem utitur his vinculis et trahit ea quae sibi cognata sunt — non ratione sed natura, ut magnes ferrum.
latin_text: Magus autem utitur his vinculis et trahit ea quae sibi cognata sunt — non ratione sed natura, ut magnes ferrum. Anima mundi omnia connectit, et qui hanc connexionem novit, potest per ea quae similia sunt dissimilia movere. Sapientia autem vera non utitur magicis artibus, sed per contemplationem puram ad Unum ascendit.
english_gloss: The magician uses these bonds and draws toward himself what is akin to him — not by reason but by nature, as a magnet draws iron. The world-soul connects all things, and he who knows this connection can move dissimilar things through what is similar. But true wisdom does not use magical arts, but ascends to the One through pure contemplation.

vocabulary.definition: fascination, bewitchment — the evil eye and binding magic that Plotinus explains through sympathy
bonds, chains — the sympathetic connections that run through the world-soul
magnet — Plotinus's paradigm for natural magical action at a distance
contemplation — the philosophical alternative to magic; direct intellectual union with the One
connection — the sympathetic network running through all things in the world-soul

source_notes: Plotinus's discussion of magic in Enneads IV.4.40-43 (c. 253-270 CE) is the most philosophically sophisticated ancient account of how magic works. Plotinus accepts that magic is real — it operates through the sympathetic connections of the world-soul — but argues the philosopher should transcend it through contemplation. His account of the magnet as paradigm for magical action at a distance influenced every subsequent Neoplatonic theory of sympathy.
bibliography: Armstrong, A.H., trans. Plotinus: Enneads, 7 vols. Loeb Classical Library. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1966–1988.

title: Metamorphoses III — Pamphile's Transformation
title_english: The Golden Ass III — A Witch Transforms Herself by Night
author: Apuleius of Madauros
representative_sentence: Pamphile exuta vestimentis, unguento quodam ex pyxide extracto perunxit sese, et mutata in noctuam avolavit.
latin_text: Pamphile exuta vestimentis, unguento quodam ex pyxide extracto perunxit sese ab unguibus imo ad summum verticem, et mutata in noctuam avolavit. Haec sunt venena Thessaliae, haec sunt carmina Circes; lunae detrahere, coelum deprimere, terram suspendere possunt sagae Thessalae. Vidi ego illas facem ardentem carmine extingui, et rursus subito accendi.
