english_gloss: Pamphile, having stripped off her garments, smeared herself from her lowest nails to the top of her head with a certain ointment drawn from a box, and transformed into an owl she flew away. These are the poisons of Thessaly, these are the charms of Circe; the Thessalian witches can pull down the moon, depress the heavens, suspend the earth. I saw with my own eyes a burning torch extinguished by their incantation and suddenly re-lit.

vocabulary.definition: ointment — the transformation unguent rubbed on the body to achieve shape-shifting
box, case — the witch's container of magical ointments and preparations
owl — the witch's animal form; owls as vehicles of nocturnal witch-flight
witches — the Latin term for female practitioners of harmful magic
Thessalian — Thessaly was the legendary homeland of witchcraft in antiquity

source_notes: Apuleius's Metamorphoses (c. 160-170 CE), the Golden Ass, is the only Latin novel to survive complete from antiquity. Book III contains one of the most vivid ancient descriptions of witch-flight: Pamphile rubs herself with an unguent and transforms into an owl. The hero Lucius attempts the same but mistakenly uses the wrong ointment and becomes a donkey. The shape-shifting ointment became a foundational image of medieval witch-flight and the sabbath.
bibliography: Hanson, J.A., trans. Apuleius: Metamorphoses. 2 vols. Loeb Classical Library. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1989.

title: De Medicamentis — Incantamenta et Remedia
title_english: On Medicines — Incantations and Remedies of Ancient Gaul
author: Marcellus Empiricus
representative_sentence: Ad herniam sanam incantato ter novies in terra et ter in hominem et ter in herbam: huat huat huat.
latin_text: Ad herniam sanam et venam sanam et sanguinem sanum incantato ter novies in terra et ter in hominem et ter in herbam. Haec verba Gallica sunt antiqua et potentissima: huat huat huat ista pista sista. Cum herba radicem eruis, dic: Tollam te, herba, et pono in loco ubi nec sol te videat nec luna.
english_gloss: For healthy rupture and healthy vein and healthy blood, chant thrice nine times into the earth and thrice into the person and thrice into the herb. These words are ancient Gaulish and most powerful: huat huat huat ista pista sista. When you pull up the herb by the root, say: I take you, herb, and place you in a spot where neither sun nor moon shall see you.

vocabulary.definition: chant, incant — speak a magical formula repeatedly over a person or thing
nine times — thrice nine is a common magical repetition formula
herb — medicinal and magical plants; herbs require ritual gathering for full potency
root — the most powerful part of a magical herb; root-cutting had its own rites
Gaulish — pertaining to Gaul; Marcellus preserves rare Celtic magical vocabulary

source_notes: Marcellus Empiricus's De Medicamentis (c. 395-410 CE), written in Bordeaux, preserves an extraordinary collection of folk charms, incantations (some in Gaulish or pseudo-Gaulish), and ritual remedies alongside Galenic medicine. The 'Huat huat huat' charm is one of the few surviving examples of Gaulish magical language. Marcellus shows how formal Greco-Roman medicine and indigenous Celtic folk magic coexisted in Late Antique Gaul.
bibliography: Niedermann, Max, ed. Marcellus: De Medicamentis Liber. Corpus Medicorum Latinorum V. Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1968.

title: Formicarius V — Malefici et Maleficae
title_english: The Anthill V — On Witches and Their Power to Harm
author: Johannes Nider OP
representative_sentence: Malefici et maleficae possunt a diabolo accipere potestatem nocendi per pactum expressum vel tacitum cum eodem diabolo initum.
latin_text: Malefici et maleficae possunt a diabolo accipere potestatem nocendi, et hoc per pactum expressum vel tacitum cum eodem diabolo initum. In Berno civitate quidam maleficus ante mortem suam confessus est se infantibus nocuisse, eorum unguento ad conventum portari et ibi diabolum in forma hominis nigri apparuisse. Mulieres simplicioris ingenii facilius in haec vitia labuntur quam viri.
english_gloss: Male and female witches can receive from the devil the power of causing harm, and this through an express or tacit pact entered into with the same devil. In the city of Bern a certain male witch before his death confessed that he had harmed infants, that their ointment carried one to the assembly, and that the devil appeared there in the form of a black man. Women of simpler disposition fall into these vices more easily than men.

vocabulary.definition: male witches, evildoers — Nider unusually recognizes both male and female witches
pact — the diabolical contract; the theological cornerstone of witch-trial theory
ointment — the flying ointment that transports witches to the sabbath assembly
assembly, gathering — the witches' sabbath; one of the earliest Latin descriptions
confessed — judicial confession under torture; the primary source of sabbath descriptions

source_notes: Johannes Nider's Formicarius (c. 1436-38) is the earliest systematic Latin account of the witches' sabbath and diabolical pact theory, preceding the Malleus Maleficarum by 50 years. Nider, a Dominican reformer at the Council of Basel, gathered accounts from the witch judge Peter of Greyerz. Book V is foundational to early modern witch-theory; studied by Norman Cohn (Europe's Inner Demons, 1975) and Richard Kieckhefer.
bibliography: Bailey, Michael D. Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2003. // Nider, Johannes. Formicarius. Cologne: Ulrich Zel, c. 1475 (editio princeps).

title: Malleus Maleficarum I — Quid Sit Maleficium
title_english: The Hammer of Witches I — The Definition of Witchcraft
source: Malleus Maleficarum, Pars Prima, Quaestio II
author: Heinrich Kramer (Institoris) OP
representative_sentence: Maleficium est actus humanus ex viribus daemonis procedens, ad nocendum alicui ordinatus per pactum cum diabolo initum.
latin_text: Maleficium est actus humanus ex viribus daemonis procedens, ad nocendum alicui ordinatus per pactum expressum vel tacitum cum diabolo initum. Haeresis est maxima non credere maleficas esse. Tria necessaria sunt ad maleficium: diabolus, maleficus, et permissio Dei Altissimi, sine qua diabolus nihil potest. Mulieres propter infidelitatem naturalem et defectum mentis magis sunt ad haec maleficia proclives.
english_gloss: Witchcraft is a human act proceeding from the powers of a demon, ordered to harm someone through an express or tacit pact entered into with the devil. It is the greatest heresy not to believe that witches exist. Three things are necessary for witchcraft: the devil, the witch, and the permission of Almighty God, without which the devil can do nothing. Women are more prone to these evils on account of their natural faithlessness and defect of mind.

vocabulary.definition: witchcraft, harmful magic — the Malleus's central legal-theological category
heresy — disbelief in witchcraft is itself heretical; the Malleus's most dangerous claim
permission — God's allowance of demonic activity; the theodicy behind the witch-persecutions
prone, inclined — women as more susceptible to diabolical temptation in the Malleus
Kramer's Latinized name — from institor, peddler; the inquisitor's self-designation

source_notes: The Malleus Maleficarum (1486) by Heinrich Kramer is the most influential and most notorious witch-hunting manual ever written. Combining scholastic theology, canon law, and descriptions of diabolical pacts, it provided both theoretical framework and procedural guidance for witch prosecution. The claim that disbelief in witchcraft is heresy was contested even in its own time. Published at least 14 times between 1487 and 1520, it shaped European witch persecution for two centuries.
bibliography: Mackay, Christopher S., trans. Malleus Maleficarum. 2 vols. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.

title: De Praestigiis Daemonum — Stultitia Sagarum
title_english: On the Deceptions of Demons — The Foolishness of Alleged Witches
source: De Praestigiis Daemonum et Incantationibus ac Veneficiis
author: Johann Weyer (Wierus)
representative_sentence: Sagae miserae et imbecilles sunt mulieres melancholica phantasia deceptae, quae diabolus persuadet ut omnia quae somniant vera sint.
latin_text: Sagae miserae et imbecilles sunt mulieres melancholica phantasia deceptae, quae diabolus eis persuadet ut omnia quae somniant vera sint. Non ipsae faciunt maleficia, sed daemon per eas; immo daemon eis persuadet se fecisse quod ipse solus fecit. Iudices qui has mulieres torquent et occidunt, ipsi in errore versantur et innocentes sanguine maculantur.
english_gloss: Wretched and feeble witches are women deceived by melancholic fantasy, whom the devil persuades that everything they dream is real. They do not themselves perform the harmful magic, but the demon acts through them; the demon persuades them that they did what he alone did. The judges who torture and kill these women are themselves in error and are stained with innocent blood.

vocabulary.definition: melancholic — the black bile humor that produces delusions; Weyer's medical-psychological explanation
fantasy, imagination — the sabbath as a diabolically-induced hallucination, not real flight
feeble, weak — Weyer's characterization of accused witches as mentally vulnerable, not guilty
torture — Weyer's explicit condemnation of judicial torture as producing false confessions
innocent people — Weyer's radical claim: the condemned are victims, not criminals

source_notes: Johann Weyer's De Praestigiis Daemonum (1563) is the most significant early modern defense of accused witches, arguing they are victims of diabolical delusion and melancholy, not perpetrators. Weyer, a physician and student of Agrippa, distinguished between genuine diabolism (which he accepted) and the delusional confessions of mentally ill women. Jean Bodin attacked him furiously. Modern historians debate whether Weyer represents proto-Enlightenment skepticism or a rearrangement of demonological categories.
bibliography: Mora, George, Benjamin Kohl, John Shea, and Erik Midelfort, eds. Witches, Devils, and Doctors in the Renaissance: Johann Weyer, De Praestigiis Daemonum. Binghamton: Medieval & Renaissance Texts & Studies, 1991.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum — Coniunctio Solis et Lunae
title_english: Philosophical Rose Garden — The Conjunction of Sun and Moon
author: Anonymous (attrib. Arnald of Villanova)
representative_sentence: Coniunctio solis et lunae est matrimonium philosophicum, ex quo filius philosophorum nascitur qui lapis vocatur.
latin_text: Coniunctio solis et lunae est matrimonium philosophicum, ex quo filius philosophorum nascitur qui lapis vocatur. Accipe de minera nostra philosophica et destilla per alembicum, et primum veniet aqua alba ut lac, postea aqua rubea ut sanguis. Solvite corpora et coagulate spiritus et habetis quod quaeritis.
english_gloss: The conjunction of sun and moon is the philosophical marriage, from which the son of the philosophers is born who is called the Stone. Take of our philosophical ore and distill through the alembic, and first will come white water like milk, then red water like blood. Dissolve the bodies and coagulate the spirits and you have what you seek.

vocabulary.definition: conjunction — the alchemical marriage of opposing principles: sol/luna, sulphur/mercury
marriage — the hierosgamos of solar and lunar principles producing the philosopher's stone
alembic — from Arabic al-anbiq; the distillation vessel central to alchemical work
coagulate, fix — condense the volatile spirit into permanent solid form
dissolve — the first half of solve et coagula; break the fixed into the fluid

source_notes: The Rosarium Philosophorum (c. 1350, attributed to Arnald of Villanova) is famous for its woodcut illustrations (published Frankfurt 1550) showing the alchemical conjunction as an erotic union between Sol (king) and Luna (queen). Jung made these images central to his psychology of alchemy in Mysterium Coniunctionis (1956). The text establishes the symbolic vocabulary of conjunction, dissolution, and rebirth that defines the late medieval alchemical tradition.
bibliography: Rosarium Philosophorum. Frankfurt: Cyriacus Jacobus, 1550. // Jung, C.G. Psychology and Alchemy. Collected Works 12. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1953.

title: Liber de Causis — Prima Causa Super Omnia
title_english: The Book of Causes — The First Cause Surpasses All Things
source: Liber de Causis (from Kitab al-Khair al-Mahd)
author: Anonymous (Arabic, trans. Gerard of Cremona)
date: Arabic c. 9th c.; Latin trans. c. 1187
representative_sentence: Prima causa superior est narratione et non deficit a rebus nisi secundum modum excellentiae, non secundum modum defectus.
latin_text: Prima causa superior est narratione et non deficit a rebus nisi secundum modum excellentiae, non secundum modum defectus. Omnis virtus unitiva fortior est virtute multiplicata, quia virtus una et simplex potentior est quam virtus per multa dispersa. Intelligentia est plena formis, et anima nobilior est corporibus quia causa est eis.
english_gloss: The first cause is above description and falls short of things only in the manner of excellence, not in the manner of deficiency. Every unifying power is stronger than a multiplied power, because a single and simple power is more potent than a power dispersed through many things. The intelligence is full of forms, and the soul is nobler than bodies because it is their cause.

vocabulary.definition: first — the first cause (God/the One) as transcending all predication
excellence — transcendence by excess; the first cause surpasses rather than falls short
unifying — power concentrated in unity is greater than the same power dispersed
intelligence — the second hypostasis after the One; the realm of eternal forms
dispersed, scattered — the weakness of multiplied power versus unified simple power

source_notes: The Liber de Causis (Arabic c. 9th century) is an Arabic adaptation of Proclus's Elements of Theology, translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona c. 1187. Falsely attributed to Aristotle throughout the Middle Ages, it was the primary vehicle for Neoplatonic metaphysics in the Latin West before Ficino's translations. Thomas Aquinas wrote a commentary recognizing its true source. Its account of causation shaped virtually all medieval natural philosophy and magical theory.
bibliography: Taylor, Richard C., trans. The Book of Causes (Liber de Causis). Milwaukee: Marquette University Press, 1984. // Bardenhewer, Otto, ed. Die pseudo-aristotelische Schrift über das reine Gute. Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 1882.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae — Laboratorium et Oratorium
title_english: Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom — Laboratory and Oratory United
author: Heinrich Khunrath
representative_sentence: Laboratorium est oratorium: nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum, frustra laborant qui aedificant eam, et Lapis sine Deo non perficitur.
latin_text: Laboratorium est oratorium: nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum, frustra laborant qui aedificant eam, et Lapis sine Deo non perficitur. Chaos nostrum philosophicum est prima materia ex qua omnia corpora mundi facta sunt, et eadem est materia Lapidis Philosophorum. Qui vult cognoscere Deum, cognoscat prius seipsum, et qui vult perficere Lapidem, perficiat prius animam suam.
english_gloss: The laboratory is an oratory: unless the Lord has built the house, they labor in vain who build it, and the Stone is not perfected without God. Our philosophical chaos is the prime matter from which all bodies of the world are made, and it is the same material as the Philosopher's Stone. He who wishes to know God, let him first know himself, and he who wishes to perfect the Stone, let him first perfect his own soul.

vocabulary.definition: laboratory — the place of alchemical work; Khunrath identifies it with the oratory
oratory, chapel — the place of prayer; for Khunrath, inseparable from the laboratory
chaos — the undifferentiated prima materia; starting point of both creation and alchemical work
is perfected — the Stone requires divine cooperation; Khunrath's Paracelsian-Protestant theology
himself — the Delphic gnoti seauton; self-knowledge as prerequisite for alchemical work

source_notes: Khunrath's Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae (1595, full edition 1609) is the most visually spectacular Hermetic work of the Renaissance, featuring five elaborate engraved plates including the famous Laboratorium-Oratorium in which an alchemist's laboratory opens into a chapel. Khunrath synthesizes Paracelsian alchemy, Lutheran piety, Kabbalah, and Hermeticism. Placed on the Catholic Index. Its central image — the laboratory as sacred space — became definitive for Rosicrucian and Masonic interpretations of alchemy.
bibliography: Khunrath, Heinrich. Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae. Hamburg, 1595; Hanau, 1609. Facsimile reprint: Graz: ADEVA, 1992.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblema III: Vento Ventrem Gestat
title_english: Atalanta Fleeing — Emblem III: The Wind Carries It in Its Womb
author: Michael Maier
representative_sentence: Vento ventrem gestat, terra nutrix eius est — haec est descriptio prima materiae quae ubique in natura latet.
latin_text: Vento ventrem gestat, terra nutrix eius est — haec est descriptio prima materiae quae ubique in natura latet. Sol pater est, luna mater, ventus portavit eam in ventre suo, terra nutrivit eam. Atalanta est argentum vivum fugax, quam Hippomenes aureis pomis decipit; sic anima mineralis per artem philosophicam retinetur et figitur.
english_gloss: The wind carries it in its womb, the earth is its nurse — this is the description of the prime matter which lies hidden everywhere in nature. The sun is its father, the moon its mother, the wind carried it in its womb, the earth nurtured it. Atalanta is the fleeting quicksilver, whom Hippomenes deceives with golden apples; thus the mineral soul is retained and fixed by the philosophical art.

vocabulary.definition: emblem — a combination of motto, image, and poem; Maier's format of 50 alchemical emblems
prime — prima materia: the undifferentiated first matter of alchemical work
silver; argentum vivum (quicksilver) — the fleeting principle that must be fixed
fleeting, fleeing — mercury as volatile principle that eludes the alchemist (Atalanta fleeing)
is fixed — the alchemical operation of fixing the volatile; the goal of the work

source_notes: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (Frankfurt, 1617) is the most artistically ambitious alchemical work ever produced, combining 50 emblems (each with a copper engraving, a Latin motto, an epigram, and a musical fugue) with prose commentaries. Maier, physician to Emperor Rudolf II, reinterpreted Greek mythology as encoded alchemical allegory. Central to Rosicrucian studies. The work is the subject of the AtalantaClaudiens digital humanities project at C:/Dev/Claudiens/.
bibliography: Godwin, Joscelyn, trans. Atalanta Fugiens: An Edition of the Fugues, Emblems and Epigrams. Grand Rapids: Phanes Press, 1989. // Maier, Michael. Atalanta Fugiens. Oppenheim: Johann Theodor de Bry, 1617.

title: Introductio in Geomantiam — De Sedecim Figuris
title_english: Introduction to Geomancy — On the Sixteen Figures and Their Meanings
source: Introductio in Geomantiam (Arabic tradition; trans. 12th c.)
author: Anonymous (trans. from Arabic)
representative_sentence: Geomantia est ars divinandi per puncta in terra vel arena, ex quibus sedecim figurae formantur, quaelibet diversam significationem habens.
latin_text: Geomantia est ars divinandi per puncta in terra vel arena, ex quibus sedecim figurae formantur, quaelibet diversam significationem habens. Prima figura est Via, significans iter et mutationem; secunda est Populus, significans multitudinem. Per has figuras in duodecim domibus dispositas, respondentur quaestiones de rebus occultis et futuris.
english_gloss: Geomancy is the art of divining through points marked in earth or sand, from which sixteen figures are formed, each having a different meaning. The first figure is Via (the Way), signifying journey and change; the second is Populus (the People), signifying a multitude. Through these figures arranged in twelve houses, questions about hidden and future matters are answered.

vocabulary.definition: geomancy — from Greek ge (earth) + manteia (divination); divination by marks in earth or sand
points, dots — random marks made in earth or sand, counted odd/even to generate figures
figures — the sixteen geomantic figures, each a pattern of odd/even points in four rows
houses — the twelve astrological houses into which geomantic figures are arranged
Via (the Way) — one of sixteen figures; four even rows; signifies travel and change

source_notes: Geomancy (Arabic: ilm al-raml, science of the sand) entered Latin Europe through 12th-century translations in Spain, notably by Hugo of Santalla and Gerard of Cremona. It became the most widely practiced form of learned divination in the Latin Middle Ages, used by Albert the Great and Henry of Langenstein. The sixteen geomantic figures map onto astrological and elemental correspondences, arranged in a shield chart to answer questions about past, present, and future.
bibliography: Charmasson, Thérèse. Recherches sur une technique divinatoire: La géomancie dans l'Occident médiéval. Paris: Champion, 1980. // Burnett, Charles. "The Earliest Chiromancy in the West." Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 50 (1987): 189–195.

title: Tabella Defixionis Aquae Sulis — Voces Magicae et Imprecatio
title_english: Curse Tablet from Bath — Barbarous Words and Ritual Imprecation
author: Anonymous (Romano-British)
representative_sentence: Dea Sulis Minerva, tibi dono nomen eius qui involaverit, nec somnum nec sanitatem donet donec ad fanum tuum pertulerit.
latin_text: Dea Sulis Minerva, tibi dono qui involaverit sive servum sive liberum si masculinum si femininum. Nec somnum nec sanitatem ei concedas donec ad fanum tuum pertulerit. ADIXOVI DEIAMVS ANDOSSOCI VOBEDE DELORE. Nomen eius si paganus si Christianus hic scriptum est in plumbo.
english_gloss: Goddess Sulis Minerva, I give you the one who has stolen, whether slave or free, whether male or female. Grant neither sleep nor health until they have brought it to your temple. ADIXOVI DEIAMVS ANDOSSOCI VOBEDE DELORE. Their name, whether pagan or Christian, is written here in lead.

vocabulary.definition: curse tablet — from defigo, to fix/nail down; a written curse inscribed on lead and deposited in sacred water or a tomb
I give, donate — ritual transfer of the target to the deity's jurisdiction for punishment
magical words — strings of foreign, invented, or divine names of uncertain meaning used to summon or coerce divine power
lead — the material of curse tablets; its heaviness and darkness symbolize the desired fate of the target
has stolen — theft was the most common cause for depositing curse tablets at sacred sites

source_notes: Over 130 lead curse tablets have been recovered from the sacred spring of Sulis Minerva at Bath (Aquae Sulis), deposited from the 2nd to 4th centuries CE. They represent the best-preserved collection of Latin curse tablets and include strings of voces magicae — nonsense or foreign syllables of ritual force. The texts reveal ordinary people (not elite practitioners) using written magic for theft recovery, love, and justice. Edited by Roger Tomlin (Tabellae Sulis, 1988). The voces 'ADIXOVI DEIAMVS ANDOSSOCI' may be Celtic, Latin-influenced, or purely invented ritual language.
bibliography: Tomlin, Roger S.O. "The Curse Tablets." In Cunliffe, Barry, ed. The Temple of Sulis Minerva at Bath, Vol. 2: The Finds. Oxford: Oxford University Committee for Archaeology Monograph 16, 1988. Pp. 59–277.

title: De Correctione Rusticorum — Superstitiones et Idolorum Cultus
title_english: On the Correction of Rustics — Superstitions and Idol Worship
author: Martin of Braga
representative_sentence: Omnia quae praeter Dei cultum observantur — auguria, dies, lunas, stellas — haec omnia superstitiones diabolicae sunt.
latin_text: Omnia quae praeter Dei cultum observantur — auguria, dies, lunas, stellas — haec omnia superstitiones diabolicae sunt et daemonum invitamenta. Infelix homo, quid tibi proderit si diem Iovis observes et operas ei des, quem coluerunt Gentiles? Quomodo Christiani ad templum eorum venire possunt et daemones invocare? Haec religio Christiana non habet, nec debet habere.
english_gloss: All things observed apart from the worship of God — auguries, days, moons, stars — all these are diabolical superstitions and invitations to demons. Unhappy man, what will it profit you to observe the day of Jupiter and do work for him, whom the pagans worshipped? How can Christians go to their temples and invoke demons? Christian religion does not have this, nor should it have it.

vocabulary.definition: superstitions — religious practices outside Christianity; the Roman term adopted by the Church for pagan/magical observances
auguries — divination by birds and omens; a Roman practice continuing in Christianized Gaul and Iberia
of demons — Martin identifies all pagan gods and nature-spirits as demons in disguise
of rustics — country people; pastoral care for rural populations who maintained pre-Christian practices
correction — the bishop's pastoral duty to identify and reform sinful practices among laypeople

source_notes: Martin of Braga's De Correctione Rusticorum (c. 572-74 CE), addressed to Bishop Polemius of Astorga, is the earliest comprehensive pastoral guide to combating folk magical practices in the Latin West. Written for rural Galicia (northwest Spain), it identifies day-observances, augury, lunar superstitions, and nature spirits as demonic survivals requiring correction. Together with Caesarius of Arles's sermons, it established the pastoral template for identifying and condemning magical practices that dominated medieval confessional literature.
bibliography: Barlow, Claude W., trans. Iberian Fathers, Vol. 1. Fathers of the Church 62. Washington: Catholic University of America Press, 1969. Pp. 63–85.

title: Decretum X — Corrector et Medicus: Superstitiones Muliebres
title_english: Decretum X — The Corrector: Women's Superstitions and Folk Magic
author: Burchard of Worms
representative_sentence: Fecisti quod quaedam mulieres facere solent — mensam cum cibis et potu tribus cultellis apparatus ut sorores quas Parcas dicunt ibi refici possint?
latin_text: Fecisti quod quaedam mulieres facere solent — mensam cum cibis et potu tribus cultellis apparatus ut sorores quas Parcas dicunt ibi refici possint? Credidisti ut aliquae maleficae sint quae noctu super bestias vel super ligna equitare possint, et in aliquam aliam terram transferri valeant? Fecisti aliquam ligaturam vel aliquam herbam vel aliud maleficium propter amorem vel propter odium?
english_gloss: Have you done what some women are accustomed to do — prepared a table with food and drink and three knives so that the sisters they call Parcae could be refreshed there? Have you believed that there are certain sorceresses who at night can ride on beasts or on wooden poles and be transported to another land? Have you made any ligature or herb-charm or other maleficium for the purpose of love or hatred?

vocabulary.definition: corrector — the confessor whose duty is to identify and correct penitent's sins, including magical ones
Parcae — the three Fates; here surviving pagan belief in fate-goddesses who visit at night; see also Norns
to ride — women riding at night over animals or poles; an early reference to witch-flight
ligature, binding — a charm object (knot, herb bundle, amulet) tied to produce love, hate, or harm
harmful magic — the broad penitential category for magical offenses requiring confession and penance

source_notes: Burchard of Worms's Decretum Book X (the Corrector sive Medicus, c. 1008-12) is the most detailed early medieval penitential catalogue of magical practices. Designed as a confessor's guide, it poses direct questions about specific acts — feeding the Parcae, night-riding, love charms, herb-magic, weather-working — with specified penances for each. It is one of the primary sources for our knowledge of 11th-century folk magical practice in the Latin West and was enormously influential on later confessional literature. Edited and studied by Cyrille Vogel and Regino of Prüm scholarship.
bibliography: McNeill, John T., and Helena M. Gamer, trans. Medieval Handbooks of Penance. New York: Columbia University Press, 1938. // Schmitz, Herman Joseph, ed. Die Bussbücher und das kanonische Bussverfahren. Vol. 2. Düsseldorf: Schwann, 1898.

title: Rituale Romanum — Ordo Exorcizandi Obsessos
title_english: Roman Ritual — The Order for Exorcizing the Possessed
source: Rituale Romanum, Tit. XI, Cap. I
author: Church of Rome (promulgated under Paul V)
representative_sentence: Exorcizo te, omnis immunde spiritus, in nomine Dei Patris omnipotentis, et in nomine Jesu Christi Filii eius, et in virtute Spiritus Sancti.
latin_text: Exorcizo te, omnis immunde spiritus, omnis satanica potestas, omnis incursio infernalis adversarii, omnis legio, omnis congregatio et secta diabolica, in nomine et virtute Domini nostri Jesu Christi: eradicare et effugare ab hoc plasmate Dei. Dic mihi nomen tuum, diem et horam exitus tui. Audi ergo et time, Satana, inimice fidei, hostis generis humani.
english_gloss: I exorcize you, every impure spirit, every satanic power, every incursion of the infernal adversary, every legion, every diabolical congregation and sect, in the name and power of our Lord Jesus Christ: be uprooted and put to flight from this creature of God. Tell me your name, the day and hour of your departure. Hear therefore and fear, Satan, enemy of the faith, enemy of the human race.

vocabulary.definition: I exorcize — from Greek ex + horkizo, to adjure; the authoritative commanding of a demon to depart
impure, unclean — the demon as a source of ritual and moral pollution; contrast with purity requirements
legion — the demonic army (cf. Mark 5:9: 'My name is Legion, for we are many')
creature, what is formed — the possessed body as God's creation being violated by the demon
to uproot — the metaphor of violent extraction; the demon as a weed to be pulled out by the root

source_notes: The Rituale Romanum (1614, under Paul V) codified the Catholic exorcism rite, but the ordo exorcizandi draws on medieval precedents going back to the 4th century (Apostolic Constitutions) and through the medieval Roman Pontifical. Key medieval sources include the Pontifical of Durandus of Mende (c. 1294). The exorcist's demand to know the demon's name reflects the same logic as Solomonic magic: naming compels. The formula 'Exorcizo te, omnis immunde spiritus' remains the opening of the Roman Rite of Exorcism (revised 1999 as De Exorcismis et Supplicationibus Quibusdam).
bibliography: Weller, Philip T., trans. The Roman Ritual. Vol. 2. Milwaukee: Bruce Publishing Co., 1950. // Rituale Romanum, De Exorcismis et Supplicationibus Quibusdam. Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 1999.

title: Sortes Sanctorum — Divinatio per Scripturas
title_english: Holy Lots — Divination by Sacred Scripture
source: Sortes Sanctorum (various manuscript traditions); Council of Vannes (461 CE)
author: Anonymous (conciliar tradition)
representative_sentence: Clerici qui sortes codicibus canonicis divinare praesumpserint, quod nec Christiana religio nec ratio sinit, a communione pellantur.
latin_text: Clerici qui sortes codicibus canonicis — quos vulgo sortes sanctorum vocant — divinare praesumpserint, quod nec Christiana religio nec ratio sinit, a communione pellantur. Haec enim superstitio est aperire librum casualiter et primum versum qui ante oculos apparet pro responso Dei accipere. Augustinus autem dicit: Melius est uti sorte quam ad daemones ire, sed melius est ab omni sorte se abstinere.
english_gloss: Clerics who have presumed to divine by lot from canonical books — which the common people call holy lots — which neither Christian religion nor reason permits, shall be expelled from communion. For this is a superstition: to open a book at random and to take the first verse that appears before one's eyes as God's answer. But Augustine says: It is better to use lots than to go to demons, but it is better still to abstain from all lots.

vocabulary.definition: lots — objects or texts used for random selection in divination; from the same root as 'sorcerer' (sortiarius)
of the saints — the 'holy lots' used scripture or saints' writings as the oracle text
by chance — the random opening of the book is the operative mechanism of the oracle
superstition — improper religious practice; here misuse of Scripture for divination
to abstain — Augustine's reluctant position: better not to use lots at all

source_notes: The Sortes Sanctorum (practiced from at least the 5th century) involved opening a Bible or saint's life at random and reading the first verse as a divine response to a question. The Council of Vannes (461 CE) condemned clerical use of this practice. Despite repeated condemnations, bibliomancy with scripture remained enormously popular throughout the Middle Ages — Rabelais mocks it in the 16th century. Augustine's ambiguous position (sortes are bad but better than demons) meant theologians continued to debate the practice. The related tradition of Sortes Virgilianae used Virgil's Aeneid as oracle-text.
bibliography: Klingshirn, William E. "Defining the Sortes Sanctorum: Gibbon, Du Cange, and Early Christian Lot Divination." Church History 77 (2008): 39–74. // Council of Vannes, Canon XVI. In Mansi, J.D., ed. Sacrorum Conciliorum Nova et Amplissima Collectio. Vol. 7. Florence, 1762.

title: Articuli Condemnati Parisiis 1277 — Magia et Astrologia Prohibita
title_english: Articles Condemned at Paris 1277 — Prohibited Magic and Astrology
source: Syllabus Errorum a Stephano Episcopo Parisiensi Condemnatorum, 1277
author: Étienne Tempier, Bishop of Paris
representative_sentence: Quod per figuras et imagines magicas ad effectus astronomiae pervenitur, quod error est.
latin_text: Quod per figuras et imagines magicas ad effectus astronomiae pervenitur, quod error est. Item, quod experimenta magica non sunt contemnenda. Item, quod daemones compelluntur ad respondendum per characteres et figuras, et hoc non est illicitum. Item, quod astronomia pars est philosophiae quae potest praedicere de voluntate hominis, quod falsum est. Haec omnia erronea sunt et a catholicis magistris reicienda.
english_gloss: That through magical figures and images one arrives at the effects of astronomy — this is an error. Likewise, that magical experiments are not to be condemned. Likewise, that demons are compelled to answer through characters and figures, and this is not illicit. Likewise, that astronomy is a part of philosophy that can predict the human will — this is false. All these are erroneous and to be rejected by Catholic masters.

vocabulary.definition: condemned — the 219 propositions officially prohibited by the Bishop of Paris in 1277
figures — ritual images, diagrams, or characters used in magic; the subject of condemnation
images — astral images/talismans used to channel celestial influence; condemned as illicit
characters — magical letters or symbols used to compel demons; condemned as demonic
to be rejected — the language of official doctrinal condemnation by ecclesiastical authority

source_notes: The Condemnations of 1277 were issued by Étienne Tempier, Bishop of Paris, on March 7, 1277, listing 219 propositions to be condemned as errors. They targeted radical Aristotelianism and included articles on astrology, image magic, and the compulsion of demons through characters. The condemnations were prompted partly by Pope John XXI's concern about astrological determinism and partly by debates about Averroism. Historians debate their effect: they may have stimulated rather than suppressed natural philosophy by forcing theologians to consider divine omnipotence vs natural necessity. The Speculum Astronomiae (attributed to Albertus Magnus) was written partly in response to earlier condemnation threats.
bibliography: Hissette, Roland. Enquête sur les 219 articles condamnés à Paris le 7 mars 1277. Louvain: Publications Universitaires, 1977. // Denifle, Henri, and Emile Chatelain, eds. Chartularium Universitatis Parisiensis. Vol. 1. Paris: Delalain, 1889. Pp. 543–558.

title: Introductiones Apotelesmaticae — Chiromantia
title_english: Apotelesmatic Introductions — Reading Fate in the Human Hand
source: Introductiones Apotelesmaticae in Chyromantiam, Physiognomiam, Astrologiam
author: Johannes ab Indagine (Johann Hagen)
representative_sentence: In manu humana tanquam in libro aperto, qui legere novit, totius vitae humanae seriem — vitam, mortem, amorem, fortunam — legere potest.
latin_text: In manu humana tanquam in libro aperto, qui legere novit, totius vitae humanae seriem legere potest. Linea vitae a pollice usque ad digitum minimum protenditur, et qualis sit haec linea, talis erit vita. Linea mentis ingenium et intellectum ostendit; linea cordis amorem et affectus regit. Ex monte Veneris amor nascitur, ex monte Iovis honor et dignitas.
english_gloss: In the human hand, as in an open book, one who knows how to read can read the entire sequence of human life — life, death, love, fortune. The line of life extends from the thumb to the little finger, and what kind this line is, such will be the life. The line of the mind shows intellect and intelligence; the line of the heart governs love and emotions. From the mount of Venus love is born, from the mount of Jupiter honor and dignity.

vocabulary.definition: chiromancy — from Greek kheir (hand) + manteia (divination); palmistry; reading fate from the lines and mounts of the hand
line of life — the life line running from thumb to wrist, indicating health and lifespan
mount — the fleshy raised areas of the palm, each associated with a planet and its qualities
thumb — the starting point of the life line and a symbol of the will and character
apotelesmatic — concerning effects or outcomes; the technical term for predictive arts including astrology and chiromancy

source_notes: Johannes ab Indagine's Introductiones Apotelesmaticae (Strasbourg, 1522) is the most widely read Latin chiromancy manual of the Renaissance, translated into English, French, German, and Italian. Indagine (1467-1537), a German priest and humanist, systematizes palm-reading with the seven planetary mounts (Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, etc.) and the major lines (life, head, heart, fate). The work went through at least 16 Latin editions. Chiromancy (also spelled cheiromancy) was a legitimate learned divination alongside physiognomy and astrology, practiced by Cardano and described by Agrippa in De Occulta Philosophia.
bibliography: Indagine, Johannes ab. Introductiones Apotelesmaticae in Chyromantiam, Physiognomiam, Astrologiam. Strasbourg: Johannes Schottus, 1522. // English trans.: A Brief Introduction to Chiromancy. London: Thomas Marshe, 1558.

title: De Occulta Philosophia I.15 — De Hydromantia
title_english: On Occult Philosophy I.15 — On Water Divination
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber I, Caput xv
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
representative_sentence: Hydromantia est divinationis genus per aquam, varia in se phantasmata et imagines exprimentem, in quibus futura praedicuntur et absentes cognosci possunt.
latin_text: Hydromantia est divinationis genus per aquam, varia in se phantasmata et imagines exprimentem, in quibus futura praedicuntur et absentes cognosci possunt. Fiebat autem hydromantia olim in basem aqua plena, aut speculo, aut pelvi aliisque vasis quibuscumque — modo aquam intuendo, modo in eam cadere sinendo guttam olei vel cerae. Huc pertinent et divinationes quae fiunt per lacus, fontes sacros, flumina et maris aequora.
english_gloss: Hydromancy is a type of divination by water, expressing in itself various phantasms and images, through which future things are predicted and absent persons can be known. Hydromancy was performed in ancient times in a basin full of water, or in a mirror, or in basins and other vessels of any kind — sometimes by gazing into the water, sometimes by letting a drop of oil or wax fall into it. To this category belong also the divinations that are done by lakes, sacred springs, rivers, and the expanse of the sea.

vocabulary.definition: hydromancy — from Greek hydor (water) + manteia (divination); scrying by water in various forms
phantasms, visions — images seen in the water surface or in mirror-like reflections during scrying
mirror — polished metal or crystal used in scrying; mirror-divination (catoptromancy) is a subtype
basin, bowl — any water-filled vessel can serve for hydromantic scrying
springs, fountains — sacred springs (like Delphi) had long oracular associations; hydromancy preserves this tradition

source_notes: Agrippa's account of hydromancy in De Occulta Philosophia I.15 (1531) synthesizes classical and medieval accounts. He describes multiple forms: lecanomancy (bowl of water), catoptromancy (mirror), and natural spring oracles. The passage is part of Agrippa's comprehensive taxonomy of divinatory arts organized by element (geomancy=earth, pyromancy=fire, aeromancy=air, hydromancy=water). Sacred springs had been oracular sites in the ancient world (Delphi, Dodona), and their Christian successors — healing wells, saints' fountains — often preserved traces of the oracular tradition.
bibliography: Tyson, Donald, ed. Three Books of Occult Philosophy Written by Henry Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim. St. Paul: Llewellyn, 1993.

title: Liber de Nymphis — Spiritus Elementales et Familiari
title_english: Book of the Nymphs — Elemental Spirits and Their Familiar Nature
source: Liber de Nymphis, Sylphis, Pygmaeis et Salamandris et de Caeteris Spiritibus
author: Paracelsus (Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim)
representative_sentence: Quatuor sunt genera spirituum elementalium: nymphae in aqua, sylphi in aere, gnomi in terra, salamandri in igne — nec daemones nec angeli sed creaturae suae naturae.
latin_text: Quatuor sunt genera spirituum elementalium: nymphae in aqua vivunt, sylphi in aere habitant, gnomi in terra morantur, salamandri in igne versantur — nec daemones nec angeli, sed creaturae suae propriae naturae. Hi spiritus hominibus apparere possunt, eos docere artes occultas, et cum illis conversari quasi familiares. Qui unum eorum sibi familiarem efficit, habet ducem in scientiis occultis et interpretem naturae.
english_gloss: There are four kinds of elemental spirits: nymphs live in water, sylphs inhabit the air, gnomes dwell in earth, salamanders move in fire — neither demons nor angels, but creatures of their own proper nature. These spirits can appear to humans, teach them occult arts, and converse with them almost as familiars. He who makes one of them his familiar has a guide in the occult sciences and an interpreter of nature.

vocabulary.definition: nymphs — water elemental beings; Paracelsus's category for undines/water spirits
sylphs — air elemental beings; Paracelsus coined or popularized this term for aerial spirits
gnomes — earth elemental beings; Paracelsus's term for underground spirits (also: pygmies, dwarves)
salamanders — fire elemental beings; the fire-resistant lizard became symbol of the fire spirit
familiars — spirits that serve individual practitioners; from familia (household); the spirit as domestic companion

source_notes: Paracelsus's Liber de Nymphis (c. 1530, published 1566) introduces the doctrine of elemental spirits: four classes of beings inhabiting each element, neither demonic nor angelic but a distinct category of nature-spirit. These beings can become 'familiars' — personal spirit companions who guide practitioners in occult knowledge. Paracelsus's framework became enormously influential: the Rosicrucian Confessio references sylphs and salamanders, Pope invented them in The Rape of the Lock, and the Golden Dawn incorporated the elemental spirit system. The familiar spirit concept here is explicitly naturalized: not a demon pact but a relationship with a created being.
bibliography: Waite, Arthur Edward, trans. The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus. 2 vols. London: James Elliott, 1894. // Sudhoff, Karl, ed. Paracelsus: Sämtliche Werke, I. Abt., Vol. 14. Munich: Oldenbourg, 1933.

title: Clavicula Salomonis — De Characteribus et Sigillis
title_english: The Key of Solomon — On Characters, Seals, and Their Consecration
source: Clavicula Salomonis, Liber II, Caput x
author: Anonymous (attrib. Solomon)
representative_sentence: Sigillum Solomonis est figura stellae sex radiorum, in qua nomina angelorum inscripta sunt, et per quam daemones coguntur ad obedientiam.
latin_text: Sigillum Solomonis est figura stellae sex radiorum ex duobus triangulis composita, in qua nomina Dei et angelorum inscripta sunt, et per quam daemones ad obedientiam coguntur. Characteres autem sunt figurae occultae quae vim suam accipiunt ex potestate divina et ex planetis sub quibus sculpta sunt. Haec sigilla in metallo planetae sui hora et die eius sculpi debent, et aqua, igne, et suffumigationibus consecranda sunt.
english_gloss: The Seal of Solomon is a six-pointed star figure composed of two triangles, on which the names of God and the angels are inscribed, and through which demons are compelled to obedience. Characters are hidden figures which receive their power from divine authority and from the planets under which they are engraved. These seals must be engraved in the metal of their planet at its hour and day, and must be consecrated with water, fire, and suffumigations.

vocabulary.definition: seal — a ritual figure embodying divine or angelic power; engraved on metal for use in conjuration
characters — magical script or symbols; includes both letter-forms and abstract figures with occult force
to be engraved — characters must be physically cut into the metal while the corresponding planet is dominant
to be consecrated — the ritual of dedicating the seal through prayer, incense, and lustration to activate its power
are compelled, forced — the seal's function is compulsory, not merely petitionary; it commands spirits

source_notes: The Clavicula Salomonis (Key of Solomon) dedicates extensive sections to the creation and consecration of 'pentacles' — ritual seals combining divine names, angelic names, astrological symbols, and abstract characters. The text specifies the metal, planetary hour, day, and ritual procedure for each seal. The 72 pentacles of Solomon (in Book II) became among the most copied magical images in the grimoire tradition. The hexagram (Star of David) appears here as a Solomonic magical seal centuries before its adoption as a Jewish religious symbol. Studied by S.L. MacGregor Mathers (1888), Skinner and Rankine (2008).
bibliography: Mathers, S.L. MacGregor, trans. The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis). London: George Redway, 1888. // Skinner, Stephen, and David Rankine. The Veritable Key of Solomon. Singapore: Golden Hoard Press, 2008.

title: Picatrix III — Suffumigationes Planetarum
title_english: Picatrix III — Planetary Suffumigations and Incense Formulas
author: Anonymous (Arabic, attrib. al-Majriti; trans. c. 1256)
representative_sentence: Ad Saturnum pertinent ex suffumigiis: castor, galbasum, asaphoetida, storace; haec fumiga hora Saturni in ascendente, et spiritus Saturni ad te descendet.
latin_text: Ad Saturnum pertinent ex suffumigiis: castor, galbasum, asaphoetida, storace, magnet et nux vetula. Haec fumiga hora Saturni quando in ascendente est, et spiritus Saturni ad te descendet. Ad Solem: thus, mastix, cinnamon, nardus et coronamentum. Ad Lunam: aloe, storax et camphora. Per haec suffumigia stellarum virtutes ad nos descendunt et opera nostra perficiuntur.
english_gloss: For Saturn among suffumigations belong: castor, galbanum, asafoetida, storax, magnet, and old nut. Burn these at Saturn's hour when it is in the ascendant, and the spirit of Saturn will descend to you. For the Sun: frankincense, mastic, cinnamon, nard, and garland. For the Moon: aloe, storax, and camphor. Through these suffumigations of the stars, the virtues of the stars descend to us and our works are perfected.

vocabulary.definition: suffumigations — the burning of incense and aromatic substances to attract planetary spirits; from suffumigo, to fumigate below
castor — beaver musk; a Saturn-associated substance used in Saturnian magical operations
galbanum — a resinous gum with a harsh smell; associated with Saturn's cold, dry, dark qualities
frankincense — the primary Solar suffumigation; associated with the sun's purity and divine presence
in the ascendant — when the planet is rising on the eastern horizon; its most powerful position for magical operation

source_notes: The Picatrix (Latin translation 1256) dedicates Book III to practical astral magic including elaborate planetary suffumigation formulas. Each planet has its associated substances: Saturn (dark, cold things — asafoetida, castor), Sun (bright, noble things — frankincense, gold), Moon (moist things — aloe, camphor). The theory is that the aromatic smoke, composed of substances in sympathy with a given planet, creates a medium through which the planetary spirit can descend. These formulas draw on Arabic, Greek (Hermetic corpus), and ultimately Egyptian temple traditions of divine incense.
bibliography: Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: Miraculum de Theophilo — Pactum cum Diabolo
title_english: The Miracle of Theophilus — The First Diabolical Pact
source: Miraculum S. Mariae de Theophilo (Latin versions after Paul the Deacon)
author: Paul the Deacon (earliest Latin version)
representative_sentence: Theophilus chartulam suae animae diabolici scripti caractere consignavit, abrenuntians Christo et Matri eius, ut dignitatem perditam recuperaret.
latin_text: Theophilus chartulam suae animae diabolici scripti caractere consignavit, abrenuntians Christo et Matri eius, ut dignitatem perditam recuperaret. Et diabolus ei dedit litteras testimonio subscriptas, et statim honore pristino restitutus est. Sed postea compunctus ad imaginem Virginis Mariae confugit, et illa chartula de pectore eius dum dormiret extracta et ei reddita est.
english_gloss: Theophilus sealed a little document of his soul with the character of diabolical writing, renouncing Christ and His Mother, in order to recover the dignity he had lost. And the devil gave him letters confirmed by witness, and immediately he was restored to his former honor. But afterward, struck with remorse, he fled to the image of the Virgin Mary, and that little document was extracted from his chest while he slept and returned to him.

vocabulary.definition: little document — the written pact document; a physically signed contract transferring the soul to the devil
renouncing — the formal verbal renunciation of baptism, Christ, and the saints required in the diabolical pact
character, sign — magical writing used to seal the pact; possibly demonic script
struck with remorse — the moment of contrition that initiates the Virgin's rescue
dignity, office — Theophilus sold his soul to recover a church office; the first Faustian bargain

source_notes: The Theophilus legend (Greek original c. 6th-7th c., Latin translations from 8th c. onward) is the archetype of the Faustian demonic pact narrative: a church official sells his soul in writing to the devil to regain lost office, then is rescued by Mary's intervention. The story was extraordinarily popular throughout the Middle Ages — Hroswitha of Gandersheim dramatized it, Rutebeuf wrote a French play about it, and it appears in the Golden Legend. The written pact (chartula) with the devil prefigures the formal pact theology of the witch trials and the later Faust legend. The Virgin's retrieval of the document from Theophilus's chest became a standard Marian miracle.
bibliography: Ward, Benedicta. Miracles and the Medieval Mind: Theory, Record and Event, 1000–1215. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1982. // Paulus Diaconus. Homiliarius. In Patrologia Latina 95, cols. 1159–1566.

title: Epistulae Morales — De Magis
title_english: Moral Letters — On Magicians
source: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, Epistula CVIII
author: Lucius Annaeus Seneca
representative_sentence: Non debes his credere qui magos evocant et umbras inferorum in cenam invitant.
latin_text: Non debes his credere qui magos evocant et umbras inferorum in cenam invitant. Non sunt ista miracula, sed praestigiae.
english_gloss: You should not believe those who summon magicians and invite the shades of the dead to dinner. These are not miracles, but tricks.

vocabulary.definition: magus — practitioner of magic arts; in Roman usage, a term of suspicion often applied to Persian-derived divination and necromantic practices
praestigiae — conjuring tricks, illusions; Seneca's rationalist dismissal of magical performance as mere deception

source_notes: Seneca's Epistulae Morales (c. 65 CE) contain multiple passages dismissing magical practices as superstition incompatible with Stoic philosophy. This dismissal illustrates the elite Roman sceptical tradition that ran alongside widespread belief in magic. Seneca distinguishes vera philosophia from the credulity of those who consult magi, a term covering both Persian-derived astrologers and local wonder-workers.
bibliography: Seneca, Lucius Annaeus. Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium. Ed. L.D. Reynolds. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1965.

title: Annales — De Mathematicis
title_english: Annals — On Astrologers
author: Publius Cornelius Tacitus
representative_sentence: Mathematici quoque et harioli pellebantur Italia, genus hominum potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax.
latin_text: Mathematici quoque et harioli pellebantur Italia, genus hominum potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax.
english_gloss: Astrologers and soothsayers too were expelled from Italy, a class of men untrustworthy to the powerful and deceitful to those who hope.

vocabulary.definition: mathematicus — astrologer; in Roman imperial usage specifically those who cast horoscopes and predict futures, repeatedly subject to senatorial expulsion
hariolus — soothsayer, diviner; practitioner of informal prediction, often associated with low-status or foreign religious practices

source_notes: Tacitus records repeated imperial expulsions of astrologers (mathematici) from Rome under Tiberius, Claudius, Vitellius, and Domitian. These expulsions reveal the political danger of predictive arts in a monarchical context: knowing the emperor's future implied plotting against him. The phrase 'genus hominum potentibus infidum' became a standard formulation in later medieval discussions of why divination was politically threatening.
bibliography: Tacitus. Annales. Ed. C.D. Fisher. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1906.

title: Divus Tiberius — De Mathematicis
title_english: Life of Tiberius — On Astrologers
author: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus
representative_sentence: Mathematicos Italia summovit, deprecantibus et in posterum emendaturos se promittentibus veniam dedit.
latin_text: Mathematicos Italia summovit, deprecantibus et in posterum emendaturos se promittentibus veniam dedit.
english_gloss: He expelled astrologers from Italy, but granted pardon to those who begged forgiveness and promised to reform in the future.

vocabulary.definition: summovere — to drive away, expel; the technical term for official Roman expulsion orders against diviners and foreign religious practitioners
deprecari — to beg off, to plead for exemption; the legal mechanism by which expelled practitioners could petition for readmission

source_notes: Suetonius's biography of Tiberius documents the expulsion of astrologers from Italy as part of a broader campaign against foreign cults and divinatory practices. The expulsion was not absolute: practitioners could plead for reinstatement by promising reform, revealing that the Roman state sought to control rather than eliminate divination. Suetonius is a key source for understanding how imperial Rome treated magical and divinatory practitioners legally.
bibliography: Suetonius. De Vita Caesarum. Ed. M. Ihm. Leipzig: Teubner, 1908.

title: Eclogae — Pharmaceutria
title_english: Eclogues — The Sorceress
author: Publius Vergilius Maro
representative_sentence: Ducite ab urbe domum, mea carmina, ducite Daphnin.
latin_text: Ducite ab urbe domum, mea carmina, ducite Daphnin. Limus ut hic durescit, et haec ut cera liquescit, uno eodemque igni.
english_gloss: Lead Daphnis home from the city, my incantations, lead him home. As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts, in one and the same fire.

vocabulary.definition: carmen — incantation, charm; the Latin word for both poetry and magical spell, capturing the ancient unity of rhythmic language and operative power
limus — ritual clay; used in binding spells (defixiones) alongside wax images to represent and compel the target

source_notes: Eclogue VIII contains Vergil's Pharmaceutria ('sorceress'), modeled on Theocritus's Idyll II and describing a binding love spell with alternating clay and wax figures. The refrain 'ducite ab urbe domum' is the oldest surviving Latin example of the iterative binding formula. The passage was central to medieval and Renaissance debates about whether Roman poets had knowledge of real magical techniques or were merely imitating Greek literary conventions.
bibliography: Virgil. Opera. Ed. R.A.B. Mynors. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1969.

title: Aeneis — Descensus ad Inferos
title_english: Aeneid — Descent to the Underworld
author: Publius Vergilius Maro
representative_sentence: Di, quibus imperium est animarum, umbraeque silentes, et Chaos et Phlegethon.
latin_text: Di, quibus imperium est animarum, umbraeque silentes, et Chaos et Phlegethon, loca nocte tacentia late, sit mihi fas audita loqui.
english_gloss: Gods, who hold dominion over souls, and you silent shades, and Chaos and Phlegethon, places silent with wide night — may it be permitted me to speak of what I have heard.

vocabulary.definition: umbra — shade, ghost; the Latin term for the soul of the dead summoned in necromantic practice, equivalent to Greek psyche in underworld contexts
fas — divine permission, sacred lawfulness; the invocation marks the narrator's speech as ritually authorized, a formula replicated in later conjuration literature

source_notes: Aeneid VI is the most influential underworld narrative in Western literature. The Sibyl's invocation formula before the descent provided a template for later Latin necromantic literature. Medieval writers read the Aeneid's katabasis as an encoded account of actual divinatory or necromantic practice; Servius's commentary and later Christian allegorizations both grappled with the ritual-seeming detail. The influence runs through Dante's Inferno and Renaissance interest in underworld descent as theurgical metaphor.
bibliography: Virgil. Opera. Ed. R.A.B. Mynors. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1969.

title: Epodi — Canidia
title_english: Epodes — Canidia's Rite
author: Quintus Horatius Flaccus
representative_sentence: Quae saga, quis te solvere Thessalis magus venenis, quis poterit deus?
latin_text: At o deorum quidquid in caelo regit terras et humanum genus, o sol qui currus nitedum temperas anteire noctis, ibo reditum nusquam habiturus ad domos.
english_gloss: O you who are whatever rules the heavens, the earth and the human race, O sun who guides your chariot gleaming before the night, I shall go and never return to these homes.

vocabulary.definition: saga — witch, wise woman; the Latin term for a female practitioner of magic, related to sagire (to perceive acutely), suggesting augury and herb-knowledge
Thessalis — Thessalian; proverbially the homeland of powerful witches in Graeco-Roman literature, especially associated with moon-drawing and herb-magic

source_notes: Horace's Epodes feature the witch Canidia in several poems (Epodes III, V, XVII), making her the most developed witch-figure in Latin poetry alongside Vergil's Pharmaceutria. Canidia appears as a veneficia (poison-witch) who performs nocturnal rites involving human sacrifice, wax images, and herb-gathering. Scholars debate whether Canidia is a real person satirized or a literary construct; John G. Griffiths argued for real-person satirical intent.
bibliography: Horace. Opera. Ed. D.R. Shackleton Bailey. Stuttgart: Teubner, 1985.

title: Elegiae — De Saga
title_english: Elegies — On the Wise Woman
author: Albius Tibullus
representative_sentence: Hanc ego de caelo ducentem sidera vidi, fluminaque occulto permutantem alveo cursu.
latin_text: Hanc ego de caelo ducentem sidera vidi, fluminaque occulto permutantem alveo cursu.
english_gloss: I have seen her drawing down stars from the sky, and reversing the course of rivers in their hidden channel.

vocabulary.definition: ducere sidera — drawing down the stars; a stock image of the powerful witch in Latin poetry, referring to moon-drawing rituals associated with Thessalian magic
flumen — river; the reversal of rivers was a proverbial demonstration of supreme magical power in ancient literature

source_notes: Tibullus's first book of elegies (c. 26 BCE) includes a portrait of a saga (wise woman) who performs traditional Latin magical services: love-magic, healing, and star-drawing. The description follows the conventional inventory of witch-powers found also in Horace and Vergil and directly influenced later catalogues of magical abilities in medieval demonological literature. Tibullus differs from Horace in presenting the saga as primarily a service-provider for the lover rather than a threatening figure.
bibliography: Tibullus. Elegiae. Ed. G. Luck. Stuttgart: Teubner, 1988.

title: Amores — Dipsas Lena
title_english: Amores — Dipsas the Procuress
author: Publius Ovidius Naso
representative_sentence: Illa magas artes Aeaeaque carmina novit, inque caput liquidas arte recurvat aquas.
latin_text: Illa magas artes Aeaeaque carmina novit, inque caput liquidas arte recurvat aquas.
english_gloss: She knows the arts of the mage and the spells of Aeaea, and by skill turns the flowing waters back to their source.

vocabulary.definition: Aeaeaque carmina — the spells of Aeaea; reference to Circe's island, marking the procuress-witch as heir to the most powerful magical tradition of Greek mythology
recurvat aquas — turns back the waters; like Tibullus's river-reversal, a stock proof of supreme magical competence in Roman literary portrayals of witches

source_notes: Ovid's portrait of the lena (procuress) Dipsas in Amores I.8 combines the comic figure of the interfering old woman with the threatening attributes of the witch: Circean knowledge, star-drawing, and herb-lore. This fusion of the domestic witch with elite mythological magical traditions is characteristic of Ovid's ironic handling of erotic magic and influenced later literary witches including those of Lucan and Apuleius.
bibliography: Ovid. Amores. Ed. E.J. Kenney. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994.

title: Pharsalia — Erictho Thessala
title_english: Civil War — Thessalian Herbs
author: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus
representative_sentence: Haec sibi, non superis, iuris natura relinquit, nudos ferre greges, haec in dente tenere.
latin_text: Haec sibi, non superis, iuris natura relinquit, nudos ferre greges, haec in dente tenere. Dissimilis cunctis, Erictho fuit.
english_gloss: Nature has left the right to these things to herself, not to the gods above — to carry naked herds, to hold these things in the tooth. Unlike all others, Erictho was.

vocabulary.definition: Erictho — the Thessalian witch of Pharsalia VI; Lucan's most extreme literary witch, who inhabits tombs and reanimates corpses, influencing all later literary necromancers
superi — the gods above; Erictho's power is contrasted with divine authority, presenting the witch as operating in a domain of nature outside divine jurisdiction

source_notes: Lucan's Pharsalia VI (c. 65 CE) contains the most extensive ancient literary treatment of necromancy, centered on the witch Erictho who reanimates a corpse to prophesy Pompey's fate at Pharsalus. Lucan's Erictho is deliberately transgressive: she inhabits graves, mutilates corpses, and compels even the gods. Frederick Ahl and Sarah Johnston have analyzed how the scene subverts Roman religious norms. The passage was a key literary source for medieval necromantic imagination.
bibliography: Lucan. Bellum Civile. Ed. D.R. Shackleton Bailey. Stuttgart: Teubner, 1988.

title: Naturalis Historia — Origo Magiae
title_english: Natural History — Origin of Magic
author: Gaius Plinius Secundus
representative_sentence: Magia, ut arbitror, orta in Perside a Zoroastre; id satis constat, sed unum an et alium fuisse eo nomine, inter auctores non convenit.
latin_text: Magia, ut arbitror, orta in Perside a Zoroastre; id satis constat, sed unum an et alium fuisse eo nomine, inter auctores non convenit.
english_gloss: Magic, as I believe, originated in Persia from Zoroaster; that much is agreed, but whether there was one or another of that name, scholars do not agree.

vocabulary.definition: magia — the art of magic; in Pliny the term is explicitly associated with Persian origins (via Zoroaster), a genealogy that influenced all subsequent Western accounts of magic's origins
Zoroaster — the Persian founder of magic in ancient Western tradition; Pliny's attribution made Zoroaster a standard figure in learned discussions of magic's origins through the Renaissance

source_notes: Pliny's Natural History Book XXX opens with a historical survey of magic that became one of the most influential ancient texts for the history of magic. His attribution of magic's origins to Zoroaster (citing also Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato) shaped Renaissance accounts of prisca magia. The same chapter lists Roman senatorial decrees against magic and argues for magic's fraudulent character while simultaneously recording hundreds of magical remedies throughout the work.
bibliography: Pliny the Elder. Naturalis Historia. Ed. L. Jan and C. Mayhoff. Leipzig: Teubner, 1892–1909.

title: Naturalis Historia — De Ligaturis
title_english: Natural History — On Amulets and Ligatures
author: Gaius Plinius Secundus
representative_sentence: Ligaturis quoque et quibusdam remediis similibus oculis obstare et efficere multa credimus.
latin_text: Ligaturis quoque et quibusdam remediis similibus oculis obstare et efficere multa credimus.
english_gloss: We believe that amulets and certain similar remedies can block the eyes and accomplish many things.

vocabulary.definition: ligatura — amulet, binding; physical objects tied or fastened to the body for protective or operative magical purposes; the term was adopted in medieval medical-magical discourse
obstare oculis — to block the eyes; protection against the evil eye (fascinatio), one of the most widely attested magical concerns in ancient and medieval medicine

source_notes: Pliny's Natural History is the single most important ancient source for Roman magical practices, recording amulet use, incantations, and sympathetic procedures throughout Books XXVIII–XXX. His ambivalent position — recording magical remedies while theoretically dismissing magic as fraud — shaped how medieval encyclopedists like Isidore of Seville and Bartholomaeus Anglicus handled magical material: preserving it as natural knowledge while condemning its religious dimensions.
bibliography: Pliny the Elder. Naturalis Historia. Ed. L. Jan and C. Mayhoff. Leipzig: Teubner, 1892–1909.

title: Naturalis Historia — De Fascino
title_english: Natural History — On the Evil Eye
author: Gaius Plinius Secundus
representative_sentence: Esse homines eiusdem generis in Africa, familias quasdam effascinantium, quorum laudatione intereant prata.
latin_text: Esse homines eiusdem generis in Africa, familias quasdam effascinantium, quorum laudatione intereant prata, arescant arbores, emoriantur infantes.
english_gloss: There are people of this kind in Africa, certain families of those who fascinate by the evil eye, at whose praise meadows perish, trees wither, and infants die.

vocabulary.definition: effascinare — to bewitch by the evil eye; the strongest form of fascination in ancient belief, capable of killing through praise alone
fascinum — the evil eye, also the protective phallic amulet against it; one of the most universal and well-attested magical beliefs in ancient Mediterranean culture

source_notes: The evil eye (fascinum, fascination) was one of the most universal beliefs in ancient magic, attested across Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, and North African sources. Pliny locates particularly powerful evil-eye families in Africa, a trope repeated in later ethnographic-magical literature. The belief that praise could harm — invidia or 'envy' — connected the evil eye to social tensions around wealth, beauty, and livestock; Matthew Dickie has analyzed evil-eye belief as a social-regulation mechanism.
bibliography: Pliny the Elder. Naturalis Historia. Ed. L. Jan and C. Mayhoff. Leipzig: Teubner, 1892–1909.

title: Naturalis Historia — De Verbis
title_english: Natural History — On the Power of Words
author: Gaius Plinius Secundus
representative_sentence: Iam ipsa verba incantationesque efficaces putamus, quaeque Cato docuit in luxationibus subveniendis.
latin_text: Iam ipsa verba incantationesque efficaces putamus, quaeque Cato docuit in luxationibus subveniendis.
english_gloss: We now believe that words and incantations themselves are efficacious, and those which Cato taught for treating dislocations.

vocabulary.definition: incantatio — incantation, verbal charm; etymologically 'singing into/over,' referring to the operative use of rhythmic speech over a patient, object, or procedure
luxatio — dislocation; Pliny's reference to Cato's healing charm for dislocations (De Agri Cultura 160) is the earliest attestation of a Latin incantatory text in a medical context

source_notes: Pliny's observation that 'words and incantations are efficacious' is significant precisely because he is a rationalist sceptic elsewhere critical of magic. His acknowledgment of verbal charm efficacy, with a reference to Cato's agricultural healing charm, reflects the impossibility of fully separating Roman medicine from magical practice. This passage was cited by later theorists of voces magicae and by scholastic writers debating whether words have inherent power.
bibliography: Pliny the Elder. Naturalis Historia. Ed. L. Jan and C. Mayhoff. Leipzig: Teubner, 1892–1909.

title: De Agri Cultura — Carmen Luxationi
title_english: On Farming — Charm for Dislocation
author: Marcus Porcius Cato
representative_sentence: Luxum siquid est, hac cantione sanum fiet: huat hauat huat ista pista sista damia bodannaustra.
latin_text: Luxum siquid est, hac cantione sanum fiet: huat hauat huat ista pista sista damia bodannaustra.
english_gloss: If there is any dislocation, it will be healed by this incantation: huat hauat huat ista pista sista damia bodannaustra.

vocabulary.definition: cantio — incantation, singing-charm; the earliest Latin term for an operative verbal formula, predating carmen in technical magical usage

huat hauat huat — a nonsense or archaic incantatory sequence; representative of voces magicae — meaningless syllables whose power derives from sound, repetition, and ritual context rather than semantic content

source_notes: Cato's healing charm in De Agri Cultura (c. 160 BCE) is the oldest surviving Latin incantatory text. It consists of a nonsense syllable sequence repeated over the injured body part during specific manual manipulations. The text is a key witness for pre-literary Latin folk healing practice and for the Roman use of voces magicae (meaningless operative syllables) alongside more intelligible charms. Pliny cited it as proof that Romans of an earlier age believed in verbal magic.
bibliography: Cato. De Agri Cultura. Ed. A. Mazzarino. Leipzig: Teubner, 1982.

title: De Divinatione — Definitio
title_english: On Divination — Definition
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
representative_sentence: Est profecto quiddam etiam si qua de re controversia est, quod certo scimus: et in somnio et in ostento et in oraculo aut futura praedicuntur aut, dum fiunt, ostenduntur.
latin_text: Est profecto quiddam, etiam si qua de re controversia est: in somnio et in ostento et in oraculo aut futura praedicuntur aut, dum fiunt, ostenduntur.
english_gloss: There is surely something, even if on the matter there is controversy: in dream, in omen, and in oracle, either future things are predicted or, while they are happening, they are shown.

vocabulary.definition: ostentum — omen, portent; a divinely significant occurrence that reveals the future through unusual natural events; one of the main categories of Roman divinatory practice
oraculum — oracle; prophetic utterance at a sacred site; Cicero analyzes oracular divination alongside dream-interpretation and augury in the first systematic ancient treatise on divination

source_notes: Cicero's De Divinatione (44 BCE) is the most important ancient philosophical treatment of divination, presenting both a Stoic defense (Book I, via his brother Quintus) and a sceptical Academic critique (Book II, Cicero's own voice). The work provides the fullest ancient taxonomy of divinatory methods and the most sophisticated ancient philosophical debate about whether foreknowledge is possible. It was central to medieval and Renaissance discussions of licit and illicit divination.
bibliography: Cicero. De Divinatione. Ed. W. Ax. Leipzig: Teubner, 1938.

title: Apologia — Quid Est Magus
title_english: Defense Speech — What Is a Magician
author: Lucius Apuleius
representative_sentence: Magus est qui communione loquendi cum dis immortalibus ad omnia quae velit incredibili quadam vi cantaminum polleat.
latin_text: Magus est qui communione loquendi cum dis immortalibus ad omnia quae velit incredibili quadam vi cantaminum polleat.
english_gloss: A magician is one who through communion of speech with the immortal gods is powerful in all that he wishes by the incredible force of incantations.

vocabulary.definition: communio loquendi — communion of speech; Apuleius's definition of the magician's power as resting on an intimate verbal relationship with the gods, anticipating later theurgical theory
cantamen — incantation, verbal charm; a rare intensive form emphasizing the power-laden quality of the magician's speech

source_notes: Apuleius was tried for magical practices at Sabratha (North Africa) c. 158–159 CE after marrying a wealthy widow; the Apologia is his court speech defending himself. His definition of a magician as one who speaks with the gods through incantations represents a rationalized, philosophically respectable version of magic: the legitimate magus as Platonic sage rather than criminal operator. The speech is a critical document for understanding how Roman intellectuals navigated the tension between philosophical theurgy and legal proscription of magic.
bibliography: Apuleius. Apologia. Ed. R. Helm. Leipzig: Teubner, 1905.

title: Papyri Graecae Magicae — Agoge
title_english: Greek Magical Papyri — Love-Drawing Spell
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Veni ad me, NN, quam peperit NN, nunc, cito, cito, festina, festina.
latin_text: Veni ad me, NN, quam peperit NN, nunc, cito, cito, festina, festina.
english_gloss: Come to me, NN (name of the desired person), whom NN (name of her mother) bore, now, quickly, quickly, hasten, hasten.

vocabulary.definition: NN — the magical blank for the operator's insertion of real names; a convention in papyrological spell texts marking where personal names are written, preserving the spell as a transferable template
festina — hasten; the doubling 'festina, festina' is an urgency formula that recurs throughout ancient and medieval love spells, commanding the supernatural agent to act immediately

source_notes: The Greek Magical Papyri (PGM), a collection of Egyptian-Greek-Roman magical texts from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE, are the richest surviving source for ancient operative magic. The agoge (leading-away spell) is one of the most common PGM spell types, designed to compel a desired person to come to the practitioner. The NN convention — placeholders for personal names — shows these were template spells for professional copyist-magicians. Hans Dieter Betz's translation made the PGM accessible to scholars of ancient religion and magic.
bibliography: Betz, Hans Dieter, ed. The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1986.

title: Papyri Graecae Magicae — Voces Magicae
title_english: Greek Magical Papyri — Magical Words
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: ABERAMENTHOOULERTHEXANAXETHRELLUOOTHNEMAREBA.
latin_text: ABERAMENTHOOULERTHEXANAXETHRELLUOOTHNEMAREBA.
english_gloss: [Untranslatable voces magicae sequence; operative by sound and divine name, not by semantic meaning.]

vocabulary.definition: voces magicae — magical words; untranslatable sequences of Greek, Coptic, Semitic, and invented syllables used as names or invocations of supernatural powers throughout the PGM
voces magicae — an unanalyzable syllable chain; the palindromic and repetitive structure of such sequences suggests they were understood as resonating with divine nature rather than human language

source_notes: Voces magicae (magical words) are one of the most distinctive features of the PGM and of ancient magical practice generally. These unanalyzable sequences combine elements of Greek, Coptic, Hebrew, Aramaic, and invented syllables, often in palindromic or anagrammatic arrangements. Their operative power was understood as residing in sound-resemblance to divine names or in the specific resonant frequencies of certain syllable combinations. The category of voces magicae was discussed by Origen, Porphyry, and Iamblichus, all of whom debated whether divine names could be translated.
bibliography: Betz, Hans Dieter, ed. The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1986.

title: Tabella Defixionis — Aquae Sulis
title_english: Curse Tablet — Bath (Aquae Sulis)
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Qui mihi Vilbiam involavit ita liquescas ut aqua, sive Vinna sive Exsupereus sive Verianus sive Severianus.
latin_text: Qui mihi Vilbiam involavit ita liquescas ut aqua, sive Vinna sive Exsupereus sive Verianus sive Severianus.
english_gloss: Whoever has stolen my Vilbia from me, may they melt like water, whether Vinna or Exsupereus or Verianus or Severianus.

vocabulary.definition: involare — to steal, fly off with; the legal-criminal vocabulary of theft adapted to ritual cursing, common in British curse tablets directed to the goddess Sulis
liquescas — may you melt, dissolve; a standard imprecatory formula directing the curse's physical destructive effect to the body of the unknown thief

source_notes: The curse tablets from the sacred spring at Bath (Aquae Sulis) are among the best-preserved examples of Romano-British magic, with over a hundred lead tablets consigning thieves to the goddess Sulis Minerva for punishment. They provide evidence for the social function of binding magic: petitioning a deity to enforce justice in cases where legal remedies were unavailable. R.S.O. Tomlin's edition and John G. Gager's collection contextualise these tablets within the broader Mediterranean tradition of defixio.
