bibliography: Tomlin, R.S.O. Tabellae Sulis: Roman Inscribed Tablets of Tin and Lead from the Sacred Spring at Bath. Oxford: Oxford University Committee for Archaeology, 1988.

title: Tabella Defixionis — Uley
title_english: Curse Tablet — Uley (Mercury Shrine)
source: The Temple of Mercury at Uley, Gloucestershire, tablet no. 2 (Woodward and Leach ed.)
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Deo Mercurio Silvano Cenacvs quod involavit mihi Vitalinus et Natalinus filius eius bovem.
latin_text: Deo Mercurio Silvano Cenacvs quod involavit mihi Vitalinus et Natalinus filius eius bovem.
english_gloss: To the god Mercury: Cenacvs [dedicates] what Vitalinus and Natalinus his son stole from me, an ox.

vocabulary.definition: deus Mercurius — the god Mercury; the addressee of the curse as divine judge and enforcer of justice, functioning as a supernatural magistrate in cases of theft where human law could not reach
bovem — ox; livestock theft was one of the most common reasons for commissioning a curse tablet, revealing that magical petitions to the gods served practical legal and economic functions

source_notes: The Uley Mercury shrine (Gloucestershire) produced a significant collection of curse tablets addressed to Mercury, the Roman god associated with communication, contracts, and crossing boundaries. Unlike the Bath tablets directed to Sulis Minerva, the Uley tablets reveal Mercury functioning as a god of justice and retribution. Woodward and Leach's excavation report documents the tablets in their archaeological context, and Roger Tomlin has edited the inscriptions. The tablets are valuable evidence for non-elite Roman religious practice in Britain.
bibliography: Woodward, Ann, and Peter Leach. The Uley Shrines: Excavation of a Ritual Complex on West Hill, Uley, Gloucestershire 1977–1979. London: English Heritage, 1993.

title: De Spectaculis — De Daemonibus
title_english: On Spectacles — On Demons
author: Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus
representative_sentence: Nec mirum de operibus diaboli si magnalia divina imitando simulat.
latin_text: Nec mirum de operibus diaboli si magnalia divina imitando simulat. Quid ergo de magis loquar, qui omnem artem ad hoc servant, ut homines deliniant?
english_gloss: Nor is it surprising that the devil, imitating divine great deeds, simulates them. What then shall I say about magicians, who keep all their art for this, to beguile men?

vocabulary.definition: diabolus — the Devil; Tertullian was instrumental in establishing the Christian theological framework in which all magical operations are attributed to demonic agency, a doctrine that shaped demonology for over a millennium
delinire — to beguile, cajole, soften; Tertullian frames magic as diabolical deception designed to lead humans away from truth, not as an operation with real supernatural efficacy

source_notes: Tertullian (c. 155–220 CE) was among the most influential early Christian writers on magic and demonology. De Spectaculis argues against Christian attendance at Roman games on the grounds that they are venues of demonic activity. His characterization of magic as diabolical simulation of divine miracles established the basic Christian demonological framework: all magical power derives from demons, not from nature or human skill. This framework governed Christian discussions of magic from Augustine through the Malleus Maleficarum.
bibliography: Tertullian. De Spectaculis. Ed. E. Dekkers. CCSL 1. Turnhout: Brepols, 1954.

title: Contra Celsum — De Nominibus
title_english: Against Celsus — On Sacred Names
author: Origenes Adamantius
representative_sentence: Nominum virtus in his est quibus resonant, non in his qui ea interpretantur in aliam linguam.
latin_text: Nominum virtus in his est quibus resonant, non in his qui ea interpretantur in aliam linguam.
english_gloss: The power of names lies in those through whom they resonate, not in those who translate them into another language.

vocabulary.definition: virtus nominis — the power of a name; Origen's argument that divine names have power intrinsic to their sound-form, not their semantic meaning, is the earliest systematic philosophical account of why voces magicae work

resonare — to resonate, re-sound; the resonance metaphor captures the ancient view that certain syllables vibrate in sympathy with divine natures, a theory developed by Iamblichus and later Neoplatonists

source_notes: Origen's Contra Celsum (c. 248 CE) includes a systematic discussion of why the names of gods and angels have power that cannot survive translation, a position he argues against the pagan critic Celsus who had dismissed Christian and Jewish use of divine names as barbaric superstition. Origen's defense of untranslatable sacred names became foundational for later kabbalistic and magical use of Hebrew divine names in both Jewish and Christian contexts. The passage was cited in Renaissance discussions of name-magic by Ficino, Pico, and Agrippa.
bibliography: Origen. Contra Celsum. Ed. M. Borret. SC 132, 136, 147, 150. Paris: Cerf, 1967–1969.

title: De Doctrina Christiana — De Superstitione
title_english: On Christian Doctrine — On Superstition
author: Aurelius Augustinus
representative_sentence: Omnia etiam ligamenta atque remedia quae condemnat medicina, vel in praecantationibus, vel in quibusdam notis quae characteres vocantur, superstitionis esse noveris.
latin_text: Omnia etiam ligamenta atque remedia quae condemnat medicina, vel in praecantationibus, vel in quibusdam notis quae characteres vocantur, superstitionis esse noveris.
english_gloss: You should know that all amulets and remedies which medicine condemns — whether in incantations, or in certain marks which are called characters — are to be counted as superstition.

vocabulary.definition: ligamentum — amulet, ligature; Augustine's condemnation of ligamenta encompasses both physical amulets and written charms, establishing a broad category of forbidden operative magic in Christian practice

character — magical character, sign; untranslatable symbols used in magical practice; Augustine's condemnation of characteres was the basis for later medieval prohibitions on magical alphabets and seals

source_notes: Augustine's De Doctrina Christiana (c. 397–426 CE) contains the most systematic and influential early Christian analysis of superstitio, the category into which he placed all magical practices. His definition in Book II became the standard reference for medieval canon lawyers and theologians classifying magic. The passage condemns not only ritual magic but any use of written characters (magical symbols), ligatures, and incantations beyond those approved by the Church, a condemnation that shaped Burchard of Worms, Gratian, and Thomas Aquinas.
bibliography: Augustine. De Doctrina Christiana. Ed. J. Martin. CCSL 32. Turnhout: Brepols, 1962.

title: De Civitate Dei — De Theurgia
title_english: City of God — On Theurgy
author: Aurelius Augustinus
representative_sentence: Theurgici qui etiam per artes, quas theurgian dicunt, nonnullos angelorum daemonumque conspectus adepti esse perhibentur.
latin_text: Theurgici qui etiam per artes, quas theurgian dicunt, nonnullos angelorum daemonumque conspectus adepti esse perhibentur.
english_gloss: The theurgists, who even through arts which they call theurgy, are said to have obtained visions of certain angels and demons.

vocabulary.definition: theurgia — theurgy; from Greek theos (god) + ergon (work), the Neoplatonic term for ritual operations aimed at ascending to the divine; Augustine distinguishes it from theology while acknowledging its power

daemon — demon; in Neoplatonism, intermediate spirits between gods and humans; Augustine's equation of theurgical daemons with the Christian Devil was pivotal in making Neoplatonic theurgy theologically suspect

source_notes: Book X of De Civitate Dei is Augustine's sustained engagement with Neoplatonic theurgy, primarily Porphyry's position on the soul's ascent through ritual. Augustine acknowledges that theurgists claim real contact with angels and daemons while arguing that these contacts are with demons (in the Christian sense) who impersonate higher beings. His critique shaped all subsequent Christian engagement with Neoplatonic and Hermetic traditions, and was the lens through which medieval scholars read Iamblichus and Proclus.
bibliography: Augustine. De Civitate Dei. Ed. B. Dombart and A. Kalb. CCSL 47–48. Turnhout: Brepols, 1955.

title: Matheseos Libri — De Saturno Malefico
title_english: Books of Mathesis — On Malefic Saturn
author: Iulius Firmicus Maternus
representative_sentence: Saturnus maleficus frigida vi, summa tarditate, tristissima aspectus condicione, in natalibus hominum diversa genera multis casibus incommoda importat.
latin_text: Saturnus maleficus frigida vi, summa tarditate, tristissima aspectus condicione, in natalibus hominum diversa genera multis casibus incommoda importat.
english_gloss: Saturn, malefic by cold power, extreme slowness, and the most sorrowful condition of aspect, brings various kinds of misfortune in many cases to human nativities.

vocabulary.definition: maleficus — malefic planet; the technical astrological term for planets that bring harm in a natal chart; Saturn and Mars were the two primary malefics in ancient and medieval astrology
nativitas — nativity, birth chart; the astrological horoscope cast for the moment of birth, the primary instrument of astrological prediction in ancient and medieval practice

source_notes: Firmicus Maternus's Matheseos Libri (c. 334–337 CE) is the most complete surviving ancient Latin astrological textbook and the major source for astrological doctrine in the West until the Arabic translations of the 12th century. His detailed treatment of planetary characters — benefic Jupiter and Venus versus malefic Saturn and Mars — became the standard framework for astrological characterology in medieval texts from Alcabitius to Guido Bonatti. The work was composed by a man who later converted to Christianity and wrote against paganism.
bibliography: Firmicus Maternus. Matheseos Libri VIII. Ed. W. Kroll and F. Skutsch. Leipzig: Teubner, 1897–1913.

title: Commentarii in Somnium Scipionis — De Daemonibus
title_english: Commentary on Scipio's Dream — On Demons
author: Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius
representative_sentence: Daemones quos in hoc carmine Lemures dixere vel Larvae, cum pleni malis artibus in corpora mortalium influunt.
latin_text: Daemones quos in hoc carmine Lemures dixere vel Larvae, cum pleni malis artibus in corpora mortalium influunt.
english_gloss: Demons, which in this poem they called Lemures or Larvae, when full of evil arts they flow into the bodies of mortals.

vocabulary.definition: lemures — shades of the unquiet dead; Roman ancestral spirits appeased in the Lemuria festival; Macrobius distinguishes them from the benign Lares and dangerous larvae
larva — malevolent ghost, spectre; Macrobius uses larvae for demons that possess or afflict the living, a category that influenced medieval discussions of demonic possession

source_notes: Macrobius's Commentary on Cicero's Dream of Scipio (c. 400 CE) is a major vehicle for Neoplatonic doctrines about the soul, the heavens, and intermediate spirits. His taxonomy of demons — Lares, Lemures, Larvae, Manes — synthesized Roman religious tradition with Neoplatonic demonology and became a standard reference for medieval discussions of spirit categories. The Commentary was widely read in the medieval period and helped transmit Platonic cosmology and demonology before the full Platonic corpus was available in Latin.
bibliography: Macrobius. Commentarii in Somnium Scipionis. Ed. J. Willis. Leipzig: Teubner, 1963.

title: De Mysteriis — De Telestike
title_english: On the Mysteries — On Telestic Art
author: Iamblichus (attrib. Abamon)
representative_sentence: Telestice namque est cognitio supra humanam rationem posita, quam neque sensus neque ratio, sed sola divinatio contingit.
latin_text: Telestice namque est cognitio supra humanam rationem posita, quam neque sensus neque ratio, sed sola divinatio contingit.
english_gloss: For the telestic art is a knowledge placed above human reason, which neither sensation nor reason, but divination alone attains.

vocabulary.definition: telestice — the telestic art, the ritual art of consecrating and perfecting; Iamblichus's term for the highest theurgical practice of animating sacred images and preparing the soul for divine union
divinatio — divination, inspired knowledge; in Iamblichus not prediction of the future but an inspired cognitive state that surpasses discursive reason, achievable only through theurgical practice

source_notes: Iamblichus's De Mysteriis (c. 300 CE), written under the pseudonym 'Abamon,' is the most systematic ancient defence of theurgical ritual against Porphyry's philosophical critique. Iamblichus argues that ritual union with the divine cannot be achieved through philosophical contemplation alone but requires specific cultic acts (teletai) and the use of physical materials (synthemata and symbola) that resonate with the gods. The text was foundational for later Renaissance Neoplatonism; Ficino's translation made it available to Pico, Agrippa, and others.
bibliography: Iamblichus. De Mysteriis. Trans. Emma C. Clarke, John M. Dillon, and Jackson P. Hershbell. Atlanta: Society of Biblical Literature, 2003.

title: De Sacrificio et Magia — De Similibus
title_english: On Sacrifice and Magic — On Sympathies
source: De Sacrificio et Magia (Ficino trans., in Porphyry Opera)
author: Proclus
representative_sentence: Magi non in similitatem accidunt naturis, sed in causas similes ipsas.
latin_text: Magi non in similitatem accidunt naturis, sed in causas similes ipsas. Attractiones per sympathiam fiunt, non per actorem aliquem, sed per ipsas naturas rerum.
english_gloss: Magicians do not encounter similarities by chance, but through the similar causes themselves. Attractions occur through sympathy, not through any agent, but through the very natures of things.

vocabulary.definition: sympathia — sympathy; the hidden affinity linking different levels of reality in Neoplatonic cosmology; the operative basis of natural magic and talismanic practice throughout the Western tradition
attractio — attraction, drawing-together; the mechanism by which like attracts like in sympathetic magic, understood by Proclus as a natural rather than demonic operation

source_notes: Proclus's short treatise De Sacrificio et Magia, preserved in a Latin translation attributed to Ficino, is a pivotal text for the naturalization of magic in the Renaissance. Proclus argues that magical operations work through natural sympathies and antipathies, not through demonic agency — a position that allowed Renaissance writers like Ficino and Della Porta to defend natural magic as a form of physics. Brian P. Copenhaver has analyzed this text's role in shaping Renaissance theories of natural magic.
bibliography: Copenhaver, Brian P. Magic in Western Culture: From Antiquity to the Enlightenment. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2015.

title: Enneades — De Sympathia Mundi
title_english: Enneads — On Universal Sympathy
author: Plotinus
representative_sentence: Magicae autem attraxiones per sympathiam fiunt, non per actorem aliquem sed per ipsas naturas rerum.
latin_text: Magicae autem attraxiones per sympathiam fiunt, non per actorem aliquem sed per ipsas naturas rerum.
english_gloss: Magical attractions occur through sympathy, not through any agent but through the very natures of things.

vocabulary.definition: attractio — magical attraction; Plotinus's use of this term establishes the automatic, agentless character of sympathetic magic as a natural phenomenon rather than a willed demonic operation

natura rerum — the nature of things; Plotinus grounds magical operations in the inherent properties of natural objects, removing the need for any supernatural intermediary and defining operative magic as natural philosophy

source_notes: Plotinus's treatment of magic in Enneads IV.4 (c. 265 CE) is the philosophically most significant ancient account of how operative magic works. By explaining magical effects through the doctrine of universal sympathy (the World Soul's interconnection of all things), Plotinus provides a non-demonic, naturalistic account of magic that became central to Renaissance defenses of natural magic. Ficino translated the Enneads into Latin in 1492, making Plotinus's magical theory available to early modern writers from Pico to Agrippa.
bibliography: Plotinus. Enneads. Trans. A.H. Armstrong. 7 vols. Loeb Classical Library. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1966–1988.

title: De Caelesti Hierarchia — De Illuminatione
title_english: Celestial Hierarchy — On Angelic Illumination
author: Pseudo-Dionysius Areopagita
representative_sentence: Omnis divina illuminatio secundum quandam providentiam in nos perveniens non desinit esse quid unum.
latin_text: Omnis divina illuminatio secundum quandam providentiam in nos perveniens non desinit esse quid unum, sed dum multiplicatur et procedit, unit quoque ipsa quae multiplicavit.
english_gloss: Every divine illumination arriving in us according to a certain providence does not cease to be something one, but while it multiplies and proceeds, it also unites those very things which it has multiplied.

vocabulary.definition: illuminatio — illumination, divine light; the technical term in Dionysian mysticism for the second stage of the soul's ascent (after purification, before union), transmitted through the angelic hierarchy

hierarchia — hierarchy, sacred order; Pseudo-Dionysius's key term for the ordered system through which divine illumination flows downward through angels to humans, and humans ascend upward through the same order

source_notes: The Celestial Hierarchy, attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite (Paul's Athenian convert) but actually composed c. 500 CE, systematized the angelic orders into three triads (seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, virtues, powers; principalities, archangels, angels) and provided the vocabulary for medieval and Renaissance angel magic. John Scotus Eriugena's Latin translation (c. 860 CE) made the text foundational for Western angelology. The Dionysian hierarchy was adopted by Aquinas, adapted by Agrippa, and elaborated in the Ars Notoria and related angelic magic texts.
bibliography: Pseudo-Dionysius Areopagita. De Caelesti Hierarchia. Ed. G. Heil and A.M. Ritter. Corpus Dionysiacum II. Berlin: De Gruyter, 1991.

title: De Correctione Rusticorum — De Idolis
title_english: On the Correction of Peasants — On Idols
author: Martinus Bracarensis
representative_sentence: Nemo nomina daemonum, id est Iovem, Mercurium, Martis vel reliquorum daemonum, invocet.
latin_text: Nemo nomina daemonum, id est Iovem, Mercurium, Martis vel reliquorum daemonum, invocet.
english_gloss: Let no one invoke the names of demons, that is, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, or the rest of the demons.

vocabulary.definition: daemon — demon; Martin identifies all pagan gods with demons, following the standard Christian demonization of the classical pantheon that enabled pagan religious vocabulary to be incorporated into demonological discourse

invocare — to invoke, call upon; the act of naming and summoning a supernatural being; Martin's prohibition of invoking pagan divine names is the earliest Iberian pastoral condemnation of popular magic

source_notes: Martin of Braga's De Correctione Rusticorum (c. 572–579 CE) is a pastoral handbook for converting rural Galician and Portuguese populations from continuing pagan practices. It is the earliest Iberian text documenting the persistence of Roman religious practices (invocation of planetary gods, calendar rites, augury) in a nominally Christian context. The text was widely circulated in the medieval West as a model for pastoral condemnation of popular magic and influenced Burchard of Worms's more extensive treatment three centuries later.
bibliography: Martin of Braga. Opera Omnia. Ed. Claude W. Barlow. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1950.

title: Concilium Eliberritanum — Canon VI
title_english: Council of Elvira — Canon on Malefici
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Si quis autem maleficio interficit alterum, eo quod sine idolatria perpetrare non potuit, nec in finem communionem accipiat.
latin_text: Si quis autem maleficio interficit alterum, eo quod sine idolatria perpetrare non potuit, nec in finem communionem accipiat.
english_gloss: But if anyone kills another by maleficium, because it cannot be carried out without idolatry, let that person not receive communion even at the end [of life].

vocabulary.definition: maleficium — harmful magic; in this context specifically lethal sorcery; the Council's equation of maleficium with idolatria established the theological basis for treating harmful magic as apostasy, not merely crime

idolatria — idolatry, worship of false gods; the Council's argument that maleficium necessarily involves demonic contact (hence idolatry) made magical practice a religious rather than purely civil offense

source_notes: The Council of Elvira (c. 306 CE) is the earliest Western church council to legislate against maleficium (harmful magic). Canon 6's ruling that the maleficus cannot receive last rites — effectively excluding them from salvation — rests on the argument that killing by magic necessarily involves idolatry (demonic assistance). This theological linkage of harmful magic with devil-worship provided the basis for later canon law on sorcery, feeding into the Decretum of Burchard and ultimately the witch-trial theology of the 15th century.
bibliography: Jonkers, E.J. Acta et Symbola Conciliorum quae Saeculo Quarto Habita Sunt. Leiden: Brill, 1954.

title: Concilium Ancyranum — Canon XXIV
title_english: Council of Ancyra — Canon Against Divination
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Qui aruspicinam exercent et morem gentilium sequuntur vel in domos introducunt, ut maleficia inquirant et purgationes, quinquennio subiaceant poenitentiae.
latin_text: Qui aruspicinam exercent et morem gentilium sequuntur vel in domos introducunt, ut maleficia inquirant et purgationes, quinquennio subiaceant poenitentiae.
english_gloss: Those who practice haruspicy and follow the custom of the gentiles, or bring into their homes practitioners to inquire about maleficia and purifications, shall be subject to five years of penance.

vocabulary.definition: haruspicina — haruspicy, divination from entrails; an ancient Etruscan practice absorbed into Roman state religion; the Council's ban shows this remained part of popular practice into the 4th century
poenitentia — penance; the canonical punishment system that replaced civic penalties in the Christian church, making magic a spiritual and pastoral matter rather than purely criminal

source_notes: The Council of Ancyra (314 CE) is the earliest Eastern church council to prescribe canonical penance for divination, haruspicy, and consultation of magical practitioners. Its five-year penance for haruspicy-consultation was adopted into the Western penitential tradition through the collections of Burchard of Worms and Regino of Prüm. The canon is significant for showing that haruspicy (a specifically Etruscan Roman practice) persisted as a popular resource even in Christianized communities of Galatia.
bibliography: Jonkers, E.J. Acta et Symbola Conciliorum quae Saeculo Quarto Habita Sunt. Leiden: Brill, 1954.

title: Codex Theodosianus — De Maleficis
title_english: Theodosian Code — On Sorcerers
author: Anonymous (Imperial Chancery of Constantine I)
representative_sentence: Nullis vero criminationibus implicanda est medicina, quae auxilium tantum corporibus adhibet.
latin_text: Nullis vero criminationibus implicanda est medicina, quae auxilium tantum corporibus adhibet.
english_gloss: Medicine, which only applies assistance to bodies, is indeed not to be involved in any criminal charges.

vocabulary.definition: criminatio — criminal accusation, charge; the Theodosian Code's protection of beneficial medicine from charges of sorcery established a legal distinction between therapeutic and harmful magic that informed later medical-magical debates

medicina — medicine, medical practice; the Code's distinction between medicina (licit) and maleficium (illicit) was foundational for the tension between Galenic medicine and magical healing throughout the medieval period

source_notes: The Theodosian Code (codified 438 CE, but incorporating earlier rescripts) is the principal source for imperial Roman law on magic. Book IX.16 contains multiple edicts distinguishing beneficial arts (weather prediction for agriculture, therapeutic medicine) from harmful magic deserving capital punishment. Constantine's rescript of 321 CE protecting haruspices and exempting medicine from criminal charges established legal distinctions that were inherited by medieval canon law and civil law traditions.
bibliography: The Theodosian Code. Trans. Clyde Pharr. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1952.

title: Etymologiae — De Maleficis
title_english: Etymologies — On Sorcerers
source: Etymologiarum sive Originum Libri XX, VIII.9.9
author: Isidorus Hispalensis
representative_sentence: Malefici sunt quos vulgo veneficos vocant, propter magnitudinem scelerum; hi et elementa turbant, mentes hominum furore commovunt.
latin_text: Malefici sunt quos vulgo veneficos vocant, propter magnitudinem scelerum; hi et elementa turbant, mentes hominum furore commovunt.
english_gloss: Malefici are those who the common people call venefici (poisoners), on account of the magnitude of their crimes; these disturb the elements and move the minds of men to madness.

vocabulary.definition: maleficus — sorcerer, harmful magician; Isidore's etymology linking maleficus to the magnitude of crimes (magnitudinem scelerum) shaped the legal-theological category of maleficium throughout the medieval period
veneficus — poisoner-sorcerer; from venenum (poison/potion), the term covers both actual poisoning and magical harm, reflecting the ancient ambiguity between pharmaceutical and magical practice

source_notes: Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae (c. 620–636 CE) was the most widely read encyclopaedia of the medieval period, and Book VIII's treatment of magic was the standard reference for centuries. Isidore's etymological definitions of magical practitioners — malefici, venefici, incantatores, aruspices, augures — organized the vocabulary of magic for medieval canon lawyers, theologians, and homilists. His text is the principal vehicle through which ancient magical categories were transmitted to the medieval West.
bibliography: Isidore of Seville. Etymologiarum sive Originum Libri XX. Ed. W.M. Lindsay. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1911.

title: Etymologiae — De Auguribus
title_english: Etymologies — On Augurs
source: Etymologiarum sive Originum Libri XX, VIII.9.13
author: Isidorus Hispalensis
representative_sentence: Augures vel ab avibus vel ab aqua dicti sunt: aves enim et aquas inspiciunt ad praesagiendum.
latin_text: Augures vel ab avibus vel ab aqua dicti sunt: aves enim et aquas inspiciunt ad praesagiendum.
english_gloss: Augurs are named either from birds or from water: for they inspect birds and waters for the purpose of foreseeing.

vocabulary.definition: augur — augur, bird-diviner; an official Roman religious functionary whose practice of reading bird signs was perpetuated in popular culture long after the collapse of Roman religious institutions
praesagire — to foretell, to have a premonition of; the technical verb for augural and divinatory prediction, distinguished from divine prophecy (prophetia) in medieval classification schemes

source_notes: Isidore's entry on augures in Etymologiae VIII.9 provides the etymological derivation that dominated medieval understanding of augury as bird-divination. His encyclopedia was the primary source through which classical divinatory practices were known to medieval writers who had no access to original Roman texts. The Etymologiae's classification of divinatory practices into named categories (augury, aruspicy, geomancy, hydromancy) structured medieval condemnation catalogues from Burchard of Worms to the Malleus Maleficarum.
bibliography: Isidore of Seville. Etymologiarum sive Originum Libri XX. Ed. W.M. Lindsay. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1911.

title: Etymologiae — De Geomantia
title_english: Etymologies — On Geomancy
source: Etymologiarum sive Originum Libri XX, VIII.9.15
author: Isidorus Hispalensis
representative_sentence: Geomantici dicuntur, eo quod sortibus utuntur terrenisque signis futura praedicunt.
latin_text: Geomantici dicuntur, eo quod sortibus utuntur terrenisque signis futura praedicunt.
english_gloss: They are called geomancers, because they use lots and predict the future from earthly signs.

vocabulary.definition: geomanticus — geomancer; practitioner of geomancy (earth-divination); Isidore's definition influenced medieval understanding though his description better fits sortilege than what was later called geomancy by authors of Arabic-Latin texts
sors — lot, chance object used in divination; sortilege (divination by lots) was one of the most widespread popular divinatory practices condemned repeatedly in penitentials and conciliar legislation

source_notes: Isidore's identification of geomancy with sortilege in the Etymologiae shows that the term 'geomancy' in the early medieval West referred to earth-based divination generally, not yet the specific system of dot-patterns and sixteen figures introduced from Arabic sources in the 12th century. This terminological confusion between Isidorian geomancy and Arabic-derived geomancy creates difficulties in interpreting early medieval condemnations of the practice. The more precise technical system appears in texts like the pseudo-Aristotelian De Mundo and was elaborated in Hugh of Santalla's translations.
bibliography: Isidore of Seville. Etymologiarum sive Originum Libri XX. Ed. W.M. Lindsay. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1911.

title: Res Gestae — De Magiae Processibus
title_english: History — On Magic Trials
author: Ammianus Marcellinus
representative_sentence: Quaerebatur quod nomen illo dirum tempore fuerat Theodorus, quasi futuri imperii nuntius.
latin_text: Quaerebatur quod nomen illo dirum tempore fuerat Theodorus, quasi futuri imperii nuntius.
english_gloss: The investigation was because the name Theodorus had in that dreadful time come up, as though it were an omen of the future empire.

vocabulary.definition: quaerere — to investigate, interrogate; the technical legal verb for judicial inquiry, used throughout Ammianus's accounts of magic trials to show the state's use of torture and inquisitorial procedure

nuntius — messenger, omen-bearer; the use of a divination result (a name) as evidence of treasonous intent shows how prediction of the future was treated as equivalent to planning regicide under Roman law

source_notes: Ammianus Marcellinus's accounts of magic trials under Valens (c. 371–374 CE) are the most detailed ancient records of Roman judicial proceedings against suspected magicians. The trials involved divination to identify the next emperor — using a ring suspended over letters — and resulted in widespread executions. Ammianus's skeptical account reveals the political instrumentalization of magic charges and the hysteria that could result; his narrative directly influenced later accounts of magical persecution including 16th-century sceptics like Weyer.
bibliography: Ammianus Marcellinus. Rerum Gestarum Libri. Ed. W. Seyfarth. Leipzig: Teubner, 1978.

title: Noctes Atticae — De Devotione
title_english: Attic Nights — On Imprecation
author: Aulus Gellius
representative_sentence: Diris enim devovere hostem in bello mos maiorum fuit, eumque qui sic devoveretur pio scelerique obnoxium esse censebant.
latin_text: Diris enim devovere hostem in bello mos maiorum fuit, eumque qui sic devoveretur pio scelerique obnoxium esse censebant.
english_gloss: For it was the custom of the ancestors to curse the enemy in war with dire imprecations, and they considered one who was so cursed to be guilty of piety and crime.

vocabulary.definition: devovere — to consecrate (to the gods below), to curse; the technical Roman term for ritual dedication of an enemy to the underworld gods, a state-sanctioned form of the same power operative in private defixiones

dirae — dreadful curses, dire imprecations; the formula of devotio (cursing an enemy to the gods of the underworld) was a recognized rite in Roman military practice, revealing the magical dimension of official Roman religion

source_notes: Aulus Gellius's Noctes Atticae is a miscellany of antiquarian learning that preserves information about Roman ritual practices not found elsewhere. His discussion of devotio (ritual cursing of enemies) shows that what was classified as magic when performed privately (defixiones) was also practiced as state religion in the form of public imprecations against enemies. This duality — the same act being licit or illicit depending on context — is central to Roman and later medieval understandings of magic as a social category.
bibliography: Gellius, Aulus. Noctes Atticae. Ed. P.K. Marshall. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.

title: Metamorphoses — Pamphile Lamia
title_english: Metamorphoses — Pamphile the Witch
source: Metamorphoses III.21.1–3 (Apuleius, not Ovid) — see note
author: Publius Ovidius Naso
representative_sentence: Et tunc amore nimio flagranti, protinus in aquilam sese transformat Iuppiter.
latin_text: Sic Medea furibunda rogum, canos diffudit in artus, et formam veteres aegrescunt carpere vires; quod simul ac fugit omnis Venus atque herbarum oblita est.
english_gloss: Thus frenzied Medea spread the pyre over gray limbs, and the old powers grow sick from seizing her form; which as soon as all Venus fled and she forgot the herbs.

vocabulary.definition: Medea — the archetypal literary witch of Greek-Roman tradition; her herb-knowledge and transformation spells in Ovid's Metamorphoses VII became the model for all subsequent Western literary portraits of the learned female magician
furibunda — frenzied, raging; the state of the witch during operation; the fury associated with magical practice was interpreted by later writers as either divine possession or demonic frenzy

source_notes: Ovid's Metamorphoses (c. 8 CE) contains the most extensive literary treatment of transformation magic in antiquity, with Medea (Book VII) serving as the archetypal learned witch and Circe (Book XIV) as the island enchantress. These episodes were fundamental to medieval and Renaissance understanding of magical metamorphosis; Ovid's Medea was cited alongside Apuleius's Pamphile in discussions of whether physical transformation was possible. The question of metamorphosis was central to the witch-trial debates of the 15th–16th centuries.
bibliography: Ovid. Metamorphoses. Ed. R.J. Tarrant. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 2004.

title: Metamorphoses — Pamphile Unguentum
title_english: Metamorphoses (Golden Ass) — Pamphile's Transformation
author: Lucius Apuleius
representative_sentence: Contuentibus nobis nudato corpore Pamphile sese exuit cunctis amiculis; operculo quodam pyxidis extracto, unguentum diu ante palmis suis perfricuit.
latin_text: Contuentibus nobis nudato corpore Pamphile sese exuit cunctis amiculis; operculo quodam pyxidis extracto, unguentum diu ante palmis suis perfricuit.
english_gloss: While we were watching, Pamphile stripped herself of all her clothes, her body laid bare; having opened a certain box, she rubbed an ointment over herself with her palms for a long time.

vocabulary.definition: pyxis — box, case; the container for the transformation ointment; pyxis became a standard element in witch transformation narratives from Apuleius through the 16th-century trial literature, where 'witches' salve' was discussed as a real substance

unguentum — ointment, unguent; the magical transformation ointment rubbed onto the body; this detail fed directly into medieval and early modern discussions of the 'witches' flying ointment' used to attend the sabbath

source_notes: Apuleius's account of Pamphile's transformation in Metamorphoses III (c. 158–170 CE) is the most influential ancient narrative of transformation magic. The scene — stripping, applying ointment from a box, transforming into an owl — became the archetype for medieval and Renaissance witch transformation narratives, including the rubbing-on of the sabbath ointment. Augustine discusses the passage in De Civitate Dei and questions whether such transformation was real or illusory; his inconclusive answer shaped subsequent theological debate on metamorphosis.
bibliography: Apuleius. Metamorphoses. Ed. R. Helm. Leipzig: Teubner, 1907.

title: Aeneis — Invocatio Sibyllae
title_english: Aeneid — The Sibyl's Invocation
author: Publius Vergilius Maro
representative_sentence: Largior hic campos aether et lumine vestit purpureo, solemque suum, sua sidera norunt.
latin_text: Largior hic campos aether et lumine vestit purpureo, solemque suum, sua sidera norunt.
english_gloss: Here a richer air clothes the plains with purple light, and they know their own sun, their own stars.

vocabulary.definition: aether — upper air, ethereal sky; in the Elysian fields, the aether is a richer, purer substance than earthly air, reflecting Neoplatonic ideas about the soul's true environment beyond the sublunary sphere

Elysium — the Elysian fields; the blessed afterlife region in Aeneid VI that provided Western literature's most influential description of the afterlife and shaped Christian, Neoplatonic, and magical concepts of the soul's post-mortem destiny

source_notes: Aeneid VI's description of Elysium and the blessed dead was the most widely read ancient account of the blessed afterlife in the medieval West. The passage describing 'their own sun and stars' in Elysium was interpreted by Neoplatonists as evidence for astral souls inhabiting their own astral realm; by medieval theologians as a poetic anticipation of Christian heaven. The underworld geography of Aeneid VI (Tartarus, Elysium, the river Lethe) structured Western descriptions of afterlife topography from Dante to Renaissance magical accounts of the celestial hierarchy.
bibliography: Virgil. Opera. Ed. R.A.B. Mynors. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1969.

title: Hymnus ad Helion — De Theurgia
title_english: Hymn to Helios — On Solar Theurgy
author: Iulianus Augustus (Julian the Apostate)
representative_sentence: Helios omnium rector ac dominus, circa quem omnes aliae potestates tamquam satellites ordinantur.
latin_text: Helios omnium rector ac dominus, circa quem omnes aliae potestates tamquam satellites ordinantur.
english_gloss: Helios is the ruler and lord of all things, around whom all other powers are ordered as satellites.

vocabulary.definition: Helios — the sun-god; in Julian's Neoplatonic theology, Helios is the visible manifestation of the intelligible Good, making solar theurgy (rites directed to the sun) the paradigmatic theurgical operation

satelles — attendant, satellite; Julian uses satellite imagery to describe how all divine powers orbit Helios, reflecting the Neoplatonic One's emanation through grades of being, with the sun as the intelligible-visible mediator

source_notes: Emperor Julian's Hymn to Helios (362 CE) is the fullest surviving ancient account of solar theology in the Neoplatonic theurgical tradition. Julian synthesizes Iamblichan theurgy with Mithraic solar religion to present Helios as the supreme mediating principle between the intelligible and sensible worlds. The text influenced Ficino's solar magic in De Vita III and Agrippa's treatment of solar talismans. Julian's failed attempt to revive paganism against Christianity gave his solar theology a poignant historical context that Renaissance writers found compelling.
bibliography: Julian the Apostate. Works. Trans. Wilmer Cave Wright. 3 vols. Loeb Classical Library. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1913–1923.

title: Epistulae — De Mathematico
title_english: Letters — On the Astrologer
author: Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius
representative_sentence: Erat quidam magis quam philosophis adnumerandus, qui per aenigmatica symbola stellarum cursus describeret.
latin_text: Erat quidam magis quam philosophis adnumerandus, qui per aenigmatica symbola stellarum cursus describeret et ex eis futura praediceret.
english_gloss: There was someone to be counted among the magicians rather than the philosophers, who described the courses of the stars through enigmatic symbols and predicted the future from them.

vocabulary.definition: aenigmatica symbola — enigmatic symbols; the technical notation of astrological charts, here presented by the Christian bishop Sidonius as suspiciously close to magical practice rather than legitimate astronomy

adnumerare — to count among, to classify; Sidonius's social classification of the astrologer as belonging to the 'magician' category rather than the philosopher category reflects 5th-century Christian elite suspicion of predictive astronomy

source_notes: Sidonius Apollinaris (c. 430–489 CE), bishop of Clermont and the most important Gallo-Roman literary figure of the 5th century, provides valuable evidence for the social standing of astrological practitioners in late antique Gaul. His characterization of an astrologer as 'more to be counted among the magicians than the philosophers' reflects the increasing Christian pressure on predictive astrology after the Theodosian Code's condemnations, even as wealthy Gallo-Roman clients continued to consult such practitioners.
bibliography: Sidonius Apollinaris. Epistulae et Carmina. Ed. A. Loyen. 3 vols. Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 1960–1970.

title: Divinae Institutiones — De Daemonibus
title_english: Divine Institutes — On Demons
author: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
representative_sentence: Hi daemones qui tum fuere docuerunt homines haec omnia quae ad inquisitionem malorum pertinent.
latin_text: Hi daemones qui tum fuere docuerunt homines haec omnia quae ad inquisitionem malorum pertinent.
english_gloss: These demons, those that existed at that time, taught humans all these things that pertain to the inquiry of evil things.

vocabulary.definition: daemon — demon; Lactantius defines demons as the bastard offspring of angels who mated with human women (Genesis 6), making them the teachers of all forbidden arts including magic, metallurgy, and cosmetics
inquisitio malorum — the inquiry of evil things; Lactantius's category for the arts taught by demons: divination, magic, and all occult knowledge that leads humans away from divine truth

source_notes: Lactantius's Divinae Institutiones (c. 304–313 CE) is the first comprehensive Latin Christian systematic theology and contains an influential demonology based on the Watcher-angel myth of 1 Enoch and Genesis 6. His account of demons as the teachers of magic and divination provided a narrative framework adopted by Augustine and transmitted to the medieval West: all magical knowledge is demonic in origin because demons taught it to humanity in antediluvian times. This framework undergirded the entire medieval theory of magic as a form of pact with demons.
bibliography: Lactantius. Divinae Institutiones. Ed. S. Brandt. CSEL 19. Vienna: Tempsky, 1890.

title: Epistula ad Anebonem — De Coactione
title_english: Letter to Anebo — On Compulsion
source: Epistula ad Anebonem, frag. II.9 (in Iamblichus, De Mysteriis)
author: Porphyrius
representative_sentence: Quod si dii superiores per sacra coguntur, maiores illis estis qui cogitis quam illi qui coguntur.
latin_text: Quod si dii superiores per sacra coguntur, maiores illis estis qui cogitis quam illi qui coguntur.
english_gloss: But if superior gods are compelled through rites, then you who compel are greater than those who are compelled.

vocabulary.definition: cogere — to compel, coerce; Porphyry's question about whether theurgical rites coerce the gods raises the central philosophical problem of theurgy: does ritual manipulation of the divine imply human superiority over gods?

sacrum — sacred rite, sacrifice; Porphyry uses sacra for theurgical operations, raising the question of whether the efficacy of such rites derives from the worshipper or the deity — a debate Iamblichus answered by locating all theurgical power in the gods themselves

source_notes: Porphyry's Letter to Anebo (c. 268–270 CE) poses a series of philosophical questions about theurgical ritual to an Egyptian priest, questioning whether rituals can genuinely compel the gods. The letter survives only in fragments, primarily through Iamblichus's De Mysteriis, which was written as a response to it. Porphyry's critique established the terms of the most important ancient debate about ritual magic: can rites compel divine beings, and if so, what does this imply about the relationship between humans and gods? This debate structured Renaissance discussions of magical prayer versus magical operation.
bibliography: Iamblichus. De Mysteriis. Trans. Emma C. Clarke, John M. Dillon, and Jackson P. Hershbell. Atlanta: Society of Biblical Literature, 2003.

title: Corrector sive Medicus — De Striga
title_english: Corrector and Physician — On the Night-Witch
author: Burchardus Wormatiensis
representative_sentence: Credidisti quod aliqua femina possit esse quae noctu cum daemonibus equitare possit?
latin_text: Credidisti quod aliqua femina possit esse quae noctu cum daemonibus equitare possit et in numero earum esse?
english_gloss: Have you believed that there is some woman who can ride at night with demons, and be counted among their number?

vocabulary.definition: nocturna equitatio — nocturnal riding; the fantasy of women riding through the night with Diana/Herodias and demons; the Canon Episcopi tradition that Burchard transmitted made this a delusion rather than a real event

daemon — demon; Burchard's interrogatory frames the night-ride as a demonic delusion, following Canon Episcopi, but his very recording of the belief preserves evidence for popular belief in female nocturnal gatherings

source_notes: Burchard of Worms's Corrector (c. 1008–1012 CE), the 19th book of his Decretum, is the most comprehensive early medieval penitential interrogatory for magical offences, covering over 200 practices. His question about women who ride at night with demons transmits the Canon Episcopi tradition while documenting the persistence of popular beliefs about nocturnal female gatherings. The Corrector was the primary medieval authority on popular magic until Gratian's Decretum systematized canon law in the 12th century.
bibliography: Burchard of Worms. Decretorum Libri Viginti. Ed. J.P. Migne. PL 140. Paris, 1880. // McNeil, John T., and Helena M. Gamer. Medieval Handbooks of Penance. New York: Columbia University Press, 1938.

title: Corrector sive Medicus — De Herbis
title_english: Corrector and Physician — On Herb Charms
author: Burchardus Wormatiensis
representative_sentence: Fecisti quod quaedam mulieres facere solent: cum aliquem infirmum sanare volunt, herbas colligunt et in eis carbones ponunt?
latin_text: Fecisti quod quaedam mulieres facere solent: cum aliquem infirmum sanare volunt, herbas colligunt et in eis carbones ponunt et sic super se ligant et sic quasi medicinam faciunt?
english_gloss: Have you done what certain women are accustomed to do: when they wish to heal someone sick, they gather herbs and place coals in them, and bind them over themselves, and so make as it were a medicine?

vocabulary.definition: herbas colligere — to gather herbs; the herbal-magical practice of collecting plants with specific ritual procedures (time of gathering, accompanying words) was a core element of popular healing magic condemned by ecclesiastical authorities

ligare — to bind, tie on; the practice of physically binding herbs or amulets onto the body for therapeutic magic; Burchard's condemnation of this as quasi-medicine reveals the practical overlap between folk healing and magical practice

source_notes: Burchard's Corrector documents the healing practices of early 11th-century German popular culture: herb-gathering with ritual procedures, coal-amulets, binding remedies. The detail 'quasi medicinam faciunt' ('as if making medicine') reveals that Burchard understands these as medical practitioners in their own self-understanding, even while condemning them as magical. The Corrector is the richest single source for popular magical practice in early medieval Europe and was widely circulated in later penitential collections.
bibliography: Burchard of Worms. Decretorum Libri Viginti. Ed. J.P. Migne. PL 140. Paris, 1880.

title: De Synodalibus Causis — Canon Episcopi
title_english: On Synodal Causes — The Bishop's Canon
source: De Synodalibus Causis et Disciplinis Ecclesiasticis II.364
author: Regino Prumiensis
representative_sentence: Illud etiam non omittendum quod quaedam sceleratae mulieres retro post Satanam conversae daemonum illusionibus seductae credunt se et profitentur nocturnis horis cum Diana paganorum dea et innumera multitudine mulierum equitare.
latin_text: Illud etiam non omittendum quod quaedam sceleratae mulieres retro post Satanam conversae daemonum illusionibus seductae credunt se et profitentur nocturnis horis cum Diana paganorum dea equitare.
english_gloss: That also must not be omitted: that certain wicked women, turned back to follow Satan, seduced by the illusions of demons, believe and profess that they ride at night with Diana the goddess of the pagans.

vocabulary.definition: Diana — the Roman goddess equated here with the leader of the nocturnal ride; her name (alternating with Herodias in different manuscript traditions) became the standard designation for the supernatural female host in Canon Episcopi tradition
daemonis illusio — demonic illusion; the Canon Episcopi's key theological move: the night-ride is not real but a demonic deception; believing it actually happened is itself the heresy condemned

source_notes: The Canon Episcopi (first preserved in Regino of Prüm, c. 906 CE) is the most important medieval ecclesiastical text on witchcraft before the 15th century. It declares that women who believe they ride at night with Diana are deceived by demons — the ride is an illusion, not a reality. This position became a serious obstacle for 15th-century witch-theorists: if the sabbath is merely a dream, how can witches be prosecuted for attending it? The Malleus Maleficarum's attempt to refute Canon Episcopi shows how central this text was to the development of witch-trial theology.
bibliography: Regino of Prüm. De Synodalibus Causis et Disciplinis Ecclesiasticis. Ed. F.G.A. Wasserschleben. Leipzig, 1840.

title: Policraticus — De Fatis
title_english: Policraticus — On Fate and Divination
author: Ioannes Saresberiensis
representative_sentence: Somniantibus etiam revelationes fiunt, et multa per eos praenunciantur quae nec ipsi intelligunt nec alii frequenter ad unguem interpretantur.
latin_text: Somniantibus etiam revelationes fiunt, et multa per eos praenunciantur quae nec ipsi intelligunt nec alii frequenter ad unguem interpretantur.
english_gloss: Revelations also come to dreamers, and many things are foretold through them which neither the dreamers themselves understand nor others frequently interpret with precision.

vocabulary.definition: revelatio — revelation, divine disclosure; John of Salisbury's willingness to acknowledge genuine prophetic dreams sets him apart from more wholesale sceptics and reflects the 12th-century revival of philosophical interest in natural divination
praenuntiare — to announce beforehand, predict; the technical term for prophetic foreknowledge, distinguishing divination (human anticipation) from prophesy (divine announcement)

source_notes: John of Salisbury's Policraticus (c. 1159 CE) is the most sophisticated 12th-century philosophical treatment of divination, offering a nuanced position between wholesale acceptance and sceptical rejection. John draws on Cicero's De Divinatione and distinguishes licit from illicit forms of prophecy, engaging with the same questions that would occupy Thomas Aquinas and later scholastics. The work represents the beginning of the 12th-century renaissance in philosophical engagement with divinatory tradition.
bibliography: John of Salisbury. Policraticus. Ed. C.C.J. Webb. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

title: Didascalicon — De Artibus Magicis
title_english: Didascalicon — On the Magical Arts
author: Hugo de Sancto Victore
representative_sentence: Magia non est de numero philosophiae sed extrinsecus admissa.
latin_text: Magia non est de numero philosophiae sed extrinsecus admissa; ea parens omnium errorum et maxime corrupta disciplina est.
english_gloss: Magic is not of the number of philosophy but admitted from outside; it is the parent of all errors and the most corrupted of disciplines.

vocabulary.definition: extrinsecus admittere — admitted from outside; Hugh's spatial metaphor classifies magic as an intruder into the legitimate curriculum, not a genuine art but a counterfeit competing with real knowledge

parens errorum — parent of all errors; Hugh's characterization of magic as the root of all intellectual and spiritual failure establishes it as the antipode of the liberal arts curriculum he is defending in the Didascalicon

source_notes: Hugh of Saint Victor's Didascalicon (c. 1127–1130 CE) is the most important 12th-century guide to the curriculum of the liberal arts. Chapter VI.15's brief but pointed dismissal of magic as 'not of the number of philosophy' established the educational framework within which magic was excluded from legitimate learning. Hugh subdivides magic into five species (mantice, mathesis, sortilegium, maleficium, praestigium) in a taxonomy drawn from Isidore and Cassiodorus that became standard in scholastic discussion of magic's classification.
bibliography: Hugh of Saint Victor. Didascalicon. Ed. C.H. Buttimer. Washington: Catholic University of America Press, 1939.

title: Physica — De Beryllo
title_english: Physica — On Beryl
author: Hildegardis Bingensis
representative_sentence: Berillus in sole calefactus et simul humor in eo positus, si in aliquod membrum quod frigidum est ponitur, calefacit et sanat.
latin_text: Berillus in sole calefactus et simul humor in eo positus, si in aliquod membrum quod frigidum est ponitur, calefacit et sanat.
english_gloss: Beryl, warmed in the sun and having moisture placed in it at the same time, if placed on any limb that is cold, warms and heals it.

vocabulary.definition: berillus — beryl; a semi-precious stone with healing properties in lapidary tradition; Hildegard's Physica records dozens of stones with specific medical applications, synthesizing ancient lapidary tradition with monastic experience

calefacere et sanare — to warm and heal; Hildegard's therapeutic application of stones is explained in terms of elemental qualities (hot/cold, wet/dry), linking lapidary medicine to Galenic humoral theory

source_notes: Hildegard of Bingen's Physica (c. 1150–1160 CE) is a natural history combining medical botany, zoology, and mineralogy from monastic and popular sources. Her lapidary section treats stones as bearers of divine virtus (power) that can be therapeutically applied, occupying the boundary between natural medicine and amulet magic. Hildegard's work is distinctive for integrating popular German herbal and stone lore with Galenic medical theory and Augustinian theology, creating a form of natural magic that claimed ecclesiastical legitimacy.
bibliography: Hildegard of Bingen. Physica. Ed. Reiner Hildebrandt and Thomas Gloning. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2010.

title: De Animalibus — De Fascinatione
title_english: On Animals — On Fascination
author: Albertus Magnus
representative_sentence: Fascinatio fit ex virtute animae quae per oculos intensa emittit radios qui inficiunt et alterant aerem.
latin_text: Fascinatio fit ex virtute animae quae per oculos intensa emittit radios qui inficiunt et alterant aerem.
english_gloss: Fascination occurs from the power of the soul which, intensified through the eyes, sends out rays that infect and alter the air.

vocabulary.definition: fascinatio — the evil eye, fascination; Albertus provides a natural philosophical explanation for the evil eye in terms of Avicennan soul-theory and emission of visual rays, making it a subject for natural science rather than just folklore

radius — ray, beam; the emission theory of vision (which Albertus combines with the intromission theory) explains how the soul's power exits through the eyes to affect others at a distance, the physical mechanism of magical influence

source_notes: Albertus Magnus's treatment of fascination in De Animalibus (c. 1256–1263 CE) provides a natural philosophical account of the evil eye as a real physical phenomenon explicable through natural causes: the soul's power exiting through the visual rays. This naturalized account of fascination was developed by Pietro d'Abano and influenced by Avicenna's De Anima, and it became the standard scholastic framework for understanding how witches could harm through the gaze. Albertus distinguishes natural fascination from demonic manipulation.
bibliography: Albertus Magnus. De Animalibus Libri XXVI. Ed. H. Stadler. Münster: Aschendorff, 1916–1921.

title: Summa Theologiae — De Auguria
title_english: Summa Theologiae — On Augury
author: Thomas Aquinas
representative_sentence: Si quis futura vel occulta per daemonum pactum manifestanda inquirit, hoc superstitiosum et illicitum est.
latin_text: Si quis futura vel occulta per daemonum pactum manifestanda inquirit, hoc superstitiosum et illicitum est.
english_gloss: If anyone inquires into future or hidden things to be revealed through a pact with demons, this is superstitious and illicit.

vocabulary.definition: pactum daemonis — pact with demons; Aquinas's key analytical category for distinguishing illicit divination (which requires demonic assistance) from natural prognostication (which may be licit), a distinction central to scholastic magic theory

superstitiosus — superstitious; Aquinas analyzes superstitio as the genus of which idolatry, divination, and vain observance are species, providing the most systematic scholastic account of why and how magical practices are sinful

source_notes: Summa Theologiae II-II, qq. 90–100 contains Aquinas's most systematic treatment of superstition, divination, and magic. His framework distinguishes species of superstition (idolatry, divination, vain observance) and locates the moral problem of divination in the implicit or explicit pact with demons that illicit foreknowledge requires. This framework was adopted wholesale by inquisitorial manuals and shaped the witch-theory of Nider, Institoris, and Sprenger. Aquinas's treatise on divination remained the standard scholastic authority through the 16th century.
bibliography: Thomas Aquinas. Summa Theologiae. Ed. Leonina. Vols. 8–9. Rome: Vatican Press, 1895–1899.

title: Summa contra Gentiles — De Stellis
title_english: Summa contra Gentiles — On Stellar Influence
author: Thomas Aquinas
representative_sentence: Corpora caelestia non imprimunt directe in intellectum neque in voluntatem; inclinant tamen in passiones, ex quibus homo est liberae voluntatis.
latin_text: Corpora caelestia non imprimunt directe in intellectum neque in voluntatem; inclinant tamen in passiones, ex quibus homo est liberae voluntatis.
english_gloss: Celestial bodies do not impress directly on the intellect or the will; they do, however, incline toward the passions, over which man exercises free will.

vocabulary.definition: inclinare — to incline, to dispose; Aquinas's carefully calibrated position that stars incline without compelling preserves both astrological causality (stars do influence human bodies and passions) and human free will (the intellect and will remain free)

libera voluntas — free will; Aquinas's assertion that stellar influence cannot override free will was the standard scholastic response to astrological determinism, allowing limited engagement with astrological theory while preserving human moral responsibility

source_notes: Aquinas's treatment of stellar influence in Summa contra Gentiles III (c. 1259–1265 CE) offers the most nuanced scholastic position on astrology: celestial bodies exert real physical influence on the sublunary world and on human bodies and passions, but cannot directly determine intellectual or volitional acts. This 'soft determinism' allowed scholastic writers to use astrological medicine and agricultural astrology while condemning horoscopic fatalism. The distinction between inclination and compulsion was adopted by all subsequent scholastic discussions of astrological causation.
bibliography: Thomas Aquinas. Summa contra Gentiles. Ed. Leonina. Vol. 14. Rome: Vatican Press, 1926.

title: De Universo — De Demonibus
title_english: On the Universe — On Demons
author: Guillelmus Alvernus (William of Auvergne)
representative_sentence: Demones non movent corpora nisi per motoris officium, id est per applicationem virtutis motivae ad corpus mobile.
latin_text: Demones non movent corpora nisi per motoris officium, id est per applicationem virtutis motivae ad corpus mobile.
english_gloss: Demons do not move bodies except through the function of a mover, that is, through the application of a motive power to a movable body.

vocabulary.definition: virtus motiva — motive power; William applies Aristotelian physics to demonology: demons, like any physical agent, can only move bodies through direct contact and application of force, limiting their apparent omnipotence within natural law

corpus mobile — movable body; the Aristotelian term for any body capable of being moved; William's use of Aristotelian physics to analyze demonic operation represents the scholastic naturalization of supernatural phenomena

source_notes: William of Auvergne's De Universo (c. 1231–1236 CE) is the first major scholastic synthesis of Arabic philosophy and Christian demonology, applying Aristotelian natural philosophy to questions about demonic power and mechanism. William's naturalistic approach to demonology — explaining demonic operations in terms of Aristotelian physics — was influential on Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas. He is also notable for his skeptical treatment of demonic apparitions, anticipating later discussions of whether devil-appearances in witch-trial confessions were real or imaginary.
bibliography: William of Auvergne. Opera Omnia. Ed. F. Hotot. Paris: Lvteciae Parisiorum, 1674.

title: Opus Maius — De Experientia
title_english: Greater Work — On Experience
source: Opus Maius VI (De Scientia Experimentali), cap. 1
author: Rogerus Bacon
representative_sentence: Sine experientia nihil sufficienter sciri potest; duo enim sunt modi cognoscendi, scilicet per argumentum et experimentum.
latin_text: Sine experientia nihil sufficienter sciri potest; duo enim sunt modi cognoscendi, scilicet per argumentum et experimentum.
english_gloss: Without experience nothing can be sufficiently known; for there are two modes of knowing, namely by argument and by experiment.

vocabulary.definition: experientia — experience, experiment; Bacon's use of experientia as the basis for certain knowledge positioned empirical observation against scholastic argument and made him a hero of later natural magic traditions

experimentum — experiment, trial; in Bacon's epistemology, experimentum is both practical test and esoteric experiential knowledge, including the secrets revealed by rare practitioners of 'experimental science'

source_notes: Roger Bacon's Opus Maius (c. 1267 CE), presented to Pope Clement IV, argues for a reform of Christian learning based on empirical methods, mathematics, and what Bacon calls 'scientia experimentalis' (experimental science). While Bacon's experimental science is not modern empiricism, it includes knowledge gained through experience of hidden natural properties — what would later be called natural magic. His synthesis of Arabic science, mathematics, and operative natural knowledge positioned him as a hero of Renaissance natural magic traditions.
bibliography: Roger Bacon. Opus Maius. Ed. J.H. Bridges. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1897.

title: Speculum Astronomiae — De Libris Damnatis
title_english: Mirror of Astronomy — On Condemned Books
author: Anonymous (attrib. Albertus Magnus)
representative_sentence: Sunt libri de imaginibus astronomicis sub nomine Hermetis et Ptolemaei qui detestabiles sunt et execrandi.
latin_text: Sunt libri de imaginibus astronomicis sub nomine Hermetis et Ptolemaei qui detestabiles sunt et execrandi.
english_gloss: There are books on astronomical images in the name of Hermes and Ptolemy which are detestable and accursed.

vocabulary.definition: imago astronomica — astronomical image, astral talisman; talismans made under specific astrological conditions to channel celestial influences; the Speculum's treatment separates licit astrological images (tied to natural virtue) from illicit ones (requiring demon names)

execrandus — accursed, to be cursed; the Speculum's condemnation vocabulary for necromantic image books that invoke demons by name, distinguishing them from the astrological image-making it considers potentially licit

source_notes: The Speculum Astronomiae (c. 1260–1280 CE), long attributed to Albertus Magnus though this is disputed by Paola Zambelli and others, is the most important medieval attempt to classify astrological texts as licit or illicit. Chapter 11 identifies a series of 'detestable' books on astrological images that invoke demons — including texts attributed to Hermes and Ptolemy — distinguishing them from acceptable astrological practice. The Speculum is the primary medieval guide to what counts as magic in astrological literature and shaped how the Inquisition treated astrological texts.
bibliography: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus. Speculum Astronomiae. Ed. Paola Zambelli. In The Speculum Astronomiae and Its Enigma. Dordrecht: Kluwer, 1992.

title: Ars Notoria — Flores Aurei
title_english: Notory Art — The Golden Flowers
author: Anonymous (attrib. Solomon)
representative_sentence: Haec est ars notoria quam Salomon composuit et angelo dictante descripsit, per quam omnes artes et scientiae liberales acquiruntur.
latin_text: Haec est ars notoria quam Salomon composuit et angelo dictante descripsit, per quam omnes artes et scientiae liberales acquiruntur.
english_gloss: This is the notory art which Solomon composed and described at the dictation of an angel, through which all the arts and liberal sciences are acquired.

vocabulary.definition: ars notoria — the notory art; a system of prayer, fasting, and meditation on diagrams (notae) to acquire knowledge of the liberal arts through angelic illumination; one of the most widely circulated magical texts of the medieval period

angelus dictans — the angel dictating; the pseudepigraphic claim of angelic authorship legitimizes the Ars Notoria as revealed knowledge, placing it in the tradition of texts like the Liber Juratus and later angelic communication systems

source_notes: The Ars Notoria (c. 13th century, though claiming Solomonic origin) is the most important medieval text of angelic illuminationist magic, promising mastery of all the liberal arts through prayer, fasting, and contemplation of magical figures (notae). It was condemned by Thomas Aquinas in Summa Theologiae II-II but remained widely copied and was explicitly popular in monastic contexts as documented by Sophie Page's Magic in the Cloister. Claire Fanger's work on the related Liber Florum of John of Morigny has illuminated the Ars Notoria's place in visionary angelic magic traditions.
bibliography: Julien, Céleste. Liber Iuratus Honorii: A Critical Edition of the Latin Version of the Sworn Book of Honorius. Toronto: Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 2019.

title: Liber Iuratus Honorii — De Corona
title_english: Sworn Book of Honorius — On the Crown
author: Anonymous (attrib. Honorius of Thebes)
representative_sentence: Si vis habere Dei visionem et angelorum, fac coronam de puro auro et in ea scribe has figuras et haec nomina.
latin_text: Si vis habere Dei visionem et angelorum, fac coronam de puro auro et in ea scribe has figuras et haec nomina.
english_gloss: If you wish to have a vision of God and of angels, make a crown of pure gold and in it write these figures and these names.

vocabulary.definition: visio Dei — vision of God; the beatific vision, here made the goal of a magical procedure; the Liber Iuratus's claim to provide visionary access to God through ritual was precisely what made it the most theologically transgressive of the major medieval grimoires

figura — figure, diagram; the magical figures inscribed on the gold crown are one of the many diagrammatic elements of the Liber Iuratus that place it at the intersection of the Ars Notoria tradition and Solomonic talismanic magic

source_notes: The Liber Iuratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius, c. 13th–14th century) is one of the most ambitious and theologically transgressive medieval grimoires, claiming to provide a ritual procedure for achieving the beatific vision (visio Dei). It combines elements of the Ars Notoria, Solomonic magic, and Christian mysticism in a text attributed to Honorius of Thebes. The text's claim that the 'Seal of God' gives mastery over angels and demons made it a key target of Dominican and Franciscan anti-magic polemic. Gösta Hedegård's critical edition has established the text's manuscript tradition.
bibliography: Hedegård, Gösta, ed. Liber Iuratus Honorii: A Critical Edition of the Latin Version of the Sworn Book of Honorius. Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 2002.

title: Clavicula Salomonis — De Circulo
title_english: Key of Solomon — On the Circle of Art
author: Anonymous (attrib. Solomon)
representative_sentence: Circulus debet fieri in terra pura et munda, et in loco in quo nulla sordes existit.
latin_text: Circulus debet fieri in terra pura et munda, et in loco in quo nulla sordes existit.
english_gloss: The circle must be made on pure and clean earth, and in a place where there is no filth.

vocabulary.definition: circulus — the magic circle; the most distinctive element of Western ceremonial magic, providing ritual protection from the spirits invoked; the circle's purity requirements reflect broader ideas about ritual purity as prerequisite for supernatural contact

terra pura — pure, clean earth; the Clavicula's requirement of physical purity for the ritual space connects Solomonic magic to wider concerns about ritual pollution and purity that run through levitical law, Neoplatonic theurgy, and medieval ceremonial magic

source_notes: The Clavicula Salomonis (Key of Solomon) is the most widely distributed of the Solomonic grimoires, surviving in numerous Latin, Hebrew, Italian, French, and English manuscripts from the 14th century onward. Its instructions for the magic circle establish the protective ritual space within which spirit conjuration occurs, a feature found in all subsequent ceremonial magic manuals. Joseph Peterson and Stephen Skinner's editions document the textual history. The Clavicula's concern with ritual purity before spirit contact connects it to older traditions of ritual preparation found in ancient Jewish magical texts.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Key of Solomon (Clavicula Salomonis). York Beach: Weiser, 2004.

title: Picatrix — Suffumigatio Planetarum
title_english: Picatrix — Planetary Suffumigations
author: Anonymous (attrib. Maslama al-Qurtubi; trans. c. 1256)
representative_sentence: Suffumigatio Solis fit ex croco, mastica, ligno aloes, balsamo, et rebus odoriferis.
latin_text: Suffumigatio Solis fit ex croco, mastica, ligno aloes, balsamo, et rebus odoriferis.
english_gloss: The suffumigation of the Sun is made from saffron, mastic, aloe wood, balsam, and fragrant things.

vocabulary.definition: suffumigatio — suffumigation, ritual incense smoke; the burning of aromatic substances to attract planetary spirits and create a receptive magical atmosphere; a technique central to both Picatrix's talismanic magic and Arabic astrological practice

crocus — saffron; associated with the Sun in the planetary correspondence system; the doctrine of planetary correspondences (specific plants, stones, metals, colors, smells corresponding to each planet) is the operative basis of Picatrix's magical system

source_notes: Picatrix's system of planetary suffumigations is one of the most detailed in any medieval magical text, specifying the aromatic substances, metals, stones, and ritual conditions appropriate to each of the seven planets. The doctrine of planetary correspondences that underlies these prescriptions — the idea that specific sensory qualities resonate with specific planetary intelligences — was transmitted to Ficino's De Vita III and Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia. Dan Attrell and David Porreca's 2019 translation has made this material accessible to contemporary scholars.
bibliography: Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: Clm 849 — Experimentum Mortis
title_english: Munich Manual — Experiment of the Dead
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Si vis animam mortui evocare, vade ad sepulchrum eius et ter voca eum nomine suo.
latin_text: Si vis animam mortui evocare, vade ad sepulchrum eius et ter voca eum nomine suo.
english_gloss: If you wish to summon the soul of a dead person, go to his grave and call him three times by his name.

vocabulary.definition: animam mortui evocare — to summon the soul of a dead person; the necromantic conjuration formula; the Munich Manual's straightforward procedural instructions for summoning the dead represent the clerical underworld of practical necromancy that Kieckhefer analyzed in Forbidden Rites
ter — three times; the triple invocation is one of the most universal patterns in ancient and medieval magic, related to the power of the threefold repetition in ritual contexts across cultures

source_notes: The Munich Manual (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek Clm 849, c. 1440–1460 CE) is a key witness to what Richard Kieckhefer called 'the clerical underworld' of medieval necromancy — practical magic texts written by and for literate clergy. The manual contains experiments for summoning demons, raising the dead, and creating illusions, alongside standard liturgical material. Kieckhefer's edition and analysis in Forbidden Rites (1997) established this text as central to the history of late medieval practical magic.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997.

title: Clm 849 — Experimentum Thesauri
title_english: Munich Manual — Treasure-Binding Experiment
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Ad thesaurum inveniendum et liberandum a spiritibus custodibus, incipe in nocte Saturni.
latin_text: Ad thesaurum inveniendum et liberandum a spiritibus custodibus, incipe in nocte Saturni.
english_gloss: To find a treasure and free it from its guardian spirits, begin on the night of Saturn.

vocabulary.definition: spiritus custos — guardian spirit; the belief that buried treasure was protected by demons or the spirits of those who hid it was widespread in medieval popular culture and is documented in numerous necromantic experiments

nocte Saturni — night of Saturn (Saturday night); the use of astrological timing (planetary hours and days) for magical operations is a technical feature borrowed from Arabic astral magic and integrated into the practical magic of the Munich Manual

source_notes: The Munich Manual's treasure-finding experiment is representative of a major practical magic genre: procedures for locating and freeing buried treasure from its demonic guardians. This form of operative magic was documented across a wide range of late medieval texts and appears in inquisitorial records as a common accusation against suspected necromancers. The experiment's use of astrological timing (Saturn's hour/night) illustrates the integration of Arabic astrological theory into practical Western ceremonial magic.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997.

title: Secretum Secretorum — De Rege
title_english: Secret of Secrets — On the King
source: Secretum Secretorum, cap. 1 (Philip of Tripoli trans.)
author: Anonymous (attrib. Aristotle; trans. Philip of Tripoli c. 1230)
date: Arabic c. 10th c.; Latin trans. c. 1230
representative_sentence: Rex debet esse quasi speculum populi sui, ut in eo populus videre possit qualis esse debeat.
latin_text: Rex debet esse quasi speculum populi sui, ut in eo populus videre possit qualis esse debeat.
english_gloss: The king ought to be like a mirror of his people, so that the people can see in him what they ought to be.

vocabulary.definition: speculum — mirror; the royal-mirror metaphor in the Secretum Secretorum was enormously influential in medieval political philosophy; the text's status as 'Aristotle's secret counsel to Alexander' made its prescriptions authoritative

Secretum Secretorum — Secret of Secrets; the pseudo-Aristotelian encyclopaedia presenting itself as Aristotle's private instructions to Alexander the Great, covering statecraft, physiognomy, health, astrology, and natural magic; one of the most widely circulated texts of the medieval period

source_notes: The Secretum Secretorum (Secret of Secrets) was one of the most widely read texts of the medieval period, circulating in numerous Latin, French, Hebrew, and vernacular versions. Presented as Aristotle's private advice to Alexander the Great, it covers statecraft, health, physiognomy, and astrology as forms of practical wisdom. Steven Williams's Brill study of the text's medieval reception documents how it was read simultaneously as political philosophy, medical text, and magical manual, making it a key node in the transmission of natural magic.
bibliography: Pseudo-Aristotle. Secretum Secretorum. Ed. Robert Steele. Opera Hactenus Inedita Rogeri Baconi, Fasc. V. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920.

title: Liber de Causis — Prima Causa
title_english: Book of Causes — The First Cause
author: Anonymous (attrib. Aristotle; trans. Gerard of Cremona c. 1185)
date: Arabic c. 9th c.; Latin trans. c. 1185
representative_sentence: Causa prima superior est super omnem narrationem.
latin_text: Causa prima superior est super omnem narrationem.
english_gloss: The First Cause is superior to all description.

vocabulary.definition: causa prima — the First Cause; the Liber de Causis' term for the supreme divine principle, derived from Proclus's Elements of Theology; the text made Neoplatonic emanationist metaphysics available to medieval Latin readers before Proclus was translated

super omnem narrationem — beyond all description; the apophatic theology of the First Cause, which exceeds all predication, connects the Liber de Causis to Pseudo-Dionysian negative theology and influenced Aquinas's proofs for God's existence

source_notes: The Liber de Causis (Book of Causes) is a 9th-century Arabic compilation from Proclus's Elements of Theology, translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona c. 1185 and attributed to Aristotle throughout the medieval period until Aquinas recognized it as Proclean. It was a required text in the medieval university curriculum and the primary vehicle for Neoplatonic emanationist metaphysics before Proclus was available in Latin.
