Its doctrine of causation — the First Cause acts through secondary causes — was fundamental to scholastic accounts of how magic and astrology work through created intermediary causes.
bibliography: Anon. Liber de Causis. Ed. Adriaan Pattin. Louvain: Tijdschrift voor Filosofie, 1966.

title: Formicarius — De Strigibus
title_english: Formicary — On Strigas
author: Ioannes Nider
representative_sentence: Striga est mulier quae per diaboli pactum infantes necat et de eorum corporibus sibi et sociis suis cibum parat.
latin_text: Striga est mulier quae per diaboli pactum infantes necat et de eorum corporibus sibi et sociis suis cibum parat.
english_gloss: A striga is a woman who through a pact with the devil kills infants and prepares food from their bodies for herself and her associates.

vocabulary.definition: striga — witch, night-hag; originally a Roman term for a nocturnal creature that fed on infant blood; Nider's use of striga in Formicarius V marks the transition from folkloric night-hag to the theologically defined devil-worshipper of the emerging witch concept

pactum diaboli — devil's pact; the defining theological element of the early modern witch: the explicit or implicit contract with Satan that gives the witch her powers; Nider's Formicarius is one of the earliest texts to make this pact-based definition systematic

source_notes: Johannes Nider's Formicarius (c. 1435–1437 CE) is the first major text of what would become the 15th-century witch-hunting movement, building on testimonies from the Alpine witch-trials and the inquisitor Peter of Berne. Book V's discussion of strigas (witches) articulates the key elements of the cumulative witch concept: devil's pact, infanticide, cannibalism, and membership in a sect. Michael Bailey's Battling Demons (2003) demonstrates how Nider synthesized traditional concerns about heresy and demonology to produce the first coherent theory of organized witchcraft.
bibliography: Bailey, Michael D. Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2003.

title: Formicarius — De Pacto
title_english: Formicary — On the Demonic Pact
author: Ioannes Nider
representative_sentence: Magister meus iuravit diabolum venerari et ei obedire in omnibus et Christum abnegavit.
latin_text: Magister meus iuravit diabolum venerari et ei obedire in omnibus et Christum abnegavit.
english_gloss: My master swore to venerate the devil and obey him in all things, and denied Christ.

vocabulary.definition: diabolum venerari — to venerate the devil; the apostatic act at the center of the witch pact in Nider's account, combining the legal concept of oath-taking with the theological concept of apostasy from baptism

Christum abnegare — to deny Christ; the renunciation of baptismal faith required by the devil as the foundational act of the witch's pact; this element connects witch-theory to earlier heresiology and the persecution of apostates

source_notes: Nider's Formicarius records testimony from witch suspects that includes detailed accounts of the initiatory pact with the devil, including oath, renunciation of Christ, and receiving diabolical instruction. These testimonies, whether produced by torture, suggestion, or genuine belief, provided the template for all subsequent witch-trial confessions. Nider's presentation of this material in dialogue form gave it the authority of direct witness testimony rather than theoretical speculation, and the Formicarius became a key source for the Malleus Maleficarum.
bibliography: Bailey, Michael D. Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2003.

title: Summa Perfectionis — De Mercurio
title_english: Sum of Perfection — On Mercury
source: Summa Perfectionis Magisterii, Liber I, cap. 12
author: Pseudo-Geber (Paulus de Taranto, attrib. Jabir ibn Hayyan)
representative_sentence: Argentum vivum, quod in omnibus metallis latet, est materia prima et causa omnium metallorum.
latin_text: Argentum vivum, quod in omnibus metallis latet, est materia prima et causa omnium metallorum.
english_gloss: Quicksilver, which lies hidden in all metals, is the prime matter and the cause of all metals.

vocabulary.definition: argentum vivum — quicksilver, mercury; in Geber's mercury-sulphur theory of metals, mercury (combined with sulphur) is the material principle of all metals; the theory dominated Latin alchemy until the 16th century

materia prima — prime matter; the substrate underlying all physical substance in Aristotelian philosophy; alchemists identified prime matter with mercury (or mercury-and-sulphur) as the substrate of metallic transformation

source_notes: The Summa Perfectionis (c. 1270–1300 CE), attributed to the Arabic alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber) but identified by William R. Newman as a Latin original probably by Paulus de Taranto, is the most technically sophisticated Latin alchemical text and the foundation of the Western theoretical alchemy tradition. Its mercury-sulphur theory of metallic composition, derived from Arabic alchemy, dominated alchemical theory from the 13th through the 16th centuries. Newman's Gehennical Fire (1991) established the text's Latin authorship and its importance for the history of chemistry.
bibliography: Newman, William R. The Summa Perfectionis of Pseudo-Geber: A Critical Edition, Translation and Study. Leiden: Brill, 1991.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum — De Fermentatione
title_english: Rosary of the Philosophers — On Fermentation
author: Anonymous (attrib. Arnald of Villanova)
representative_sentence: Aurum est fermentum solis, argentum est fermentum lunae; sine fermento nulla perfectio fieri potest.
latin_text: Aurum est fermentum solis, argentum est fermentum lunae; sine fermento nulla perfectio fieri potest.
english_gloss: Gold is the leaven of the sun, silver is the leaven of the moon; without leaven no perfection can be achieved.

vocabulary.definition: fermentum — ferment, leaven; the alchemical term for the catalyst that transforms base metals into noble ones, analogous to bread-leavening; gold and silver as fermenta connect alchemical theory to natural processes of biological transformation

perfectio — perfection; the goal of the alchemical work — the achievement of the perfect metal (gold) through the completion of the Philosopher's Stone; perfectio carries both material and spiritual implications in the alchemical tradition

source_notes: The Rosarium Philosophorum (c. 14th century, attributed to Arnald of Villanova though this is uncertain) is one of the most widely cited Latin alchemical texts of the medieval and Renaissance periods, notable for its extensive use of dialogue, allegory, and illustration (in the 1550 Frankfurt printed edition). The fermentation doctrine — that gold and silver act as catalysts for the transformation of base metals — is one of the technical mechanisms of the Great Work. Barbara Obrist and Chiara Crisciani have analyzed the Rosarium's place in the medieval alchemical tradition.
bibliography: Anon. Rosarium Philosophorum. In Artis Auriferae. Basel: Waldkirch, 1593. // Obrist, Barbara. Les débuts de l'imagerie alchimique. Paris: Le Sycomore, 1982.

title: Liber Lunae — Mansio Tertia
title_english: Book of the Moon — Third Lunar Mansion
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: In tertia mansione fac imaginem gladii stricti et pone sub eo nomen inimici et effigiem eius.
latin_text: In tertia mansione fac imaginem gladii stricti et pone sub eo nomen inimici et effigiem eius.
english_gloss: In the third mansion, make an image of an unsheathed sword and place under it the name of the enemy and his likeness.

vocabulary.definition: mansio — lunar mansion; one of the 28 divisions of the moon's monthly path through the zodiac used in Arabic-derived astral image magic; each mansion has specific operative properties and appropriate magical images

imago gladii — image of a sword; the specific talisman appropriate to the third lunar mansion, used for aggressive operations against enemies; the correspondence of mansion images to martial operations is a core feature of the Liber Lunae system

source_notes: The Liber Lunae (Book of the Moon) is an Arabic-Latin magical text that assigns specific magical images and operations to each of the 28 lunar mansions. It is one of a cluster of texts (with Picatrix, the Liber Razielis, and the Magical Calendar) that brought Arabic lunar mansion astrology into the Latin West in the 12th–13th centuries. The text was cited in the Speculum Astronomiae's list of 'detestable' books as particularly dangerous because of its combination of astral images with demon invocation.
bibliography: Lory, Pierre, and Charles Burnett. 'Al-Kindi's Book of the Degrees of the Sword' and Related Material. Forthcoming. // Burnett, Charles. Magic and Divination in the Middle Ages. Aldershot: Variorum, 1996.

title: Sortes Sanctorum — Formula
title_english: Lots of the Saints — Lot-Casting Formula
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Aperi librum sanctum et mitte digitum super versum et quaere quod Deus tibi in illo ostenderit.
latin_text: Aperi librum sanctum et mitte digitum super versum et quaere quod Deus tibi in illo ostenderit.
english_gloss: Open the holy book and place your finger on a verse and seek what God will show you in it.

vocabulary.definition: Sortes Sanctorum — lots of the saints; random selection of Bible verses or saint texts for divination; condemned by councils but widely practiced, representing the tension between orthodox condemnation of sortilege and popular desire for divine guidance

liber sanctus — holy book; in Sortes practice, the Bible or a psalter opened at random; the sanctity of the text was used to legitimize what was in practice sortilege, a form of divination repeatedly condemned by councils from Vannes (461) onward

source_notes: Sortes Sanctorum (lots of the saints) refers to a variety of practices using sacred texts for divination, from random Bible-opening to dedicated sortilege books organized around numerical keys. The practice was condemned by the Council of Vannes (461 CE) and repeatedly by later councils and penitentials, yet it persisted throughout the medieval period and beyond, attested in manuscript collections alongside psalters and Books of Hours. The persistence of this practice despite condemnation illustrates the gap between ecclesiastical prohibition and popular religious practice.
bibliography: Klingshirn, William E. 'Defining the Sortes Sanctorum: Gibbon, Du Cange, and Early Christian Lot Divination.' Journal of Early Christian Studies 10 (2002): 77–130.

title: Condemnatio Parisiensis — De Imaginibus
title_english: Paris Condemnation — On Magical Images
author: Stephanus Tempier (Bishop of Paris)
representative_sentence: Quod per caracteres et figuras magicos et per carmina aliqua fieri potest operatio miraculosa.
latin_text: Quod per caracteres et figuras magicos et per carmina aliqua fieri potest operatio miraculosa.
english_gloss: That through magical characters and figures and through certain incantations a miraculous operation can be performed.

vocabulary.definition: caracteres et figuras magicos — magical characters and figures; the specific textual and diagrammatic elements of Solomonic and astrological talismanic magic; condemned by Tempier as implying that material instruments can produce supernatural effects without divine will

operatio miraculosa — miraculous operation; the article condemns the claim that magical procedures can produce genuinely miraculous effects, i.e., effects that exceed natural causation, which would imply demonic assistance or rival divine power

source_notes: The Paris Condemnation of 1277, issued by Bishop Étienne Tempier at the behest of Pope John XXI, condemned 219 philosophical and theological propositions including several bearing on magic, astrology, and talismanic practice. Article 154 explicitly condemns the claim that magical characters can produce miraculous effects, targeting the Solomonic and Hermetic talisman tradition. The Condemnation disrupted the development of naturalistic astrological magic at Paris and was the most important single act of academic anti-magic censorship in the medieval period.
bibliography: Piché, David, ed. La condamnation parisienne de 1277. Paris: Vrin, 1999.

title: Geomantia — Via
title_english: Geomancy — The Figure Via
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Via significat viam, iter, et transitum, et est figura lunae complentis, indicans res in motu positas.
latin_text: Via significat viam, iter, et transitum, et est figura lunae complentis, indicans res in motu positas.
english_gloss: Via signifies way, journey, and passage, and it is the figure of the completing moon, indicating things set in motion.

vocabulary.definition: via — the geomantic figure Via (Way); one of the sixteen figures of Arabic-Latin geomancy, consisting of four pairs of points, assigned lunar and other astrological correspondences in geomantic tradition

luna complens — the completing moon; the full moon as planetary ruler of the Via figure; the assignment of each geomantic figure to a planet and zodiacal sign was the primary interpretive framework for reading the geomantic chart

source_notes: Geomancy (earth-divination) was introduced to the Latin West from Arabic sources in the 12th century and became the most widely practiced learned divination system of the medieval and Renaissance periods, documented in hundreds of manuscripts. The system generates sixteen figures (each a pattern of odd/even dot-rows) through randomized dot-making, assembles them into a shield-chart, and reads their interactions according to astrological correspondences. Teodoro Bonatti's Liber Astronomicus (c. 1282) and numerous anonymous treatises defined the Latin geomantic tradition that Agrippa synthesized in De Occulta Philosophia II.
bibliography: Burnett, Charles. 'The Earliest Chiromancy in the West.' Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 50 (1987): 189–195. // Skinner, Stephen. Geomancy in Theory and Practice. Singapore: Golden Hoard Press, 2011.

title: De Proprietatibus Rerum — De Adamante
title_english: On the Properties of Things — On the Diamond
author: Bartholomaeus Anglicus
representative_sentence: Adamas est lapis omni tempore aquis vel sanguini immixtus venena dissolvit et fantasmata nocturna repellit.
latin_text: Adamas est lapis omni tempore aquis vel sanguini immixtus venena dissolvit et fantasmata nocturna repellit.
english_gloss: The diamond is a stone which, mixed at any time with water or blood, dissolves poisons and repels nocturnal phantoms.

vocabulary.definition: adamas — diamond; literally 'unconquerable' in Greek; the hardest stone in the lapidary tradition, assigned protective and counter-magical properties in sources from Pliny through Bartholomaeus and Albertus Magnus

fantasmata nocturna — nocturnal phantoms, night-terrors; demonic or spectral appearances during the night; the diamond's protective power against night-phantoms connects lapidary medicine to demonological concerns about demonic visitation

source_notes: Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De Proprietatibus Rerum (c. 1230–1240 CE) was the most popular medieval encyclopaedia of natural properties and one of the first books printed in the vernacular. Its entries on stones, plants, and animals consistently blend Galenic medicine, Aristotelian natural philosophy, and lapidary magical tradition into a synthetic natural magic of properties. Along with Hildegard's Physica and Vincent of Beauvais's Speculum Naturale, it was the primary vehicle for natural magical lore among non-specialist medieval readers.
bibliography: Bartholomaeus Anglicus. On the Properties of Things: John Trevisa's Translation of Bartholomaeus Anglicus, De Proprietatibus Rerum. Ed. M.C. Seymour. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1975.

title: Speculum Naturale — De Magis
title_english: Natural Mirror — On the Magi
author: Vincentius Bellovacensis
representative_sentence: Magi in principio ex gentibus erant qui in observatione siderum callentes futura praedicebant.
latin_text: Magi in principio ex gentibus erant qui in observatione siderum callentes futura praedicebant.
english_gloss: The magi were in the beginning from among the gentiles, those skilled in the observation of the stars who predicted the future.

vocabulary.definition: magus — magus, the Magi; Vincent uses the term for both the wise men of Matthew 2 and the general class of astrologer-diviners, reflecting the ambiguity in medieval usage between the honorable Magi of the Epiphany and the condemned practitioners of magic

observatio siderum — observation of the stars; the oldest definition of the magi's craft as stellar observation; this characterization allowed medieval writers to treat the Magi of Matthew's Gospel as legitimate astronomers while condemning contemporary astrologers as magicians

source_notes: Vincent of Beauvais's Speculum Maius (c. 1244–1259 CE) is the most extensive medieval encyclopaedia, gathering material from patristic, classical, and Arabic sources into a vast synthesis. Its treatment of magic in the Speculum Naturale draws primarily on Isidore and Augustine while incorporating newer Arabic-Latin material. As the largest single gathering of medieval learning, the Speculum was a key vehicle for transmitting both condemnatory and descriptive material about magic to educated medieval readers across Europe.
bibliography: Vincent of Beauvais. Speculum Naturale. Douai: Balthazar Bellerus, 1624 (repr. Graz: Akademische Druck- und Verlagsanstalt, 1964).

title: Physiognomia — De Facie
title_english: Physiognomy — On the Face
author: Michael Scottus
representative_sentence: Qui habent oculos viridem colorem sicut aqua profunda, astuti sunt et in rebus occultis prudentes.
latin_text: Qui habent oculos viridem colorem sicut aqua profunda, astuti sunt et in rebus occultis prudentes.
english_gloss: Those who have eyes of a green color like deep water are shrewd and prudent in occult matters.

vocabulary.definition: physiognomia — physiognomy; the art of reading character and fortune from physical features, especially the face; a major Arabic-derived divinatory art transmitted to the Latin West by Michael Scot and Peter of Abano

rebus occultis — occult matters; the term occultus (hidden) applied to natural properties beyond ordinary perception; Michael Scot's physiognomy treats the face as a legible map of the soul's hidden qualities, connecting the divinatory with the natural-philosophical

source_notes: Michael Scot (c. 1175–c. 1232 CE) was the most important Latin translator and adaptor of Arabic science in the early 13th century, translating Aristotle, Averroes, and Avicenna for the court of Frederick II. His Physiognomia draws on Arabic physiognomic tradition to describe how bodily features reveal character and occult qualities. Scot was associated with magical practice in later legend (Dante places him in Hell among the diviners) and his reputation as a court astrologer and natural philosopher made him a liminal figure between learned science and magical practice.
bibliography: Thorndike, Lynn. Michael Scot. London: Nelson, 1965.

title: Conciliator — De Astrologia Medica
title_english: Conciliator — On Medical Astrology
author: Petrus de Abano
representative_sentence: Caelestia corpora esse causas efficientes omnium rerum in hac inferiori generatione, nemo sapiens negabit.
latin_text: Caelestia corpora esse causas efficientes omnium rerum in hac inferiori generatione, nemo sapiens negabit.
english_gloss: That celestial bodies are the efficient causes of all things in this lower generation, no wise person will deny.

vocabulary.definition: causa efficiens — efficient cause; Aristotelian causal category applied to astrological causation; Peter of Abano's claim that planets are efficient causes of sublunary events is a strong astrological determinism that he sought to reconcile with free will and Christian doctrine

generatio — generation, the sublunary sphere; Aristotelian term for the region below the moon where generation and corruption occur, under the influence of celestial movements — the basis for astrological medicine

source_notes: Peter of Abano's Conciliator (c. 1303–1310 CE) is the most ambitious medieval attempt to reconcile Greek medicine (especially Galen) with Arabic astrology and Aristotelian natural philosophy. His strong astrological position — that celestial bodies are efficient causes of all sublunary events including human diseases — brought him into conflict with the Inquisition. He was posthumously condemned as a heretic. The Conciliator was nevertheless widely read and taught at the University of Padua, making Peter a key figure in the Paduan tradition of naturalistic astral causation.
bibliography: Peter of Abano. Conciliator Differentiarum Philosophorum et Medicorum. Venice: Giunta, 1565.

title: Dialogus Miraculorum — De Daemonibus
title_english: Dialogue of Miracles — On Demons
author: Caesarius Heisterbacensis
representative_sentence: Daemon in specie mulieris pulcherrimae iuveni apparuit dicens: Ego sum domina tua, quam tu semper amasti.
latin_text: Daemon in specie mulieris pulcherrimae iuveni apparuit dicens: Ego sum domina tua, quam tu semper amasti.
english_gloss: A demon appeared to a young man in the form of a most beautiful woman, saying: I am your lady, whom you have always loved.

vocabulary.definition: in specie mulieris — in the form of a woman; demonic shape-shifting into beautiful women was one of the most commonly recorded forms of demonic seduction in medieval exempla literature, related to later accounts of the succubus

species — outward form, appearance; the theological question of whether demons have real bodies or merely adopt appearances was central to scholastic demonology, bearing directly on whether demonic seduction and pacts were physically real

source_notes: Caesarius of Heisterbach's Dialogus Miraculorum (c. 1219–1223 CE) is the most important collection of exempla (moral tales) from the Cistercian tradition, containing hundreds of stories about demonic apparitions, possessions, and temptations. Its demonological tales were influential in shaping popular and clerical understanding of how demons operate: appearing in disguise, tempting through the senses, creating illusions, and sometimes entering into explicit compacts. The Dialogus was a major source for subsequent preachers and writers on demonic activity.
bibliography: Caesarius of Heisterbach. Dialogus Miraculorum. Ed. J. Strange. Cologne: Heberle, 1851.

title: De Nugis Curialium — De Fata
title_english: Courtiers' Trifles — On Fairies
author: Walterus Mapes
representative_sentence: Gens illa antiqua Morganis nomen habet, quae per silvas et montes et speluncas oberrat.
latin_text: Gens illa antiqua Morganis nomen habet, quae per silvas et montes et speluncas oberrat.
english_gloss: That ancient people has the name of Morgan, which wanders through forests and mountains and caves.

vocabulary.definition: Morgan — the fairy woman, Morgan le Fay; Walter Map's reference to the Arthurian fairy Morgan as leader of a spirit people represents the intersection of learned Latin culture with vernacular fairy tradition in 12th-century court literature

gens antiqua — ancient people; the identification of fairies as an ancient supernatural race (rather than demons or souls of the dead) is one of several competing medieval theories about fairy nature, with different implications for magical practice involving them

source_notes: Walter Map's De Nugis Curialium (c. 1181–1193 CE) is a miscellany of court gossip, folklore, and exempla that preserves early Arthurian material alongside accounts of encounters with supernatural beings. His references to Morgan and fairy people are among the earliest Latin witnesses to the fairy mythology that flourished in 12th–13th-century vernacular literature. Map's work documents the interface between learned clerical Latin culture and the vernacular fairy traditions that would later intersect with witch-trial testimony about spirit familiars.
bibliography: Walter Map. De Nugis Curialium. Ed. M.R. James, rev. C.N.L. Brooke and R.A.B. Mynors. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1983.

title: Liber Florum — Visio Mariae
title_english: Book of Flowers — Vision of the Virgin
source: Liber Florum Caelestis Doctrinae, Liber Visionum, cap. 1
author: Ioannes de Morigiis (John of Morigny)
representative_sentence: Apparuit mihi Virgo Maria et dixit: Liber quem scribis non est diaboli sed dei, quia ego dedi tibi eum.
latin_text: Apparuit mihi Virgo Maria et dixit: Liber quem scribis non est diaboli sed dei, quia ego dedi tibi eum.
english_gloss: The Virgin Mary appeared to me and said: The book you are writing is not the devil's but God's, because I gave it to you.

vocabulary.definition: Virgo Maria — the Virgin Mary; John of Morigny's visionary authorization of his magical system through Marian apparitions is a remarkable strategy for legitimizing a text closely related to the condemned Ars Notoria by replacing angelic authority with Marian patronage

non est diaboli sed dei — it is not the devil's but God's; John's self-defense against the charge that his visionary magic is demonic; the Liber Florum was burned by the Bishop of Orléans c. 1323, showing that the Marian legitimization strategy failed to satisfy ecclesiastical authorities

source_notes: John of Morigny's Liber Florum Caelestis Doctrinae (c. 1301–1315 CE) is a remarkable text at the intersection of Ars Notoria tradition and Christian visionary literature. John, a Benedictine monk, began using the Ars Notoria and claimed to receive visions from the Virgin Mary authorizing a reformed magical practice. The book was condemned and burned, but John revised it to make it more orthodox. Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson's critical edition has established it as a central document in the history of medieval angelic magic and its relationship to Christian mysticism.
bibliography: John of Morigny. Liber Florum Caelestis Doctrinae: The Flowers of Heavenly Teaching. Ed. Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson. Toronto: Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 2015.

title: Liber Razielis — Sigillum Angeli
title_english: Book of Raziel — Seal of the Angel
author: Anonymous (attrib. Raziel; trans. from Hebrew c. 13th century)
date: Hebrew c. 7th–13th c.; Latin c. 13th century
representative_sentence: Qui portaverit hoc sigillum in se securum se credat ab omni periculo et a potentia malignorum spirituum.
latin_text: Qui portaverit hoc sigillum in se securum se credat ab omni periculo et a potentia malignorum spirituum.
english_gloss: Whoever carries this seal on them may consider themselves safe from all danger and from the power of malicious spirits.

vocabulary.definition: sigillum — seal, magical sigil; in the Liber Razielis tradition, sigils are diagrammatic representations of angelic names and powers with protective and operative functions; the sigil tradition connects Hebrew angel magic to the broader Western magical character tradition

spiritus malignus — malicious spirit, evil spirit; the primary threat against which the Liber Razielis's protective seals are directed; the text's combination of Jewish angelology with protective amulet practice made it widely popular in both Jewish and Christian magical contexts

source_notes: The Liber Razielis Angeli (Book of the Angel Raziel) is a Latin compilation based partly on Hebrew magical texts, including the Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh, produced at the court of Alfonso X of Castile in the mid-13th century. It combines Jewish angelology and demonology with Arabic astrological magic and Christian liturgical elements into a comprehensive system of angel-magic and amulet production. The text was one of the channels through which Jewish kabbalistic angel lore entered the Latin magical tradition; Agrippa drew on it in De Occulta Philosophia III.
bibliography: Hamori, Esther J. Women's Divination in Biblical Literature: Prophecy, Necromancy, and Other Arts of Knowledge. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2015. // Véronèse, Julien. 'Magic, Theurgy and Spirituality in the Medieval Ritual of the Ars Notoria.' In Invoking Angels. Ed. Claire Fanger. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2012.

title: Ars Generalis Ultima — De Principiis
title_english: Final Great Art — On the Principles
author: Raimundus Lullus
representative_sentence: Haec ars est generalis ad omnes scientias, quia continet principia communia quae in omnibus scientiis reperiuntur.
latin_text: Haec ars est generalis ad omnes scientias, quia continet principia communia quae in omnibus scientiis reperiuntur.
english_gloss: This art is general to all sciences, because it contains common principles that are found in all sciences.

vocabulary.definition: ars generalis — the general art; Lull's combinatorial system for generating all knowledge by rotating diagrams of divine attributes (Bonitas, Magnitudo, etc.); the mechanical generation of knowledge through divine-name combinations made Lull's Ars a model for later kabbalistic and magical memory systems

principia communia — common principles; Lull's nine divine attributes (B-K) that serve as the foundation for all knowledge; their combinatorial manipulation through the rotating circles of the Ars was designed to prove all propositions of natural philosophy, theology, and ethics

source_notes: Ramon Lull's Ars Generalis Ultima (c. 1308 CE) is the final and most complete version of his combinatorial philosophical system (the 'Ars'), which uses rotating diagrams to generate all possible combinations of divine attributes as the basis for universal knowledge. While not a magical text, Lull's Ars was appropriated by Renaissance writers (especially Agrippa and Giorgi) as a model for kabbalistic and magical combination of divine names. Frances Yates's The Art of Memory (1966) traced the influence of Lull's combinatorial system on Renaissance memory arts and magical philosophy.
bibliography: Lull, Ramon. Selected Works of Ramon Llull. Ed. and trans. Anthony Bonner. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1985.

title: Causae et Curae — De Mania
title_english: Causes and Cures — On Madness
author: Hildegardis Bingensis
representative_sentence: Si diabolus nimium operatur in aliquo, per ministerium humorum eius id facit.
latin_text: Si diabolus nimium operatur in aliquo, per ministerium humorum eius id facit.
english_gloss: If the devil operates excessively in someone, he does so through the medium of that person's humours.

vocabulary.definition: ministerium humorum — the medium of the humours; Hildegard's psycho-medical theory that demonic activity works through natural bodily channels (humoral imbalance) represents a characteristic medieval integration of natural medicine with demonology

diabolus — the devil; in Hildegard's medical theology, the devil can exploit natural bodily weaknesses rather than directly possessing the body, a more nuanced demonology than simple possession theories

source_notes: Hildegard of Bingen's Causae et Curae (Causes and Cures, c. 1150–1158 CE) is a medical cosmology that explains diseases, including mental illness, in terms of humoral theory interacting with cosmic forces and demonic activity. Her position that the devil operates through natural channels (humours) rather than direct possession was a sophisticated integration of medical and theological frameworks. Hildegard's medical texts show how the boundary between natural healing and magical-religious practice was navigated by a major 12th-century religious intellectual.
bibliography: Hildegard of Bingen. Causae et Curae. Ed. Laurence Moulinier. Berlin: Akademie Verlag, 2003.

title: De Radiis — Prima Propositio
title_english: On Rays — First Proposition
source: De Radiis Stellarum (De Radiis), Propositio I
author: Alcindi (al-Kindi; attrib.)
date: Arabic c. 830–870 CE; Latin c. 12th century
representative_sentence: Mundus iste inferior est quasi speculum obtusum et densum, in quo caelestes influentiae et virtutes rebus imprimuntur.
latin_text: Mundus iste inferior est quasi speculum obtusum et densum, in quo caelestes influentiae et virtutes rebus imprimuntur.
english_gloss: This lower world is like a dull and dense mirror, in which celestial influences and powers are imprinted on things.

vocabulary.definition: radii stellarum — rays of the stars; al-Kindi's thesis that all celestial bodies emit rays that carry their specific influences throughout the sublunary world provided the physical mechanism for both astrological influence and talismanic magic

speculum obtusum — dull mirror; the sublunary world as imperfect reflector of celestial light and power; the mirror metaphor connects al-Kindi's ray theory to Neoplatonic emanation and to the broader medieval theme of the created world as a mirror of divine order

source_notes: Al-Kindi's De Radiis (On Rays, c. 830–870 CE; Latin c. 12th century) is the most systematic ancient or medieval account of astral causation as a physical process of ray-emission. Its first proposition — that all objects emit rays that influence their surroundings — provides a universal theory of sympathy and antipathy, a mechanism for both natural magic and talismanic practice. The text was a major source for the 13th-century natural magic tradition and was cited by Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus, and the author of the Speculum Astronomiae.
bibliography: al-Kindi. De Radiis. Ed. M.-T. d'Alverny and F. Hudry. Archives d'Histoire Doctrinale et Littéraire du Moyen Age 41 (1975): 139–260.

title: De Vita — Sol Talisman
title_english: On Life — The Solar Talisman
source: De Vita Libri Tres, Liber III (De Vita Coelitus Comparanda), cap. 8
author: Marsilius Ficinus
representative_sentence: Imaginem solis ex auro vel electro quae formam regis habeat in pectore vel in annulo gestare prodest.
latin_text: Imaginem solis ex auro vel electro quae formam regis habeat in pectore vel in annulo gestare prodest.
english_gloss: It is beneficial to wear an image of the sun made from gold or electrum having the form of a king, on the breast or in a ring.

vocabulary.definition: imago solis — solar image, sun talisman; the astral talisman made under solar influence is central to Ficino's practical magic in De Vita III; the solar image channels the Sun's vivifying spirit to counteract the melancholy associated with Saturn

electrum — electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy; Ficino's specification of solar metals (gold, electrum) for the solar talisman reflects the doctrine of planetary correspondences at the heart of his astral-magical system

source_notes: Ficino's De Vita Coelitus Comparanda (1489 CE) is the most important Renaissance text on astral-talismanic magic, offering a naturalistic account of how solar and Jovial images can attract beneficial celestial spirit (spiritus mundi). Ficino was careful to defend his position as natural philosophy rather than demonic magic, following Proclus and Plotinus on sympathetic action. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (1958) remains the standard analysis of Ficino's magical theory and its Renaissance influence.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Three Books on Life. Trans. Carol V. Kaske and John R. Clark. Binghamton: MRTS, 1989.

title: De Vita — Spiritus Mundi
title_english: On Life — World Spirit
source: De Vita Libri Tres, Liber III, cap. 1
author: Marsilius Ficinus
representative_sentence: Est et in toto mundi corpore spiritus quidam universalis qui per omnia penetrat atque omnia vivificat.
latin_text: Est et in toto mundi corpore spiritus quidam universalis qui per omnia penetrat atque omnia vivificat.
english_gloss: There is also in the whole body of the world a certain universal spirit which penetrates through all things and vivifies all things.

vocabulary.definition: spiritus universalis — universal world-spirit; Ficino's key concept for how celestial influence is transmitted to the sublunary world; the spiritus mundi mediates between the purely immaterial World Soul and material bodies, making it the vehicle of all magical operations

omnia vivificat — vivifies all things; the animating function of the world-spirit identifies Ficino's magic with a form of pneumatic medicine — attracting more world-spirit through diet, music, scent, and astrological images to counteract melancholic depletion

source_notes: The doctrine of spiritus mundi (world-spirit) in De Vita III is Ficino's central theoretical contribution to Renaissance magic: a pneumatic substrate filling the cosmos that transmits celestial influence and can be attracted or repelled through sensory and astrological means. The doctrine synthesizes Stoic pneumatology, Neoplatonic world-soul theory, and Galenic medical pneumatics. Brian P. Copenhaver's analysis in 'Scholastic Philosophy and Renaissance Magic in the De Vita of Marsilio Ficino' (1984) remains essential for understanding the technical background.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Three Books on Life. Trans. Carol V. Kaske and John R. Clark. Binghamton: MRTS, 1989.

title: Conclusiones — De Magia
title_english: Nine Hundred Conclusions — On Magic
author: Ioannes Picus Mirandulanus
representative_sentence: Magia naturalis nil aliud est quam perfecta cognitio omnium rerum naturalium.
latin_text: Magia naturalis nil aliud est quam perfecta cognitio omnium rerum naturalium.
english_gloss: Natural magic is nothing other than the perfect knowledge of all natural things.

vocabulary.definition: magia naturalis — natural magic; Pico's definition identifies natural magic with the highest form of natural knowledge, a position that made him the Renaissance's most influential defender of magic as philosophy rather than sorcery

perfecta cognitio — perfect knowledge; natural magic for Pico is epistemic perfection about nature, not mere technique; this intellectualist definition elevated magic to the status of natural philosophy and shaped the entire subsequent Renaissance magical tradition

source_notes: Pico della Mirandola's Conclusiones Nongentae (1486 CE) — 900 theses he proposed to debate publicly in Rome — include the first systematic defense of natural magic and the first explicit combination of magic with Kabbalah as complementary paths to natural and divine knowledge. The theses provoked papal condemnation of thirteen propositions and Pico's subsequent imprisonment. His Apologia defending the condemned theses is the founding document of the Renaissance natural magic tradition. Brian P. Copenhaver has edited and analyzed the magical and kabbalistic theses.
bibliography: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Syncretism in the West: Pico's 900 Theses. Ed. and trans. S.A. Farmer. Tempe: MRTS, 1998.

title: Oratio de Dignitate Hominis — De Mago
title_english: Oration on Human Dignity — On the Magus
author: Ioannes Picus Mirandulanus
representative_sentence: Magus enim est naturae minister, et non quasi per externa aliqua miracula, sed per intimam rerum naturam ad effectus operatur.
latin_text: Magus enim est naturae minister, et non quasi per externa aliqua miracula, sed per intimam rerum naturam ad effectus operatur.
english_gloss: For the magus is the servant of nature, and works toward effects not as if through external miracles, but through the intimate nature of things.

vocabulary.definition: naturae minister — servant of nature; Pico's redefinition of the magus as nature's servant rather than its master is a key move in legitimizing natural magic as a form of natural science that works with rather than against natural order

intimam rerum naturam — the intimate nature of things; the hidden occult properties of natural objects that the natural magician exploits; 'intimate' here means inner and essential rather than superficial and visible

source_notes: Pico's Oratio de Dignitate Hominis (c. 1486–1487 CE), often called the 'Manifesto of the Renaissance,' includes a celebrated passage on the magus as nature's minister that was fundamental to the subsequent Renaissance defense of natural magic. The passage redefines magic from demonic pact to mastery of natural philosophy, making the magus a kind of proto-scientist who understands nature's hidden causes. The Oratio was not published until after Pico's death in 1494.
bibliography: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Oration on the Dignity of Man. Trans. Francesco Borghesi et al. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012.

title: De Verbo Mirifico — Tetragrammaton
title_english: On the Wonder-Working Word — The Tetragrammaton
author: Ioannes Reuchlin
representative_sentence: Nomen Dei Tetragrammaton est quod Hebraei ineffabile esse dicunt, quod ego Schemhamphoras vocabo.
latin_text: Nomen Dei Tetragrammaton est quod Hebraei ineffabile esse dicunt, quod ego Schemhamphoras vocabo.
english_gloss: The Tetragrammaton is the name of God which the Hebrews say is ineffable, which I shall call Schemhamphoras.

vocabulary.definition: Tetragrammaton — the four-letter divine name (YHWH); Reuchlin's treatment of the Tetragrammaton as the supreme divine name was foundational for Christian Kabbalah and the Renaissance tradition of sacred name magic

Schemhamphoras — the 72-letter or 216-letter name of God derived from Exodus 14; Reuchlin's use of this kabbalistic term introduced it into Christian magical discourse where it became associated with the most powerful operative divine names in grimoire tradition

source_notes: Johannes Reuchlin's De Verbo Mirifico (1494 CE) is the first major Christian Kabbalist text, presenting a dialogue between a Pythagorean, a Jew, and a Christian on the power of divine names. Reuchlin argues that the name Jesus (Yehoshua) is the most powerful of all divine names because it contains the Tetragrammaton with an added letter. His work was foundational for the Christian Kabbalist tradition developed by Pico, Agrippa, and Giorgi, and for Renaissance magic's use of Hebrew divine names.
bibliography: Reuchlin, Johann. De Verbo Mirifico. In On the Art of the Kabbalah. Trans. Martin and Sarah Goodman. New York: Abaris, 1983.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — Sympathia Elementorum
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — Elemental Sympathy
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber I, caput 14
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Quemadmodum magnes ferrum ad se trahit, sic et quaelibet res occultam et propriam ad se rapit virtutem.
latin_text: Quemadmodum magnes ferrum ad se trahit, sic et quaelibet res occultam et propriam ad se rapit virtutem.
english_gloss: Just as the magnet draws iron to itself, so too does every thing seize its own hidden and proper virtue to itself.

vocabulary.definition: magnes — magnet; the loadstone's attraction to iron was the universal ancient and Renaissance example of hidden natural sympathy; Agrippa uses it as the paradigm case for all occult properties that operate without apparent contact or mechanism

virtus occulta — occult virtue, hidden power; the technical term for the specific, non-manifest properties of natural objects that form the basis of natural magic; 'occult' here means simply 'hidden from the senses,' not 'supernatural'

source_notes: Book I of Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia (1531 CE, written c. 1510) is devoted to elemental and natural magic: the occult properties of substances, their sympathies and antipathies, and how these can be manipulated for magical effects. The magnet-iron analogy was the paradigm case for all natural magical operations in the Western tradition from Pliny through Ficino and Agrippa. Vittoria Perrone Compagni's critical edition (1992) is the standard text.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — De Suffumigationibus
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — On Suffumigations
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber I, caput 43
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Suffumigatio convocatoria daemonum fit ex radicibus coriandri, aconiti, cicutae et aliis veneno actis.
latin_text: Suffumigatio convocatoria daemonum fit ex radicibus coriandri, aconiti, cicutae et aliis veneno actis.
english_gloss: The suffumigation for convoking demons is made from roots of coriander, aconite, hemlock, and other poisonous substances.

vocabulary.definition: suffumigatio convocatoria — convocatory suffumigation; the class of incense-burning operations designed to attract or summon supernatural beings; Agrippa systematizes the correspondence between specific aromatic substances and specific supernatural entities

cicuta — hemlock; a poisonous plant whose dangerous fumes were believed to attract and please demonic entities; the association of poison with demons reflects the ancient link between veneficium (poisoning/magic) and demonic pact

source_notes: Agrippa's treatment of suffumigations in De Occulta Philosophia I.43 systematizes the correspondence between aromatic substances and supernatural beings across the spectrum from benefic angels (sweet, solar aromatics) to malefic demons (foul, poisonous substances). This synthesis drew on Picatrix, al-Kindi's De Radiis, and the herbal tradition to create the most comprehensive Renaissance account of olfactory magic. The chapter illustrates how Agrippa integrated Arabic, Neoplatonic, and folk-magical elements into a single system.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — Characteres Planetarum
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — Planetary Characters
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber II, caput 22
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Planetarum characteres sunt signa specialia quae magici solent pingere in laminis metallicis sub aspectu planetarum confectis.
latin_text: Planetarum characteres sunt signa specialia quae magici solent pingere in laminis metallicis sub aspectu planetarum confectis.
english_gloss: The characters of the planets are special signs which magicians customarily paint on metallic plates made under the aspect of the planets.

vocabulary.definition: character — magical character, planetary sign; the diagrammatic symbols associated with each planet used to inscribe talismans; Agrippa's systematic treatment of planetary characters drew on the Picatrix, Sefer Raziel, and other sources to produce the most comprehensive Renaissance catalogue

lamina metallica — metallic plate; the material substrate for planetary talismans; each planet corresponds to a specific metal (Saturn-lead, Jupiter-tin, Mars-iron, Sun-gold, Venus-copper, Mercury-quicksilver, Moon-silver), and talismans must be made from the appropriate metal

source_notes: Book II of Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia covers celestial magic: the astrological correspondences, planetary characters, angelic names, and magical squares associated with each of the seven planets. This synthesis of Arabic astral magic (from Picatrix and related texts) with Neoplatonic and Hermetic planetary theology produced the most systematic Renaissance account of celestial magic and became the standard reference for talismanic practice from the 16th century to the present. Wouter Hanegraaff has analyzed Agrippa's synthetic methodology.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — Kabbalah
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — On Kabbalah
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber III, caput 10
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Kabbalah est acceptio traditionis, disciplina de rebus divinis maxime contemplativa.
latin_text: Kabbalah est acceptio traditionis, disciplina de rebus divinis maxime contemplativa.
english_gloss: Kabbalah is the reception of tradition, a discipline most highly contemplative of divine things.

vocabulary.definition: Kabbalah — Jewish mystical tradition; Agrippa's definition captures the esoteric character of Kabbalistic knowledge as received, traditional wisdom; his treatment in DOP III synthesizes Jewish Kabbalah with Christian angelology and ceremonial magic

acceptio traditionis — reception of tradition; the literal meaning of 'Kabbalah' (Hebrew: qabbalah, 'receiving'); Agrippa's etymological definition emphasizes the revealed, non-speculative character of kabbalistic knowledge as transmitted wisdom rather than philosophical argument

source_notes: Book III of Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia is devoted to ceremonial and divine magic: the names of God and angels, Kabbalah, divine names in Hebrew and their operative uses, and the theory of the immortal soul's magical capacities. Agrippa's synthesis of Christian Kabbalah (from Pico and Reuchlin) with practical ceremonial magic (from the grimoire tradition) was the most ambitious Renaissance attempt to unify speculative and operative magic in a single philosophical framework. Wouter Hanegraaff's Agrippa's Occult Philosophy and the History of Magic (2012) is the authoritative modern study.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: De Incertitudine — De Artibus Magicis
title_english: On the Uncertainty — On the Magical Arts
source: De Incertitudine et Vanitate Omnium Scientiarum et Artium, cap. 42
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Magia nihil aliud est quam connectio naturalium rerum per applicationem unius ad aliam.
latin_text: Magia nihil aliud est quam connectio naturalium rerum per applicationem unius ad aliam.
english_gloss: Magic is nothing other than the connection of natural things through the application of one to another.

vocabulary.definition: connectio naturalium rerum — the connection of natural things; Agrippa's minimal definition of natural magic as simply the practical application of sympathies and antipathies, stripped of demonic or supernatural elements

applicationem — application; the practical, operative side of natural magic: bringing things with natural affinity into contact to produce desired effects; Agrippa's language here prefigures Francis Bacon's definition of magic as applied natural philosophy

source_notes: Agrippa's De Incertitudine et Vanitate Omnium Scientiarum et Artium (1530 CE) is a sceptical deconstruction of all human knowledge, published the year before his De Occulta Philosophia. Its chapter on magic provides a condensed naturalistic definition of magic while simultaneously attacking the pretensions of magical practitioners. The apparent contradiction between the two books has generated much scholarly debate; Charles Nauert and Paola Zambelli have analyzed how the two works complement rather than contradict each other in Agrippa's broader intellectual project.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Incertitudine et Vanitate Omnium Scientiarum et Artium. Cologne: Gymnicus, 1531.

title: Steganographia — Angelus Pamersiel
title_english: Steganography — The Angel Pamersiel
author: Ioannes Trithemius
representative_sentence: Pamersiel ost Delmuson thafloyn machariel bolvuln labonai balumnus Omeran.
latin_text: Pamersiel ost Delmuson thafloyn machariel bolvuln labonai balumnus Omeran.
english_gloss: [Spirit conjuration formula for the angel Pamersiel — a cipher text whose surface reading is an angelic name-sequence and whose hidden reading is an encoded message.]

vocabulary.definition: Pamersiel — a spirit name in Trithemius's Steganographia; like all the 'spirit names' in the Steganographia, Pamersiel is simultaneously a genuine angelic name in the magical tradition and a carrier for encrypted textual information in Trithemius's cipher system

steganographia — hidden writing, steganography; Trithemius coined the term for his system that disguises secret messages as angel-conjuration texts; the work's dual identity (magical grimoire and cipher manual) made it one of the most debated texts of the Renaissance

source_notes: Trithemius's Steganographia (c. 1499 CE, published posthumously 1606) is one of the most enigmatic Renaissance texts, presenting itself as a grimoire for communicating with angelic spirits while actually containing an elaborate cryptographic system for sending secret messages. The question of whether the 'magic' is a cover for cryptography or vice versa was debated for centuries; Jim Reeds's 1998 decipherment of Book I and II showed that the spirit operations encode cipher tables. The work illustrates the Renaissance intersection of magic, learned secrecy, and information science.
bibliography: Trithemius, Johannes. Steganographia. Frankfurt: Becker, 1606. // Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999.

title: Monas Hieroglyphica — Theorema
title_english: Hieroglyphic Monad — Theorem
author: Ioannes Dee
representative_sentence: Punctum et linea hic ab uno et eodem signo producuntur, et utraque ad circulum aptissima.
latin_text: Punctum et linea hic ab uno et eodem signo producuntur, et utraque ad circulum aptissima.
english_gloss: Point and line are here produced from one and the same sign, and both are most fittingly applied to the circle.

vocabulary.definition: monas hieroglyphica — the hieroglyphic monad; Dee's symbol combining sun, moon, cross, and Aries sign into a single hieroglyph that encodes all natural and divine knowledge; the monad is simultaneously a mathematical symbol, an alchemical operator, and a cosmological diagram

punctum et linea — point and line; Dee begins his analysis with the most fundamental geometrical elements, arguing that the monad sign contains within itself all geometrical and hence all natural relationships; his Euclidean-magical synthesis is characteristic of Renaissance mathematical magic

source_notes: John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica (1564 CE) is the most hermetic of his published works, presenting twenty-four theorems that unfold the cosmic significance of a single hieroglyphic symbol. The work synthesizes Neoplatonic mathematics, alchemy, astronomy, and kabbalistic letter-symbolism into a demonstration that a single sign contains all natural knowledge. Deborah Harkness's analysis of Dee's angel conversations in John Dee's Conversations with Angels shows how the Monas relates to his broader pursuit of prisca sapientia through mathematical-magical means.
bibliography: Dee, John. Monas Hieroglyphica. Trans. C.H. Josten. Ambix 12 (1964): 84–221.

title: De Umbris Idearum — Imago Memoriae
title_english: On the Shadows of Ideas — Memory Image
author: Giordanus Brunus
representative_sentence: Umbrae idelarum sunt rerum omnium species et formae quae in materia sensibili apparent.
latin_text: Umbrae idearum sunt rerum omnium species et formae quae in materia sensibili apparent.
english_gloss: The shadows of ideas are the species and forms of all things which appear in sensible matter.

vocabulary.definition: umbrae idearum — shadows of ideas; Bruno's title concept: the forms appearing in material reality are mere shadows of the Platonic Ideas, but for the magus-philosopher they serve as ascent-points toward the Ideas themselves; this reverses the usual negative valuation of shadows in Platonic tradition

species — form, image; in Bruno's magical memory art, species are not abstract forms but active image-forces that can be manipulated to work on the imagination and through imagination on nature; the magical efficacy of images depends on their status as species bearing intelligible power

source_notes: Giordano Bruno's De Umbris Idearum (1582 CE) is the first of his memory arts works and already reveals his ambitious synthesis of Lullian combinatory method, Hermetic philosophy, and Neoplatonic image theory. The memory art it proposes is simultaneously a practical mnemonic system and a theurgical procedure: by filling the mind with images organized according to cosmic principles, the practitioner aligns their inner life with the structure of reality. Frances Yates's Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964) remains the foundational study of Bruno's magical philosophy.
bibliography: Bruno, Giordano. De Umbris Idearum. Ed. Rita Sturlese. Florence: Olschki, 1991.

title: De Vinculis in Genere — Amor
title_english: On Bonds in General — Love as Bond
author: Giordanus Brunus
representative_sentence: Amor est vinculum vinculorum, et omnis boni principium et finis.
latin_text: Amor est vinculum vinculorum, et omnis boni principium et finis.
english_gloss: Love is the bond of bonds, and the beginning and end of all good.

vocabulary.definition: vinculum vinculorum — bond of bonds; Bruno's culminating formula for love as the supreme magical force; the magus who understands love can bind and unbind all things, making love not just an emotion but a cosmic operative principle

vinculum — bond, chain, ligature; Bruno's theory of vincula (bonds) analyzes all social, psychological, and magical influence in terms of chains binding minds together; the magus operates by attaching and detaching these chains rather than by physical manipulation

source_notes: Bruno's De Vinculis in Genere (c. 1590 CE) is the most sophisticated Renaissance theory of magical influence through bonds (vincula). Bruno analyzes how all forms of social and magical influence — persuasion, love, fear, religious devotion — operate through the same mechanism: attaching bonds to the imagination. The magus is thus a psychologist of desire who can bind and release minds through the systematic deployment of images that excite love or fear. Ioan Couliano's Eros and Magic in the Renaissance (1987) developed Bruno's model into a general theory of Renaissance magic.
bibliography: Bruno, Giordano. Cause, Principle and Unity: And Essays on Magic. Trans. Robert de Lucca and Richard J. Blackwell. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

title: Magia Naturalis — Sympathia
title_english: Natural Magic — Sympathy
author: Ioannes Baptista Porta
representative_sentence: Est praeterea quaedam occulta et vere admiranda vis per quam res se invicem trahunt vel fugant.
latin_text: Est praeterea quaedam occulta et vere admiranda vis per quam res se invicem trahunt vel fugant.
english_gloss: There is moreover a certain hidden and truly wonderful force through which things attract or repel each other.

vocabulary.definition: vis occulta — occult force; Della Porta's empiricist version of sympathetic force as an observable but inexplicable natural phenomenon; his approach treats occult properties as data to be collected and classified rather than theoretically explained

trahunt vel fugant — attract or repel; the fundamental polarity of sympathy and antipathy; in natural magic theory, all operative procedures exploit this binary by bringing sympathetic things together or using antipathetic things to drive away unwanted effects

source_notes: Giambattista della Porta's Magia Naturalis (first edition 1558; expanded 4-volume edition 1589) is the most popular Renaissance natural magic compendium, combining classical and Arabic natural lore with contemporary empirical observations. Della Porta's systematic collection of sympathies and antipathies, medical recipes, and optical experiments positioned natural magic as an empirical discipline. William Eamon's Science and the Secrets of Nature (1994) analyzes Della Porta's work in the context of the 'books of secrets' tradition and the emergence of modern experimental science.
bibliography: Della Porta, Giambattista. Magia Naturalis. Naples: Cancer, 1558. // Eamon, William. Science and the Secrets of Nature. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1994.

title: Philosophia Sagax — Astrum Corporis
title_english: Profound Philosophy — The Astrum of the Body
author: Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (Paracelsus)
representative_sentence: In homine est sol et luna et omnia planetae, omnes stellae firmamenti.
latin_text: In homine est sol et luna et omnia planetae, omnes stellae firmamenti.
english_gloss: In man there is the sun and the moon and all the planets, all the stars of the firmament.

vocabulary.definition: astrum — star, but also the inner stellar principle; Paracelsus's key term for the microcosmic counterpart of each celestial body within the human body; medicine is possible because the inner astrum responds to the outer star through sympathy

firmamentum — the firmament; the sphere of the fixed stars; Paracelsus's claim that all celestial bodies are mirrored within the human body is his version of the macrocosm-microcosm correspondence, driving both his medicine and his astrology

source_notes: Paracelsus's Astronomia Magna (Philosophia Sagax, c. 1537–1538 CE) is his most systematic account of the relationship between macrocosm and microcosm. His claim that each planet and star has an inner counterpart (astrum) within the human body was the basis for his astrological medicine, in which celestial observation diagnoses the inner astral condition. Charles Webster's From Paracelsus to Newton (1982) and Walter Pagel's Paracelsus (1958) remain standard analyses of his natural philosophy.
bibliography: Paracelsus. Sämtliche Werke. Ed. Karl Sudhoff. 14 vols. Munich: Barth, 1922–1933.

title: Liber de Nymphis — De Sylphis
title_english: Book of Nymphs — On Sylphs
source: Liber de Nymphis, Sylphis, Pygmaeis et Salamandris, cap. 2
author: Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (Paracelsus)
representative_sentence: Sylphi habitant in aere, sunt quasi natura aeria, neque visibiles neque tangibiles.
latin_text: Sylphi habitant in aere, sunt quasi natura aeria, neque visibiles neque tangibiles.
english_gloss: Sylphs inhabit the air, they are of an airy nature as it were, neither visible nor tangible.

vocabulary.definition: sylphus — sylph; Paracelsus coined or popularized the term for elemental spirits of air; his four elemental spirits (undines/water, sylphs/air, gnomes/earth, salamanders/fire) became the standard Renaissance and modern magical taxonomy of nature spirits

natura aeria — airy nature; Paracelsus explains the invisibility and intangibility of sylphs through their elemental constitution: they are composed of a different material than humans, explaining why human senses cannot normally perceive them

source_notes: Paracelsus's Liber de Nymphis, Sylphis, Pygmaeis et Salamandris (c. 1530 CE) is the source of the modern magical taxonomy of elemental spirits: nymphs/undines (water), sylphs (air), gnomes (earth), and salamanders (fire). Paracelsus presents these as natural beings — not demons — inhabiting the four elemental realms with specific physiological constitutions. His naturalization of elemental spirits as a fourth kind of being (between humans and animals) was influential on Renaissance natural philosophy and on later occultist traditions from Rosicrucian texts to 18th-century Sylphide literature.
bibliography: Paracelsus. Four Treatises. Trans. C. Lilian Temkin et al. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1941.

title: Malleus Maleficarum — De Pacto
title_english: Malleus Maleficarum — On the Pact with the Devil
author: Henricus Institoris et Iacobus Sprenger
representative_sentence: Maleficae per pactum expressum vel tacitum cum diabolo contrahunt.
latin_text: Maleficae per pactum expressum vel tacitum cum diabolo contrahunt.
english_gloss: Witches enter into a contract with the devil through an express or tacit pact.

vocabulary.definition: pactum expressum vel tacitum — explicit or implicit pact; the Malleus's distinction between a formal ritual pact (express) and an implicit reliance on demonic assistance without formal contract (tacit) allowed any magical operation to be classified as involving demonic collaboration

malefica — witch; the Malleus consistently uses the feminine form, reflecting its famous claim that women are more susceptible to demonic seduction due to their weakness of faith and natural carnality; the gendering of the witch was one of the Malleus's most influential and most criticized contributions

source_notes: The Malleus Maleficarum (Hammer of Witches, 1486 CE) by Heinrich Institoris (Kramer) and Jacob Sprenger is the most influential witch-hunting manual ever written, combining canon law, scholastic demonology, and trial procedure. Its systematic elaboration of the witch's pact with the devil as both express and tacit provided the theological framework for prosecuting witchcraft without a formal signed contract. Christopher Mackay's critical translation and commentary (2006) is the standard modern scholarly edition.
bibliography: Institoris, Heinrich, and Jacob Sprenger. Malleus Maleficarum. Trans. Christopher S. Mackay. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.

title: Malleus Maleficarum — De Sabbato
title_english: Malleus Maleficarum — On the Witches' Sabbath
source: Malleus Maleficarum, Pars II, Quaestio 1, cap. 3
author: Henricus Institoris et Iacobus Sprenger
representative_sentence: Multa maleficae noctu in synagogam suam quasi corporaliter deferuntur et coram diabolo apparent.
latin_text: Multa maleficae noctu in synagogam suam quasi corporaliter deferuntur et coram diabolo apparent.
english_gloss: Many witches are carried at night to their synagogue as if bodily, and appear before the devil.

vocabulary.definition: synagoga — the witches' sabbath, assembly; the use of 'synagogue' for the witch-gathering reflects the anti-Semitic conflation of Jewish religious assembly with demonic worship common in 15th-century demonology; the term was used alongside sabbat, conventus, and ludus

quasi corporaliter — as if bodily; the Malleus's careful qualification of the sabbath's reality as 'as if bodily' ('quasi corporaliter') attempts to navigate Canon Episcopi's denial of real nocturnal transport while asserting the sabbath's genuine occurrence

source_notes: The Malleus's treatment of the witches' sabbath represents a pivotal development in the history of witchcraft theory. The problem of how to reconcile Canon Episcopi's statement that nocturnal rides are mere dreams with the Malleus's insistence on their reality is navigated through the phrase 'quasi corporaliter' — the transport is real enough to be prosecuted, but the authors hedge on its precise ontological status. Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons (1997) provides the fullest analysis of witch-trial literature's treatment of the sabbath.
bibliography: Institoris, Heinrich, and Jacob Sprenger. Malleus Maleficarum. Trans. Christopher S. Mackay. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.

title: De Praestigiis Daemonum — Illusio
title_english: On the Illusions of Demons — Demonic Deception
source: De Praestigiis Daemonum, Liber I, cap. 5
author: Ioannes Wierus
representative_sentence: Daemones non vere transmutant homines in bestias, sed per phantasiam cerebri id efficiunt.
latin_text: Daemones non vere transmutant homines in bestias, sed per phantasiam cerebri id efficiunt.
english_gloss: Demons do not truly transform humans into beasts, but they accomplish this through the imagination of the brain.

vocabulary.definition: phantasia cerebri — imagination of the brain; Weyer's rationalization of demonic transformation as a disorder of the internal senses (imagination, memory) rather than a real physical event; this medical-psychological explanation anticipated later naturalistic accounts of witch delusions

non vere transmutant — do not truly transform; Weyer's sceptical position on metamorphosis, following Augustine, that apparent animal transformation is always an illusion or delusion; his application of this to witch confessions was his central argument against execution

source_notes: Johann Weyer's De Praestigiis Daemonum (1563 CE) is the most important 16th-century sceptical text on witchcraft. Weyer, a physician and former student of Agrippa, argued that accused witches are typically mentally ill old women deceived by demons into believing they have committed crimes they have not performed. His medical-psychological approach to witch confessions as symptoms of imagination disorder was condemned by Bodin and others but influenced later sceptics including Reginald Scot. H.C. Erik Midelfort's introduction to the English translation is a standard reference.
bibliography: Weyer, Johann. Witches, Devils, and Doctors in the Renaissance. Trans. John Shea. Ed. George Mora. Binghamton: MRTS, 1991.

title: Compound of Alchymy — Calcination
title_english: Compound of Alchymy — On Calcination
source: The Compound of Alchymy, Second Gate (Calcination)
author: Georgius Ripley
representative_sentence: Calcinatio est corporis in pulverem comminuti per ignem reductio, absque omni humiditate substantiali.
latin_text: Calcinatio est corporis in pulverem comminuti per ignem reductio, absque omni humiditate substantiali.
english_gloss: Calcination is the reduction of a body comminuted into powder by fire, without any substantial moisture.

vocabulary.definition: calcinatio — calcination; the first of the twelve gates (operations) in Ripley's Compound of Alchymy; the reduction of a substance to powder or ash through heat, destroying its gross elemental constitution to reveal the purer principle underneath

humiditas substantialis — substantial moisture; the Aristotelian quality whose removal by calcination exposes the dry, pure essence of the substance; the twelve gates of Ripley's system correspond to the twelve stages of the alchemical Work from prima materia to philosopher's stone

source_notes: George Ripley's Compound of Alchymy (c. 1470–1480 CE) is the most important late medieval English alchemical text, organizing the Great Work into twelve allegorical 'gates' corresponding to twelve alchemical operations from calcination to projection. Written in English verse, the Compound was translated into Latin and circulated widely in both languages. Stanton Linden and Jennifer Rampling have analyzed Ripley's place in the English alchemical tradition and his influence on later writers including Ben Jonson.
bibliography: Ripley, George. The Compound of Alchymy. Ed. Stanton J. Linden. Aldershot: Ashgate, 2001.

title: Amphitheatrum — Lux Divinorum
title_english: Amphitheatre — The Divine Light
author: Henricus Khunrath
representative_sentence: Lux tenebrarum divinarum est lux Dei in seipso immanens, quam nemo mortalium videre potest.
latin_text: Lux tenebrarum divinarum est lux Dei in seipso immanens, quam nemo mortalium videre potest.
english_gloss: The light of divine darkness is the light of God immanent in himself, which no mortal can see.

vocabulary.definition: lux tenebrarum divinarum — light of divine darkness; Khunrath's paradoxical theology, derived from Pseudo-Dionysius's apophatic mysticism, identifies the philosopher's stone with the hidden divine light that is simultaneously the darkest darkness and the most brilliant light

amphitheatrum — amphitheatre; the circular theatre of wisdom in Khunrath's title is both a memory-art concept (the memory theatre) and an alchemical laboratory: the circular space where all wisdom, divine and natural, is performed and revealed

source_notes: Heinrich Khunrath's Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae (1595/1609 CE) is the most mystically elaborate of the late Renaissance alchemical texts, combining Paracelsian alchemy with Lutheran Pietism, Kabbalah, and Hermetic philosophy. Its famous allegorical engravings (including the Oratorium-Laboratorium showing prayer and laboratory work as complementary) make it a visual as well as textual monument to spiritual alchemy. Peter Forshaw's extensive research on Khunrath and his context is the primary modern scholarship.
bibliography: Forshaw, Peter J. 'Kabbalah and Renaissance Alchemy.' In Kabbalah and Modernity. Ed. Boaz Huss et al. Leiden: Brill, 2010.

title: Arbatel — Aphorismi Magici
title_english: Arbatel — First Magic Aphorism
source: Arbatel de Magia Veterum, Aphorismus I
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Tota magicae artis summa in cognitione Dei et naturae consistit.
latin_text: Tota magicae artis summa in cognitione Dei et naturae consistit.
english_gloss: The whole sum of the magical art consists in the knowledge of God and nature.

vocabulary.definition: cognitio Dei et naturae — knowledge of God and nature; the Arbatel's foundational definition identifies magic with a fundamentally theistic and natural-philosophical enterprise, not with demonic pact; this definition made the Arbatel relatively acceptable even to Protestant readers

summa — sum, complete account; the Arbatel presents itself as the 'summa' of magic in aphoristic form, a compressed wisdom text; its structure as numbered aphorisms (like Proverbs or Hippocratic aphorisms) gives it a gnomic authority

source_notes: The Arbatel de Magia Veterum (1575 CE) is a Protestant-inflected grimoire of angelic/spirit magic notable for its relatively theologically innocent framing of magic as knowledge of God and nature. It describes seven Olympic Spirits (Aratron, Bethor, Phaleg, Och, Hagith, Ophiel, Phul) associated with the seven planets and outlines a procedure for their invocation. Frank Klaassen has analyzed the Arbatel in the context of the Protestant engagement with learned magic, showing how its theistic framework made it more acceptable to Reformed readers than more explicitly grimoiric texts.
bibliography: Joseph H. Peterson, ed. Arbatel: Concerning the Magic of Ancients. Lake Worth: Ibis Press, 2009.

title: Arbatel — Spiritus Aratron
title_english: Arbatel — The Olympic Spirit Aratron
source: Arbatel de Magia Veterum, Aphorismus XLII–XLIII
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Aratron est spiritus Saturni qui gubernat quae in mundo Saturno subiecta sunt.
latin_text: Aratron est spiritus Saturni qui gubernat quae in mundo Saturno subiecta sunt.
english_gloss: Aratron is the spirit of Saturn who governs those things in the world that are subject to Saturn.

vocabulary.definition: Aratron — the Olympic Spirit of Saturn; one of seven planetary spirits in the Arbatel system who govern the influence of their respective planets; the Olympic Spirits occupy a position between the purely astrological planetary intelligences and the fully personal angels of the grimoire tradition

Saturno subiecta — subject to Saturn; the doctrine that all natural phenomena correspond to a planetary ruler; Aratron governs lead, black things, the aged, melancholy, and agriculture — the full Saturnian correspondence table from ancient astrology

source_notes: The Arbatel's description of the seven Olympic Spirits (one per planet) is the most widely cited Renaissance account of planetary spirit beings, providing names and attributes that became standard in Western occultism. The Olympic Spirit concept bridges astrological influence (the spirits govern what belongs to their planet) with the personal angel model of the grimoire tradition (the spirits can be invoked and petitioned). Agrippa had laid theoretical groundwork for planetary spirits in De Occulta Philosophia II; the Arbatel gave them specific names and attributes.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. Arbatel: Concerning the Magic of Ancients. Lake Worth: Ibis Press, 2009.

title: Chiromantia — Mons Veneris
title_english: Chiromancy — Mount of Venus
author: Ioannes ab Indagine
representative_sentence: Mons Veneris in manu dextra et magnus, latus ac elevatus, significat valetudinem firmam et amorem validum.
latin_text: Mons Veneris in manu dextra et magnus, latus ac elevatus, significat valetudinem firmam et amorem validum.
english_gloss: The Mount of Venus in the right hand, large, broad, and elevated, signifies robust health and strong love.

vocabulary.definition: mons Veneris — Mount of Venus; the fleshy area at the base of the thumb; in chiromantic theory, each planetary mount corresponds to a planet and reveals the subject's constitution and character with respect to that planet's qualities

chiromantia — chiromancy, palm reading; divination from the lines and mounts of the hand; introduced to the Latin West from Arabic sources and organized into a systematic discipline by Johann von Hagen (Indagine) and others in the Renaissance

source_notes: Johann von Hagen's (Indagine) Introductiones Apotelesmaticae (1522 CE) is the most popular Renaissance chiromancy manual, going through over 50 editions by 1600. His systematic treatment of the lines (Linea Vitae, Mensalis, Jovis, etc.) and mounts of the hand in terms of planetary correspondences became the standard framework for European chiromancy. The Speculum Astronomiae had condemned chiromancy as a form of divination; Indagine's enormously popular work normalized it as a form of astromancy — divination through the body's astral signatures.
bibliography: Indagine, Johann. Introductiones Apotelesmaticae in Chyromantiam. Strasburg: Schott, 1522.

title: Utriusque Cosmi Historia — Macrocosmos
title_english: History of Both Worlds — The Macrocosm
source: Utriusque Cosmi Maioris Scilicet et Minoris Historia, Tractatus I
author: Robertus Fludd
representative_sentence: Homo est mundus minor, in quo maior mundus omnes suas vires et proprietates contractas habet.
latin_text: Homo est mundus minor, in quo maior mundus omnes suas vires et proprietates contractas habet.
english_gloss: Man is the lesser world, in which the greater world has all its powers and properties contracted.

vocabulary.definition: mundus minor — microcosm, lesser world; the human being as a concentrated image of the universe; the macrocosm-microcosm correspondence was the organizing principle of Fludd's natural philosophy and the basis for his medical and magical applications

contractas — contracted, compressed; Fludd's term for the way the macrocosm's powers are condensed and present in the human body in miniature form, allowing the body's symptoms to reveal cosmic conditions and cosmic techniques to heal bodily diseases

source_notes: Robert Fludd's Utriusque Cosmi Historia (1617 CE) is the most encyclopaedic of the early 17th-century Hermetic philosophical systems, presenting the entire cosmos as a series of correspondences between the macrocosm (universe) and microcosm (man). Fludd's elaborate diagrams and his defense of the Rosicrucian pamphlets provoked a famous controversy with Johannes Kepler over the status of visual analogy versus mathematical demonstration in natural philosophy. William Huffman's Robert Fludd and the End of the Renaissance (1988) is the standard modern biography.
bibliography: Fludd, Robert. Utriusque Cosmi Maioris Scilicet et Minoris Metaphysica. Oppenheim: de Bry, 1617.

title: De Sensu Rerum — Anima Mundi
title_english: On the Sense of Things — World Soul
source: De Sensu Rerum et Magia, Liber I, cap. 1
author: Thomas Campanella
representative_sentence: Mundus est animal magnum et perfectum, sensu et vita praedita.
latin_text: Mundus est animal magnum et perfectum, sensu et vita praedita.
english_gloss: The world is a great and perfect animal, endowed with sense and life.

vocabulary.definition: animal magnum — great animal; Campanella's hylozoist position that the world as a whole is a living, sensing being; this animist cosmology, derived from Plato's Timaeus and Stoic philosophy, was the philosophical basis for his natural magic

sensus et vita — sense and life; Campanella attributes to the world both vita (biological life, also attributed by Aristotle to plants) and sensus (sensation, typically animal), making the cosmos not just alive but sentient; this radical animism made him dangerous to the Inquisition
