source_notes: Tommaso Campanella's De Sensu Rerum et Magia (first Italian version c. 1590; Latin 1620 CE) presents the most radical animist philosophy of the Renaissance: all natural objects possess sensation and the world as a whole is a conscious animal. This panpsychist position made natural magic not just possible but necessary — if everything senses, then sympathetic operations on the world-animal's body are simply communications with a sentient cosmos. Campanella's magical philosophy brought him into repeated conflict with the Inquisition; he spent 27 years imprisoned for heresy and conspiracy.
bibliography: Campanella, Tommaso. On the Sense of Things and on Magic. Trans. Margaret Rees. Aldershot: Ashgate, 2004.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblema I
title_english: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem I
author: Michael Maierus
representative_sentence: Portavit eum ventus in ventre suo.
latin_text: Portavit eum ventus in ventre suo.
english_gloss: The wind carried it in its belly.

vocabulary.definition: ventus in ventre suo — the wind in its belly; the first emblem of Atalanta Fugiens illustrates the alchemical dictum from the Emerald Tablet, showing the infant philosopher's stone carried by wind — the volatile, pneumatic principle that bears the seed of transformation

Atalanta Fugiens — Atalanta Fleeing; Maier's allegorical title draws on the myth of the footrace of Atalanta; the work combines 50 alchemical emblems with fugues composed for each emblem, making it the most multimedia alchemical work of the Renaissance

source_notes: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1617 CE) is the most elaborate alchemical emblem book, combining 50 copperplate emblems with Latin epigrams and fugal musical compositions — each emblem has its own three-voice musical setting. The first emblem's motto 'Portavit eum ventus in ventre suo' quotes the Emerald Tablet, establishing the Hermetic alchemical tradition's authority for the whole work. H.M.E. de Jong's Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1969) is the standard iconographic analysis.
bibliography: Maier, Michael. Atalanta Fugiens. Oppenheim: de Bry, 1617. // de Jong, H.M.E. Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens. Leiden: Brill, 1969.

title: De Incantationibus — De Miraculis
title_english: On Incantations — On Miracles as Natural Effects
author: Petrus Pomponatius
representative_sentence: Miracula quae per daemones fieri dicuntur, per stellarum virtutes et naturalem philosophiam explicari possunt.
latin_text: Miracula quae per daemones fieri dicuntur, per stellarum virtutes et naturalem philosophiam explicari possunt.
english_gloss: Miracles which are said to be performed through demons can be explained through the powers of the stars and natural philosophy.

vocabulary.definition: per stellarum virtutes — through the powers of the stars; Pomponazzi's astrological naturalism attributes all apparently miraculous phenomena to stellar causation, eliminating both divine and demonic explanations in favor of a purely natural account

naturalem philosophiam — natural philosophy; Pomponazzi's reduction of magic and miracle to natural philosophy was the most radical 16th-century naturalist position and influenced later sceptical tradition; his use of 'natural philosophy' prefigures the modern use of 'science' as the ultimate explanatory framework

source_notes: Pietro Pomponazzi's De Incantationibus (c. 1520 CE, published posthumously 1556) is the most radical naturalistic reduction of magic in the Renaissance: all apparently supernatural effects — including miracles, magic, and demonic operations — are explained by stellar causation and Aristotelian natural philosophy. Written in the Paduan Averroist tradition, it was suppressed in his lifetime but circulated in manuscript and was influential on later naturalist thinkers. Brian P. Copenhaver's analysis places it at the extreme naturalist end of the Renaissance spectrum of magical theory.
bibliography: Pomponazzi, Pietro. De Naturalium Effectuum Admirandorum Causis seu de Incantationibus. Basle: Henricpetri, 1567.

title: Oedipus Aegyptiacus — Hieroglyphica
title_english: Egyptian Oedipus — On Hieroglyphs as Magic
author: Athanasius Kircher
representative_sentence: Hieroglyphica non alia arte intelligenda sunt quam per mysticam Aegyptiorum philosophiam.
latin_text: Hieroglyphica non alia arte intelligenda sunt quam per mysticam Aegyptiorum philosophiam.
english_gloss: Hieroglyphs are to be understood by no other art than through the mystical philosophy of the Egyptians.

vocabulary.definition: hieroglyphica — hieroglyphs; for Kircher, Egyptian hieroglyphs are not a writing system but a mystical symbolic language encoding universal divine wisdom; his decipherment (largely incorrect) treated each sign as an allegorical philosophical statement rather than a phonetic element

mysticam philosophiam — mystical philosophy; the Hermetic-Neoplatonic Egyptian wisdom that Kircher believed hieroglyphs encoded; his project was the recovery of the prisca theologia through the most ancient symbolic language

source_notes: Athanasius Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus (1652–1654 CE) is the most ambitious 17th-century synthesis of Egyptian, Hermetic, kabbalistic, and Neoplatonic learning. Kircher's 'decipherment' of hieroglyphs as philosophical allegories (now known to be entirely wrong) represents the final flower of the Renaissance Hermetic tradition's belief in Egyptian prisca sapientia. Despite its errors, the work was enormously influential and helped create modern Egyptomania. Paula Findlen's edited volume Athanasius Kircher: The Last Man Who Knew Everything (2004) provides the standard modern assessment.
bibliography: Kircher, Athanasius. Oedipus Aegyptiacus. Rome: Mascardi, 1652–1654.

title: Diarii — Angelus Uriel
title_english: Spirit Diaries — The Angel Uriel
source: A True and Faithful Relation... (Casaubon ed. 1659), entry for March 10, 1582
author: Ioannes Dee
representative_sentence: Angelus Uriel ad nos descendit, splendens ut sol, in medio speculi apparuit.
latin_text: Angelus Uriel ad nos descendit, splendens ut sol, in medio speculi apparuit.
english_gloss: The angel Uriel descended to us, shining like the sun, appearing in the middle of the mirror.

vocabulary.definition: speculum — mirror, scrying crystal; Dee and Kelley used a polished obsidian mirror (and later a crystal ball) as the medium for angelic visions; the use of reflective surfaces for spirit contact is one of the oldest divinatory techniques and connects the Dee-Kelley sessions to ancient catoptromancy

Uriel — the archangel Uriel, 'Fire of God'; one of the four archangels associated with the cardinal directions; Uriel's first appearance to Dee via Kelley inaugurated the decade-long series of angelic conversations that produced the Enochian language and angelic system

source_notes: John Dee's Spirit Diaries (1581–1583 and 1583–1589, published by Meric Casaubon in 1659) record the angelic communication sessions conducted by Dee with his scryer Edward Kelley. The sessions produced what Dee believed was the original Adamic language (Enochian), tables of angelic names, and instructions for spiritual and material operations. Deborah Harkness's John Dee's Conversations with Angels (1999) is the standard modern study, situating the diaries in the context of Elizabethan natural philosophy, Reformation spirituality, and intelligence work.
bibliography: Dee, John. A True and Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Years between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits. Ed. Meric Casaubon. London, 1659.

title: De Subtilitate — De Occultis
title_english: On Subtlety — On Hidden Causes
source: De Subtilitate Libri XXI, Liber XIX
author: Hieronymus Cardanus
representative_sentence: Subtilitas est quaedam ratio, qua sensibilia a sensu aegre percipiuntur.
latin_text: Subtilitas est quaedam ratio, qua sensibilia a sensu aegre percipiuntur.
english_gloss: Subtlety is a certain principle by which sensible things are scarcely perceived by the senses.

vocabulary.definition: subtilitas — subtlety, fineness; Cardano's key category for natural phenomena that exceed ordinary sensory perception; his 'De Subtilitate' covers the same territory as natural magic but presents it as natural philosophy — the study of properties too fine and hidden for gross sensory observation

aegre percipiuntur — scarcely perceived; the epistemological definition of occult quality as that which the senses can barely grasp; Cardano's definition effectively naturalizes the 'occult' by redefining it as a limitation of sense rather than a supernatural category

source_notes: Girolamo Cardano's De Subtilitate (1550 CE) is the most systematic Renaissance attempt to explain 'occult' natural phenomena — sympathies, antipathies, and hidden properties — as extreme instances of natural subtlety, too fine for ordinary sensory detection but amenable to rational investigation. Its definition of subtlety as the limiting case of natural perception effectively dissolved the boundary between natural magic and natural philosophy. The work was enormously popular and went through numerous editions, establishing Cardano as a major figure in the naturalization of magical thinking.
bibliography: Cardano, Girolamo. De Subtilitate. Nuremberg: Petreius, 1550.

title: Heptameron — Angeli Horarum
title_english: Heptameron — Angels of the Hours
author: Anonymous (attrib. Pietro d'Abano)
representative_sentence: Haec sunt nomina angelorum qui praesunt horis diei et noctis et qui invocari debent pro operationibus magicis.
latin_text: Haec sunt nomina angelorum qui praesunt horis diei et noctis et qui invocari debent pro operationibus magicis.
english_gloss: These are the names of the angels who preside over the hours of day and night and who must be invoked for magical operations.

vocabulary.definition: angeli horarum — angels of the hours; the Heptameron's system assigns specific angelic rulers to each planetary hour, each day of the week, and each direction of the compass, providing a precise timing-and-orientation framework for magical operations

operationibus magicis — magical operations; the Heptameron's practical focus on specific operations (gaining treasure, love, illness, etc.) represents the grimoire tradition's operational orientation in contrast to the philosophical magic of Agrippa or Bruno

source_notes: The Heptameron seu Elementa Magica (published 1496 CE, attributed to Pietro d'Abano though probably not his) is a practical grimoire of planetary angel magic organized around the seven days of the week. Each day has its associated planet, angel, seal, metal, and perfume, with full conjuration formulas. The text was widely circulated alongside Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia (to which it was sometimes appended) and represents the operational rather than theoretical dimension of Renaissance ceremonial magic.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H. 'Heptameron, or Magical Elements.' Available at esotericarchives.com. // Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: De Harmonia Mundi — Sephirot
title_english: On the Harmony of the World — The Sephirot
source: De Harmonia Mundi Totius, Tomus I, Cantus I
author: Franciscus Georgius Venetus (Francesco Giorgi)
representative_sentence: Sephirot sunt decem emanationes divinae per quas Deus mundum creavit et gubernat.
latin_text: Sephirot sunt decem emanationes divinae per quas Deus mundum creavit et gubernat.
english_gloss: The Sephirot are ten divine emanations through which God created and governs the world.

vocabulary.definition: Sephirot — the ten divine attributes/emanations of Kabbalah; Giorgi's incorporation of the Sephirot into a Christian-Neoplatonic metaphysics makes De Harmonia the most comprehensive Renaissance synthesis of Kabbalah with Platonic cosmology

emanationes divinae — divine emanations; the Neoplatonic metaphysical framework Giorgi uses to interpret the Sephirot, presenting kabbalistic theory as a version of Plotinian emanationism and thereby making Kabbalah legible to Christian readers steeped in Neoplatonism

source_notes: Francesco Giorgi's De Harmonia Mundi (1525 CE) is the most comprehensive Renaissance synthesis of Christian Kabbalah, Neoplatonism, Hermetism, and Franciscan theology. Combining the kabbalistic Sephirot with Platonic musical harmony and scriptural typology, Giorgi creates a total account of cosmic order in which number, music, and divine names all express the same underlying harmony. The work was used by Agrippa and influenced the Rosicrucian tradition; Daniel Stein Kokin has provided the fullest modern analysis.
bibliography: Giorgi, Francesco. De Harmonia Mundi Totius. Venice: de Sabio, 1525.

title: De Septem Secundeis — Angeli Saeculi
title_english: On the Seven Secondary Causes — Angels of the Ages
author: Ioannes Trithemius
representative_sentence: Septem sunt angeli principales qui orbem terrarum et omnia in eo a Deo ordinate gubernant.
latin_text: Septem sunt angeli principales qui orbem terrarum et omnia in eo a Deo ordinate gubernant.
english_gloss: There are seven principal angels who govern the sphere of the earth and all things in it in an ordered way from God.

vocabulary.definition: Septem Secundeadei — the seven secondary beings; Trithemius's term for the seven planetary angels who govern world history in sequence, each reigning for approximately 354 years; the system provides an astrological philosophy of history

orbem gubernant — they govern the sphere; the seven angels' governance of the world identifies them as the intermediaries between divine providence and historical events, making world history itself a form of angelic magic in Trithemius's system

source_notes: Trithemius's De Septem Secundeis (1508 CE) presents a philosophy of history based on the sequential rulership of seven planetary angels, each governing a period of approximately 354 years. The system allows for prediction of future historical trends based on the incoming angel's planetary character. Trithemius was the teacher of both Agrippa and Paracelsus; his angelic historiography influenced Renaissance prophetic and magical thought and fed into later discussions of world ages and astrological historical causation.
bibliography: Trithemius, Johannes. De Septem Secundeis. Cologne, 1567. // Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999.

title: De Consideratione Quintae Essentiae — Definitio
title_english: On the Consideration of the Fifth Essence — Definition
source: De Consideratione Quintae Essentiae, Liber I
author: Ioannes de Rupescissa
representative_sentence: Quinta essentia est incorruptibilis, quae si recte preparatur, corpus humanum a corruptione praeservat.
latin_text: Quinta essentia est incorruptibilis, quae si recte preparatur, corpus humanum a corruptione praeservat.
english_gloss: The fifth essence is incorruptible; if rightly prepared, it preserves the human body from corruption.

vocabulary.definition: quinta essentia — the fifth essence, quintessence; John of Rupescissa's term for the incorruptible distillate extracted from wine (i.e., ethanol) that he believed could preserve human health and even extend life; his quintessence concept was foundational for Paracelsian pharmaceutical alchemy

a corruptione praeservare — preserves from corruption; the medical application of the quintessence as a preservative and restorative; Rupescissa's quasi-medical alchemy anticipated the Paracelsian program of replacing Galenic medicine with chemical remedies

source_notes: John of Rupescissa's De Consideratione Quintae Essentiae (c. 1351–1352 CE) is the foundational text of pharmaceutical alchemy, introducing the concept of the quinta essentia (quintessence) as a distilled incorruptible substance capable of preserving human health. Rupescissa, a Franciscan imprisoned for prophetic activities, framed his alchemical program within Joachimite eschatology — the quintessence would preserve bodies through the tribulations of the end times. Leah DeVun's Prophecy, Alchemy, and the End of Time analyzes his dual role as alchemist and prophet.
bibliography: Rupescissa, John of. De la consideration de la quinte essence. Ed. and trans. Leah DeVun. In Prophecy, Alchemy, and the End of Time. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

title: Discoverie of Witchcraft — De Ligatura
title_english: Discoverie of Witchcraft — On the Binding Spell
source: The Discoverie of Witchcraft, Booke XII, chap. 18
author: Reginaldus Scotus
representative_sentence: Ligatura quaedam est per quam vir cum uxore sua coire impeditur per artes magicas.
latin_text: Ligatura quaedam est per quam vir cum uxore sua coire impeditur per artes magicas.
english_gloss: Ligature is a certain thing by which a man is prevented from lying with his wife through magical arts.

vocabulary.definition: ligatura — the ligature, the binding; a specific magical spell preventing sexual intercourse, one of the most commonly prosecuted forms of maleficium in medieval and early modern courts; the ligature combined folk herbal magic with knotting rituals and written charms

artes magicae — magical arts; Scot uses the term to encompass both the popular folk magic he is debunking and the learned ceremonial magic he critiques; his sceptical approach treats both as either fraud or delusion rather than genuine supernatural operation

source_notes: Reginald Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584 CE) is the most important Elizabethan sceptical text on witchcraft and magic, arguing that witches have no real power and that witch-trial executions are unjust. Written in response to the wave of English witch-trials, the book paradoxically preserves detailed descriptions of magical operations (including conjurations and charms) precisely in order to debunk them. Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic analyses the book's relationship to the learned magic tradition it critiques.
bibliography: Scot, Reginald. The Discoverie of Witchcraft. Ed. Brinsley Nicholson. London: Elliot Stock, 1886.

title: De la Démonomanie — De Pacto
title_english: On Demonomany — On the Pact
source: De la Démonomanie des Sorciers, Livre I, chap. 2 (Latin abstract)
author: Ioannes Bodinus
representative_sentence: Pactum cum diabolo expressam et liberam voluntatem includit qua quis a fide Christiana recedit.
latin_text: Pactum cum diabolo expressam et liberam voluntatem includit qua quis a fide Christiana recedit.
english_gloss: A pact with the devil includes an express and free act of will by which someone departs from the Christian faith.

vocabulary.definition: expressam et liberam voluntatem — express and free act of will; Bodin insists on the voluntary character of the witch's pact to distinguish it from mere delusion; this emphasis on free choice made the pact an act of apostasy deserving capital punishment

a fide Christiana recedit — departs from the Christian faith; the pact as apostasy, not merely as crime; Bodin's strong position that anyone who doubts the reality of witchcraft is either deceived or complicit was directed specifically against Weyer's sceptical arguments

source_notes: Jean Bodin's De la Démonomanie des Sorciers (1580 CE) was the most vigorous Renaissance response to Weyer's scepticism, arguing for the reality of witchcraft, the validity of witch-trial procedures, and the justice of capital punishment for witches. Bodin's political theory (sovereignty) and his witch-theory are related: just as political sovereignty is absolute and non-negotiable, so the devil's pact is a real transfer of sovereignty over the soul. Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons analyzes Bodin's demonology in its political context.
bibliography: Bodin, Jean. De la Démonomanie des Sorciers. Paris: du Puys, 1580.

title: Compendium Maleficarum — De Sabbato
title_english: Compendium Maleficarum — On the Sabbath
author: Franciscus Maria Guazzo
representative_sentence: In sabbato strigum diabolus in forma hirci vel alterius animalis praeest.
latin_text: In sabbato strigum diabolus in forma hirci vel alterius animalis praeest.
english_gloss: At the witches' sabbath the devil presides in the form of a goat or another animal.

vocabulary.definition: forma hirci — in the form of a goat; the devil's goat-form at the sabbath is the most culturally pervasive image from early modern witch-trial literature; the goat associated with Azazel and wilderness connected the sabbath iconography to biblical as well as folkloric traditions

sabbato strigum — witches' sabbath; the formal term for the gathered assembly of witches and their devil; Guazzo's Compendium includes famous engravings depicting the sabbath, making it one of the most visually influential witch-trial texts

source_notes: Francesco Maria Guazzo's Compendium Maleficarum (1608 CE) is a late witch-theory text notable for its extensive use of visual illustration: its engravings of the witches' sabbath (including the devil as goat, the kiss of shame, and the trampling of the cross) became among the most widely reproduced images in the history of witchcraft. The text synthesizes the accumulated demonological tradition from the Malleus to Bodin while its illustrations provided the visual vocabulary for 17th-century representations of the sabbath.
bibliography: Guazzo, Francesco Maria. Compendium Maleficarum. Trans. E.A. Ashwin. Ed. Montague Summers. London: Rodker, 1929.

title: Disquisitiones Magicae — De Maleficio
title_english: Magical Investigations — On Maleficium
author: Martinus Antonius Delrio
representative_sentence: Maleficium est operatio miraculosa quam daemon ex pacto, vel tacito vel expresso, humano auxilio facit.
latin_text: Maleficium est operatio miraculosa quam daemon ex pacto, vel tacito vel expresso, humano auxilio facit.
english_gloss: Maleficium is a miraculous operation which a demon performs through a pact, either tacit or express, with human assistance.

vocabulary.definition: operatio miraculosa — miraculous operation; Del Rio's definition of maleficium as a genuinely supernatural (miraculous) event performed by demons distinguishes him from naturalist accounts; for Del Rio, the reality of demonic operations is axiomatic and their supernatural character is precisely what makes them so dangerous

ex pacto — through a pact; Del Rio's careful legal analysis of the pact mechanism — express (formal ritual) or tacit (reliance on demonic assistance without explicit contract) — made the Disquisitiones the most legally sophisticated of all witch-trial manuals

source_notes: Martin del Rio's Disquisitiones Magicae (1599–1600 CE) is the most systematic and legally sophisticated of all early modern witch-hunting manuals, drawing on Jesuit training in scholastic theology and law. Del Rio provides extensive analysis of all forms of magic, classified by demonic involvement, with detailed guidance for judicial procedure. His work was the standard authority for 17th-century witch trials in Catholic Europe. Alison Rowlands and other historians have assessed its influence on judicial practice.
bibliography: Del Rio, Martín. Investigations into Magic. Trans. P.G. Maxwell-Stuart. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 2000.

title: De Magia — Classificatio
title_english: On Magic — Classification of Magic
source: Adversus Fallaces et Superstitiosas Artes, cap. 1
author: Benedictus Pererius
representative_sentence: Magia alia est naturalis quae per naturales causas operatur, alia est daemoniaca quae per daemonum pactum.
latin_text: Magia alia est naturalis quae per naturales causas operatur, alia est daemoniaca quae per daemonum pactum.
english_gloss: Some magic is natural, which operates through natural causes; other magic is daemonic, which operates through a pact with demons.

vocabulary.definition: naturalis causas — natural causes; the key distinction in Renaissance classification of magic: operations that can be explained by natural philosophy are natural magic (potentially licit); those that require supernatural assistance are demonic magic (always illicit)

daemoniacus — daemonic, diabolical; Pererius's category for all magic that exceeds natural causes and therefore requires demonic assistance; the boundary between natural and daemonic magic was the central contested issue in Renaissance discussions of licit magical practice

source_notes: Benedetto Pereira (Pererius), a Jesuit professor at the Collegio Romano, wrote Adversus Fallaces et Superstitiosas Artes (1591 CE) as the most systematic Jesuit critique of magical practices. His classification distinguishes natural magic, divination, and demonic magic, arguing that apparent natural magic always conceals demonic involvement when it exceeds natural causes. The work represents the Counter-Reformation Catholic position on magic: rigorous scepticism about natural magic's extent combined with strong affirmation of demonic reality.
bibliography: Pereira, Benedetto. Adversus Fallaces et Superstitiosas Artes. Ingolstadt: Sartorius, 1591.

title: De Amore — Amor Magus
title_english: On Love — Love the Magician
source: De Amore (Commentarium in Convivium Platonis), Oratio VI, cap. 10
author: Marsilius Ficinus
representative_sentence: Amor magus est, quia tota vis magiae in amore consistit.
latin_text: Amor magus est, quia tota vis magiae in amore consistit.
english_gloss: Love is the magician, because the whole power of magic consists in love.

vocabulary.definition: amor magus — love the magician; Ficino's identification of the cosmic force of love with the operative power of magic; his reading of Plato's Symposium argues that the magician works by exciting and channeling the same Eros that binds the cosmos together

vis magiae — the power of magic; Ficino's claim that magic's power is love redefines magic as fundamentally erotic — the manipulation of desire and attraction rather than technical manipulation of substances; this definition influenced Bruno's De Vinculis and the whole Renaissance theory of magical bonds

source_notes: Ficino's De Amore (c. 1469 CE, published 1484), his commentary on Plato's Symposium, contains the famous claim that 'love is the magician' — the force of cosmic Eros is the same force that operates in magical practice. By identifying magic with the Platonic force of cosmic attraction, Ficino elevates magical practice to a form of Platonic cosmology and love theory. This identification was developed by Bruno in De Vinculis in Genere and by Ioan Couliano's modern analysis in Eros and Magic in the Renaissance.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Commentary on Plato's Symposium on Love. Trans. Sears Jayne. Dallas: Spring Publications, 1985.

title: Liber Secretorum — De Herbis Magicis
title_english: Book of Secrets — On Magical Herbs
source: Libellus de Mirabilibus Mundi (Secreta Mulierum et Alberti), cap. 2
author: Anonymous (attrib. Albertus Magnus)
representative_sentence: Herba quam Graeci mandragoram dicunt, sub terra humanam effigiem habet.
latin_text: Herba quam Graeci mandragoram dicunt, sub terra humanam effigiem habet.
english_gloss: The herb which the Greeks call mandrake has a human likeness beneath the ground.

vocabulary.definition: mandragora — mandrake; the plant with a human-shaped root was the most magical of all herbs in ancient and medieval tradition; Pseudo-Albertus repeats the stock magical lore about mandrake's human form, sympathetic properties, and dangerous harvesting procedure

humanam effigiem — human likeness; the doctrine of signatures applied to the mandrake root: its human form indicates its sympathetic connection to human beings and explains its power in operations involving persons; the signature doctrine was foundational for both magical botany and Paracelsian medicine

source_notes: The Book of Secrets attributed to Albertus Magnus (Pseudo-Albertus, c. 13th–14th century) is not genuinely Albertus's work but a popular compilation of natural magic recipes organized around plants, stones, and animals with wonderful properties. It is one of the most widely printed books of the early modern period and a key vehicle for the popular transmission of natural magic lore. William Eamon's Science and the Secrets of Nature traces the 'books of secrets' tradition of which Pseudo-Albertus is the medieval foundation.
bibliography: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus. The Book of Secrets. Ed. Michael R. Best and Frank H. Brightman. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.

title: Antipalus Maleficiorum — Remedia
title_english: Defender against Maleficia — Remedies
author: Ioannes Trithemius
representative_sentence: Contra maleficia praesidium optimum est fides firma, poenitentia sincera, et orationes ad Deum.
latin_text: Contra maleficia praesidium optimum est fides firma, poenitentia sincera, et orationes ad Deum.
english_gloss: The best protection against maleficia is firm faith, sincere penance, and prayers to God.

vocabulary.definition: antipalus — defender, champion against; Trithemius uses this rare term for his counter-magic manual, positioning himself as a defender of Christian communities against magical attack through orthodox spiritual means

maleficia — harmful magical acts; Trithemius accepts the reality of maleficium (demonic-assisted harmful magic) while arguing that the best counter-measures are spiritual rather than counter-magical; his position distinguishes orthodox counter-magic (prayer, penance) from superstitious counter-magic

source_notes: Trithemius's Antipalus Maleficiorum (c. 1508 CE) is a pastoral manual for protecting communities against magical harm, recommending orthodox spiritual practices (faith, penance, prayer, sacramentals) rather than counter-magic. This position distinguished Trithemius's approach from folk anti-magical practices that would themselves be condemned as superstitious. The Antipalus reveals the practical pastoral problem that demonological theory created: if demons cause real harm through witches, what can the Church offer as genuine protection?
bibliography: Trithemius, Johannes. Antipalus Maleficiorum. In Johannis Trithemii Opera Historica. Frankfurt, 1601. // Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999.

title: Theatrum Chemicum — Musaeum Hermeticum
title_english: Chemical Theatre — Hermetic Museum
author: Anonymous (various)
representative_sentence: Lapis philosophorum est pater et mater omnium metallorum et fons omnium metallicae perfectionis.
latin_text: Lapis philosophorum est pater et mater omnium metallorum et fons omnium metallicae perfectionis.
english_gloss: The philosopher's stone is the father and mother of all metals and the source of all metallic perfection.

vocabulary.definition: lapis philosophorum — philosopher's stone; the ultimate product of the alchemical Great Work, capable of transmuting base metals into gold and (in spiritual alchemy) of perfecting the soul; the stone's dual role as material and spiritual perfecting agent is the central paradox of alchemical symbolism

pater et mater — father and mother; alchemical gender symbolism presenting the stone as simultaneously the masculine (sulphur/Sol) and feminine (mercury/Luna) principles; the coincidence of opposites in the stone is a standard alchemical theme from the Tabula Smaragdina onward

source_notes: The Musaeum Hermeticum (1625 CE, reprinted 1677 as Musaeum Hermeticum Reformatum et Amplificatum) is the most important anthology of alchemical texts published in the 17th century, collecting key texts including the Tabula Smaragdina, the Rosarium Philosophorum, Thomas Norton's Ordinal, and numerous German and Latin texts. It served as the standard reference collection for late Renaissance and early modern alchemy and has been the subject of Arthur Edward Waite's translation (1893) and more recently of C.J.R. Armstrong's analysis.
bibliography: Waite, Arthur Edward, trans. The Hermetic Museum. London: James Elliott, 1893.

title: Testamentum — De Lapide
title_english: Testament — On the Philosopher's Stone
source: Testamentum (attrib. Ramon Lull), Liber I, cap. 1
author: Anonymous (attrib. Ramon Lull)
representative_sentence: Lapis noster non est lapis, nec ex metallis, nec ex animalibus, nec ex vegetabilibus; sed est corpus quoddam incomprehensibile.
latin_text: Lapis noster non est lapis, nec ex metallis, nec ex animalibus, nec ex vegetabilibus; sed est corpus quoddam incomprehensibile.
english_gloss: Our stone is not a stone, nor is it from metals, animals, or vegetables; but it is a certain incomprehensible body.

vocabulary.definition: lapis noster non est lapis — our stone is not a stone; the standard alchemical apophatic formula for the philosopher's stone, which systematically denies that the stone is any known category of substance; this negative definition is a deliberate paradox designed to protect the secret while pointing toward it

incomprehensibilis — incomprehensible, not to be grasped; the stone's incomprehensibility indicates its transcendent character — it exceeds ordinary Aristotelian categories just as God exceeds ordinary predication; alchemical apophasis mirrors theological apophasis

source_notes: The alchemical Testamentum attributed to Ramon Lull (c. 14th century) is not by the historical Lull (who explicitly rejected alchemy) but is a pseudepigraphic text that appropriated Lull's enormous prestige for alchemical purposes. The text became one of the most cited alchemical authorities, and 'Lullian alchemy' became a recognized school. Michela Pereira's The Alchemical Corpus Attributed to Raymond Lull (1989) is the definitive account of how Lull's name was co-opted by the alchemical tradition.
bibliography: Pereira, Michela. The Alchemical Corpus Attributed to Raymond Lull. London: Warburg Institute, 1989.

title: Ordinall of Alchemy — Prohemium
title_english: Ordinal of Alchemy — Prologue
source: Ordinall of Alchemy (Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum), Prohemium
author: Thomas Norton
representative_sentence: Philosophi occultaverunt artem suam sub copertis verbis sicut placuit eis.
latin_text: Philosophi occultaverunt artem suam sub copertis verbis sicut placuit eis.
english_gloss: The philosophers have hidden their art under covered words as it pleased them.

vocabulary.definition: copertis verbis — covered words, veiled language; the deliberate obscuration of alchemical knowledge through allegory, symbolism, and technical jargon is acknowledged here as a conscious strategy; alchemists justified this secrecy by the danger of the knowledge and the unworthiness of the uninitiated

philosophus — alchemical philosopher; the term used by English alchemists like Norton for the wise masters of the alchemical tradition; the alchemist as philosopher situates the Great Work within the tradition of philosophical contemplation rather than mere craft

source_notes: Thomas Norton's Ordinall of Alchemy (c. 1477 CE) is the most important English alchemical poem of the 15th century, written in English verse but presenting alchemical teaching through metaphor and allegory. Norton explicitly discusses and justifies the tradition of alchemical obscurity — the deliberate hiding of the Work's secrets under covered words. Elias Ashmole included it in his Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum (1652), which preserved many English alchemical texts. Jennifer Rampling's recent work on English alchemy provides essential context.
bibliography: Norton, Thomas. The Ordinall of Alchemy. Ed. John Reidy. London: Oxford University Press (EETS), 1975.

title: Isagoge — De Universalibus
title_english: Introduction — On Universals
author: Porphyrius
representative_sentence: De generibus et speciebus illud quidem sive subsistunt sive in nudis intellectibus posita sunt sive subsistentia corporalia an incorporalia, et utrum separata a sensibilibus an in sensibilibus posita, dicere recusabo.
latin_text: De generibus et speciebus illud quidem sive subsistunt sive in nudis intellectibus posita sunt, dicere recusabo.
english_gloss: Whether genera and species subsist in reality or are placed in bare intellects only — this I shall decline to say.

vocabulary.definition: generibus et speciebus — genera and species; Porphyry's refusal to answer whether universals have real existence beyond the mind is the famous source of the medieval problem of universals, which shaped all scholastic epistemology including the theory of occult properties and hidden forms

subsistunt — subsist, have real existence; the question of whether categories like sympathy, species, and virtue subsist in things themselves (realism) or in the mind (nominalism) determined how magic was theorized: realists could posit real occult virtues; nominalists had to explain them differently

source_notes: Porphyry's Isagoge (c. 270 CE), his introduction to Aristotle's Categories translated into Latin by Boethius, posed the famous problem of universals — whether genera and species have real existence — that dominated medieval philosophy. The question mattered for magic theory: if occult properties (sympathy, virtue) are real universal forms inherent in things, natural magic has a genuine physical basis; if they are merely mental categories, natural magic requires different justification. Boethius's translation and commentary made this text central to medieval education.
bibliography: Porphyry. Isagoge. Trans. Jonathan Barnes. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 2003.

title: Arbor Scientiae — De Radice
title_english: Tree of Science — On the Root
author: Raimundus Lullus
representative_sentence: Scientia est quasi arbor quae ex radice divina in ramos et flores et fructus dispanditur.
latin_text: Scientia est quasi arbor quae ex radice divina in ramos et flores et fructus dispanditur.
english_gloss: Knowledge is like a tree which spreads from a divine root into branches and flowers and fruits.

vocabulary.definition: radix divina — divine root; Lull's tree metaphor grounds all knowledge in God as the ultimate source; the diagram of knowledge as a tree with roots in divine attributes and branches in the various sciences was one of the most influential diagrammatic concepts in medieval and Renaissance encyclopaedism

quasi arbor — as if a tree; the tree as metaphor for organic, connected, hierarchical knowledge — all branches deriving from a single root — prefigures the Sephirot-tree of Kabbalah and the arbor porphyriana of scholastic logic; Lull may have been influenced by kabbalistic tree imagery

source_notes: Ramon Lull's Arbor Scientiae (1295–1296 CE) is a comprehensive classification of knowledge organized around the metaphor of a tree with divine roots spreading into branches of the sciences. The work's tree diagrams, with roots in Lull's divine attributes (Bonitas, Magnitudo, etc.), branches in natural philosophy and theology, and flowers in specific sciences, provided a powerful visual model for the unity of knowledge. Its influence on Renaissance syncretism and kabbalistic tree-diagrams has been analyzed by Harvey Hames and others.
bibliography: Lull, Ramon. Selected Works of Ramon Llull. Ed. and trans. Anthony Bonner. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1985.

title: Liber Runarum — De Hydromantia
title_english: Book of Runes — On Hydromancy
source: Liber Antimaquis (De Arte Notoria et Hydromantia), frag.
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: In aqua pura et stagnante speculum praeparas et per eam occulta cognoscis.
latin_text: In aqua pura et stagnante speculum praeparas et per eam occulta cognoscis.
english_gloss: You prepare a mirror in pure and still water, and through it you come to know hidden things.

vocabulary.definition: hydromantia — hydromancy, water divination; one of the standard categories in medieval magical taxonomies from Isidore onward; the practice ranges from simple reflection-scrying in still water to elaborate procedures involving bowls, oils, and invocations

speculum in aqua — mirror in water; the use of still water as a scrying mirror is one of the most ancient divinatory practices, attested from ancient Egypt and the Near East through Greek and Roman literature and into medieval and Renaissance practice

source_notes: Hydromancy (water divination) was one of the standard categories in medieval magical taxonomies, listed alongside geomancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy as one of the four elemental divination types. The practice of gazing into still water to see visions — essentially a form of catoptromancy (mirror divination) — is among the oldest recorded divinatory methods. Medieval condemnation of hydromancy drew on Isidore's taxonomy and was incorporated into penitential literature; the practice persisted and was recorded by Roger Bacon and later by Agrippa in De Occulta Philosophia I.
bibliography: Klaassen, Frank. 'English Manuscripts of Magic, 1300–1500.' In Conjuring Spirits. Ed. Claire Fanger. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1998.

title: De Incertitudine — De Astrologia
title_english: On Uncertainty — Against Astrology
source: De Incertitudine et Vanitate Omnium Scientiarum, cap. 31
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Astrologi de stellis et eorum effectibus loquuntur tanquam explorati et certa, cum nihil sit incertius.
latin_text: Astrologi de stellis et eorum effectibus loquuntur tanquam explorati et certa, cum nihil sit incertius.
english_gloss: Astrologers speak about the stars and their effects as if they were known and certain, when nothing is more uncertain.

vocabulary.definition: astrologus — astrologer; Agrippa's sceptical attack on astrology in De Incertitudine ch. 31 is a reversal of his De Occulta Philosophia II's extensive use of astrological doctrine, illustrating his use of radical scepticism as a rhetorical strategy rather than a consistent position

nihil sit incertius — nothing is more uncertain; Agrippa's paradox: the discipline that claims to reveal cosmic certainty is itself the most uncertain of all, because the human capacity to read celestial signs is fatally compromised by the complexity of combinations and the fallibility of observation

source_notes: Agrippa's critique of astrology in De Incertitudine ch. 31 attacks practitioners who claim certainty about celestial influences despite the impossibility of precise observation and the infinite complexity of planetary combinations. His sceptical argument draws on Pico's Disputationes against astrology and anticipates later Renaissance critiques by Pomponazzi and Cardano. The juxtaposition of this attack on astrology with De Occulta Philosophia II's extensive use of astrological doctrine illustrates the rhetorical and philosophical tensions in Agrippa's work.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Incertitudine et Vanitate Omnium Scientiarum et Artium. Cologne: Gymnicus, 1531.

title: De Augmentis — Magia Naturalis
title_english: On the Advancement — Natural Magic
source: De Augmentis Scientiarum, Liber III, cap. 5
author: Franciscus Bacon
representative_sentence: Magia naturalis nil aliud est quam applicatio activa passivis, rerum naturalium cognitione suffulta.
latin_text: Magia naturalis nil aliud est quam applicatio activa passivis, rerum naturalium cognitione suffulta.
english_gloss: Natural magic is nothing other than the active application to passives, supported by knowledge of natural things.

vocabulary.definition: applicatio activa passivis — the application of actives to passives; Francis Bacon's definition of natural magic as the operative application of natural knowledge; this formula, which echoes Agrippa, redefines natural magic as what we would call applied science

rerum naturalium cognitione — supported by knowledge of natural things; Bacon grounds operative magic in natural philosophical knowledge, completing the Renaissance project of naturalizing magic by subordinating it to scientific investigation; this made Bacon's natural magic continuous with the emerging experimental program

source_notes: Francis Bacon's De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623 CE) is the Latin expansion of The Advancement of Learning and contains the clearest statement of Bacon's view of natural magic as applied natural philosophy. Bacon's definition of natural magic as 'the application of actives to passives' directly echoes Agrippa and represents the final naturalization of the natural magic tradition into what would become experimental science. Brian Vickers has analyzed the continuities and discontinuities between Renaissance natural magic and Baconian science.
bibliography: Bacon, Francis. De Augmentis Scientiarum. In Works. Ed. J. Spedding et al. London: Longman, 1857–1874.

title: De Natura Rerum — De Draconibus
title_english: On the Nature of Things — On Dragons
source: De Natura Rerum, Liber VI (De Serpentibus)
author: Thomas Cantipratanus
representative_sentence: Draco maximus omnium serpentium est, qui multa venena non habet sed viribus suis et cauda interficit.
latin_text: Draco maximus omnium serpentium est, qui multa venena non habet sed viribus suis et cauda interficit.
english_gloss: The dragon is the greatest of all serpents, which has no great poison but kills with its own strength and tail.

vocabulary.definition: draco — dragon; in medieval natural history, the dragon is a natural creature (the greatest serpent) rather than a purely mythological one; its appearance in bestiaries and encyclopaedias alongside wolves and lions reflects the medieval genre's inclusion of fabulous alongside real animals as vehicles for moral allegory

venenum — poison, venom; the distinction between venomous and non-venomous serpents was practically important for medieval medicine; Thomas's observation that the dragon kills by constriction rather than venom echoes ancient zoological sources and was repeated in Renaissance natural histories

source_notes: Thomas of Cantimpré's De Natura Rerum (c. 1228–1244 CE) is a comprehensive medieval natural history combining Aristotelian zoology, Plinian natural history, and Christian allegory. Like Bartholomaeus Anglicus's roughly contemporary encyclopaedia, it treats animals, plants, and stones as bearers of natural magical properties with spiritual significance. Its material on marvellous animals, including dragons and basilisks, fed into the Renaissance natural magic tradition that treated fabulous creatures as witnesses to nature's hidden powers.
bibliography: Thomas of Cantimpré. Liber de Natura Rerum. Ed. H. Boese. Berlin: De Gruyter, 1973.

title: Otia Imperialia — De Mirabilibus
title_english: Imperial Leisure — On Marvels
author: Gervasius Tilberiensis
representative_sentence: Mirabilia dicimus quae nostrae cognitioni non subiacent, etiam cum sint naturalia.
latin_text: Mirabilia dicimus quae nostrae cognitioni non subiacent, etiam cum sint naturalia.
english_gloss: We call things marvellous which are not subject to our cognition, even though they may be natural.

vocabulary.definition: mirabilia — marvels, wonders; the category of natural phenomena that exceed ordinary understanding; Gervase's definition of mirabilia as natural yet incomprehensible is a key step in the medieval naturalization of the marvelous, separating it from the miraculous (divine) while preserving its wonder

nostrae cognitioni non subiacent — not subject to our cognition; Gervase's epistemological definition of the marvelous as that which exceeds current human understanding; this definition implies that marvels are potentially explicable by natural philosophy rather than permanently mysterious

source_notes: Gervase of Tilbury's Otia Imperialia (c. 1210–1214 CE), composed for the Emperor Otto IV, is a miscellany of geography, history, and natural wonders that was an important vehicle for learning about marvelous phenomena in the 13th century. His definition of mirabilia as natural but incomprehensible phenomena contributed to the medieval category of natural wonders that stood between miracula (divine) and natural operations. Lorraine Daston and Katharine Park's Wonders and the Order of Nature analyzes mirabilia literature of which Gervase is a key example.
bibliography: Gervase of Tilbury. Otia Imperialia. Ed. S.E. Banks and J.W. Binns. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 2002.

title: Summa Theologiae — De Ligaturis
title_english: Summa Theologiae — On Amulets
author: Thomas Aquinas
representative_sentence: Ligaturae quae in collo geruntur vel ad sanitatem vel ad alias causas sunt superstitiosae nisi ex sola vi naturalium rerum operentur.
latin_text: Ligaturae quae in collo geruntur vel ad sanitatem vel ad alias causas sunt superstitiosae nisi ex sola vi naturalium rerum operentur.
english_gloss: Amulets worn around the neck, whether for health or other causes, are superstitious unless they operate solely through the power of natural things.

vocabulary.definition: ligatura — amulet, ligature worn around the neck; Aquinas's treatment distinguishes natural-property amulets (licit if they work by natural virtue alone) from superstitious amulets (those that work only through implicit demonic association or written characteres)

vi naturalium rerum — through the power of natural things; the criterion for licit amulet use; if a stone's protective property can be explained by its natural virtue (warmth, etc.), wearing it is medicine; if it works only through written symbols or unknown causes, it is superstition

source_notes: Aquinas's treatment of amulets in Summa Theologiae II-II q. 96 provides the most careful medieval scholastic analysis of when wearing an amulet is licit natural medicine versus illicit superstition. His criterion — whether the amulet operates through natural virtue alone — created a workable boundary that allowed natural medicine to incorporate lapidary therapeutic objects while condemning written characteres and unknown-operation amulets. This distinction was adopted by Renaissance medical writers who wanted to legitimize natural magic while condemning demonic practice.
bibliography: Thomas Aquinas. Summa Theologiae. Blackfriars ed. 61 vols. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode, 1964–1981.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — De Numeris
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — On Numbers
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber II, caput 3
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Numerus est res praecipua et divina, sine qua nihil vel fieri vel intelligi potest.
latin_text: Numerus est res praecipua et divina, sine qua nihil vel fieri vel intelligi potest.
english_gloss: Number is a principal and divine thing, without which nothing can either be done or understood.

vocabulary.definition: numerus divinus — divine number; Agrippa's Pythagorean-Neoplatonic identification of number with divine reality; the magical squares of planets, the numerological values of divine names, and the geometric figures of talismans all rest on this theological status of number as the structure of divine order

praecipuus — principal, preeminent; number's primacy in Agrippa's system reflects the Pythagorean-Platonic tradition from Nicomachus of Gerasa through Boethius to Ficino in which number underlies all reality; mathematical magic is therefore the most fundamental form of natural magic

source_notes: Book II of Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia opens with a treatment of number as the divine principle underlying all reality, establishing the Pythagorean-Platonic basis for mathematical magic. The subsequent chapters elaborate magical squares (tabulae), the numerological values of letters in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, and the astrological significance of numbers. This mathematical magic draws on Cornelius Agrippa's sources in Reuchlin, Ficino, Pico, and ultimately in the Neoplatonist Nicomachus's Introduction to Arithmetic.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — De Sigillis
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — On Magical Seals
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber II, caput 52
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Sigillis caelestibus inscriptis iuxta characteres planetarum, virtutes eorum conciliantur.
latin_text: Sigillis caelestibus inscriptis iuxta characteres planetarum, virtutes eorum conciliantur.
english_gloss: By the heavenly seals inscribed according to the characters of the planets, their virtues are gathered.

vocabulary.definition: sigillum caeleste — celestial seal; a diagrammatic symbol engraved or drawn to capture and concentrate a planet's virtue; Agrippa's magical seals derive from the numerical-geometrical relationships within each planet's magic square, linking mathematical and talismanic magic

conciliantur — are gathered, attracted; the operative mechanism of the seal: inscribing the planetary seal on the appropriate metal under the appropriate astrological conditions creates an object that attracts and concentrates the planet's specific virtue or influence

source_notes: Agrippa's treatment of magical seals (sigilla) in De Occulta Philosophia II.52 provides a systematic account of how planetary characters and seals are derived from the numerical patterns of magic squares associated with each planet. The Saturn square (3×3), Jupiter square (4×4), Mars square (5×5), Sun square (6×6), Venus square (7×7), Mercury square (8×8), and Moon square (9×9) each generate distinctive geometrical patterns that serve as the planetary seals. This numerological derivation of seals was Agrippa's most original contribution to talismanic theory.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: Utriusque Cosmi — De Unguentum Armarium
title_english: History of Both Worlds — Weapon Salve
source: Utriusque Cosmi Historia, Tractatus II (De Technica Macrocosmi), cap. 4
author: Robertus Fludd
representative_sentence: Unguentum armarium applicatur non vulneri sed armi, et tamen vulnus per sympathiam sanatur.
latin_text: Unguentum armarium applicatur non vulneri sed armi, et tamen vulnus per sympathiam sanatur.
english_gloss: The weapon salve is applied not to the wound but to the weapon, and yet the wound is healed through sympathy.

vocabulary.definition: unguentum armarium — weapon salve; one of the most famous and controversial demonstrations of natural magic in the 17th century: healing a wound by applying salve to the weapon that caused it rather than to the wound itself; the action at a distance it implied was used by Fludd and Paracelsians as evidence for natural sympathy

per sympathiam — through sympathy; Fludd's explanation of the weapon salve's action at a distance; the sympathetic connection between wound and weapon allows the salve applied to the weapon to act on the wound; this was the paradigm case in 17th-century debates about action at a distance in natural magic

source_notes: The weapon salve controversy of the early 17th century — whether a salve applied to a weapon could heal the wound it caused — was one of the major debates in natural magic, involving Fludd, Paracelsians, and critics including William Foster and Marin Mersenne. Fludd defended the salve as a demonstration of natural sympathy and the world-soul's operations; critics argued it was either fraud or demonic assistance. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella analyzes the theoretical context, and Hiro Hirai has studied the specific debate.
bibliography: Foster, William. Hoplocrisma-Spongus, or A Sponge to Wipe Away the Weapon-Salve. London, 1631. // Walker, D.P. Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella. London: Warburg Institute, 1958.

title: Basilica Chymica — Prooemium
title_english: Royal Chemistry — Preface
source: Basilica Chymica, Prooemium de Signaturis Internis Rerum
author: Oswaldus Crollius
representative_sentence: Omnis herba, planta, arbor, lapis et animal characterem internum habet, quo medicus scire potest ad quam morborum curationem sint ordinata.
latin_text: Omnis herba, planta, arbor, lapis et animal characterem internum habet, quo medicus scire potest ad quam morborum curationem sint ordinata.
english_gloss: Every herb, plant, tree, stone, and animal has an internal character, by which the physician can know for the cure of which diseases they are ordained.

vocabulary.definition: characterem internum — internal character, inner signature; Crollius's version of the Paracelsian doctrine of signatures: every natural thing bears an inner mark that reveals its therapeutic purpose; this doctrine made natural magic and medicine identical — reading nature's 'signatures' is both magic and medicine

signatura — signature; Paracelsus's doctrine that each natural object bears a visible or invisible mark (signature) indicating its relationship to specific organs or diseases; the walnut's resemblance to a brain indicates its use for brain diseases; the doctrine was systematized by Crollius and remained influential through the 17th century

source_notes: Oswald Crollius's Basilica Chymica (1609 CE) is the most systematic Paracelsian pharmaceutical treatise of the early 17th century and contains the fullest account of the doctrine of signatures — the theory that natural objects bear visible marks revealing their therapeutic applications. Crollius's signatures doctrine synthesized Paracelsian magical medicine with natural magic's tradition of correspondence, making it simultaneously a medical manual and a system of natural magic. William Eamon analyzes Crollius in the context of Renaissance natural magical medicine.
bibliography: Crollius, Oswald. Basilica Chymica. Frankfurt: Palthenius, 1609.

title: Archidoxis Magicae — Sigilla
title_english: Archidoxis of Magic — Planetary Seals
author: Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (Paracelsus; attrib.)
representative_sentence: Sigillum Solis est forma circularis cum charactere suo et imago regis sedens in throno.
latin_text: Sigillum Solis est forma circularis cum charactere suo et imago regis sedens in throno.
english_gloss: The seal of the Sun is a circular form with its own character and the image of a king sitting on a throne.

vocabulary.definition: sigillum solis — the seal of the Sun; a planetary talisman in the Paracelsian tradition; the Archidoxis Magicae's solar seal combines a diagrammatic character with an anthropomorphic image (a king), connecting it to the Arabic tradition of planetary images in Picatrix

archidoxis magica — the magical arcana; a probably spurious Paracelsian text on planetary seals and characters; while attributed to Paracelsus, modern scholars doubt its authenticity, but it represents a widespread popularization of Paracelsian natural magic into practical talisman-making

source_notes: The Archidoxis Magicae (published 1570 CE, attributed to Paracelsus) is one of several probably spurious texts published under Paracelsus's name that brought his natural-magical philosophy into the practical grimoire tradition. Its planetary seals and characters drew on Arabic-derived talismanic traditions (Picatrix, Agrippa) while presenting them as Paracelsian natural medicine. Whether or not it is authentically Paracelsian, it illustrates how Paracelsian medicine and natural magic were received as continuous practices by 16th–17th-century readers.
bibliography: Paracelsus. Archidoxis Magicae. Trans. Robert Turner. London, 1656.

title: Signatura Rerum — Definitio
title_english: Signature of All Things — Definition
author: Iacobus Böhme
representative_sentence: Omnia quae subsistunt in lumine et obscuritate suam signuram in exteriori forma habent.
latin_text: Omnia quae subsistunt in lumine et obscuritate suam signuram in exteriori forma habent.
english_gloss: All things that subsist in light and darkness have their signature in their external form.

vocabulary.definition: signatura — signature; Böhme's universal doctrine that every created thing bears a visible signature of its inner spiritual principle; his signatures are not merely medical (Crollius's doctrine) but ontological — the outer form is a revelation of the inner spiritual being

lumine et obscuritate — in light and darkness; Böhme's fundamental polarity of divine light and divine wrath that structures all reality; every created thing participates in both principles and its signature reveals the balance between them

source_notes: Jakob Böhme's Signatura Rerum (1621 CE) is the most mystically profound treatment of the doctrine of signatures, extending it from a medical-magical tool into a general ontology: all created things bear signatures of their inner spiritual principles, and reading these signatures is reading the language in which God wrote the world. Böhme's theosophical elaboration of signatures influenced Rosicrucian natural philosophy, 17th-century Protestant mysticism, and the Western esoteric tradition through Swedenborg and beyond.
bibliography: Böhme, Jakob. The Signature of All Things. Trans. John Ellistone. London: Clarke, 1651.

title: De Arte Cyclognomica — De Cometis
title_english: On Cyclognomic Art — On Comets
source: De Arte Cyclognomica, Liber I, cap. 2
author: Cornelius Gemma
representative_sentence: Cometae non solum ex naturalibus causis sed ex divina providentia apparent et futura praenuntiant.
latin_text: Cometae non solum ex naturalibus causis sed ex divina providentia apparent et futura praenuntiant.
english_gloss: Comets appear not only from natural causes but from divine providence and announce future events.

vocabulary.definition: divina providentia — divine providence; Gemma's argument that comets have both natural causes and providential significance reconciles Aristotelian natural philosophy with the divinatory tradition of reading celestial signs as messages from God

futura praenuntiant — they announce future events; the traditional interpretation of comets as portents of disaster (war, plague, death of rulers) that Gemma defends against purely naturalistic accounts; his position allows both natural philosophy and divination to be simultaneously valid

source_notes: Cornelius Gemma's De Arte Cyclognomica (1569 CE) attempts to create a comprehensive science of prognostication from natural signs, combining Aristotelian natural philosophy with the divinatory tradition. His treatment of comets as both natural phenomena and divine signs represents the Renaissance compromise between scientific and prophetic accounts of unusual natural events. Gemma's work influenced later discussions of the relationship between natural philosophy and providential interpretation of natural phenomena in early modern Europe.
bibliography: Gemma, Cornelius. De Arte Cyclognomica. Antwerp: Plantin, 1569.

title: Disquisitiones Magicae — De Goetia
title_english: Magical Investigations — On Goetia
author: Martinus Antonius Delrio
representative_sentence: Goetia est ars per quam daemones ad infima quaeque poscenda compellit illusaque sensuum actiones efficit.
latin_text: Goetia est ars per quam daemones ad infima quaeque poscenda compellit illusaque sensuum actiones efficit.
english_gloss: Goetia is the art by which one compels demons to supply any low things one seeks and produces illusory actions on the senses.

vocabulary.definition: goetia — from Greek goeteia (wailing, sorcery); the lower form of magic involving compulsion of demons for material or sensory effects, as opposed to theurgy (working with divine beings for spiritual ends); Del Rio's definition follows the standard Renaissance distinction between high and low magic

compellit daemones — compels demons; the claim that demons can be compelled by magical operations was theologically controversial: if demons obey the magician, this implies either that the magician has power over demons (denied by Aquinas) or that demons consent to appear willing to be compelled (the standard scholastic answer)

source_notes: Del Rio's Disquisitiones Magicae provides the most systematic Renaissance classification of magical arts, distinguishing theurgy (high magic, working with angels or God), goetia (low magic, compelling demons), and natural magic. His analysis of goetia draws on the ancient Greek-Roman distinction between theurgy and goeteia and applies it to contemporary grimoire magic. The Solomonic tradition — conjuring and compelling spirits by divine names — occupies a middle position in Del Rio's classification that he ultimately condemns as disguised goetia.
bibliography: Del Rio, Martín. Investigations into Magic. Trans. P.G. Maxwell-Stuart. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 2000.

title: Lemegeton — Ars Goetia
title_english: Lemegeton — First Art (Goetia)
source: The Lemegeton (Lesser Key of Solomon), Ars Goetia, cap. 1
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Primus spiritus est rex potens ac terribilis, Bael nomine, qui imperare facit invisibilitati.
latin_text: Primus spiritus est rex potens ac terribilis, Bael nomine, qui imperare facit invisibilitati.
english_gloss: The first spirit is a mighty and terrible king, Bael by name, who makes one able to command invisibility.

vocabulary.definition: Bael — the first of the 72 spirits in the Ars Goetia; the name derives from Ba'al (Lord), the Canaanite deity condemned in Hebrew scripture; his ability to confer invisibility is a typical magical attribute connecting the demon list to ancient traditions of occultation spells

rex potens ac terribilis — mighty and terrible king; the Goetia's spirit descriptions follow a consistent formula including title (king, duke, marquis, etc.), appearance, and abilities; the hierarchical structure reflects the social organization of the demonic realm modeled on European feudal hierarchy

source_notes: The Lemegeton or Lesser Key of Solomon (c. 17th century) is a compilation of five books of ceremonial magic of which the Ars Goetia — the list of 72 bound demons — is the most famous. The Goetia's 72 spirits, organized by rank and listed with seals and abilities, became the standard reference for ceremonial demon-summoning from the 17th century to the present. The text synthesizes earlier Solomonic material from the Clavicula, Pseudomonarchia Daemonum, and other sources. Joseph Peterson's critical edition is the standard scholarly text.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Lesser Key of Solomon (Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis). York Beach: Weiser, 2001.

title: Pseudomonarchia Daemonum — Rex Bael
title_english: False Kingdom of Demons — On the Demon Kings
source: Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (appendix to De Praestigiis Daemonum), entry 1
author: Ioannes Wierus
representative_sentence: Daemones ordines et honores habent quasi militares et multa diversa operantur.
latin_text: Daemones ordines et honores habent quasi militares et multa diversa operantur.
english_gloss: Demons have orders and ranks as if military and perform many diverse operations.

vocabulary.definition: ordines et honores quasi militares — orders and ranks as if military; the hierarchical organization of the demonic realm in the Pseudomonarchia (and later the Goetia) mirrors feudal-military organization; Weyer's 'quasi' marks scepticism about whether demons actually have such ranks or merely appear to

pseudomonarchia — false monarchy; Weyer's ironic title for his appendix on the demonic hierarchy; by calling it a 'false monarchy,' Weyer simultaneously records the demon list (for sceptical purposes) and signals that the whole system is deceptive — demons lie about their ranks and powers

source_notes: Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1577 CE, appendix to the expanded De Praestigiis) is an alphabetical list of 69 demons with their ranks, appearances, and abilities, derived from an earlier grimoire called the Liber Officiorum Spirituum. Weyer's stated purpose was to expose the grimoire tradition as fraudulent by cataloguing its claims; his appendix thus preserves the most important pre-Goetia demon list in a context of explicit debunking. Paradoxically, it became one of the most used reference texts for subsequent demonologists and magicians.
bibliography: Weyer, Johann. Witches, Devils, and Doctors in the Renaissance. Trans. John Shea. Ed. George Mora. Binghamton: MRTS, 1991.

title: Conclusiones — Kabbalah et Magia
title_english: Nine Hundred Conclusions — Kabbalah and Magic
author: Ioannes Picus Mirandulanus
representative_sentence: Nulla scientia magis certificat de divinitate Christi quam magia et cabala.
latin_text: Nulla scientia magis certificat de divinitate Christi quam magia et cabala.
english_gloss: No science certifies the divinity of Christ more than magic and Kabbalah.

vocabulary.definition: certificat de divinitate — certifies the divinity; Pico's controversial thesis that magic and Kabbalah provide stronger proof of Christ's divinity than conventional theological argument was one of the thirteen condemned propositions, raising fears that it subordinated faith to magical evidence

magia et cabala — magic and Kabbalah; Pico's most famous and provocative thesis about the complementarity of natural magic (which demonstrates divine power in nature) and Jewish Kabbalah (which reveals divine names and structures) as convergent proofs of Christian theology

source_notes: Pico's Conclusio 9 of the kabbalistic theses — that no science certifies Christ's divinity more than magic and Kabbalah — was among the thirteen propositions condemned by Pope Innocent VIII in 1487. The papal condemnation was driven less by anti-magical sentiment than by the proposition's apparent claim that kabbalistic and magical argument supersedes orthodox theological proof. Pico's Apologia defending the condemned theses is a key document in the history of Renaissance heresy and of Christian Kabbalah's relationship to Church authority.
bibliography: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Syncretism in the West: Pico's 900 Theses. Ed. and trans. S.A. Farmer. Tempe: MRTS, 1998.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — Alphabetum Magicum
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — Magical Alphabet
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber III, caput 29
author: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Habent Hebraei proprium characterum et figurarum modum qui characteres Malachim et Transitus fluvii et aliis nominibus appellati sunt.
latin_text: Habent Hebraei proprium characterum et figurarum modum qui characteres Malachim et Transitus fluvii et aliis nominibus appellati sunt.
english_gloss: The Hebrews have their own way of characters and figures which are called the characters of Malachim and the Passing of the River and by other names.

vocabulary.definition: characteres Malachim — characters of Malachim (angels); one of the several magical Hebrew alphabets that Agrippa describes in De Occulta Philosophia III, alongside the Celestial alphabet and the Transitus Fluvii; these alphabets were used to inscribe angelic names on talismans and ritual objects

Transitus Fluvii — Passage of the River; another magical alphabet described by Agrippa, believed to be based on ancient Hebrew characters used before the Babylonian captivity; the multiple magical alphabets represent different modes of encoding divine names in physical inscription

source_notes: Agrippa's treatment of magical alphabets in De Occulta Philosophia III.29–30 provides descriptions and illustrations of several magical writing systems including the Celestial alphabet, the Malachim, and the Transitus Fluvii. These scripts, presented as ancient Hebrew writing systems with magical properties, became the most widely used magical alphabets in Western occultism from the Renaissance to the present. Their use on talismans and in ritual inscriptions rests on the kabbalistic principle that letters are not mere signs but ontologically active structures with divine power.
bibliography: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: Decretum — De Sortilegiis
title_english: Decretum — On Sortilege
source: Decretum Gratiani, Causa XXVI, Quaestio 2, canon 1
author: Gratianus
representative_sentence: Qui sortilegio vel augurio seu incantationibus utuntur a communione ecclesiastica penitus arceantur.
latin_text: Qui sortilegio vel augurio seu incantationibus utuntur a communione ecclesiastica penitus arceantur.
english_gloss: Those who use sortilege or augury or incantations shall be completely barred from ecclesiastical communion.

vocabulary.definition: sortilegium — sortilege, divination by lots; the canon's placement of sortilege before augury and incantations reflects the frequency with which lot-casting was used as a divinatory practice across medieval Europe; from Sortes Sanctorum to dice-casting, sortilege was the most democratically accessible form of divination

a communione ecclesiastica — from ecclesiastical communion; excommunication-equivalent punishment for magical practices; Gratian's Decretum systematized canon law and made its condemnations of magic the standard reference for ecclesiastical courts throughout the medieval period

source_notes: Gratian's Decretum (c. 1140 CE) is the foundational document of medieval canon law, systematizing and reconciling the accumulated canons of councils, papal decretals, and patristic authorities into a coherent legal framework. Causa XXVI deals with magic, divination, and sorcery, gathering texts from Augustine, the Councils of Ancyra and Laodicea, and Isidore into a systematic condemnation. The Decretum made canon law on magic stable and portable, providing the framework that all later inquisitorial procedure on magic built upon.
bibliography: Gratian. Decretum Magistri Gratiani. In Corpus Iuris Canonici, vol. 1. Ed. Aemilius Friedberg. Leipzig: Tauchnitz, 1879.

title: Malleus Maleficarum — Maleficium in Matrimonio
title_english: Malleus Maleficarum — Maleficium in Marriage
source: Malleus Maleficarum, Pars II, Quaestio 1, cap. 6
author: Henricus Institoris et Iacobus Sprenger
representative_sentence: Ligatura maleficalis est quando quis per artes diabolicas ab usu matrimonii impeditur.
latin_text: Ligatura maleficalis est quando quis per artes diabolicas ab usu matrimonii impeditur.
english_gloss: Maleficial binding is when someone is prevented from the use of marriage through diabolical arts.

vocabulary.definition: ligatura maleficalis — maleficial ligature; the magical binding that prevents sexual consummation of marriage; this specific form of maleficium was one of the most commonly prosecuted in medieval and early modern courts, with extensive pastoral literature on how to diagnose and cure it

ab usu matrimonii — from the use of marriage; the sacramental and legal term for marital intercourse; the Malleus devotes extensive attention to sexual maleficia because they strike at the sacrament of marriage and directly harm Christian social order

source_notes: The Malleus Maleficarum's treatment of sexual maleficium — particularly the binding spell (ligatura) preventing marital intercourse — occupies substantial portions of Part II. The Malleus's extensive discussion reflects both the pastoral importance of this issue (maleficium in matrimonio undermined the sacrament) and its prevalence in late medieval accusations. Guido Ruggiero's Binding Passions (1993) analyzes how sexual maleficium was prosecuted in Renaissance Venice, showing how widespread anxiety about this form of harmful magic was.
bibliography: Institoris, Heinrich, and Jacob Sprenger. Malleus Maleficarum. Trans. Christopher S. Mackay. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.

title: Picatrix — Oratio Planeti
title_english: Picatrix — Prayer to a Planet
author: Anonymous (attrib. Maslama al-Qurtubi; trans. c. 1256)
representative_sentence: O Iuppiter, tu es iustus et sapiens, da mihi de virtute tua secundum quod habes.
latin_text: O Iuppiter, tu es iustus et sapiens, da mihi de virtute tua secundum quod habes.
english_gloss: O Jupiter, you are just and wise, give me of your virtue according to what you have.

vocabulary.definition: O Iuppiter — invocation of Jupiter; Picatrix's prayers address planets as persons — an animistic theology that identifies the planets with divine intelligences who can receive petitions; this personal address to planetary beings was central to the talismanic magic the Speculum Astronomiae condemned

da mihi de virtute tua — give me of your virtue; the operative request of the planetary prayer: that the planet transmit some of its specific quality (Jupiter's justice and wisdom) to the petitioner; the mechanics of talismanic magic depend on this transmission of planetary virtue through the medium of a specially prepared image

source_notes: Picatrix's planetary prayers are among the most important evidence for the religious-magical dimension of medieval astral magic: the planets are addressed as divine persons who can be petitioned, praised, and asked for gifts. These prayers reveal the theological layer beneath the technical apparatus of astrological image-making: the talisman works because the planet-spirit accepts and responds to the petition embedded in its creation. Charles Burnett's work on Picatrix's Latin transmission has illuminated how Arabic astral religion was adapted for Western Christian contexts.
bibliography: Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: De Rerum Varietate — De Auguriis
title_english: On the Variety of Things — On Omens
source: De Rerum Varietate, Liber XVI, cap. 93
author: Hieronymus Cardanus
representative_sentence: Si quidem rebus omnibus naturales virtutes insunt, et caelestibus influxibus singula reguntur, auguria non penitus inaniter accipiuntur.
latin_text: Si quidem rebus omnibus naturales virtutes insunt, et caelestibus influxibus singula reguntur, auguria non penitus inaniter accipiuntur.
english_gloss: If indeed natural virtues inhere in all things, and each thing is governed by celestial influences, auguries are not received entirely in vain.

vocabulary.definition: naturales virtutes — natural virtues; Cardano's claim that augury is not entirely vain rests on the Aristotelian-astrological position that all natural things have specific virtues given by celestial influences; if birds respond to the same astral causes as human affairs, bird-signs may genuinely indicate future events

caelestibus influxibus — celestial influences; the astrological theory of how heavenly bodies cause sublunary events; Cardano uses this to provide a naturalistic justification for augury — birds respond to the same planetary conditions that determine human outcomes, so their behavior can indicate those conditions

source_notes: Cardano's De Rerum Varietate (1557 CE) is a comprehensive natural history of marvels and unusual phenomena, covering augury, divination, dreams, and occult properties alongside meteorology, geology, and medicine. His naturalistic defense of augury as potentially valid — if all things are governed by celestial influences, bird behavior may indeed reflect the same influences as human affairs — is characteristic of his willingness to take divinatory practices seriously as natural phenomena while remaining sceptical of their practitioners.
bibliography: Cardano, Girolamo. De Rerum Varietate. Basle: Petri, 1557.

title: Summa Theologiae — De Verbis Incantationum
title_english: Summa Theologiae — On Words of Incantation
author: Thomas Aquinas
representative_sentence: Verba ut verba nullam habent ex natura sua virtutem ad aliquem naturalem effectum producendum.
latin_text: Verba ut verba nullam habent ex natura sua virtutem ad aliquem naturalem effectum producendum.
english_gloss: Words, as words, have no power from their own nature to produce any natural effect.
