vocabulary.definition: verba ut verba — words as words; Aquinas's anti-magical language theory: words have no inherent natural power beyond their semantic and social functions; any apparent operative power of words requires an external cause — divine grace for prayer, demonic assistance for magic

naturalem effectum — natural effect; the key distinction in Aquinas's analysis of incantation: words can produce natural effects through their semantic content (conveying information, persuading) but not through their physical sound; incantations that claim to produce effects by their mere utterance therefore imply non-natural (supernatural or demonic) causation

source_notes: Aquinas's analysis of verbal charms in Summa Theologiae II-II q. 96 is the most rigorous medieval philosophical treatment of incantatory power. His argument that words have no inherent physical virtue directly contradicts popular belief in the operative power of spoken formulas and the learned tradition of voces magicae. Aquinas allows words to produce effects through meaning (prayer achieving divine effects) or through natural acoustic properties (sound causing physical vibration) but denies any other mode of verbal causation — a position that made all incantatory magic theologically suspect.
bibliography: Thomas Aquinas. Summa Theologiae. Blackfriars ed. 61 vols. London: Eyre and Spottiswoode, 1964–1981.

title: Polygraphia — Scriptura Secreta
title_english: Polygraphia — Secret Writing
author: Ioannes Trithemius
representative_sentence: Scriptura secreta per ipsam litterarum varietatem in iis maxime locis adhibetur ubi secreta celanda sunt.
latin_text: Scriptura secreta per ipsam litterarum varietarum in iis maxime locis adhibetur ubi secreta celanda sunt.
english_gloss: Secret writing through the variety of letters itself is most employed in those places where secrets must be concealed.

vocabulary.definition: scriptura secreta — secret writing; Trithemius's Polygraphia is the first book on cryptography and polygraphy (multiple writing systems) published in Europe; its subject matter — hiding messages in various writing forms — connects to the magical secrecy tradition even as Trithemius frames it as natural art

litterarum varietatem — variety of letters; the principle that any alternative script system can serve as a cipher; Trithemius documents dozens of alternative writing systems including magical alphabets, making Polygraphia a bridge between the cryptographic and the magical alphabets traditions

source_notes: Trithemius's Polygraphia (1518 CE) is the first printed book on cryptography and steganography in Europe, documenting numerous cipher systems including many magical alphabets. While distinct from his Steganographia (which disguised ciphers as magical operations), the Polygraphia shares with it the theme of secret communication through writing. Trithemius positioned his work as a natural art serving the needs of diplomacy and scholarship rather than magic, but the overlap between magical alphabets and cryptographic scripts made the boundary porous.
bibliography: Trithemius, Johannes. Polygraphia. Oppenheim: Köbel, 1518. // Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999.

title: Introductorium in Astronomiam — De Planetarum Effectibus
title_english: Introduction to Astronomy — On the Effects of the Planets
author: Abu Ma'shar (trans. Hermann of Carinthia)
date: Arabic c. 9th c.; Latin trans. c. 1140
representative_sentence: Saturnus autem ex planetis summum tenet locum, et eius natura frigida et sicca est, maleficaque in rebus humanis.
latin_text: Saturnus autem ex planetis summum tenet locum, et eius natura frigida et sicca est, maleficaque in rebus humanis. Omnia quae ad tristitionem, tarditatem, et senium pertinent sub eius dominio ponuntur.
english_gloss: Saturn holds the highest place among the planets, and its nature is cold and dry, and malefic in human affairs. All things pertaining to sadness, slowness, and old age are placed under its dominion.

vocabulary.definition: malefic — harmful or evil in influence; standard astrological term for Saturn and Mars as planets of ill omen
dominion — planetary rulership over specific substances, qualities, and human activities; the operative basis of astrological medicine and image magic

source_notes: Abu Ma'shar (Albumasar, d. 886) was the most influential Arabic astrologer in the Latin West; his Introductorium, translated by Hermann of Carinthia in 1140, transmitted Aristotelian and Ptolemaic astrology to medieval Europe. Charles Burnett has traced how this text shaped the entire medieval understanding of celestial causation and astrological medicine.
bibliography: Lemay, Richard. Abu Ma'shar and Latin Aristotelianism in the Twelfth Century. Beirut: American University of Beirut, 1962. // Burnett, Charles. 'The Coherence of the Arabic-Latin Translation Program in Toledo in the Twelfth Century.' Science in Context 14 (2001): 249–288.

title: De Imaginibus — De Opere Imaginum
title_english: On Images — On the Work of Talismanic Images
author: Thabit ibn Qurra (attrib.; trans. from Arabic)
date: Arabic c. 9th c.; Latin trans. c. 12th c.
representative_sentence: Imago sub electa hora et gradu ascendente confecta virtutem caelestis figurae in se recipit, et effectum in rebus inferioribus producit.
latin_text: Imago sub electa hora et gradu ascendente confecta virtutem caelestis figurae in se recipit, et effectum in rebus inferioribus producit.
english_gloss: An image made under a chosen hour and ascending degree receives into itself the virtue of the celestial figure, and produces its effect in lower things.

vocabulary.definition: ascending degree — the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of an image's creation; the most critical factor in talismanic timing
talismanic image — an engraved figure made at an astrologically elected moment to capture and transmit celestial influence; the central subject of Arabic-Latin image magic

source_notes: De Imaginibus, attributed to the ninth-century Sabian mathematician Thabit ibn Qurra, is the foundational Latin text on talismanic image magic. It specifies the astrological conditions under which engraved images acquire celestial virtues. The Speculum Astronomiae treated it as a borderline work; Paola Zambelli analysed its reception in the context of Albert the Great's engagement with image magic.
bibliography: Greer, John Michael, trans. De Imaginibus: Astral High Magic. Tempe: Renaissance Astrology, 2012. // Zambelli, Paola. The Speculum Astronomiae and Its Enigma. Dordrecht: Kluwer, 1992.

title: De Causis Mirabilium — Contra Superstitionem
title_english: On the Causes of Wonders — Against Superstition
author: Nicole Oresme
representative_sentence: Omnia quae hominibus mira videntur ex naturali causa procedunt, et non ex pactione daemonis aut arte magica.
latin_text: Omnia quae hominibus mira videntur ex naturali causa procedunt, et non ex pactione daemonis aut arte magica.
english_gloss: All things that seem wondrous to people proceed from a natural cause, and not from a demonic pact or the magical arts.

vocabulary.definition: wondrous/miraculous — the category of preternatural events Oresme sought to explain naturalistically, distinguishing marvel from miracle and from demonic intervention
demonic pact — the theoretical basis for learned magic's illegitimacy; Oresme's critique aimed to remove this explanation from natural phenomena entirely

source_notes: Nicole Oresme (c. 1320–1382), bishop of Lisieux and Aristotelian natural philosopher, wrote De Causis Mirabilium as a systematic naturalistic explanation of apparently supernatural events, arguing that marvels require no demonic cause. His approach represents the scholastic naturalist wing of medieval thought on magic, usefully contrasted with Aquinas and William of Auvergne by Michael D. Bailey.
bibliography: Hansen, Bert, ed. Nicole Oresme and the Marvels of Nature. Toronto: Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 1985.

title: De Lamiis et Phitonicis Mulieribus — De Natura Lamiarum
title_english: On Witches and Female Soothsayers — On the Nature of Witches
author: Ulrich Molitor
representative_sentence: Lamiae et striges non vere transformantur, sed diaboli illusione et phantasmate se volare et mutari putant.
latin_text: Lamiae et striges non vere transformantur, sed diaboli illusione et phantasmate se volare et mutari putant.
english_gloss: Witches and night-hags are not truly transformed, but believe themselves to fly and change form through the devil's illusion and phantasm.

vocabulary.definition: witch/lamia — a term for female night-demons or witches; Molitor's use reflects the contested late medieval demonology that questioned whether such figures acted physically or only in illusion
phantasm — diabolical illusion; in Molitor's cautious demonology, the devil acts on the imagination rather than producing real physical transformation

source_notes: Ulrich Molitor's De Lamiis (1489), written as a dialogue dedicated to Archduke Sigismund, argues that witches' feats are diabolical illusions rather than real physical acts—a position more conservative than the Malleus Maleficarum. It is notable as one of the earliest illustrated printed witchcraft treatises. Michael D. Bailey discusses it in the context of early modern demonological debate.
bibliography: Molitor, Ulrich. De Lamiis et Phitonicis Mulieribus. Constance, 1489. // Bailey, Michael D. Magic and Superstition in Europe. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2007.

title: Buch aller verbotenen Kunst — De Arte Chiromantiae
title_english: Book of All Forbidden Arts — On the Art of Chiromancy
source: Buch aller verbotenen Kunst, Unglaubens und der Zauberei (Latin summary passages)
author: Johannes Hartlieb
representative_sentence: Chiromantia est ars ex lineis et figuris manus fortunam et mores hominis praedicendi, quam aliqui ex daemonum illusione procedere dicunt.
latin_text: Chiromantia est ars ex lineis et figuris manus fortunam et mores hominis praedicendi, quam aliqui ex daemonum illusione procedere dicunt.
english_gloss: Chiromancy is the art of predicting the fortune and character of a person from the lines and figures of the hand, which some say proceeds from the illusion of demons.

vocabulary.definition: chiromancy — divination from the lines of the palm; classified among the seven forbidden arts (nigromancy, geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, pyromancy, scapulamancy, chiromancy) by Hartlieb
lines — the major and minor lines of the palm (vita, mentis, cordis) read as indices of fate; the empirical substrate of palmistic practice

source_notes: Johannes Hartlieb (c. 1400–1468), court physician to the Wittelsbach dukes, wrote the Buch aller verbotenen Kunst in German, but it circulated with Latin chapter summaries and influenced the later Latin demonological tradition. It is one of the first systematic vernacular classifications of the seven forbidden divinatory arts and demonstrates how learned magic discourse filtered into lay and courtly contexts.
bibliography: Hartlieb, Johannes. Das Buch aller verbotenen Künste. Ed. Frank Fürbeth. Frankfurt: Insel, 1998. // Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: De Grandine et Tonitruis — Contra Magos Tempestarii
title_english: On Hail and Thunder — Against Weather-Magicians
author: Agobard of Lyon
representative_sentence: Vulgus credit quosdam homines, quos tempestarios vocant, valere excitare grandines et tonitrua, et posse transferre fruges de agro in agrum.
latin_text: Vulgus credit quosdam homines, quos tempestarios vocant, valere excitare grandines et tonitrua, et posse transferre fruges de agro in agrum.
english_gloss: The common people believe that certain men, whom they call storm-makers, have the power to stir up hail and thunder, and to transfer crops from one field to another.

vocabulary.definition: storm-maker/weather-magician — a person popularly believed to control storms; Agobard's treatise is a key early Carolingian critique of such beliefs as superstition incompatible with Christian natural theology
common people — the populace whose beliefs Agobard is attempting to correct; distinguishing elite theological knowledge from popular credulity

source_notes: Agobard, Archbishop of Lyon (769–840), wrote De Grandine et Tonitruis as a rationalistic critique of popular belief in weather magicians, arguing such effects are beyond human power and attributing storm damage solely to natural causes governed by God. The text is a landmark in the Carolingian policing of popular magic and is discussed by Valerie Flint in her study of the rise of magic in early medieval Europe.
bibliography: Van Acker, Lieven, ed. Agobardi Lugdunensis Opera Omnia. CCCM 52. Turnhout: Brepols, 1981. // Flint, Valerie I.J. The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991.

title: De Divortio Lotharii — De Maleficiis et Ligaturis
title_english: On the Divorce of Lothar — On Maleficia and Ligatures
source: De Divortio Lotharii Regis et Theutbergae Reginae
author: Hincmar of Reims
representative_sentence: Malefici per daemonum ministerium ligare possunt homines ne copulam coniugalem perficere valeant, et haec ligatura vera esse creditur.
latin_text: Malefici per daemonum ministerium ligare possunt homines ne copulam coniugalem perficere valeant, et haec ligatura vera esse creditur.
english_gloss: Malefactors, through the service of demons, are able to bind people so that they cannot complete the conjugal act, and this binding is believed to be real.

vocabulary.definition: to bind — the central operation of malefic magic (ligatura); Hincmar affirmed that demonic binding of sexual function was real, with significant implications for canon law on marriage impediments
malefactors/sorcerers — those who perform harmful magic; Hincmar's discussion contributed to defining maleficium as a concrete canonical and legal offense

source_notes: Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims (806–882), addressed questions of magical impediment to marriage in his treatise on the divorce of King Lothar II. His affirmation that demonic ligature could genuinely prevent consummation entered canonical tradition and shaped subsequent discussions in Gratian and later canonists. This is a key text for the history of maleficium in ecclesiastical law.
bibliography: Böhringer, Letha, ed. De Divortio Lotharii Regis et Theutbergae Reginae. MGH Concilia IV Suppl. 1. Hanover: Hahn, 1992.

title: Sermones — De Superstitione Pagana
title_english: Sermons — On Pagan Superstition
author: Caesarius of Arles
representative_sentence: Nemo nomina daemonum, nemo caracteres, nemo herbas aut lapides colligat, sed omnia haec velut venena diaboli respuat.
latin_text: Nemo nomina daemonum, nemo caracteres, nemo herbas aut lapides colligat, sed omnia haec velut venena diaboli respuat.
english_gloss: Let no one gather the names of demons, let no one collect characters, let no one gather herbs or stones, but let all these things be rejected as the poisons of the devil.

vocabulary.definition: characters — magical signs or symbols; Caesarius's condemnation of characters alongside demonic names is an early attestation of Christian hostility to the use of graphical magical notations
poisons of the devil — Caesarius's rhetorical framing of magical practices as spiritually toxic; a template for later pastoral anti-magic discourse

source_notes: Caesarius of Arles (c. 470–542), bishop and monastic reformer, left a large corpus of sermones addressed to lay audiences that are among the richest sources for popular magical practice in sixth-century Gaul. His repeated condemnations of amulets, characters, and healing spells demonstrate the persistence of non-Christian practice and shaped Carolingian pastoral policing of magic.
bibliography: Morin, Germain, ed. Caesarii Arelatensis Opera Omnia I: Sermones. CCSL 103–104. Turnhout: Brepols, 1953. // Klingshirn, William E. Caesarius of Arles: The Making of a Christian Community in Late Antique Gaul. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1994.

title: Concilium Laodicense — Canon XXXVI
title_english: Council of Laodicea — Canon 36
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Non oportet sacerdotes vel clericos esse magos, vel incantatores, vel mathematicos, vel astrologos.
latin_text: Non oportet sacerdotes vel clericos esse magos, vel incantatores, vel mathematicos, vel astrologos.
english_gloss: Priests and clergy ought not to be magicians, or enchanters, or mathematicians, or astrologers.

vocabulary.definition: mathematicians/astrologers — in late antique Latin usage, mathematicus regularly denotes an astrologer or caster of horoscopes, not a mathematician in the modern sense; the semantic slippage reflects anxiety about the divinatory implications of astronomical knowledge
enchanters — those who use spoken spells or charms; the canon's enumeration classifies magic into operative categories that recur in later canonical and penitential literature

source_notes: The Council of Laodicea (c. 363 CE) issued canons regulating clerical conduct, including this prohibition on clerical involvement in magic and astrology. The grouping of magus, incantator, mathematicus, and astrologus became a standard canonical taxonomy repeated in later conciliar and penitential texts. It exemplifies the institutional church's effort to define and police the boundary between legitimate liturgy and illicit manipulation.
bibliography: Joannou, Périclès-Pierre. Discipline Générale Antique (IVe–IXe s.), Vol. I/2. Grottaferrata: Tipografia Italo-Orientale, 1962.

title: De Magicis Artibus — Enumeratio Artium Magicarum
title_english: On the Magical Arts — Enumeration of the Magical Arts
author: Hrabanus Maurus
representative_sentence: Magicae artes multa genera habent: sunt enim necromantici, hydromantici, aeromantici, pyromantici, geomantici, et qui aruspicia vel auguria sequuntur.
latin_text: Magicae artes multa genera habent: sunt enim necromantici, hydromantici, aeromantici, pyromantici, geomantici, et qui aruspicia vel auguria sequuntur.
english_gloss: The magical arts have many kinds: for there are necromancers, hydromancers, aeromancers, pyromancers, geomancers, and those who follow augury or haruspicy.

vocabulary.definition: necromancers — diviners through the dead; Hrabanus draws from Isidore to catalogue divinatory arts as a taxonomy of prohibition that influenced the entire subsequent encyclopaedic tradition

haruspicy — divination from entrails; Hrabanus's inclusion of classical Roman divinatory practices in a Carolingian classification shows the persistence of antique categories as models for organizing forbidden knowledge

source_notes: Hrabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), Abbot of Fulda and later Archbishop of Mainz, compiled De Magicis Artibus drawing heavily on Isidore's Etymologiae to classify and condemn the magical arts. His work transmitted late antique encyclopaedic classification of magic into the Carolingian educational tradition and formed a bridge to later medieval taxonomies of forbidden knowledge.
bibliography: PL 110, cols. 1095–1110. // Flint, Valerie I.J. The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991.

title: Epistulae — De Imaginibus Tutandis
title_english: Letters — On Protective Images
author: Anonymous (attrib. Apollonius of Tyana)
representative_sentence: Imago in aere sub ascendente Scorpii facta et in muro posita urbem a serpentibus et animalibus venenatis perpetuo tuebitur.
latin_text: Imago in aere sub ascendente Scorpii facta et in muro posita urbem a serpentibus et animalibus venenatis perpetuo tuebitur.
english_gloss: An image made in bronze under the ascendant of Scorpio and placed in a wall will protect the city from serpents and venomous creatures forever.

vocabulary.definition: ascendant of Scorpio — the moment Scorpio rises on the eastern horizon; astrological election of the right zodiacal ascendant is essential for crafting effective talismanic images
bronze — the metal corresponding to Venus in some systems, though here used for a city-protective talisman; the Apollonius correspondence treats metal selection as integral to talismanic power

source_notes: Texts attributed to Apollonius of Tyana (c. 15–100 CE), the neo-Pythagorean sage, circulated in Arabic and Latin as authorities on talismanic magic. The pseudo-Apollonian correspondence on protective city-images entered Picatrix and the broader Arabic-Latin talismanic tradition. Charles Burnett and David Pingree have traced the transmission of Apollonius as a magical authority through Arabic intermediaries.
bibliography: Pingree, David. 'The Diffusion of Arabic Magical Texts in Western Europe.' La diffusione delle scienze islamiche nel medio evo europeo. Rome: Accademia dei Lincei, 1987. 57–102.

title: Ars Almadel — De Invocatione Angelorum per Altitudines
title_english: The Ars Almadel — On the Invocation of Angels through the Altitudes
author: Anonymous (attrib. Solomon)
representative_sentence: Fac tabulam de cera alba mundissima in qua sculpes characteres et nomina angelorum altitudinis primae, et eos per incensum thymiamatis invoca.
latin_text: Fac tabulam de cera alba mundissima in qua sculpes characteres et nomina angelorum altitudinis primae, et eos per incensum thymiamatis invoca.
english_gloss: Make a table of the purest white wax in which you will engrave the characters and names of the angels of the first altitude, and invoke them through the incense of frankincense.

vocabulary.definition: altitude — in the Almadel system, one of four celestial divisions each governed by a class of angels; the altitudes correspond to seasons and cardinal directions

frankincense/incense — the aromatic suffumigation required for angelic contact; the Almadel, like many grimoires, specifies particular incenses for each angelic group to establish sympathetic correspondence

source_notes: The Ars Almadel is a short Solomonic grimoire describing the construction of a wax tablet inscribed with angelic names and characters to serve as a ritual instrument for invoking angels of the four celestial altitudes. It circulated as part of the Lemegeton compilation and represents the angelic invocation current within the broader Solomonic tradition. Frank Klaassen and Joseph Peterson have edited and contextualized the text.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser, 2001. // Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Liber de Angelis — De Operatione per Lunam
title_english: Book of Angels — On Operation through the Moon
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: In hora Lunae, luna existente in signo aqueo, exerce operationem tuam cum characteribus et nominibus angelis Lunae deputatis, et effectum desideratum obtinebis.
latin_text: In hora Lunae, luna existente in signo aqueo, exerce operationem tuam cum characteribus et nominibus angelis Lunae deputatis, et effectum desideratum obtinebis.
english_gloss: In the hour of the Moon, when the moon is in a watery sign, perform your operation with the characters and names assigned to the angels of the Moon, and you will obtain the desired effect.

vocabulary.definition: hour of the Moon — a planetary hour corresponding to lunar governance; timing magical operations to planetary hours is a widespread medieval practice linking astrological election to angelic invocation
characters — inscribed signs specific to each angelic power; the Liber de Angelis integrates astrological timing with Solomonic character-writing as joint prerequisites for effective ritual

source_notes: The Liber de Angelis is a fourteenth-century Latin ritual text prescribing operations for invoking planetary angels through a combination of astrological timing, characters, and suffumigation. It belongs to the learned ritual magic tradition examined by Frank Klaassen and Sophie Page and illustrates how Solomonic and astrological elements were fused in late medieval clerical magic.
bibliography: Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013. // Page, Sophie. Magic in the Cloister. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: De Naturis Rerum — De Virtutibus Herbarum
title_english: On the Natures of Things — On the Virtues of Plants
author: Alexander Neckam
representative_sentence: Virtutes occultas plantarum et lapidum non ex composito elementorum, sed ex influentia caelesti originem habere philosophi tradiderunt.
latin_text: Virtutes occultas plantarum et lapidum non ex composito elementorum, sed ex influentia caelesti originem habere philosophi tradiderunt.
english_gloss: Philosophers have handed down that the occult virtues of plants and stones have their origin not from the composition of elements, but from celestial influence.

vocabulary.definition: occult virtues — hidden properties of natural substances that cannot be reduced to the four elemental qualities; attributed to celestial imprinting rather than elemental composition in the Aristotelian-Arabic synthesis

celestial influence — the downward flow of power from stars to terrestrial substances; the standard explanation for hidden natural virtues in medieval natural philosophy from al-Kindi through Albertus Magnus

source_notes: Alexander Neckam (1157–1217), Augustinian canon and master at Paris and Oxford, wrote De Naturis Rerum as an encyclopaedic natural philosophy engaging with the newly translated Arabic-Aristotelian corpus. His discussion of occult virtues illustrates how the concept was integrated into high medieval natural philosophy before Albertus Magnus gave it its fullest scholastic elaboration.
bibliography: Wright, Thomas, ed. Alexandri Neckam De Naturis Rerum. Rolls Series 34. London: HMSO, 1863.

title: De Sortibus — Utrum Sortes Sint Licitae
title_english: On Lots — Whether Divination by Lots Is Licit
author: Thomas Aquinas
representative_sentence: Sortes dividentes, quibus quaerit homo quid agere debet aut quid ei eventurum sit, superstitiosae sunt et illicitae, nisi forte ex divina providentia aliquid manifestetur.
latin_text: Sortes dividentes, quibus quaerit homo quid agere debet aut quid ei eventurum sit, superstitiosae sunt et illicitae, nisi forte ex divina providentia aliquid manifestetur.
english_gloss: Dividing lots, by which a person seeks to know what he ought to do or what will happen to him, are superstitious and illicit, unless perhaps something is manifested by divine providence.

vocabulary.definition: dividing lots — one of three Thomistic categories of sortilege (consulting, dividing, poetic); lots used to determine future outcomes or courses of action fall under the general prohibition of divination

superstitious — involving implicit or explicit demonic pact by presuming to access knowledge God has not sanctioned to be revealed; Aquinas's category of superstitio organizes his entire treatment of divination

source_notes: Aquinas's De Sortibus is a short treatise distinguishing three types of lots and assessing their liceity. His careful taxonomy—sortes consultoriae, divisoriae, and divinatoriae—became standard in later scholastic and canonistic discussions of divination. The text exemplifies the scholastic project of rationally categorizing and adjudicating magical practices rather than simply condemning them wholesale.
bibliography: Aquinas, Thomas. Opera Omnia. Ed. Leonine Commission. Vol. 43. Rome: Commissio Leonina, 1976.

title: Lapidario — De Virtutibus Lapidum sub Stellis
title_english: Lapidary — On the Virtues of Stones under the Stars
author: Alfonso X of Castile (attrib.; trans. from Arabic)
representative_sentence: Cada piedra tiene su vertud del signo o del planeta que es su señor, et quando la luna es en aquel signo et en aquel grado, entonces es la piedra de mayor vertud.
latin_text: Quaelibet gemma virtutem suam a signo vel planeta qui dominus eius est accipit, et quando luna est in illo signo et in illo gradu, tunc gemma summam suam virtutem habet.
english_gloss: Each gemstone receives its virtue from the sign or planet that is its lord, and when the moon is in that sign and degree, then the gemstone has its greatest virtue.

vocabulary.definition: lord/ruler — the astrological rulership linking each stone to a particular planet or zodiacal sign; the causal basis for the stone's medicinal and magical power
virtue/power — the specific hidden property of the gemstone activated by astral alignment; the Lapidario bridges natural-magical and astrological frameworks

source_notes: Alfonso X of Castile's Lapidario (c. 1250), compiled under royal patronage from an Arabic source attributed to the sage Abolays, is the most extensive medieval lapidary organized by astrological correspondence. Each stone is linked to a specific degree of the zodiac and acquires its virtue when the moon transits that degree. The text illustrates how Arabic astrological mineralogy was integrated into Iberian Latin learned culture.
bibliography: Brey Mariño, María, ed. Alfonso X el Sabio: Lapidario. Madrid: Castalia, 1982. // Burnett, Charles, and Danielle Jacquart, eds. Constantine the African and 'Ali ibn al-'Abbas al-Magusi. Leiden: Brill, 1994.

title: Determinatio de Superstitione — Paris 1398
title_english: Determination on Superstition — Paris 1398
source: Determinatio Facultatis Theologiae Parisiensis de Superstitione
author: University of Paris, Faculty of Theology
representative_sentence: Ars magica quae communicat cum daemonibus, sive per expressum pactum sive per implicitum, omnino illicita est et fidei christianae contraria.
latin_text: Ars magica quae communicat cum daemonibus, sive per expressum pactum sive per implicitum, omnino illicita est et fidei christianae contraria.
english_gloss: The magical art that communicates with demons, whether through an explicit or implicit pact, is entirely illicit and contrary to the Christian faith.

vocabulary.definition: explicit pact — a formal, consciously made agreement with a demon; distinguished from the implicit pact, which the Paris theologians argued is involved in any use of magic even without knowing it

implicit — the expansion of the demonic pact doctrine to cover cases where the practitioner had not consciously contracted with demons; this concept, developed at Paris in 1398, enormously broadened the scope of illicit magic

source_notes: The 1398 Determinatio of the Paris Theology Faculty, associated with Jean Gerson and Pierre d'Ailly, is a landmark document in the history of demonology. It extended the doctrine of the demonic pact to cover practitioners who did not consciously invoke demons, making nearly all learned ritual magic formally heretical. Michael D. Bailey and Kieckhefer have analysed its role in shaping the fifteenth-century witch-craze.
bibliography: Hansen, Joseph. Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns. Bonn: Georgi, 1901. // Bailey, Michael D. 'From Sorcery to Witchcraft: Clerical Conceptions of Magic in the Later Middle Ages.' Speculum 76 (2001): 960–990.

title: Cosmographia — De Natura Animae Mundi
title_english: Cosmographia — On the Nature of the World Soul
author: Bernard Silvestris
representative_sentence: Noys, divinae mentis speculum, et secundum ipsum exemplar quo mundus informatur, in rerum naturas et arcanas efficacias velut in thesauros proprios intuetur.
latin_text: Noys, divinae mentis speculum, et secundum ipsum exemplar quo mundus informatur, in rerum naturas et arcanas efficacias velut in thesauros proprios intuetur.
english_gloss: Noys, the mirror of the divine mind, and the model according to which the world is formed, gazes into the natures of things and their hidden efficacies as into her own treasures.

vocabulary.definition: Noys (Nous) — Bernard's Latinization of the Neoplatonic divine Intellect; she mediates between the first principle and matter, organizing the world through ideal forms
hidden efficacies — the hidden powers embedded in natural things by the world-soul; this concept provides a Neoplatonic foundation for natural magic theory in the twelfth-century Schools

source_notes: Bernard Silvestris of Tours (fl. c. 1147) composed the Cosmographia, a prosimetrum (alternating prose and verse) describing the creation of the universe through the World Soul (Noys) and Nature (Natura). The text draws on the Timaeus in Calcidius's translation and was a vehicle for Neoplatonic ideas about hidden natural powers that influenced subsequent natural magic theory. Winthrop Wetherbee's edition and commentary remains standard.
bibliography: Wetherbee, Winthrop, ed. The Cosmographia of Bernardus Silvestris. New York: Columbia University Press, 1973.

title: Quaestiones Naturales — De Virtutibus Naturalibus
title_english: Natural Questions — On Natural Virtues
author: Adelard of Bath
representative_sentence: Si quid mirabile in rebus humanis apparet, non daemonum operibus sed naturae rationibus adscribendum est, quarum rationes nos latent.
latin_text: Si quid mirabile in rebus humanis apparet, non daemonum operibus sed naturae rationibus adscribendum est, quarum rationes nos latent.
english_gloss: If anything marvellous appears in human affairs, it must be attributed not to the works of demons but to the reasons of nature, which are hidden from us.

vocabulary.definition: marvellous — the preternatural event whose cause is hidden; Adelard's naturalistic programme, derived from Arabic science, sought to replace demonic and supernatural explanation with rational natural causes

reasons of nature — the rational principles underlying natural phenomena; Adelard's key epistemological claim that marvels have natural explanations not yet discovered represents an early Latin rationalism about magic

source_notes: Adelard of Bath (fl. c. 1116–1142), one of the first major Latin translators of Arabic science, framed his Quaestiones Naturales as a dialogue between old (authority-based) and new (reason-based) approaches to natural philosophy. His insistence on natural explanation of marvels, derived from his Arabic studies, marks an important shift toward naturalistic accounts of magical phenomena in the early twelfth century.
bibliography: Burnett, Charles, ed. Adelard of Bath: Conversations with His Nephew. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

title: L'Acerba — De Stellis et Fato
title_english: The Harsh One — On Stars and Fate
author: Cecco d'Ascoli
representative_sentence: Stellae non cogunt sed inclinant, nisi quis per virtutem mentis supra fatum se erigat; plerique tamen fato cedunt et sub astris vivunt.
latin_text: Stellae non cogunt sed inclinant, nisi quis per virtutem mentis supra fatum se erigat; plerique tamen fato cedunt et sub astris vivunt.
english_gloss: The stars do not compel but incline, unless someone raises himself above fate through the virtue of the mind; most people, however, yield to fate and live under the stars.

vocabulary.definition: incline — the standard Aristotelian-Arabic limitation on stellar determinism; stars incline without compelling, preserving human free will while granting astrology practical predictive power
fate — in Cecco's astrology, the totality of stellar influence over human life; his borderline determinism led to condemnation by the Inquisition and his execution in Florence in 1327

source_notes: Francesco Stabili, known as Cecco d'Ascoli (c. 1269–1327), was an astrologer and professor at Bologna whose encyclopaedic poem L'Acerba developed an astrological cosmology pushing toward determinism that the Inquisition found heretical. He was burned at Florence as a relapsed heretic. His case illustrates the fine line between licit astrological influence and heterodox fatalism in the fourteenth century.
bibliography: Albertazzi, Marco, ed. L'Acerba. Lavis: La Finestra, 2002.

title: Oracula Chaldaica — De Theurgica Ascensione
title_english: Chaldaean Oracles — On the Theurgic Ascent
source: Oracula Chaldaica (fragments preserved in Neoplatonic commentators)
author: Anonymous (attrib. Julian the Theurgist)
representative_sentence: Μὴ κλῖναι κάτω — Ne inclina te deorsum; in lucem enim puram ascende, ex qua Pater tibi praeclara signa misit.
latin_text: Ne inclina te deorsum: in lucem enim puram ascende, ex qua Pater tibi praeclara signa misit.
english_gloss: Do not incline yourself downward: ascend into the pure light, from which the Father has sent you clear signs.

vocabulary.definition: pure light — the noetic realm of the Chaldaean Father-principle; the theurgic ascent moves from matter toward this fiery intelligible light
signs/symbols — the synthemata or symbola, divine signatures embedded in creation that allow the theurgist to ascend; equivalent to the iynges (divine intermediaries) of the Chaldaean system

source_notes: The Chaldaean Oracles, a second-century hexameter collection attributed to Julian the Theurgist and his father, provided the scriptural authority for late antique Neoplatonic theurgy. Preserved only in fragments quoted by Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Damascius, they describe a triadic theology and a programme of ritual ascent through divine symbols. Hans Lewy's study and Ruth Majercik's edition remain foundational.
bibliography: Majercik, Ruth. The Chaldaean Oracles: Text, Translation, and Commentary. Leiden: Brill, 1989. // Lewy, Hans. Chaldaean Oracles and Theurgy. Paris: Études Augustiniennes, 1978.

title: De Bono — De Descensu Animae
title_english: On the Good — On the Descent of the Soul
source: De Bono (fragments preserved in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica)
author: Numenius of Apamea
representative_sentence: Anima in corpus descendens velut nauta in navigium intrat, et vim caelestis originis suae sub pondere materiae obliviscitur.
latin_text: Anima in corpus descendens velut nauta in navigium intrat, et vim caelestis originis suae sub pondere materiae obliviscitur.
english_gloss: The soul descending into the body enters as a sailor into a ship, and forgets the power of its celestial origin under the weight of matter.

vocabulary.definition: sailor into a ship — Numenius's influential analogy for the soul-body relationship; the soul retains its identity while using the body as an instrument, a Middle Platonic formulation taken up by Porphyry and Iamblichus

power of celestial origin — the divine potency the soul carries from its pre-incarnate life; recovering this through philosophy or theurgy is the goal of Middle Platonic and Neoplatonic spiritual practice

source_notes: Numenius of Apamea (fl. c. 160–200 CE) was a Middle Platonist whose fragments, preserved mainly in Eusebius of Caesarea's Praeparatio Evangelica, anticipate the Neoplatonic triad and the soul's descent and return. His synthesis of Platonic, Pythagorean, and Eastern religious themes was influential on Plotinus and the entire Neoplatonic tradition. É. des Places's edition is standard.
bibliography: Des Places, Édouard, ed. Numénius: Fragments. Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 1973.

title: Hymni Orphici — Hymnus in Hecaten
title_english: Orphic Hymns — Hymn to Hecate
author: Anonymous (Orphic tradition)
representative_sentence: Ἑκάτη τριοδῖτι — Hecate trioditis, tribus viis praesidens, virgo et matrona et crona, noctis regina, cara nobis esto.
latin_text: Hecate, triviis praesidens, virgo et matrona et anus, noctis et inferorum regina, his sacris accede propitia.
english_gloss: Hecate, presiding over the crossroads, virgin and matron and crone, queen of night and the underworld, draw near propitiously to these rites.

vocabulary.definition: crossroads — Hecate's sacred domain; crossroads were sites of her worship, magical rites, and the deposition of magical materials; the triple-formed goddess rules three realms (heaven, earth, underworld)
propitious/favourable — the goal of hymnic invocation; to render a divine power favorably disposed through ritual address

source_notes: The Orphic Hymns, a collection of 87 hexameter hymns addressed to Greek deities and used in ritual contexts, survive from the second or third century CE and reflect mystery-religion and theurgic practice. The Hymn to Hecate is the opening text and establishes the triple-formed goddess as mistress of magic and crossroads. The hymns were used in magical rituals and were cited by Renaissance Neoplatonists including Ficino and Pico.
bibliography: Athanassakis, Apostolos N., and Benjamin M. Wolkow. The Orphic Hymns. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2013.

title: De Rebus Coelestibus — De Fato et Astris
title_english: On Celestial Things — On Fate and Stars
author: Giovanni Pontano
representative_sentence: Astra non necessitant sed inclinant hominum voluntates, et prudens astrologus futura ex caelestibus signis coniicit, non praenuntiat.
latin_text: Astra non necessitant sed inclinant hominum voluntates, et prudens astrologus futura ex caelestibus signis coniicit, non praenuntiat.
english_gloss: The stars do not compel but incline the wills of people, and the prudent astrologer conjectures future things from celestial signs, he does not foretell them.

vocabulary.definition: do not compel — the crucial distinction preserving human free will in astrology; Pontano articulates the standard Renaissance defence of judicial astrology against theological objections
conjectures — epistemic humility; Pontano frames astrological prediction as probable inference rather than certain foreknowledge, defending it on Aristotelian probabilistic grounds

source_notes: Giovanni Pontano (1429–1503), Neapolitan humanist and poet, wrote several major astrological works including De Rebus Coelestibus and Urania. His sophisticated defence of judicial astrology engaged with the Aristotelian tradition and anticipated the debates Pico della Mirandola would ignite with his Disputationes adversus astrologiam. Anthony Grafton analyses Pontano's astrology in his study of Renaissance horoscopy.
bibliography: Pontano, Giovanni. De Rebus Coelestibus. Naples, 1512. // Grafton, Anthony. Cardano's Cosmos: The Worlds and Works of a Renaissance Astrologer. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1999.

title: Propaedeumata Aphoristica — De Virtute Radiante
title_english: Preliminary Aphoristic Teaching — On Radiant Virtue
author: John Dee
representative_sentence: Omnia quae in mundo inferiori existunt sub radiatione caelesti constant, et quicquid hic agitur ex influxu stellarum ortum habet.
latin_text: Omnia quae in mundo inferiori existunt sub radiatione caelesti constant, et quicquid hic agitur ex influxu stellarum ortum habet.
english_gloss: All things that exist in the lower world subsist under celestial radiation, and whatever is done here has its origin from the influence of the stars.

vocabulary.definition: celestial radiation — Dee's Neoplatonic-mathematical concept of stellar influence as a form of radiation following optical laws; draws on al-Kindi's De Radiis and proposes a mathematical foundation for natural magic
stellar influence — the downward flow of astral power; Dee sought to mathematize this influence and develop a quantitative science of magic as part of his programme for reforming natural philosophy

source_notes: John Dee's Propaedeumata Aphoristica (1558, rev. 1568) is his earliest major published work, presenting a programme for a mathematical science of celestial influence drawing on al-Kindi, Roger Bacon, and Neoplatonic optics. It represents Dee's ambition to place natural magic on a rigorous mathematical foundation. Deborah Harkness analyses it as key to understanding Dee's scientific programme before his angelic experiments.
bibliography: Dee, John. Propaedeumata Aphoristica. Ed. and trans. Wayne Shumaker. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1978. // Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999.

title: De Vinculis in Genere — De Amore ut Vinculo
title_english: On Bonds in General — On Love as a Bond
author: Giordano Bruno
representative_sentence: Qui vult vincire, per amorem vincit; amor autem est primum et potissimum vinculum quo homo in hominem agit, et quo magus in animas operatur.
latin_text: Qui vult vincire, per amorem vincit; amor autem est primum et potissimum vinculum quo homo in hominem agit, et quo magus in animas operatur.
english_gloss: He who wishes to bind, binds through love; for love is the first and most powerful bond by which a person acts upon a person, and by which the magician operates upon souls.

vocabulary.definition: to bind — the central metaphor of Bruno's magical psychology; the magician works by binding the soul through the same emotional and imaginative mechanisms operative in natural love

bond — Bruno's term for any force creating attachment between beings; De Vinculis classifies and analyses bonds (love, fear, hope, wonder) as the operative instruments of natural magic working through the imagination

source_notes: De Vinculis in Genere, written c. 1591 and unpublished in Bruno's lifetime, is his most systematic treatment of practical magic. It analyses the imagination as the key mechanism by which the magician operates on souls through bonds (vincula) — love, fear, hope, admiration. Richard Blackwell and Robert de Lucca have discussed it in the context of Bruno's broader natural magic and it is central to Ioan Couliano's study of Renaissance Eros and Magic.
bibliography: Couliano, Ioan P. Eros and Magic in the Renaissance. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1987. // Bruno, Giordano. Opere Magiche. Ed. Simonetta Bassi et al. Milan: Adelphi, 2000.

title: De Amore — De Spiritu Mundi et Amore
title_english: On Love — On the World Spirit and Love
source: De Amore, Oratio VI, Caput x
author: Marsilio Ficino
representative_sentence: Spiritus mundi, subtilissima res, per calorem solis in lucem quasi productus, omnibus rebus vitam et vigorem infundit, et amor ipse nihil aliud est quam huius spiritus in nos attractio.
latin_text: Spiritus mundi, subtilissima res, per calorem solis in lucem quasi productus, omnibus rebus vitam et vigorem infundit, et amor ipse nihil aliud est quam huius spiritus in nos attractio.
english_gloss: The spirit of the world, a most subtle thing, produced as it were into light by the heat of the sun, pours life and vigour into all things, and love itself is nothing other than the attraction of this spirit into us.

vocabulary.definition: world spirit — the subtle, luminous intermediary between soul and body in Ficino's cosmology; it flows through the universe carrying celestial influences and is the medium of both natural magic and love

attraction — the drawing of cosmic spirit; Ficino's account of love as spirit-attraction provides the physical mechanism behind sympathetic magic, medical astrology, and the manipulation of the spiritus through music and image

source_notes: Ficino's De Amore (Commentary on Plato's Symposium, c. 1469, pub. 1484) develops the concept of spiritus mundi as the medium of cosmic love and magical sympathy. This passage connects his Neoplatonic cosmology directly to the theory of natural magic developed in De Vita III, where stellar spiritus is drawn down through ritual. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic remains the foundational study of this nexus.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Commentary on Plato's Symposium on Love. Trans. Sears Jayne. Dallas: Spring, 1985. // Walker, D.P. Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella. London: Warburg Institute, 1958.

title: Liber de Nymphis — De Natura Spirituum Elementarium
title_english: Book of Nymphs — On the Nature of Elemental Spirits
source: Liber de Nymphis, Sylphis, Pygmaeis ac Salamandris et de Caeteris Spiritibus
author: Paracelsus
representative_sentence: Quattuor sunt genera spirituum: undinae in aqua habitant, silvestres in terra, gnomi sub terra, vulcani in igne — et omnia haec sunt inter hominem et daemonem media.
latin_text: Quattuor sunt genera spirituum elementarium: undinae in aqua habitant, silvestres in silva, gnomi in montibus, vulcani in igne — omnia haec sunt inter hominem et daemonem media naturalia.
english_gloss: There are four kinds of elemental spirits: undines dwell in water, sylphs in forests, gnomes in mountains, vulcans in fire — all these are natural intermediaries between humans and demons.

vocabulary.definition: elemental spirits — Paracelsus's naturalistic category of beings inhabiting the four elements; unlike demons they are material (flesh and blood) and unlike angels they lack immortal souls, occupying a unique ontological middle position

natural intermediaries — Paracelsus frames elemental beings as natural rather than supernatural, attempting to remove them from demonological discourse and situate them within his philosophy of nature

source_notes: Paracelsus's Liber de Nymphis (c. 1530, published 1566) describes four classes of elemental beings — undines, sylphs, gnomes, and salamanders — inhabiting the four elements. Paracelsus attempts to naturalise what earlier writers had classified as demons, situating elemental beings within his broader philosophy of nature. The text influenced later esoteric spirit taxonomies and is analysed by Walter Pagel and Charles Webster.
bibliography: Pagel, Walter. Paracelsus: An Introduction to Philosophical Medicine in the Era of the Renaissance. Basel: Karger, 1982. // Weeks, Andrew. Paracelsus: Speculative Theory and the Crisis of the Early Reformation. Albany: SUNY Press, 1997.

title: De Verbo Mirifico — De Nomine Tetragrammaton
title_english: On the Wonder-Working Word — On the Tetragrammaton
author: Johann Reuchlin
representative_sentence: Nomen ineffabile Dei, quod Hebraei per quattuor litteras scribunt, est fons omnis virtutis et efficaciae in mundo, et per hoc nomen Christus miracula operatus est.
latin_text: Nomen ineffabile Dei, quod Hebraei per quattuor litteras scribunt, est fons omnis virtutis et efficaciae in mundo, et per hoc nomen Christus miracula operatus est.
english_gloss: The ineffable name of God, which the Hebrews write with four letters, is the source of all virtue and efficacy in the world, and through this name Christ worked miracles.

vocabulary.definition: ineffable name — the Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the unspeakable divine name; Reuchlin argues that adding the letter shin to produce YHSWH (Yehoshua/Jesus) makes the Incarnation legible in the divine name itself
virtue and efficacy — the power and operative capacity of the divine name; Reuchlin's Christian Kabbalah grounds the efficacy of magical names in their participation in the divine name

source_notes: Reuchlin's De Verbo Mirifico (1494) is the first major work of Christian Kabbalah in Latin, arguing that the Hebrew divine name YHWH contains the secret of the Incarnation through the addition of shin. The text initiated the Christian Kabbalist tradition that ran through Pico, Agrippa, and Dee. Joseph Dan and Allison Coudert have traced its influence on subsequent Renaissance esotericism.
bibliography: Reuchlin, Johann. De Verbo Mirifico. Stuttgart: Frommann-Holzboog, 1996. // Dan, Joseph. The Christian Kabbalah. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1997.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — De Purificatione ad Magiam
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — On Purification for Magic
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber III, Caput lviii
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Qui magicis operationibus se applicat, debet prius animum a perturbationibus purgare, corpus a sordibus lavare, et mentem in contemplationem divinam erigere.
latin_text: Qui magicis operationibus se applicat, debet prius animum a perturbationibus purgare, corpus a sordibus lavare, et mentem in contemplationem divinam erigere.
english_gloss: Whoever applies himself to magical operations must first purge the mind of disturbances, wash the body of impurities, and raise the intellect toward divine contemplation.

vocabulary.definition: to purge/purify — the ritual preparation required before magical operations; Agrippa integrates Neoplatonic katharsis (purification of the soul) with physical cleansing as prerequisites for effective magical work
divine contemplation — the elevation of the intellect toward God; for Agrippa the magician must first become a philosopher and contemplative before ritual operations can be effective

source_notes: Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia III (1531) addresses the religious and moral preconditions for magical practice, requiring purification of body, mind, and spirit. This section draws on Neoplatonic and Hermetic traditions of ritual purity as prerequisites for theurgy. Brian Copenhaver and Charles Nauert have analysed how Agrippa integrates these requirements into his comprehensive theory of magical practice.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: De Sensu Rerum et Magia — Omnia Sentiunt
title_english: On the Sense of Things and Magic — All Things Have Sense
source: De Sensu Rerum et Magia, Liber IV
author: Tommaso Campanella
representative_sentence: Magia naturalis nil aliud est quam sapientia rerum naturalium ab experientia derivata, qua homo in sympathias et antipathias rerum ingressus earum viribus utitur.
latin_text: Magia naturalis nil aliud est quam sapientia rerum naturalium ab experientia derivata, qua homo in sympathias et antipathias rerum ingressus earum viribus utitur.
english_gloss: Natural magic is nothing other than wisdom of natural things derived from experience, by which a person, having entered into the sympathies and antipathies of things, makes use of their powers.

vocabulary.definition: sympathies and antipathies — the hidden affinities and repulsions structuring natural magic; Campanella's hylozoism (all things have sensation) grounds sympathetic magic in universal sentience
natural magic — the benign, philosophical manipulation of natural sympathies; Campanella's definition echoes Della Porta but situates it within his panpsychist natural philosophy

source_notes: Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639), Dominican friar and philosopher, developed a panpsychist natural philosophy in De Sensu Rerum et Magia (1620) arguing that all nature is sentient and that natural magic exploits universal sympathy grounded in this universal sentience. Campanella's defence of natural magic as a form of applied experience connects him to Della Porta and anticipates early modern empiricism. D.P. Walker analyses his position in Spiritual and Demonic Magic.
bibliography: Campanella, Tommaso. Del Senso delle Cose e della Magia. Ed. Antonio Bruers. Bari: Laterza, 1925. // Walker, D.P. Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella. London: Warburg Institute, 1958.

title: Utriusque Cosmi Historia — Homo ut Microcosmus
title_english: History of Both Worlds — Man as Microcosm
source: Utriusque Cosmi Maioris et Minoris Historia, Tractatus II
author: Robert Fludd
representative_sentence: Homo est speculum totius universi, et quicquid in macrocosmo existit, hoc in corpore humano quasi in minori mundo continetur et repraesentatur.
latin_text: Homo est speculum totius universi, et quicquid in macrocosmo existit, hoc in corpore humano quasi in minori mundo continetur et repraesentatur.
english_gloss: Man is the mirror of the whole universe, and whatever exists in the macrocosm is contained and represented in the human body as in a smaller world.

vocabulary.definition: mirror — the human body as reflective representation of the universe; Fludd's elaboration of the microcosm-macrocosm analogy into a comprehensive visual and symbolic system
macrocosm — the great world; Fludd's two-volume Utriusque Cosmi Historia maps correspondences between macrocosm and microcosm as the theoretical basis for his Hermetic natural philosophy and medicine

source_notes: Robert Fludd (1574–1637) produced the monumental Utriusque Cosmi Historia (1617–1621), an elaborately illustrated Hermetic encyclopaedia mapping correspondences between macrocosm and microcosm, including music, medicine, and natural magic. His engagement with Kepler on the mathematical versus qualitative understanding of the cosmos is analysed by Peter Ammann and Joscelyn Godwin. Frances Yates treated Fludd as a key figure in the Rosicrucian enlightenment.
bibliography: Yates, Frances A. The Rosicrucian Enlightenment. London: Routledge, 1972. // Godwin, Joscelyn. Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher and Surveyor of Two Worlds. Boulder: Shambhala, 1979.

title: Contra Astrologiam Divinatricem — De Illusione Magiae
title_english: Against Divinatory Astrology — On the Illusion of Magic
author: Girolamo Savonarola
representative_sentence: Astrologi divinatores et magi fallunt populum, promittentes eis ea quae scire non possunt, et per daemones aut per vanas artes operantur.
latin_text: Astrologi divinatores et magi fallunt populum, promittentes eis ea quae scire non possunt, et per daemones aut per vanas artes operantur.
english_gloss: Divinatory astrologers and magicians deceive the people, promising them things they cannot know, and operate through demons or through vain arts.

vocabulary.definition: divinatory astrologers — those who use astrology to predict individual fate rather than describing general celestial patterns; Savonarola's critique distinguishes licit from illicit astronomy
vain arts — frivolous or worthless arts; a category of forbidden practice linking magic to deceit and false promise, echoing Augustine's condemnation of the curiositas that drives magical inquiry

source_notes: Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), Dominican friar and prophet of Florence, attacked judicial astrology and magic as demonic deception in several treatises including Contra Astrologiam Divinatricem. His position represents the puritanical reform wing of the Italian Renaissance, counterpoint to the Hermetic enthusiasm of Ficino and Pico. Anthony Grafton contextualises Savonarola's anti-astrological polemic within Renaissance debates.
bibliography: Savonarola, Girolamo. Contra Astrologiam Divinatricem. Florence, 1497. // Grafton, Anthony. Defenders of the Text. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1991.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae — De Laboratorio Oratorio
title_english: Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom — On the Laboratory-Oratory
author: Heinrich Khunrath
representative_sentence: Laboratorium et oratorium idem sunt: sine oratione nulla perfecta operatio chimica, sine labore nulla vera contemplatio divina.
latin_text: Laboratorium et oratorium idem sunt: sine oratione nulla perfecta operatio chimica, sine labore nulla vera contemplatio divina.
english_gloss: The laboratory and the oratory are one: without prayer there is no perfect chemical operation, without labour there is no true divine contemplation.

vocabulary.definition: laboratory — the practical alchemical workspace; Khunrath's famous engraving shows a combined laboratory-chapel, literalizing his insistence that chemical and spiritual work are inseparable

oratory/prayer room — the devotional space; Khunrath's union of laboratory and oratory defines Paracelsian spiritual alchemy's claim that true transmutation requires both chemical skill and divine grace

source_notes: Heinrich Khunrath's Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae (1595, expanded 1609) is one of the most visually elaborate works of Renaissance spiritual alchemy. Its famous engraving of the combined laboratory-oratory embodies Khunrath's thesis that alchemical and spiritual transformation are inseparable. Pamela Smith and Lawrence Principe have analysed the practical and devotional dimensions of this Paracelsian alchemy.
bibliography: Khunrath, Heinrich. Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae. Hamburg, 1595. // Forshaw, Peter J. 'Alchemy in the Amphitheatre: Some Considerations of the Alchemical Content in the Works of Heinrich Khunrath.' Alchemy and Early Modern Chemistry. Ed. J. Rampling. Ambix 60 (2013): 44–79.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblema VIII
title_english: Atalanta Fleeing — Emblem VIII
source: Atalanta Fugiens, Emblema VIII: Accipe ovum et igneo percute gladio
author: Michael Maier
representative_sentence: Accipe ovum et igneo percute gladio; inde enim fiet lapis philosophorum ex quo omnia metalla in aurum verum transmutantur.
latin_text: Accipe ovum et igneo percute gladio; inde enim fiet lapis philosophorum ex quo omnia metalla in aurum verum transmutantur.
english_gloss: Take the egg and pierce it with a fiery sword; for from this comes the philosophers' stone, from which all metals are transmuted into true gold.

vocabulary.definition: egg — the Philosophical Egg; a central alchemical symbol for the sealed vessel in which the prima materia undergoes transformation; corresponds to the world-egg of Orphic cosmogony in Maier's emblematic system

philosophers' stone — the ultimate product of alchemical work capable of universal transmutation; Maier embeds its production in a sequence of mythological emblems where Atalanta's race represents the alternation of opposites in the work

source_notes: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1617) is a collection of fifty alchemical emblems each accompanied by a motto, epigram, prose discourse, and musical fugue. It integrates classical mythology (Atalanta's race with Hippomenes) into a dense allegorical encoding of the alchemical work. H.M.E. de Jong's commentary and Joscelyn Godwin's edition with music remain essential references.
bibliography: Maier, Michael. Atalanta Fugiens. Ed. Joscelyn Godwin. Grand Rapids: Phanes, 1989. // de Jong, H.M.E. Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems. Leiden: Brill, 1969.

title: Liber Iuratus Honorii — De Visione Dei
title_english: Sworn Book of Honorius — On the Vision of God
author: Anonymous (attrib. Honorius of Thebes)
representative_sentence: Per hanc artem sacram et sanctam, quam spiritus angelici magistris nostris revelaverunt, visum dei et beatorum spirituum meremur attingere in hac vita.
latin_text: Per hanc artem sacram et sanctam, quam spiritus angelici magistris nostris revelaverunt, visum dei et beatorum spirituum meremur attingere in hac vita.
english_gloss: Through this sacred and holy art, which angelic spirits revealed to our masters, we merit to attain the vision of God and the blessed spirits in this life.

vocabulary.definition: sacred art — the Liber Iuratus frames its ritual magic as a divinely revealed sacred art rather than demonic practice, distinguishing it from nigromancy through its angelic and visionary character

vision of God — the beatific vision sought through the Liber Iuratus's ritual programme; the text promises practitioners a direct vision of the divine, situating the magical operations within a Christian soteriology

source_notes: The Liber Iuratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius), a thirteenth-century compilation attributed to Honorius of Thebes, claims to transmit an angelic revelation for attaining the vision of God and achieving practical magical ends. Its complex ritual system combining prayer, fasting, and divine name invocation represents the summit of learned medieval angelic magic. Gösta Hedegård's edition and Julien Veronese's studies are the standard references.
bibliography: Hedegård, Gösta, ed. Liber Iuratus Honorii. Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 2002. // Veronese, Julien. L'Ars Notoria au Moyen Âge. Florence: SISMEL, 2007.

title: De Praestigiis Daemonum — De Spiritu Familiari
title_english: On the Illusions of Demons — On the Familiar Spirit
author: Johann Weyer
representative_sentence: Spiritus familiaris est daemon qui certo pacto homini adhaeret, eumque in artibus magicis instruit, et ad scelera aut ad vanas curiositates impellit.
latin_text: Spiritus familiaris est daemon qui certo pacto homini adhaeret, eumque in artibus magicis instruit, et ad scelera aut ad vanas curiositates impellit.
english_gloss: The familiar spirit is a demon who cleaves to a person through a specific pact, instructs him in the magical arts, and drives him toward crimes or toward vain curiosities.

vocabulary.definition: familiar spirit — a demon bound to an individual practitioner through pact; the concept consolidates scholastic demonology's insistence that all magical power ultimately derives from demonic assistance

specific pact — the contractual basis of the familiar spirit relationship; the specificity of the pact (as opposed to a general demonic alliance) defines the familiar spirit as a particular form of demonic servitude

source_notes: Johann Weyer's De Praestigiis Daemonum (1563) is a landmark of Renaissance demonology, notable for arguing that alleged witches were mentally ill women deceived by demons rather than genuine pact-makers. His account of the familiar spirit preserves traditional demonological categories while redirecting their application. George Mora's translated edition with essays and H.C. Erik Midelfort's contextual work are key.
bibliography: Weyer, Johann. On Witchcraft (De Praestigiis Daemonum). Trans. John Shea. Ed. Benjamin Kohl and H.C. Erik Midelfort. Asheville: Pegasus, 1998.

title: Summa Theologiae — De Efficacia Verborum in Magia
title_english: Summa Theologiae — On the Efficacy of Words in Magic
source: Summa Theologiae, IIa IIae, q. 96, a. 2
author: Thomas Aquinas
representative_sentence: Verba in magicis operationibus vim habent non ex natura sua, sed ex tacita vel expressa daemonum invocatione, ad quam omnes superstitiosae observationes ordinantur.
latin_text: Verba in magicis operationibus vim habent non ex natura sua, sed ex tacita vel expressa daemonum invocatione, ad quam omnes superstitiosae observationes ordinantur.
english_gloss: Words in magical operations have power not from their own nature, but from the tacit or express invocation of demons, to which all superstitious observances are ordered.

vocabulary.definition: tacit invocation — Aquinas's concept that magic words carry implicit demonic power even without explicit summoning; this extends the category of demonic pact to cover all magical language regardless of the practitioner's conscious intent
superstitious observances — the broad Thomistic category encompassing magical practices; Aquinas's systematic treatment here became the standard scholastic analysis of how magical words function

source_notes: Aquinas's treatment of magical words in Summa Theologiae IIa IIae q. 96 established the standard scholastic account: magical words derive their power not from linguistic form or natural virtue but from implicit demonic invocation. This analysis shaped the entire subsequent canonical and demonological tradition's understanding of incantations, voces magicae, and ritual language.
bibliography: Aquinas, Thomas. Summa Theologiae. Ed. Leonine Commission. Vol. 9. Rome: Commissio Leonina, 1897. // Torrell, Jean-Pierre. Saint Thomas Aquinas. Vol. 1. Washington: Catholic University of America Press, 1996.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — De Arte Mathematica et Magia
title_english: On Occult Philosophy — On Mathematical Art and Magic
source: De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres, Liber II, Caput ii
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
representative_sentence: Mathematica non solum ad naturales sed etiam ad magicas operationes necessaria est, per numeros enim et figuras geometricas virtutes rerum attinguntur.
latin_text: Mathematica non solum ad naturales sed etiam ad magicas operationes necessaria est, per numeros enim et figuras geometricas virtutes rerum attinguntur et in effectum deducuntur.
english_gloss: Mathematics is necessary not only for natural but also for magical operations, for through numbers and geometric figures the virtues of things are reached and brought into effect.

vocabulary.definition: geometric figures — shapes like circles, triangles, and pentagrams used in magical operations; Agrippa's Book II grounds image magic, talismans, and ritual diagrams in the mathematical structure of reality
virtues of things — the hidden powers of natural substances accessed through mathematical proportion; Agrippa follows Roger Bacon and al-Kindi in treating mathematics as the key to natural magic

source_notes: Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia II (1531) is devoted to celestial magic operating through mathematical structures — numbers, figures, and musical proportions — as intermediaries between the natural and divine worlds. This section illustrates the Renaissance fusion of mathematical arts and magical practice that Agrippa inherited from Roger Bacon, al-Kindi, and Ficino. Brian Copenhaver and Charles Nauert provide the essential scholarly context.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: Ars Notoria — De Notis Sacris et Figuris
title_english: The Notory Art — On Sacred Notes and Figures
author: Anonymous (attrib. Solomon)
representative_sentence: Notae istae sacrae, quas angeli Salomoni revelaverunt, per contemplationem et orationem memoriam et intellectum illuminant et omnem scientiam liberalium artium infundunt.
latin_text: Notae istae sacrae, quas angeli Salomoni revelaverunt, per contemplationem et orationem memoriam et intellectum illuminant et omnem scientiam liberalium artium infundunt.
english_gloss: These sacred notes, which angels revealed to Solomon, through contemplation and prayer illuminate memory and intellect and pour in knowledge of all the liberal arts.

vocabulary.definition: sacred notes — the diagrammatic figures (notae) central to the Ars Notoria; complex visual symbols to be contemplated during prayer rituals, said to imprint the knowledge of a liberal art directly into the practitioner's memory

liberal arts — the seven medieval university disciplines (grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy); the Ars Notoria promises instant mastery of all through angelic infusion rather than study

source_notes: The Ars Notoria Salomonis is a thirteenth-century ritual magic text prescribing a complex regime of fasting, prayer, and contemplation of sacred diagrammatic figures (notae) said to grant instant mastery of the seven liberal arts through angelic infusion. It represents a learned, quasi-liturgical form of ritual magic explicitly claiming angelic rather than demonic agency. Julien Veronese has produced the definitive critical study and edition.
bibliography: Veronese, Julien. L'Ars Notoria au Moyen Âge: Introduction et Édition Critique. Florence: SISMEL, 2007. // Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Opus Maius — De Scientia Experimentali
title_english: Great Work — On Experimental Science
source: Opus Maius, Pars VI: De Scientia Experimentali
author: Roger Bacon
representative_sentence: Scientia experimentalis omnium aliarum scientiarum domina est et potest multa admiranda perficere, quae vulgo magica videri possunt sed sunt naturalia.
latin_text: Scientia experimentalis omnium aliarum scientiarum domina est et potest multa admiranda perficere, quae vulgo magica videri possunt sed ex naturis rerum procedunt.
english_gloss: Experimental science is the mistress of all other sciences and can accomplish many marvellous things, which may appear magical to the common people but proceed from the natures of things.

vocabulary.definition: experimental science — Bacon's concept of a science based on direct experience rather than mere authoritative argument; his third prerogative of experimental science describes the ability to produce marvels that appear magical

marvellous things — preternatural feats achievable through knowledge of natural causes; Bacon's naturalistic programme distinguishes true natural science from demonic magic while claiming many of the same effects

source_notes: Roger Bacon's Opus Maius (c. 1267), written for Pope Clement IV, devotes its sixth part to scientia experimentalis as the master science capable of validating all other knowledge through experience. Bacon's experimental science claims the ability to produce magical-seeming effects through natural means, positioning natural magic as the apex of scientific knowledge. Jeremiah Hackett and Sophia Coward have analysed Bacon's place in the history of science and magic.
bibliography: Bridges, John Henry, ed. Opus Maius Rogeri Baconis. Oxford: Clarendon, 1897. // Hackett, Jeremiah. Roger Bacon and the Sciences. Leiden: Brill, 1997.

title: Liber Razielis — De Nominibus Secretis Creationis
title_english: Book of Raziel — On the Secret Names of Creation
author: Anonymous (attrib. Raziel)
representative_sentence: Nomina secreta quibus Deus mundum creavit Raziel angelo ad Adam tradidit, et per haec nomina omnis creatura ligatur et solvitur.
latin_text: Nomina secreta quibus Deus mundum creavit Raziel angelo ad Adam tradidit, et per haec nomina omnis creatura ligatur et solvitur.
english_gloss: The secret names by which God created the world Raziel handed down to the angel Adam, and through these names every creature is bound and loosed.

vocabulary.definition: secret names — the divine names used in creation, transmitted from God through Raziel to Adam; the text presents knowledge of these names as the ultimate source of magical power over all creation
bound and loosed — the binding and releasing power of the secret names; echoes the keys of the kingdom (Matt. 16:19) and the principle underlying both angelic magic and Solomonic exorcism

source_notes: The Liber Razielis Archangeli is a thirteenth-century Latin compilation drawing on Jewish mystical and magical traditions, presenting itself as the angelic book of secret names given to Adam at the Fall. It circulated widely in learned magical circles and influenced the Kabbalistic current within Christian magic. Bill Rebiger and Peter Schäfer have analysed the Hebrew sources; Liana De Girolami Cheney has studied the Latin tradition.
bibliography: Rebiger, Bill, and Peter Schäfer, eds. Sefer ha-Razim I und II. Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2009. // Burnett, Charles. 'Arabic, Greek and Latin Works on Astrological Magic Attributed to Aristotle.' Pseudo-Aristotle in the Middle Ages. Ed. Jill Kraye et al. London: Warburg Institute, 1986.

title: De Sacrificio et Magia — De Operatione Symbolis
title_english: On Sacrifice and Magic — On Working through Symbols
author: Proclus Diadochus
representative_sentence: Theurgus per symbola et synthemata divinis viribus utitur, non quasi cogendo deos sed quia participat eis per similitudinem et per ipsam sympathiam.
latin_text: Theurgus per symbola et synthemata divinis viribus utitur, non quasi cogendo deos sed quia participat eis per similitudinem et per ipsam sympathiam.
english_gloss: The theurgist uses divine powers through symbols and tokens, not as if compelling the gods, but because he participates in them through likeness and through sympathy itself.

vocabulary.definition: tokens/symbols (Greek) — divine signs embedded in the natural world that serve as vehicles for theurgic contact; distinct from arbitrary human symbols, synthemata are intrinsic to the divine order
sympathy — the universal affinity linking all levels of reality; Proclus grounds theurgic efficacy in cosmic sympathy rather than mechanical compulsion, distinguishing theurgy from goetic magic

source_notes: Proclus's short treatise De Sacrificio et Magia (preserved in Latin by Ficino, who translated it as part of his Neoplatonic programme) provides the most concise account of theurgic practice in the late Neoplatonic tradition. It distinguishes the theurgist's use of divine symbols from compulsive magic, grounding efficacy in cosmic sympathy and ontological participation. Ficino's translation was influential in the Renaissance revival of Neoplatonic theurgy.
bibliography: Proclus. De Sacrificio et Magia. Trans. Marsilio Ficino. In: Opera Omnia. Venice, 1497. // Lewy, Hans. Chaldaean Oracles and Theurgy. Paris: Études Augustiniennes, 1978.

title: Decretum — De Sortilegiis et Divinis
title_english: Decree — On Sortilege and Divination
source: Decretum Gratiani, Causa XXVI, Quaestio V
author: Gratian
representative_sentence: Qui sortes vel auguria inquirunt, daemonibus se obligant et a Deo recedunt; tales si in fide persistere volunt, poenitentiam agant.
latin_text: Qui sortes vel auguria inquirunt, daemonibus se obligant et a Deo recedunt; tales si in fide persistere volunt, poenitentiam agant et ab his omnibus cessent.
english_gloss: Those who consult lots or auguries bind themselves to demons and depart from God; if such persons wish to persist in the faith, let them do penance and cease from all these things.

vocabulary.definition: lots — consultation of lots for divination; Gratian's Decretum assembled patristic and conciliar authorities on sortilege into a canonical synthesis that defined its legal status in the medieval church
bind themselves to demons — the standard canonical formula for why divination is illicit; any recourse to prohibited knowledge-seeking implies a compact with demonic powers

source_notes: Gratian's Decretum (c. 1140), the foundational text of medieval canon law, includes in Causa XXVI a systematic assembly of patristic and conciliar texts on divination and magic. Gratian's harmonization of these authorities created the canonical basis for subsequent ecclesiastical treatment of magic as demonic pact. It was the standard reference for canonists, confessors, and inquisitors throughout the later Middle Ages.
bibliography: Friedberg, Emil, ed. Corpus Iuris Canonici, Vol. I. Leipzig: Tauchnitz, 1879. // Kéry, Lotte. Canonical Collections of the Early Middle Ages. Washington: Catholic University of America Press, 1999.

title: Defixio Circensis Carthaginensis — Devotio Aurigarum
title_english: Circus Curse Tablet from Carthage — Binding of Charioteers
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Adiuro vos daemones qui in hoc loco habitatis ut ligatis equos et aurigas adversariorum meorum ne possint currere neque vincere.
latin_text: Adiuro vos daemones qui in hoc loco habitatis ut ligatis equos et aurigas adversariorum meorum ne possint currere neque vincere in crastino die.
english_gloss: I adjure you, demons who dwell in this place, that you bind the horses and charioteers of my opponents so that they cannot run or win on the next day.

vocabulary.definition: I adjure — the performative verb of binding in defixiones; the formal invocation that activates the curse by commanding demonic powers through a ritual speech act
bind — the central operation of the defixio (literally 'binding tablet'); the binding verb mirrors the physical act of inscribing the lead tablet and folding or piercing it to seal the curse

source_notes: Circus curse tablets (defixiones circenses) are among the most numerous surviving Latin magical texts, primarily from North Africa (Carthage, Hadrumetum) and dating to the third and fourth centuries CE. They invoke demons to bind the horses and drivers of opposing circus factions. John Gager's collection and Celia Sánchez Natalías's Sylloge of Defixiones from the Roman West provide the standard documentary editions.
bibliography: Gager, John G. Curse Tablets and Binding Spells from the Ancient World. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992. // Sánchez Natalías, Celia. Sylloge of Defixiones from the Roman West. 2 vols. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2022.

title: Defixio Hadrumentina — Devotio Amoris
title_english: Curse Tablet from Hadrumetum — Love Binding
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Adiuro te spiritus qui hic iacis ut excites Sextilius ut amet me ardentem et non possit dormire nisi venerit ad me.
latin_text: Adiuro te spiritus qui hic iacis ut excites Sextilius ut amet me ardentem et non possit dormire nisi venerit ad me.
