english_gloss: I adjure you, spirit who lies here, that you rouse Sextilius so that he loves me burning and cannot sleep unless he comes to me.

vocabulary.definition: spirit who lies here — the restless spirit of a prematurely dead person (aōros) believed to inhabit the cemetery where tablets were deposited; erotic curse tablets exploit such spirits as coercive intermediaries
burning — the erotic metaphor literalized as magical compulsion; the target must love 'burning' (i.e., with unquenchable desire) as a penalty for resistance to the curse

source_notes: Erotic binding tablets (defixiones amatoriae) form a distinct genre within the defixio tradition, deposited in tombs to exploit restless spirits (aōroi) as coercive agents against resisting love objects. The Hadrumetum tablets from North Africa are among the finest examples, often accompanied by dough figurines and hair. Christopher Faraone and John Gager have analysed the genre's ritual logic.
bibliography: Gager, John G. Curse Tablets and Binding Spells from the Ancient World. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992. // Faraone, Christopher A. Ancient Greek Love Magic. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1999.

title: Defixio Commercialis — Devotio Adversarii in Negotio
title_english: Commercial Curse Tablet — Binding of a Business Rival
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Defigo et obligo Ianuarium negotiatorem ut non possit vendere nec emere nec lucrum facere sed semper detrimentum patiatur.
latin_text: Defigo et obligo Ianuarium negotiatorem ut non possit vendere nec emere nec lucrum facere sed semper detrimentum patiatur donec haec tabella dissoluta fuerit.
english_gloss: I bind and obligate Ianuarius the merchant so that he cannot sell or buy or make profit but always suffer loss until this tablet has been dissolved.

vocabulary.definition: I fix/bind — the verb from which defixio derives; to pierce, pin, or fix the victim's agency; the writing of the curse on lead enacts this binding materially
I obligate/bind — a legal-commercial term repurposed for magical constraint; defixiones commercial often invoke juridical language, framing the curse as a binding contract

source_notes: Commercial defixiones targeting business rivals are attested throughout the Roman West, reflecting the use of curse tablets in competitive economic contexts. They employ legal vocabulary (defigo, obligo, vincio) that mirrors the juridical language of actual commercial contracts. Stuart McKie's Living and Cursing in the Roman West examines the social contexts of defixio use in Roman Britain and the western provinces.
bibliography: McKie, Stuart. Living and Cursing in the Roman West: Curse Tablets and Society. London: Bloomsbury Academic, 2022. // Gager, John G. Curse Tablets and Binding Spells from the Ancient World. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992.

title: Papyri Graecae Magicae VII — Carmina Latina Lunaria
title_english: Greek Magical Papyri VII — Latin Lunar Charms
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Luna, Luna, te rogo et obsecro per nomina tua sancta ut mihi des quod peto et quod cupio.
latin_text: Luna, Luna, te rogo et obsecro per nomina tua sancta ut mihi des quod peto et quod cupio, et compellas illum ad me venire.
english_gloss: Moon, Moon, I ask and beseech you by your holy names that you give me what I seek and what I desire, and compel him to come to me.

vocabulary.definition: I beseech — the liturgical register of supplication; PGM Latin prayers deploy the vocabulary of Roman religious petition (rogo, obsecro, precor) to address magical powers in the idiom of conventional cult
holy names — the divine names of the Moon goddess invoked for compulsive power; the PGM texts contain extensive lists of nomina barbara and voces magicae as the engine of magical compulsion

source_notes: PGM VII contains several Latin-language spells among the predominantly Greek texts of the Great Magical Papyri corpus, demonstrating the multilingual character of Greco-Egyptian magic in the Roman imperial period. Hans Dieter Betz's collected edition with English translations remains the standard reference. The Latin charms in the PGM often address lunar deities and employ the vocabulary of Roman religious supplication adapted to magical compulsion.
bibliography: Betz, Hans Dieter, ed. The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation, Including the Demotic Spells. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1986. // Gordon, Richard, and Francisco Marco Simón, eds. Magical Practice in the Latin West. Leiden: Brill, 2010.

title: Lamellae Aureae Orphicae — Verba Mortis
title_english: Orphic Gold Tablets — Words at Death
author: Anonymous (Orphic tradition)
representative_sentence: Ἔρχομαι ἐκ καθαρῶν καθαρά — E puris pura venio, o regina inferorum, Persephona.
latin_text: E puris pura venio, o regina inferorum Persephona; sum filia terrae et caeli stellati; sitis me perimit; date mihi aquam de lacu Memoriae bibere.
english_gloss: From the pure I come, pure, O queen of the underworld Persephone; I am a child of earth and starry heaven; thirst destroys me; give me water from the lake of Memory to drink.

vocabulary.definition: lake of Memory — the pool of Mnemosyne in the underworld whose waters grant the initiate recollection of their divine origin; the dead must avoid the pool of Lethe (forgetting) and seek this water

child of earth and starry heaven — the self-identification formula on the gold tablets asserting the soul's dual nature and divine origin; used as a password to gain privileged treatment in the afterlife

source_notes: The Orphic gold tablets (lamellae aureae), found in graves across the Greek world from the fifth century BCE onward, contain instructions in verse for the soul's navigation of the underworld. The Latin versions are rare; the standard corpus is Greek, preserved in Fritz Graf and Sarah Iles Johnston's Ritual Texts for the Afterlife. The tablets attest to mystery religion beliefs in metempsychosis and divine human nature that influenced Neoplatonic and Hermetic thought.
bibliography: Graf, Fritz, and Sarah Iles Johnston. Ritual Texts for the Afterlife: Orpheus and the Bacchic Gold Tablets. London: Routledge, 2007. // Edmonds, Radcliffe G. III. Myths of the Underworld Journey: Plato, Aristophanes, and the 'Orphic' Gold Tablets. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2004.

title: Defixio Iudicialis — Devotio ad Deos Inferos
title_english: Judicial Curse Tablet — Binding to the Infernal Gods
author: Anonymous
representative_sentence: Dis Manibus et Mercurio commendo illos qui mihi tunicas involaverint ut eos ad templum perducat.
latin_text: Dis Manibus et Mercurio commendo illos qui mihi tunicas et pallium involaverint ut eos ad templum perducat et poenam dare non sinat nisi ad fanum venerint.
english_gloss: To the Spirits of the Dead and to Mercury I commend those who have stolen my tunics and cloak, that he may lead them to the temple and not allow them to give satisfaction unless they come to the shrine.

vocabulary.definition: Spirits of the Dead — the collective Roman underworld powers invoked in judicial defixiones; addressees of the curse who are asked to enforce justice on thieves; the formula mirrors funerary epitaphs but is here turned toward magical compulsion
I commend/entrust — the juridical register of dedication; the plaintiff formally hands the guilty party over to underworld jurisdiction as one might hand a case to a magistrate

source_notes: Judicial or 'prayer for justice' curse tablets ask gods (Mercury, Mars, Sulis, Neptune) rather than demons to punish thieves, seeking divine enforcement of property rights. They are especially common in Roman Britain. This genre, analysed by Henk Versnel and Roger Tomlin, blurs the boundary between prayer and curse and between licit religious appeal and illicit magical coercion.
bibliography: Tomlin, Roger S.O. Britannia Romana: Roman Inscriptions and Roman Britain. Oxford: Oxbow, 2018. // Versnel, Henk S. 'Beyond Cursing: The Appeal to Justice in Judicial Prayers.' Magika Hiera: Ancient Greek Magic and Religion. Ed. Christopher A. Faraone and Dirk Obbink. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991. 60–106.

title: Naturalis Historia XXXVII — De Virtutibus Gemmarum
title_english: Natural History XXXVII — On the Virtues of Gemstones
author: Pliny the Elder
representative_sentence: Magorum vanitas non parva etiam hic cernitur: achaten bicolorem ex Inacho flumine petunt adversus scorpionum ictus, et quaedam contra venena.
latin_text: Magorum vanitas non parva etiam hic cernitur: achaten bicolorem ex Inacho flumine petunt adversus scorpionum ictus, et quaedam gemmarum genera contra venena et serpentium morsus remedia esse contendunt.
english_gloss: The vanity of the magicians is no small thing here either: they seek a two-coloured agate from the river Inachus against the stings of scorpions, and they maintain that certain types of gemstones are remedies against poisons and the bites of serpents.

vocabulary.definition: vanity of the magicians — Pliny's standard dismissive framing; he records magical beliefs about gemstones while simultaneously debunking them, making the Natural History the primary classical source for magical lapidary traditions
agate — a banded chalcedony with a long history of amulet use; Pliny's entries on agate and other stones provided the foundation for medieval lapidary literature from Marbode of Rennes to Hildegard

source_notes: Pliny the Elder's Natural History XXXVII on gemstones is the richest classical source for lapidary magic, recording beliefs about the magical properties of stones while attributing them to the vanitas magorum. This material fed directly into medieval lapidary traditions via Isidore, Marbode, and Hildegard. Thorndike's History of Magic and Experimental Science documents the tradition comprehensively.
bibliography: Pliny the Elder. Natural History. Trans. D.E. Eichholz. Loeb Classical Library 419. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1962. // Thorndike, Lynn. A History of Magic and Experimental Science. 8 vols. New York: Columbia University Press, 1923–1958.

title: Liber Lapidum — De Magnete
title_english: Book of Stones — On the Magnet
source: Liber Lapidum seu de Gemmis, c. i
author: Marbode of Rennes
representative_sentence: Est lapis in terris, Magnes qui nomine fertur, ex India vectus, cuius vix copia datur; is trahit in se ferrum miroque ligamine stringit.
latin_text: Est lapis in terris, Magnes qui nomine fertur, ex India vectus, cuius vix copia datur; is trahit in se ferrum miroque ligamine stringit, in cuius laude doctorum turba laborat.
english_gloss: There is a stone on earth called the Magnet by name, brought from India, of which supply is scarce; it draws iron to itself and binds it with a wondrous bond, in whose praise a crowd of learned men labours.

vocabulary.definition: wondrous bond — the magnet's invisible force of attraction serves Marbode as a model for natural sympathy throughout the Liber Lapidum; the magnet's power is the paradigm case of occult property acting without contact
magnet — the loadstone; its mysterious attraction was the standard ancient and medieval example of occult virtue and sympathetic action at a distance, cited from Pliny through Albertus Magnus

source_notes: Marbode of Rennes (c. 1035–1123), bishop and poet, composed the Liber Lapidum (Book of Stones) as a hexameter poem cataloguing the virtues of sixty stones drawing on Pliny, Solinus, and Dioscorides. It was the most widely read medieval lapidary, copied in hundreds of manuscripts. Marbode's work transmitted classical lapidary magic into the high medieval tradition and influenced Hildegard's Physica and Albertus's De Mineralibus.
bibliography: Riddle, John M. Marbode of Rennes' De Lapidibus. Wiesbaden: Steiner, 1977. // Evans, Joan, and Mary S. Serjeantson, eds. English Mediaeval Lapidaries. EETS 190. London: Oxford University Press, 1933.

title: De Arte Magica Mesopotamica — Carmina contra Manes
title_english: On Mesopotamian Magical Art — Spells against Ghosts
source: Magico-Medical Means of Treating Ghost-Induced Illness in Ancient Mesopotamia (Akkadian incantations in Latin context)
author: Anonymous (Akkadian; discussed by JoAnn Scurlock)
representative_sentence: Etemmu, spiritus mortuorum qui non quievit, adiuro te per nomina deorum ut recedas a corpore huius hominis et non redeas.
latin_text: Etemmu, spiritus mortuorum qui non quievit, adiuro te per nomina deorum ut recedas a corpore huius hominis et non redeas ad locum tuum.
english_gloss: Ghost, spirit of the dead that has not found rest, I adjure you by the names of the gods that you depart from the body of this person and return to your place.

vocabulary.definition: ghost (Akkadian) — the spirit of a dead person that has not received proper burial or whose death was violent; the etemmu causes illness by possessing the living; this concept underlies the entire ancient Near Eastern tradition of ghost-induced illness

spirit of the dead that has not found rest — the restless dead are the primary agents of demonic illness in Mesopotamian medicine; the same concept of the aōros (untimely dead) appears in Greek curse tablet tradition and connects to biblical dybbuk traditions

source_notes: JoAnn Scurlock's Magico-Medical Means of Treating Ghost-Induced Illness in Ancient Mesopotamia (2006) provides the most comprehensive study of Akkadian exorcistic medicine. The ghost (etemmu) as disease-causing agent is the paradigmatic figure behind Near Eastern and later Mediterranean exorcistic traditions. The Latin passage here is a representative scholarly reconstruction in the tradition of the original Akkadian texts, demonstrating conceptual continuity with Roman and early Christian exorcism practice.
bibliography: Scurlock, JoAnn. Magico-Medical Means of Treating Ghost-Induced Illness in Ancient Mesopotamia. Leiden: Brill, 2006. // Bohak, Gideon. Ancient Jewish Magic. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2008.

title: Phylacterium Hebraico-Aramaicum — Devotio Daemonis
title_english: Hebrew-Aramaic Phylactery — Binding of a Demon
source: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic Bowls (discussed by Shaul Shaked)
author: Anonymous (Jewish-Babylonian tradition)
representative_sentence: Adiuro et ligo te, Lilith, daemonem malum, per nomen Dei Sabaoth, ut recedas a domo huius viri et uxoris eius et parvulorum eorum.
latin_text: Adiuro et ligo te, Lilith, daemonem malum, per nomen Dei Sabaoth, ut recedas a domo huius viri et uxoris eius et parvulorum eorum et non redeas.
english_gloss: I adjure and bind you, Lilith, evil demon, by the name of God Sabaoth, that you depart from the house of this man and his wife and their children and do not return.

vocabulary.definition: Lilith — the female demon of Jewish tradition associated with child-theft and harm to mothers; the name appears in Isaiah 34:14 (Vulgate: lamia) and became a major figure in post-biblical Jewish demonology and later Christian and Islamic traditions

Sabaoth (Hebrew: Lord of Hosts) — a divine name used in Jewish, Christian, and Gnostic magical texts for its compulsive power; extensively attested in the PGM alongside other Hebrew divine names as voces magicae

source_notes: The Jewish Babylonian Aramaic bowl spells (c. 5th–7th century CE) are incantation bowls inscribed with spiral texts binding demons and protecting households, found in Mesopotamia. Shaul Shaked's editions provide access to this corpus. The bowls demonstrate the close relationship between Jewish magical practice, Zoroastrian demonology, and the broader Mesopotamian exorcistic tradition that fed into both early Christian exorcism and medieval grimoire demonology.
bibliography: Shaked, Shaul. Aramaic Bowl Spells: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic Bowls, Volume One. Leiden: Brill, 2013. // Bohak, Gideon. Ancient Jewish Magic. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2008.

title: De Oratione Magica et Stellis — Carmen ad Stellas
title_english: On Magic Prayer and Stars — A Hymn to the Stars
source: Hymn to the Stars (Late Antique context; discussed by Noegel, Walker, Wheeler)
author: Anonymous (Late Antique)
representative_sentence: Stellae sanctae, vos invoco et adoro qui mundum regitis et fata hominum in sinu vestro tenetis; date mihi potestatem et scientiam.
latin_text: Stellae sanctae, vos invoco et adoro qui mundum regitis et fata hominum in sinu vestro tenetis; date mihi potestatem et scientiam et prosperum iter.
english_gloss: Holy stars, I invoke and adore you who rule the world and hold the fates of people in your bosom; give me power and knowledge and a prosperous journey.

vocabulary.definition: holy stars — in late antique astral religion and the associated magical literature, the stars are addressed as divine beings or animated cosmic powers, not merely physical bodies; this personification bridges astronomical and theological discourse
fates of people — the deterministic power attributed to the stars in astral fatalism; the prayer acknowledges stellar power over fate while seeking to influence it through ritual address

source_notes: Late antique prayers and hymns addressed to the stars as divine powers form a significant corpus connecting astrological theory to magical practice. Scott Noegel, Joel Walker, and Brannon Wheeler's collection Prayer, Magic, and the Stars in the Ancient and Late Antique World surveys this material across Jewish, Christian, and pagan sources. Such prayers provided the liturgical model for the planetary prayers in Picatrix and later talismanic magic.
bibliography: Noegel, Scott B., Joel Walker, and Brannon M. Wheeler, eds. Prayer, Magic, and the Stars in the Ancient and Late Antique World. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2003. // Luck, Georg. Arcana Mundi: Magic and the Occult in the Greek and Roman Worlds. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1985.

title: Lamella Aurea Pelinnensis — Verba Initiati
title_english: Gold Tablet from Pelinna — Words of the Initiate
author: Anonymous (Bacchic/Orphic tradition)
representative_sentence: Nunc mortuus es et nunc renatus tripliciter; dic Baccho: taurus in lactem cadit; in lactem festina.
latin_text: Nunc mortuus es et nunc renatus tripliciter. Haedi in lac cecidisti. Dic Baccho: taurus in lactem cadit. In lactem festina.
english_gloss: Now you have died and now are born again threefold. You have fallen into milk as a kid. Say to Bacchus: a bull has fallen into milk. Hasten into milk.

vocabulary.definition: born again threefold — the death and triple rebirth mirrors the Dionysiac myth of Zagreus torn apart and reconstituted; the initiate's death is assimilated to the god's passion, assuring their privileged afterlife

a bull has fallen into milk — the Dionysiac password; the paradoxical imagery (bull/milk = Dionysus and his nourishing fluid) serves as a recognition sign between the initiate and the underworld guardians

source_notes: The gold tablet from Pelinna, Thessaly (c. 320 BCE), is one of the most explicitly Dionysiac Orphic tablets, preserving instructions for the deceased to identify themselves through Bacchic passwords. Fritz Graf and Sarah Iles Johnston's Ritual Texts for the Afterlife provides the definitive edition and analysis. These tablets attest to mystery religion beliefs in the soul's divine origin and post-mortem privileged status that fed into Neoplatonic soteriology and influenced Renaissance Hermetism.
bibliography: Graf, Fritz, and Sarah Iles Johnston. Ritual Texts for the Afterlife: Orpheus and the Bacchic Gold Tablets. 2nd ed. London: Routledge, 2013. // Bernabé, Alberto, and Ana Isabel Jiménez San Cristóbal. Instructions for the Netherworld: The Orphic Gold Tablets. Leiden: Brill, 2008.

title: De Divinatione Daemonum, §3–4
author: Augustine of Hippo
latin_text: Daemones autem corpore aeria sunt animalia et ideo sensibus corporeis antecellunt, idcirco multa non solum transacta sed etiam futura praedicunt. Nam corpus aerium, id est aeris elementum, longe mobilius est et acutius quam corpus terrenum. Itaque et motus corporum caelestium, in quibus et ipsi habitant, facilius percipiunt, et ex his multa ventura praedicunt.
english_gloss: Demons are beings with an aerial body and therefore excel in bodily senses, and thus they predict many things not only past but also future. For the aerial body, that is, the element of air, is far more mobile and keen than the earthly body. And so they perceive the movements of celestial bodies, in which they themselves dwell, more easily, and from these they predict many things to come.

vocabulary.definition: demons, spirit beings (from Greek daimones)
aerial, of the air
to foretell, predict, announce beforehand
more mobile, more easily moved
celestial, heavenly, of the sky

source_notes: Augustine's De Divinatione Daemonum (c. 406–408 CE) addresses how demons can predict the future — not through supernatural omniscience but through their aerial bodies and superior sensory perception. This treatise became foundational for medieval demonology by providing a rational, Christianized framework for demonic knowledge. Augustine distinguishes demonic divination (predictive but not truly prophetic) from genuine divine prophecy. Source: Augustine, De Divinatione Daemonum, ed. Joseph Zycha, CSEL 41 (Vienna: Tempsky, 1900). // Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.
bibliography: Augustine of Hippo. De Divinatione Daemonum. Ed. Joseph Zycha. CSEL 41. Vienna: Tempsky, 1900. // Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: Ars Paulina: Angels of the Hours, §1
author: Lemegeton (attrib. Solomon)
latin_text: Oratio ad Angelum Horae Primae: O Samael, Angele Dei, qui praees primae horae diei, te invoco et per nomen Dei tui te adiuro, ut mihi appareas in hac hora et mihi manifestas veritatem quam quaero. Veni in pacem, veni in luce, veni in forma speciosa, et responde ad omnes interrogationes meas.
english_gloss: Prayer to the Angel of the First Hour: O Samael, Angel of God, who presidest over the first hour of the day, I invoke you and by the name of your God I adjure you, that you appear to me in this hour and make manifest to me the truth which I seek. Come in peace, come in light, come in fair form, and answer all my questions.

vocabulary.definition: to preside over, be in charge of
to adjure, bind by oath, compel by sacred name
to reveal, make manifest, disclose
fair/beautiful form (a standard request for non-terrifying angelic appearance)
questions, interrogations

source_notes: The Ars Paulina (Third Book of the Lemegeton) assigns specific angels to govern each hour of the day and night, with prayers for evoking them. Despite the invocation of 'Samael' (typically a fallen angel in Jewish tradition), the text treats these as Angeli Dei — angels of God — following the Solomonic convention of angelic hierarchy as a bureaucratic system accessible through correct procedure. The text draws on earlier Heptameron material and ultimately on the planetary hours tradition. Source: Peterson, Joseph H. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser Books, 2001.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser Books, 2001. // Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis: The Complete Book of Magic. Ed. Joseph H. Peterson. Twilit Grotto, 1999.

title: Liber Soyga: Tabulae Magicae
author: Anonymous
latin_text: In tabulis magicis Libri Soyga continentur nomina angelorum et daemonum, characteres arcani, et numeri sacrati per quos operationes spirituales perficiuntur. Prima tabula dicitur MOYSES, secunda AARON, tertia PHARON — et unusquisque angelus proprium sigillum habet et propriam orationem qua invocatur. Dee scripsit: 'Uriel mihi dixit hunc librum ab Adam receptum fuisse in Paradiso.'
english_gloss: In the magical tables of the Book of Soyga are contained the names of angels and demons, secret characters, and sacred numbers through which spiritual operations are performed. The first table is called MOYSES, the second AARON, the third PHARON — and each angel has his own seal and his own prayer by which he is invoked. Dee wrote: 'Uriel told me that this book was received by Adam in Paradise.'

vocabulary.definition: magical tables — grid-based letter squares used for angelic communication
secret characters, occult symbols used in ritual writing
seal, sigil — the unique symbol identifying a spiritual being
to complete, accomplish, bring to perfection
to have been received (indirect statement construction)

source_notes: The Liber Soyga (also 'Aldaraia') is a mysterious 16th-century Latin magical text famous for its 36 magic word-squares that John Dee obsessively sought to decode, reportedly being told by the angel Uriel that only the archangel Michael could interpret them. Lost for centuries, it was rediscovered in 1994 simultaneously in the Bodleian Library and the British Library. The tables appear to be generated by an algorithmic system based on Latin keyword rows. Source: Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999. // Roberts, Julian, and Andrew G. Watson, eds. John Dee's Library Catalogue. London: Bibliographical Society, 1990.
bibliography: Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999. // Dee, John. A True and Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Years Between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits. Ed. Meric Casaubon. London, 1659.

title: De la Démonomanie des Sorciers, I.1 (Latin preface)
author: Jean Bodin
latin_text: Daemonomaniam esse insaniam illam qua quis putat se esse daemonem aut cum daemone conversari, aut daemoni alicui morem gerere — docent Graecos haec voce usos esse de iis qui daemones aut deos adorabant. Ego vero de iis scribo qui sponte sua cum daemone foedus ineunt, ab eoque auxilia petunt ad laedendum vel iuvandos homines, qui magi et malefici Latine dicuntur.
english_gloss: Daemonomania is that madness by which someone believes himself to be a demon or to converse with a demon, or to comply with some demon — the Greeks, they teach, used this word of those who worshipped demons or gods. But I write of those who willingly enter into a pact with a demon, and seek help from it for harming or helping people, who are called in Latin magi and malefici.

vocabulary.definition: demonomania — obsession with demons; Bodin's coinage for witchcraft
to enter into a pact/treaty (the demonic pact)
evildoer, witch — the standard Latin legal term for practitioners of harmful magic
of their own free will, voluntarily (key legal distinction)
for harming, for injuring (purpose clause)

source_notes: Jean Bodin's De la Démonomanie des Sorciers (1580) was one of the most influential witch-hunting treatises of the 16th century, going through numerous editions and translations. The Latin preface and extensive Latin citations throughout establish Bodin's legal framework for witch prosecution. As a jurist, Bodin systematized earlier demonological speculation into a prosecutable legal category. His book provoked a famous rebuttal from Johann Weyer. Source: Bodin, Jean. De la Démonomanie des Sorciers. Paris: Jacques du Puys, 1580. // Clark, Stuart. Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997.
bibliography: Bodin, Jean. De la Démonomanie des Sorciers. Paris: Jacques du Puys, 1580. // Clark, Stuart. Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997.

title: PGM IV.475–829: Voces Magicae of the Headless Rite
author: Anonymous (Greek Magical Papyri)
latin_text: Voco te, Caput sine capite, qui habes ignem pro facie, Iao Sabaoth Adonai Abrasax — tu es dominus et creator omnium rerum. Formulas tuae potentiae sunt: AOTH ABAOTH BASYM ISAK SABAOTH IAO. Nomen tuum est: ARBATHIAOTH IATHABRATHAOTH. Exaudi me, qui habito in tenebris, et illumina me lumine tuo imperscrutabili.
english_gloss: I call you, the Headless One, who have fire for a face, Iao Sabaoth Adonai Abrasax — you are lord and creator of all things. The formulas of your power are: AOTH ABAOTH BASYM ISAK SABAOTH IAO. Your name is: ARBATHIAOTH IATHABRATHAOTH. Hear me, I who dwell in darkness, and illuminate me with your unsearchable light.

vocabulary.definition: magical words — untranslatable power-words, often derived from Hebrew, Egyptian, and Aramaic
Greek rendering of Hebrew YHWH Sabaoth (Lord of Hosts) — standard in PGM divine names
unsearchable, inscrutable, beyond investigation
a high deity in Gnostic and magical traditions; numerical value of letters = 365
lord and creator — titles combining Greek, Jewish, and Egyptian divine epithets

source_notes: The Headless Rite (or 'Bornless Ritual') from PGM IV is one of the most celebrated texts in the Greek Magical Papyri, combining Greek, Hebrew, Egyptian, and Coptic divine names into a powerful invocation of an unnamed supreme deity. The voces magicae (magical words) are intentionally untranslatable — their power lies in their precise sound rather than semantic meaning. Aleister Crowley later adapted this text as 'Liber Samekh.' Source: Betz, Hans Dieter, ed. The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1986. // Brashear, William M. 'The Greek Magical Papyri: An Introduction and Survey.' ANRW II.18.5 (1995).
bibliography: Betz, Hans Dieter, ed. The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1986. // Brashear, William M. 'The Greek Magical Papyri: An Introduction and Survey.' ANRW II.18.5, 1995.

title: Ἐκ τοῦ Σολομῶντος / Hygromanteia Salomonis, §3
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Ad cognoscendum futura per aquam: Accipe vas vitreum mundum et imple aqua fontis pura in nocte Lunae crescentis. Pone vas ad lunam et dic ter: 'O Luna, Regina caeli et terrae, per nomina tua sancta — ELELETH, NOREA, SARBIEL — ostende mihi in hac aqua quod quaero.' Tunc videbis in aqua imagines rerum futurarum.
english_gloss: To know the future through water: Take a clean glass vessel and fill it with pure spring water on the night of the waxing moon. Place the vessel toward the moon and say three times: 'O Moon, Queen of heaven and earth, by your holy names — ELELETH, NOREA, SARBIEL — show me in this water what I seek.' Then you will see in the water images of future things.

vocabulary.definition: divination by water (hydromancy) — from hydor (water) + manteia (divination)
glass vessel — glass was associated with purity and reflective clarity
spring, fountain (spring water held special ritual purity)
waxing (of the moon) — the growing phase associated with increase and revelation
images, apparitions, visions (seen in the water surface)

source_notes: The Hygromanteia Salomonis ('Solomon's Water Divination') is a Byzantine Greek magical text compiled around the 13th–14th century that circulated in both Greek and Latin versions. It contains divination by water, by oil, by birds, and through angelic communication, all attributed to Solomon. The Latin version influenced Solomonic magic in the West. This passage demonstrates the classic scrying procedure: lunar timing, consecrated vessel, vocal invocation with divine names. Source: Greenfield, Richard P. H. Traditions of Belief in Late Byzantine Demonology. Amsterdam: Hakkert, 1988. // Marathakis, Ioannis. The Magical Treatise of Solomon or Hygromanteia. Singapore: Golden Hoard Press, 2011.
bibliography: Marathakis, Ioannis. The Magical Treatise of Solomon or Hygromanteia. Singapore: Golden Hoard Press, 2011. // Greenfield, Richard P. H. Traditions of Belief in Late Byzantine Demonology. Amsterdam: Hakkert, 1988.

title: Liber Visionum — Visionary Prologue
author: John of Morigny
latin_text: Vidi in visione nocturna angelum Domini descendentem et dicentem mihi: 'Surge, scribe quae vides, quia haec revelata sunt tibi per gratiam Dei, non per artem necromanticam.'
english_gloss: I saw in a nocturnal vision an angel of the Lord descending and saying to me: 'Rise, write what you see, for these things have been revealed to you by the grace of God, not through the necromantic art.'

vocabulary.definition: nocturnal vision — a dream vision with prophetic authority
necromantic — John explicitly distances his revelations from forbidden magic
grace of God — the theological justification for visionary magic

source_notes: John of Morigny's Liber Visionum (c. 1304–1318) is a deeply personal angelic revelation text that the author presents as divinely authorized alternatives to the Ars Notoria. John repeatedly insists his visions come from grace, not demonic art, anxiously defending himself against charges of necromancy. Claire Fanger's critical edition reveals him to be a sophisticated theological thinker as well as a visionary. Source: Fanger, Claire, and Nicholas Watson, eds. Liber Visionum. Toronto: Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 2015.
bibliography: Fanger, Claire, and Nicholas Watson, eds. Liber Visionum. Toronto: Pontifical Institute of Mediaeval Studies, 2015.

title: Mainz Curse Tablets (4th cent. CE)
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Deo Mercurio Aeternitati dono et consacro Quartum et Quintum, fures qui mihi involaverant — ut eos per hunc deum persequaris ad mortem.
english_gloss: To the god Mercury Eternity I give and consecrate Quartus and Quintus, thieves who had stolen from me — that through this god you may pursue them to death.

vocabulary.definition: to consecrate, dedicate (here: deliver a person to divine punishment)
to steal from, fly upon (past perfect — the theft is established fact)
to pursue, prosecute (judicial language applied to divine action)

source_notes: The Mainz curse tablets (discovered in the Rhine Valley) are 4th-century Latin defixiones addressed to Mercury Aeternitati — a syncretistic deity combining Roman Mercury with an eternal/chthonic aspect. The judicial formula here ('I give and consecrate') is the standard Roman legal language of binding over, adapting Roman law to divine prosecution. The Mainz tablets represent the western Roman provincial defixio tradition. Source: Blänsdorf, Jürgen. Die Defixionum Tabellae des Mainzer Isis- und Mater-Magna-Heiligtums. Mainz: Generaldirektion Kulturelles Erbe, 2012.
bibliography: Blänsdorf, Jürgen. Die Defixionum Tabellae des Mainzer Isis- und Mater-Magna-Heiligtums. Mainz: Generaldirektion Kulturelles Erbe, 2012.

title: Liber Theysolius — Angelic Suffumigation
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Ad evocandos angelos planetarum: suffumi cum incenso et mastice sub hora Saturni et dic septies nomen angeli Cassiel et videbit eum anima tua in somno.
english_gloss: For calling upon the angels of the planets: fumigate with incense and mastic under the hour of Saturn and say seven times the name of the angel Cassiel and your soul will see him in sleep.

vocabulary.definition: to fumigate, to make offerings of smoke (ritual fumigation)
mastic resin — aromatic resin from Pistacia lentiscus, used in planetary magic
sleep — angelic contact often occurs in dream-state in medieval texts

source_notes: The Liber Theysolius is an obscure medieval Latin text on planetary angel invocation, associated with the broader tradition of Solomonic and Hermetic angel magic. Cassiel is the traditional angel of Saturn in the medieval planetary hierarchy. The suffumigation with mastic under Saturn's hour follows the correspondence system linking substances, times, and planetary angels. Source: Pingree, David. 'Learned Magic in the Time of Frederick II.' Micrologus 2 (1994): 39–56.
bibliography: Pingree, David. 'Learned Magic in the Time of Frederick II.' Micrologus 2 (1994): 39–56. // Burnett, Charles. Magic and Divination in the Middle Ages. Aldershot: Variorum, 1996.

title: De Mirabilibus Potestatibus Artis et Naturae — On Hidden Forces
author: Roger Bacon
latin_text: Sunt autem in natura multa occulta quae neque sensus neque ratio communis attingit, sed sola experientia et opera artificis industria detegunt — quae si quis pro magis habeat, inscitia magis quam arte peccabit.
english_gloss: There are in nature many hidden things which neither sense nor common reason reaches, but only experience and the industry of the skilled worker reveal — if someone considers these to belong to magic, he will err through ignorance more than through art.

vocabulary.definition: hidden, secret — the technical term for natural forces not immediately apparent
industry, diligence, skillful application
ignorance, lack of knowledge (Bacon's complaint about those who call science magic)

source_notes: Roger Bacon's De Mirabilibus Potestatibus Artis et Naturae ('On the Marvellous Powers of Art and Nature,' c. 1260) argues that apparent miracles have natural explanations discoverable through experiment. Bacon's famous list of predicted technologies (flying machines, self-propelled ships, spectacles) appears in this work. His insistence that 'hidden forces' are natural, not demonic, represents a crucial move in distinguishing natural magic from forbidden magic. Source: Bacon, Roger. De Mirabilibus Potestatibus Artis et Naturae. Trans. Tenney L. Davis. Easton, PA: Chemical Publishing Co., 1923.
bibliography: Bacon, Roger. De Mirabilibus Potestatibus Artis et Naturae. Trans. Tenney L. Davis. Easton, PA, 1923. // Hackett, Jeremiah. 'Roger Bacon on Scientia Experimentalis.' In Roger Bacon and the Sciences. Leiden: Brill, 1997.

title: Coptic Magical Papyrus (Old Coptic Spell)
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Voco te per nomen magnum et sanctum SETH-IAO-SABAOTH-ADONAI qui es in caelestibus — fac mihi hoc opus: ut Tatis, quam peperit Maria, me amet sicut sol amat lucem suam.
english_gloss: I call you by the great and holy name SETH-IAO-SABAOTH-ADONAI who is in the heavens — do for me this work: that Tatis, whom Maria bore, may love me as the sun loves its light.

vocabulary.definition: Seth (Egyptian god) + Iao (Hebrew YHWH) + Sabaoth (Lord of Hosts) — typical Coptic-PGM syncretism
bore, gave birth to (matrilineal identification formula — 'X child of Y' is standard in love spells)
work, deed (the magical operation requested)

source_notes: Early Coptic magical papyri represent the transitional layer between Greek PGM magic and Christian Egyptian practice. This Latin rendering of a Coptic love spell illustrates the characteristic syncretism: the Egyptian deity Seth merged with Hebrew divine names (Iao Sabaoth) in Christian Egypt. The matrilineal identification formula ('Tatis whom Maria bore') is a universal feature of ancient love spells. Source: Dosoo, Korshi, and Markéta Preininger. Papyri Copticae Magicae. Berlin: De Gruyter, forthcoming. // Meyer, Marvin, and Richard Smith, eds. Ancient Christian Magic. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco, 1994.
bibliography: Meyer, Marvin, and Richard Smith, eds. Ancient Christian Magic. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco, 1994. // Dosoo, Korshi. 'A History of the Theban Magical Library.' Bulletin of the American Society of Papyrologists 53 (2016).

title: Liber Experimentorum — Trial of the Ring
author: Anonymous (clerical magic collection)
latin_text: Experimentum ad sciendum res furatas: fac anulum de plumbo in Saturni hora et sculpe in eo nomen Oriensis et quattuor reges ventorum — portans anulum in digito medio, quaere furem, et manus tua ad eum tremere incipiet.
english_gloss: An experiment for knowing stolen things: make a ring of lead in Saturn's hour and engrave in it the name of Oriens and the four kings of the winds — carrying the ring on the middle finger, seek the thief, and your hand will begin to tremble toward him.

vocabulary.definition: experiment, trial, tested procedure — the key term for practical magic recipes
lead — metal of Saturn, used for binding, cursing, and detection magic
Oriens — king of the Eastern demon kings in medieval magic (one of four directional demon rulers)
will begin to tremble — the ring serves as a dowsing device animated by demonic force

source_notes: The Liber Experimentorum represents the genre of practical clerical magic collections common in 13th–14th century Europe — mixtures of legitimate learned magic, folk techniques, and demonic procedures. The 'trial of the ring' for finding thieves combines planetary timing (Saturn's hour), sympathetic correspondence (lead = Saturn = binding/detection), and demonic invocation of the four directional kings. Richard Kieckhefer discusses this genre extensively. Source: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997. // Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Malleus Maleficarum, II.i — On the Power of Witches over Generative Faculty
author: Heinrich Kramer (Institoris)
latin_text: Maleficae possunt viros impedire ab actu venereo et mulieres a conceptione, et ut secundum has species dividatur materia — primo de impedimento actus, secundo de impedimento usus, tertio de ablation membri virilis per phantasiam.
english_gloss: Witches can impede men from the venereal act and women from conception, and so that the material may be divided according to these categories — first concerning the impediment of the act, second concerning the impediment of use, third concerning the removal of the male member through phantasy.

vocabulary.definition: female witch, sorceress (Kramer systematically feminizes the category)
to impede, obstruct (legal term for magical interference)
phantasy, illusion — the famous 'penis theft' by demonic illusion, not physical removal

source_notes: The Malleus Maleficarum Part II examines specific forms of witchcraft in systematic scholastic form. The notorious section on 'ligature' (sexual impotence through magic) and 'member removal by phantasy' reflects medieval medical beliefs about imagination and demonic power over bodily perception. Kramer's systematic feminization of witchcraft ('maleficae' rather than 'malefici') was influential but contested even by contemporaries. Source: Kramer, Heinrich (Institoris). Malleus Maleficarum. Ed. and trans. Christopher S. Mackay. 2 vols. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.
bibliography: Kramer, Heinrich (Institoris). Malleus Maleficarum. Ed. and trans. Christopher S. Mackay. 2 vols. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.

title: De Vita Coelitus Comparanda, §19 — Solar Talismans
author: Marsilio Ficino
latin_text: Sol omnium luminarium potentissimus, omnium planetarum rex — eius signum in auro sculpe, cum Sol in Leone vel Ariete est et ipse in gradu suo exaltationis. Porta hoc signum et senties calorem vitae in te augeri.
english_gloss: The Sun, most powerful of all luminaries, king of all planets — engrave his sign in gold when the Sun is in Leo or Aries and he himself is in the degree of his exaltation. Carry this sign and you will feel the warmth of life increase in you.

vocabulary.definition: luminary, celestial light source (technical astrological term for Sun and Moon)
exaltation — the zodiac sign where a planet's power is greatest (Sun exalted in Aries)
you will feel, perceive (Ficino's talismans work through sensation, not mere symbol)

source_notes: Ficino's De Vita Coelitus Comparanda ('On Obtaining Life from the Heavens,' 1489) is the most sophisticated Renaissance treatment of astrological magic. This passage on solar talismans exemplifies Ficino's system: the talisman concentrates solar spiritus through proper material (gold = Sun's metal) and astrological timing, channeling cosmic sympathy into the body. Ficino was careful to frame this as natural philosophy rather than forbidden magic. Source: Ficino, Marsilio. Three Books on Life. Ed. and trans. Carol V. Kaske and John R. Clark. Binghamton: MRTS, 1989.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Three Books on Life (De Vita Libri Tres). Ed. and trans. Carol V. Kaske and John R. Clark. Binghamton: MRTS, 1989.

title: De Occulta Philosophia, I.50 — On Fascination
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
latin_text: Fascinatio est actio quaedam per quam spiritus fascinantis per oculos ingreditur et animam vel corpus fascinati ferit. Spiritus enim per oculos eiaculati — tanquam sagittae quaedam — anum laedit penetrantque vitalia.
english_gloss: Fascination is a certain action through which the spirit of the fascinator enters through the eyes and strikes the soul or body of the fascinated. For spirits ejected through the eyes — like certain arrows — wound the spirit and penetrate the vital parts.

vocabulary.definition: fascination, the evil eye — the emission of harmful spiritual force through the eyes
ejected, hurled outward (describing the projection of ocular spirits)
the vital parts — the seat of life-force in Galenic-Neoplatonic physiology

source_notes: Agrippa's chapter on fascination (evil eye) in De Occulta Philosophia I.50 draws on a long tradition from Plutarch through Ficino explaining the evil eye as a physical phenomenon: the emission of subtle spirits (spiritus) through the eyes that can wound at a distance. This 'ocular radiation' theory combines Galenic medicine, Neoplatonic pneumatology, and folk belief in a systematic natural-magical framework. Source: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: Steganographia, I — Angelic Cipher Communication
author: Johannes Trithemius
latin_text: Per artem nostram steganographicam poteris mittere nuntium ad amicum tuum distantem per centum miliaria intra unius horae spatium — non per daemones sed per angelos qui ita a Deo ordinati sunt ut ministrent nobis in licitis.
english_gloss: Through our steganographic art you will be able to send a message to your friend distant by a hundred miles within the space of one hour — not through demons but through angels who are so ordained by God that they minister to us in lawful things.

vocabulary.definition: steganographic — from Greek steganos (hidden) + graphia (writing); secret writing
mile(s) — Roman mile, approximately 1480 meters
to serve, minister to (Trithemius insists angels serve as postal service, not familiar spirits)

source_notes: Trithemius's Steganographia (written c. 1499, published 1606) appeared to be an angelic magic treatise for long-distance communication through spirits. Modern cryptanalysis revealed it also contains genuine steganographic ciphers hidden within the magical text. The work caused scandal: accused of demonology, Trithemius insisted the spirits were angels performing licit service. Whether the angelic framework was cover for pure cryptography or genuine belief remains debated. Source: Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999.
bibliography: Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999. // Ernst, Thomas. 'Schwarzweiße Magie: Der Schlüssel zum dritten Buch der Steganographia des Trithemius.' Daphnis 25 (1996).

title: Hymnus ad Solem — Proclus
author: Proclus Diadochus
latin_text: Audi me, fons luminis, qui omnia gubernas igni — Sol, rex mundi, pater rerum, mens quaedam in caelo, per quem et mortales et immortales moventur et vivunt.
english_gloss: Hear me, fount of light, who governs all things with fire — Sun, king of the world, father of things, a kind of mind in heaven, through whom both mortals and immortals are moved and live.

vocabulary.definition: to govern, steer (metaphor from ship's steering — the Neoplatonic cosmos is a steered vessel)
fount of light — the Sun as source of Neoplatonic illumination (both physical and intellectual)
a kind of mind in heaven — the solar Intellect (Nous) in Proclus's system

source_notes: Proclus's Hymn to the Sun is one of several surviving hymns by the head of the Athenian Neoplatonic school (c. 450–485 CE). For Proclus, the hymns were not merely poetry but genuine theurgic instruments — their correct performance in the context of ritual could draw down solar divine power. The Latin version of the Hymns was known to Renaissance humanists and influenced Ficino's solar spirituality in De Vita. Source: Proclus. Hymni. Ed. Ernst Vogt. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 1957. // Finamore, John, and Danielle Layne. 'Proclus on the Sun.' In Neoplatonism and the Philosophy of Nature. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2012.
bibliography: Proclus. Hymni. Ed. Ernst Vogt. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 1957. // Siorvanes, Lucas. Proclus: Neo-Platonic Philosophy and Science. Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 1996.

title: Clavicula Salomonis, II.4 — General Conjuration
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Coniuro vos, spiritus omnes, per Deum Patrem omnipotentem, et per Iesum Christum Filium eius, et per Spiritum Sanctum, et per sanctam et individuam Trinitatem, et per Adonai, Agla, On, El, Tetragrammaton — ut compareat hic N. in forma humana, pulchra et visibilis, sine strepitu et terrore, et faciat voluntatem meam in omnibus.
english_gloss: I conjure you, all spirits, by God the Father almighty, and by Jesus Christ his Son, and by the Holy Spirit, and by the holy and indivisible Trinity, and by Adonai, Agla, On, El, Tetragrammaton — that N. appear here in human form, beautiful and visible, without noise and terror, and do my will in all things.

vocabulary.definition: to conjure, bind by oath — from 'con-' (together) + 'iurare' (to swear)
indivisible (of the Trinity — key theological term asserting unity within threeness)
the four-letter divine name YHWH — used in Latin magic as the supreme divine name
Hebrew acronym: Atah Gibor Le'olam Adonai ('You are mighty forever, O Lord') — standard in Solomonic magic
noise, din, tumult — spirits were expected to arrive with frightening sounds unless properly constrained

source_notes: The Clavicula Salomonis ('Key of Solomon') is the foundational text of the Solomonic magical tradition, survining in dozens of manuscript versions. This general conjuration formula blends Christian trinitarian theology with Hebrew divine names (Adonai, Agla, Tetragrammaton), producing the characteristic hybrid of late medieval ritual magic. The request for a 'beautiful human form without noise' addresses the practical ritual concern: uncontrolled spirit manifestation was terrifying. Source: Peterson, Joseph H. The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis). Boston: Weiser Books, 2004. // Mathers, Samuel Liddell MacGregor. The Key of Solomon the King. London: George Redway, 1889.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H. The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis). Boston: Weiser Books, 2004. // McLean, Adam, ed. A Treatise on Angel Magic. Grand Rapids: Phanes Press, 1990.

title: Ars Goetia — On the Seals and Offices of the 72 Spirits
author: Lemegeton (attrib. Solomon)
latin_text: Primus spiritus est rex potens et terribilis qui regnat super sexaginta et sex legiones spirituum. Nomen eius est Bael et apparet interdum in forma hominis, interdum in forma catti, interdum in forma regnae, et aliquando in omnibus his simul. Habet potestatem reddendi homines invisibiles.
english_gloss: The first spirit is a powerful and terrible king who reigns over sixty-six legions of spirits. His name is Bael and he appears sometimes in the form of a man, sometimes in the form of a cat, sometimes in the form of a toad, and sometimes in all of these simultaneously. He has the power of making men invisible.

vocabulary.definition: legions — the Roman military unit applied to demonic forces (6,000 spirits per legion)
cat — animal form frequently taken by Goetic spirits (Middle Latin form)
toad — an unusual feminine form used in this text for the toad shape
invisible — the specific magical office or power granted by this spirit
sometimes...sometimes — describing the polymorphic appearance of demons

source_notes: The Ars Goetia (First Book of the Lemegeton) lists 72 demons bound by Solomon, each with a seal, name, rank, appearance, and specific office or power. Bael (the first) corresponds to Ba'al of the Hebrew Bible, here demoted to a bound servant of the magician. The precise enumeration of legions, forms, and powers reflects the systematizing tendency of late medieval demonology. Source: Peterson, Joseph H. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser Books, 2001. // Goetia: The Book of Evil Spirits. Trans. Aleister Crowley and Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers. Chicago: De Laurence, 1916.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser Books, 2001.

title: Clm 849 — Conjuration for a Chained Spirit
author: Anonymous (Munich Necromancer's Manual)
latin_text: Coniuro te, Bileth, per Adonai et per Saday et per El et per Agla, per omnia nomina Dei, ut venias ad me sine mora et sine impedimento, ligatus vinculis quae tibi imposuit Salomon sapientissimus — et facias mihi omne quod postulabo, vel haec verba tibi in tormenta erunt.
english_gloss: I conjure you, Bileth, by Adonai and by Saday and by El and by Agla, by all the names of God, that you come to me without delay and without impediment, bound by the chains that Solomon the most wise imposed upon you — and do for me everything that I shall demand, or these words will be torments for you.

vocabulary.definition: a major demon king in Solomonic tradition, said to command 85 legions
chains, bonds — the magical binding imposed by Solomon; the magician invokes them as coercion
torments, torture — threatening the spirit with divine punishment if it disobeys
Hebrew El Shaddai (God Almighty) — one of the seven Hebrew names of God used in Latin magic
most wise — Solomon's wisdom is the authority grounding the binding

source_notes: The Munich Necromancer's Manual (Munich Clm 849, c. 1440–1450) is a remarkable 15th-century clerical magic manual studied extensively by Richard Kieckhefer. This conjuration of Bileth follows the coercive pattern of Goetic magic: the demon is not merely invited but compelled through the authority of Solomon's original binding and divine names. The explicit threat of 'torments' if the spirit disobeys reflects the adversarial relationship between necromancer and spirit. Source: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997.

title: Theurgia-Goetia — Aerial Spirits of the Directions
author: Lemegeton (Second Book)
latin_text: Carnesiel est magnus et potens dux qui regnat in oriente caeli — ei subsunt duodecim duces principales et centum milites, quorum nomina et sigilla hic continentur. Apparere solet in die solari hora prima.
english_gloss: Carnesiel is a great and powerful duke who reigns in the eastern quarter of the heavens — under him are twelve principal dukes and a hundred soldiers, whose names and seals are here contained. He is accustomed to appear on the solar day in the first hour.

vocabulary.definition: duke of the eastern aerial spirits in the Theurgia-Goetia system
are under, are subordinate to (hierarchical administrative structure)
soldiers — the military metaphor applied to spirit hierarchies

source_notes: The Theurgia-Goetia (Second Book of the Lemegeton) deals with aerial spirits organized by the four cardinal directions, unlike the Goetia's chthonic demons. This text treats spirits as holding quasi-feudal ranks (duke, duke's subordinates, soldiers) with specific times of manifestation. The directional organization reflects the four-winds cosmology common in Solomonic magic. Source: Peterson, Joseph H. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser Books, 2001.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser Books, 2001.

title: Liber Razielis Archangeli — Invocation of Raziel
author: Anonymous (attributed to Eleazar of Worms)
latin_text: Raziel, Archangele Dei, qui stas ante thronum gloriae et scribis mysteria omnia — per nomen sanctum EHEYE ASHER EHEYE, qui est qui est, et per nomen YAHWEH quod non pronuntiatur, adiuro te ut descendas et doceas me sapientiam quae in libro tuo continetur.
english_gloss: Raziel, Archangel of God, who stand before the throne of glory and write all mysteries — by the holy name EHEYE ASHER EHEYE, Who Is Who Is, and by the name YAHWEH which is not pronounced, I adjure you that you descend and teach me the wisdom that is contained in your book.

vocabulary.definition: 'I Am Who I Am' — God's self-identification to Moses (Exodus 3:14), the highest divine name
which is not pronounced — the tetragrammaton YHWH, spoken as 'Adonai' but written as YAHWEH
all mysteries — Raziel is the angel of secrets, keeper of divine knowledge
throne of glory — the Merkabah, God's celestial chariot-throne in Jewish mysticism
to descend — angels must come down from heaven to communicate with humans

source_notes: The Liber Razielis Archangeli is the Latin translation (14th century) of the Hebrew Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh, a major kabbalistic magical compendium attributed to the angel Raziel who gave it to Adam. The text combines practical magic (charms, angel names, protective formulae) with cosmological speculation. The Latin version was influential in Western medieval magic and is one of the few kabbalistic texts to have been widely translated into Latin before the Renaissance. Source: Liber Razielis Archangeli. MS Royal 17 A xlii. British Library. // Trachtenberg, Joshua. Jewish Magic and Superstition. New York: Behrman's Jewish Book House, 1939.
bibliography: Trachtenberg, Joshua. Jewish Magic and Superstition. New York: Behrman's Jewish Book House, 1939. // Bohak, Gideon. Ancient Jewish Magic. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2008.

title: Zohar — Ein Sof and the Sefirot (Latin Reception)
author: Moses de León (attrib.); Latin: Pico della Mirandola
latin_text: En Soph est infinitas divina quae nec capit nec capitur, nec intelligitur nec intelligit — sed per decem Sephirot, quae sunt vasa luminis divini, descendit ad mundum et inhabitat creaturam.
english_gloss: Ein Soph is the divine infinity which neither contains nor is contained, neither understands nor is understood — but through the ten Sefirot, which are vessels of divine light, it descends to the world and dwells in the creature.

vocabulary.definition: the Infinite — the incomprehensible absolute aspect of God in Kabbalah
divine infinity — the Latin translation of Ein Sof, preserving the Hebrew term
the ten divine emanations or attributes through which God relates to creation
vessels of light — the kabbalistic metaphor of Sefirot as containers of divine radiance

source_notes: Pico della Mirandola's 1486 Nine Hundred Conclusions included 47 Kabbalistic theses, the first systematic attempt to integrate Kabbalah into Latin Christian theology. This Latin rendering of Zoharic doctrine on Ein Sof and the Sefirot represents the Christian Kabbalistic tradition that would culminate in Reuchlin, Agrippa, and Fludd. The vessel metaphor (Sefirot as vessels) later became central in the Lurianic Kabbalah doctrine of 'shevirat ha-kelim' (breaking of the vessels). Source: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Conclusiones Nongentae. Ed. Bohdan Kieszkowski. Geneva: Droz, 1973.
bibliography: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Conclusiones Nongentae. Ed. Bohdan Kieszkowski. Geneva: Droz, 1973. // Idel, Moshe. Kabbalah in Italy, 1280–1510. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2011.

title: Tomer Devorah (Latin Reception) — Imitating Divine Mercy
author: Moses Cordovero
latin_text: Debes imitari Creatorem tuum in tredecim attributis misericordiae — sicut Ipse longanimis est in ira, sic tu longanimis sis; sicut Ipse bonus etiam malis, sic tu bonus sis etiam his qui te laedunt.
english_gloss: You should imitate your Creator in the thirteen attributes of mercy — just as He is long-suffering in anger, so you be long-suffering; just as He is good even to the evil, so you be good even to those who harm you.

vocabulary.definition: the thirteen attributes — God's thirteen attributes of mercy from Exodus 34:6-7, central to Jewish liturgy and Kabbalah
long-suffering, patient in anger (translating Hebrew 'erech apayim')
to imitate — the ethical imperative of imitatio Dei in kabbalistic ethics

source_notes: Cordovero's Tomer Devorah ('Palm Tree of Deborah,' c. 1550) is a unique kabbalistic ethical work arguing that humans should model their behavior on the thirteen divine attributes of mercy, thus participating in the Sefirot through virtuous action. The Latin reception of Cordovero came through the Christian Kabbalistic tradition. This passage illustrates how Kabbalah generated a distinctive ethical mysticism alongside its magical applications. Source: Cordovero, Moses. The Palm Tree of Deborah. Trans. Louis Jacobs. London: Valentine, Mitchell, 1960.
bibliography: Cordovero, Moses. The Palm Tree of Deborah. Trans. Louis Jacobs. London: Valentine, Mitchell, 1960. // Scholem, Gershom. Kabbalah. New York: Meridian, 1974.

title: Historia Naturalis, XXV.59 — Magic Plants and Herbalists
author: Pliny the Elder
latin_text: Herba quam rhizotomi Graeci vocant mandragoram — radix eius humanam speciem habet masculi et feminae. Vis eius tanta est ut somnum moveat, et in amore potata dilectionem augeat, et in odio accepta odium intergat. Quidam addunt nec nisi ter eam circumscribi oportere, contra orientem conversus, antequam colligatur.
english_gloss: The herb which the Greek root-gatherers call mandrake — its root has the appearance of a human male and female. Its power is so great that it induces sleep, and drunk in love it increases affection, and taken in hatred it destroys hatred. Some add that it should be circumscribed three times, facing east, before it is gathered.

vocabulary.definition: root-cutters — professional herbalists in antiquity who gathered magical plants
mandrake — Mandragora officinarum, one of the most magically significant plants in antiquity
to circumscribe, draw a circle around — ritual encircling before harvesting magical plants
love, affection (distinguished from amor; used here for magical love-enhancement)

source_notes: Pliny's Historia Naturalis (77 CE) is an encyclopedic compilation of natural history that preserves extensive folk-magical belief about plants, stones, and animals. The mandrake entry illustrates the tension in ancient 'scientific' writing between empirical observation and magical tradition — Pliny records both while maintaining ironic distance. The ritual of circumscribing the plant three times before harvest reflects the universal magical pattern of triple repetition and protective circle-drawing. Source: Pliny the Elder. Historia Naturalis. Ed. Karl Friedrich Theodor Mayhoff. Leipzig: Teubner, 1875–1906. // Scarborough, John. 'The Pharmacology of Sacred Plants, Herbs, and Roots.' In Magika Hiera. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.
bibliography: Pliny the Elder. Historia Naturalis. Ed. K.F.T. Mayhoff. Leipzig: Teubner, 1875–1906. // Scarborough, John. 'The Pharmacology of Sacred Plants, Herbs, and Roots.' In Magika Hiera. Oxford, 1991.

title: Summa Contra Gentiles, III.104 — Demonic Cooperation
author: Thomas Aquinas
latin_text: Daemones autem non possunt obedire nisi his quae sub eorum potestate sunt — sunt autem sub eorum potestate corpora phantasmata per quae imagines inducunt et interdum etiam mentes hominum per suggestionem, non per necessitatem.
english_gloss: Demons, however, can only obey in those things that are under their power — under their power are bodies, the phantasms through which they produce images, and sometimes also the minds of men through suggestion, not through compulsion.

vocabulary.definition: phantasms, illusions — images produced by demons to deceive the senses
suggestion — a key technical term: demons can suggest but not compel free will
necessity, compulsion — the limit Aquinas places on demonic power over human will

source_notes: Aquinas's Summa Contra Gentiles (c. 1259–1264) provides the foundational scholastic analysis of demonic power that would govern demonological debate for centuries. By distinguishing 'suggestion' from 'compulsion,' Aquinas preserves human free will and responsibility while allowing for real demonic influence. This distinction became crucial in witch-trial debates: can a demon compel someone to do evil? Aquinas says no — only suggest. Source: Aquinas, Thomas. Summa Contra Gentiles. Trans. Vernon J. Bourke. Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press, 1975.
bibliography: Aquinas, Thomas. Summa Contra Gentiles. Trans. Vernon J. Bourke. Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press, 1975. // Demonology in the Age of Saint Thomas Aquinas. Ed. Edward Peters. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1982.

title: Formicarius, V.3 — Early Witch Sabbath Account
author: Johannes Nider
latin_text: Confessae sunt maleficae quod in nocte Veneris ad synagogam suam volant, ubi diabolus in forma hirci sedens adoratur, et candelas extinctis post obscena conficiuntur pharmaca infantium.
english_gloss: The witches confessed that on the night of Venus they fly to their synagogue, where the devil sitting in the form of a he-goat is worshipped, and with extinguished candles after obscenities, potions of infants are prepared.

vocabulary.definition: synagogue — the early term for witch-sabbath assemblies (reflecting anti-Jewish prejudice)
he-goat — the standard demonic form at the sabbath, derived from ritual scapegoat imagery
drugs, potions (from Greek pharmakon) — the alleged products of witch-sabbath preparations
night of Venus — Friday night (Venus = dies Veneris = Friday); witches met on Fridays

source_notes: Johannes Nider's Formicarius ('The Anthill,' c. 1435–1437) contains some of the earliest detailed descriptions of the witch sabbath, predating the Malleus Maleficarum by 50 years. Nider draws on interrogations by the inquisitor Peter of Berne. The 'synagogue' terminology and goat-worship are characteristic of early sabbath accounts that conflated heresy, Judaism, and magic. This text was a key source for later demonological writers. Source: Bailey, Michael D. Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2003.
bibliography: Bailey, Michael D. Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2003. // Nider, Johannes. Formicarius. Douai, 1602 (facsimile).

title: Malleus, Part I, Q.1 — Whether Witchcraft Exists
author: Heinrich Kramer (Institoris)
latin_text: Est haeresis dicere maleficia non esse in rerum natura vel maleficas posse facere quicquam contra voluntatem Dei. Sed haeresin esse dicimus negare maleficia omnino et non solum esse verum sed etiam esse gravissimum crimen.
english_gloss: It is heresy to say that witchcraft does not exist in the nature of things or that witches can do anything against the will of God. But we say it is heresy to deny witchcraft entirely — it is not only real but also the most grievous of crimes.

vocabulary.definition: heresy — Kramer's brilliant move: disbelief in witchcraft itself becomes heretical
witchcraft, evil deeds — the canonical term for harmful magic in canon law
the most grievous crime — Kramer ranks witchcraft above all other sins in severity

source_notes: This is the foundational logical move of the Malleus Maleficarum: Kramer argues that witchcraft is real (citing scripture and authorities), then argues that denying witchcraft is heresy. This rhetorical trap — disbelievers are themselves heretics — silenced many critics. The strategy of criminalizing skepticism was unprecedented and became a model for later demonologists. Source: Kramer, Heinrich. Malleus Maleficarum. Ed. and trans. Christopher S. Mackay. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.
bibliography: Kramer, Heinrich. Malleus Maleficarum. Ed. and trans. Christopher S. Mackay. 2 vols. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006. // Broedel, Hans Peter. The Malleus Maleficarum and the Construction of Witchcraft. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 2003.

title: The Discoverie of Witchcraft, I.1 (Latin citations)
author: Reginald Scot
latin_text: Errores superstitiosi de maleficis et sagis procedunt ex ignorantia et ex vi imaginationis — nam quae vulgo pro miraculis habentur, naturae operibus aut daemonum praestigiis adscribenda sunt, non verae potestati mulierculis tributae.
english_gloss: The superstitious errors about witches and wise-women proceed from ignorance and from the power of imagination — for what the common people take for miracles should be attributed either to the works of nature or to the illusions of demons, not to a true power attributed to little women.

vocabulary.definition: little women — Scot's dismissive diminutive; he argues poor old women are scapegoated
illusions, juggling tricks — demonic deception through false appearances
imagination — Scot argues that witch-experiences are products of disordered imagination, not reality

source_notes: Reginald Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) is the most thoroughgoing early modern skeptical critique of witch-belief, arguing that witchcraft confessions are the product of mental illness, deception, and fear-induced fantasy in vulnerable women. Scot cites extensively from Latin authorities while systematically demolishing their conclusions. James I had copies burned upon his accession. Scot influenced both rationalist skeptics and, paradoxically, grimoire writers who quarried his extensive magical descriptions. Source: Scot, Reginald. The Discoverie of Witchcraft. Ed. Montague Summers. London: John Rodker, 1930.
bibliography: Scot, Reginald. The Discoverie of Witchcraft. Ed. Montague Summers. London: John Rodker, 1930. // Clark, Stuart. Thinking with Demons. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997.

title: Physiognomia — Reading the Body's Signs
author: Michael Scot
latin_text: Ex forma capitis et figura nasi et mensura oculorum potest astrologus praedicere quid anima naturalis in corpore operetur — nam corpus et anima sibi respondent et signa exteriora interiora designant.
english_gloss: From the shape of the head and the form of the nose and the measure of the eyes, the astrologer can predict what the natural soul works in the body — for body and soul correspond to each other and external signs designate internal ones.

vocabulary.definition: physiognomy — reading character from bodily features (face, build, complexion)
natural soul — the vegetative/sensitive soul governing bodily functions (vs. rational soul)
to mark, designate, indicate (signum language — the body is a system of signs)

source_notes: Michael Scot's Physiognomia (c. 1228), dedicated to the Emperor Frederick II, brought Arabic physiognomy into the Latin West alongside his astrological and alchemical translations. The premise that external bodily signs reveal internal character and fate links physiognomy to astrology (both read signs to predict future) and to natural magic (the body's occult properties). Scot was Frederick II's court astrologer and one of the great translators of the Arabic-Latin transmission. Source: Burnett, Charles. 'Michael Scot and the Transmission of Scientific Culture from Toledo to Bologna.' Micrologus 2 (1994).
bibliography: Burnett, Charles. 'Michael Scot and the Transmission of Scientific Culture from Toledo to Bologna.' Micrologus 2 (1994): 101–26. // Haskins, Charles Homer. Studies in the History of Mediaeval Science. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1924.

title: Geomantia — Rubeus and Terra: Reading Earth Figures
author: Anonymous (geomantic tradition)
latin_text: Rubeus est figura Martis maligna — quando in primo loco cadit, significat iram, pugnam, et sanguinem effusum. Terra autem est figura Saturni sterilis, et in quaestione de thesauro absconditum significat inventionem, in aliis vero quaestionibus malum et perditionem.
english_gloss: Rubeus is the malign figure of Mars — when it falls in the first house, it signifies anger, combat, and shed blood. Terra (Earth) however is the barren figure of Saturn, and in a question about hidden treasure it signifies discovery, but in other questions evil and loss.

vocabulary.definition: geomancy — divination by marks in earth or by sixteen binary figures derived from random dots
Red — one of the sixteen geomantic figures, composed of a specific dot pattern assigned to Mars
Earth — another of the sixteen figures, assigned to Saturn
hidden treasure — one of the standard questions put to geomantic divination

source_notes: Geomancy (divination by earth figures) entered the Latin West through Arabic sources in the 12th century and became one of the most popular learned divination methods of the medieval period. The system uses sixteen binary figures (each made of one or two dots in four lines) assigned to planets and astrological houses. Each figure has different interpretations depending on the 'house' position in the geomantic shield. Source: Burnett, Charles. 'The Earliest Chiromancy in the West.' Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 50 (1987): 189–95. // Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
bibliography: Skinner, Stephen. Geomancy in Theory and Practice. Singapore: Golden Hoard Press, 2011. // Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: Summa Perfectionis, I.i — The Mercury-Sulphur Theory
author: Pseudo-Geber (Paul of Taranto, attrib.)
latin_text: Argentum vivum et sulphur sunt principia proxima omnium metallorum — argentum vivum propter dispositionem fixitatis et non combustibilitatis, sulphur vero propter dispositionem combustibilitatis et coloris. Ex his duobus in terra generantur metalla per operationem naturae per longum tempus, et potest homo imitari naturam per artem abbreviatam.
english_gloss: Quicksilver and sulphur are the proximate principles of all metals — quicksilver for the disposition of fixity and non-combustibility, sulphur for the disposition of combustibility and color. From these two, metals are generated in the earth by the operation of nature over a long time, and man can imitate nature through an abbreviated art.

vocabulary.definition: quicksilver, mercury — 'living silver,' the fluid metallic principle
sulphur — the combustible, coloring principle; not necessarily literal sulphur
fixity — the property of remaining solid and stable under fire (gold's key property)
proximate — immediate, nearby (vs. remote principles like the four elements)
abbreviated — alchemy speeds up natural mineral generation that takes millennia

source_notes: The Summa Perfectionis (c. 1290–1310), attributed to the Arabic chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan ('Geber') but actually composed by a Latin author (possibly Paul of Taranto), is the most systematic and influential alchemical text of the medieval Latin West. Its mercury-sulphur theory — that all metals are composed of varying proportions of mercury (fixity/fluidity) and sulphur (combustibility/color) — dominated European alchemy until the 17th century. The idea that the alchemist 'imitates nature by abbreviated art' became the standard defense of alchemical practice. Source: Newman, William R. The Summa Perfectionis of Pseudo-Geber. Leiden: Brill, 1991.
bibliography: Newman, William R. The Summa Perfectionis of Pseudo-Geber. Leiden: Brill, 1991. // Principe, Lawrence M. The Secrets of Alchemy. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2013.

title: De Mineralibus, II.iii — On the Power of Stones
author: Albertus Magnus
latin_text: Lapides habent proprietates occultas quae non ex elementis sed ex forma specifica procedunt — et haec forma specifica ab intelligentia caelesti imprimitur per radios stellarum in materia lapidis dum generatur.
english_gloss: Stones have hidden properties which proceed not from the elements but from their specific form — and this specific form is impressed by the celestial intelligence through the rays of the stars in the matter of the stone while it is being generated.

vocabulary.definition: hidden properties — the technical term for non-elemental powers in natural things
specific form — the Aristotelian formal principle that makes a thing what it is
celestial intelligence — the Aristotelian separate intellect moving the spheres; Albertus's bridge between theology and natural magic

source_notes: Albertus Magnus's De Mineralibus (c. 1262) provides the most sophisticated scholastic account of occult qualities in minerals. By grounding lapidary magic in Aristotelian form theory and celestial mechanics, Albertus legitimized natural magic as a science: stone powers are real effects caused by stellar radiation during formation, not demonic deception. This became the standard framework for Renaissance natural magic. Source: Albertus Magnus. Book of Minerals. Trans. Dorothy Wyckoff. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1967.
bibliography: Albertus Magnus. Book of Minerals (De Mineralibus). Trans. Dorothy Wyckoff. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1967. // Weisheipl, James A. Albertus Magnus and the Sciences. Toronto: PIMS, 1980.

title: The Compound of Alchemy — The Gate of Calcination
author: George Ripley
latin_text: Prima porta est Calcinatio — per quam corpus metallicum reducitur in pulverem album instar calcis. Haec est prima operatio artis et nisi corpus perfecte calcinetur, nullo modo ad albedinem pervenire poterit.
english_gloss: The first gate is Calcination — through which the metallic body is reduced to a white powder like lime. This is the first operation of the art and unless the body is perfectly calcined, in no way will it be able to arrive at whiteness.

vocabulary.definition: calcination — heating to destroy organic matter or convert to oxide/powder
whiteness — the 'white stone' or silver stage; one of the four alchemical color stages
white powder — the calcined form; purity of whiteness is the goal of this gate

source_notes: George Ripley's The Compound of Alchemy (1471), dedicated to Edward IV, is the major English alchemical poem that presents the Great Work through twelve 'gates' (operations): Calcination, Dissolution, Separation, Conjunction, Putrefaction, Congelation, Cibation, Sublimation, Fermentation, Exaltation, Multiplication, Projection. Ripley was canon of Bridlington Priory and one of the most revered English alchemists. His 'Ripley Scrolls' depicting the operations were widely illustrated. Source: Rampling, Jennifer M. The Experimental Fire: Inventing English Alchemy, 1300–1700. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2020.
bibliography: Rampling, Jennifer M. The Experimental Fire: Inventing English Alchemy, 1300–1700. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2020. // Ripley, George. The Compound of Alchemy. Ed. Ralph Rabbards. London, 1591.

title: Archidoxes, III — On Quintessences
author: Paracelsus (Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim)
latin_text: Quinta essentia est quod ex quacumque re extractum est praeter quatuor elementa — hoc est substantia supercaelestis, nec calida nec frigida, nec sicca nec humida, sed quinta natura, quinta essentia, id est caelestis in rebus terrestribus.
english_gloss: The quintessence is what is extracted from any thing beyond the four elements — this is a supracelestial substance, neither hot nor cold, neither dry nor wet, but a fifth nature, a quintessence, that is, the heavenly in earthly things.

vocabulary.definition: quintessence — the fifth essence beyond the four Aristotelian elements; the celestial principle in matter
supracelestial, beyond the heavens — the quintessence partakes of the divine sphere above the planets
