extracted — the quintessence must be drawn out from gross matter through distillation

source_notes: Paracelsus's Archidoxes (c. 1524, published 1570) presents his theory of quintessences — refined extracts from natural substances that concentrate their healing and magical powers. This directly challenged Galenic medicine by replacing the four-humor system with a three-principle system (Sulfur, Mercury, Salt) plus the quintessence. The medical-alchemical reform Paracelsus proposed had enormous influence on 16th–17th century chemistry and hermetic philosophy. Source: Paracelsus. The Archidoxes of Magic. Trans. Robert Turner. London, 1655 (facsimile, Weiser, 1975). // Weeks, Andrew. Paracelsus: Speculative Theory and the Crisis of the Early Reformation. Albany: SUNY Press, 1997.
bibliography: Weeks, Andrew. Paracelsus: Speculative Theory and the Crisis of the Early Reformation. Albany: SUNY Press, 1997. // Webster, Charles. Paracelsus: Medicine, Magic and Mission at the End of Time. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2008.

title: A True and Faithful Relation — First Enochian Call
author: John Dee (Edward Kelley, medium)
latin_text: Loquutus est angelus Uriel et dixit: 'Haec lingua Angelica est in qua Adam locutus est in Paradiso — vocatur Enochiana quia Enochus eam primus post Adamum scripsit. Characteres eius non sunt characteres linguarum humanarum sed voces potentiae primordiales.'
english_gloss: The angel Uriel spoke and said: 'This Angelic language is that in which Adam spoke in Paradise — it is called Enochian because Enoch first wrote it after Adam. Its characters are not the characters of human languages but primordial voices of power.'

vocabulary.definition: the Angelic language — Enochian, the language of the angels received by Dee and Kelley
Enochian — from Enoch, the biblical patriarch who walked with God; the name for Dee's angelic language system
primordial, of the first creation — the angelic language predates all human tongues
the archangel Uriel ('God is my light') — one of Dee's primary angelic contacts

source_notes: John Dee's spiritual diaries record his angelic communications (1582–1589) conducted with the medium Edward Kelley. The angels delivered the 'Enochian' language with its unique alphabet, grammar, and 'calls' or invocations. Dee believed this was the original Adamic language, the tongue of angels and of prelapsarian humanity. The Enochian system was later adopted by the Golden Dawn and has become the most influential angelic communication system in modern Western esotericism. Source: Dee, John. A True and Faithful Relation. Ed. Meric Casaubon. London, 1659. // Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999.
bibliography: Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999. // Laycock, Donald C. The Complete Enochian Dictionary. London: Askin, 1978.

title: Corpus Hermeticum I (Poimandres) — The Primal Vision
author: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.)
latin_text: Vidi lucem infinitam, et oblectatus sum in ea. Post haec vidi tenebras, tetras et tremebundas, obliquo modo descendentes, et timui. Deinde ex luce loquebatur mihi vox, vox inenarrabiliter suavis, et dicebat: 'Ego sum Poimandres, intellectus potentiae summae — quod vis videre, docebo te.'
english_gloss: I saw an infinite light, and I was delighted in it. After these things I saw darkness, foul and trembling, descending in an oblique manner, and I was afraid. Then from the light there spoke to me a voice, a voice of indescribably sweet character, and it said: 'I am Poimandres, the mind of supreme power — what you wish to see, I will teach you.'

vocabulary.definition: the divine Mind or Intellect — possibly from Greek 'poimen andron' (shepherd of men) or Coptic origin
in an oblique manner — the darkness descends at an angle, not straight down (cosmological detail)
indescribably, beyond narration — the classical marker of mystical ineffability
the Intellect of supreme power — Nous, the divine Mind, first emanation of the One in Hermetic theology
delighted, taking pleasure — the soul's natural response to divine light

source_notes: The Poimandres (Corpus Hermeticum I) is the foundational Hermetic cosmogonic text, presenting a visionary revelation of the origin of the cosmos and the nature of the divine Mind. Marsilio Ficino's Latin translation (1463), commissioned by Cosimo de' Medici, created the Renaissance Hermetic movement by introducing this text to Western scholars. Ficino believed (as did most Renaissance readers) that Hermes Trismegistus was an Egyptian contemporary of Moses. Source: Ficino, Marsilio, trans. Pimander [Corpus Hermeticum]. Florence: Antonio Miscomini, 1471. // Copenhaver, Brian P. Hermetica. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1992.
bibliography: Copenhaver, Brian P. Hermetica: The Greek Corpus Hermeticum and the Latin Asclepius. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1992. // Yates, Frances A. Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition. London: Routledge, 1964.

title: Epistolae, V.7 — The Spiritus Mundi and Solar Magic
author: Marsilio Ficino
latin_text: Spiritus mundi est quoddam caeleste corpus tenuissimum, quasi nexus inter animam mundi et corpus mundi — per hunc spiritum Sol influit in omnia, et qui spiritum solis in se colligit per congruos colores, odores, sapores, et cantus, is Solis vires in se trahit.
english_gloss: The spirit of the world is a certain finest celestial body, like a bond between the world-soul and the world-body — through this spirit the Sun flows into all things, and whoever gathers the spirit of the Sun in himself through suitable colors, odors, tastes, and songs, draws the powers of the Sun into himself.

vocabulary.definition: world-spirit — the subtle medium between soul and body in Ficino's Neoplatonic cosmology
bond, link — the spiritus is the middle term binding immaterial soul to material body
suitable, fitting, congruent — things must 'fit' the planet to channel its power
draws in, attracts — the spiritus flows like a current; the right 'receiver' attracts it

source_notes: Ficino's Epistolae (Letters) develop his practical solar magic in a more personal and less systematic mode than De Vita. This letter articulates the theory of how solar spiritus can be 'gathered' through sensory correspondences — appropriate colors (gold, yellow), odors (saffron, balsam), flavors (sweet, golden wine), and music (bright, clear modes). This is Ficino's natural-magical framework for what he calls 'Orphic' therapy: feeding the spiritus on solar influences. Source: Ficino, Marsilio. The Letters of Marsilio Ficino. Vol. 5. London: Shepheard-Walwyn, 1994.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. The Letters of Marsilio Ficino. 8 vols. London: Shepheard-Walwyn, 1975–2010. // Walker, D.P. Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella. London: Warburg Institute, 1958.

title: Introductorium Maius, I — On the Power of the Stars
author: Abu Ma'shar (Albumasar)
date: c. 848 CE (Arabic); 12th cent. (Latin trans. Herman of Carinthia)
latin_text: Stellae non solum significant futura sed etiam causant per radios suos in haec inferiora descendentes — nam caelum est virtus activa, terra virtus passiva, et inter eas spiritus mundi qui impressiones caelestes ad terram defert.
english_gloss: The stars not only signify future things but also cause them through their rays descending into these lower realms — for heaven is the active power, earth is the passive power, and between them is the world-spirit that carries celestial impressions to earth.

vocabulary.definition: to signify, indicate — the semiotic role of stars (reading signs vs. causing effects)
to cause — Albumasar's key claim: stars don't just predict, they produce effects
lower things — the sublunar world beneath the moon's orbit
active/passive power — the Aristotelian schema applied to celestial (active) and terrestrial (passive)

source_notes: Abu Ma'shar's Introductorium Maius ('Great Introduction to Astrology,' c. 848 CE) was translated by Herman of Carinthia in 1140 and became the foundational Arabic astrological text in the medieval Latin West. Albumasar's causal astrology — distinguishing mere prediction ('signification') from actual causal influence ('causation') — was philosophically crucial for legitimizing astrological practice as natural science rather than divination. Source: Lemay, Richard. Abu Ma'shar and Latin Aristotelianism in the Twelfth Century. Beirut: American University of Beirut, 1962.
bibliography: Lemay, Richard. Abu Ma'shar and Latin Aristotelianism in the Twelfth Century. Beirut: American University of Beirut, 1962. // Abu Ma'shar. The Abbreviation of the Introduction to Astrology. Ed. Charles Burnett. Leiden: Brill, 1994.

title: De Mysteriis Aegyptiorum, II.11 — Why the Gods are Moved by Ritual
author: Iamblichus of Chalcis
latin_text: Non igitur ut homines, qui persuasionibus et blanditiis flectuntur, ita et dii moveri putandi sunt — dii enim rationibus neque moventur neque flectuntur: sed divinum lumen per suam naturam descendit, ex se ipso undique diffusum, et in iis qui capaces sunt, permanet. Theurgus igitur non persuadet deos, sed praeparat animam suam ut divinum lumen capiat.
english_gloss: The gods, therefore, are not to be thought moved as men who are swayed by persuasions and flatteries — for the gods are moved and swayed by neither reasonings nor flattery: but divine light descends through its own nature, diffused everywhere from itself, and remains in those who are capable. The theurgist therefore does not persuade the gods, but prepares his soul to receive divine light.

vocabulary.definition: flatteries, coaxing — Iamblichus refutes the prayer-as-flattery view of pagan critics
theurgist — the ritual practitioner who uses divine names and acts to unite with divinity
capable, receptive — only properly prepared souls can receive divine illumination
diffused, spread in all directions — divine light radiates universally but is received selectively
prepares — the theurgist's role is not manipulation but self-preparation

source_notes: Iamblichus's De Mysteriis Aegyptiorum ('On the Mysteries of the Egyptians,' c. 300 CE) is the foundational text of Neoplatonic theurgy — the use of ritual actions, divine names, and sacred objects to unite the soul with the gods. Iamblichus's key move here is redefining ritual: it doesn't 'move' the gods (who are immutable) but prepares the practitioner to receive divine presence. This transforms magic from manipulation to spiritual purification. Ficino translated portions in the 15th century. Source: Iamblichus. On the Mysteries. Trans. Emma C. Clarke, John M. Dillon, and Jackson P. Hershbell. Atlanta: SBL, 2003.
bibliography: Iamblichus. On the Mysteries. Trans. Emma C. Clarke, John M. Dillon, and Jackson P. Hershbell. Atlanta: SBL, 2003. // Shaw, Gregory. Theurgy and the Soul: The Neoplatonism of Iamblichus. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1995.

title: Bath Curse Tablets — Offering to Sulis Minerva
author: Anonymous (Bath, Roman Britain)
latin_text: Deae Suli Minervae Uricalus donat partem togae suae et paenulae qui ilam involavit, sive puer sive puella, sive homo liber sive servus — ut dea eum sanguine et vita sua puniat.
english_gloss: To the goddess Sulis Minerva, Uricalus donates part of his toga and cloak — [from] whoever stole it, whether boy or girl, whether free man or slave — that the goddess may punish that person by their blood and their life.

vocabulary.definition: Sulis Minerva — the syncretized Celtic-Roman goddess of the Bath springs; Sulis (Celtic) identified with Minerva
cloak — a heavy traveling cloak; the stolen item dedicated to the goddess
stole, flew upon (with theft sense) — same verb used in Mainz tablets
whether...or — the all-inclusive formula covering all possible perpetrators
blood and life — the maximum penalty; giving the thief to the goddess in body and soul

source_notes: The Bath (Aquae Sulis) curse tablets are one of the largest and best-preserved collections of Romano-British defixiones, deposited in the sacred spring of Sulis Minerva at Bath. Over 130 tablets have been recovered, mostly written in lead, addressing thefts from the temple precinct. They represent the intersection of Roman legal practice (deditio — handing over to divine justice) with Celtic religious tradition (Sulis's spring). Source: Tomlin, Roger S.O. Tabellae Sulis: Roman Inscribed Tablets of Tin and Lead from the Sacred Spring at Bath. Oxford: Oxford University Committee for Archaeology, 1988.
bibliography: Tomlin, Roger S.O. Tabellae Sulis: Roman Inscribed Tablets of Tin and Lead from the Sacred Spring at Bath. Oxford: OUCA, 1988. // Cunliffe, Barry, ed. The Temple of Sulis Minerva at Bath. Vol. 2. Oxford: OUCA, 1988.

title: Divinae Institutiones, II.15 — Christian Classification of Demonic Arts
author: Lactantius
latin_text: Daemones docuerunt homines artes maleficas — vaticinationes, auguria, auspicia, magiam, goetiam, necromantiam. His artibus delectati homines deos putabant esse qui docebant, sed erant angeli Dei lapsi qui sibi numen vindicabant.
english_gloss: Demons taught humans the evil arts — prophecy, augury, auspices, magic, goetia, necromancy. Delighted by these arts, people thought those who taught them were gods, but they were fallen angels of God who claimed divine authority for themselves.

vocabulary.definition: prophetic utterances, vaticinations (pagan oracular prophecy)
augury — divination by observing birds (Roman official practice)
goetia — low or demonic magic (from Greek goes, a wailing mourner/magician), distinct from high magic
claimed divine power for themselves — the key Christian demonological error: taking the gods' place

source_notes: Lactantius's Divinae Institutiones (c. 304–311 CE) is an early Christian apologist's systematic classification of pagan magic arts as demonic deceptions. His list — vaticinatio, augury, auspices, magic, goetia, necromancy — became one of the earliest systematic taxonomies of magical arts in Latin Christian thought and influenced Augustine, Isidore, and ultimately the entire medieval classification tradition. Source: Lactantius. Divine Institutes. Trans. Anthony Bowen and Peter Garnsey. Liverpool: Liverpool University Press, 2003.
bibliography: Lactantius. Divine Institutes. Trans. Anthony Bowen and Peter Garnsey. Liverpool: Liverpool University Press, 2003. // Flint, Valerie I.J. The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991.

title: Compendium Maleficarum, I.7 — The Witches' Sabbath
author: Francesco Maria Guazzo
latin_text: In synagoga maleficorum diabolus in throno residet in forma hirci vel canis nigri, et maleficae coram eo genuflectunt et osculantur eum sub cauda. Tunc negant fidem christianam et conculcant crucifixum et aquam benedictam aspergunt in saniem conversam.
english_gloss: In the assembly of witches the devil sits on a throne in the form of a he-goat or black dog, and the witches kneel before him and kiss him beneath the tail. Then they deny the Christian faith and trample the crucifix and sprinkle holy water converted into filth.

vocabulary.definition: assembly of witches (sabbath) — the anti-Jewish term for witch-gathering continued in use
kneel before him — the obscene parody of genuflection; ritual inversion of Christian worship
trample, tread underfoot — ritual desecration of Christian symbols
pus, putrid fluid — holy water ritually inverted into its opposite, corruption

source_notes: Francesco Maria Guazzo's Compendium Maleficarum (1608) is one of the last major demonological texts before skepticism began to dominate, and is famous for its detailed woodcut illustrations of the sabbath. Guazzo systematically describes the witch's pact, the sabbath, the sexual relationship with the devil, and the various forms of maleficium. His text exemplifies the fully elaborated sabbath mythology that had developed over 200 years from Nider. Source: Guazzo, Francesco Maria. Compendium Maleficarum. Ed. Montague Summers. London: John Rodker, 1929.
bibliography: Guazzo, Francesco Maria. Compendium Maleficarum. Ed. Montague Summers. London: John Rodker, 1929. // Ginzburg, Carlo. Ecstasies: Deciphering the Witches' Sabbath. New York: Pantheon, 1991.

title: Quaestio de Strigibus — Are Witches Real?
author: Bernardo Basin
latin_text: Strigae verae esse possunt et non solum in phantasia existere — quia diabolus virtute naturali et permissione Dei potest homines de loco ad locum transportare, et hoc expertis confessoribus et iudicibus probatum est.
english_gloss: True witches can exist and not exist only in phantasy — because the devil by natural power and with the permission of God can transport people from place to place, and this has been proven by experienced confessors and judges.

vocabulary.definition: witches — from Latin strix (screech-owl), the night-flying hag who fed on children
natural power — demonic power is natural, not supernatural; an important theological distinction
permission of God — Satan can act only within divine permission; theodicy of demonic power
confessors — priests hearing confessions; judicial as well as sacramental role in witch-trials

source_notes: Bernard Basin's Quaestio de Strigibus (1483) is a short but important early demonological text that argues for the reality of physical witchcraft against the Canon Episcopi tradition that treated night-flying as illusion. Basin's argument — that demonic power can cause real physical transport — became the standard theological position supporting witch-trial prosecution. Source: Hansen, Joseph. Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns. Bonn: Georgi, 1901. // Bailey, Michael D. Magic and Superstition in Europe. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2007.
bibliography: Hansen, Joseph. Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns. Bonn: Georgi, 1901. // Bailey, Michael D. Magic and Superstition in Europe. Lanham: Rowman and Littlefield, 2007.

title: Clavicula Salomonis, IV — Making the Pentacles
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Pentacula in die et hora Mercurii scribuntur in pergameno virginis vel in lamina aeris — et scribantur characteres cum sanguine chamaeleontis vel cum tinctura croci. Postea suffumigantur et recitantur super eis psalmi Davidici designati.
english_gloss: Pentacles are written on the day and hour of Mercury on virgin parchment or on a plate of bronze — and the characters are written with the blood of a chameleon or with saffron dye. Afterward they are fumigated and the designated Psalms of David are recited over them.

vocabulary.definition: pentacles — magical talismans, typically inscribed circles with divine names and symbols (from Greek penta = five)
virgin parchment — unused parchment from an unborn animal; ritual purity requirement
chameleon — the chameleon's blood was believed to have color-changing (adaptable) magical properties
saffron dye — golden ink for solar purposes; crocus/saffron associated with Sun and Mercury
are fumigated — ritual consecration by smoke; smoke carries the object into sacred space

source_notes: The Clavicula Salomonis devotes an entire section to the manufacture and consecration of pentacles — the most complex objects in the Solomonic toolkit. The prescription for virgin parchment, chameleon blood, and Davidic psalms combines ritual purity requirements (virginity = uncorrupted material), animal magic (chameleon's color-changing), and scriptural authority (Psalms as divine speech). This multi-layered consecration is characteristic of high medieval magic. Source: Peterson, Joseph H. The Key of Solomon the King. Boston: Weiser Books, 2004.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H. The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis). Boston: Weiser Books, 2004.

title: Liber Iuratus Honorii — The 72 Divine Names in Sequence
author: Honorius of Thebes (pseudo-author)
latin_text: Nomina Dei iuxta ordinem angelorum: ADONAI SABAOTH EL ELION SHADDAI TETRAGRAMMATON EHYEH ASHER EHYEH — per haec nomina sancta omnia virtute tua continentur et nihil est in caelo vel terra quod his nominibus non obediat.
english_gloss: Names of God in the order of the angels: ADONAI SABAOTH EL ELION SHADDAI TETRAGRAMMATON EHYEH ASHER EHYEH — through these holy names all things are contained in your power and there is nothing in heaven or earth that does not obey these names.

vocabulary.definition: God Most High — a title of God appearing in Genesis 14:18-22, used especially in Canaanite/patriarchal texts
God Almighty — a pre-Mosaic divine name; translated as 'the Almighty' in Septuagint
are held, contained — all things are in God's grasp through the names

source_notes: The Liber Iuratus Honorii ('Sworn Book of Honorius,' c. 13th cent.) claims to preserve the secret angelic teachings almost suppressed by Pope Boniface VIII. Its sequence of Hebrew divine names — drawn from Kabbalistic and Solomonic sources — became a standard repertoire in Western magical tradition. The claim that 'nothing in heaven or earth' disobeys these names reflects the Solomonic premise that divine names are the key to all power. Source: Gösta Hedegård, ed. Liber Iuratus Honorii. Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 2002.
bibliography: Hedegård, Gösta, ed. Liber Iuratus Honorii. Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 2002. // Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Heptameron — Constructing the Magic Circle
author: Pietro d'Abano (attrib.)
latin_text: Circulus magicus debet esse in terra scriptus stilo eboris vel calamo novo — et in gyro eius scribantur nomina angelorum diei illius et nomina planetarum et signa zodiaci regnantia. Extra circulum scribantur quatuor nomina Dei versa ad quatuor ventos: YHVH ad orientem, ADONAI ad meridiem, EHYEH ad occidentem, AGLA ad septentrionem.
english_gloss: The magic circle should be drawn on the ground with a style of ivory or a new reed — and around its circumference should be written the names of the angels of that day and the names of the planets and the ruling zodiac signs. Outside the circle should be written the four names of God facing the four winds: YHVH to the east, ADONAI to the south, EHYEH to the west, AGLA to the north.

vocabulary.definition: ivory stylus — ivory (non-ferrous, pure material) for drawing protective circles
new reed — an unused reed pen; ritual purity requires unused implements
in the circumference, around the circle (from Greek gyros, circular movement)
north — literally 'the seven plowing oxen' (Ursa Major); the northern direction

source_notes: The Heptameron ('Seven Days,' attributed to Pietro d'Abano but actually c. 14th century) is one of the most influential ritual magic handbooks, describing operations for each day of the week corresponding to its planetary angel. The magic circle described here — with divine names at the four cardinal directions — became the standard Western ritual magic protective structure, inherited by the Golden Dawn and Wicca. Source: d'Abano, Pietro (attrib.). Heptameron. In Three Books of Occult Philosophy by Agrippa. Trans. James Freake. London, 1651.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., and Dan Harms, eds. The Book of Magic with Instructions for Invoking Spirits. Lake Worth: Ibis Press, 2015. // Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Ring of Solomon — The Tetragrammaton Seal
author: Anonymous (Solomonic tradition)
latin_text: Salomon habuit annulum in quo sculptum erat nomen Dei quadriliterum YHVH — et per hunc annulum daemones cogere poterat ad obediendum. Qui habet annulum similem, sculptum in die Iovis sub hora Saturni ex metallo Iovis, habebit potestatem super spiritus.
english_gloss: Solomon had a ring in which was engraved the four-letter name of God YHVH — and through this ring he was able to compel demons to obey. Whoever has a similar ring, engraved on the day of Jupiter under the hour of Saturn from the metal of Jupiter, will have power over spirits.

vocabulary.definition: the four-letter name — the Tetragrammaton YHVH; the most sacred divine name
to compel, coerce — the ring gives coercive (not persuasive) power over spirits
metal of Jupiter — tin; each planet has its associated metal in alchemical correspondence

source_notes: The Ring of Solomon is one of the most persistent elements in Solomonic magical tradition, appearing in the Testament of Solomon (3rd–5th cent. CE), Islamic legend (the ring of Sulayman), and numerous European grimoires. The ring's power comes from the engraved Tetragrammaton — God's name serves as the ultimate binding authority. The prescriptions for specific day, hour, and metal demonstrate how Solomonic magic integrates astrological timing with talismanic practice. Source: Duling, D.C. 'Testament of Solomon.' In Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1. Ed. James H. Charlesworth. Garden City: Doubleday, 1983.
bibliography: Duling, D.C. 'Testament of Solomon.' In Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 1. Ed. James H. Charlesworth. Garden City: Doubleday, 1983. // Skinner, Stephen, and David Rankine. The Keys to the Gateway of Magic. London: Golden Hoard Press, 2005.

title: Ritual for Raising a Spirit from the Dead
author: Anonymous (necromantic manual)
latin_text: Ad evocandum spiritum mortui: Vade ad sepulcrum in nocte Saturni et circumda sepulcrum circulo et dic: 'Coniuro te, anima N., per Deum viventem et verum, per Deum vivificantem mortuos, ut exeas de loco tuo et venias ad me in forma placida et mihi respondeas ad omnia quae interrogabero.' Expecta in silentio et audies vocem.
english_gloss: For summoning the spirit of a dead person: Go to the grave on a night of Saturn and surround the grave with a circle and say: 'I conjure you, soul of N., by the living and true God, by the God who raises the dead, that you come out of your place and come to me in a peaceful form and answer me in all things that I shall ask.' Wait in silence and you will hear a voice.

vocabulary.definition: to the grave — necromantic operations typically take place at the burial site
night of Saturn — Saturday night; Saturn governs death and the dead
who raises the dead — the invocation uses Christian resurrection doctrine as magical authority
in peaceful form — the request prevents terrifying manifestations
wait in silence — the operative instruction; voices from the dead are subtle

source_notes: This type of grave-necromancy ritual appears in multiple medieval magical manuscripts, typically in collections with other illicit practices. The pattern — Saturday night, circle around the grave, Christian-framed conjuration — represents the standard form of learned necromancy. Unlike classical necromancy (which summoned shades), medieval necromancy typically seeks information, treasure location, or assistance from the recently dead. Source: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997. // Fanger, Claire, ed. Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1998.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997. // Fanger, Claire, ed. Conjuring Spirits. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1998.

title: Pharsalia, VI.507–568 — Erichtho the Necromancer
author: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus
latin_text: Erichtho haec effata silet. Pallensque cadaver erexit in tenebroso lumine et corpus sanguine tinctum circumdat, lunari rore madefacta. Tunc haec verba iacit: 'Tisiphoneque et Megaera vacuas pulsante catervas, Persephone nolens nostrique Hecate conscia vulgi, concutite has umbras et cogite redire.'
english_gloss: When Erichtho had spoken these things she fell silent. And she raised the pale corpse in the dark light and surrounded the blood-stained body with lunar dew, and sprinkled it. Then she uttered these words: 'Tisiphone and Megaera, striking the empty throngs, Persephone who is unwilling and Hecate who knows our band — shake these shades and force them to return.'

vocabulary.definition: the witch of Thessaly in Lucan — archetype of the necromancer in Latin literature
lunar dew — moisture associated with the moon and death; a necromantic reagent
Tisiphone — one of the three Furies (Erinyes), avengers of the dead
Hecate — goddess of crossroads, magic, and the underworld; patron of necromancers
shades, ghosts — the souls of the dead as shadows in the underworld

source_notes: Lucan's Pharsalia (c. 61–65 CE) contains the most extended literary treatment of necromancy in Latin literature — the night-time raising of a dead soldier by the witch Erichtho for the benefit of Sextus Pompey. Lucan's elaborate description of Erichtho's rites (herbal mixtures, invocations of infernal deities, verbal commands to the underworld) became the canonical portrait of the classical necromancer and influenced medieval treatises on necromancy. Source: Lucan. Pharsalia (Civil War). Trans. Susan H. Braund. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992. // Gordon, Richard. 'Imagining Greek and Roman Magic.' In Witchcraft and Magic in Europe, Vol. 2. London: Athlone, 1999.
bibliography: Lucan. Pharsalia. Trans. Susan H. Braund. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992. // Gordon, Richard. 'Imagining Greek and Roman Magic.' In Witchcraft and Magic in Europe, Vol. 2. London: Athlone, 1999.

title: Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), I.8 — Pamphile the Witch
author: Apuleius of Madaura
latin_text: Haec Pamphile artem magicam profitetur: aiunt illam per quaedam carminum potestates lumina superna dimittere in profundum Tartari et corpora iam tradita sepulcro per temporaria rursus damna seniorum reviviscere, ac rursum per haec incantamenta stellas detrahere et fontium cursus inhibere.
english_gloss: This Pamphile professes the magic art: they say that through certain powers of incantations she sends the lights above down into the depths of Tartarus and causes bodies already consigned to the tomb to revive again through temporary setbacks of age, and again through these enchantments to draw down the stars and check the courses of fountains.

vocabulary.definition: professes, practices openly — Pamphile doesn't hide her art; Latin magic could be semi-public
Tartarus — the deepest region of the underworld (Roman equivalent of Hades)
to come back to life again — temporary necromantic revival, not true resurrection
enchantments, spells — from 'incantare' (to sing/chant over), the verbal element of magic
to draw down the stars — the classic claim of the supreme witch; lunar and stellar command

source_notes: Apuleius's Metamorphoses or 'Golden Ass' (c. 158–170 CE) is the only complete Latin novel to survive from antiquity, and its witch Pamphile is one of the most vivid portraits of the ancient sorceress. The capabilities listed — sending heavenly lights to Tartarus, reviving the dead, drawing down stars, stopping springs — represent the full repertoire of witchcraft in the ancient literary imagination. Apuleius himself was prosecuted for magic (and acquitted, as his Apologia demonstrates). Source: Apuleius. The Golden Ass. Trans. P.G. Walsh. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1994. // Dickie, Matthew W. Magic and Magicians in the Greco-Roman World. London: Routledge, 2001.
bibliography: Apuleius. The Golden Ass (Metamorphoses). Trans. P.G. Walsh. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1994. // Dickie, Matthew W. Magic and Magicians in the Greco-Roman World. London: Routledge, 2001.

title: Speculum Necromanticum — The Magic Mirror of Spirits
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Fac speculum de metallo Veneris sub hora Veneris et consacra illud fumigando cum ligno aloes. Tunc puer virginis ante speculum ponas et dic nomina spirituum: videbit puer in speculo quidquid quaesiveris — vel thesauros absconditos vel personas absentes vel futura.
english_gloss: Make a mirror of Venus's metal under the hour of Venus and consecrate it by fumigating with aloe wood. Then place a virgin boy before the mirror and say the names of spirits: the boy will see in the mirror whatever you have asked about — whether hidden treasures, or absent persons, or future things.

vocabulary.definition: metal of Venus — copper; each planet has its associated metal in the seven-metal system
aloe wood — aromatic wood (Aquilaria agallocha), associated with Venus and purification
a virgin boy — children were used as scryers because of their ritual purity and receptivity
mirror — the standard scrying device in necromantic and Solomonic magic

source_notes: The magic mirror (speculum) appears in numerous medieval and Renaissance magical texts as a device for clairvoyance: seeing absent persons, finding treasure, or predicting the future. The use of a virgin boy as scryer reflects the belief that ritual purity (sexual inexperience) made children more receptive to spiritual vision. The technique resembles Islamic and Jewish crystal-gazing practices that entered the Latin West with other magical texts. Source: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997. // Camille, Michael. 'The Image and the Self: Unwriting Late Medieval Bodies.' In Framing Medieval Bodies. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1994.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1997.

title: De Nigromantia (Canon Law Perspective) — What Necromancy Is
author: Anonymous (canonist)
latin_text: Nigromantia est ars vel potius impietas evocandi animas mortuorum per sacrificia vel carmina ad praedicendum futura — et haec ars expresse prohibetur in lege Dei et in iure canonico et exercentes eam tamquam haereticos puniendos esse doctores tradunt.
english_gloss: Necromancy is the art or rather impiety of calling up the souls of the dead through sacrifices or incantations for the purpose of predicting the future — and this art is expressly forbidden in the law of God and in canon law and the doctors hand down that those practicing it are to be punished as heretics.

vocabulary.definition: necromancy — from nekromanteia (divination by the dead); Latin 'nigro-' (black) replaced 'nekro-' (dead) in some manuscripts
impiety — the canonist substitutes a moral-theological term for the neutral 'art'
heretics — the classification that brings necromancers under Inquisitorial jurisdiction
the doctors hand down — citing patristic and scholastic authorities for the prohibition

source_notes: This canonist definition of necromancy reflects the gradual criminalization of the art through canon law. The key legal move is classifying necromancers as heretics — not merely as practitioners of a forbidden art, but as enemies of the faith punishable by the Inquisition. This reclassification happened gradually through 13th–14th century canon law development and made necromancy a capital offense in ecclesiastical courts. Source: Peters, Edward. The Magician, the Witch, and the Law. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1978. // Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.
bibliography: Peters, Edward. The Magician, the Witch, and the Law. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1978. // Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: De Imaginum, Signorum et Idearum Compositione — Memory and Magic
author: Giordano Bruno
latin_text: Imagines non solum ad memoriam sed ad magiam faciunt — nam imago quae cum affectu et intentione formatur recipit virtutem ex spiritu formantis et operatur in animam alterius per similitudinem. Sic magus interior per imagines extrinsecas mundum interiorem movet.
english_gloss: Images serve not only for memory but also for magic — for an image which is formed with feeling and intention receives power from the spirit of the one forming it and operates on the soul of another through similitude. Thus the inner magician moves the inner world through external images.

vocabulary.definition: with feeling and intention — the two subjective requirements that activate the magic image
similitude, likeness — sympathetic magic works through resemblance
the inner magician — Bruno's concept of the imaginative faculty as inherently magical

source_notes: Bruno's De Imaginum Compositione (1591) is the culmination of his art of memory and magic, arguing that mental images can operate magically on the world through the spiritus linking all things. For Bruno, the memory magician and the ritual magician use the same faculty — the imagination — to different ends. This work anticipates modern concepts of mental magic and influenced Dee, Agrippa's posthumous reputation, and the Cambridge Platonists. Source: Yates, Frances A. The Art of Memory. London: Routledge, 1966. // Bruno, Giordano. De Imaginum, Signorum et Idearum Compositione. Frankfurt, 1591.
bibliography: Yates, Frances A. The Art of Memory. London: Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1966. // Ciliberto, Michele. Giordano Bruno: Il teatro della vita. Milan: Mondadori, 2007.

title: Enneads, I.6.1 — On Beauty
author: Plotinus
latin_text: Pulchritudo maxima versatur in his quae visu percipiuntur; est autem aliqua et in his quae non videntur, sed audienda — cantus namque et voces pulchrae. Qui autem ulterius procedunt invenient pulchritudinem in studiis ac moribus ac in scientiarum speciebus. Est et pulchritudo ipsius virtutis. Unde his omnibus maior est pulchritudo quae non cadit sub sensum, sed sub intellectum solum.
english_gloss: Beauty is found chiefly in those things that are perceived by sight; but there is also some beauty in those things that are not seen but heard — for beautiful songs and voices. Those who proceed further find beauty in studies and conduct and in the forms of the sciences. There is also the beauty of virtue itself. Whence greater than all these is the beauty which does not fall under the senses but under intellect alone.

vocabulary.definition: beauty — Plotinus distinguishes sensible from intelligible beauty throughout Enneads I.6
sight, the visual sense — beauty enters first through the eyes
beautiful, fair in appearance (related to species, form)
under intellect — belonging to the intelligible realm, accessible only to the mind
forms of the sciences — the structural beauty of mathematics, philosophy

source_notes: Plotinus's Enneads I.6 'On Beauty' is the founding text of Neoplatonic aesthetics and the source of the Renaissance doctrine of spiritual beauty. Plotinus argues that sensible beauty participates in intelligible Beauty — the Form of Beauty emanating from the One. Ficino translated the Enneads in the 1480s and they became a primary source for Renaissance Platonism. Pico, Ficino, and Bruno all drew directly on this treatise. Source: Plotinus. Enneads. Trans. A.H. Armstrong. 7 vols. Cambridge: Harvard University Press (Loeb), 1966–1988. // Ficino, Marsilio. Opera Omnia. Basel, 1576.
bibliography: Plotinus. Enneads. Trans. A.H. Armstrong. 7 vols. Cambridge: Harvard University Press (Loeb), 1966–1988. // Ficino, Marsilio. Opera Omnia. Basel, 1576. Repr. Turin: Bottega d'Erasmo, 1959.

title: Elementatio Theologica, Props. 1–3 — The First Principles
author: Proclus Diadochus
latin_text: Omnis multitudo participat uno modo. Si enim nullo modo participaret uno, nec totum esset nec partes haberent ad invicem communionem ullam. Principium autem omnium est unum, quod est ante omnem multitudinem, quod nec ipsum est multitudo sed prius multitudine — hoc est principium et causa omnium.
english_gloss: Every multiplicity participates in unity in some way. For if it participated in unity in no way, it would not be a whole nor would its parts have any communion with each other. The principle of all things, however, is the One, which is before all multiplicity, which is not itself a multiplicity but prior to multiplicity — this is the principle and cause of all things.

vocabulary.definition: multiplicity, manifold — the derived realm of many things
participates in the One — Neoplatonic participation: derived things share in their source
before all multiplicity — the One's absolute priority as unconditioned source
communion, shared participation — what unity gives to the multiple

source_notes: Proclus's Elementatio Theologica (Elements of Theology) is a systematic axiomatization of Neoplatonic metaphysics into 211 propositions, translated by William of Moerbeke in 1268. It was the primary source through which Aristotelian and scholastic thinkers encountered rigorous Neoplatonic logic. The Liber de Causis (a medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle) was extracted from it. Ficino, Pico, and Agrippa all drew on the Elements. Source: Proclus. The Elements of Theology. Ed. E.R. Dodds. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1963.
bibliography: Proclus. The Elements of Theology. Ed. and trans. E.R. Dodds. 2nd ed. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1963. // Siorvanes, Lucas. Proclus: Neo-Platonic Philosophy and Science. Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 1996.

title: Liber de Causis, Prop. I — The First Cause and Being
author: Pseudo-Aristotle (after Proclus; trans. Gerard of Cremona, c. 1167)
latin_text: Omnis causa primaria plus est influens super causatum suum quam causa universalis secunda. Cum ergo removet causa universalis secunda virtutem suam a re, causa prima non removet virtutem suam ab ea, quia causa prima est fixior et stabilior in sua virtute. Causa ergo prima antecedit causam secundam.
english_gloss: Every primary cause has more influence over its effect than the universal second cause. When therefore the universal second cause removes its power from a thing, the first cause does not remove its power from it, because the first cause is more fixed and stable in its power. The first cause therefore precedes the second cause.

vocabulary.definition: primary cause — God or the One, the absolute source; always more powerful than intermediate causes
the caused thing, the effect — Arabic-Latin technical term absent from classical Latin
more fixed and more stable — the first cause's unchanging permanence vs. secondary variability
flows in, influences — celestial causation conceived as a fluid influx

source_notes: The Liber de Causis ('Book of Causes') is an Arabic text based on Proclus's Elements of Theology, translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona around 1167. For three centuries it was believed to be Aristotle's work, influencing Albertus Magnus, Aquinas (who first identified it as pseudo-Aristotelian), Ficino, and all Renaissance Neoplatonists. Proposition I's argument — that the First Cause always exceeds all secondary causes — became a cornerstone of both scholastic and Renaissance magical cosmology. Source: Liber de Causis. Ed. Adriaan Pattin. Leuven: Tijdschrift voor Filosofie, 1966.
bibliography: Liber de Causis. Ed. Adriaan Pattin. Leuven: Tijdschrift voor Filosofie, 1966. // Taylor, Richard C. 'The Liber de Causis: A Preliminary List of Extant MSS.' Bulletin de philosophie médiévale 25 (1983).

title: De Docta Ignorantia, I.4 — The Maximum and the Infinite
author: Nicholas of Cusa
latin_text: Maximum autem absolutum unum est, cui nihil opponitur, ultra quod nihil esse potest; hoc est infinitum. In hoc enim infinito coincidit omnis oppositio. Deus igitur est Maximum absolutum et infinitum, cui omnia conveniunt et quod omnia sunt; et qui deum attingere vult, oportet eum super omnem contradictionem elevari.
english_gloss: The absolute maximum, however, is one, to which nothing is opposed, beyond which nothing can exist; this is the infinite. For in this infinite all opposition coincides. God therefore is the absolute Maximum and infinite, to whom all things converge and which all things are; and whoever wishes to reach God must be elevated above all contradiction.

vocabulary.definition: the absolute Maximum — Cusa's term for God as the greatest possible being, unconstrained by opposition
coincides — Cusa's key doctrine: opposites coincide in the infinite God (coincidentia oppositorum)
opposition, contradiction — in the finite world all things have contraries; in God contraries coincide
to be elevated — mystical ascent beyond rational contradiction toward divine simplicity
the infinite — Cusa's God as infinite being, beyond all finite measure

source_notes: Nicholas of Cusa's De Docta Ignorantia ('On Learned Ignorance,' 1440) argues that the highest knowledge is the recognition of our ignorance before the infinite God — the 'learned ignorance' of the title. His key concept of coincidentia oppositorum (the coincidence of opposites in the infinite) deeply influenced Bruno's cosmology (the infinite universe), Ficino's Theologia Platonica, and Agrippa. Cusa also proposed that the Earth moves and that the universe has no fixed center — 150 years before Copernicus. Source: Nicholas of Cusa. De Docta Ignorantia. Trans. Jasper Hopkins. Minneapolis: Banning Press, 1985.
bibliography: Nicholas of Cusa. De Docta Ignorantia. Trans. Jasper Hopkins. Minneapolis: Banning Press, 1985. // Biechler, James E. The Religious Language of Nicholas of Cusa. Missoula: Scholars Press, 1975.

title: Theologia Platonica, XIV.1 — The Soul's Immortality Proven
author: Marsilio Ficino
latin_text: Anima nostra immortalis est — primo quia capax est intelligendi veritas aeterna; secundo quia amat bonum infinitum nec satiatur bono finito; tertio quia ex suo corpore migrat ad similitudinem Dei tendendo. Quicumque autem tendit ad infinitum et aeternum, ipse infinitus et aeternus esse debet.
english_gloss: Our soul is immortal — first because it is capable of understanding eternal truth; second because it loves infinite good and is not satisfied by finite good; third because it migrates from its body tending toward the likeness of God. But whoever tends toward the infinite and eternal must itself be infinite and eternal.

vocabulary.definition: capable of understanding — the soul's capacity for truth is evidence of its divine nature
infinite good — the soul desires more than any finite object can satisfy; only God satisfies
migrates, departs — the soul's natural motion away from the body toward God
likeness of God — the soul's destination in the Platonic-Christian synthesis

source_notes: Ficino's Theologia Platonica (1482) is the most ambitious work of the Florentine Renaissance — a systematic philosophical theology arguing that Platonic philosophy and Christian doctrine agree on the soul's immortality. The triple argument here (capacity for eternal truth, desire for infinite good, migration toward God) became the standard Renaissance proof for immortality. Pico, Reuchlin, and all subsequent Christian Platonists relied on Ficino's synthesis. Source: Ficino, Marsilio. Platonic Theology. Ed. James Hankins. 6 vols. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2001–2006.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Platonic Theology. Ed. James Hankins. Trans. Michael J.B. Allen. 6 vols. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2001–2006. // Kristeller, Paul Oskar. The Philosophy of Marsilio Ficino. New York: Columbia University Press, 1943.

title: De Vita Coelitus Comparanda, I — World-Soul and the Magician's Art
author: Marsilio Ficino
latin_text: Anima mundi et stellarum daemonumque animae facile alliciuntur corporum formis accommodatis. Si tantum haec duo sint in mundo, hinc quidem intellectus, inde vero corpus, sed absit anima, tunc neque intellectus trahetur ad corpus — immobilis enim est omnino caretque affectu — neque corpus trahetur ad intellectum. Verum si interponatur anima utrique conformis, facile utrinque et ad utraque fiet attractus.
english_gloss: The world-soul and the souls of the stars and daemons are easily attracted by bodily forms fitted to them. If in the world there were only these two things — intellect on one side and body on the other — but the soul were absent, then intellect would not be drawn to body, for it is entirely motionless and without feeling — nor would body be drawn to intellect. But if a soul conformable to both is placed between them, attraction toward both easily occurs from both sides.

vocabulary.definition: are attracted, lured — the key term for celestial magic: the right material 'lures' divine power
fitted forms — materials that correspond to a star's nature attract its daemonic power
is placed between — the soul's mediating role as the middle term in magical causation
attraction, drawing power — Ficino's name for the mechanism of sympathetic magic
souls of daemons — intermediate spirits attached to stars that transmit celestial power

source_notes: This is the opening argument of De Vita Coelitus Comparanda Book III — the theoretical foundation of Ficino's astrological magic. By positing that the World-Soul mediates between pure Intellect and gross Body, Ficino explains how ritual magic works: the right material ('accommodated form') attracts daemonic soul-powers that channel stellar influence. This passage is from the critical Kaske-Clark edition, which shows the Latin text directly from the Ficino manuscript tradition. Source: Ficino, Marsilio. Three Books on Life. Ed. and trans. Carol V. Kaske and John R. Clark. Binghamton: MRTS, 1989.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Three Books on Life. Ed. and trans. Carol V. Kaske and John R. Clark. Binghamton: MRTS, 1989. // Walker, D.P. Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella. London: Warburg Institute, 1958.

title: Ars Magna, Pars I — The Combinatory Art
author: Ramon Llull
latin_text: In hac arte figurae rotantes continent omnia principia: B significat Bonitatem, C Magnitudinem, D Aeternitatem, E Potestatem, F Sapientiam — et per combinationem harum litterarum omnes propositiones de Deo et creaturis demonstrari possunt sine errore.
english_gloss: In this art the rotating figures contain all principles: B signifies Goodness, C Greatness, D Eternity, E Power, F Wisdom — and through the combination of these letters all propositions about God and creatures can be demonstrated without error.

vocabulary.definition: rotating figures — concentric paper wheels encoding Llull's combinatory system
combination — the mechanical generation of all possible propositions from a finite set
principles — the divine attributes (Goodness, Greatness, etc.) encoded as letters
can be demonstrated — Llull claims his art yields necessary demonstrations of theological truth

source_notes: Ramon Llull's Ars Magna (1305) proposes a combinatory system for generating all possible true propositions about God and the world by mechanically combining divine attributes encoded as letters on rotating paper wheels. The system was intended as a universal apologetics tool for converting Muslims and Jews. Bruno was fascinated by the Ars Magna and used it as the basis for his own combinatory memory art. Agrippa criticized it; Leibniz later credited Llull as a forerunner of symbolic logic. Source: Llull, Ramon. Opera Omnia. Ed. Ivo Salzinger. 8 vols. Mainz, 1721–1742.
bibliography: Bonner, Anthony. The Art and Logic of Ramon Llull: A User's Guide. Leiden: Brill, 2007. // Yates, Frances A. 'Ramon Lull and John Scotus Erigena.' Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 23 (1960): 1–44.

title: Monas Hieroglyphica, Theorema I — The Point and the Line
author: John Dee
latin_text: Primo et summo, punctum monadicum considerandum est. Ex puncto et linea fit circulus — sol enim in figura monadis per circulum exprimitur. Deinde linea recta, quae per centrum transit, solem a luna distinguit. Aries autem, qui in capite monadis apparet, zodiacum signum est in quo sol per exaltationem regnat. Haec monas omnia in seipsa continet et per omnia tendit.
english_gloss: First and foremost, the monadic point is to be considered. From a point and a line a circle is made — for the Sun in the figure of the Monad is expressed through the circle. Then the straight line, which passes through the center, distinguishes the Sun from the Moon. Aries, moreover, which appears at the head of the Monad, is the zodiac sign in which the Sun reigns through its exaltation. This Monad contains all things in itself and extends through all things.

vocabulary.definition: the monadic point — the mathematical point as the origin of all geometric and cosmological construction
the Monad — Dee's composite hieroglyphic symbol uniting Sun, Moon, cross, and Aries in one sign
exaltation — the zodiac sign where a planet's power is greatest; Sun exalted in Aries
extends through all things — the Monad's universal scope as a symbol of cosmic unity
distinguishes, separates — the cross-line that differentiates solar from lunar aspects

source_notes: John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564) is one of the most obscure and densely symbolic works of the Renaissance, presenting a single composite hieroglyphic sign that Dee claims encodes all mathematical, astronomical, alchemical, and magical knowledge. Written in thirteen days in Antwerp, it was presented to Emperor Maximilian II. The Monad integrates the astronomical symbols for Sun (circle), Moon (crescent), elements (cross), and Aries (fire sign) into a single figure that Dee treats as a key to nature. Source: Dee, John. The Hieroglyphic Monad. Trans. J.W. Hamilton-Jones. London: Watkins, 1947. // Josten, C.H. 'A Translation of John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica.' Ambix 12 (1964): 83–221.
bibliography: Josten, C.H. 'A Translation of John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica.' Ambix 12 (1964): 83–221. // Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999.

title: De Vanitate Scientiarum, §42 — On the Uncertainty of Magic
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
latin_text: Magia quam philosophi naturalis operatrices vocant — haec prima de qua loquimur et laudabilis — iam tanto errorum labyrintho involuta est et tam multis mendaciis maculata, ut nihil in ea verum, nihil certum, nihil non periculosum relinquatur. Sapientior ergo qui nihil scit.
english_gloss: Magic which philosophers call the operator of natural philosophy — this first kind about which we speak and which is laudable — has now been enveloped in so great a labyrinth of errors and stained with so many lies, that nothing true, nothing certain, nothing not dangerous remains in it. More wise therefore is he who knows nothing.

vocabulary.definition: operator, practitioner (feminine form) — Agrippa's praise-term for legitimate natural magic
labyrinth of errors — the maze of corruption that has overtaken what was once noble
stained, defiled — moral pollution imagery for magic's corruption
'More wise is he who knows nothing' — Agrippa's paradox, echoing Socratic ignorance and Cusa's docta ignorantia

source_notes: De Vanitate Scientiarum ('On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences,' 1530) appeared one year before Agrippa published De Occulta Philosophia, creating an apparent paradox: he published both a comprehensive magical encyclopedia and its apparent recantation nearly simultaneously. The relationship between the two works has been endlessly debated — was De Vanitate sincere, satirical, or political cover? The closing 'sapientior qui nihil scit' echoes Cusa's docta ignorantia. Source: Agrippa, Heinrich Cornelius. De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum. Cologne, 1527. Ed. Fumaroli, Marc. Paris, 1981.
bibliography: Nauert, Charles G. Agrippa and the Crisis of Renaissance Thought. Urbana: University of Illinois Press, 1965. // Bowen, Barbara C. 'Cornelius Agrippa's De Vanitate: Polemic or Paradox?' Bibliothèque d'Humanisme et Renaissance 34 (1972).

title: Heptaplus, Proem — The Seven Worlds of Moses
author: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
latin_text: Septem mundos intellexit Moses sub sex diebus creationis, et hi sunt: mundus angelicus, mundus caelestis, mundus sublunaris, mundus hominis, mundus temporis, mundus verbi, mundus legis — et omnes hi connectuntur vinculo unitatis quae in Deo est.
english_gloss: Moses understood seven worlds under the six days of creation, and these are: the angelic world, the celestial world, the sublunar world, the world of man, the world of time, the world of the word, the world of the law — and all these are connected by the bond of unity which is in God.

vocabulary.definition: seven worlds — Pico's heptapartite scheme applied to the six days of Genesis
bond of unity — God as the unifying link connecting all the levels of creation
world of man — the human being as a micro-cosmos summing all seven worlds within itself
the Word — the divine Logos as a cosmic level, combining Johannine and Kabbalistic theologies

source_notes: Pico's Heptaplus (1489) applies the Kabbalistic doctrine of four worlds (Azilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, Assiyah) and Christian angelology to the six days of Genesis, arguing that each day describes the same creative act on seven different ontological levels simultaneously. The hermeneutical method — multiple simultaneous levels of meaning — is directly derived from the Kabbalistic pardes (PaRDeS: literal, allegorical, allusive, mystical). Source: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Heptaplus. Trans. Douglas Carmichael. Indianapolis: Bobbs-Merrill, 1965.
bibliography: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Heptaplus. Trans. Douglas Carmichael. Indianapolis: Bobbs-Merrill, 1965. // Wirszubski, Chaim. Pico della Mirandola's Encounter with Jewish Mysticism. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1989.

title: De Arte Cabalistica, I — Pythagoras and Kabbalist Agree
author: Johannes Reuchlin
latin_text: Simon dixit: 'Pythagorici et Cabalistae eadem fere docent — ambo enim dicunt numerum esse principium omnium et ambo per numeros ad divinam sapientiam ascendere volunt. Sed Pythagorici numeros rerum causas esse ponunt; Cabalistae vero literas Hebraicas, quae idem sunt ac numeri, esse principia creationis per quae Deus mundum fecit.'
english_gloss: Simon said: 'Pythagoreans and Kabbalists teach nearly the same things — for both say that number is the principle of all things and both wish to ascend to divine wisdom through numbers. But Pythagoreans hold that numbers are the causes of things; the Kabbalists indeed hold that Hebrew letters, which are the same as numbers, are the principles of creation through which God made the world.'

vocabulary.definition: Pythagoreans and Kabbalists — Reuchlin's central thesis: these two wisdom traditions agree on number-mysticism
principle of all things — number as the ontological foundation (Pythagorean thesis)
Hebrew letters — in Kabbalah, each of the 22 letters is both a number and a cosmic principle
wish to ascend — the anagogic purpose of both traditions: numerical contemplation leads to God

source_notes: Reuchlin's De Arte Cabalistica (1517) is presented as a dialogue between the Pythagorean Philolaus, a Muslim scholar Marranus, and the Kabbalist Simon, each bringing different mystical traditions into conversation. Reuchlin argues that Pythagorean number-mysticism and Jewish Kabbalah are fundamentally the same wisdom tradition — both use mathematical structure to ascend to God. This work was the mature statement of Christian Kabbalism and directly influenced Agrippa's Book II (Celestial Magic). Source: Reuchlin, Johannes. De Arte Cabalistica. Trans. Martin and Sarah Goodman. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1983.
bibliography: Reuchlin, Johannes. De Arte Cabalistica. Trans. Martin and Sarah Goodman. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1983. // Secret, François. Les Kabbalistes chrétiens de la Renaissance. Paris: Dunod, 1964.

title: Aurora, Prooemium — The Dark Ground of God
author: Jacob Boehme
latin_text: Ante omnem lucem est Ungrund — abyssus infinita, voluntas sine fundamento quae non est Deus sed terra Dei, matrix prima ex qua Deus procedit. Ex hac obscuritate et silentio oritur Verbum primum quod est Lux prima, et ex Luce prima fit Mundus.
english_gloss: Before all light is the Ungrund — the infinite abyss, the will without foundation which is not God but the ground of God, the primal matrix from which God proceeds. From this darkness and silence arises the first Word which is the first Light, and from the first Light the World is made.

vocabulary.definition: the Unground — Boehme's term for the primordial abyss/void before even God's self-manifestation; German 'ohne Grund' (without ground)
infinite abyss — the Latin rendering of the Ungrund, drawing on Neoplatonic and Kabbalistic abyss-imagery
will without foundation — the pre-cosmic Will that precedes even divine being
primal matrix, womb — the creative void from which God's self-revelation proceeds
the first Word — the Logos/Verbum emerging from divine darkness as the first act of creation

source_notes: Jacob Boehme's Aurora (1612) is the first and most visionary of his works, describing God's self-manifestation from the dark 'Unground' (Ungrund) — the abyss that precedes even God's being. The Latin reception came through English Behmenists like John Sparrow and Dutch-Latin translators, influencing the Cambridge Platonists (Henry More, Ralph Cudworth), Leibniz, Hegel, and Schelling. Boehme's theosophy was the final major current feeding into Western esoteric tradition. Source: Boehme, Jacob. Aurora. Trans. John Sparrow. London: John Streater, 1656. // Weeks, Andrew. Boehme: An Intellectual Biography. Albany: SUNY Press, 1991.
bibliography: Boehme, Jacob. Aurora. Trans. John Sparrow. London, 1656. // Weeks, Andrew. Boehme: An Intellectual Biography. Albany: SUNY Press, 1991.

title: Oedipus Aegyptiacus, II.2 — The Hermetic Wisdom of Egypt
author: Athanasius Kircher, S.J.
latin_text: Aegyptii per hieroglyphica non vocabula rerum notabant sed rerum essentias et proprietates occultas — ita ut Mercurius Trismegistus, Pythagoras, Plato, et omnes antiquitatis sapientes ex hac Aegyptia philosophia biberint, et tota philosophia Graeca nihil aliud sit quam Aegyptiaca translata.
english_gloss: The Egyptians through hieroglyphics were noting not the words of things but the hidden essences and properties of things — so that Hermes Trismegistus, Pythagoras, Plato, and all the wise men of antiquity drank from this Egyptian philosophy, and all Greek philosophy is nothing other than Egyptian philosophy translated.

vocabulary.definition: hieroglyphics — sacred carvings; Kircher believed they encoded esoteric wisdom (his translations were mostly wrong)
hidden essences — Kircher's thesis: hieroglyphs directly encode natural occult properties
drank (from) — the image of wisdom as a spring or river flowing from Egypt to Greece
translated, transferred — Greek philosophy as Egyptian wisdom in new linguistic clothing

source_notes: Athanasius Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus (1652–1654) is the most ambitious and most spectacularly wrong work of 17th-century Hermeticism — Kircher's 'translation' of hieroglyphics, which proved to be almost entirely invented. Yet his work was enormously influential, synthesizing Hermetic philosophy, Kabbalah, Neoplatonism, and Egyptology into a grand unified system. The 'Egyptian origin' thesis — that all wisdom came from Egypt — was a founding myth of the prisca theologia tradition. Source: Kircher, Athanasius. Oedipus Aegyptiacus. 4 vols. Rome: Vitalis Mascardi, 1652–1654. // Godwin, Joscelyn. Athanasius Kircher: A Renaissance Man and the Quest for Lost Knowledge. London: Thames and Hudson, 1979.
bibliography: Godwin, Joscelyn. Athanasius Kircher: A Renaissance Man and the Quest for Lost Knowledge. London: Thames and Hudson, 1979. // Findlen, Paula, ed. Athanasius Kircher: The Last Man Who Knew Everything. New York: Routledge, 2004.

title: Utriusque Cosmi Historia, I.3 — The Great and Small Worlds
author: Robert Fludd
latin_text: Homo est minor mundus: habet enim in se caelum et terram, ignem et aquam, angelos et daemones — totius mundi imaginem. Mundus autem maior est homo expansus: sicut homo habet animam et corpus, sic mundus habet animam mundi et corpus mundi; sicut homo spirat, sic mundus spirat per ventos et tonitrua.
english_gloss: Man is a small world: for he has in himself heaven and earth, fire and water, angels and demons — the image of the whole world. The greater world, however, is an expanded man: just as man has soul and body, so the world has world-soul and world-body; just as man breathes, so the world breathes through winds and thunders.

vocabulary.definition: small world — the microcosm; man as a compressed image of the whole cosmos
an expanded man — the macrocosm as man extended to cosmic scale (reciprocal definition)
world-soul — the Neoplatonic/Hermetic cosmic soul animating the universe
breathes through winds — the world's breath as cosmic respiration, analogous to human respiration

source_notes: Robert Fludd's Utriusque Cosmi Historia (History of the Two Worlds, 1617–1621) presents the most visually spectacular synthesis of Renaissance Hermetic philosophy — illustrated with extraordinary engravings mapping the macrocosm-microcosm correspondence. Fludd's debt to Ficino, Pico, and Paracelsus is explicit; his visualizations of the World Monochord, the divine proportions, and the cosmic architecture became canonical images of the Hermetic worldview. Source: Fludd, Robert. Utriusque Cosmi Maioris scilicet et Minoris Metaphysica. Oppenheim: de Bry, 1617. // Godwin, Joscelyn. Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher. London: Thames and Hudson, 1979.
bibliography: Godwin, Joscelyn. Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher and Surveyor of Two Worlds. London: Thames and Hudson, 1979. // Huffman, William H. Robert Fludd and the End of the Renaissance. London: Routledge, 1988.

title: Sefer Yetzirah — Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom (Latin Reception)
author: Anonymous (attributed to Abraham); Latin: Pico / Reuchlin tradition
latin_text: Per triginta duas semitas sapientiae mirabiles sculpsit Deus, Deus Israelis, Deus vivens et Rex seculi — sculpsit per tres formas: scriptura et numerus et narratio. Viginti duae literae fundamentales sunt et decem sunt Sephirot Belimah.
english_gloss: By thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom God engraved — God, God of Israel, living God and King of the world — He engraved by three forms: script and number and narrative. Twenty-two are the fundamental letters and ten are the Sefirot Belimah.

vocabulary.definition: thirty-two paths — 22 Hebrew letters + 10 Sefirot = 32 paths of creation
engraved, carved — God's creation as inscription/engraving in the fabric of reality
Sefirot of nothingness — the ten divine emanations, 'Belimah' meaning 'without what' (ineffable)
script, number, and narrative — the three domains through which God creates (later: Sefer, Sippur, Sephirah)

source_notes: The Sefer Yetzirah ('Book of Formation,' c. 3rd–6th century CE) is the earliest extant Jewish mystical-cosmological text, describing creation through the 32 paths (22 Hebrew letters + 10 Sefirot). Its Latin reception came through Pico's Kabbalistic theses and Reuchlin's De Arte Cabalistica. The system of 22 letters as cosmic principles became fundamental to all subsequent Kabbalah and Christian Kabbalism. Source: Sefer Yetzirah. Trans. Aryeh Kaplan. York Beach: Weiser Books, 1990. // Scholem, Gershom. On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism. New York: Schocken, 1965.
bibliography: Sefer Yetzirah. Trans. Aryeh Kaplan. York Beach: Weiser Books, 1990. // Scholem, Gershom. On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism. New York: Schocken, 1965.

title: Eros and Magic: The Interiorization of Magic
author: Ioan Petru Couliano (Culianu)
latin_text: Magia amoris est ars qua magus per phantasiam et imagines desideria hominum movet et regit — nam spiritus per oculos intrat et in memoria haeret et voluntatem trahit quasi catena invisibili. Ficinus hoc bene novit quando de vita caelesti scripsit.
english_gloss: Love magic is the art by which the magician through imagination and images moves and governs the desires of people — for the spirit enters through the eyes and clings in the memory and draws the will as if by an invisible chain. Ficino knew this well when he wrote about celestial life.

vocabulary.definition: love magic — Couliano's central thesis: Renaissance magic is primarily a technology of desire
imagination and images — the psychological mechanism underlying all magical efficacy
invisible chain — the spiritus-chain binding the fascinated person to the magician's will
clings in the memory — Couliano's point: effective magic lodges itself in the memory/imagination

source_notes: Ioan Petru Couliano's Eros and Magic in the Renaissance (French 1984, English 1987) argues that Renaissance magic was fundamentally a technology of desire and persuasion operating through the imagination and spirit — and that modern advertising and propaganda are its secular successors. Couliano died under mysterious circumstances in 1991, shortly after writing political commentary. His book remains a major reinterpretation of Renaissance magic alongside Yates. Source: Couliano, Ioan P. Eros and Magic in the Renaissance. Trans. Margaret Cook. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1987.
bibliography: Couliano, Ioan P. Eros and Magic in the Renaissance. Trans. Margaret Cook. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1987. // Marius, Richard. 'Review of Eros and Magic.' Journal of the History of Ideas 50 (1989).

title: Tabula Smaragdina — The Emerald Tablet
author: Hermes Trismegistus (attr.)
latin_text: Verum, sine mendacio, certum et verissimum: Quod est inferius est sicut quod est superius, et quod est superius est sicut quod est inferius, ad perpetranda miracula rei unius. Et sicut res omnes fuerunt ab uno, meditatione unius, sic omnes res natae ab hac una re adaptatione. Pater eius est sol. Mater eius est luna. Portavit illud ventus in ventre suo. Nutrix eius terra est. Pater omnis telesmi totius mundi est hic. Vis eius integra est si versa fuerit in terram.
english_gloss: True, without falsehood, certain and most true: That which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing. And as all things were from one, by the mediation of one, so all things born from this one thing by adaptation. Its father is the sun. Its mother is the moon. The wind carried it in its belly. The earth is its nurse. The father of all perfection of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if turned toward earth.

vocabulary.english: that which is below, the lower realm
vocabulary.notes: Key term for the as above, so below correspondence

vocabulary.english: that which is above, the higher realm
vocabulary.notes: The celestial counterpart to the terrestrial

vocabulary.english: perfection, completion (from Greek teleiosis)
vocabulary.notes: The goal of alchemical and hermetic work

vocabulary.english: by adaptation, through fitting/application
vocabulary.notes: The Neoplatonic descent of unity into multiplicity

vocabulary.english: by the meditation/contemplation of
vocabulary.notes: Cognitive-cosmological act unifying the one and the many

source_notes: The Tabula Smaragdina is the foundational text of Western alchemy and hermeticism. The earliest Latin version appears in the Liber de compositione alchimiae (c. 1140, tr. Robert of Chester). The text was quoted and commented by Albertus Magnus, Roger Bacon, and became the cornerstone of Paracelsian medicine. Its formula 'as above, so below' encapsulates the hermetic doctrine of universal correspondence.
bibliography: Ruska, Julius. Tabula Smaragdina: Ein Beitrag zur Geschichte der hermetischen Literatur. Heidelberg: Winter, 1926.
Holmyard, E.J. Alchemy. Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1957.

title: Timaeus — On the World Soul (Anima Mundi)
author: Plato (tr. Calcidius)
latin_text: Deus itaque, quantum ex ea parte qua bonum est, nihil invidum in sese habens, omnia sibi quam simillima esse voluit. Hanc igitur causam esse principalemque rationem a prudentibus viris referendam mundi fabricationis, dum ex instinctu bonitatis deus optime fabricare noluit. Intuens igitur deus in id omne quod motum haberet nec quieti obnoxium esset, confusumque passim et inordinate agitaretur, ex inordinatione in ordinem adduxit, melius putans ordinatum inordinato.
english_gloss: God therefore, inasmuch as he has no envy in himself from the side of goodness, wished all things to be as similar to himself as possible. This therefore is the primary cause and chief reason, to be cited by wise men, for the fashioning of the world — that God, from the impulse of his goodness, willed to fashion all things in the best way. Looking therefore upon all that which had motion and was not subject to rest, agitated everywhere confusedly and without order, he led it from disorder into order, thinking ordered better than disordered.

vocabulary.english: world soul
vocabulary.notes: Timaeus 34b–37c; the soul Demiurge infuses into the cosmos

vocabulary.english: fashioning, construction (as of a craftsman)
vocabulary.notes: Plato's Demiurge as cosmic artisan

vocabulary.english: disorder, the primal chaos before cosmic order
vocabulary.notes: Contrast with ordo — the Platonic cosmos emerges from bringing order to disorder

vocabulary.english: envious, grudging
vocabulary.notes: Plato's rejection of divine envy as the cosmogonic motive

vocabulary.english: most similar, as like as possible
vocabulary.notes: The Neoplatonic doctrine of assimilation (homoiosis) to the divine

source_notes: Calcidius's fourth-century Latin translation of the Timaeus (with commentary) was the primary Platonic text available to medieval Western scholars. It transmitted the Demiurge, world soul, and four elements doctrines that structured natural philosophy, cosmology, and the doctrine of correspondences through the Renaissance. Ficino, Pico, and the Florentine Platonists worked from this text.
bibliography: Plato. Timaeus. Trans. Calcidius. Ed. J. H. Waszink. London: Warburg Institute, 1975.
Gersh, Stephen. Middle Platonism and Neoplatonism: The Latin Tradition. 2 vols. Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press, 1986.

title: Oratio de Hominis Dignitate — The Dignity of Man
author: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
latin_text: Legi, Patres colendissimi, in Arabum monumentis, interrogatum esse Abdalam Sarracenum, quid in hac quasi mundana scaena admirandum maxime spectaretur, nihil spectari homine admirabilius respondisse. Cui sententiae illud Mercurii adstipulatur: 'Magnum, o Asclepi, miraculum est homo.' Harum sententiarum causam cogitanti mihi, non satis faciebant ea quae afferuntur a multis de hominis praestantia: esse hominem creaturarum internuntium, superis familiarem, regem inferiorum, sensuum perspicacitate, rationis indagine, intelligentiae lumine, naturae interpretem, stabilis aevi et fluxae temporis interstitium, et, quod Persae dicunt, mundi copulam, immo hymeneum ab angelis, teste Davide, paullo imminutum.
english_gloss: I have read, most reverend fathers, in the records of the Arabs that Abdala the Saracen, when asked what thing on this worldly stage seemed most worthy of wonder, replied that nothing seemed more wonderful than man. This verdict is confirmed by the saying of Hermes: 'A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man.' Thinking over the reasons for these sayings, I was not satisfied by the many arguments put forward for man's excellence: that he is the intermediary between creatures, intimate with the higher beings, king of the lower, by keenness of sense, by the discernment of reason, by the light of intelligence, interpreter of nature, fixed interval between the flowing time and the stable eternity, and, as the Persians say, the bond of the world, its marriage knot — little lower than the angels, in David's testimony.

vocabulary.english: intermediary, go-between
vocabulary.notes: Man as mediator between heaven and earth — the Hermetic-Neoplatonic doctrine

vocabulary.english: bond, link, fastening
vocabulary.notes: The technical term for man's function as cosmic connector in Pico's thought

vocabulary.english: marriage bond, the knot of union
vocabulary.notes: Pico's striking metaphor for man as the marriage of the divine and material

vocabulary.english: excellence, preeminence, superiority
vocabulary.notes: Central term in the Renaissance dignity-of-man discourse

vocabulary.english: tracking, investigation, searching out
vocabulary.notes: The verb indagare — to track, search — metaphor for reason as hunter

source_notes: The Oratio (c. 1486) was Pico's proposed introduction to the 900 Theses debate, never delivered as planned when Pope Innocent VIII suspended it. It synthesizes Hermeticism ('great miracle is man,' from Asclepius), Neoplatonism, Kabbalah, and Scholasticism into the Renaissance ideal of human self-determination. Burkhardt cited it as the manifesto of Renaissance individualism, though modern scholars (Borghesi, Copenhaver) caution against anachronistic readings.
bibliography: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Oration on the Dignity of Man. Trans. A. Robert Caponigri. Chicago: Regnery, 1956.
Copenhaver, Brian P. Magic and the Dignity of Man: Pico della Mirandola and His Oration in Modern Memory. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2019.

title: Conclusiones Nongentae — On Natural Magic
author: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
latin_text: Magia naturalis nihil aliud est quam absoluta consummatio philosophiae naturalis. Nihil est in caelo et terra quod non possit per philosophiam naturalem cogi atque comprehendi. Nulla est scientia quae nos magis certificet de divinitate Christi quam magia et cabala.
english_gloss: Natural magic is nothing other than the absolute consummation of natural philosophy. There is nothing in heaven and earth that cannot be compelled and comprehended through natural philosophy. No science certifies us more fully of the divinity of Christ than magic and Kabbalah.

vocabulary.english: natural magic
vocabulary.notes: Pico's distinction: natural magic (legitimate) vs. demonic magic (condemned)

vocabulary.english: completion, perfection, culmination
vocabulary.notes: Magic as the apex of natural philosophy, not its rejection

vocabulary.english: Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition
vocabulary.notes: Pico's Christian Kabbalah synthesis — unique in 15th-century Latin scholarship

source_notes: These theses from Pico's 900 Conclusions (1486) defined natural magic as legitimate scientia and sparked the papal condemnation. Thesis 9.1 ('natural magic is the consummation of natural philosophy') became the standard defense of learned magic through the 16th century.
bibliography: Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni. Conclusiones Nongentae. Ed. Albano Biondi. Florence: Olschki, 1995.

title: A True and Faithful Relation — The First Call
author: John Dee
work: A True and Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Years Between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits
latin_text: Madimi dixit: Ecce ego venio. Respice Angelos tuos, nam gubernatores rerum humanarum sunt, et tu eorum instrumentum es. Da gloriam Deo et non tibi ipsi. Noli timere. Fortitudo Dei est in te. Fac quod facis. In nomine Altissimi.
english_gloss: Madimi said: Behold, I come. Look to your angels, for they are the governors of human affairs, and you are their instrument. Give glory to God and not to yourself. Fear not. The strength of God is in you. Do what you do. In the name of the Most High.

vocabulary.english: Madimi, the child-spirit or angel who appeared to Dee and Kelley
vocabulary.notes: One of the principal spirits in the Dee-Kelley sessions

vocabulary.english: governors, rulers, those who steer
vocabulary.notes: Angels as cosmic administrators — a standard Neoplatonic-Enochian doctrine

vocabulary.english: instrument, tool
vocabulary.notes: Dee as passive vehicle for angelic will — a recurrent theme in the diaries

source_notes: A True and Faithful Relation (published posthumously by Meric Casaubon, 1659) records Dee's scrying sessions with Edward Kelley from 1582–1587. The text is problematic as a source — Casaubon selected and framed the material to discredit Dee.
