Deborah Harkness's John Dee's Conversations with Angels (1999) provides the modern scholarly reassessment.
bibliography: Dee, John. A True and Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Years Between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits. Ed. Meric Casaubon. London, 1659.
Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999.

title: Pimander — Vision of the Primal Light
author: Hermes Trismegistus (attr.)
latin_text: Et vidi lumen ingens candidissimum, quod mihi valde gratum erat. Et post pusillum tenebras ex parte contraria descendere video, in infernum vergentes, et obliquas, undulatas, tortasque, ut serpentem. Postea tenebras mutari video in quandam naturam humidam, ineffabiliter agitatam ac fumum emittentem, quasi ex igne. Erat autem vox quaedam indistincta de luce emissa, quam vocem Pimandri spiritum esse credidi.
english_gloss: And I saw a boundless light, most white and bright, which was very pleasant to me. And after a short time I see darkness descend from the opposite direction, verging downward into the deep, oblique, undulating, and twisted, like a serpent. Then I see the darkness change into a certain moist nature, indescribably agitated and emitting smoke, as from fire. But there was a certain indistinct voice emitted from the light, which voice I believed to be the spirit of Pimander.

vocabulary.english: Pimander, the divine Mind (Nous) who reveals cosmic truth to Hermes
vocabulary.notes: From Coptic p-eime-nte-re, 'the knowledge of Ra'; or Greek poimen, 'shepherd'

vocabulary.english: moist nature, the watery primal matter
vocabulary.notes: The dark, moist, serpentine matter is identified with hyle in Neoplatonic cosmogony

vocabulary.english: a vast most-brilliant light
vocabulary.notes: The primal divine light — the hermetic equivalent of the Neoplatonic One

vocabulary.english: indistinct voice, wordless sound from the divine light
vocabulary.notes: The logos before articulation — cf. John 1:1

source_notes: Pimander (CH I) is the programmatic vision-text of the Corpus Hermeticum, transmitted in Ficino's 1471 Latin translation. The vision of light and dark, the serpentine matter, and the voice of divine Mind established the hermetic cosmogony distinct from Genesis — though Renaissance readers often harmonized the two.
bibliography: Hermes Trismegistus. Pimander. Trans. Marsilio Ficino. Florence, 1471.
Copenhaver, Brian P., trans. Hermetica: The Greek Corpus Hermeticum and the Latin Asclepius. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1992.

title: De la Causa, Principio et Uno — The Infinite Cause
author: Giordano Bruno
work: De la Causa, Principio et Uno
latin_text: Causa efficiens universalis est ille intellectus universalis, qui est prima et principale facultas animae mundi. Materia prima in rebus naturalibus est illa quae neque forma est neque privatio, sed subiectum et fundamentum commune, quo omnia corpora naturalia subnixa sunt. Unum infinitum est, in quo omnia sunt, ex quo omnia sunt.
english_gloss: The universal efficient cause is that universal intellect which is the first and principal faculty of the world soul. Prime matter in natural things is that which is neither form nor privation, but the common subject and foundation upon which all natural bodies rest. The one infinite is that in which all things are, from which all things are.

vocabulary.english: universal efficient cause (the active cosmic principle)
vocabulary.notes: Bruno's term for the divine intellect animating the cosmos

vocabulary.english: universal intellect
vocabulary.notes: The Aristotelian-Neoplatonic nous translated into Bruno's infinite universe

vocabulary.english: world soul
vocabulary.notes: The soul infusing all matter with life and intelligibility

vocabulary.english: prime matter, the formless substratum
vocabulary.notes: Bruno reverses the Aristotelian hierarchy: matter is primary, form secondary

vocabulary.english: the one infinite
vocabulary.notes: Bruno's radical monotheism: God = the infinite cosmos, not a creator outside it

source_notes: De la Causa (1584, written in Italian but building on Latin Scholastic vocabulary) is Bruno's most systematic philosophical work. His arguments for an infinite universe and the identification of matter with the divine principle brought him before the Inquisition. Unlike Ficino's hierarchical Neoplatonism, Bruno collapses the Great Chain: matter and spirit are ultimately one substance.
bibliography: Bruno, Giordano. De la Causa, Principio et Uno. Ed. and trans. Richard J. Blackwell and Robert de Lucca. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
Gatti, Hilary. Giordano Bruno: Philosopher of the Renaissance. Aldershot: Ashgate, 2002.

title: Sefer Yetzirah — The Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom
author: Anon. (attrib. Abraham or Adam)
latin_text: In triginta duabus semitis sapientiae mirabilis sculpsit Iah Dominus exercituum, Deus Israel, Deus vivens et rex mundi, El Shaddai, misericors et clemens, excelsus et sublimis, habitans aeternitate, excelsum et sanctum nomen eius, creando mundum suum in tribus libris: in scriptione et numero et narratione.
english_gloss: In thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom did Yah, the Lord of Hosts, God of Israel, living God and King of the World, El Shaddai, merciful and gracious, high and exalted, dwelling in eternity, and whose Name is holy and exalted — engrave his world through three modes: through text (sepher), number (sephar), and communication (sippur).

vocabulary.english: paths of wisdom (from Hebrew netivot chokhmah)
vocabulary.notes: The 32 = 22 Hebrew letters + 10 sefirot; the structural grammar of creation

vocabulary.english: engraved, carved out
vocabulary.notes: Haqaq — the divine 'engraving' is ontological, not merely linguistic

vocabulary.english: in three books (sepher, sephar, sippur)
vocabulary.notes: The famous triple pun: text, number, speech — three modes of divine creative articulation

vocabulary.english: Yah, the abbreviated divine name
vocabulary.notes: Yah (Jah) — the contracted form of YHWH, used in Sefer Yetzirah's opening formula

vocabulary.english: narrative, speech, communication
vocabulary.notes: Sippur — often understood as 'story' but here the divine communicative act

source_notes: Sefer Yetzirah (Book of Formation, possibly 3rd–6th century CE) was the foundational text of Jewish Kabbalah. Its Latin versions circulated in the Renaissance through Pico della Mirandola's Kabbalist collaborators (Johanan Alemanno, Mithridates) and Johannes Reuchlin's De Arte Cabalistica. The 32 paths = 22 Hebrew letters + 10 sefirot became the structural grammar of Christian Kabbalah.
bibliography: Sefer Yetzirah. Trans. Aryeh Kaplan. York Beach: Samuel Weiser, 1990.
Idel, Moshe. Kabbalah: New Perspectives. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1988.

title: De Radiis Stellarum — The Theory of Rays
author: Al-Kindi (Alkindus)
latin_text: Omnia quae in hoc mundo sensibili fiunt, velut quidam nexus et ligamen universalis, efficiuntur per harmoniam et concordiam siderum. Stellae enim per radios suos et impressiones in elementis inferioribus effectus varios producunt. Verba igitur et voces habent vim operativam in rerum natura per communicationem cum radiis stellarum.
english_gloss: All things that come about in this sensible world are accomplished, as if by a universal bond and link, through the harmony and concord of the stars. For the stars through their rays and impressions produce various effects in the lower elements. Words and sounds therefore have operative power in the nature of things through their communication with the rays of the stars.

vocabulary.english: rays of the stars, stellar emanations
vocabulary.notes: Al-Kindi's central concept: stars act on lower matter through invisible ray-like forces

vocabulary.english: universal bond/connection
vocabulary.notes: The cosmic sympathy binding all levels of the universe through stellar influence

vocabulary.english: impressions, stamps — the marks stellar rays leave in matter
vocabulary.notes: The physical mechanism: rays imprint qualities on receptive matter

vocabulary.english: operative power, efficacious force
vocabulary.notes: The key term justifying spoken magic — words share in stellar correspondence

vocabulary.english: concord of the stars, celestial harmony
vocabulary.notes: Pythagorean-Islamic synthesis: the cosmos is a musical-mathematical order

source_notes: Al-Kindi's De Radiis (9th century, tr. Latin c. 12th century) is the foundational theoretical treatise on how stellar forces operate on terrestrial matter and on spoken/written symbols. It provided the philosophical basis for talisman magic, spoken incantations, and ceremonial ritual by grounding them in natural science. Ficino, Agrippa, and the entire natural magic tradition depended on this framework.
bibliography: Al-Kindi. De Radiis Stellarum. Ed. M.-Th. d'Alverny and F. Hudry. Archives d'histoire doctrinale et littéraire du Moyen Âge 41 (1975): 139–260.
Travaglia, Pinella. Magic, Causality and Intentionality: The Doctrine of Rays in al-Kindi. Florence: SISMEL, 1999.

title: Speculum Astronomiae — On the Books of Magic
author: Albertus Magnus (attr.)
latin_text: Sciendum est etiam quod sunt libri de imaginibus, quorum alii sunt tractabiles et alii non. Tractabiles sunt qui non nisi figuram et formam et ordinem stellarum et characteres ac inscriptiones continent et nihil quod ex iudicio prohibito sumptum sit. Non tractabiles sunt qui invocationes daemonum continent aut characteres qui non sunt ex virtute caelesti sed ex expresso vel tacito daemonum pacto.
english_gloss: It should also be known that there are books on images, of which some are acceptable and some are not. Acceptable are those which contain only the figure and form and position of the stars, and characters and inscriptions, and nothing drawn from forbidden judgment. Unacceptable are those which contain invocations of demons, or characters which do not derive from celestial power but from the explicit or tacit pact of demons.

vocabulary.english: images, talismans (engraved figures)
vocabulary.notes: The technical term for astrological talismans — images engraved at astrologically propitious moments

vocabulary.english: acceptable, permissible, handle-able
vocabulary.notes: Albertus's legal category for legitimate astrological image magic

vocabulary.english: characters, magical signs
vocabulary.notes: Symbolic characters inscribed on talismans — their legitimacy depends on stellar vs. demonic origin

vocabulary.english: demonic pact, agreement with devils
vocabulary.notes: The decisive criterion distinguishing natural from demonic magic (from Augustine through Aquinas)

vocabulary.english: forbidden judgment — judicial astrology on free will questions
vocabulary.notes: Church prohibition: predicting human choices from stars crosses into determinism

source_notes: The Speculum Astronomiae (c. 1260, attrib. Albertus Magnus) was the most important medieval classification of legitimate vs. forbidden magical books. By distinguishing talismanic image magic (legitimate, if only celestial) from demonic pact magic (forbidden), it provided the theoretical framework for the natural magic tradition. Crucial to the Ficino-Agrippa defense of learned magic.
bibliography: Albertus Magnus. The Speculum Astronomiae and Its Enigma. Ed. and trans. Paola Zambelli. Dordrecht: Kluwer, 1992.

title: Formicarius — The Demonic Pact
author: Johannes Nider
latin_text: Quicumque ergo voluerit magiae artibus uti, primo daemoni per pactum expressum vel tacitum se obligat, et daemonicum auxilium invocat. Pactum autem hoc potest esse expressum, quando quis verbo vel scripto se daemoni dedicat; vel tacitum, quando quis, advertens opera sua non posse fieri sine daemonis ope, scienter in his perseverat. Huiusmodi pacta sunt gravissima peccata et contra fidem christianam directe pugnant.
english_gloss: Whoever therefore wishes to make use of the arts of magic first binds himself to a demon through an explicit or tacit pact, and invokes demonic assistance. This pact can be explicit, when someone dedicates himself to a demon by word or writing; or tacit, when someone, knowing his works cannot be accomplished without demonic assistance, knowingly persists in them. Pacts of this kind are the gravest sins and fight directly against the Christian faith.

vocabulary.english: explicit pact, formal agreement with a demon
vocabulary.notes: Augustine's category; formalized in late medieval demonology as the legal basis of magic

vocabulary.english: tacit pact, implicit agreement through persistent use of demonic means
vocabulary.notes: Key expansion: using magic at all implies consent to demonic assistance

vocabulary.english: binds, obligates — the legal metaphor of the demonic pact
vocabulary.notes: Contract law applied to the supernatural — the soul as the currency of the deal

vocabulary.english: dedicates, consecrates to — the pact as an act of worship
vocabulary.notes: The language of sacrifice and devotion inverted: worshiping the devil

source_notes: Nider's Formicarius (c. 1437) is one of the earliest systematic demonological treatises and a crucial source for the Malleus Maleficarum. The explicit/tacit pact distinction, inherited from Augustine and Aquinas, became the mechanism by which all non-ecclesiastical ritual was potentially criminalized — any sufficiently strange act implies demonic cooperation.
bibliography: Nider, Johannes. Formicarius. Douai: Belleri, 1602.
Bailey, Michael D. Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2003.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — Tables of Characters and Seals
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
latin_text: Characteres autem et sigilla quidam vocant sacras scripturas angelorum, eo quod per haec nomina angelorum et spirituum in lapidibus et metallis inscribuntur. Haec autem ex numeris, figuris geometricis, ex signis caelestibus et stellarum radiis componuntur, et vim habent ex concordantia cum numeris caelestibus et ex impressione rerum caelestium in materiis inferioribus.
english_gloss: Characters and seals are called by some the sacred scripts of angels, since through them the names of angels and spirits are inscribed on stones and metals. These are composed from numbers, geometric figures, celestial signs, and stellar rays, and have power from their concordance with celestial numbers and from the impression of celestial things on lower materials.

vocabulary.english: characters, magical signs, non-alphabetic symbols with power
vocabulary.notes: Distinguished from ordinary letters by their direct celestial derivation

vocabulary.english: seals, sigils — bound images of a spirit's 'signature'
vocabulary.notes: Each angel or spirit has a characteristic seal derived from its name-number

vocabulary.english: sacred scripts of angels, angelic writing systems
vocabulary.notes: The claim that magical characters are the actual script used in heaven

vocabulary.english: impression, stamp — the celestial quality pressed into matter
vocabulary.notes: Aristotelian causation: the seal impresses the celestial force into the metal

source_notes: Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia II.22–52 provides the most comprehensive Renaissance systematization of magical characters, planetary seals, and angelic scripts. The 'Theban alphabet' (attributed to Honorius), the Malachim script, and the Celestial script all appear here as legitimate tools for talisman-making. The theoretical justification (celestial impression through number and figure) links directly to Al-Kindi's De Radiis.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Page, Sophie. Magic in the Cloister: Pious Motives, Illicit Interests, and Occult Approaches to the Medieval Universe. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — Magical Alphabets
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
latin_text: Tria sunt alphabeta magica praecipua: primum Hebraeorum est, quod sanctum et divinum appellatur; secundum est Malachim, scriptura regum et angelorum; tertium Transitus Fluvii dicitur, quasi transitus per aquas. His autem addunt scripturam Thebanam, quam Honorius Thebanus invenit ut dicunt, et est quasi scriptura monachorum nigromantiae studentium.
english_gloss: There are three principal magical alphabets: the first is Hebrew, which is called holy and divine; the second is Malachim, the script of kings and angels; the third is called Transitus Fluvii, as if a crossing through waters. To these they add the Theban script, which Honorius of Thebes is said to have invented, and is as it were the script of monks studying necromancy.

vocabulary.english: magical alphabets, scripts with supernatural properties
vocabulary.notes: Alphabets whose letter-forms encode celestial or angelic correspondences

vocabulary.english: Malachim — 'kings' or 'angels' in Hebrew; the angelic script
vocabulary.notes: One of three celestial scripts given in Agrippa II.30 — derives letter forms from astrological positions

vocabulary.english: Crossing of the River — script linked to the celestial river/Milky Way
vocabulary.notes: The third magical alphabet, associated with the threshold between worlds

vocabulary.english: Theban script, attributed to Honorius of Thebes
vocabulary.notes: Used in medieval grimoires; often called 'witches' alphabet' in modern practice

source_notes: Agrippa's catalogue of magical alphabets in De Occulta Philosophia III.29–30 synthesized the various scripts circulating in late medieval magical manuscripts (Theban, Malachim, celestial, passing-the-river). The claim that these are authentic angelic scripts raised them above the status of cipher and into the category of sacred language.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Skemer, Don C. Binding Words: Textual Amulets in the Middle Ages. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2006.

title: De Praestigiis Daemonum — Familiar Spirits
author: Johann Weyer
latin_text: Spiritus familiares vocantur qui certis hominibus, maxime maleficis, assistere ac famulari dicuntur, ab iis qui haec credunt. Ii vel in forma animalium apparent, ut cattorum, murium, ranarum, mustelae; vel in forma homunculi pusilli. Sed haec omnia ex melancholia et imaginatione aegra provenire arbitror potius quam ex vera daemonis praesentia.
english_gloss: Familiar spirits are called those which are said by those who believe in such things to attend and serve certain persons, especially witches. They appear either in the form of animals, such as cats, mice, frogs, weasels; or in the form of a tiny little man. But I judge that all these things arise rather from melancholy and sick imagination than from the true presence of a demon.

vocabulary.english: familiar spirits, attending daemon-servants
vocabulary.notes: The concept merges classical daimon, Islamic qarin, and late medieval witch trial testimony

vocabulary.english: witches, malefactors — those who cause harm through magic
vocabulary.notes: Maleficus/malefica: the gendered Latin term for the harmful witch

vocabulary.english: melancholy, the black bile humor
vocabulary.notes: Weyer's key medical explanation: witch confessions are symptoms of illness not crime

vocabulary.english: sick imagination, diseased fantasy
vocabulary.notes: Medical-skeptical category: the witch's experience is subjective, not demonic

source_notes: Johann Weyer's De Praestigiis Daemonum (1563) is one of the earliest sustained arguments against witch persecution. His medical-skeptical framework (confessions arise from melancholy) was unusual and controversial. He did not deny demons or magic — he denied the legal validity of torture-induced confessions from mentally ill women. Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons (1997) provides the definitive analysis of this discourse.
bibliography: Weyer, Johann. De Praestigiis Daemonum. Trans. Benjamin Mora. Binghamton: MRTS, 1991.
Clark, Stuart. Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997.

title: De Mineralibus — Occult Properties of Stones
author: Albertus Magnus
latin_text: Proprietates occultae in rebus naturalibus sunt quas nec calor nec frigus nec humiditas nec siccitas neque aliqua qualitas elementaris producit, sed producuntur a forma speciei, quae derivatur ex virtute caelesti in materiam sublunem. Magnes enim trahit ferrum non per calorem vel frigus, sed per proprietatem occultam quae est in eius forma specifica, a stella quadam caelesti impressa.
english_gloss: Occult properties in natural things are those which neither heat nor cold nor moisture nor dryness nor any elementary quality produces, but which are produced by the form of the species, derived from celestial power into sublunary matter. For the magnet draws iron not through heat or cold, but through an occult property which is in its specific form, impressed by a certain celestial star.

vocabulary.english: hidden/occult properties — powers that cannot be explained by the four qualities
vocabulary.notes: The key natural philosophical concept: some powers are real but non-Aristotelian

vocabulary.english: the form of the species — what makes a thing the kind of thing it is
vocabulary.notes: The Aristotelian form is the bearer of occult powers; it derives from celestial influence

vocabulary.english: celestial virtue/power — force transmitted from stars to matter
vocabulary.notes: The mechanism connecting Al-Kindi's rays to Aristotelian natural philosophy

vocabulary.english: magnet — the stock example of occult property in all medieval discussions
vocabulary.notes: Magnetism is the paradigm case: real, powerful, observable, but inexplicable by heat/cold

source_notes: Albertus Magnus's De Mineralibus (c. 1262) is the foundational medieval treatise on occult properties of stones and minerals. The concept of 'occult qualities' — real powers derived from celestial influence, not explicable by the four Aristotelian elements — became the theoretical cornerstone for distinguishing natural magic (licit) from demonic magic (illicit). Everything from talismans to herbal remedies depended on this framework.
bibliography: Albertus Magnus. Book of Minerals. Trans. Dorothy Wyckoff. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1967.
Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: Clavicula Salomonis — Ritual Purification of the Operator
author: Anon. (attrib. Solomon)
latin_text: Ante omnia igitur opus est ut Magister sive operarius per novem dies ieiunet, et a mulierum consortio abstineat, et ab omni immunditia carnis se custodiat. Item debet confiteri sacerdoti et penitentiam agere de peccatis suis. Deinde lavacro mundetur, et vestes mundas et novas induat, et cincturam de nova virgine linea habeat. Haec omnia necessaria sunt ad operationem magicam rite peragendam.
english_gloss: Before all else, it is necessary that the Master or operator fast for nine days, and abstain from the company of women, and keep himself free from all uncleanness of flesh. Likewise he should confess to a priest and do penance for his sins. Then he should be cleansed by washing, and put on clean and new clothes, and have a belt of new virgin linen. All these things are necessary for a magical operation to be rightly performed.

vocabulary.english: purification, ritual cleansing of the operator
vocabulary.notes: The Solomonic tradition requires purity as precondition for angelic cooperation

vocabulary.english: fast, abstention from food
vocabulary.notes: Nine days: the novena structure derived from biblical patterns

vocabulary.english: uncleanness of flesh, bodily impurity
vocabulary.notes: Sexual abstinence as required by Levitical purity codes transposed into magical practice

vocabulary.english: confession — the Christianizing element in the Solomonic tradition
vocabulary.notes: Uniquely medieval addition: sacramental preparation for angel-conjuration

source_notes: The Clavicula Salomonis (Key of Solomon, medieval version) requires elaborate purification of the operator before conjuration. The nine-day fast, sexual abstinence, confession, and new white clothing blend Levitical purity law (Exodus, Leviticus), monastic asceticism, and ancient Greek theurgy into a specifically Christian ritual framework. This distinguishes Solomonic magic from mere divination or trickery.
bibliography: Solomon. The Key of Solomon (Clavicula Salomonis). Ed. S. L. MacGregor Mathers. London: Kegan Paul, 1888.
Leitch, Aaron. Secrets of the Magickal Grimoires. Woodbury: Llewellyn, 2005.

title: Papyri Graecae Magicae — Voces Magicae and the Power of Secret Names
author: Anon.
latin_text: Nomina barbara, id est voces magicae, sunt nomina deorum et angelorum in linguis ignotis — Aegyptia, Hebraica, Chaldaica — quae vim magicam retinent propter antiquitatem et sanctitatem. Haec nomina non transferenda sunt in alias linguas, quia in translatione vim amittunt. AOTH ABAOTH BASYM ISAK SABAOTH IAO.
english_gloss: Barbarous names, that is magical words/voices, are names of gods and angels in unknown languages — Egyptian, Hebrew, Chaldaean — which retain their magical power through antiquity and holiness. These names are not to be translated into other languages, because in translation they lose their power. AOTH ABAOTH BASYM ISAK SABAOTH IAO.

vocabulary.english: barbarous names — magical words in foreign/unknown languages
vocabulary.notes: 'Barbarous' means non-Greek/non-Latin; the foreignness IS the efficacy

vocabulary.english: magical voices/words — spoken formulae with autonomous power
vocabulary.notes: The technical term for untranslatable ritual utterances in the Greek magical papyri

vocabulary.english: lose their power — translation destroys efficacy
vocabulary.notes: Iamblichus De Mysteriis VII.4-5 provides the theoretical justification for untranslated divine names

vocabulary.english: IAO — the Greek rendering of the Hebrew divine name YHWH
vocabulary.notes: The most common voces magicae in the PGM; appears in Gnostic and Christian contexts as well

source_notes: The untranslatability and power of barbarous names (voces magicae, nomina barbara) is a doctrine running from the Greek magical papyri through Iamblichus's defense of theurgy to the Solomonic grimoires and Agrippa. The names AOTH, IAO, SABAOTH are recycled from the PGM into medieval Christian conjurations with only minor modification — a direct textual transmission across 1500 years.
bibliography: Betz, Hans Dieter, ed. The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1986.
Frankfurter, David. Religion in Roman Egypt: Assimilation and Resistance. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1998.

title: Antipalus Maleficarum — On False Attribution in Magic Books
author: Johannes Trithemius
latin_text: Multi libri magici sub nomine Salomonis, Hermetis, Apollonii et aliorum sapientum circumferuntur, qui ab his viris numquam scripti sunt, sed ab impostoribus suppositi, qui auctoritatem illorum nominum praetexuerunt. Haec est consuetudo pseudepigraphorum: quia propria opera in lucem prodire non audent, alienis nominibus ea ornant. Sic Clavicula Salomonis, sic Liber Razielis, sic multa alia.
english_gloss: Many magical books are circulated under the name of Solomon, Hermes, Apollonius, and other wise men, which were never written by these men but were falsely ascribed by imposters, who used the authority of those names as a pretext. This is the custom of pseudepigraphers: because they do not dare to bring forth their own works into the light, they adorn them with others' names. Thus the Clavicula Salomonis, thus the Liber Razielis, thus many others.

vocabulary.english: pseudepigrapha — texts falsely attributed to famous authors
vocabulary.notes: From Greek pseudepigraphos: 'falsely inscribed'; applies across biblical, magical, and philosophical traditions

vocabulary.english: falsely ascribed, substituted, forged
vocabulary.notes: Legal term: suppositio = fraudulent substitution; the grimoire as a legal forgery

vocabulary.english: authority, the borrowed weight of a great name
vocabulary.notes: Pseudepigraphy works because authority, not content, legitimizes a text in medieval epistemology

vocabulary.english: imposters, deceivers — authors who hide behind false attributions
vocabulary.notes: Trithemius identifies a category of writer who knows their work is fraudulent

source_notes: Trithemius's Antipalus Maleficarum (c. 1508) is a rare Renaissance critique of magical pseudepigraphy from within the learned magic tradition. His analysis of how grimoires borrowed authority from Solomon and Hermes remains a starting point for modern source criticism of the grimoire corpus. Ironically, Trithemius's own works (Steganographia, Polygraphia) were accused of containing hidden magical content.
bibliography: Trithemius, Johannes. Antipalus Maleficarum. In Opera Historica. Frankfurt, 1601.
Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages and Renaissance. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Didascalicon — The Illicit Arts
author: Hugh of St. Victor
latin_text: Sunt autem et aliae artes quas non recte artes sed potius adulterinae artium species vocaverim, quae ex quibusdam rationibus et documentis sub certa forma collectae sunt et usum habent aliquem, licet non sine dolo. Inter eas computatur magia cum suis speciebus, quae sunt mantice, mathesis, sortilegia, prestigia et similia, quae omnia sub malo daemonis auspicio operantur.
english_gloss: There are also other arts which I would not rightly call arts, but rather adulterated species of arts, which have been collected under a certain form from certain reasonings and precepts and have some use, although not without deception. Among them is counted magic with its species, which are divination, astrology, sortilege, prestidigitation and similar things, which all operate under the evil auspice of the demon.

vocabulary.english: adulterated/bastard species of arts — illegitimate imitations of true knowledge
vocabulary.notes: Hugh's elegant category: not non-knowledge but corrupted knowledge

vocabulary.english: divination (from Greek mantike) — the art of reading signs for future knowledge
vocabulary.notes: The broad category: includes astrology, augury, necromancy, geomancy

vocabulary.english: judicial astrology — predicting human fate from stars (not astronomy)
vocabulary.notes: Distinguished from legitimate astronomy by its deterministic claims about free will

vocabulary.english: sortilege — divination by lots
vocabulary.notes: Condemned because it either uses natural coincidence (deceptive) or demonic influence (sinful)

vocabulary.english: under the evil auspice of the demon
vocabulary.notes: Hugh's final criterion: all illicit knowledge requires demonic mediation

source_notes: Hugh of St. Victor's Didascalicon (c. 1128) was the standard medieval classification of the arts and sciences. His distinction between legitimate arts and 'adulterated' magic arts shaped every subsequent medieval classification. The list (magia, mantice, mathesis, sortilegia, praestigia) derives from Isidore's Etymologiae VIII.9 and was transmitted through Gratian's Decretum into canon law.
bibliography: Hugh of St. Victor. Didascalicon: A Medieval Guide to the Arts. Trans. Jerome Taylor. New York: Columbia University Press, 1961.
Flint, Valerie I.J. The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991.

title: Corrector — Pastoral Questions on Superstitious Practice
author: Burchard of Worms
latin_text: Fecisti quod quaedam mulieres facere solent? Id est, herbas et cetera ligamina cum quibusdam incantationibus sub pedibus tuis vel in veste sua ligatas portare, ut per eas te vel alios a morte vel periculo liberares? Si fecisti, unum annum per legitimas ferias poeniteas.
english_gloss: Have you done what certain women are accustomed to do? That is, carrying herbs and other bindings tied beneath your feet or bound in your clothing, along with certain incantations, in order to free yourself or others from death or danger by means of them? If you have done this, do penance for one year on the prescribed fast days.

vocabulary.english: ligatures, bindings — amulets tied to the body
vocabulary.notes: A recurring category in pastoral condemnations: tied herbal bundles worn for protection

vocabulary.english: incantations, spoken charms accompanying the physical object
vocabulary.notes: The amulet + spoken formula combination is the folk magic baseline

vocabulary.english: prescribed fast days, the canonical penance schedule
vocabulary.notes: Graduated penance: serious sins get years on Fridays; superstition is relatively light

vocabulary.english: women — the gendered subject of most pastoral magic prohibitions
vocabulary.notes: The Corrector consistently addresses women's folk practice; men appear in different question-forms

source_notes: Burchard of Worms's Corrector et Medicus (c. 1010), Book 19 of his Decretum, is the most detailed source for early medieval popular magic practice, preserved in the interrogatory questions a priest should ask in confession. It reveals an extensive world of herb-bundles, love charms, weather magic, and protective amulets that the Church repeatedly condemned but never eradicated. The penance is light — one year — suggesting pastoral pragmatism.
bibliography: Burchard of Worms. Decretum. In Patrologia Latina, vol. 140. Ed. J.-P. Migne. Paris, 1853.
McNeill, John T. and Helena M. Gamer, trans. Medieval Handbooks of Penance. New York: Columbia University Press, 1938.

title: Summa contra Gentiles — On the Influence of the Stars
author: Thomas Aquinas
latin_text: Corpora caelestia non agunt super intellectum et voluntatem directe, sed agunt super corpora inferiora per motum et lumen, et per hunc modum indirecte aliquam influentiam habent in animam: sicut ex dispositione corporis consequitur dispositio appetitus sensitivi, et haec est causa quare astrologi multa vera praedicunt de moribus hominum qui sequuntur passiones corporis.
english_gloss: Celestial bodies do not act directly on intellect and will, but act upon lower bodies through motion and light, and through this means have some indirect influence on the soul: just as from the disposition of the body the disposition of the sensitive appetite follows, and this is why astrologers predict many true things about the characters of people who follow bodily passions.

vocabulary.english: celestial bodies, heavenly spheres — the stars and planets
vocabulary.notes: Aquinas carefully distinguishes what stars CAN do (affect body) from what they CANNOT (override free will)

vocabulary.english: influence — the flowing-in of celestial power into lower matter
vocabulary.notes: The word 'influence' derives from this Latin concept: astral power 'flows into' receptive matter

vocabulary.english: sensitive appetite, the bodily-emotional side of the soul
vocabulary.notes: Aquinas allows star-influence on emotion and temperament but not on rational choice

vocabulary.english: habits, character, moral dispositions
vocabulary.notes: The astrologer correctly predicts character (mores) shaped by temperament; cannot predict free acts

source_notes: Aquinas's Summa contra Gentiles III.84–85 provides the standard Scholastic position on celestial influence: stars affect the body, the body affects the passions, the passions affect character — but free will remains inviolable. This nuanced position allowed legitimate astrological medicine and temperament analysis while condemning deterministic judicial astrology. Ficino and the entire medical astrology tradition depended on exactly this Thomistic framework.
bibliography: Aquinas, Thomas. Summa contra Gentiles. Trans. Anton C. Pegis et al. Garden City: Doubleday, 1955–57.
North, J.D. Horoscopes and History. London: Warburg Institute, 1986.

title: Opus Majus — On Experimental Science
author: Roger Bacon
latin_text: Sine experientia nihil sufficienter sciri potest. Duplex est enim modus cognoscendi, scilicet per argumentum et per experientiam. Argumentum concludit et facit nos concedere conclusionem, sed non certificat neque removet dubitationem ut quiescat animus in intuitu veritatis, nisi eam inveniat via experientiae. Scientia experimentalis, praeter tres speculativas modos, habet tria magnifica opera: unum est cognitio futurorum, praesentium et praeteritorum; secundum est opera miranda super admiranda naturae; tertium est detectio maleficiorum et incantationum.
english_gloss: Without experience nothing can be sufficiently known. For there are two modes of knowing: through argument and through experience. Argument concludes and causes us to grant the conclusion, but does not certify nor remove doubt so that the mind rests in the intuition of truth, unless it finds it through the way of experience. Experimental science, beyond the three speculative modes, has three magnificent works: one is knowledge of future, present and past things; the second is wondrous operations beyond the wonders of nature; the third is the detection of maleficia and incantations.

vocabulary.english: experimental science — knowledge derived from direct experience/observation
vocabulary.notes: Bacon's foundational epistemological claim; links empiricism to natural magic

vocabulary.english: certifies, makes certain — the verification function of experience
vocabulary.notes: Argument gives logical certainty; experience gives existential certainty

vocabulary.english: wondrous works/operations — effects that exceed ordinary nature
vocabulary.notes: Bacon's space for natural magic: science can produce apparent miracles without demons

vocabulary.english: detection of harmful magic — a legitimizing function of experimental knowledge
vocabulary.notes: Using science against magic: the irony of Bacon's third magnificent work

source_notes: Roger Bacon's Opus Majus (1267) prefigures Francis Bacon's experimental program by 350 years. His scientia experimentalis legitimizes the study of natural wonders as a branch of philosophy, creating intellectual space for natural magic between theology and Scholastic philosophy. The claim that experimental science can detect maleficia gave the tradition a defensive, ecclesiastically acceptable function.
bibliography: Bacon, Roger. Opus Majus. Trans. Robert Belle Burke. 2 vols. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1928.
Hackett, Jeremiah, ed. Roger Bacon and the Sciences. Leiden: Brill, 1997.

title: Decretum — Canon on Prohibited Arts
author: Gratian
latin_text: Qui artes magicas exercent vel his qui eas exercent consulunt, sive malefici sive arioli sive augures sive incantatores fuerint, vel qui phylacteria facere praesumunt, penitentiam agant. Artes enim prohibitae his nominibus comprehenduntur, et exercitores earum a communione fidei separantur quamdiu in hac observatione permanserint.
english_gloss: Those who practice magical arts or consult those who practice them, whether they are sorcerers, soothsayers, augurs, or enchanters, or those who presume to make phylacteries, shall do penance. For the prohibited arts are comprehended under these names, and their practitioners are separated from the communion of the faith as long as they persist in this observance.

vocabulary.english: prohibited arts — the canonical category for forbidden magical practices
vocabulary.notes: The formal legal term in canon law for the class of practices under ecclesiastical prohibition

vocabulary.english: sorcerers, workers of harm through magic
vocabulary.notes: Maleficium: harmful magic — distinguished from beneficial charm-work

vocabulary.english: soothsayers, diviners who use altars or shrines
vocabulary.notes: From ara (altar): diviners who sought answers from sacrificial rites

vocabulary.english: phylacteries, amulets — objects worn for magical protection
vocabulary.notes: Condemned throughout canon law; the term derives from Jewish tefillin but applied broadly to all amulets

source_notes: Gratian's Decretum (c. 1140), the foundational text of medieval canon law, compiled biblical, patristic, and conciliar texts condemning magic into Causa XXVI. The formal category artes prohibitae ('prohibited arts') gave inquisitors and confessors the legal framework for prosecution. It draws on the Burchard of Worms tradition while systematizing it into enforceable ecclesiastical law.
bibliography: Gratian. Decretum. In Corpus Iuris Canonici. Ed. Emil Friedberg. Leipzig: Tauchnitz, 1879.
Kors, Alan C. and Edward Peters, eds. Witchcraft in Europe, 400-1700: A Documentary History. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2001.

title: De Umbris Idearum — The Wheel of Memory
author: Giordano Bruno
latin_text: Intentio mea est ut per hanc artem non solum rerum species in memoria conserventur sed etiam in animo quaedam impressio virtutum et potentiarum rerum fiat. Imagines enim non sunt tantum signa sed etiam vehicula virtutum: per imagines planetarum et daemonum et heroum disponit se animus ad recipiendas eorum virtutes. Qui enim Solis imaginem vivacem et magnam in memoria locat, is Solis naturam et virtutem quodammodo participat.
english_gloss: My intention is that through this art not only are the species of things preserved in memory but also a certain impression of the virtues and powers of things is made in the soul. For images are not merely signs but also vehicles of powers: through images of planets, daemons, and heroes, the soul disposes itself to receive their virtues. For whoever places a vivid and great image of the Sun in memory participates in some measure in the nature and power of the Sun.

vocabulary.english: vehicles of powers/virtues — images as transmission channels for celestial force
vocabulary.notes: Bruno's key innovation: memory images are talismanic, not merely mnemonic

vocabulary.english: impression, imprint — the celestial virtue stamped into the soul through imagination
vocabulary.notes: The same term as for talisman-making; the soul itself becomes the talismanic receptacle

vocabulary.english: species, the visible forms/representations of things
vocabulary.notes: Aristotelian-Scholastic: the species (form) is what is received in knowledge

vocabulary.english: participates in, shares in — the Neoplatonic language of grade-participation
vocabulary.notes: Neoplatonic participation logic: the image doesn't imitate but genuinely shares in the original

vocabulary.english: daemons — intermediate divine spirits between humans and gods
vocabulary.notes: Bruno follows Iamblichus: daemons are real powers accessed through their images

source_notes: Bruno's De Umbris Idearum (1582) transforms the medieval ars memorativa into a magical-Neoplatonic system. Where Ciceronian mnemonics used images as signs to remember words, Bruno's images are charged with the actual virtues of the planets and daemons they represent. The practitioner who 'places' the Sun in memory is doing theurgy, not just mnemonics. Frances Yates's The Art of Memory (1966) established the scholarship on this tradition.
bibliography: Bruno, Giordano. De Umbris Idearum. Ed. and trans. Scott Gosnell. Sequim: Holmes, 2013.
Yates, Frances A. The Art of Memory. London: Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1966.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — What is Magic?
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
latin_text: Magia est facultas potestate plena admirandos effectus praestandi, naturae superioris et inferioris vinculis arctissimis connectens res. Haec est summum culmen et perfectio philosophiae naturalis, nec nisi philosopho bene experto et in philosophia naturali radicato concessa. Triplex etiam haec ars secundum triplicem mundi naturam est distincta: in naturalem, quae circa naturalia tantum versatur, in caelestem vel mathematicam, quae motuum et luminum caelestium virtutibus utitur, et in ceremonialem, quae ritus et ceremonias adhibet.
english_gloss: Magic is a faculty full of power, producing admirable effects by connecting things through the tightest bonds of the superior and inferior nature. This is the highest summit and perfection of natural philosophy, granted only to the philosopher who is well experienced and well rooted in natural philosophy. This art is also distinguished according to the triple nature of the world: into natural, which deals only with natural things; into celestial or mathematical, which uses the virtues of celestial motions and lights; and into ceremonial, which employs rites and ceremonies.

vocabulary.english: bond, chain, link — the chain of sympathies connecting upper and lower
vocabulary.notes: The vinculum (bond) is central to Bruno's love magic and the whole sympathetic tradition

vocabulary.english: faculty full of power — magic as a positive discipline with real efficacy
vocabulary.notes: Agrippa opposes this to skeptics: magic is a real faculty (capability), not illusion

vocabulary.english: the highest summit of natural philosophy
vocabulary.notes: Direct echo of Pico's thesis — magic is science perfected, not science rejected

vocabulary.english: natural magic — the first level, working only with natural powers
vocabulary.notes: Licit; distinguished from ceremonial magic which involves spirits

vocabulary.english: ceremonial magic — the third level, involving ritual, spirits, and divine names
vocabulary.notes: Most controversial; Agrippa defends it in Book III as legitimate religion

source_notes: Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia I.1 (1531) opens by defining magic as the 'absolute consummation of natural philosophy' — directly echoing Pico's 1486 thesis. The tripartite division (natural / celestial-mathematical / ceremonial) became the standard Renaissance taxonomy of magical practice. Agrippa's project was to create a unified science of the hidden forces of nature, drawing on Ficino, Pico, Trithemius, and the Neoplatonist tradition.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Amore — Love as Daimonic Force
author: Marsilio Ficino
latin_text: Amor daemon quidam magnus est, ut ait Diotima in Platonis Convivio. Genus enim daemonis est medium inter deum et mortalem hominem. In medio duorum extremorum versatur, et interpretis officium gerit inter superos et inferos, transferens hinc illuc vota et munera, inde huc responsa et beneficia. Per ipsum fit omnis divinatio atque sacerdotum varietas. Daemon enim perpetuus est, mortalis autem homo non semper eadem virtute pollet. Amor autem daemon non pauper, non sordidus, non ignobilis, sed rector quidam totius naturae est.
english_gloss: Love is a certain great daemon, as Diotima says in Plato's Symposium. For the race of the daemon is intermediate between god and mortal man. It moves in the middle between two extremes, and performs the function of interpreter between those above and those below, transferring from this side vows and gifts, and from that side responses and benefits. Through it comes all divination and the variety of priestly functions. For the daemon is perpetual, but mortal man does not always excel in the same virtue. But Love as daemon is not poor, not sordid, not ignoble, but is a certain ruler of the whole of nature.

vocabulary.english: great daemon — intermediate divine being between God and humans
vocabulary.notes: Ficino translates Plato's daimon as 'daemon' and elevates it from pagan intermediary to cosmic force

vocabulary.english: the function of interpreter — daemon as cosmic messenger
vocabulary.notes: The daemon does not just carry messages but actively interprets, translates, mediates

vocabulary.english: divination — in this context, divine inspiration and prophetic knowing
vocabulary.notes: Per daemones: all oracles, prophecy, and priestly inspiration flows through daimonic mediation

vocabulary.english: ruler of nature — love as the governing principle of the cosmos
vocabulary.notes: Ficino elevates Platonic Eros from a human feeling to a cosmological principle

vocabulary.english: vows and gifts — the upward prayers flowing toward the divine
vocabulary.notes: The daemon carries offerings upward and responses downward: cosmic postal service

source_notes: Ficino's Commentary on Plato's Symposium (De Amore, 1469) developed the concept of Platonic love as both a cosmological force and a daimonic intermediary. The Renaissance concept of 'Platonic love' derives from this text — but Ficino's intention was philosophical-theological, not sentimental. By identifying Love as a great daemon, he validated the entire daimonic universe of Renaissance magic.
bibliography: Ficino, Marsilio. Commentary on Plato's Symposium on Love (De Amore). Trans. Sears Jayne. Dallas: Spring, 1985.
Allen, Michael J.B. The Platonism of Marsilio Ficino. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1984.

title: De Occulta Philosophia — Fascination and the Power of the Eye
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
latin_text: Fascinatio est quaedam potentia transmittendi spiritus proprios in rem alterius, per aspectum. Hi spiritus ex oculis emissi, utpote acutissimi et puri, primo attingunt oculos fascinati, inde ad cor penetrant, et sanguinem totum inficiunt. Sic fit ut aspectus aliquorum hominum venenatorum aut invidorum noceat infantibus et iis qui debile corpus habent. Hoc potissimum contingit ubi spiritus fascinantis sortitus est qualitatem venenosam aut ubi vehemens affectio et intensa imaginatio ad nocendum dirigitur.
english_gloss: Fascination is a certain power of transmitting one's own spirits into the thing of another through the gaze. These spirits, emitted from the eyes, being most sharp and pure, first touch the eyes of the fascinated person, then penetrate to the heart, and infect the whole blood. Thus it happens that the gaze of certain poisonous or envious people harms infants and those who have a weak body. This happens especially when the spirit of the fascinator has obtained a venomous quality, or when a strong feeling and intense imagination is directed toward causing harm.

vocabulary.english: fascination, the evil eye — harm through the gaze
vocabulary.notes: From Latin fascinare; related to Greek baskania; one of the oldest attested magical beliefs

vocabulary.english: spirits — the subtle vaporous medium between soul and body
vocabulary.notes: The Galenic spiritus as the mechanism of fascination: real, physical, transmissible

vocabulary.english: gaze, aspect — the directed look as the vehicle of transmission
vocabulary.notes: Aspectus in astrology too: planets 'aspect' each other through geometric angles of transmission

vocabulary.english: infects, contaminates — the medical metaphor for magical transmission
vocabulary.notes: Fascination as a disease model: the evil eye literally infects the blood

vocabulary.english: intense imagination — the concentrated mental force directing the harmful spiritus
vocabulary.notes: Following Avicenna: strong imagination can affect matter directly through spiritus

source_notes: Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia I.50 provides a natural-philosophical account of the evil eye through Galenic spirit medicine. The spiritus — a warm, vaporous substance mediating between soul and body — is the physical mechanism of fascination. This medicalizes what was superstition and makes it amenable to natural philosophy. The same mechanism underlies love at first sight, voluntary fascination, and maternal imagination impressing the unborn child.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. V. Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Dundes, Alan, ed. The Evil Eye: A Folklore Casebook. New York: Garland, 1981.

title: De Mysteriis — On the Efficacy of Theurgic Prayer
author: Iamblichus
latin_text: Non cogitatio est quae coniungit theurgos cum diis. Quid enim impediret quominus qui philosophantur theoria contemplantes fruantur theurgica unione cum diis? Res vero ita habet. Perfectio theurgia non per intellectum sed per operationem sacratissimam fit, et per tacitum et ineffabilem signum. Signa enim symbolica non ad intellectum sed ad deos ipsos sonant.
english_gloss: It is not thought that conjoins theurgists with the gods. For what would prevent those who philosophize, contemplating through theory, from enjoying theurgic union with the gods? The matter is rather thus: the perfection of theurgy comes not through intellect but through the most sacred operation, and through silent and ineffable signs. For symbolic signs resound not toward the intellect but toward the gods themselves.

vocabulary.english: theurgy — divine work; ritual that effects union with the divine (opp. theology)
vocabulary.notes: Iamblichus's key distinction: theurgy (doing divine work) vs. theologia (speaking about the divine)

vocabulary.english: symbolic signs — ritual actions and objects that connect to the divine directly
vocabulary.notes: The symbolic signs do not mean the divine for the intellect; they ARE the divine for the gods

vocabulary.english: ineffable, that which cannot be spoken — the beyond-language character of theurgy
vocabulary.notes: Apophatic theology applied to ritual: the deepest operations pass beyond human speech

vocabulary.english: conjoins with the gods, achieves union
vocabulary.notes: Theurgic union (henosis) is the goal — not knowledge of the gods but merger with them

source_notes: Iamblichus's De Mysteriis (c. 300 CE) is the foundational theoretical defense of theurgy against Porphyry's purely intellectual Neoplatonism. The key argument: you cannot think your way to union with the One; you must act theurgy into being. This anti-intellectualist mysticism validated ritual magic for the entire subsequent tradition — from late antique paganism through Renaissance Hermeticism to modern ceremonial magic.
bibliography: Iamblichus. De Mysteriis. Trans. Emma C. Clarke, John M. Dillon, and Jackson P. Hershbell. Atlanta: SBL, 2003.
Shaw, Gregory. Theurgy and the Soul: The Neoplatonism of Iamblichus. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1995.

title: Secreta Mulierum — Occult Powers of the Female Body
author: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus
latin_text: Mulier menstruata si aspiciat speculum novum, videbitur in speculo quasi sanguis ruber. Oculi enim mulieris menstruatae emittunt spiritum infectum qui superficiem speculi tangit et maculat. Similiter infantem in cunabulis aspiciens mulier menstruata nocere potest, si spiritus eius per oculos emissus tener corpus infantis penetrat. Haec omnia ex qualitate spiritus proveniunt, non ex maleficio.
english_gloss: If a menstruating woman looks at a new mirror, a red bloodlike color will be seen on the mirror. For the eyes of a menstruating woman emit an infected spirit that touches and stains the surface of the mirror. Similarly, a menstruating woman looking at an infant in its cradle can harm it, if the spirit emitted through her eyes penetrates the tender body of the infant. All these things arise from the quality of the spirit, not from maleficium.

vocabulary.english: menstruating woman — subject of extensive medieval medical-magical discourse
vocabulary.notes: From Pliny Natural History VII.13: menstrual blood was the paradigm of natural 'occult' property

vocabulary.english: infected/tainted spirit — the medical mechanism for the menstrual taboo
vocabulary.notes: Galenic spiritus theory: the menstruating woman emits harmful vapor from her eyes

vocabulary.english: stains, spots, taints — the mirror as diagnostic surface
vocabulary.notes: The mirror test was a practical method cited as proof of the doctrine

vocabulary.english: not from sorcery/harmful magic — the naturalizing disclaimer
vocabulary.notes: Pseudo-Albertus carefully distinguishes natural effects from demonic intervention

source_notes: The Secreta Mulierum (c. 1300, falsely attributed to Albertus Magnus) was widely circulated in manuscript and print, presenting gynecological knowledge as a form of natural philosophy. Its discussion of menstrual 'fascination' connects the Pliny tradition (Natural History) to Galenic medicine and Aristotelian natural philosophy. The text was used both to understand and to pathologize female biology.
bibliography: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus. Women's Secrets: A Translation of Pseudo-Albertus Magnus's De Secretis Mulierum. Trans. Helen Rodnite Lemay. Albany: SUNY Press, 1992.
Cadden, Joan. Meanings of Sex Difference in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.

title: Malleus Maleficarum — Witches' Night-Flight to the Sabbath
author: Heinrich Kramer
latin_text: Qualiter autem strigae et lamiae de loco ad locum transferantur, quatuor sunt modi. Primo modo corporaliter et realiter, transportante eas daemone. Secundo modo per phantasiam solum et imaginationem. Tertio modo per lunam sive per quemdam spiritum qui lunae assimilatur. Quarto modo per aliquam unguentum. Et notandum quod primi tres modi a theologis conceduntur, quartus autem inter superstitiosa computatur.
english_gloss: As for how witches and night-demons are transferred from place to place, there are four modes. In the first mode, bodily and really, the demon transporting them. In the second mode, through fantasy alone and imagination. In the third mode through the moon or through a certain spirit that resembles the moon. In the fourth mode through some ointment. And note that the first three modes are conceded by theologians, but the fourth is counted among superstitions.

vocabulary.english: witches and night-spirits — the classical supernatural women conflated in medieval witch doctrine
vocabulary.notes: Striga: screech-owl, witch; lamia: child-devouring female demon; both become terms for the sabbath witch

vocabulary.english: bodily and really — the theological claim that flight was physical, not illusory
vocabulary.notes: The key demonological question: is the sabbath real or merely dreamed?

vocabulary.english: through an ointment — the flying ointment (unguentum sabbati)
vocabulary.notes: The pharmacological explanation for the sabbath: ointments with solanaceous alkaloids producing hallucinations

vocabulary.english: through fantasy/imagination alone — the skeptical alternative
vocabulary.notes: The Canon Episcopi position: sabbath flight is diabolical illusion, not real movement

source_notes: The Malleus Maleficarum's taxonomy of sabbath transportation modes reflects genuine theological controversy: was the witch's sabbath a real physical journey or a diabolic illusion? The Canon Episcopi (c. 900) had said illusion; the Malleus (1487) argued for real physical transport as more useful for prosecution. The flying ointment theory (mode 4) was treated skeptically even by inquisitors — Emma Wilby's work on cunning folk traditions is essential for modern assessment.
bibliography: Kramer, Heinrich. Malleus Maleficarum. Trans. Christopher S. Mackay. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006.
Cohn, Norman. Europe's Inner Demons. 2nd ed. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1993.

title: De Anima — The Power of Imagination Over Matter
author: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
latin_text: Manifestum est enim quod anima humana potest habere dominium et potestatem super corpus alienum, non solum supra corpus proprium, per virtutem imaginativam et per intentionem fortem, maxime quando anima fuerit fortis et nobilis. Intentio enim fortis et imaginatio intensa convertuntur in rem extra animam et in corpore alieno signum relinquunt. Hoc videmus in fascinantibus qui per solum aspectum et intentionem infirmitates generant.
english_gloss: For it is evident that the human soul can have dominion and power over a foreign body, not only over its own body, through the imaginative faculty and through strong intention, especially when the soul is strong and noble. For strong intention and intense imagination are converted into a thing outside the soul and leave a mark in a foreign body. This we see in those who fascinate, who generate illnesses through gaze and intention alone.

vocabulary.english: imaginative faculty — the power of mental image-forming
vocabulary.notes: For Avicenna the imagination is not passive but can act causally on matter through the soul

vocabulary.english: strong intention, concentrated mental will directed outward
vocabulary.notes: The technical mechanism: intention is a real physical-psychological force in Avicennan medicine

vocabulary.english: dominion over a foreign body — psychic influence on others
vocabulary.notes: The philosophical basis for evil eye, love magic, and healing-at-a-distance

vocabulary.english: strong and noble soul — the prerequisite for effective imagination
vocabulary.notes: Natural hierarchy: some people's souls are more powerful than others; the magician has an exceptional soul

vocabulary.english: they leave a mark — the physical trace of imaginative action
vocabulary.notes: The imagination's effect is genuinely physical: birth marks, disease symptoms, visible changes

source_notes: Avicenna's De Anima (Latin translation of the psychological section of Kitab al-Shifa, c. 1020) was the most influential psychological text in medieval Europe. His claim that strong imagination can affect external bodies provided the natural-philosophical foundation for the entire tradition of learned magic in the West. Agrippa, Ficino, and Pomponazzi all cite Avicenna's imaginatio theory to explain magic without demons.
bibliography: Avicenna. Liber de Anima seu Sextus de Naturalibus. Ed. S. Van Riet. 2 vols. Leiden: Brill, 1968–72.
Hasse, Dag Nikolaus. Avicenna's De Anima in the Latin West. London: Warburg Institute, 2000.

title: Introductorium Maius — Saturn's Significations
author: Abu Mashar (Albumasar)
latin_text: Saturnus significat patres et avos et homines antiquos, et scientiam occultam et philosophiam naturalem et investigationem secretorum naturae. Significat etiam agriculturam et labores graves et diuturnas peregrinationes et sepultura et mortem lentam. Inter homines, significat monachos et heremitas et eos qui solitariam vitam ducunt. Color eius est niger vel plumbeus. Metallum eius plumbum. Lapis eius onyx.
english_gloss: Saturn signifies fathers and grandfathers and ancient men, and hidden knowledge and natural philosophy and the investigation of the secrets of nature. It also signifies agriculture and heavy labors and long pilgrimages and burial and slow death. Among men, it signifies monks and hermits and those who lead a solitary life. Its color is black or leaden. Its metal is lead. Its stone is onyx.

vocabulary.english: signifies — the astrological verb of correspondence and rulership
vocabulary.notes: The planet doesn't cause these things directly; it 'signifies' them by correspondence

vocabulary.english: hidden knowledge, occult science
vocabulary.notes: Saturn rules esoteric study — hence the melancholic scholar archetype

vocabulary.english: investigation of secrets — natural philosophical inquiry into hidden causes
vocabulary.notes: Saturn's melancholic temperament predisposes its natives to depth of thought

vocabulary.english: hermits, those who withdraw from society for spiritual practice
vocabulary.notes: The link: Saturn's solitary, contemplative nature matches the hermit's withdrawal

vocabulary.english: its metal is lead — the correspondence system linking planets to materials
vocabulary.notes: Lead works alchemically under Saturn; Saturn's talisman uses lead; Saturn rules leadworkers

source_notes: Abu Mashar's Introductorium Maius in Astrologiam (c. 850, tr. John of Seville c. 1133) was the most widely used astrological textbook in medieval Europe. Its systematic tables of planetary significations — each planet linked to body parts, metals, stones, plants, professions, character types — provided the fundamental correspondence system underlying natural magic, talisman-making, and medical astrology. The Ficino-Agrippa tradition depends directly on this schema.
bibliography: Abu Mashar. The Abbreviation of the Introduction to Astrology. Ed. and trans. Charles Burnett. Leiden: Brill, 1994.
Lemay, Richard. Abu Mashar and Latin Aristotelianism in the Twelfth Century. Beirut: American University of Beirut, 1962.

title: Conciliator Controversiarum — Astrology as Natural Science
author: Pietro d'Abano
work: Conciliator Controversiarum Quae inter Philosophos et Medicos Versantur
latin_text: Astrologia non est ars superstitiosa sed scientia naturalis, quia demonstrat qualiter corpora caelestia per suos motus et radios qualitates in corporibus inferioribus inducunt, et qualiter ex his qualitatibus dispositiones physicae et morales in hominibus sequuntur. Haec scientia ideo licit est, quia non utitur daemoniis vel pacto implicito, sed solis causis naturalibus.
english_gloss: Astrology is not a superstitious art but a natural science, since it demonstrates how celestial bodies through their motions and rays induce qualities in lower bodies, and how from these qualities physical and moral dispositions follow in human beings. This science is therefore licit, since it does not make use of demons or implicit pact, but of natural causes alone.

vocabulary.english: natural science — the Aristotelian classification of legitimate rational inquiry into nature
vocabulary.notes: Pietro's key argumentative move: astrology is natural science, not magic

vocabulary.english: rays, stellar emissions — al-Kindi's framework redeployed in medical astrology
vocabulary.notes: The rays transmit celestial qualities to terrestrial matter, including human bodies

vocabulary.english: moral dispositions — character tendencies arising from celestial influence
vocabulary.notes: Follows Aquinas: free will is not cancelled, but temperament is shaped by the stars

vocabulary.english: without implicit pact — the key canonical criterion for licit magic
vocabulary.notes: From Augustine through Aquinas: licit if only natural; illicit if it implies demonic cooperation

source_notes: Pietro d'Abano's Conciliator (1310) applied Aristotelian natural philosophy to reconcile disagreements between philosophers and physicians, including the status of astrology. As both a philosopher and physician at Padua, he was uniquely positioned to argue that astrological medicine was natural science, not superstition. He was posthumously condemned by the Inquisition — an indicator of how contentious this position remained.
bibliography: Pietro d'Abano. Conciliator Controversiarum. Venice: Giunta, 1521.
Thorndike, Lynn. A History of Magic and Experimental Science. Vol. 2. New York: Columbia University Press, 1923.

title: Liber Misericordiae — Theory of the Four Natures
author: Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber)
latin_text: Quatuor sunt naturae simplices ex quibus omnia composita fiunt: calor, frigus, humiditas et siccitas. Ex his quatuor fit omnis lapis et omne metallum. Aurum enim ex calore et siccitate perfectis praevalet, et ideo non corrumpitur. Argentum vero ex humiditate et frigore mixtis sequitur. Plumbum autem ex frigore praedominante fit, et ideo facile corruptioni obnoxium est.
english_gloss: There are four simple natures from which all composite things are made: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. From these four every stone and every metal is made. Gold indeed excels from perfect heat and dryness, and therefore is not corrupted. Silver truly follows from mixed moisture and cold. Lead is made from predominant cold, and therefore is easily subject to corruption.

vocabulary.english: four simple natures — the Aristotelian primary qualities
vocabulary.notes: Jabir's alchemy grounds metallurgy in Aristotelian physics, making it a rational science

vocabulary.english: heat, cold, moisture, dryness — the four primary qualities
vocabulary.notes: All metals are combinations of these; the alchemist manipulates their ratios to transmute

vocabulary.english: is not corrupted — gold's incorruptibility as the goal of alchemical work
vocabulary.notes: Gold = perfect elemental balance; to make gold = to perfect the elemental proportions of base metal

vocabulary.english: predominating, having the upper hand — quality imbalance as the cause of imperfection
vocabulary.notes: Lead's coldness 'predominates'; heating lead is literally correcting its elemental imbalance

source_notes: Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 8th–9th century CE) is the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy. His Latin translations (circulating as 'Geber' in the West) introduced systematic elemental theory into alchemical practice. The 'sulfur-mercury theory' of metals and the four-natures framework became the theoretical backbone of Western alchemy through Roger Bacon, Arnald of Villanova, and Paracelsus.
bibliography: Jabir ibn Hayyan. The Arabic Works of Jabir ibn Hayyan. Trans. and ed. Eric J. Holmyard. Paris: Geuthner, 1928.
Kraus, Paul. Jabir ibn Hayyan. 2 vols. Cairo: Institut Français d'Archéologie Orientale, 1942–43.

title: Livre des Figures Hiéroglyphiques — The Alchemical Vision
author: Nicolas Flamel
latin_text: Vidi in somnis angelum Dei qui mihi librum quendam dedit lucidum et fulgidum valde, foliis ex subtilissima papyra factis, scriptum calamo ferreo, et literis elegantissimis. Tunc angelus dixit mihi: Flamelle, intuere hunc librum, nihil intelliges ex eo, sed aliquando videbis in eo quod nemo alius videbit. Liber erat vetus et scriptus in lingua quam non intelligebam, et characteres erant diversi et sigilla multa.
english_gloss: I saw in a dream an angel of God who gave me a certain book, very bright and shining, with pages made of the finest papyrus, written with an iron stylus, and in most elegant letters. Then the angel said to me: Flamel, look upon this book, you will understand nothing from it, but someday you will see in it what no one else will see. The book was old and written in a language I did not understand, and the characters were various and there were many seals.

vocabulary.english: angel of God — divine messenger who reveals the alchemical book
vocabulary.notes: The dream-vision revelation is a standard legitimizing device for esoteric texts

vocabulary.english: various/diverse characters — the mysterious script of the alchemical manuscript
vocabulary.notes: Flamel claims to have received the 'Book of Abraham the Jew' — full of Kabbalistic and alchemical symbols

vocabulary.english: seals, sigils — the symbolic images in the text that encode the alchemical process
vocabulary.notes: Flamel spent years having the symbols interpreted before he claimed to achieve the Work

vocabulary.latin: intelligibis in eo quod nemo alius
vocabulary.english: you will see in it what no one else will see — the personal illumination theme
vocabulary.notes: The text is decipherable only to the initiated; the angel designates Flamel as the chosen interpreter

source_notes: Nicolas Flamel (1330–1418) was a Parisian scrivener whose modest historical wealth became, through post-mortem legend, evidence that he had achieved the alchemical Philosopher's Stone. The Livre des Figures Hiéroglyphiques (1612, but retroactively attributed to him) presents his dream-revelation of the 'Book of Abraham the Jew.' Modern scholarship (Principe, Kahn) demonstrates Flamel's alchemical writings are 17th-century fabrications — but this makes the legend all the more interesting as a case of alchemical myth-making.
bibliography: Flamel, Nicolas. His Exposition of the Hieroglyphical Figures. London: T. Walkley, 1624.
Kahn, Didier. Alchimie et Paracelsisme en France. Geneva: Droz, 2007.

title: Currus Triumphalis Antimonii — The Antimony Process
author: Basil Valentine (attr.)
latin_text: Antimonium est minerale sulphureum, plumbo simile, in montibus nascitur et a natura habet proprietatem purgandi aurum ab impuritatibus. Si aurum cum antimonio funditur, omnes impuritates ad antimonium transeunt et aurum purum manet. Similiter corpus humanum purgari potest per antimonii praeparata, si rite et cum scientia praeparentur. Nam antimonia est lupus metallorum, quia devorat et consumit impuras partes.
english_gloss: Antimony is a sulfurous mineral, similar to lead, born in the mountains, and has from nature the property of purifying gold from impurities. If gold is fused with antimony, all impurities pass to the antimony and the pure gold remains. Similarly, the human body can be purified through prepared antimony, if it is rightly and skillfully prepared. For antimony is the wolf of metals, since it devours and consumes the impure parts.

vocabulary.english: antimony (stibium) — the mineral used both as metallurgical flux and iatrochemical medicine
vocabulary.notes: The 'antimony controversy' of the 16th-17th c: Paracelsians vs. Galenists on whether antimony was poison or cure

vocabulary.english: wolf of metals — antimony's literary-alchemical epithet
vocabulary.notes: The 'wolf' that devours impure metal; by analogy, cleanses the human body of disease-matter

vocabulary.english: purging, purification — the dual literal and alchemical-medical meaning
vocabulary.notes: Alchemical purification and medical purgation are the same operation at different scales

vocabulary.english: sulfurous — containing sulfur in the Jabir/Paracelsian theory of mineral composition
vocabulary.notes: In Paracelsian tria prima theory, sulfur is the principle of combustibility

source_notes: Basil Valentine's Currus Triumphalis Antimonii (1604) — attributed to a 15th-century Benedictine monk but almost certainly 17th-century — was central to the Paracelsian iatrochemistry movement. The 'wolf of metals' metaphor for antimony's purifying property became one of the most famous alchemical images. The text's promotion of antimonial medicines was controversial: antimony in unprepared form is toxic, and the iatrochemical Paracelsian school fought the Galenic establishment over its use.
bibliography: Valentine, Basil. The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony. Trans. A.E. Waite. London: Vincent Stuart, 1962.
Moran, Bruce T. Distilling Knowledge: Alchemy, Chemistry, and the Scientific Revolution. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2005.

title: Magia Adamica — The Ancient Magic of Adam
author: Thomas Vaughan
latin_text: Magia est scientia quam Adamus habuit in paradiso, qua cognoscebat naturam omnium rerum et potestatem habebat in omnia animalia et in tota natura. Haec scientia per Cain filium eius corrupta est et demoniaca facta est; per Seth autem filio per tradita est et conservata usque ad Moysen et Salomonem. Haec est vera et legitima magia, quae non est ars superstitiosa sed cognitio primorum principiorum naturae.
english_gloss: Magic is the science which Adam had in Paradise, by which he knew the nature of all things and had power over all animals and over the whole of nature. This science was corrupted through his son Cain and made demonic; but through his son Seth it was handed down and preserved even to Moses and Solomon. This is the true and legitimate magic, which is not a superstitious art but knowledge of the first principles of nature.

vocabulary.english: Adam's science — the primal knowledge given to the first man before the Fall
vocabulary.notes: The Adamic knowledge tradition: naming the animals = knowing their natures = mastering nature

vocabulary.english: corrupted through Cain — the Fall of magic from Adamic perfection to demonic practice
vocabulary.notes: The Cainite-Sethite split: one line preserves true magic (Seth→Moses→Solomon), one corrupts it

vocabulary.english: first principles of nature — the deep structural laws underlying physical reality
vocabulary.notes: Vaughan's naturalistic claim: magic is not supernatural but supra-rational natural science

vocabulary.english: true and legitimate magic — the defended category distinguished from superstition
vocabulary.notes: The standard apologetic move from Pico through Agrippa: there is a true magic that is not demonic

source_notes: Thomas Vaughan's Magia Adamica (1650) represents the English Hermeticist tradition of the mid-17th century, influenced by Agrippa, Paracelsus, and Rosicrucian thought. His reconstruction of an 'Adamic' original magic — pristine knowledge of nature given at creation, preserved through Seth, corrupted through Cain — is characteristic of Renaissance-era attempts to legitimize occult study by grounding it in pre-Fall perfection rather than demonic pact.
bibliography: Vaughan, Thomas. The Works of Thomas Vaughan. Ed. A.E. Waite. London: Theosophical Publishing House, 1919.
Linden, Stanton J. The Alchemy Reader. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003.

title: Magia Naturalis — Sympathy and Antipathy in Nature
author: Giambattista della Porta
latin_text: Est inter res naturales admirabilis quaedam concordia et discordia, quam Graeci sympatheian et antipatheian appellant. Haec occulta qualitas rebus innata est ab ipsa rerum creatione. Magnes ferrum trahit per sympathiam; adamas vero maximo adversatur odio magneti per antipatheiam. Herba heliotropium solem sequitur per totum diem; canes lupos naturaliter oderint. Ex his sympathiis et antipathiis naturae tota magia naturalis pendeat, et qui eas noverit, multa miranda praestare poterit.
english_gloss: Among natural things there is a certain admirable concord and discord, which the Greeks call sympathy and antipathy. This hidden quality is innate in things from the very creation of things. The magnet draws iron through sympathy; but the diamond opposes the magnet with the greatest hatred through antipathy. The herb heliotrope follows the sun through the whole day; dogs naturally hate wolves. From these sympathies and antipathies of nature all natural magic depends, and whoever knows them will be able to produce many wonders.

vocabulary.english: sympathy and antipathy — the twin principles of hidden attraction and repulsion
vocabulary.notes: Porta's key theoretical framework: all of nature is structured by occult attraction and repulsion

vocabulary.english: occult quality innate from creation — hidden powers built into things at their creation
vocabulary.notes: God inscribed sympathies into nature at creation; the magician reads this divine code

vocabulary.english: heliotrope — the sun-following herb, paradigm case of natural sympathy
vocabulary.notes: Plants following the sun: the strongest natural-world example of sympathy (solar correspondence)

vocabulary.english: great wonders — the results of applying sympathetic knowledge
vocabulary.notes: Maraviglie: the Renaissance natural marvels tradition, distinct from miracles (divine) and tricks (demonic)

vocabulary.english: all natural magic depends upon these — sympathy as the foundation of the whole discipline
vocabulary.notes: Porta reduces all natural magic to a single explanatory principle: sympathetic resonance

source_notes: Giambattista della Porta's Magia Naturalis (1558, expanded 1589) was the most popular natural magic compendium of the Renaissance, translated into six languages. Its claim that all magical effects reduce to natural sympathy and antipathy — rather than demonic pact — was the definitive public defense of natural magic. The book covers optics, cryptography, magnetism, plant lore, and practical chemistry, presenting them all as branches of a unified science of hidden correspondences.
bibliography: Della Porta, Giambattista. Natural Magick. London, 1658. Reprint New York: Basic Books, 1957.
Eamon, William. Science and the Secrets of Nature: Books of Secrets in Medieval and Early Modern Culture. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1994.

title: Astronomia Magna — The Light of Nature
author: Paracelsus
