latin_text: Homo habet duas luces: lumen naturae et lumen fidei. Per lumen naturae cognoscit res naturales et occultas, et potest praedicere futura ex signis naturalibus, et hoc est opus astrologorum et magorum. Per lumen fidei autem cognoscit ea quae sunt supra naturam et ultra rationem humanam. Lumen naturae vero non est inferius lumine fidei, quia est donum Dei pariter. Et qui lumen naturae habet perfecte, is aliquam partem Dei in se habet.
english_gloss: Man has two lights: the light of nature and the light of faith. Through the light of nature he knows natural and hidden things, and can predict the future from natural signs, and this is the work of astrologers and magi. But through the light of faith he knows those things which are above nature and beyond human reason. The light of nature is no inferior to the light of faith, since it too is a gift of God equally. And whoever has the light of nature perfectly, has in himself some part of God.

vocabulary.english: light of nature — Paracelsus's term for the innate knowledge given to man at creation
vocabulary.notes: A kind of natural revelation parallel to scriptural revelation; both are divine gifts

vocabulary.english: light of faith — theological knowledge, scripture and revelation
vocabulary.notes: Paracelsus insists both lights are equal gifts of God — a provocative equalizing of magic and religion

vocabulary.english: magi — those who possess and use the light of nature professionally
vocabulary.notes: Paracelsus uses magus positively: the physician-philosopher who reads nature's hidden text

vocabulary.english: predict the future from natural signs
vocabulary.notes: Natural prophecy: not demonic divination but reading the signatures God has written into nature

vocabulary.english: some part of God — the divine spark in the human who perfects natural knowledge
vocabulary.notes: Paracelsus's pantheistic streak: the perfected natural philosopher participates in divinity

source_notes: Paracelsus's Astronomia Magna (1537) is his most comprehensive philosophical work, also known as Philosophia Sagax. The 'two lights' doctrine — lumen naturae and lumen fidei as equal divine gifts — was his theological justification for the magician-physician's project. By arguing that natural knowledge is as divine as scripture, Paracelsus challenged both Scholastic philosophy and Protestant-era skepticism about natural magic.
bibliography: Paracelsus. Astronomia Magna. In Sämtliche Werke, ed. Karl Sudhoff. Munich: Barth, 1922–33. Vol. 12.
Webster, Charles. Paracelsus: Medicine, Magic and Mission at the End of Time. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2008.

title: Liber Iuratus — Achieving the Beatific Vision by Magic
author: Honorius of Thebes (attr.)
latin_text: Ad videndum faciem Dei et beatitudinem aeternam consequendam, hoc modo procedat operarius. Primo per novem dies ieiunet et oret continue, et a mulierum consortio abstineat. Post novem dies in loco mundo et secreto circulum componat cum nominibus Dei magnis et signo crucis in quatuor partibus. Deinde orationem magnam dicat quae incipit: O Deus qui es in caelis. Tunc angelus tuus appareat et ostendat tibi visionem gloriae tuae.
english_gloss: To see the face of God and obtain eternal beatitude, let the operator proceed in this way. First let him fast for nine days and pray continuously, and abstain from the company of women. After nine days in a clean and secret place let him compose a circle with the great names of God and the sign of the cross in four parts. Then let him say the great prayer which begins: O God who art in the heavens. Then your angel shall appear and show you a vision of your glory.

vocabulary.english: beatific vision — the direct sight of God, normally reserved for heaven
vocabulary.notes: The Liber Iuratus claims to achieve in this life what theology reserves for the afterlife — an enormously ambitious claim

vocabulary.english: nine-day fast — the extended preparatory ascesis
vocabulary.notes: Nine = 3x3: the triple Trinity; the number appears throughout Solomonic preparation requirements

vocabulary.english: magical circle — the protective geometric space for ritual operation
vocabulary.notes: The circle protects the operator from hostile forces while concentrating divine presence

vocabulary.english: great names of God — the divine names used in circle construction
vocabulary.notes: The Liber Iuratus contains a 'seal of God' (sigillum Dei) composed of 72 divine names

vocabulary.english: your angel — the personal guardian angel who effects the vision
vocabulary.notes: The Liber Iuratus frames its operation as summoning one's own holy guardian angel, not a demon

source_notes: The Liber Iuratus (Sworn Book of Honorius, c. 13th century) claims to achieve the beatific vision — the direct sight of God — through an elaborate magical operation combining fasting, prayer, and ritual circle-work. It represents the extreme of the angelic magic tradition: not merely communicating with angels but achieving, in this life, the state of divine union normally reserved for death. It influenced Dee's angelology and the entire tradition of 'holy guardian angel' magic.
bibliography: Sworn Book of Honorius: Liber Iuratus Honorii. Trans. Joseph H. Peterson. Twilit Grotto, 2004.
Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages and Renaissance. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: 1 Samuel 28 — Saul and the Witch of Endor
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Et dixit Saul servis suis: Quaerite mihi mulierem habentem pythonem, et vadam ad eam et sciscitabor per eam. Et dixerunt servi eius: Est mulier Pythonem habens in Aendor. Igitur mutavit Saul habitum suum, induitque se vestimentis alienis et abiit ipse et duo viri cum eo, veneruntque ad mulierem nocte. Et ait: Divina mihi in pythone, et suscita mihi quem dixero tibi. Dixit autem mulier ad eum: Ascende Samuel. Cumque vidisset mulier Samuelem, exclamavit voce magna.
english_gloss: And Saul said to his servants: Seek me a woman who has a familiar spirit, and I will go to her and inquire through her. And his servants said to him: There is a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor. Therefore Saul changed his appearance, putting on other garments, and went out, he and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night. And he said: Divine for me through a familiar spirit, and raise up for me the one I shall name. And the woman said to him: Bring up Samuel. And when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a great voice.

vocabulary.english: familiar spirit, divining spirit (from Greek Python)
vocabulary.notes: The Vulgate's rendering of the Hebrew ob — the spirit used in necromantic consultation; also the spirit of the Delphic oracle

vocabulary.english: divine for me — the technical term for the necromantic consultation
vocabulary.notes: Divinare: the same root as 'divination'; here specifically 'make inquiry of the dead'

vocabulary.english: raise up for me — the act of necromantic summoning of the dead
vocabulary.notes: Suscitare: to raise, rouse; the Vulgate's term for the necromantic act of raising Samuel

vocabulary.english: having a python/familiar spirit — the biblical term for the necromantic specialist
vocabulary.notes: The Witch of Endor was the paradigm case cited in every medieval and Renaissance discussion of necromancy

source_notes: 1 Samuel 28 — Saul's consultation with the Witch of Endor to raise the ghost of Samuel — was the most cited biblical text in all medieval and Renaissance discussions of necromancy. Its interpretation was deeply contested: did Samuel actually appear, or was it a demon imitating him? Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin, and Luther all argued about it. The passage established the scriptural precedent for both the possibility and the sinfulness of necromantic consultation.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. R. Weber and R. Gryson. Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994.
Schmitt, Jean-Claude. Ghosts in the Middle Ages: The Living and the Dead in Medieval Society. Trans. Teresa Lavender Fagan. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1998.

title: Testament of Solomon — Solomon Binds Asmodeus
author: Anon. (attrib. Solomon)
latin_text: Et adduxi Asmodeum ante me, et interrogavi eum: Qui es tu? Et respondit: Ego sum Asmodeus, daemon princeps, et nomen meum est odium. Suscito uxores adversus maritos earum et segregate eos; stringo virgines et non patior eas nuptum ire. Et dixi ei: In nomine Dei vivi, in annulo tuo quid sit scribe. Et scripsit: Raffael archangelus sub regem Salomonem ligabit me et vinciet me in oleum septuaginta dies.
english_gloss: And I led Asmodeus before me, and questioned him: Who are you? And he replied: I am Asmodeus, a prince of daemons, and my name means hatred. I stir up wives against their husbands and separate them; I bind virgins and do not permit them to be married. And I said to him: In the name of the living God, write what is contained in your ring. And he wrote: The archangel Raphael, under King Solomon, will bind me and chain me in oil for seventy days.

vocabulary.english: Asmodeus — the prince of daemons associated with lust and marital discord
vocabulary.notes: From Hebrew Ashmedai; identified with the demon in the Book of Tobit who killed Sarah's seven husbands

vocabulary.english: prince of daemons — Asmodeus's rank in the demonic hierarchy
vocabulary.notes: Each demon has a rank and a specific sphere of harmful activity

vocabulary.english: will bind me — the demonic confession of its own future defeat
vocabulary.notes: The testament genre: demons confess their weaknesses and the names of angels that bind them

vocabulary.english: Raphael the archangel — the specific divine power that neutralizes Asmodeus
vocabulary.notes: From Tobit: Raphael binds Asmodeus in Upper Egypt; the testament systematizes these angel-demon pairings

source_notes: The Testament of Solomon (Greek original, c. 1st–5th century CE, later Latin versions) presents Solomon as a master demonologist who interrogates and binds demons using God's power. Each demon confesses its harmful activities and the angel that defeats it — a systematic demonological catalogue in narrative form. It was foundational for Solomonic magic, providing the template of hierarchical demon-binding that runs from the Ars Goetia to the grimoire tradition.
bibliography: Testament of Solomon. Trans. D.C. Duling. In The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, ed. J.H. Charlesworth. Garden City: Doubleday, 1983.
Torijano, Pablo A. Solomon the Esoteric King. Leiden: Brill, 2002.

title: Sacred Magic of Abramelin — Obtaining the Holy Guardian Angel
author: Abraham of Worms (attr.)
work: The Book of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage
latin_text: Si vis angelum tuum sanctum et custodem tuum videre et habere, per sex menses oportet te ieiunare et orare et ab omnibus mundanis rebus abstinere et in castitate et puritate vivere. Et in ultimo die operationis, post matutinas orationes, sedebis in oratorio tuo quod praeparasti, et veniet angelus tuus in forma lucis et loquetur tecum et dabit tibi sigillum suum et nomen suum, et inde eris protectus ab omnibus daemonibus et potestatem habebis super omnes spiritus.
english_gloss: If you wish to see and have your holy angel and guardian, for six months you must fast and pray and abstain from all worldly things and live in chastity and purity. And on the last day of the operation, after the morning prayers, you will sit in your oratory which you have prepared, and your angel will come in the form of light and speak with you and give you his seal and his name, and thereafter you will be protected from all daemons and will have power over all spirits.

vocabulary.english: holy angel and guardian — the holy guardian angel (HGA) of the Abramelin operation
vocabulary.notes: Every soul has a personal guardian angel; the Abramelin operation makes this relationship conscious and direct

vocabulary.english: oratory, prayer room — the specially prepared ritual space
vocabulary.notes: The Abramelin operation requires a purpose-built oratory: a room with specific dimensions and ritual equipment

vocabulary.english: in the form of light — the angel's mode of appearance
vocabulary.notes: Angels appear as light: the association with Lucifer (light-bearer) and the divine radiance

vocabulary.english: seal and name — the angel's two identifying elements
vocabulary.notes: Name = power to call; seal = graphic signature through which the angel acts

vocabulary.english: you will have power over all spirits — the result of HGA contact
vocabulary.notes: The HGA grants mastery over all inferior spirits — the prerequisite for demonic operations in the Abramelin system

source_notes: The Book of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage (German original c. 1458, French 17th-century version, English translation by MacGregor Mathers 1897) describes an 18-month (or 6-month) operation to contact one's Holy Guardian Angel. It became enormously influential on modern ceremonial magic through Aleister Crowley. The concept of the HGA as the true self and master of all demonic operations derives from this text.
bibliography: Abraham of Worms. The Book of Abramelin. Trans. Georg Dehn and Steven Guth. Lake Worth: Ibis Press, 2006.
Hanegraaff, Wouter J. Esotericism and the Academy: Rejected Knowledge in Western Culture. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012.

title: Munich Necromancer's Manual — Experiment at the Tomb
author: Anon.
latin_text: Ad evocandum spiritum mortui: Vade ad sepulcrum eius in nocte media et percute super lapidem sepulcri ter cum cultello et dic: N. qui in hoc sepulcro iaces, per Deum vivum et verum et per virtutem animarum purgatorii, resurge et responde mihi quaesitioni meae. Et si non venerit, dic iterum; et si adhuc non venerit, springe tres guttas de sanguine tuo super lapidem.
english_gloss: To evoke the spirit of a dead person: Go to his tomb at midnight and strike upon the gravestone three times with a knife and say: N. who lies in this tomb, by the living and true God and by the power of the souls of purgatory, rise up and answer my question. And if he does not come, say it again; and if he still does not come, sprinkle three drops of your blood upon the stone.

vocabulary.english: tomb, grave, sepulchre — the site of the necromantic operation
vocabulary.notes: The grave as liminal space: the boundary between the living world and the dead

vocabulary.english: midnight, the middle hour of night — the traditional time for necromantic work
vocabulary.notes: Midnight inverts midday (God's hour); it is the hour of the dead in folklore across cultures

vocabulary.english: by the power of the souls of purgatory
vocabulary.notes: Uniquely medieval: invoking purgatory as an adjuration — those trapped between worlds are summoned

vocabulary.english: three drops of blood — the necromancer's self-sacrifice to compel the spirit
vocabulary.notes: Blood = life = bargaining chip; offering your own life-force to the dead in exchange for speech

source_notes: The Munich Manual (Clm 849, c. 1440s) is one of the most complete surviving necromantic handbooks. This tomb experiment combines the classical tradition (midnight, graveside conjuration) with specifically Christian elements (purgatory, divine adjuration). Richard Kieckhefer's analysis in Magic in the Middle Ages established the standard scholarly reading of such texts as part of a 'clerical underworld' — learned men using university-acquired techniques outside institutional channels.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.
Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1998.

title: Discovery of Witchcraft — Skepticism About Necromancy
author: Reginald Scot
latin_text: Necromantici asserunt se per artem suam mortuos suscitare et eis loqui posse, et ita futura praenoscere. Sed haec omnia illusiones sunt et fraudes, quia anima semel ex corpore egressa nunquam in corpus redit per humanam artem. Si autem aliquid apparet, aut est diabolus in forma mortui, aut melancholica imaginatio spectantis. Vera scientia talia miracula reiicit et solis naturae viribus confidit.
english_gloss: Necromancers assert that through their art they can raise the dead and speak with them, and thus foreknow the future. But all these things are illusions and frauds, because a soul once departed from the body never returns to the body through human art. If something does appear, it is either the devil in the form of the dead, or the melancholic imagination of the observer. True science rejects such miracles and trusts in the powers of nature alone.

vocabulary.english: illusions and frauds — Scot's categorical rejection of necromantic claims
vocabulary.notes: Scot's skepticism is empiricist before its time: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence

vocabulary.english: once departed — the soul's one-way exit from the body
vocabulary.notes: The Aristotelian-Christian premise: death is irreversible; what appears must be illusion or demon

vocabulary.english: the devil in the form of the dead
vocabulary.notes: The standard alternative to real ghost: if something appears, it's a demon pretending to be the deceased

vocabulary.english: melancholic imagination — the medical-psychological alternative explanation
vocabulary.notes: Following Weyer: the 'ghost' is a subjective hallucination produced by the mourner's disordered imagination

source_notes: Reginald Scot's Discovery of Witchcraft (1584) was the most thorough Renaissance skeptical treatment of magic, witchcraft, and necromancy. Arguing from natural philosophy, scripture, and common sense, Scot denied the reality of demonic pact, witches' sabbath, and necromantic contact with the dead. King James I had copies burned on his accession in 1603 — the book's influence was nevertheless pervasive, and it became a handbook for those who wished to expose fraudulent practitioners.
bibliography: Scot, Reginald. The Discovery of Witchcraft. Ed. Brinsley Nicholson. London, 1886. Reprint New York: Dover, 1972.
Clark, Stuart. Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997.

title: Clavicula Salomonis — Preparation of the Instruments
author: Anon. (attrib. Solomon)
latin_text: Instrumenta ad operationes necessaria haec sunt: gladius, virgula, candela, incensum, oleum, et pergamenum virgineum. Gladius ex ferro novo fieri debet in die Saturni in hora Saturni, et in ipso sculpantur characteres quinque planetarum et nomina angeli qui eum consecravit. Virgula ex avellana recens crescente luna scindenda est in aurora ante solis ortum. Haec omnia in aqua cum sale et hyssopo purificanda sunt ante usum.
english_gloss: The instruments necessary for operations are these: sword, wand, candle, incense, oil, and virgin parchment. The sword must be made of new iron on the day of Saturn in the hour of Saturn, and on it shall be engraved the characters of the five planets and the names of the angel who consecrated it. The wand must be cut from a fresh hazel at the waxing moon, in the dawn before sunrise. All these things must be purified before use in water with salt and hyssop.

vocabulary.english: instruments of the operation — the magical tools required for ritual
vocabulary.notes: Each Solomonic instrument is ritually constructed at the correct astrological time and consecrated

vocabulary.english: day of Saturn, hour of Saturn — Saturday at the Saturnine hour
vocabulary.notes: Planetary timing: each operation and its tools must align with the relevant planetary influence

vocabulary.english: virgin parchment — unborn-calf skin, never previously used for writing
vocabulary.notes: The extreme purity requirement: the parchment must be ritually virgin to receive the sacred characters

vocabulary.english: hyssop — the biblical purifying herb (Psalm 51:7: purge me with hyssop)
vocabulary.notes: Hyssop in ritual purification connects Solomonic magic directly to the Mosaic cultic purity code

source_notes: The Clavicula Salomonis, Book 2, details the ritual preparation of every magical instrument — each tied to planetary hours, lunar phases, and specific materials. The precision of this preparatory system (new iron on Saturday at Saturn's hour; hazel wand at waxing moon before dawn) shows how deeply medieval astrological theory penetrated practical ritual. The hyssop purification connects explicitly to Psalm 51, anchoring the operation in biblical precedent.
bibliography: Solomon. The Key of Solomon (Clavicula Salomonis). Ed. S. L. MacGregor Mathers. London: Kegan Paul, 1888.
Mathiesen, Robert. 'A Thirteenth-Century Ritual to Attain the Beatific Vision from the Key of Solomon.' Traditio 41 (1985): 175–200.

title: Ars Goetia — Bael, First Spirit of the 72
author: Anon.
latin_text: Primus spiritus et rex orientis vocatur Bael. Regit sexaginta sex legiones spirituum. Apparet in formis diversis, scilicet hominis et catti et ranae, et aliquando in omnibus simul. Loquitur voce rauca. Facit hominem invisibilem. Sigillum eius hoc est: [sigillum]. Et in ritu vocandus est in prima hora diei Iovis, et habetur in annulo aureo sub pollice dextrae manus et fumigetur cum ligno aloes.
english_gloss: The first spirit and king of the east is called Bael. He rules sixty-six legions of spirits. He appears in various forms, namely of a man and a cat and a frog, and sometimes in all at once. He speaks in a hoarse voice. He makes a man invisible. His seal is this: [seal]. And in rite he is to be called in the first hour of Thursday, and held in a gold ring under the right thumb and fumigated with aloe-wood.

vocabulary.english: king of the East — Bael's directional rulership in the demonic hierarchy
vocabulary.notes: The 72 spirits are organized by direction (East/West/North/South) and hierarchical rank

vocabulary.english: sixty-six legions — the number of spirits under Bael's command
vocabulary.notes: Each Goetic spirit commands legions; 72 spirits total with specific legion-counts

vocabulary.english: makes invisible — Bael's specific power or gift to the summoner
vocabulary.notes: Each Goetic spirit offers a specific magical service; invisibility is Bael's primary function

vocabulary.english: fumigated with aloe-wood — the specific incense for Bael's ritual
vocabulary.notes: Each spirit has its proper incense, derived from planetary correspondence (aloe = solar/lunar)

source_notes: The Ars Goetia (Part I of the Lemegeton, 17th century) presents the 72 spirits bound by Solomon's ring, each with their seal, rank, legion-count, and specific powers. The entry format — form of appearance, voice quality, powers, ritual requirements — is standardized across all 72, creating a systematic demonological database. The Goetia was influential on John Dee (via the earlier Weyer source) and became central to modern ceremonial magic through MacGregor Mathers's 1904 edition.
bibliography: Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis: The Lesser Key of Solomon. Ed. Joseph H. Peterson. York Beach: Weiser, 2001.
Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

title: Inferno XX — The Punishment of Diviners and Necromancers
author: Dante Alighieri
latin_text: Vidi Anfiarao, Tiresias, Aronta, Manto, la Sibilla, Michel Scotto, e altri molti. Costoro che lagrimando a forza tendono il viso in dietro, perché 'l volere vedere innanzi tolto lor fu: così quel colui che de l'arte magica era sì bello. Similiter latinorum poetarum tradicio habet divinatores et nectomanticos in circulo quarto Malebolge puniri, conversis capitibus post tergum.
english_gloss: I saw Amphiaraus, Tiresias, Aruns, Manto, the Sibyl, Michael Scot, and many others. These who weeping are forced to turn their faces backward, because the desire to see ahead was taken from them: such is the punishment of those who in the art of magic were so beautiful. Similarly the Latin poetic tradition holds that diviners and necromancers are punished in the fourth ditch of Malebolge, with their heads twisted backward.

vocabulary.english: Michael Scot — the 13th-century astrologer and translator placed in Hell by Dante
vocabulary.notes: Michael Scot translated Aristotle and served at Frederick II's court; his reputation for magic sent him to Inferno XX

vocabulary.english: necromancers — those who attempted to know the future through the dead
vocabulary.notes: Dante's term echoes the Greek nekromanteia; the spelling 'necto-' appears in some manuscripts

vocabulary.english: with heads turned backward — the contrapasso (fitting punishment)
vocabulary.notes: The diviners who looked too far forward now can only look backward: Dante's moral poetics at work

vocabulary.english: Malebolge — the 8th circle of Hell, the Pit of Evil Pouches
vocabulary.notes: The 10 ditches of Malebolge punish different forms of fraud; divination occupies the fourth

source_notes: Inferno XX places diviners, astrologers, and necromancers in the 8th circle (Malebolge, 4th pit), their heads permanently twisted backward as a contrapasso for presuming to see forward in time. Dante specifically names Michael Scot (Frederick II's court astrologer) and references Tiresias, Amphiaraus, and Manto. The canto is a canonical medieval statement on the theological-moral status of prophetic arts.
bibliography: Dante Alighieri. The Divine Comedy, Inferno. Trans. Robert Hollander and Jean Hollander. New York: Doubleday, 2000.
Freccero, John. Dante: The Poetics of Conversion. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1986.

title: Munich Necromancer's Manual — Image Magic to Harm
author: Anon.
latin_text: Ut hominem infirmes vel occidas per imaginem: Fac imaginem de cera alba ad similitudinem eius quem infirmare vis, et in ipsa imagine iunge membra sicut in homine vivo iunguntur. Deinde baptiza imaginem nomine eius quem significat, et dic: Sicut haec imago languescit, ita languescit N. Et transfige imaginem acu ferrea in locis ubi vis eum infirmari.
english_gloss: To make a person ill or kill them through an image: Make an image from white wax in the likeness of the one you wish to make ill, and in that image join the limbs as they are joined in a living person. Then baptize the image with the name of the one it represents, and say: As this image languishes, so languishes N. And pierce the image with an iron needle in the places where you wish him to be ill.

vocabulary.english: wax image, effigy — the substrate of image magic (voodoo doll)
vocabulary.notes: From Greek kolossoi: ritual substitutes with the power of the original through naming

vocabulary.english: baptize the image — the Christianizing perversion of the sacrament
vocabulary.notes: Ritual naming through mock-baptism creates a magical link (correspondence) between image and person

vocabulary.english: as the image languishes — the sympathetic magic formula
vocabulary.notes: The simile-formula: 'as X does, so Y does' is the structural grammar of sympathetic magic across cultures

vocabulary.english: iron needle — the instrument of harm, piercing the representative image
vocabulary.notes: Iron in magic: cold iron repels fairies, but worked iron (forged) concentrates and directs harmful force

source_notes: Wax image magic (imago cerae) — making a doll resembling the target, naming it for them, and then harming the doll — is one of the oldest and most widespread magical practices documented. The Munich Manual's version adds the uniquely medieval element of mock-baptism: by giving the image a name through the baptismal formula, it becomes magically identified with the target person. This is the basis for countless witch trial accusations of image magic.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. University Park: Penn State University Press, 1998.
Faraone, Christopher A. Talismans and Trojan Horses: Guardian Statues in Ancient Greek Myth and Ritual. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum — The Nature of the Philosopher's Stone
author: Arnald of Villanova (attr.)
latin_text: Lapis philosophorum non est lapis nec metal sed est spiritus et corpus et anima simul. Est medicina universalis quae omnia metalla ad perfectionem perducit et omnes infirmitates humanas curat. Non invenietur in montibus nec in silvis, sed in mente solis philosophi qui intelligit quod antiqui sapientes scripserunt. Est vilis in pretio et in omni loco haberi potest ab illis qui oculos intelligentiae habent.
english_gloss: The philosopher's stone is not a stone nor a metal but is spirit and body and soul simultaneously. It is the universal medicine which leads all metals to perfection and cures all human illnesses. It will not be found in mountains nor in forests, but in the mind of the true philosopher who understands what the ancient wise men wrote. It is cheap in price and can be obtained in every place by those who have the eyes of understanding.

vocabulary.english: philosopher's stone — the supreme goal of alchemical work
vocabulary.notes: The 'stone' is paradoxically not a stone; the name is itself an enigma or riddle

vocabulary.english: spirit, body, and soul — the tripartite alchemical constitution mirroring human nature
vocabulary.notes: Paracelsian tria prima (mercury/sulphur/salt) is a later version of this trinity

vocabulary.english: universal medicine, panacea — the stone's healing function
vocabulary.notes: The stone transmutes metals AND heals diseases: physical and human-medical gold-making are one operation

vocabulary.english: in the mind of the philosopher — the stone is as much a mental as a physical achievement
vocabulary.notes: The spiritual/psychological interpretation: the stone represents the philosopher's own purification

source_notes: The Rosarium Philosophorum (c. 1350, attributed to Arnald of Villanova) was one of the most widely circulated alchemical texts of the late medieval period. Its description of the philosopher's stone as simultaneously stone/not-stone, cheap/precious, everywhere/nowhere encapsulates the paradoxical, riddling language of alchemical writing. The famous illustrated 1550 printed edition with its woodcuts of the royal couple in the bath became canonical for alchemical iconography.
bibliography: Arnald of Villanova. Rosarium Philosophorum. In Theatrum Chemicum, vol. 1. Ursel, 1602.
Obrist, Barbara. Les débuts de l'imagerie alchimique (XIVe–XVe siècles). Paris: Le Sycomore, 1982.

title: Consolatio Philosophiae — Fortune and Divine Providence
author: Boethius
latin_text: Haec nostra vis est, hunc continuum ludum ludimus. Rotam volubili orbe versamus; infima summis, summa infimis mutare gaudemus. Ascende si placet, sed ea lege ne utique cum lusum meum exegerit, descendere iniuriam putes. An tu mores ignorabas meos? Nesciebas Croesum regem Lydorum Cyro paulo ante formidabilem mox deinde victori flebilem fuisse? Quid nisi fortunae crimen expectas?
english_gloss: This is our power, this is the continuous game we play. We turn the wheel with whirling orbit; we take delight in changing high things to low, and low to high. Rise if you wish, but with this condition, that you think it no injustice when by the rule of my play you descend. Did you not know my ways? Did you not know that Croesus, king of the Lydians, shortly before formidable to Cyrus, was soon after pitiful to the victor? What do you expect but Fortune's crime?

vocabulary.english: Fortune's wheel — the image of constant revolution of good and bad
vocabulary.notes: The most influential medieval image of fate: the wheel that raises and lowers all worldly fortune

vocabulary.english: whirling orbit, rolling sphere — the wheel's unstoppable revolution
vocabulary.notes: Volubilis: from volvere (to roll); the wheel as time's visible embodiment

vocabulary.english: changing low things to high — Fortune's constitutional nature is reversal
vocabulary.notes: Fortune cannot be just or unjust because reversal IS her nature; she has no other mode

vocabulary.english: Fortune's crime — what a foolish person blames, not understanding Fortune's nature
vocabulary.notes: Boethius's therapeutic argument: Fortune is not criminal; only our attachment to her gifts is the problem

source_notes: Boethius's Consolatio Philosophiae (524 CE), written while awaiting execution, was the most-read philosophical text in medieval Europe after the Bible. Fortune's Wheel became the central medieval image for the instability of earthly goods — cited in every discussion of fate, astrology, and providence. The Consolatio shaped the intellectual framework within which medieval scholars discussed whether astral fate was compatible with free will and divine providence.
bibliography: Boethius. The Consolation of Philosophy. Trans. V.E. Watts. Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1969.
Courcelle, Pierre. La Consolation de Philosophie dans la tradition littéraire. Paris: Études Augustiniennes, 1967.

title: De Sphaera — On the Fixed Stars and Their Power
author: Johannes de Sacrobosco
latin_text: Sphaera igitur stellarum fixarum est ultima et nobilissima inter sphaeras corporeas, et virtutes suas influentes in omnes alias sphaeras et in mundum subsolarem per radios suos transmittit. Stellae autem fixae non moventur per motum proprium sed per motum firmamenti communem in motu diurno. Stellae errantes autem, id est planetae, praeter motum communem motus proprios habent in zodiacum contra firmamentum.
english_gloss: The sphere of the fixed stars is therefore the highest and most noble among the corporeal spheres, and transmits its influencing powers into all other spheres and into the sublunar world through its rays. But the fixed stars are not moved by their own motion but by the common motion of the firmament in the daily revolution. The wandering stars, however, that is the planets, besides the common motion, have their own motions in the zodiac against the firmament.

vocabulary.english: sphere of the fixed stars — the eighth heaven in Ptolemaic cosmology
vocabulary.notes: The fixed stars = eighth sphere; beyond are the primum mobile and empyreum

vocabulary.english: wandering stars — the planets (from Greek planetes, 'wanderers')
vocabulary.notes: Planets = those that wander against the background of fixed stars; 7 in classical cosmology

vocabulary.english: zodiac — the belt of 12 constellations through which the planets travel
vocabulary.notes: Greek zoidiakon kyklos: the circle of animals through which planets pass, forming horoscopes

vocabulary.english: daily motion — the apparent revolution of the whole sky from east to west in 24 hours
vocabulary.notes: Caused by the primum mobile (first mover) rotating the entire celestial sphere

source_notes: Sacrobosco's De Sphaera (c. 1230) was the standard introductory astronomy text at every medieval European university for 400 years. It provided the cosmological framework — geocentric spheres, fixed stars, planetary orbits, zodiacal belt — that every educated person shared, including every practitioner of astrology, talisman magic, and medical astrology. Without this shared cosmological vocabulary, Renaissance magic is unintelligible.
bibliography: Sacrobosco, Johannes de. The Sphere of Sacrobosco and Its Commentators. Ed. Lynn Thorndike. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1949.
Grant, Edward. Planets, Stars, and Orbs: The Medieval Cosmos, 1200–1687. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1994.

title: Commentarium Magnum — The Active Intellect
author: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
work: Commentarium Magnum in Aristotelis De Anima
latin_text: Intellectus agens est substantia separata ab omnibus corporeis rebus, unica et communis omnibus hominibus, non multiplicabilis in multis. Per hunc intellectum agentem, qui est quasi sol animarum, illuminantur intellectus materiales hominum et fiunt actu intelligentes. Ideo qui velit perficere animam suam et attingere intelligentiam perfectam, debet se disponere ad receptionem influxus intellectus agentis per puritatem et studium.
english_gloss: The active intellect is a substance separate from all bodily things, single and common to all humans, not capable of multiplication in many. Through this active intellect, which is as it were the sun of souls, the material intellects of men are illuminated and become actually intelligent. Therefore whoever wishes to perfect his soul and attain perfect intelligence must dispose himself to receive the influx of the active intellect through purity and study.

vocabulary.english: active intellect (nous poietikos) — the divine intelligence that illuminates human thought
vocabulary.notes: Averroes's controversial thesis: one single agent intellect shared by all humans, not individual

vocabulary.english: separate substance — a non-material, non-bodily being (an angel in Scholastic terms)
vocabulary.notes: The active intellect is angelic-level in nature; human souls are illuminated from above, not self-illuminating

vocabulary.english: sun of souls — the metaphor for the active intellect as light-source for human minds
vocabulary.notes: The active intellect is to souls as the sun is to eyes; it makes actual intelligibility possible

vocabulary.english: influx of the intellect — the downward radiation of intelligibility
vocabulary.notes: Influxus: the same word as for stellar influence; intellectual illumination and magical influence share a structure

source_notes: Averroes's Commentarium Magnum on Aristotle's De Anima (c. 1180, Latin translation c. 1225) made the 'unity of the intellect' doctrine famous and controversial in medieval Europe. The claim that all humans share one active intellect (rather than each having their own) was condemned by the Bishop of Paris in 1270 and 1277. But it was also philosophically powerful: if the active intellect is the 'sun of souls,' then magical illumination, prophetic inspiration, and rational thought all operate through the same cosmic mechanism.
bibliography: Averroes. Long Commentary on the De Anima of Aristotle. Trans. Richard C. Taylor. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2009.
Davidson, Herbert A. Alfarabi, Avicenna, and Averroes on Intellect. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992.

title: Picatrix — On the Spirits of the Hours and Talisman Making
author: Anon. (trans. from Arabic)
latin_text: Omnis hora diei et noctis habet spiritum et angelum proprium a Deo ordinatum. Et quando vis facere imaginem ad aliquem effectum, debes eligere horam et diem convenientem planete cuius est effectus quem desideras. Et debes incipere laborem tuum in hora ascensus illius planete in oriente, et debes habere in animo effectum desideratum et totam voluntatem tuam in hoc solo. Tunc imago capit virtutem a spiritu horae et a planeta dominante.
english_gloss: Every hour of day and night has its own spirit and angel ordained by God. And when you wish to make an image for some effect, you must choose the hour and day fitting to the planet whose effect you desire. And you must begin your work in the hour when that planet is rising in the east, and you must have in mind the desired effect and your whole will concentrated on this alone. Then the image takes on power from the spirit of the hour and from the ruling planet.

vocabulary.english: spirit of the hour — the presiding angelic power for each planetary hour
vocabulary.notes: Each of the 24 hours has a ruling planet (the planetary hour system); each planet has an angel-spirit

vocabulary.english: image, talisman — an object made to capture celestial power
vocabulary.notes: The imago is the physical receptacle for the celestial virtue flowing from the ruling planet and hour-spirit

vocabulary.english: the planet's rising in the east — the optimal talisman-making moment
vocabulary.notes: Rising = the planet is in maximum strength; this is the horoscopic ascendant moment

vocabulary.english: whole will — the operator's concentrated intention as a component of talisman efficacy
vocabulary.notes: Avicennan imaginatio + astrological timing: both contribute to the talisman's power

source_notes: Picatrix (Ghayat al-Hikam, 'Goal of the Wise', Arabic c. 1000, Latin translation c. 1256) is the most comprehensive handbook of astrological talismanic magic. Its doctrine that each hour has a presiding spirit/angel, and that talismans must be made at precisely the right astrological moment with the operator's full imaginative attention, synthesizes Al-Kindi's rays, Avicenna's imaginatio, and Neoplatonic spirit-theory into a complete magical system.
bibliography: Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic. Trans. Dan Attrell and David Porreca. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.
Pingree, David. 'The Diffusion of Arabic Magical Texts in Western Europe.' In La diffusione delle scienze islamiche nel medio evo europeo. Rome: Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei, 1987.

title: De Daemonibus — On the Material Daemons
author: Michael Psellus
latin_text: Daemones aliqui habent corpus aethereum et tenue, aliqui corpus aereum, aliqui corpus ignis vel aquae vel terrae. Et secundum corporis naturam variant loca ubi habitant et opera quae faciunt. Daemones aquei amant aquas et lacus et flumina, et per aquam operantur et tempestates movent. Daemones terrei habitant subterranea et fodinas metallis plenas, et hi metalla et thesauros custodiunt.
english_gloss: Some daemons have a body of ether or fine substance, some a body of air, some a body of fire or water or earth. And according to the nature of their body they vary in the places where they dwell and the works they perform. Watery daemons love waters, lakes, and rivers, and operate through water and stir up storms. Earthy daemons inhabit underground spaces and mines full of metals, and these guard metals and treasures.

vocabulary.english: ethereal daemon — highest class, composed of fine aetheric matter
vocabulary.notes: Psellus revives the Neoplatonic daemon hierarchy: daemons are real, embodied, and graduated by their matter

vocabulary.english: aerial body — a fine physical body composed of air (not mere spirit)
vocabulary.notes: Daemons have genuine bodies, just subtler than human ones; this explains their powers and limitations

vocabulary.english: watery daemons, water-spirits — the class associated with bodies of water
vocabulary.notes: Medieval nature-spirits rationalized: undines, nixies, river-spirits = daemons of the water element

vocabulary.english: they guard treasures — earth-daemons as treasure-guardians
vocabulary.notes: A universal folk-belief rationalized: dwarfs and gnomes are earth-daemons in this taxonomy

source_notes: Michael Psellus's De Daemonibus (11th century, translated to Latin c. 13th century) revived the full Neoplatonic daemon doctrine for Byzantine and then Latin Europe. By classifying daemons according to their elemental bodies (ether/air/fire/water/earth/subterranean), he provided a natural-philosophical taxonomy for beings that medieval Christianity tended to collapse into the single category of 'devil'. The text influenced Agrippa's classification of spirits in De Occulta Philosophia Book 3.
bibliography: Psellus, Michael. De Daemonibus. In Bibliotheque de Photius, ed. Henry. Paris, 1857.
Culianu, Ioan P. Eros and Magic in the Renaissance. Trans. Margaret Cook. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1987.

title: Naturalis Historia — Magical Uses of Plants
author: Pliny the Elder
latin_text: Herba verbena et herba artemisia inter omnes herbas ad magica opera potentissimae existimantur. Verbena quam Romani verbenacam appellant, si aspergitur in triclinio, laetitiam facit convivantibus. Artemisiam quam Graeci parthenion vocant, viatores sub pedibus calcant ne lassitudine in via opprimentur. Mandragora autem, quam Circe in veneficiis usus esse dicitur, si ex parte sinistra terrae effoditur cum incantationibus, soporem inducit.
english_gloss: The herb vervain and the herb artemisia are considered the most powerful of all herbs for magical works. Vervain, which the Romans call verbenacea, if sprinkled in a dining room, brings joy to those dining there. Artemisia, which the Greeks call parthenion, travelers tread beneath their feet so they are not overcome by fatigue on the road. But mandrake, which Circe is said to have used in her poisonings, if dug from the left side of the earth with incantations, induces sleep.

vocabulary.english: sacred vervain — a ritual herb used in Roman religious and magical ceremonies
vocabulary.notes: Verbena was the Roman fetial herb: carried by ambassadors and used to consecrate altars

vocabulary.english: artemisia — a genus of aromatic plants (wormwood, mugwort) with strong magical associations
vocabulary.notes: Named for Artemis/Diana; its protection of travelers = a natural quality not merely a superstition

vocabulary.english: mandrake — the paradigm magical plant, its root resembling a human body
vocabulary.notes: The mandrake 'scream' when uprooted, the human-form root, and the narcotic properties made it central to magical botany

vocabulary.english: with incantations, spoken charms — spoken words accompanying the gathering of plants
vocabulary.notes: Pliny reports the incantations but characteristically distances himself: he is recording not endorsing

source_notes: Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (77 CE) books 24–27 are the most comprehensive ancient source for the magical uses of plants, recording an enormous body of folk practice that Pliny typically distances himself from while faithfully preserving. The mandrake, vervain, artemisia, and other 'magical herbs' described here passed directly into medieval herbalism, Albertus Magnus's De Vegetabilibus, and the Renaissance natural magic tradition.
bibliography: Pliny the Elder. Natural History. Trans. H. Rackham et al. 10 vols. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1938–62.
Ogden, Daniel. Magic, Witchcraft, and Ghosts in the Greek and Roman Worlds. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2002.

title: Geomantia — The Sixteen Geomantic Figures
author: Anon. (attrib. Gerard of Cremona)
latin_text: Sedecim sunt figurae geomanticae, quarum prima vocatur Via et est omnium via et iter; secunda Populus et significat multitudinem. Tertia vocatur Laetitia et est figura benigna et fortunata; quarta Tristitia, maligna et mala. Carcer captivum et constrictum significat; Cauda Draconis exitum et finem. Caput Draconis ingressum et initium. Fortuna Minor et Maior bona et mala quidem portendunt. Ex his figurarum combinationibus omnia futura in quatuordecim domibus caeli indicantur.
english_gloss: There are sixteen geomantic figures, the first of which is called Via (Way) and is the way and path of all things; the second Populus (People) and signifies a multitude. The third is called Laetitia (Joy) and is a benign and fortunate figure; the fourth Tristitia (Sadness), malign and bad. Carcer (Prison) signifies the captive and constricted; Cauda Draconis (Tail of the Dragon) signifies exit and ending. Caput Draconis (Head of the Dragon) signifies entrance and beginning. Fortuna Minor and Fortuna Major portend good and bad respectively. From the combinations of these figures all future things are indicated in the fourteen houses of heaven.

vocabulary.english: geomantic figures — the 16 dot-patterns that are the alphabet of geomancy
vocabulary.notes: Each figure = a pattern of single/double dots in 4 rows; created by random marking and then systematically derived

vocabulary.english: Way/Road — a geomantic figure associated with travel, change, movement
vocabulary.notes: Via = 8 single dots (1.1.1.1): maximum odd points; pure motion, no fixed structure

vocabulary.english: Head and Tail of the Dragon — the lunar nodes as geomantic figures
vocabulary.notes: The lunar nodes (astronomical) became geomantic figures; Caput is always fortunate, Cauda unfortunate

vocabulary.english: fourteen houses of heaven — the geomantic houses (12 zodiacal + 2 derived)
vocabulary.notes: Geomancy maps its figures onto the 12 astrological houses, making it essentially astrological in its interpretive framework

source_notes: Medieval geomancy (from Arabic ilm al-raml, 'science of the sand') was introduced to Latin Europe c. 12th century through translations attributed to Gerard of Cremona and Hugo of Santalla. The 16 figures are generated by random dot-marking in sand or on paper, then combined through a systematic algorithm to fill 16 positions interpreted through 12 astrological houses. It was the most widely practised learned divination in medieval and Renaissance Europe.
bibliography: Burnett, Charles. 'The Earliest Chiromancy in the West.' Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 50 (1987): 189–195.
Skinner, Stephen. Terrestrial Astrology: Divination by Geomancy. London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1980.

title: Forman's Casebook — A Horary Astrological Consultation
author: Simon Forman
latin_text: Anno Domini 1597 die 15 Martii hora 3 post meridiem quaesivit a me Johanna Bulmer utrum maritus eius in peregrinatione superstes esset vel non. Ereximus figuram caeli pro hac quaestione, et ascendens erat Libra gradu 22, Luna in Cancro cum Saturno coniuncta, Sol in Piscibus. Ex his figuris iudicavi maritum adhuc vivere sed morbo laborare gravi nec ante tres menses rediturum esse.
english_gloss: In the year of Our Lord 1597, on March 15, at the third hour after noon, Johanna Bulmer asked me whether her husband was surviving on his journey abroad or not. I erected the figure of the heavens for this question, and the ascendant was Libra at degree 22, the Moon in Cancer conjoined with Saturn, the Sun in Pisces. From these figures I judged that the husband was still alive but suffering a serious illness, and would not return before three months.

vocabulary.english: we erected the figure of the heavens — the horary chart cast for the moment of the question
vocabulary.notes: Horary astrology: a chart cast for the exact moment a question is asked; the chart answers the question

vocabulary.english: the ascendant — the zodiac degree rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the question
vocabulary.notes: The ascendant = the first house cusp; it describes the querent and the immediate situation

vocabulary.english: Moon in conjunction with Saturn — unfavorable placement for travel and health
vocabulary.notes: Saturn = illness, delay, depression; Moon with Saturn in the same sign indicates difficult circumstances

vocabulary.english: question — the specific question posed by the querent that the horary chart answers
vocabulary.notes: Latin technical term for the 'quesited' in horary astrology — what is being asked about

source_notes: Simon Forman (1552–1611) was one of the most documented English astrologers and magical practitioners of the Elizabethan era. His casebooks (now in the Bodleian Library) contain thousands of consultations — clients asking whether absent loved ones were alive, whether they had been robbed, whether a business venture would succeed. Lauren Kassell's Medicine and Magic in Elizabethan London (2005) is the definitive modern study.
bibliography: Kassell, Lauren. Medicine and Magic in Elizabethan London: Simon Forman, Astrologer, Alchemist, and Physician. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 2005.
Curry, Patrick. Prophecy and Power: Astrology in Early Modern England. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1989.

title: Charitesion — A Love Charm
author: Anon.
latin_text: Ad amorem conciliandum: Scribe in tabella plumbea nomen illius quam amas et nomen matris eius, et haec verba: Atracho, Memnunebi, te per terram et mare et per ignem et per aerem adiuro, ut N. filia N. me amet et mihi soli adhaereat. Conduc tabulam sub limen eius domus aut in sepulcrum mortui recenter sepulti.
english_gloss: To bind someone in love: Write on a lead tablet the name of the one you love and the name of her mother, and these words: Atracho, Memnunebi, I adjure you through earth and sea and through fire and through air, that N. daughter of N. may love me and cling to me alone. Deposit the tablet beneath the threshold of her house or in the tomb of a recently buried dead person.

vocabulary.english: lead tablet, curse tablet — thin lead sheets inscribed with magical texts
vocabulary.notes: Lead = cold, heavy, infernal; associated with Saturn and the dead; the metal for binding and binding-charms

vocabulary.english: voces magicae — untranslatable magical names invoked as divine powers
vocabulary.notes: Drawn from the Egyptian-Greek magical papyri tradition; their power lies in their foreignness and antiquity

vocabulary.english: the mother's name — the standard magical identification using mother not father
vocabulary.notes: In ancient and medieval magic, a person is identified through their mother's name, not their father's

vocabulary.english: beneath the threshold — the liminal space between inside and outside
vocabulary.notes: The threshold is a liminal zone; depositing a binding charm there ensures the target crosses over it constantly

source_notes: Love charms on lead tablets (defixiones amatoria) are among the most abundant magical documents from antiquity. The PGM versions systematize older practice: the four-element adjuration, the mother's name identification, the burial with the dead — all draw on the principle that the powerful forces of death and the underworld can be mobilized for erotic purposes. The practice continued into medieval Europe with remarkably little modification.
bibliography: Faraone, Christopher A. Ancient Greek Love Magic. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1999.
Gager, John G., ed. Curse Tablets and Binding Spells from the Ancient World. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1992.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum — The Chemical Wedding (Coniunctio)
author: Anon.
latin_text: Rex et regina, sol et luna, sulphur et mercurius, debet in coniunctionem venire sicut mas et femina in matrimonium. Et ex hac coniunctione nascitur puer Hermetis, lapis philosophorum, perfectissima et nobilissima omnium rerum sublunarium. Haec coniunctio appellatur a philosophis nuptiae chymicae, et est principalissimus actus totius artis nostrae.
english_gloss: King and queen, sun and moon, sulphur and mercury, must come into conjunction like male and female in marriage. And from this conjunction is born the child of Hermes, the philosopher's stone, most perfect and most noble of all sublunary things. This conjunction is called by the philosophers the chemical wedding, and is the principal act of our entire art.

vocabulary.english: conjunction — the alchemical union of opposites (sulphur/mercury, king/queen)
vocabulary.notes: The great Work = the marriage and reunion of opposites that were separated at the Fall/beginning of matter

vocabulary.english: king and queen — the paired opposites (gold/silver, active/passive, fixed/volatile)
vocabulary.notes: The alchemical royal couple: Sol (gold, sulphur, fixed) marries Luna (silver, mercury, volatile)

vocabulary.english: child of Hermes — the philosopher's stone as the offspring of the alchemical marriage
vocabulary.notes: The 'Hermetic child' or filius philosophorum: what results from the perfect union of opposites

vocabulary.english: chemical wedding (nuptiae chymicae) — the alchemical marriage as the central operation
vocabulary.notes: The term Rosarium uses; later popularized in Andreae's Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosenkreutz (1616)

source_notes: The 'chemical wedding' — the union of the red king (sulphur, gold, fixed principle) with the white queen (mercury, silver, volatile principle) — is the central image of late medieval alchemy. The Rosarium Philosophorum's sequence of woodcuts showing the royal couple bathing, embracing, dying, and resurrecting together was the visual grammar of alchemical allegory. C.G. Jung's Psychology and Alchemy (1944) is the most famous modern interpretation of these images.
bibliography: Rosarium Philosophorum. Facsimile ed. with German commentary. Frankfurt: Insel, 1967.
Jung, C.G. Psychology and Alchemy. Trans. R.F.C. Hull. London: Routledge, 1953.

title: Exodus 22:18 — Maleficos Non Patieris Vivere
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Maleficos non patieris vivere. Qui coierit cum iumento morte moriatur. Qui immolat diis occidetur, praeter Domino soli. Advenae molestus non eris neque affliges eum: advenae enim et ipsi fuistis in terra Aegypti.
english_gloss: You shall not permit witches/sorcerers to live. Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death. Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone. You shall not wrong a stranger nor afflict him, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

vocabulary.english: witch, sorcerer, worker of harmful magic (from malum + facere)
vocabulary.notes: The Vulgate's rendering of the Hebrew mekhashef (one who uses sorcery); this single verse drove centuries of witch prosecution

vocabulary.english: you shall not permit to live — the death mandate
vocabulary.notes: The terse legal formula that Heinrich Kramer quoted in the Malleus Maleficarum as the scriptural basis for witch execution

vocabulary.english: sacrifices to gods — the idolatry/magic nexus in biblical law
vocabulary.notes: Sacrifice to any being other than YHWH = death; the theological ground for treating magic as equivalent to apostasy

vocabulary.english: let him die the death — the emphatic death formula (infinitive absolute)
vocabulary.notes: The Hebrew mot yumat translated as morte moriatur: the doubled death-word emphasizes absolute certainty of execution

source_notes: Exodus 22:18 — 'Maleficos non patieris vivere' — is the single most cited biblical verse in the entire history of European witch-hunting. The Malleus Maleficarum opens Part II by quoting it. The Hebrew mekhashef probably referred to a specific type of practical sorcerer, but the Vulgate's 'maleficus/malefica' was interpreted broadly to encompass all dealings with supernatural power outside the Church. The KJV's 'Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live' continues this interpretive tradition.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. R. Weber and R. Gryson. Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994.
Kors, Alan C. and Edward Peters, eds. Witchcraft in Europe, 400-1700: A Documentary History. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2001.

title: Deuteronomy 18:10–12 — The Catalogue of Forbidden Arts
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Nec inveniatur in te qui lustret filium suum aut filiam, ducens per ignem, aut qui ariolos sciscitetur et observet somnia atque auguria, nec sit maleficus, nec incantator, nec qui pythones consulat, nec divinos, aut quaerat a mortuis veritatem. Omnia enim haec abominatur Dominus, et propter istiusmodi scelera delebit eos in introitu tuo.
english_gloss: There shall not be found among you one who makes his son or daughter pass through fire, or who consults soothsayers, or who observes dreams and omens, or a sorcerer, or an enchanter, or one who consults those with familiar spirits, or diviners, or who seeks truth from the dead. For the Lord abhors all these things, and on account of these crimes he will destroy them at your entering in.

vocabulary.english: soothsayers, haruspices — those who observe entrails or signs for divination
vocabulary.notes: The Hebrew qosem: one who divines; the Vulgate's ariolus becomes Isidore's canonical term for this class of diviner

vocabulary.english: omens, augury — divination from the behavior of birds and natural signs
vocabulary.notes: The Roman augur tradition enters this biblical list; the verse became the source for all medieval catalogues of forbidden arts

vocabulary.english: enchanter, one who uses spoken charms (incantations)
vocabulary.notes: From in-cantare: to sing over, cast a spell by voice; the spoken-charm specialist

vocabulary.english: those with familiar spirits (from Greek Python — the Delphic oracle-spirit)
vocabulary.notes: The python-spirit is the same as at Endor; the Vulgate uses this Hellenistic term for the Hebrew ob (spirit of the dead)

vocabulary.english: seeks truth from the dead — necromancy as the final item on the list
vocabulary.notes: The list culminates in necromancy; the sequence from divination through enchantment to consulting the dead maps the gradient of transgression

source_notes: Deuteronomy 18:10-12 provided the canonical biblical taxonomy of forbidden magical arts. Every subsequent classification of magic in medieval and Renaissance Europe — from Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae through Hugh of St. Victor's Didascalicon to the Malleus Maleficarum — is essentially a commentary on and expansion of this Deuteronomic list. The verse's completeness made it the anchor text of the entire anti-magic tradition.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. R. Weber and R. Gryson. Stuttgart: Deutsche Bibelgesellschaft, 1994.
Flint, Valerie I.J. The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991.

title: Exodus 7:11–12 — The Magicians of Pharaoh
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Vocavit autem Pharao sapientes et maleficos, et fecerunt ipsi quoque per incantationes Aegyptias et arcana quaedam similiter. Proiecitque unusquisque virgam suam, et versae sunt in dracones: sed devoravit virga Aaron virgas eorum. Induratumque est cor Pharaonis, et non audivit eos, sicut praeceperat Dominus.
english_gloss: And Pharaoh called the wise men and the sorcerers, and they too through Egyptian incantations and certain secret arts did likewise. And each one threw down his rod, and they were turned into serpents: but Aaron's rod swallowed their rods. And Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had commanded.

vocabulary.english: wise men and sorcerers — the two categories of Pharaoh's magical court
vocabulary.notes: Hebrew chartummim (learned scribes) and mekhashefim (sorcerers); the Vulgate's pair distinguishes knowledge-magic from craft-magic

vocabulary.english: Egyptian incantations — the specific tradition of Egyptian magical speech
vocabulary.notes: Aegyptian magic was the paradigm in antiquity; the PGM is the surviving corpus of this tradition

vocabulary.english: certain secret arts — the unnamed deeper reservoir of Egyptian magical knowledge
vocabulary.notes: The deliberate vagueness: the text acknowledges real Egyptian magical power without specifying its source

vocabulary.english: Aaron's rod — the divine power through which Moses operates
vocabulary.notes: The rod-to-serpent contest was constantly cited as evidence that real magic existed — but that divine power surpassed it

vocabulary.english: Pharaoh's heart was hardened — the theological problem of divine determinism
vocabulary.notes: God hardening Pharaoh's heart: Augustine's proof-text for predestination; a crux in every theology of free will

source_notes: Exodus 7-8's contest between Moses and Pharaoh's magicians was one of the most theologically significant biblical magic passages. It established that non-Israelite magic was real but inferior to divine power — a position with enormous consequences: magic existed, it worked, but only divine power transcended it. Augustine, Aquinas, and the Malleus Maleficarum all interpreted the Egyptian magicians as demonstrating genuine demonic power subordinated to divine will.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Vulgata. Ed. Weber-Gryson. Stuttgart, 1994.
Klauck, Hans-Josef. Magic and Paganism in Early Christianity. Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 2003.

title: Numbers 22:6 — Balaam and the Power of the Curse
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Veni igitur et maledic populo huic, quia fortior me est: si quomodo possim eum percutere et eiciam de terra. Scio enim quod quem benedixeris, benedicitur, et quem maledixeris, erit maledictus. Et respondit Deus ad Balaam: Non vadas cum eis, nec maledicas populo, quoniam benedictus est.
english_gloss: Come therefore and curse this people, for they are stronger than I: perhaps I may be able to strike them and drive them out of the land. For I know that whom you bless is blessed, and whom you curse is cursed. And God answered Balaam: You shall not go with them, nor shall you curse the people, for they are blessed.

vocabulary.english: curse the people — the commissioning of professional cursing as a military weapon
vocabulary.notes: Balaam is hired as a professional curse-specialist: the curse is a real weapon in ancient Near Eastern warfare

vocabulary.english: whom you curse will be cursed — Balak's statement of the curse's efficacy
vocabulary.notes: The premise of hiring Balaam: curses are real and efficacious, not mere words; they change the metaphysical status of the target

vocabulary.english: he is blessed — God's statement that makes Balaam's curse impossible
vocabulary.notes: The theological point: divine blessing overrides human cursing; magic cannot override providence

vocabulary.english: Balaam — the Aramean diviner, paradigm case of a pagan prophet who received genuine divine communication
vocabulary.notes: Balaam is ambiguous throughout: a pagan seer who genuinely speaks God's words; later tradition made him a sorcerer

source_notes: The Balaam narrative (Numbers 22-24) was the most complex biblical magic passage — a non-Israelite professional curse-specialist who nevertheless spoke genuine divine prophecy. Later tradition (2 Peter 2:15, Jude 11, Revelation 2:14) demonized Balaam as a paradigm of magic for hire. But the text itself presents him ambiguously as a professional diviner who speaks divine truth. Philo, Origen, and rabbinic midrash all wrestled with this anomaly.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. Weber-Gryson. Stuttgart, 1994.
Levine, Baruch A. Numbers 21-36: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary. New York: Doubleday, 2000.

title: Isaiah 47:9–13 — Against the Astrologers of Babylon
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Veniant nunc astrologi tui qui contemplabantur stellas et numerabant menses, ut ab his quae ventura sunt tibi annuntient. Ecce facti sunt quasi stipula, ignis combussit eos. Non liberabunt animam suam de manu flammae. Non sunt prunae quibus calefiat homo, nec ignis ut sedeatur ad eum. Sic fuerunt tibi cum quibus laborasti, negotiatores tui a iuventute tua: unusquisque in errorem suum vadit, non est qui salvet te.
english_gloss: Let now your astrologers come, those who contemplate the stars and count the months, so that they may announce to you what is coming. Behold, they have become like stubble; fire has burned them up. They will not deliver their own soul from the hand of the flame. These are not coals to warm a man, nor a fire to sit before. Such have become to you those with whom you labored, your merchants from your youth: each goes off in his own error, there is none who saves you.

vocabulary.english: astrologers (from Greek astrologos: star-interpreter)
vocabulary.notes: The Vulgate uses the Greek loanword; in Hebrew the phrase is chozeh bakokhabim (star-gazers)

vocabulary.english: those who contemplate the stars — the meditative aspect of astrological practice
vocabulary.notes: The language of philosophical contemplation applied to star-watching: astrology as a kind of negative mysticism

vocabulary.english: counted the months — calculation of lunar/zodiacal periods for prediction
vocabulary.notes: Month-counting = the computational core of astrology: calculating zodiacal positions from calendar data

vocabulary.english: like stubble — the astrologers' inadequacy and fate made visible
vocabulary.notes: The prophetic reversal: the astrologers who predicted others' fates cannot predict their own destruction

source_notes: Isaiah 47 is the most sustained biblical polemic against Babylonian astrology. The taunt against Babylon's 'astrologers who count the months' was constantly cited by Christian anti-astrology writers — from Tertullian through Augustine to the medieval canonists. Yet the same verse system that condemned Babylonian astrology admitted that the Magi of Matthew 2 were led to Christ by a star — a tension never fully resolved.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. Weber-Gryson. Stuttgart, 1994.
Barton, Tamsyn. Ancient Astrology. London: Routledge, 1994.

title: Matthew 2:1–2 — The Magi and the Star
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Cum ergo natus esset Iesus in Bethlehem Iudaeae in diebus Herodis regis, ecce Magi ab Oriente venerunt Hierosolymam dicentes: Ubi est qui natus est rex Iudaeorum? Vidimus enim stellam eius in Oriente et venimus adorare eum. Et ecce stella quam viderant in Oriente antecedebat eos usque dum veniens staret supra ubi erat puer.
english_gloss: When therefore Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi from the East came to Jerusalem saying: Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East and have come to worship him. And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood over where the child was.

vocabulary.english: Magi from the East — astrologers/wise men from Persia, Babylon, or Arabia
vocabulary.notes: Magos from Greek magos; originally the Zoroastrian priestly caste of Persia; here Gentile star-interpreters

vocabulary.english: his star — the star that announced the birth of the king of the Jews
vocabulary.notes: The 'star of Bethlehem' was interpreted astronomically (Jupiter-Saturn conjunction), symbolically, and as a miraculous nova

vocabulary.english: in the East — both geographically (the Magi's homeland) and astrologically (heliacal rising)
vocabulary.notes: Astrological double meaning: they saw the star 'in the east' = they observed its heliacal rising, the astrologically significant moment

vocabulary.english: to worship, to prostrate before — the Magi's offering as an act of religious homage
vocabulary.notes: The paradox: pagan astrologers perform the first Gentile act of worship toward Christ

vocabulary.english: stood over — the miraculous arrest of the star above the specific house
vocabulary.notes: No natural phenomenon stops over a point; Matthew presents this as miraculous, not merely astrological

source_notes: Matthew 2:1-12 was the most powerful biblical argument for the legitimacy of astrology and astral divination: the Magi — professional star-interpreters — were led by a star to Christ, and worshipped him. Christian astronomers and astrologers from Origen through Kepler used this passage to argue that astral knowledge was divinely sanctioned. Against this stood the Isaiah 47 condemnation of Babylonian astrologers. The tension was never fully resolved in medieval or Renaissance theology.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. Weber-Gryson. Stuttgart, 1994.
Molnar, Michael R. The Star of Bethlehem: The Legacy of the Magi. New Brunswick: Rutgers University Press, 1999.

title: Acts 8:9–13 — Simon Magus
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Vir autem quidam, nomine Simon, qui ante fuerat in civitate magicis artibus praedicens, et seducens gentem Samariae, dicens esse se aliquem magnum. Cui attendebant omnes a minimo usque ad maximum, dicentes: Hic est virtus Dei quae vocatur Magna. Attendebant autem ei propter quod multo tempore magicis suis artibus dementasset eos. Cum autem credidissent Philippo evangelizanti de regno Dei et de nomine Iesu Christi, baptizabantur viri ac mulieres. Tunc Simon et ipse credidit, et cum baptizatus esset adharebat Philippo.
english_gloss: But a certain man named Simon, who had previously been in the city practicing magic arts and amazing the people of Samaria, saying he was someone great. To him all paid attention, from least to greatest, saying: This is the power of God which is called Great. They paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic arts. But when they believed Philip preaching about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptized. Then Simon himself also believed, and when he was baptized, he attached himself to Philip.

vocabulary.english: magical arts — the technical phrase for Simon's professional practice
vocabulary.notes: Magicis artibus: the Vulgate's most direct phrase for professional magic; used three times in this passage for emphasis

vocabulary.english: seducing/misleading the people — magic as deception and social manipulation
vocabulary.notes: Seducere: to lead astray; magic as a socially destructive force that diverts people from truth

vocabulary.english: the power of God which is called Great — Simon's messianic title among the Samaritans
vocabulary.notes: The Gnostic 'Great Power' title: Simonian Gnosticism made Simon a divine figure; Acts presents this as fraud

vocabulary.english: had driven them mad, crazed them — the psychological effect of magic on its audience
vocabulary.notes: Dementia through magic: magic produces a crowd-psychology of irrationality; contrast with the logos-based apostolic preaching

source_notes: Simon Magus (Acts 8) is the paradigm case of the bad magician in Christian tradition. The term 'simony' (buying church offices) derives from Acts 8:18-19, where Simon attempts to buy the apostles' power. Patristic writers (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Hippolytus) identified Simon as the first Gnostic and father of all heresies. His transformation from magician to (failed) Christian encapsulates the theological claim that Christianity supersedes magic.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. Weber-Gryson. Stuttgart, 1994.
Haar, Stephen. Simon Magus: The First Gnostic? Berlin: de Gruyter, 2003.

title: Acts 19:19 — The Burning of the Magic Books at Ephesus
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Multi autem ex eis qui fuerant curiosa sectati, contulerunt libros et combusserunt coram omnibus. Et computatis pretiis illorum invenerunt pecuniam denariorum quinquaginta milium. Ita fortiter crescebat verbum Dei et confortabatur. Ephesi autem erat multis nota urbs et magna, et erant ibi multi qui magicis artibus operam dabant.
english_gloss: But many of those who had followed curious practices brought their books together and burned them before all. And when their value was calculated, they found the sum of fifty thousand denarii. So mightily grew the word of God and was strengthened. Ephesus was a city known to many and great, and there were many there who devoted themselves to magic arts.

vocabulary.english: curious things, occult arts — the Vulgate's term for magical practices and their objects
vocabulary.notes: Curiositas = intellectual overreach into forbidden knowledge; Augustine's theological critique of magic as a form of pride

vocabulary.english: magic books — the Ephesian letters (Ephesia grammata) and other magical texts
vocabulary.notes: The Ephesian letters (a class of powerful voces magicae) were specifically associated with Ephesus in antiquity

vocabulary.english: fifty thousand denarii — a vast sum, signaling the scale of Ephesian magical commerce
vocabulary.notes: The monetary valuation tells us magic books were an expensive professional commodity, not just folk practice

vocabulary.english: the word of God grew — the book-burning as evangelistic victory
vocabulary.notes: The narrative logic: destroying magic books = space for the word of God; Christianity and magic as zero-sum

source_notes: Acts 19:19 — the Ephesian book-burning — was the scriptural precedent for every subsequent destruction of magic books in Christian history, from Diocletian's burning of alchemical texts to the bonfire of the Inquisition. The fifty thousand denarii underscored magic's economic scale. The 'Ephesian letters' (Ephesia grammata) were famous ancient voces magicae — their burning at Paul's preaching was theologically central to the idea of Christianity as the supersession of magic.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. Weber-Gryson. Stuttgart, 1994.
Arnold, Clinton E. Ephesians: Power and Magic. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: Genesis 1:3 — And God Said: Creation Through the Word
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram. Terra autem erat inanis et vacua, et tenebrae super faciem abyssi, et spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas. Dixitque Deus: Fiat lux. Et facta est lux. Et vidit Deus lucem quod esset bona, et divisit lucem ac tenebras. Appellavitque lucem Diem et tenebras Noctem.
english_gloss: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. But the earth was formless and empty, and darkness was over the face of the abyss, and the spirit of God moved over the waters. And God said: Let there be light. And there was light. And God saw the light that it was good, and he divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light Day and the darkness Night.

vocabulary.english: In the beginning — the opening formula read as the first divine Name
vocabulary.notes: Kabbalistic exegesis: Bereshit (in the beginning) contains the name of God; every letter encodes a creative act

vocabulary.english: Let there be light — the paradigm of creation through divine speech-act
vocabulary.notes: The divine fiat as the model for magical commanding speech: if God creates by saying, perhaps human words can create too

vocabulary.english: the spirit of God hovered/moved — the divine breath animating primal matter
vocabulary.notes: Ruach Elohim: the divine spirit as creative force; Ficino's anima mundi; Paracelsus's archeus — all read this verse

vocabulary.english: formless and empty (tohu wa-bohu in Hebrew) — the primordial chaos before creation
vocabulary.notes: The tohu wa-bohu of Genesis = the Neoplatonic hyle = the alchemical prima materia = the hermetic moist darkness

source_notes: Genesis 1's cosmogony through divine speech — 'And God said: let there be light, and there was light' — was the foundational text for the entire tradition of magical speech in the Jewish and Christian West. If God creates by speaking, language has ontological power. The Kabbalistic reading of Genesis 1 (each letter of Bereshit encodes a cosmic force) built the entire edifice of Jewish and later Christian Kabbalah on this premise. Sefer Yetzirah, Pico, Reuchlin, Agrippa, and Dee all circle back to this verse.
bibliography: Biblia Sacra Iuxta Vulgatam Versionem. Ed. Weber-Gryson. Stuttgart, 1994.
Scholem, Gershom. On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism. Trans. Ralph Manheim. New York: Schocken, 1965.

title: Exodus 3:14 — I Am Who I Am: The Divine Name
author: Anon. (Vulgate Bible)
latin_text: Dixit Deus ad Moysen: Ego sum qui sum. Ait: Sic dices filiis Israel: Qui est misit me ad vos. Dixitque iterum Deus ad Moysen: Haec dices filiis Israel: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac et Deus Iacob misit me ad vos. Hoc nomen mihi est in aeternum, et hoc memoriale meum in generationem et generationem.
english_gloss: God said to Moses: I am who I am. He said: So you shall say to the sons of Israel: He who is has sent me to you. And God said again to Moses: Thus shall you say to the sons of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has sent me to you. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial for generation to generation.

vocabulary.english: I am who I am — the divine self-definition as pure being
vocabulary.notes: Ehyeh asher ehyeh in Hebrew: variously translated as 'I am what I am,' 'I will be what I will be,' 'I cause to be what I cause to be'

vocabulary.english: He who is — the name given to Israel as the divine name for use
vocabulary.notes: The name for use: Yahweh = he who is/was/will be; this 'name' is the Tetragrammaton YHWH

vocabulary.english: Lord — the Vulgate's rendering of YHWH, the unpronounceable divine name
