vocabulary.notes: Damnatio: the legal/religious sentence applied to books, mirroring the condemnation of heretics

source_notes: The Index Librorum Prohibitorum (first issued 1559, maintained until 1966) placed Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia, Trithemius's Steganographia, and various Paracelsian works among prohibited texts. The Index did not prevent circulation — it drove the trade underground and to Protestant printers. The paradox is documented: condemned books sold better than permitted ones. The Index's practical effect on magic book circulation was probably more promotional than suppressive.
bibliography: Bujanda, J.M. de. Index des livres interdits. 11 vols. Sherbrooke: Éditions de l'Université de Sherbrooke, 1984–2002.
Grendler, Paul F. The Roman Inquisition and the Venetian Press, 1540–1605. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1977.

title: Grimoires: A History — On the Transmission of Magic Books
author: Owen Davies
work: Grimoires: A History of Magic Books
latin_text: Libri magici non erant scripta manu sola latentia, sed merces commerciales late diffusae per omnes ordines societatis. A typographia inventa, grimoria multiplicata sunt et per mercatores ambulantes et bibliopolos et medicos rudes distributa. Qui libros hos emebant erant non clerici docti sed agricolae, opifices, ancillae, et qui se contra sortem malam, morbum, et damnum protegere volebant. Traditio grimoriorum est ergo traditio popularis, non eruditorum solius.
english_gloss: Magic books were not manuscripts lurking in hiding alone, but commercial goods widely diffused through all orders of society. From the invention of printing, grimoires were multiplied and distributed by travelling merchants, booksellers, and unlicensed physicians. Those who bought these books were not learned clerics but farmers, craftsmen, maidservants, and those who wished to protect themselves against ill fortune, disease, and harm. The grimoire tradition is therefore a popular tradition, not of the learned alone.

vocabulary.english: commercial goods, merchandise — grimoires as marketplace commodities
vocabulary.notes: Davies's key insight: magic books are not esoteric secrets but commercial products, shaped by market demand

vocabulary.english: from the invention of printing — the printing press as the key enabling technology
vocabulary.notes: Print multiplied grimoires beyond the control of any institution; the Index's failure is partly a print-technology problem

vocabulary.english: booksellers and unlicensed physicians — the distribution network
vocabulary.notes: The 'cunning man' and the quack doctor were often the local grimoire retailers, bundling magical services with the text

vocabulary.english: popular tradition, folk tradition — grimoires as vernacular practice not elite knowledge
vocabulary.notes: The social range: from learned magus to illiterate farmer, all consumed magic books adapted to their literacy level

source_notes: Owen Davies's Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (2009) is the definitive modern history of the grimoire as a genre and commercial object. His analysis of the grimoire as a popular commodity — not an elite secret — transformed how scholars understand magical texts. The grimoire tradition did not flow down from learned magic to folk practice; it circulated horizontally across social classes through commercial networks, and was shaped as much by market demand as by esoteric tradition.
bibliography: Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.
Davies, Owen. Popular Magic: Cunning-folk in English History. London: Hambledon Continuum, 2003.

title: Steganographia — Phaleg, Spirit of Mars
author: Johannes Trithemius
latin_text: Phaleg est spiritus Martis, rex belli et praefectus omnium qui bella gerunt in terris et in alto caelo. Si vis secretum aliquod per longum spacium cum socio communicare, invoca Phaleg in hora Martis die Martis, et dic: Phaleg rex gloriosum, ito ad N. et ei dic verba mea. Tunc per aerem spiritus tuus verba tua secum feret et in aure socius tui resonabit, quasi ipse adesses. Hoc est steganographia, scriptura occulta per spiritum transmissa.
english_gloss: Phaleg is the spirit of Mars, king of war and prefect of all who wage wars on earth and in the high heaven. If you wish to communicate some secret to a companion over a long distance, invoke Phaleg in the hour of Mars on the day of Mars, and say: Phaleg the glorious king, go to N. and tell him my words. Then through the air the spirit will carry your words with him and will resound in the ear of your companion, as if you yourself were present. This is steganography: hidden writing transmitted through a spirit.

vocabulary.english: Phaleg — the Steganographia's Martial spirit, ruler of the 42 who govern Tuesday
vocabulary.notes: One of 24 planetary spirits in the Steganographia; the name appears in Trithemius's source material from earlier angel-magic

vocabulary.english: steganography — concealed writing, secret communication
vocabulary.notes: Greek: steganos (hidden) + graphia (writing); Trithemius's title claims to teach secret communication through angelic mediation

vocabulary.english: carries your words through the air — the angelic transmission medium
vocabulary.notes: The mechanism: the spirit travels through air, carrying the message to the distant recipient's ear

vocabulary.english: as if you yourself were present — the effect of spirit-mediated long-distance communication
vocabulary.notes: Renaissance anticipation of telecommunications: the spirit as message-carrier makes distance irrelevant

source_notes: Trithemius's Steganographia (written c. 1499, circulated in manuscript, published 1606) was placed on the Index of Prohibited Books in 1609. For centuries it appeared to be a genuine spirit-conjuration manual for long-distance communication; in 1998 scholars decoded the first two books as a cryptographic manual, with the angelic apparatus being a cover for cipher instructions. The third book remains genuinely magical. The Steganographia's 400-year reception history — from condemned grimoire to decoded cipher manual — is a uniquely rich case study in how grimoires are read, misread, and reread.
bibliography: Trithemius, Johannes. Steganographia. Frankfurt: Becker, 1606.
Brann, Noel L. Trithemius and Magical Theology. Albany: SUNY Press, 1999.

title: Pentacula Lunae
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Haec sunt pentacula Lunae, quae faciunt ut spiritus aquarum appareant et obediant, et ut thesauri absconditi in aquis inveniantur. Scribe haec in pergameno virginis die Lunae in hora Lunae, et odoribus Lunae suffumiga, scilicet camphorae et mentis et similium. Tunc spiritus convocati venient in forma puerorum vel mulierum, et revelabunt omnia petita.
english_gloss: These are the pentacles of the Moon, which cause the spirits of waters to appear and obey, and hidden treasures in waters to be found. Write these on virgin parchment on Monday in the hour of the Moon, and fumigate with the perfumes of the Moon, namely camphor and mint and the like. Then the spirits summoned will come in the form of boys or women, and will reveal all things asked.

vocabulary.definition: pentacles, magical seals
parchment
to fumigate, to perfume with smoke
camphor
summoned, called together

source_notes: Book II of the Key of Solomon details lunar pentacles for summoning water spirits and finding hidden treasure. The planetary hour system, virgin parchment, and planetary suffumigations are central to Solomonic ritual technology.
bibliography: Mathers, S.L. MacGregor, ed. The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis). London: Redway, 1889.
Torijano, Pablo A. Solomon the Esoteric King: From King to Magus, Development of a Tradition. Leiden: Brill, 2002.

title: Oratio Ante Opus Magicum
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: O Domine Deus meus, tu qui es ante saecula saeculorum, audi orationem meam, et exaudi vocem meam, et illumina oculos meos ne unquam obdormiam in morte, ne dicat inimicus meus: Praevalui adversus eum.
english_gloss: O Lord my God, you who are before ages of ages, hear my prayer, and listen to my voice, and illuminate my eyes lest I ever sleep in death, lest my enemy say: I have prevailed against him.

vocabulary.definition: ages, eternities
to hear favorably, to heed
to illuminate, enlighten
to prevail, to overcome

source_notes: The preliminary prayer before magical operations in the Key of Solomon blends Psalm 13:3-4 with conjuration framing, presenting the operator as a penitent servant of God. This pseudo-biblical framing is characteristic of Solomonic ritual.
bibliography: Mathers, S.L. MacGregor, ed. The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis). London: Redway, 1889.

title: Notae ad Philosophiam
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Has notas philosophiae contemplari debes et eas in corde tuo imprimere, ne eas oblivioni des. Fac orationes praescriptas cum devotione et humilitate, et per viginti dies abstine a mulieribus, ab ebrietate, ab ira, ab omni impuritate. Tunc angeli memoriae et intelligentiae tibi apparebunt in somnis et vigilando, et infundent in animam tuam perfectam memoriam omnium artium liberalium.
english_gloss: You must contemplate these notes of philosophy and impress them on your heart, lest you consign them to forgetfulness. Perform the prescribed prayers with devotion and humility, and for twenty days abstain from women, from drunkenness, from anger, from all impurity. Then the angels of memory and understanding will appear to you in dreams and waking, and will pour into your soul perfect memory of all the liberal arts.

vocabulary.definition: notes, magical figures, notae
to impress, imprint, engrave
forgetfulness, oblivion
to abstain, refrain
to pour into, infuse, instill

source_notes: The Ars Notoria (Notory Art) promised supernatural acquisition of the seven liberal arts through contemplation of magical figures (notae), prayers, and ritual purity. Condemned repeatedly but widely copied, it influenced later angelic grimoires including the Liber Juratus.
bibliography: Fanger, Claire, ed. Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic. Stroud: Sutton, 1998.
Page, Sophie. Magic in the Cloister: Pious Motives, Illicit Interests, and Occult Approaches to the Medieval Universe. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Oratio Theologiae Infundendae
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Tulburburit, Calquibistrit, Razimut — haec sunt nomina angelorum memoriae. Per haec nomina sacra et ineffabilia deprecor te, Domine Deus, ut mihi concedas perfectam memoriam Scripturae Sacrae et omnium artium.
english_gloss: Tulburburit, Calquibistrit, Razimut — these are the names of the angels of memory. Through these sacred and ineffable names I implore you, Lord God, that you grant me perfect memory of Holy Scripture and all the arts.

vocabulary.definition: ineffable, unspeakable, inexpressible
to pray earnestly, to implore
to grant, allow, concede

source_notes: The barbarous angel names in the Ars Notoria are among the earliest pseudo-Hebraic angel names in Latin magic. The text presents them as Hebrew divine names corrupted by transmission, legitimizing magical efficacy through scriptural precedent.
bibliography: Véronèse, Julien. L'Ars notoria au Moyen Âge. Florence: SISMEL, 2007.

title: Aeriel Rex Orientis
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Aeriel est rex magnus et potens spiritus Orientis, habens sub se duodecim duces et vicesimum quinque subduces. Ipse regit super omnes spiritus aeris Orientalis et imperat eis de mane usque ad meridiem. Evocandus est in circulo cum charactere suo in pelle, et obsequetur sine perturbatione, dans cognitionem rerum absconditarum in Oriente terrae.
english_gloss: Aeriel is a great and powerful king spirit of the East, having under him twelve dukes and twenty-five sub-dukes. He rules over all spirits of the eastern air and commands them from morning until midday. He is to be evoked in a circle with his character on skin, and will attend without disturbance, giving knowledge of hidden things in the East of the earth.

vocabulary.definition: sub-dukes, subordinate spirit commanders
to comply, attend, obey
magical character, sigil, seal
disturbance, confusion, disorder
hidden, concealed, secret

source_notes: The Ars Theurgia-Goetia, second book of the Lemegeton, describes aerial spirits organized by cardinal direction and time of day. Unlike the Goetia's infernal spirits, these are presented as morally ambiguous, serving in aerial hierarchies. The text survives from the 17th century.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Lesser Key of Solomon: Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis. York Beach: Weiser, 2001.
Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

title: Angeli Horarum Diei
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Samael est angelus primae horae diei Dominicae sub Michaele Principe Solis; Anael secundae horae sub Anachiele; Raphael tertiae. Hi angeli horarum dantur ad protectionem hominis nati sub illis horis et ad revelationes de thesauris caelestibus.
english_gloss: Samael is the angel of the first hour of Sunday under Michael Prince of the Sun; Anael of the second hour under Anachiels; Raphael of the third. These angels of the hours are given for protection of a person born under those hours and for revelations concerning heavenly treasures.

vocabulary.definition: of Sunday, of the Lord
prince, chief, leader
protection, defense
revelations, disclosures

source_notes: The Ars Paulina claims Pauline authorship for a system of angelic hours governing each day. It connects each planetary hour to a governing angel, synthesizing planetary magic with angelic hierarchies. The ascription to Paul legitimized contact with named angels.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Lesser Key of Solomon: Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis. York Beach: Weiser, 2001.

title: Fama Fraternitatis Rosae Crucis
author: Anonymous (Johann Valentin Andreae attr.)
latin_text: Nos Fraternitatis Rosae Crucis, quamvis ab humanis oculis celati, in lucem prodire constituimus. Librum Naturae, quam Deus per Creaturam suam aperuit, et librum Scripturae Sacrae, quam per Spiritum Sanctum dictavit, aequaliter contemplamur. Philosophia nostra non nova est, sed ipsa prisca et ab initio mundi Adamo revelata. Reformationem totius orbis terrarum propediem futuram esse annuntiamus.
english_gloss: We of the Fraternity of the Rosy Cross, although hidden from human eyes, have resolved to come into the light. We contemplate equally the Book of Nature, which God opened through His Creation, and the Book of Holy Scripture, which He dictated through the Holy Spirit. Our philosophy is not new, but is that ancient one revealed to Adam from the beginning of the world. We announce that a reformation of the entire world is soon to come.

vocabulary.definition: hidden, concealed
to resolve, decide, establish
to contemplate, meditate upon
ancient, former, of old
soon, shortly, in the near future

source_notes: The Fama Fraternitatis (1614) announced the existence of the secret Rosicrucian brotherhood and called for a universal reformation of arts, sciences, and religion. Its Latin proclamations synthesized Paracelsian medicine, Hermetic philosophy, and Protestant reform rhetoric. The manifesto sparked a pamphlet war across Europe.
bibliography: Yates, Frances A. The Rosicrucian Enlightenment. London: Routledge, 1972.
Edighoffer, Roland. Rose-Croix et société idéale selon Johann Valentin Andreae. Paris: Arma Artis, 1982.

title: Confessio Fraternitatis
author: Anonymous (Johann Valentin Andreae attr.)
latin_text: Librum M, quem per totam Europam sine titulis circumferrimus, et quem Catalogum omnium mirabilium Naturae continet, nondum publicavimus. Verum eum ita composuimus ut, si omnes bibliothecae essent combustae, ex eo sola sapientia humana posset instaurari.
english_gloss: Book M, which we carry throughout all Europe without title, and which contains a Catalogue of all the wonders of Nature, we have not yet published. But we have composed it in such a way that, if all libraries were burned, from it alone human wisdom could be restored.

vocabulary.definition: to carry around, to circulate
titles, inscriptions, labels
burned, consumed by fire
to restore, renew, rebuild

source_notes: The Confessio Fraternitatis (1615) amplified the Fama's claims, introducing the mysterious 'Book M' (Mundi?) as a universal encyclopedia. The claim that it could restore all knowledge if libraries burned echoes Paracelsus's universal medicine and the Hermetic dream of recovered Adamic wisdom.
bibliography: Yates, Frances A. The Rosicrucian Enlightenment. London: Routledge, 1972.

title: Pactum Faustii cum Diabolo
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Ego Joannes Faustus Doctor, sponte mea et libera voluntate hac die, omnia membra corporis mei, animam quoque et spiritum, post obitum meum Mephistophili Principi daemoniorum trado et donavi, ita ut ipse Mephistophilis mihi servus et minister sit per viginti quatuor annos ab hac die computandos, et quidquid petiero praestet.
english_gloss: I Johann Faust Doctor, of my own free will on this day, all members of my body, and also my soul and spirit, after my death I hand over and give to Mephistophiles Prince of demons, so that Mephistophiles himself shall be my servant and minister for twenty-four years reckoned from this day, and shall perform whatever I shall request.

vocabulary.definition: of one's own accord, voluntarily
death, departure, decease
to hand over, surrender, deliver
to give, donate, present
to be reckoned, counted, calculated

source_notes: The Historia von D. Johann Fausten (Frankfurt, 1587) contained a Latin pact formula presented as authentic. The text popularized the diabolical pact narrative and influenced Marlowe's Doctor Faustus. The 24-year term and formal legal language of 'tradere et donare' framed the soul-sale as a legal contract.
bibliography: Baron, Frank. Doctor Faustus: From History to Legend. Munich: Fink, 1978.
Durrant, Jonathan, and Michael D. Bailey, eds. Historical Dictionary of Witchcraft. Lanham: Scarecrow Press, 2012.

title: De Arte Nigromantiae
author: Johann Hartlieb
work: Buch aller verbotenen Künste (De omnibus artibus prohibitis)
latin_text: Nigromantia est ars in qua per invocationem spirituum mortuorum aut daemoniorum futura praenoscuntur et occulta revelantur. Haec ars in septem partes dividitur: nigromantia proprie dicta, geomantia, hydromantia, aeromantia, pyromantia, chiromantia, spatulamantia. Omnes autem istae artes prohibitae sunt et excommunicationi obnoxiae, quia a diabolo inventae sunt ad deceptionem humanam.
english_gloss: Necromancy is the art in which future things are foreknown and hidden things revealed through the invocation of dead spirits or demons. This art is divided into seven parts: necromancy properly so called, geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, pyromancy, chiromancy, scapulomancy. But all these arts are forbidden and subject to excommunication, because they were invented by the devil for human deception.

vocabulary.definition: to foreknow, know beforehand
scapulomancy, divination by shoulder blades
excommunication
subject to, liable to, guilty of
deception, fraud, trickery

source_notes: Johann Hartlieb's vernacular Book of All Forbidden Arts (c. 1456, written for Margrave Johann of Brandenburg-Kulmbach) survives in German but contains Latin technical terms. Hartlieb presents the sevenfold taxonomy to condemn each art while inadvertently preserving its practices. He studied medicine in Vienna and Padua.
bibliography: Hartlieb, Johann. The Book of All Forbidden Arts. Trans. Nigel Barton. Frome: Brill, 1998.
Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: Liber Soyga — Admonestatio
author: John Dee
latin_text: Angelus dixit: Liber Soyga solum ab Adamo in Paradiso lectus et ab angelis compositus est. Ego eum legi et in eo multa mirabilia de naturis spirituum et ordine hierarchiarum inveni. Sed ultima pagina, quae continet nomen Dei efficax, mihi nondum revelata est.
english_gloss: The angel said: The Book of Soyga was read only by Adam in Paradise and composed by angels. I read it and found in it many wonderful things about the natures of spirits and the order of hierarchies. But the last page, which contains the efficacious name of God, has not yet been revealed to me.

vocabulary.definition: admonition, warning, instruction
hierarchies, angelic ranks
efficacious, effective, potent
revealed, disclosed

source_notes: Dee's spiritual diaries record an angelic communication about the Liber Soyga, a Latin magical text Dee possessed. The angel Uriel told him the book was composed in Paradise. The Liber Soyga (rediscovered in the British Library in 1994) contains tables of generated letter-sequences and instructions for their use in conjuration.
bibliography: Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999.
Dee, John. A True and Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Years Between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits. London: Maxwell, 1659.

title: Apologie pour les grands hommes soupçonnez de Magie — De Libris
author: Gabriel Naudé
work: Apologie pour les grands hommes soupçonnez de Magie
latin_text: Inter libros qui de magia tractant, primum locum tenet Clavicula Salomonis, quae tamen ex tot manibus transita tot interpolationibus corrupta est ut vix centesima pars genuini operis supersit. Deinde Picatrix arabicus, et Agrippa de Occulta Philosophia, quae opera eruditis quidem ingeniis composita sed in vulgus perniciosa sunt, quia vulgus non rationes philosophicas sed operas daemonicas in eis quaerit.
english_gloss: Among books that treat of magic, first place is held by the Key of Solomon, which however, having passed through so many hands, has been so corrupted by interpolations that scarcely a hundredth part of the genuine work survives. Next the Arabic Picatrix, and Agrippa's On Occult Philosophy, which works were indeed composed by learned intellects but are dangerous for the common people, because common people seek in them not philosophical reasons but demonic operations.

vocabulary.definition: interpolations, insertions, corruptions
to survive, remain, be left
learned, erudite, educated
pernicious, dangerous, harmful
common people, the masses, the crowd

source_notes: Gabriel Naudé's Apologie (1625) defended learned men accused of magic by distinguishing philosophical magic from demonic superstition. His bibliographic assessment of the Clavicula — noting its textual corruption through manuscript transmission — anticipates modern philological criticism of grimoire traditions.
bibliography: Naudé, Gabriel. Apologie pour les grands hommes soupçonnez de magie. Paris: Targa, 1625.
Clark, Stuart. Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997.

title: Prologus Picatricis
author: Pseudo-Maslama al-Majriti
latin_text: Haec est praecipua et nobilissima scientia et altior et subtilior omnibus scientiis philosophicis. Quia per eam adquiritur sapientia et habentur vires et facultates superiorum in inferioribus, et etiam inferioribus in superioribus. Et sciendum est quod qui voluerit perfectionem huius artis attingere, oportet quod sit philosophus et astrologus et magus perfectus.
english_gloss: This is the supreme and most noble science and higher and more subtle than all philosophical sciences. Because through it wisdom is acquired and the powers and faculties of the superior things are obtained in the inferior, and also of the inferior things in the superior. And it must be known that whoever wishes to attain perfection of this art must be a philosopher and astrologer and perfect magician.

vocabulary.definition: supreme, chief, excellent, pre-eminent
more subtle, refined, precise
to be acquired, obtained
to attain, reach, touch
it is necessary, it is fitting, one must

source_notes: The Picatrix (Latin translation of the Arabic Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm, c. 1000 CE) was translated in Toledo c. 1256. Its prologue establishes the synthesis of astrology, Neoplatonic philosophy, and practical image-magic that defines the work. It was one of the most influential Arabic magical texts in the Latin West.
bibliography: Ritter, Helmut, and Martin Plessner, eds. Picatrix: Das Ziel des Weisen von Pseudo-Magriti. London: Warburg Institute, 1962.
Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: Visio Beatifica per Artem Magicam
author: Pseudo-Honorius
work: Liber Juratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius)
latin_text: Finis et intentio totius huius artis est ut homo possit videre Deum facie ad faciem et intelligere arcana caelestia, et habere potestatem super omnes spiritus tam bonos quam malos, et cognoscere omnia occulta per ministerium angelorum. Ad hoc autem obtinendum, oportet hominem esse purum et ab omni peccato mundatum, et ieiuniis et orationibus diu vacasse, et secretum artis nemini revelare.
english_gloss: The end and intention of this whole art is that a man may be able to see God face to face and understand celestial secrets, and have power over all spirits both good and evil, and know all hidden things through the ministry of angels. To obtain this, however, a man must be pure and cleansed from all sin, and have devoted himself to fasts and prayers for a long time, and reveal the secret of the art to no one.

vocabulary.definition: beatific, making blessed, heavenly
secrets, mysteries, hidden things
to have been devoted to, occupied with
cleansed, purified, made clean
ministry, service, agency

source_notes: The Liber Juratus Honorii (13th c.) presents magic as a path to the beatific vision — seeing God face to face — framing conjuration as an extreme form of contemplative piety. The text requires 140 days of ritual preparation. It influenced the Ars Notoria tradition and represents the most ambitious theurgical claim in medieval Latin magic.
bibliography: Mathiesen, Robert. 'A Thirteenth-Century Ritual to Attain the Beatific Vision.' In Conjuring Spirits, ed. Claire Fanger. Stroud: Sutton, 1998.
Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages and Renaissance. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: De Libris Magicis Suppositis
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
latin_text: Multa circumferuntur sub nomine Salomonis, ut Clavicula, Almadel, Liber Spirituum et similia, quorum maximam partem esse supposita et ab imperitis confecta non dubito, quia neque stylum regium habent neque cum vera Salomonea philosophia consentiunt.
english_gloss: Many things circulate under the name of Solomon, such as the Key, the Almadel, the Book of Spirits and similar works, the greater part of which I do not doubt are spurious and fabricated by incompetents, because they neither have the royal style nor agree with the true Solomonic philosophy.

vocabulary.definition: to circulate, be passed around
spurious, falsely attributed, substituted
incompetents, the unskilled, the ignorant
style, manner of writing
to agree with, accord, be consistent with

source_notes: Agrippa's critique of Solomonic pseudepigrapha is doubly ironic: his own De Occulta Philosophia drew on precisely such texts, and a 'Fourth Book' was later falsely attributed to him. His dismissal of the Clavicula as stylistically unworthy anticipates modern textual criticism.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.

title: Speculum Astronomiae — Libri de Maleficiis
author: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus
latin_text: Sunt quidam libri qui vocantur libri Imaginum in quibus non est astronomia, sed superstitio et idolatria. Tales sunt Liber Lune, Liber Runarum, et similes, qui petunt ab imaginibus responsiones, et faciunt sub eis suffumigationes et invocationes daemonum. Hi omnino reiiciendi sunt nec in bibliotheca sapientis retinendi. Astronomia autem legitima a maleficiis per hoc distinguitur, quod in ea nihil petitur nisi a Deo solo.
english_gloss: There are certain books called Books of Images in which there is not astronomy but superstition and idolatry. Such are the Book of the Moon, the Book of Runes, and similar works, which seek responses from images, and perform fumigations and invocations of demons under them. These are to be entirely rejected and not kept in the library of a wise man. Legitimate astronomy is distinguished from evil arts by this, that in it nothing is sought except from God alone.

vocabulary.definition: images, figures, magical images/talismans
idolatry, image-worship
runes, secret characters, magical signs
to be rejected, thrown away, cast aside
to be distinguished, separated, differentiated

source_notes: The Speculum Astronomiae (c. 1260, attributed to Albertus Magnus but disputed) created the canonical scholastic taxonomy of magical books: acceptable astronomical image-books vs. forbidden demonic image-books. This classification influenced centuries of inquisitorial and ecclesiastical responses to grimoires.
bibliography: Paravicini-Bagliani, Agostino, ed. Albertus Magnus and the Sciences. Toronto: PIMS, 1980.
Burnett, Charles. Magic and Divination in the Middle Ages. Aldershot: Variorum, 1996.

title: Coniuratio Prima
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Coniuro te, O spiritus N., per Deum Patrem omnipotentem, et per Filium eius Iesum Christum, et per Spiritum Sanctum, et per sacrosanctum nomen Dei Tetragrammaton, ut sine mora et sine strepitu et sine nocumento alicuius personae appareas hic ante circulum in forma humana pulchra et amabili. Veni ergo, veni, N., per haec nomina sacra: Adonai, Tetragrammaton, Jehova, Elohim.
english_gloss: I conjure you, O spirit N., by God the Father almighty, and by His Son Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit, and by the most holy name of God Tetragrammaton, that without delay and without noise and without harm to any person you appear here before the circle in beautiful and amiable human form. Come therefore, come, N., by these holy names: Adonai, Tetragrammaton, Jehova, Elohim.

vocabulary.definition: to conjure, swear together, adjure
noise, din, disturbance
harm, injury, damage
amiable, lovable, pleasant
the four-letter name of God (YHWH)

source_notes: The Goetia's first conjuration formula invokes Christian Trinitarian theology alongside Hebrew divine names. This blend is characteristic of Renaissance ceremonial magic: the operator does not worship demons but commands them through divine authority. The 72 demons of the Goetia derive ultimately from Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum.
bibliography: Mathers, S.L. MacGregor, and Aleister Crowley, eds. The Goetia: The Lesser Key of Solomon the King. London: Kegan Paul, 1904.
Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

title: Paimon Rex Occidentis
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Paimon est rex potentissimus Occidentis, apparens in forma hominis sedentis super dromedarium cum corona in capite. Ipse docet omnes artes et scientias et secreta. Habet sub se ducentos legiones spirituum ex parte quaedam Ordinis Angelorum, quaedam ex parte Potestatum.
english_gloss: Paimon is a most powerful king of the West, appearing in the form of a man seated on a dromedary with a crown on his head. He teaches all arts and sciences and secrets. He has under him two hundred legions of spirits, partly of the Order of Angels, partly of the Order of Powers.

vocabulary.definition: dromedary, one-humped camel
Powers (angelic order), powers
legions, military divisions

source_notes: Paimon's description in the Goetia blends demonic and angelic hierarchy: his legions include former angels of both the Order of Angels and Powers. The dromedary is his traditional mount in Arabic-influenced demonology. He appears as King #9 in the Goetia's list of 72 spirits.
bibliography: Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Lesser Key of Solomon: Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis. York Beach: Weiser, 2001.

title: Oratio Diei Solis
author: Pietro d'Abano (attrib.)
latin_text: In die Solis et hora eius prima, accipe virgam ex cornu hazel arboris, et in ea sculpito characteres angeli Michaelis et spirituum eius. Invoca Michaelem per haec verba: O Michael, angele fortis et potens, princeps militiae caelestis, qui pugnasti contra draconem, exaudi me servantem praecepta tua, et veni in hanc horam ad adiutorium meum.
english_gloss: On the day of the Sun and its first hour, take a wand from the hazel tree, and on it engrave the characters of the angel Michael and his spirits. Invoke Michael through these words: O Michael, strong and powerful angel, prince of the heavenly host, who fought against the dragon, hear me keeping your commandments, and come in this hour to my aid.

vocabulary.definition: hazel (tree), Corylus avellana
to engrave, carve, sculpt
military host, army, service
dragon, serpent (Rev. 12: Satan)
aid, help, assistance

source_notes: The Heptameron (likely 14th c., attributed to Pietro d'Abano) organizes angelic magic by planetary day and hour, each day governed by specific angels. Michael governs Sunday. The hazel wand inscribed with angelic characters is a standard tool of Solomonic practice, the allusion to Revelation 12 legitimizing Michael's invocation as scripture-sanctioned.
bibliography: Véronèse, Julien. 'Magic, Theurgy, and Spirituality in the Medieval Ritual of the Ars Notoria.' In Invoking Angels, ed. Claire Fanger. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2012.

title: De Strigibus et Lamiis — Libri Magici
author: Ulrich Molitor
latin_text: Libri magicales quos vulgus claviculas Salomonis vocat nihil aliud sunt quam daemonum illusiones in scripturam redactae, ut simplices homines decipiant. Nam daemon ipse hos libros composuit et per manus maleficorum propagavit, ut per eos cultum suum extenderet et animas perditioni addiceret.
english_gloss: The magical books which the common people call the keys of Solomon are nothing other than demonic illusions reduced to writing, in order to deceive simple people. For the demon himself composed these books and propagated them through the hands of sorcerers, so that through them he might extend his worship and consign souls to perdition.

vocabulary.definition: magical, pertaining to magic
reduced, brought, compiled (into writing)
to propagate, spread, extend
perdition, destruction, damnation
to consign, assign, condemn

source_notes: Ulrich Molitor's De Lamiis (1489, written for Archduke Sigismund of Austria) was one of the first printed witchcraft treatises. His characterization of grimoires as demonic compositions circulated by sorcerers was widely repeated and influenced early modern attitudes toward the Clavicula Salomonis and similar texts.
bibliography: Molitor, Ulrich. De Lamiis et Phitonicis Mulieribus. Constance: Murer, 1489.
Behringer, Wolfgang. Witches and Witch-Hunts: A Global History. Cambridge: Polity Press, 2004.

title: Contra Artem Notoriam
author: Thomas Aquinas
latin_text: Ars notoria nullam efficaciam habere potest ad scientias acquirendas ex vi figurarum et verborum, nec ex parte Dei qui ad haec non intendit, nec ex parte daemonum qui hanc artem operantur. Est enim contra devotionem debitam Deo, quia homo per hanc artem non studet ac laborat, sed per quaedam vana signa quaerit habere a Deo id quod debet per proprium laborem acquirere.
english_gloss: The notory art can have no efficacy for acquiring knowledge from the force of figures and words, neither on God's part who does not intend this, nor on the demons' part who operate this art. For it is against the devotion owed to God, because a man through this art does not study and labor, but through certain vain signs seeks to have from God what he ought to acquire through his own labor.

vocabulary.definition: notory (of the notory art), noted, recorded
efficacy, effectiveness, power
devotion, piety, dedication
vain, empty, worthless, futile
to acquire, obtain, gain

source_notes: Aquinas's condemnation of the Ars Notoria (ST II-II q.96 a.1) attacked not the text's demonic content but its laziness: seeking knowledge supernaturally instead of through proper study. This framing was influential, presenting the Notory Art as a kind of spiritual fraud rather than simply diabolism.
bibliography: Aquinas, Thomas. Summa Theologiae. Trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province. London: Burns, Oates & Washbourne, 1920.
Page, Sophie. Magic in the Cloister. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Liber Vaccae — De Operationibus ex Animalibus
author: Pseudo-Plato
latin_text: Philosophus dicit: Si vis facere hominem qui loquatur et ambulet sicut homo et multa secreta naturae ostendat, accipe vaccam virginem et macta eam die Iovis in hora Iovis, et extrahe ex ea sanguinem et semen taurinum mixtum, et pone in vase et claude per triginta dies. Virtus enim caelestis a stellis descendit in materiam praeparatam et opus mirabile per naturam operatur.
english_gloss: The Philosopher says: If you wish to make a man who speaks and walks like a man and reveals many secrets of nature, take a virgin cow and slaughter her on Thursday in the hour of Jupiter, and extract from her blood and bull semen mixed, and place in a vessel and close for thirty days. For celestial virtue descends from the stars into prepared matter and works a marvelous work through nature.

vocabulary.definition: cow, heifer
to slaughter, sacrifice, kill
of a bull, bovine
prepared, made ready
philosopher (here: Plato, as pseudonym)

source_notes: The Liber Vaccae (Book of the Cow, attributed to Plato) is a Latin translation of the Arabic Kitab al-Nawamis, containing instructions for creating a homunculus-like artificial being. One of the most notorious Arabic magical texts to enter Latin, it was condemned but copied extensively. The Jovian timing reflects the Arabic planetary magic tradition.
bibliography: Burnett, Charles. 'The Liber Vaccae or Book of the Cow Attributed to Plato.' In Magic and the Classical Tradition, eds. C. Burnett and W.F. Ryan. London: Warburg Institute, 2006.

title: Index Librorum Prohibitorum — Categoriae
author: Council of Trent
latin_text: In decima regula: Libri qui res magicas, sortilegia, auguria, auspicia, sortes, veneficia, artem divinatoriam, necromantiam, aut in quibus haec tractentur, vel aliquid ex his docetur, omnino prohibentur. Episcopi diligenter curent ut his libris populus Christianus quam maxime careat.
english_gloss: In the tenth rule: Books that deal with magical things, lots, auguries, auspices, divination, poisons, the divinatory art, necromancy, or in which these things are treated or anything of them is taught, are entirely prohibited. Bishops should diligently see to it that the Christian people be as much as possible deprived of these books.

vocabulary.definition: lot-casting, sortilege, divination by lots
auguries, omens, divination by birds
auspices, omens, bird-divination
poisoning, witchcraft, sorcery with potions
to lack, be without, be deprived of

source_notes: The Tridentine Index's tenth rule (1564) created a broad prohibition covering all magical texts. Its practical effect was to drive grimoire ownership underground rather than eradicate it — as Owen Davies has documented, condemned books were often hidden, copied in secret, and acquired on the clandestine book market.
bibliography: Reusch, Franz Heinrich. Die Indices Librorum Prohibitorum des sechzehnten Jahrhunderts. Tübingen: Literarischer Verein, 1886.
Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

title: Character Saturni et Virtutes Eius
author: Pseudo-Solomon
latin_text: Character Saturni in plumbo sculptus hora Saturni die Saturni habet vim ad destruendum inimicos, ad faciendum discordiam et odium inter homines, ad aperiendos carceres, et ad fugandos spiritus nocentes. Portans eum in sinistra manu in panno nigro involutum tutus erit a veneficiis.
english_gloss: The character of Saturn engraved on lead in the hour of Saturn on the day of Saturn has power to destroy enemies, to create discord and hatred among men, to open prisons, and to drive away harmful spirits. The one carrying it in the left hand wrapped in black cloth will be safe from witchcraft.

vocabulary.definition: lead (metal)
engraved, carved
discord, disagreement, strife
to drive away, put to flight
wrapped, enveloped, enclosed

source_notes: The Saturnian talisman instructions illustrate the planetary metal correspondence system central to Solomonic practice: Saturn governs lead, black color, and malefic operations. The association of Saturn with prisons, discord, and harming enemies reflects both astrological tradition and the grimoire's acceptance of magically caused harm.
bibliography: Mathers, S.L. MacGregor, ed. The Key of Solomon the King. London: Redway, 1889.
Skinner, Stephen, and David Rankine. The Veritable Key of Solomon. Singapore: Golden Hoard Press, 2008.

title: Triangulum Evocationis
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Extra circulum protectionis triangulum describis in quo spiritus appareat. Inscribis in angulis: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, et in centro: ANAPHAXETON. Spiritus citatus in triangulo stare debet nec circulum superare. Si circulum ingredi tentet, exorcizabis eum per nomen Tetragrammaton.
english_gloss: Outside the circle of protection you draw a triangle in which the spirit shall appear. In the corners you inscribe: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and in the center: ANAPHAXETON. The cited spirit must stand in the triangle and not exceed the circle. If he tries to enter the circle, you will exorcise him by the name Tetragrammaton.

vocabulary.definition: triangle
corners, angles
cited, summoned, invoked
to exceed, cross over, surpass
to exorcise, adjure

source_notes: The triangle of evocation outside the magician's protective circle is a consistent feature of the Grand Grimoire and related French grimoire traditions. The archangel names at the corners and the barbarous name ANAPHAXETON in the center constrain the demon spatially. This ritual geography appears also in the Key of Solomon and the Goetia.
bibliography: Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.
Peterson, Joseph H., ed. The Lesser Key of Solomon. York Beach: Weiser, 2001.

title: Benedictio Vulnerum et Febrium
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Ad sanandum vulnus: dic ter super vulnus: In nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti. Amen. Christus natus est, Christus passus est, Christus vulneratus est. Per has quinque plagas sacras sana hoc vulnus et remove dolorem et restingue ignem malignum.
english_gloss: To heal a wound: say three times over the wound: In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen. Christ was born, Christ suffered, Christ was wounded. By these five sacred wounds heal this wound and remove the pain and extinguish the malign fire.

vocabulary.definition: to heal, cure, restore to health
wounded, hurt
wounds, blows, the Five Wounds
to extinguish, quench, suppress
malign, evil, harmful

source_notes: The Romanusbüchlein (Roman Book) was a popular German healing grimoire circulating from the 18th century, purporting to be of ancient Roman origin. Its wound-blessing formula invokes the Five Wounds of Christ — a common medieval healing charm adapted into print-culture folk magic. Owen Davies traces such texts to the intersection of clerical and popular healing traditions.
bibliography: Davies, Owen. Popular Magic: Cunning-folk in English History. London: Hambledon Continuum, 2003.
Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

title: Sigillum Adonai
author: Anonymous
work: Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses
latin_text: Sigillum Adonai, quod est nomen Dei altissimi, portatum in corio cervi post ieiunium trium dierum, confert portanti sanitatem perfectam, victoriam in litibus, et protectionem ab omnibus inimicis visibilibus et invisibilibus. Hoc sigillum ipsemet Moses in Aegypto portavit.
english_gloss: The seal of Adonai, which is the most high name of God, carried on deer hide after a fast of three days, confers upon the bearer perfect health, victory in disputes, and protection from all visible and invisible enemies. Moses himself carried this seal in Egypt.

vocabulary.definition: hide, leather, skin
deer, stag
fast, fasting, abstinence from food
to confer, bestow, bring together
disputes, lawsuits, quarrels

source_notes: The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses (first printed 1849 in Stuttgart) presented itself as lost books of Moses, legitimizing its seals through Mosaic authorship. The Adonai seal with its deerskin carrier and three-day fast reflects the fusion of Kabbalistic divine names with practical Solomonic ritual. The text spread widely among German-American immigrant communities.
bibliography: Chireau, Yvonne P. Black Magic: Religion and the African American Conjuring Tradition. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2003.
Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

title: De Libris Magicis Confutatio
author: Balthasar Bekker
latin_text: Libri qui sub titulis magicis feruntur, ut Clavicula Salomonis et Picatrix, nihil continent praeter nugas et ineptias hominum imperitorum qui per verba barbara et figuras inutiles daemones invocare se posse credunt. Sed daemon nec verbis vincitur nec figuris coercetur, quia incorporeus est et per naturam suam extra omnem humanam potestatem manet.
english_gloss: Books that circulate under magical titles, such as the Key of Solomon and the Picatrix, contain nothing but the nonsense and foolishness of unskilled men who believe they can invoke demons through barbarous words and useless figures. But a demon is neither bound by words nor constrained by figures, because he is incorporeal and by his nature remains outside all human power.

vocabulary.definition: nonsense, trifles, foolishness
foolishness, absurdity, ineptitude
barbarous, foreign, incomprehensible
to constrain, restrain, confine
incorporeal, without a body, immaterial

source_notes: Balthasar Bekker's De Betoverde Weereld (1691-93) mounted an Enlightenment rational critique of witchcraft and magic, arguing that demons lack the power to interact with the material world. His dismissal of grimoires as 'nugae' was part of a broader Protestant-rationalist attack that inadvertently helped discredit witch-hunting.
bibliography: Bekker, Balthasar. De Betoverde Weereld. Amsterdam: Daniël van den Dalen, 1691.
Fix, Andrew C. Fallen Angels: Balthasar Bekker, Spirit Belief, and Confessionalism in the Seventeenth Century Dutch Republic. Dordrecht: Kluwer, 1999.

title: Experimentum de Spiritu Familiaris
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Ad habendum spiritum familiarem: Accipe librum mundissimum et in eo scribe haec nomina: Sathan, Beelzebub, Astaroth, Lucifer, et sub unoquoque nomen eius signum. Tunc vade ad triuium in nocte Iovis post mediam noctem et dic ter: O vos spiritus qui hunc locum inhabitatis, venite ad me N. qui vos invoco per potestatem illorum nominum quae scripsi. Et apparebit tibi unus in forma alicuius animalis.
english_gloss: To have a familiar spirit: Take the cleanest book and in it write these names: Satan, Beelzebub, Astaroth, Lucifer, and beneath each its sign. Then go to a crossroads on Thursday night after midnight and say three times: O you spirits who inhabit this place, come to me N. who invokes you by the power of those names which I wrote. And one will appear to you in the form of some animal.

vocabulary.definition: crossroads, three-way junction
to inhabit, dwell in
cleanest, purest, most spotless
familiar (spirit), household spirit, intimate
animal, living creature, beast

source_notes: The Munich Handbook of Necromancy (Clm 849, 15th c.) is one of the most complete surviving learned necromancy manuals. Kieckhefer's edition revealed the crossroads meeting with demons to be not folk magic but learned clerical practice, directly engaging the demonic hierarchy. The Thursday timing (Jovian day) reflects the planetary system.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. Stroud: Sutton, 1997.
Kieckhefer, Richard. Magic in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989.

title: Imago Cerae ad Nocendum Inimico
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Fac imaginem de cera in forma hominis et in eius fronte scribe nomen inimici tui et dic: Te N. per ignem Gehennae et per tormenta damnatorum adiuro ut tales dolores N. patiatur quales haec imago patietur. Tunc acu punges eam in parte corporis quam vexare vis.
english_gloss: Make an image from wax in the form of a man and on his forehead write the name of your enemy and say: I adjure you N. by the fire of Gehenna and by the torments of the damned that N. suffer such pains as this image will suffer. Then you will pierce it with a needle in the part of the body you wish to torment.

vocabulary.definition: Gehenna, Hell, the place of punishment
torments, tortures, agonies
of the damned, condemned persons
needle, pin
to pierce, prick, stab

source_notes: Wax image magic (imago cerae) appears throughout the Munich Manual as a link between learned Latin necromancy and ancient defixio traditions. The Christian framing — invoking Gehenna rather than the underworld gods — adapts the classical curse tablet into a medieval demonic magic framework.
bibliography: Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. Stroud: Sutton, 1997.

title: Oratio pro Defensione Corporis
author: Anonymous (attrib. Pope Leo III)
latin_text: Haec oratio a Leone Papa Summo Pontifice composita et Carolo Magno Imperatori missa defensionem corporis et animae contra omnes inimicos visibiles et invisibiles praestat. Qui eam ieiunus legit et secum defert, ab igne, ab aqua, a ferro, a veneno, a fascino et ab omni maleficio tutus erit. Per nomen Dei viventis, per virtutem Crucis Christi, per merita Virginis Mariae.
english_gloss: This prayer composed by Leo the Pope, Supreme Pontiff, and sent to Charlemagne the Emperor, provides protection of body and soul against all visible and invisible enemies. Whoever reads it fasting and carries it with him will be safe from fire, from water, from iron, from poison, from the evil eye, and from all witchcraft. By the name of the living God, by the power of the Cross of Christ, by the merits of the Virgin Mary.

vocabulary.definition: to provide, supply, perform, excel
fasting, having fasted, empty (of food)
to carry, bring, convey
evil eye, fascination, magical harm by gaze
witchcraft, evil deed, sorcery

source_notes: The Enchiridion (first printed Rome, 1523) claimed to be a collection of prayers compiled by Pope Leo III and sent as a gift to Charlemagne. Its papal and imperial authority legitimized its use as a protective amulet. The claim is certainly false — the text is a later compilation — but its association with Rome gave it extraordinary popular prestige.
bibliography: Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.
Flint, Valerie I.J. The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991.

title: Virtus Talismanum Gallinae Nigrae
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Talisman primum, quod figuram serpentis in auro continet, portanti dat loquelam in omnibus linguis et intelligentiam omnium rerum occultarum. Talisman secundum, in argento sculptum, invisibilitatem confert. Haec talisamana a sapiente Turcico in Aegypto tradita sunt et virtutes eorum per experimentum probatae.
english_gloss: The first talisman, which contains the figure of a serpent in gold, gives to the wearer speech in all languages and understanding of all hidden things. The second talisman, engraved in silver, confers invisibility. These talismans were handed down by a Turkish sage in Egypt and their virtues have been proven by experiment.

vocabulary.definition: speech, language, manner of speaking
invisibility, the state of being unseen
to confer, bestow, attribute
proven, tested, approved
wise man, sage, philosopher

source_notes: La Poule Noire (c. 1820) presented a set of talismans supposedly recovered from an Egyptian sage encountered during Napoleon's Egyptian campaign. Its talismans for speech in all languages, invisibility, and treasure-finding represent the most popular magical desires in 19th-century French popular magic. Davies traces it as the culmination of the French grimoire tradition.
bibliography: Davies, Owen. Grimoires: A History of Magic Books. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

title: Forma Pacti cum Spiritu Familiari
author: Anonymous
work: Liber Spirituum (Book of Spirits, generic tradition)
latin_text: Ego N. do et concedo tibi spiritui N. omnem potestatem meam in rebus materialibus per spatium decem annorum, ita ut tu mihi serves fideliter et obedias in omnibus quae petiero. In signum huius pacti do tibi guttam sanguinis mei ex digito sinistro et hoc chirographum manu mea scriptum. Post decem annos, anima et corpus mea libera erunt.
english_gloss: I N. give and grant to you spirit N. all my power in material things for a period of ten years, so that you faithfully serve me and obey in all things I shall request. As a sign of this pact I give you a drop of my blood from my left finger and this document written by my own hand. After ten years, my soul and body will be free.

vocabulary.definition: to give, grant, yield, concede
material, physical, relating to matter
handwritten document, autograph, deed
drop (of liquid)
left (hand), sinister

source_notes: The Liber Spirituum was a generic name for personal spirit-books used by learned necromancers, containing pacts, spirit names, and ritual instructions built up over a career. The blood-pact formula — giving a drop from the left hand as a contract signature — appears across multiple grimoire traditions and was cited as proof of diabolism in witch trials.
bibliography: Boudet, Jean-Patrice. Entre science et nigromance: Astrologie, divination et magie dans l'Occident médiéval. Paris: Publications de la Sorbonne, 2006.
Kieckhefer, Richard. Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century. Stroud: Sutton, 1997.

title: On the Operativity of Ritual in Learned Magic
author: Frank Klaassen
latin_text: Magia operativa, ut in libris nigromantiae docetur, distinguitur a magia speculativa per hoc quod habet finem practicum: non solum cognitionem rerum occultarum sed etiam mutationem status rerum in mundo. Operatores magici non philosophi sed artifices erant.
english_gloss: Operative magic, as taught in books of necromancy, is distinguished from speculative magic by having a practical end: not only knowledge of hidden things but also the change of the state of things in the world. Magical operators were not philosophers but craftsmen.

vocabulary.definition: operative, practical, action-oriented
speculative, theoretical, contemplative
craftsmen, makers, skilled practitioners
change, alteration, transformation

source_notes: Frank Klaassen's taxonomy of operative vs. speculative magic — drawn from his study of late medieval magical manuscripts — has become foundational for understanding grimoire traditions. His argument that grimoire operators were practitioners rather than philosophers reframes the study of magic books as technical literature.
bibliography: Klaassen, Frank. The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages and Renaissance. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2013.

title: Introductorium Maius — De Virtutibus Planetarum in Operibus Magicis
author: Abu Ma'shar (Albumasar)
latin_text: Stella Saturni frigidam et siccam complexionem habet et dominatur super agricolas et servos et reos et mortuos et res sepultas in terra. In operibus magicis invocatur per suffumigationes frigidas et humidas et per colores nigros, et tempora eius sunt noctes Saturni ante solis ortum.
english_gloss: The star of Saturn has a cold and dry complexion and rules over farmers and slaves and the condemned and the dead and things buried in the earth. In magical operations it is invoked through cold and moist fumigations and through black colors, and its times are Saturday nights before sunrise.

vocabulary.definition: complexion, combination of qualities, temperament
farmers, tillers of the soil
buried, interred, concealed in the ground
fumigations, smoke-offerings, incense
cold, frigid, chilling

source_notes: Abu Ma'shar's Introductorium Maius (translated by John of Seville, 1133 CE) transmitted Arabic astrological magic into Latin Europe. The Saturnian correspondences — coldness, dryness, agriculture, burial, black — became the standard basis for Solomonic planetary talisman theory in the Picatrix, the Key of Solomon, and the Grand Grimoire.
bibliography: Abu Ma'shar. The Abbreviation of the Introduction to Astrology. Ed. and trans. Charles Burnett. Leiden: Brill, 1994.
Lemay, Richard. Abu Ma'shar and Latin Aristotelianism in the Twelfth Century. Beirut: American University of Beirut, 1962.

title: Quaestiones Celeberrimae — Magia Est Impossibilis
author: Marin Mersenne
latin_text: Illi qui credunt per verba barbara et characteres inscriptos in pergameno corpora volare, metalla transmutari, daemones cogi, graviter errant. Natura enim legibus suis obedit, non verbis humanis. Daemones autem, si existunt, nec verbis ligantur nec signis coguntur, quia spiritus sunt et supra naturam corporalem agunt.
english_gloss: Those who believe that through barbarous words and characters inscribed on parchment bodies can fly, metals be transmuted, demons be compelled, err gravely. For nature obeys its own laws, not human words. Demons however, if they exist, are neither bound by words nor compelled by signs, because they are spirits and act above corporeal nature.

vocabulary.definition: barbarous, foreign, unintelligible
characters, symbols, magical signs
to be transmuted, transformed, changed
to be compelled, forced, coerced
to be bound, tied, constrained

source_notes: Marin Mersenne's massive biblical commentary (1623) devoted extensive space to refuting magic using natural philosophy. His argument — that nature follows its own laws, not magical words — anticipates the scientific revolution's reframing of nature as law-governed and thus immune to verbal manipulation.
bibliography: Mersenne, Marin. Quaestiones Celeberrimae in Genesim. Paris: Cramoisy, 1623.
Dear, Peter. Mersenne and the Learning of the Schools. Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1988.

title: De Essentia Spirituum — Hierarchia Aetheris
author: Anonymous
latin_text: Spiritus qui sunt inter nos et Deum in hierarchiam ordinantur: primi sunt angeli qui assistunt throno divino, secundi sunt qui portant mandata, tertii qui mundos regunt, quarti qui inter stellas habitant, quinti qui in aere medio conversantur, sexti qui terram incolunt, septimi qui aquas et terram subterranam custodiunt.
english_gloss: The spirits that are between us and God are arranged in a hierarchy: the first are angels who stand before the divine throne, the second are those who carry commands, the third who govern worlds, the fourth who dwell among the stars, the fifth who dwell in the middle air, the sixth who inhabit the earth, the seventh who guard the waters and the subterranean earth.

vocabulary.definition: hierarchy, sacred order, ranked structure
to stand before, assist, attend upon
throne, seat of power
commands, orders, commissions
to dwell, associate, live among

source_notes: The sevenfold hierarchy of spirits in this anonymous text — from throne-angels to subterranean guardians — represents the synthesis of Pseudo-Dionysian hierarchiology with Arabic elemental cosmology that underlies practical grimoire spirit-lists. The structure directly influenced the Liber Juratus and the Arbatel.
bibliography: Boudet, Jean-Patrice. Entre science et nigromance. Paris: Publications de la Sorbonne, 2006.
Fanger, Claire, ed. Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic. Stroud: Sutton, 1998.

title: Praefatio Editoris — De Authentica Clavicula
author: S.L. MacGregor Mathers
work: The Key of Solomon the King (1889 edition)
latin_text: Inter codices manuscriptos bibliothecarum Londinensium multos legi qui sub nomine Claviculae Salomonis feruntur; et reperi eos inter se multum discrepare et multa apocrypha continere. Tamen ex his omnibus, collatis et emendatis, veram formam operis antiqui restituere conatus sum.
english_gloss: Among the manuscript codices of the London libraries I have read many that circulate under the name of the Key of Solomon; and I found them to differ greatly among themselves and to contain much that is apocryphal. Nevertheless from all these, having compared and emended them, I have attempted to restore the true form of the ancient work.

vocabulary.definition: manuscripts, codices, bound books
to differ, disagree, be discordant
apocryphal, spurious, hidden/secret writings
compared, collated, brought together
corrected, emended, revised

source_notes: Mathers's 1889 Key of Solomon was the first printed English translation, based on British Library manuscripts. His editorial rhetoric — comparing, emending, restoring — mimics philological method while serving occult revival goals. The edition was foundational for 20th-century Solomonic practice and influenced Crowley, Waite, and the Golden Dawn.
bibliography: Mathers, S.L. MacGregor, ed. The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis). London: Redway, 1889.
Bogdan, Henrik, and Martin P. Starr, eds. Aleister Crowley and Western Esotericism. New York: Oxford University Press, 2012.

title: De Triplici Mundo — The Threefold World
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter i
latin_text: Cum triplex sit mundus, elementalis, coelestis et intellectualis, et quisque inferior a superiori regatur ac suarum virium suscipiat influxum, ita ut ipse Archetypus et summus Opifex per angelos, coelos, stellas, elementa, animalia, plantas, metalla, lapides suae omnipotentiae virtutes exinde in nos transfundat — non irrationabile putant magi nos per eosdem gradus, per singulos mundos, ad eundem ipsum archetypum mundum, omnium opificem et primam causam, a qua sumpserunt omnia et in quam tendunt omnia, posse conscendere.
english_gloss: Since the world is threefold — elemental, celestial, and intellectual — and each lower is governed by the higher and receives the influx of its powers, so that the Archetype and supreme Artificer pours through angels, heavens, stars, elements, animals, plants, metals, and stones the virtues of His omnipotence into us — the magi think it not unreasonable that we can ascend through those same degrees, through each world in turn, to that same archetypal world, the maker of all things and first cause, from which all things have taken their being and to which all things tend.

vocabulary.definition: threefold, triple
influx, flowing-in, influence
archetype, original pattern, divine exemplar
maker, craftsman, artificer (here: God)
to ascend, climb up, mount

source_notes: The opening theorem of De Occulta Philosophia establishes Agrippa's fundamental cosmological premise: the universe is structured in three linked worlds (elemental, celestial, intellectual), each governed by the one above it. Magic is the art of ascending this chain to its source. This Neoplatonic cascade—Plotinus via Ficino—underpins all three books.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: Quid Sit Magia — What Magic Is
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter ii
latin_text: Magica facultas, potestatis plurimae compos, altissimis plena mysteriis, profundissimam rerum secretissimarum contemplationem, naturam, potentiam, qualitatem, substantiam et virtutem totius naturae complectitur. Est ergo magia connexio et copulatio praedicta trium mundorum, quam qui calluerit nihil erit quod possit ignorare in naturis rerum. Haec est perfectissima summaque scientia, haec altior sanctiorque philosophia, haec denique totius nobilissimae philosophiae absoluta consummatio.
english_gloss: The magical faculty, possessing very great power, full of the highest mysteries, encompasses the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, the nature, power, quality, substance and virtue of all nature. Therefore magic is the connection and coupling of the three aforesaid worlds, and one who has mastered it will have nothing in the natures of things that he can be ignorant of. This is the most perfect and supreme science, this is a higher and more sacred philosophy, this finally is the absolute consummation of the noblest philosophy.

vocabulary.definition: faculty, power, capacity, branch of knowledge
power, authority, might
to embrace, encompass, comprehend
connection, linking, union
consummation, completion, perfection

source_notes: Agrippa's definition of magic as 'connexio et copulatio trium mundorum' — the connection of three worlds — locates magic as a synthetic science rather than a diabolical art. The definition draws on Ficino's Neoplatonism and Pico's Oration. The claim to be 'absolutam consummationem' of all philosophy made the book controversial.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Quatuor Elementis — The Four Elements and Their Qualities
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter iii
latin_text: Quatuor elementa, ignis, aqua, terra, aer, omnium rerum materiale principium apud omnes philosophos certissimum: his autem quatuor elementis quatuor primae qualitates adsistunt, caliditas, frigiditas, humiditas et siccitas. Et unumquodque elementum duas specificas qualitates habet, quarum priorem sibi propriam retinet, in altera tanquam media convenit cum sequenti: est enim ignis calidus et siccus, aer calidus et humidus, aqua frigida et humida, terra sicca et frigida.
english_gloss: The four elements, fire, water, earth, and air, are the most certain material principle of all things, according to all philosophers. To these four elements four primary qualities are assigned: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. And each element has two specific qualities, retaining the first as its own, while in the second it agrees as a middle with the following: for fire is hot and dry, air hot and moist, water cold and moist, earth dry and cold.

vocabulary.definition: principle, beginning, first cause
qualities, properties, characteristics
to be present in, attend, belong to
specific, proper to the species
moisture, dampness, humidity

source_notes: The elemental theory follows Aristotle's De Generatione et Corruptione via Avicenna. Agrippa's contribution is linking the elemental qualities to the full chain of correspondences: each element corresponds to a humor, a planet, a time of day, a wind, an animal class, and ultimately to a divine name. This system pervades all three books of DOP.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Triplici Elementorum Ratione — The Threefold Classification of Elements
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter iv
latin_text: Quatuor itaque quae diximus sunt elementa, sine quorum notitia perfecta nullum in magia producere possumus effectum. Sunt autem singula triplicia, ut sic quaternarius compleat duodenarium et, per septenarium in denarium progrediens, ad supremam unitatem, unde omnis virtus et mirabilis operatio dependet, fiat progressus. Primo igitur ordine elementa pura sunt, quae nec componuntur, nec alterantur, nec corrumpuntur — causas et virtutes habent maximas. Secundo ordine sunt quae ex mixtione primorum resultant. Tertio, quae ex utrisque composita, plurimis permixta qualitatis, omnium ultima et minime potentia.
english_gloss: So then these four that we have described are the elements, without perfect knowledge of which we can produce no effect in magic. Moreover each of them is threefold, so that the quaternary completes the duodenary and, progressing through the septenary to the decenary, makes progress to the supreme unity on which every virtue and marvelous operation depends. In the first order elements are pure, neither compounded, altered, nor corruptible — they have the greatest causes and virtues. In the second order are those that result from the mixing of the first. In the third, those composed from both, mixed with many qualities, the last of all and least powerful.

vocabulary.definition: threefold, triple
quaternary, the number four
duodenary, the number twelve
septenary, the number seven
supreme, highest, final

source_notes: The threefold classification of elements generates Agrippa's numerological cosmology: 4 × 3 = 12 (the zodiac), 4 × 7 = 28 (lunar mansions), 4 × 10 = 40 (Mosaic desert period). The ascent from quaternary to unity via septenary and denary maps the magical operator's spiritual progression.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Spiritu Mundi — The Spirit of the World
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xiv
latin_text: Est praeterea in rebus omnibus quidam spiritus occultus diffusus per universum mundum, qui quidem spiritus ipse mundus est, vivens et sentiens, et eo plenus est mundus, per quem res naturales suis virtutibus inter se agunt et patiuntur. Hunc spiritum per radios Solis, per aera et per sublimes quasdam haustiones recipimus, per quem etiam magnetica vis gignitur, per quem herba et lapis et lignum et tota natura vires suas exercet. Omnis occulta proprietas propagatur in herbas, lapides et metalla et in animantia per Solem, per Lunam, per planetas perque stellas planetis sublimiores.
english_gloss: Moreover in all things there is a certain hidden spirit diffused through the entire world, which spirit is itself the world, living and perceiving, and the world is full of it, through which natural things act on and are acted on by each other through their virtues. We receive this spirit through the rays of the Sun, through the air and through certain sublime inhalations, through which also the magnetic force is generated, through which herb and stone and wood and all of nature exercises its powers. Every hidden property is propagated into herbs, stones and metals and into living things through the Sun, through the Moon, through the planets and through the stars higher than the planets.

vocabulary.definition: hidden, concealed, secret
diffused, spread out, poured through
inhalations, draughts, absorptions
magnetic, of the lodestone
to be propagated, spread, transmitted

source_notes: The spiritus mundi doctrine — a universal pneuma or subtle vapor that transmits celestial influences to terrestrial matter — is Agrippa's key explanatory mechanism for natural magic. It synthesizes Stoic pneuma (via Ficino's De Vita III) with Neoplatonic theory of sympatheia. The lodestone example illustrates how celestial influence operates invisibly.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Ficino, Marsilio. De Vita Libri Tres. Ed. Carol Kaske and John Clark. Binghamton: MRTS, 1989.

title: De Virtutibus Occultis Rerum — Hidden Virtues in Things
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter x
latin_text: Haec est radix et fundamentum omnium corporum, naturarum, virtutum et operum mirabilium, et qui has elementorum qualitates et eorundem mixtiones cognoverit, facile perficiet opera miranda atque stupenda eritque consummatus in magia naturali. Virtus enim quaedam occulta inest rebus omnibus, quam nulla sensuum experientia observare possumus, nisi per effectus eius collatis eorum similitudinibus et differentiis per longam temporum observationem. Has autem virtutes a stellis et planetis rerum principiis ac sideribus, tum a Deo ipso rebus infusas esse arbitratur philosophia.
english_gloss: This is the root and foundation of all bodies, natures, virtues and marvelous works, and one who has known these elemental qualities and their mixtures will easily accomplish marvelous and stupendous works and will be perfected in natural magic. For a certain hidden virtue is in all things, which we cannot observe by any experience of the senses except through its effects by comparing their similarities and differences through long observation over time. Philosophy holds that these virtues have been infused into things by the stars and planets and heavenly bodies, and by God himself.

vocabulary.definition: foundation, basis, ground
perfected, completed, consummate
by comparing, collating, bringing together
similarities, likenesses, resemblances
infused, poured into, instilled

source_notes: The theory of virtutes occultae — hidden properties not reducible to elemental quality — is central to Agrippa's natural magic. These are properties knowable only by long empirical observation, making natural magic an experiential science. The term 'occultus' means 'hidden from the senses,' not 'diabolical.' Agrippa follows Albertus Magnus and Ficino.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Sympathia et Antipathia — On Sympathy and Antipathy
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xix
latin_text: Sympathy est quaedam naturalis amicitia ac familiaritas inter res, quam philosophi Graeci sympatheian vocant; antipathia vero odium quoddam naturale et repugnantia. Ex sympathia ergo fit ut res similes res sibi similes appetant, trahant, retineant et foveant; ex antipathia vero fit ut dissonantia inter se fuga et odio prosequantur. Quapropter magus ille qui novit sympathias et antipathias rerum naturalium, naturalium virium habet plenissimam cognitionem et per eam facile mirabilia producit, unitam quasi naturam per applicationem talium ad talia, nec opus habens daemonibus aut incantationibus.
english_gloss: Sympathy is a certain natural friendship and familiarity between things, which the Greek philosophers call sympatheia; antipathy is a certain natural hatred and repugnance. From sympathy it comes about that like things seek, attract, retain, and cherish things like themselves; from antipathy it comes about that discordant things pursue each other with flight and hatred. Therefore the magician who knows the sympathies and antipathies of natural things has the fullest knowledge of natural powers and through it easily produces marvels, uniting nature as it were through the application of such to such things, needing neither demons nor incantations.

vocabulary.definition: sympathy, natural affinity, fellow-feeling
antipathy, natural repugnance, opposition
repugnance, resistance, opposition
dissonance, disagreement, discordance
incantations, spells, enchantments

source_notes: Sympathia/antipathia is the physical mechanism underlying natural magic: like attracts like, unlike repels unlike. The crucial claim ('nec opus habens daemonibus') is that true natural magic requires neither demons nor incantations but only knowledge of natural affinities. Agrippa cites Pliny, Theophrastus, and Neoplatonists as authorities.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Anima Mundi et Spiritu Eius — World Soul and Its Spirit
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xii
latin_text: Plato enim et eius sectatores in mundo spiritu et rationali anima tam eum adornant vitam quam et nos: huius animae corpora omnia plena sunt, quae per totum mundum diffusa, omnibus suis partibus vitam praebet. Haec est anima mundi in toto universo et singulis partibus eius, sicut anima nostra in nobis et in qualibet parte corporis nostri.
english_gloss: For Plato and his followers adorn the world with a spirit and rational soul as much as us: all bodies are full of this soul, which being diffused through the whole world gives life to all its parts. This is the soul of the world in the whole universe and in its individual parts, just as our soul is in us and in every part of our body.

vocabulary.definition: followers, adherents, disciples
to adorn, furnish, equip
diffused, spread out, poured through
to give, provide, offer, furnish

source_notes: The anima mundi or world soul (Plato's Timaeus 34b-37c) provides the living substrate through which celestial influences reach terrestrial matter. Agrippa's use of it legitimizes natural magic: one is not dealing with demons but with the life-principle of nature itself, as Ficino had argued in his Theologia Platonica.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Plantis Solaribus — Solar Plants
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xxiv
latin_text: Solaria inter herbas et plantas sunt quae girantur ad Solem imitantes eius motum, ut heliotropium et lotos, quam quidem arbusculam solarem esse et fructuum et foliorum figura testatur. Sic paeonia, chelidonia, citraria, zinziber, gentiana, dictamnus, verbena quoque praestans vaticinium et expiationem fugansque cacodaemones; laurus etiam, Phoebo sacer, ac cedrus, palma et fraxinus et hedera et vitis et quaecunque venena et fulgura repellunt et, perpetuo virentes, hyemis algores non verentur. Item solaria sunt menta, mastix, zedoaria, crocus, balsamus, ambra, muscus, mel flavum, lignum aloes, cinnamomum, calamus aromaticus, piper, thus, amaracus.
english_gloss: Among herbs and plants, solar ones are those that turn toward the Sun imitating its motion, like the heliotrope and the lotus, which the shape of its fruits and leaves testifies to be solar. So too peony, celandine, citrus, ginger, gentian, dittany, and vervain, which also provides prophetic power and expiation and puts cacodaemons to flight; also laurel, sacred to Phoebus, and cedar, palm and ash and ivy and vine and whatever repels poisons and lightning and, ever green, fears not winter's colds.
