Also solar are mint, mastic, zedoary, saffron, balsam, amber, musk, yellow honey, aloe wood, cinnamon, aromatic calamus, pepper, frankincense, marjoram.

vocabulary.definition: heliotrope, sunflower (sun-turning plant)
prophetic power, divination, prophecy
expiation, purification, atonement
evil spirits, malevolent demons
colds, chills, freezing temperatures

source_notes: Agrippa's planetary herb list synthesizes Pseudo-Apuleius, Dioscorides, Ficino's De Vita, and the Picatrix. Each plant's solar quality is demonstrated by behavior (turning toward the sun), shape (imitating sun discs), or medicinal property (warming, illuminating, prophetic). The list was the standard reference for Renaissance botanical magic.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Plantis Saturnalibus — Saturn's Plants
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xxiii
latin_text: Saturnalia inter herbas et plantas sunt quae Saturni naturam participant, ut habentes sucos nigros et graveolentes et noxios, ut mandragora, opium, chelidonium maius. Item quae diu vivunt et tarde crescunt ac sero fructum ferunt et quibus spinae absunt aut durae surculi. Ex arboribus cupressus, pinus, abies et nux.
english_gloss: Among herbs and plants those are Saturnine that participate in Saturn's nature, such as those having dark, ill-smelling, and noxious juices, as mandrake, opium, and greater celandine. Also those that live long and grow slowly and bear fruit late, and those lacking thorns or having hard shoots. Among trees: cypress, pine, fir, and walnut.

vocabulary.definition: to share in, participate in, partake
ill-smelling, heavy-scented, malodorous
mandrake (Mandragora officinarum)
silver fir, fir tree (Abies)

source_notes: Saturnine plants are identified by slowness of growth, dark or noxious qualities, longevity, and association with cold and heaviness — all properties of the planet Saturn in astrological theory. The list correlates with Saturnine medical properties: binding, constipating, melancholy-inducing.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Lapidibus Occultis Virtutibus Donatis — Stones Endowed with Hidden Virtues
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xv
latin_text: Mirabilior quam in vegetabilibus in lapidibus quoque virtus admiranda apparet. Quis non miretur adamantem, qui ferrum impenetrabili sua duritie vincit nec igni nec acre cedit? Quis non miretur carbunculum, qui tenebras illustrat luce propria et in aqua splendore non minuitor? Quis non miretur magnetem, qui ferrum ad se trahit per occultam naturae vim? Quis non miretur catocitem, qui admotam manum sic stringit, ut declinare non possit, dum voluntas iubendo non imperat? Haec omnia non ab elementorum qualitatibus sed ab occultis rerum ideis per spiritum mundi in eas influxis derivant.
english_gloss: More marvelous even than in plants, a wonderful virtue appears in stones too. Who is not amazed by the diamond, which overcomes iron with its impenetrable hardness and yields neither to fire nor to acid? Who is not amazed by the carbuncle, which illuminates the dark with its own light and is not diminished in brightness under water? Who is not amazed by the magnet, which attracts iron through nature's hidden force? Who is not amazed by the catochite, which so grips an applied hand that it cannot pull away without the will commanding? All these derive not from elemental qualities but from the hidden ideas of things infused into them through the spirit of the world.

vocabulary.definition: diamond, the hardest stone
carbuncle, a fiery red gemstone (ruby/garnet)
magnet, lodestone
catochite, a stone said to cause adhesion
Platonic ideas, forms, archetypes

source_notes: The lapidary tradition is one of Agrippa's main sources for occult virtue: stones exhibit properties that cannot be explained by their elemental composition alone (hardness, luminosity, magnetism) and therefore prove the existence of form-derived virtues infused by celestial ideas. Sources include Albertus Magnus's De Mineralibus and the Picatrix.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Animalibus Planetis Attributis — Animals Attributed to Planets
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xxii
latin_text: Solaria inter animalia sunt leo, qui inter quadrupedia in dignitatis principatum fertur, et aries et crocodilus et cervus et calurus serpens et scarabeus. Lunaria sunt quae mutationibus Lunae parent, ut cat, lepus, rana, porcus et omnia aquatica. Iovialia sunt cervus et delphinus et aquila et gallus gallinaceus.
english_gloss: Among animals, solar ones are the lion, which is held to the first rank in dignity among quadrupeds, and the ram, crocodile, stag, calurus serpent, and scarab. Lunar are those that respond to the Moon's changes, like the cat, hare, frog, pig, and all aquatic creatures. Jovial are the stag, dolphin, eagle, and rooster.

vocabulary.definition: four-footed animals, quadrupeds
of a rooster, cockerel (gallus gallinaceus)
changes, mutations, phases
aquatic, water-dwelling, of the water

source_notes: The zoological correspondence table assigns each animal to a planet based on behavioral, morphological, or symbolic qualities. The lion's solar kingship, the cat's lunar changeability, the eagle's Jovian nobility — these are ancient correspondences from Ptolemy, Firmicus Maternus, and the Picatrix, systematized by Agrippa.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Imaginibus Coelestibus — On Celestial Images
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xxxvii
latin_text: Praeterea sunt quaedam imagines coelestium non ab humanis manibus fabricatae, sed a natura ipsa in certis lapidibus et metallis impressae, ut in magnetite imago ursi maioris et minoris aut in aetite imago aquilae, in cornachio imago vel corvus vel scarabeus. Quae imagines cum in rebus ipsis naturaliter insunt, certam in se stellae suae obtinent virtutem, ex quibus intelligere possumus quantum ad similitudinem coelestium nostri artificio fabricatae imagines valeant, quando ex ipsa natura in rebus haerentibus tam miranda efficacia reperitur.
english_gloss: Moreover there are certain images of celestial bodies not fashioned by human hands, but impressed by nature itself in certain stones and metals, as in magnetite an image of the Greater and Lesser Bear, or in the eagle-stone an image of the eagle, in the cornelian an image of a raven or scarab. These images, since they are naturally inherent in the things themselves, hold in themselves a definite virtue of their star, from which we can understand how much images fashioned by our craft to the likeness of celestial things may avail, when such wonderful efficacy is found in things inherent naturally.

vocabulary.definition: magnetite, magnetic iron ore
eagle-stone (a concretion), aetite
cornelian, carnelian (a reddish stone)
inherent, adhering, naturally present in
efficacy, effectiveness, power to act

source_notes: Natural celestial images (stones bearing natural pictures of stars or constellations) prove the principle of celestial inscription in matter. If nature herself inscribes eagle-images in eagle-stone, then artificially made images can capture stellar virtue by analogy. This argument legitimizes astrological talismanic magic by natural precedent.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: De Signaculis et Signaturis Rerum — The Signatures of Things
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xxxiii
latin_text: Quaecunque res a superioribus virtutem haurit, signum aliquod a superiori imprimitur ei, per quod virtus illa manifesta fiat et indicetur. Hinc verbena vincenti datur, hinc palma victoribus, hinc corona lauro aut myrto. Haec signacula occultorum characterum viam ac semitam aperiunt mago.
english_gloss: Whatever thing draws virtue from superiors, some sign is impressed on it by that superior, through which that virtue may be made manifest and indicated. Hence vervain is given to the victor, hence the palm to winners, hence a crown of laurel or myrtle. These seals of hidden characters open the way and path for the magician.

vocabulary.definition: signs, seals, signatures, marks
to be impressed, stamped, marked upon
manifest, evident, clear
vervain (Verbena officinalis), a magical plant
of characters, magical signs, symbols

source_notes: The doctrine of signatures holds that celestial influence leaves visible marks on terrestrial things, readable by the trained magus. Agrippa cites the use of victory-plants (vervain, laurel, palm) as evidence that nature encodes virtue in form. This doctrine is elaborated by Paracelsus and later by Oswald Croll's Basilica Chymica.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Ligaturis et Amuletis — Bindings and Amulets
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xlv
latin_text: Ligaturae ac suspensiones, quae amuleta vocantur, non negaverim habere virtutem, si tamen ex causis naturalibus profluant nec superstitioni maculatae admixtae sint. Virtus enim rerum, sicut in sensibili corpore operatur, ita etiam in aliqua distantia per sympathiam operatur; ligata enim res aut suspensa ei qui portat vim suam naturalem pro magnitudine sympathiae impertit. Praecipue autem hoc fit quando sub debitis coelestibus horis et constellationibus praeparantur et quando ex rebus conficiuntur quae naturalem vim suam ad id opus conferentes habent.
english_gloss: I would not deny that bindings and suspensions called amulets have virtue, provided they flow from natural causes and are not mixed with filthy superstition. For the virtue of things, just as it operates in the sensible body, also operates at some distance through sympathy; for a bound or suspended thing imparts its natural power to the one carrying it in proportion to the sympathy. This happens especially when they are prepared under proper celestial hours and constellations, and when they are made from things that have natural power contributing to that work.

vocabulary.definition: bindings, ties, ligatures, amulets
suspensions, things hung, pendants
amulets, talismans worn for protection
superstition, false religious practice
constellations, configurations of stars

source_notes: Agrippa's measured defense of amulets insists on the naturalness of sympathetic action at a distance: an amulet works like a magnet, transmitting virtue through the universal spiritus without supernatural agency. The caveat against 'superstitio maculata' distinguishes legitimate natural use from diabolical pact.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Fascinatione — On the Evil Eye and Fascination
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter l
latin_text: Fascinatio est virtus quaedam emanans ex spiritu fascinantis, per oculos, in spiritum fascinati, eumque inficiens et corrumpens. Est enim in oculis nostris spiritus quidam ex sanguinis purissimi flore et subtilissimo vapore cordis emanans, qui quasi scintillam lucidam emittit radios spirituales, quibus — sicut arcus sagittam — spiritus cordis nostri in spiritu alterius tanquam sagittam immittit. Et ideo fascinator multo plus potest in alios quos odio prosequitur vel quos amat vehementer; radii enim eius efficaciores sunt ut magis corroborentur ab affectibus animi.
english_gloss: Fascination is a certain virtue emanating from the spirit of the fascinator, through the eyes, into the spirit of the fascinated, infecting and corrupting it. For there is in our eyes a certain spirit flowing from the purest flower of the blood and the subtlest vapor of the heart, which emits a kind of bright spark of spiritual rays, through which — like a bow shoots an arrow — the spirit of our heart is sent like an arrow into the spirit of another. And therefore the fascinator has much more power over those he pursues with hatred or loves vehemently; for his rays are more efficacious as they are more strengthened by the emotions of the soul.

vocabulary.definition: fascination, the evil eye, magical harming by gaze
the one who fascinates, the fascinator
spark, glimmer, tiny flame
rays, beams, shafts of light
emotions, feelings, passions of the soul

source_notes: Agrippa's theory of fascination (the evil eye) is physiological: the eyes emit pneumatic rays carrying the spirit of the gazer's blood, which then penetrates the observer's spiritus. The emotional intensification — hatred and love make the rays more powerful — draws on Ficino's De Vita and Avicenna's psychology. This explains how the evil eye operates naturally.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Suffumigationibus — On Fumigations
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xliii
latin_text: Suffumigamenta, incensionum et suffituum quam multas vires habent, a physicis et Magis probatum est. Suffumigationes enim planetarum et signorum suis planetis attributae plurimum conferunt ad imaginum consecrationem et ad invocandas animas et daemonas et congregandas vel fugandas. Saturnales suffumigationes: sulphur, asphaltos, storax, arundo, styrax, mandragora, opium, oleum cicutae et omnium herbarum vel radicum quae Saturni dicuntur. Solares vero: thus, crocus, balsamus, ambar, muscus, lignum aloes. Lunares: aloe, mastix, camphora, launum, semen papaveris, thus album, sperma ceti.
english_gloss: Fumigations — how many powers incenses and suffumigations have — has been proven by physicists and magi. Fumigations of the planets and signs attributed to their planets contribute greatly to the consecration of images and to invoking souls and demons and gathering or putting them to flight. Saturnine fumigations: sulphur, asphalt, storax, reed, styrax, mandrake, opium, hemlock oil, and all herbs and roots said to belong to Saturn. Solar: frankincense, saffron, balsam, amber, musk, aloe wood. Lunar: aloe, mastic, camphor, launum, poppy seed, white frankincense, spermaceti.

vocabulary.definition: fumigations, incenses, smoke-materials
burnings, incensings, ignitions
asphalt, bitumen, mineral pitch
styrax, storax (a resinous plant)
consecration, dedication, sacred charging

source_notes: The planetary fumigation tables are sourced from the Picatrix (III.11) and Pseudo-Albertus Magnus. Fumigations work by releasing the quintessential spirit of the plant or mineral, which then attracts the corresponding planetary influence. This principle — like draws like celestially — makes suffumigation a physical procedure, not a ritual in the strictly religious sense.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: De Sacrificiis et Igni — Sacrifices and Sacred Fires
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xliv
latin_text: Sacrificia autem non solum ad placandum deos et ad invocandos daemones valent, sed etiam ad attrahendas virtutes coelestes. Ignis enim ex propriis materialibus confectus, si recte ad hoc incensus fuerit, non solum locum purgat et sanat, sed etiam spiritum magnetice trahit qui in se completam stellae suae virtutem includit.
english_gloss: Sacrifices avail not only for propitiating gods and invoking demons, but also for attracting celestial virtues. For fire made from its own proper materials, if rightly kindled for this purpose, not only purifies and heals the place, but also draws magnetically the spirit that in itself contains the complete virtue of its star.

vocabulary.definition: sacrifices, offerings, sacred rites
to propitiate, appease, calm
magnetically, by magnetic attraction
complete, full, entire

source_notes: The sacrificial fire functions as a concentrated attractor of celestial virtue: by burning materials specifically assigned to a planet, the magus creates a vortex of sympathetic resonance that draws the planet's spiritus downward. The 'magnetic' metaphor (magnetice trahit) naturalizes the sacrificial operation.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Harmonia Musica — Musical Harmony and Celestial Powers
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter lvii
latin_text: Concentus harmonicus magnam habet potestatem in animam, in corpus et in res etiam externas. Constat enim ex numero, non tali qui in quantitate consistit, sed in qualitate vocum ac temporum, quibus animam per aures penetrat et ipso spiritu atque aeris motu mentem afficit. Daemonibus autem et angelis concentus in templis atque divinis officiis usurpatus plurimum placet, quia per illum anima ad superiora elevatur, mens a corporis vinculis liberatur, et quod ex una parte abstrahit a terrenis, ex alia attrahit coelestia. Qua de causa Apollo citharista et Orpheus ob concentus potentiam etiam silvas et saxa movere dicebantur.
english_gloss: Musical harmony has great power over the soul, the body, and even external things. For it consists of number — not such number as subsists in quantity, but in the quality of sounds and times — through which it penetrates the soul through the ears and affects the mind through the very spirit and movement of air. The harmony employed in temples and divine offices most pleases demons and angels, because through it the soul is elevated to higher things, the mind is freed from the bonds of the body, and what on one side abstracts from earthly things, on the other attracts celestial ones. For this reason Apollo the citharist and Orpheus were said, through the power of harmony, to move even forests and stones.

vocabulary.definition: harmony, concord, consonance
harmonic, of harmony
quantity, amount, extension
employed, used, appropriated
to abstract, draw away, detach

source_notes: Musical magic is explained through the Pythagorean-Platonic doctrine of cosmic harmony: since the cosmos is structured by musical ratios (Timaeus 35b-36d), music can resonate with and attract celestial virtue. Agrippa draws on Ficino's astrological music therapy and on the Orphic tradition. The Orpheus/Apollo example demonstrates musical magic's ancient pedigree.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Walker, D.P. Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella. London: Warburg Institute, 1958.

title: De Virtute Verborum et Nominum — The Power of Words and Names
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter lxix
latin_text: Vox humana quandam ineffabilem vim habet ad movendas res naturales, immo et supernaturales, quia non solum vocem corpori simul et animae esse commune instrumentum natura voluit, sed etiam virtutes superiores in nos per eam diffundere. Hinc est quod magi dicunt verbum esse maximum vinculum et viaticum, quia virtute verbi possunt res quaecunque moveri et attracti. Carmina enim et verba ex animo intenso prolata magnam habent potestatem; sicut enim cogitatio intendit vim suam per imaginationem in corpus, sic animus intendit vim suam per verbum in quamcunque rem exteriorem.
english_gloss: The human voice has a certain ineffable power for moving natural — indeed supernatural — things, because nature willed the voice to be an instrument common to both body and soul together, and also to diffuse into us the virtues of higher things through it. Hence the magi say that the word is the greatest bond and viaticum, because through the virtue of the word any things whatsoever can be moved and attracted. For charms and words pronounced from an intensely focused mind have great power; just as the mind directs its power into the body through imagination, so the soul directs its power through the word into whatever external thing.

vocabulary.definition: ineffable, unspeakable, beyond expression
bond, chain, constraint, binding
viaticum, provision for a journey, medium
songs, charms, incantations, poems
imagination, image-making faculty

source_notes: The doctrine of verbal power synthesizes the Pythagorean logos theory with Neoplatonic theurgy: words are not arbitrary signs but natural conduits of pneumatic power, capable of affecting the world soul. The imagination/word parallel is crucial: Agrippa argues that the concentrated will creates real effects whether directed by imagination or by spoken word.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Nominibus Barbaris — On Barbarous Names
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter lxx
latin_text: Nomina barbara et ineffabilia multo efficaciora habentur in magia quam reliqua, quia per vetustam traditionem a suis autoribus ita recepta sunt, ut nulla translatione corrumperentur, quemadmodum in transferendo vim suam amittunt nomina sensibilia. Nomina autem barbara et ignota multo plus terrore movent daemones et spiritum magis obstupefaciunt.
english_gloss: Barbarous and ineffable names are held to be much more efficacious in magic than others, because through ancient tradition they have been received from their authors in such a way that no translation corrupts them, just as sensible names lose their power in translation. Barbarous and unknown names move demons with much greater terror and stupefy the spirit more.

vocabulary.definition: barbarous, foreign, from non-Latin languages
ineffable, unspeakable, untranslatable
translation, transfer, rendering
to stupefy, stun, overwhelm with awe
ancient, old, of long standing

source_notes: The defense of barbarous names in magic — Hebrew, Chaldean, Arabic names that cannot be translated — argues that these are not arbitrary sounds but ancient sacred designations that retain power precisely through their untranslatability. This is the theoretical basis for the voces magicae tradition in Greco-Roman magic and its medieval descendants.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Reductione Literarum ad Planetas — Letters and Planets
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter lxxiv
latin_text: Dedit Deus homini mentem atque sermonem et ea pro signaculis atque characteribus rerum constituit, in quibus virtutes rerum omnium aut inclusae aut exprimuntur. Ideo in qualibet lingua et in quolibet alphabeto quaedam literae Saturno tribuuntur, quaedam Iovi, Marti, Soli, Veneri, Mercurio et Lunae; et ex his literas singulas dividiis suis planetis respondere novimus.
english_gloss: God gave to man mind and speech and established them as the signs and characters of things, in which the virtues of all things are either enclosed or expressed. Therefore in each language and in each alphabet certain letters are attributed to Saturn, certain to Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and Moon; and from these we know that individual letters correspond to their individual planets.

vocabulary.definition: speech, language, discourse, word
signs, seals, marks, tokens
to be expressed, represented, articulated
to be attributed, assigned, distributed
to correspond to, answer to, match

source_notes: The letter-planet correspondence system draws on Kabbalistic letter mysticism (especially the Sefer Yetzirah, in which letters create the world) and Arabic astrological numerology. Agrippa assigns each letter of Hebrew, Greek, and Latin to a planet, creating a universal code by which any name can be analyzed astrologically.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Formatione Hominis — The Formation of Man
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter lx
latin_text: Homo est parvus mundus, microcosmus, ex iisdem constans elementis e quibus constat totus mundus. Sicut enim mundus ipse ex terra, aqua, igne et aere compositus est, sic et homo. Et sicut mundus coelestia habet corpora, sic homo spiritus vitales et animam rationalem. Et sicut mundus habet intelligentias et angelorum ordines, sic homo intellectum et spiritum, per quos cum divinis communicat. Hinc facile colligimus in homine singulorum virium ac virtutum omnium quae in coelo, in aethere, in elementis et omnibus eorum habitatoribus reperiuntur reflexiones expressasque imagines contineri.
english_gloss: Man is a small world, a microcosm, consisting of the same elements from which the whole world consists. For just as the world itself is composed of earth, water, fire, and air, so also is man. And just as the world has celestial bodies, so man has vital spirits and a rational soul. And just as the world has intelligences and orders of angels, so man has intellect and spirit, through which he communicates with the divine. Hence we easily gather that in man are contained reflections and expressed images of all the powers and virtues that are found in heaven, in the aether, in the elements, and in all their inhabitants.

vocabulary.definition: microcosm, small world (Greek: mikros kosmos)
vital, life-giving, pertaining to life
intellect, understanding, the highest faculty
reflections, mirror-images
expressed, articulated, clearly rendered

source_notes: The microcosm/macrocosm doctrine is Agrippa's most influential concept: man contains within himself a reflection of every level of the universe. This makes the human body itself a magical instrument — by understanding one's own microcosmic structure, the magus gains leverage over the macrocosm. Sources: Plato's Timaeus, Macrobius, Pico's Heptaplus.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Membris Planetis Attributis — Body Parts and Planets
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter xxii
latin_text: Saturno tribuuntur auris dextra, genua, ossa, dentes et quaecunque in corpore arida, frigida et tristia. Iovi adsignantur stomachus, epar et pulmones. Marti vesica, ren, sanguis. Soli cor, medulla, semen virile, spiritus animales, oculus dexter. Veneri pudenda, matrix, nates, umbilicus. Mercurio lingua, manus, pedes, nervi et sensus. Lunae cerebrum, pulmo, medulla spinae, oculus sinister.
english_gloss: To Saturn are attributed the right ear, knees, bones, teeth, and whatever in the body is dry, cold, and sorrowful. To Jupiter are assigned the stomach, liver, and lungs. To Mars the bladder, kidneys, blood. To the Sun the heart, marrow, male seed, animal spirits, right eye. To Venus the genitals, womb, buttocks, navel. To Mercury the tongue, hands, feet, nerves, and senses. To the Moon the brain, lung, spinal marrow, left eye.

vocabulary.definition: to be attributed, assigned, allotted
liver (Greek: hepar)
kidney
marrow, pith, innermost part
genitalia, private parts (literally: things to be ashamed of)

source_notes: The planetary-bodily correspondence system derives from Firmicus Maternus and Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos. It underlies astrological medicine: each planet governs specific organs and diseases, and medical-magical treatment targets the corresponding planet. This system is foundational for Renaissance medical astrology and for Paracelsian doctrine.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Divinatione per Somnia — Divination Through Dreams
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter lx
latin_text: Somnia prophetica non per se et propria natura divinant sed per supernam inspirationem quandam, qua mens humana a superioribus caelestibusque intelligentiis illustratur; quam illustrationem per quietum somniumque magis recipit, quia tunc animus totus est quietissimus ab externis perturbationibus et a sensibilibus rebus abstractus. Per ipsam ergo quietem et silentium, quo mens a sensuum tumultu, passionum impetu et corporis occupatione seiungitur et sese in seipsam colligit, divini spiritus efficitur capax et futurorum praesaga.
english_gloss: Prophetic dreams do not divine through themselves and their own nature, but through a certain supernal inspiration, by which the human mind is illuminated by superior and celestial intelligences; which illumination it receives more during sleep and dreaming, because then the mind is wholly most quiet from external disturbances and abstracted from sensible things. Through this very quiet and silence, by which the mind is separated from the tumult of the senses, the onset of passions, and the occupation of the body, and gathers itself into itself, it becomes capable of the divine spirit and prophetic of future things.

vocabulary.definition: prophetic, predictive, inspired
to be illuminated, enlightened
most quiet, most still, in deepest rest
abstracted, drawn away, detached
prophetic, foreboding, presaging

source_notes: Prophetic dream theory in DOP synthesizes Aristotle's Parva Naturalia (On Dreams), Macrobius's Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, and Neoplatonic psychology: the rational soul, freed from sensory noise during sleep, can receive illumination from higher intelligences. Agrippa distinguishes natural prophetic dreams (via this mechanism) from demonic dream-manipulation.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Furore Divino — Divine Frenzy
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter lxii
latin_text: Est et furor quidam divinus qui, mentem a sensibus seiunctam et ab ipsis corpore eiectam, facit ire in abstracta et intelligibilia penetrare: hac via Sibyllae, hac prophetae, hac philosophi illuminantur. Ficinus quatuor furoribus mentes humanas diis iunctas esse docet: amatorio, poético, mystico et prophetico.
english_gloss: There is also a certain divine frenzy which, having separated the mind from the senses and expelled it from the body itself, makes it go into abstract things and penetrate the intelligible: by this path the Sibyls, by this path prophets, by this path philosophers are illuminated. Ficino teaches that human minds are joined to the gods through four frenzies: amatory, poetic, mystical, and prophetic.

vocabulary.definition: frenzy, madness, divine inspiration
separated, disjoined, set apart
abstract things, things drawn away from matter
intelligible things, objects of intellect
amatory, of love, erotic

source_notes: Ficino's four divine frenzies (from his commentary on Plato's Phaedrus and Ion) become a standard Renaissance framework. Agrippa uses them to explain how the human mind can access superhuman knowledge without demonic intermediary: through amatory (Eros), poetic (Muses), mystical (Dionysus), and prophetic (Apollo) inspiration.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Walker, D.P. Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella. London: Warburg Institute, 1958.

title: Magia Naturalis Licita — Natural Magic is Lawful
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter ii
latin_text: Magica enim naturalis nil aliud est quam philosophia naturalis maxima et perfectissima. Non igitur magia haec est impia, sacrilega aut diabolica — nisi quod fortasse propter ignorantiam multis videtur —, sed vere divina et sublimis, quam recte Plato 'artis regiae maximum opus' vocat et Cicero 'summae artis originem'.
english_gloss: For natural magic is nothing other than the greatest and most perfect natural philosophy. Therefore this magic is not impious, sacrilegious, or diabolical — except that perhaps through ignorance it seems so to many — but truly divine and sublime, which Plato rightly calls 'the greatest work of the royal art' and Cicero 'the origin of the supreme art.'

vocabulary.definition: impious, ungodly, wicked
sacrilegious, blasphemous
diabolical, of the devil
sublime, exalted, elevated
royal, kingly, of the king

source_notes: Agrippa's explicit defense of natural magic's lawfulness invokes classical authorities (Plato, Cicero) to counter the charge of diabolism. This rhetorical move — citing pagan philosophy to defend natural magic as 'royal art' — is characteristic of Renaissance apologists including Ficino and Pico, who sought to rescue magic from its demonological associations.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Mirabilibus Aquae Naturis — The Marvelous Nature of Water
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book I, Chapter vi
latin_text: Aquae enim tanta necessitas est, ut absque illa nullum animal degere possit, nulla herba nec planta quaevis citra aquae humectationem possit progeminare. In ipsa est seminaria omnium rerum virtus. Sola siquidem terra et aqua a Mose describuntur producere animam viventem, sed aquae duplicem productionem tribuit: natantium videlicet in aquis et volantium in aere supra terram.
english_gloss: The necessity of water is so great that without it no animal can live, no herb or plant can germinate without the moistening of water. In it is the seminal virtue of all things. For only earth and water are described by Moses as producing the living soul, but to water he attributes a twofold production: of swimmers in the waters and flyers in the air above the earth.

vocabulary.definition: moistening, dampening, watering
to sprout, germinate, shoot forth
seminal, of seeds; (noun) nursery
to attribute, assign, grant

source_notes: Agrippa's account of water's seminal virtue draws on Thales via Aristotle and on the hexameron tradition of biblical commentary (Genesis 1:20-21, where Moses assigns two acts of creation to water alone). This integration of natural philosophy with scriptural authority is characteristic of Agrippa's syncretic method.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Virtute Numerorum — The Power of Numbers
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter iii
latin_text: Inquit Severinus Boethius: 'Omnia quaecunque a primaeva rerum natura constructa sunt, numerorum videntur ratione formata; hoc enim fuit principale in animo Conditoris exemplar: hinc elementorum multitudo mutuata est, hinc temporum vices, hinc motus astrorum et coeli conversio, omniumque status numerorum colligatione subsistit.' Sunt ergo numeri re ipsa et natura rationibus et formis omnium rerum — et ideo non solum naturales sed etiam daemonicae et divinae virtutes eis inesse creduntur, et per eos habetur via ad omnia scibilia indaganda et intelligenda.
english_gloss: Severinus Boethius says: 'All things whatsoever that have been constructed by the primeval nature of things seem to have been formed by the reason of numbers; for this was the chief exemplar in the mind of the Creator: from here was the multitude of elements borrowed, from here the changes of seasons, from here the motions of the stars and the revolution of the heaven, and the condition of all things subsists by the binding of numbers.' Numbers are therefore in actual reality and by nature the reasons and forms of all things — and therefore not only natural but also demonic and divine virtues are believed to be in them, and through them the path is obtained for investigating and understanding all things knowable.

vocabulary.definition: primeval, original, of the earliest time
Creator, founder, maker
exemplar, model, pattern, archetype
binding, connection, linking together
knowable things, objects of knowledge

source_notes: Agrippa opens Book II with Boethius's Arithmetic to establish the ontological reality of numbers: they are not human inventions but the mind of the Creator. This Pythagorean-Platonic position (numbers as ideas in the divine mind) makes mathematical magic — using numbers to access divine patterns — a form of theophany rather than superstition.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Boethius. De Institutione Arithmetica. Ed. Jean-Yves Guillaumin. Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 1995.

title: De Monade — On the Monad
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter iv
latin_text: Unitas enim omnem numerum simplicissime penetrat omniumque numerorum communis mensura, fons et origo, omnem numerum in se unice coniunctum continet, multitudinis omnis insors, semper eadem et immutabilis; unde etiam in seipsam multiplicata nihil producit nisi seipsam. Indivisibilis est, partium omnium expers: quod si dividi aliquando fingatur, non secatur sed multiplicatur. Haec apud theologos est Deus ipse: unus, trinus, principium et finis omnium, origo et mensura omnium quae sunt, intelligentia et intelligibile, omnia simul, alpha et omega.
english_gloss: For unity penetrates every number in the simplest way and is the common measure, font, and origin of all numbers, containing every number uniquely conjoined in itself, having no part in multitude, always the same and unchangeable; whence also when multiplied by itself it produces nothing but itself. It is indivisible, lacking all parts: if one imagines it to be divided at any time, it is not cut but multiplied. This among theologians is God Himself: one, triple, beginning and end of all things, origin and measure of all that is, intelligence and intelligible, all things at once, alpha and omega.

vocabulary.definition: monad, unity, the One (Pythagorean first principle)
measure, standard, criterion
without a share in, having no part of
immutable, unchangeable, constant
intelligible, thinkable, object of intellect

source_notes: The monad (One) as divine principle synthesizes Pythagoras (via Nicomachus), Plato's Parmenides, Plotinus's One, and Christian Trinitarian theology. Agrippa's equation of the mathematical monad with God the Trinity — via the triple unity of Father/Son/Spirit — is a characteristic Renaissance synthesis of Pythagorean and Christian metaphysics.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Triade — The Power of Three
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter vi
latin_text: Tribus corporalia et spiritualia constant, principio, medio, fine. Tribus, ut Trismegistus ait, perficitur mundus: hemarmene, necessitate et ordine — hoc est, conventione causarum adinvicem, quam plerique fatum dicunt, et executione ad foetum ac foeturae debita distributione. Tota temporis mensura ternario concluditur, videlicet praeterito, praesenti, futuro. Omnis magnitudo tribus continetur, linea, superficie, corpore. Tres symphonias continet harmonia, diapason, hemiolion, diatessaron. Tria quoque sunt animarum genera: vegetativa, sensitiva, rationalis.
english_gloss: Things corporeal and spiritual consist of three: beginning, middle, end. The world is perfected, as Trismegistus says, by three things: hemarmene, necessity, and order — that is, by the agreement of causes among themselves (which most call fate), by their execution toward offspring, and by the due distribution of offspring. The whole measure of time is concluded in the ternary: past, present, future. Every magnitude is contained by three: line, surface, body. Harmony contains three symphonies: diapason, hemiolia, diatessaron. There are also three kinds of souls: vegetative, sensitive, rational.

vocabulary.definition: fate, destiny (Greek: heimarmenē), cosmic necessity
ternary, the number three
octave, the interval of eight tones
hemiolia, the ratio 3:2 (musical fifth)
diatessaron, the musical fourth (ratio 4:3)

source_notes: The ternary's universal significance — time, space, harmony, soul — follows Pythagorean number mysticism as systematized by Nicomachus and transmitted by Macrobius and Boethius. The Hermetic triad 'hemarmene/necessity/order' (from the Asclepius) gives the cosmic framework a Trismegistan sanction.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Tetrade — The Fourfold Principle
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter vii
latin_text: Quaternarius numerus apud Pythagoreos iuramentum sacratissimum erat, quem tetractyn vocabant, in quo fons et radix omnis naturae latere putabatur. Ex quatuor elementis mundus constitit, quatuor temporibus annus, quatuor partibus coelum, quatuor humores corpus humanum. Quaternarius est solidissimus numerus et immobilis fundamentum, basis et radix omnium numerorum.
english_gloss: The quaternary number was the most sacred oath among the Pythagoreans, whom they called the tetractys, in which the font and root of all nature was thought to lie hidden. From four elements the world was constituted, the year by four seasons, the heaven by four parts, the human body by four humors. The quaternary is the most solid number and the immovable foundation, base, and root of all numbers.

vocabulary.definition: tetractys, the sum 1+2+3+4=10, Pythagorean sacred symbol
oath, swearing, solemn pledge
most sacred, most holy
most solid, firmest, most stable
immovable, fixed, unchanging

source_notes: The tetractys (1+2+3+4=10) was the Pythagoreans' supreme oath: swearing by 'him who gave us the tetractys, the fountain and root of ever-flowing nature.' Agrippa follows Iamblichus's Life of Pythagoras. The four as foundation of the physical world (elements, seasons, humors) makes it the most 'solid' and 'material' of sacred numbers.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Quintario — The Number Five
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter viii
latin_text: Quinarius a Pythagoreis est Dei numerus, quo Deum honorabant et quem Hermum vocabant, idest interpretationem, quia per eum omnes res intelliguntur et ex eo totus numerus resultat. Quinque etiam sunt sensus corporis, quinque digiti manus, quinque zonae coeli, quinque planitia mundi. Est hic numerus et Martis, qui bellicosissimus habetur.
english_gloss: The quinary is for the Pythagoreans the number of God, by which they honored God and which they called Hermus, that is, interpretation, because through it all things are understood and from it the whole number results. Five also are the senses of the body, five the fingers of the hand, five the zones of the heaven, five the planes of the world. This number is also that of Mars, who is held most warlike.

vocabulary.definition: quinary, the number five
Hermus (Pythagorean name for five, from Hermes as interpreter)
interpretation, explanation, mediation
zones (of the earth/sky), belts
most warlike, most martial

source_notes: The number five connects divine interpretation (Hermes, the mediator between gods and men) with the human microcosm (five senses, five fingers) and the cosmos (five zones, five Platonic solids). Its Martian association is counter-intuitive but follows the Pythagorean pairing of odd numbers with male/active principles.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Septenario — The Number Seven
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter x
latin_text: Septenarius numerus est plenus omnis veneratione divina et omnium rerum perfectione. In eo enim Pythagoras Mineruam collocabat et virginem vocat, quia nec ex parte aliquam nec in aliquam primorum denarij numerorum multiplicando procedit. A physicis vero vehemens et potens habetur: nam is circulus vitae humanae omnes in septenarios digeritur et septem planetae septem coelorum sphaeras et septem stellas pliadis et septem dies hebdomadam conficiunt. Ob haec septennio etiam animarum beatitudinem iudicabant.
english_gloss: The septenary number is full of all divine veneration and the perfection of all things. For in it Pythagoras placed Minerva and called it a virgin, because it neither proceeds from any part nor to any part of the first numbers of the decad by multiplication. By natural philosophers it is held powerful and potent: for this circle of human life is distributed in sevens, and the seven planets compose the seven spheres of the heavens and the seven stars of the Pleiades and the seven days of the week. On account of these things they also judged the blessedness of souls by the seventh.

vocabulary.definition: septenary, the number seven
veneration, reverence, worship
week, period of seven days
the Pleiades, a star cluster of seven stars
blessedness, happiness, bliss

source_notes: Seven is the most cosmically resonant number in Agrippa's system: it governs planetary spheres, the week, the stages of human life (infancy to old age in seven-year increments), musical octave-intervals, and celestial hierarchies. The Pythagorean epithet 'virgin' for seven — not born from any number below ten and bearing none — makes it uniquely self-sufficient.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Denario — The Decade
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter xiii
latin_text: Denarius dicitur omnis numerus sive universus; hic numerus apud Hebraeos Iod, decimus character divini nominis, qui characterem primum in se retinens in numeris per denarium sibi similis iteratur. Decem sunt Sefirot et decem mandata legis Moysis et decem spherae mundi et decem Angeli ordines.
english_gloss: The decad is called every number or the universal number; this number among the Hebrews is Yod, the tenth character of the divine name, which retaining the first character in itself is repeated like itself through the decad in numbers. There are ten Sefirot and ten commandments of the Law of Moses and ten spheres of the world and ten orders of Angels.

vocabulary.definition: denarius (a coin), the decade, number ten
Sefirot, the ten divine attributes in Kabbalah
commandments, orders, precepts
spheres, orbs (of the cosmos)
Yod, the tenth Hebrew letter (י)

source_notes: The decade synthesizes Pythagorean perfect number theory (10 = 1+2+3+4) with the Kabbalistic Sefirot and the Mosaic Decalogue. The identification of 10 with the Hebrew letter Yod (the initial of the Tetragrammaton) links arithmetic, Kabbalah, and scripture in Agrippa's characteristic synthetic method.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Mensularum Planetarum Quadratis — Magic Squares of the Planets
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter xxii
latin_text: Retulerunt magi et ex talibus mensularum formationibus extrahi posse caracteres planetarum spirituumque eorum et talis lamina vel imago in talibus formata confert qui eam fert virtutem planeti illius. Prima tabula est Saturni ex numeris novem in quadrato trium distributa, cuius numerorum summa undecunque computetur triginta ac quinque efficit, ex qua extrahuntur caracteres spiritus Saturni et intelligentiae eius. Secunda est Iovis ex sedecim numeris in quadrato quatuor, summa cuius quadraginta quatuor est ubique. Tertia est Martis quinquies viginti quinque in quadrato quinque, summa ubique sexagintaquinque.
english_gloss: The magi have reported that from such formations of tablets the characters of the planets and their spirits can be extracted, and such a plate or image formed in this way confers on the one carrying it the virtue of that planet. The first table is of Saturn, distributed from nine numbers in a square of three, the sum of whose numbers however computed always makes thirty-five, from which are extracted the characters of the spirit of Saturn and its intelligence. The second is of Jupiter, from sixteen numbers in a square of four, whose sum is everywhere forty-four. The third is of Mars, twenty-five numbers in a square of five, the sum everywhere sixty-five.

vocabulary.definition: small tables, tablets; magic squares
squares, four-sided figures
plate, sheet, thin piece of metal
intelligence, angelic spirit governing a planet
everywhere, in every direction, always

source_notes: The seven planetary magic squares (kameas) — each producing a constant sum in every row, column, and diagonal — are one of Agrippa's most influential contributions. From the number arrangement he derives the sigils of each planet's ruling intelligence and spirit. The Saturn square (3×3, sum 15) is the oldest, appearing in Chinese mathematics and medieval Arabic magic.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Skinner, Stephen. Sacred Geometry: Deciphering the Code. New York: Sterling, 2006.

title: De Animae Humanae Compositione et Harmonia — Soul's Composition and Harmony
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter xxviii
latin_text: Anima humana secundum Platonem et Pythagoreos constat ex harmonia musicali: sicut enim mundus ex contrariarum qualitatum elementali conflictu in harmoniam quandam redactus est, sic ex contrariis animis anima temperata est. Hinc et ex musica nos ad morales virtutes et morum honestatem duci docet Plato: nam ut concentus certa proportione temperatae vocis movet mentes nostras motusque eos exprimit quibus consonat, ita anima, quorum virtutibus vel vitiis affecta est, eisdem facilius movetur et afficitur per musicam.
english_gloss: The human soul according to Plato and the Pythagoreans consists of musical harmony: for just as the world has been reduced to a certain harmony from the elemental conflict of contrary qualities, so the soul is tempered from contrary elements. Hence Plato also teaches that we are led by music to moral virtues and the honorableness of character: for just as the concord of voice tempered in a certain proportion moves our minds and expresses those motions with which it is consonant, so the soul, affected by the virtues or vices to which it has been conditioned, is more easily moved and affected by the same through music.

vocabulary.definition: conflict, clash, collision
tempered, moderated, balanced
honorableness, virtue, moral integrity
to be consonant with, resonate, agree
to be affected, moved, conditioned

source_notes: The soul-as-harmony doctrine (Plato's Phaedo 85e-86d, Timaeus 35a-36d) makes music the most direct instrument for affecting the rational soul, since both are constituted by the same numerical proportions. Agrippa links this to Ficino's musical therapy and to the Orphic tradition of soul-healing through song.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Viginti Octo Mansionibus Lunae — The 28 Mansions of the Moon
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter xxxiii
latin_text: Luna viginti octo dierum spatio cursum suum conficit per stellas fixas dividendo zodiaci circulum in viginti octo partes aequaliter, quas mansiones Lunae appellant. In prima igitur mansione, quam Alnath vocant, id quod ponitur in ea cornu arietis — facit ad iter bonum. In secunda, quam Allothaim vocant — vinculum fugitivi et ad infirmitatem et impedimentum. In tertia, Azoraya — super thesauros et ad iram regum. In quarta, Aldebaran — ad destructionem et impediendum alicuius. Haec traditio est Arabum et magis antiquorum.
english_gloss: The Moon completes its course in twenty-eight days through the fixed stars, dividing the circle of the zodiac into twenty-eight equal parts, which they call the mansions of the Moon. In the first mansion therefore, which they call Alnath, which is placed at the horn of Aries — it is good for a journey. In the second, which they call Allothaim — for the binding of a fugitive and for illness and impediment. In the third, Azoraya — for treasures and for the anger of kings. In the fourth, Aldebaran — for destruction and impeding anyone. This tradition is from the Arabs and ancient magi.

vocabulary.definition: mansions (of the Moon), stations, lodgings
Alnath (Arabic al-naṭḥ: the horn), first lunar mansion
Aldebaran (Arabic: the follower), star in Taurus
fugitive, runaway, escaped slave
treasures, stores, hoards

source_notes: The 28 lunar mansions are Arabic astronomical divisions (manāzil al-qamar) transmitted through Mashallah, Abu Ma'shar, and the Picatrix. Each mansion — defined by a prominent fixed star — governs specific magical operations. Agrippa's list follows Picatrix Book IV, chapter 9, though with some adaptations.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Attrell, Dan, and David Porreca, trans. Picatrix. University Park: Penn State University Press, 2019.

title: De Imaginibus Coelestibus sub Divo Factas — Celestial Images Made Under Open Sky
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter xlvii
latin_text: Imagines a veteribus in metallis aut lapidibus sub determinatis constellationibus fabricatae ac characteribus et nominibus spirituum inscriptae coelestium gratiam et virtutem in se contrahunt. Hoc sciebant Aegyptii qui statuarum suarum animandis quasi animas a supernis atque aetheriis traxerunt, per quas prophetias edebant et multa praestabant. Iamblichus haec in libro suo De Mysteriis Aegyptiorum probavit.
english_gloss: Images made by the ancients in metals or stones under determined constellations and inscribed with characters and names of spirits draw to themselves the grace and virtue of the celestial bodies. This the Egyptians knew, who animated their statues drawing their souls as it were from the supernal and ethereal regions, through which they issued prophecies and performed many things. Iamblichus proved these things in his book On the Mysteries of the Egyptians.

vocabulary.definition: constellations, star-configurations at a moment
made, crafted, fashioned
for animating, giving life to
ethereal, of the aether, celestial
prophecies, inspired utterances

source_notes: The animation of Egyptian statues — drawing celestial souls into stone images — is the example Agrippa uses to legitimize astrological talisman making. The source is Iamblichus's De Mysteriis (V.23), mediated through Ficino. The Egyptian priests' knowledge of how to attract stellar daemon into statues provides the theoretical model for all Renaissance image magic.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Iamblichus. De Mysteriis. Trans. Emma Clarke, John Dillon, and Jackson Hershbell. Atlanta: SBL Press, 2003.

title: De Sorte — The Art of Lots
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book II, Chapter liv
latin_text: Sors non est fortuita nec casu fit, sed divina necessitate et providentia dirigitur, ut per eam rerum latentium veritas manifestetur. Hinc in electione apostoli Mathiae loco Iudae in apostolorum locum sortibus usus est Ecclesia primitiva, et per sortes multorum temporum observationes multa praedicta sunt quae postea evenerunt. Sed sors per sacras scripturas facta efficacissima habetur.
english_gloss: A lot is not fortuitous nor does it happen by chance, but is directed by divine necessity and providence, so that through it the truth of hidden things may be made manifest. Hence in the election of the apostle Matthias to the place of Judas, the primitive Church used lots, and through lots many observations of many times have predicted things that afterward came to pass. But a lot cast through holy scriptures is held most efficacious.

vocabulary.definition: fortuitous, by chance, accidental
providence, foresight, divine governance
apostle, messenger, one sent
to be made manifest, revealed, evident
lots, divination by lots, fate

source_notes: The legitimacy of sortilege (divination by lots) is established by the Acts of the Apostles 1:26, where Matthias is chosen by lot. Agrippa uses this to defend the 'Sortes Sanctorum' practice — opening the Bible at random for divine guidance — as proper religious divination distinct from condemned pagan sortilege.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Necessitate Religionis — Religion as Foundation of Magic
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter i
latin_text: Tempus est nunc ad altiora nos convertere et ad eam magiae portionem, quae nos docet callere et scire leges religionum et quomodo veritatem religione divina debeamus adipisci et quomodo animum et mentem a rebus terrenis et corporalibus abstrahere atque ad divina sublimia converti possimus. Nam qui coelestium et divinorum mysterio caret et nomen Dei sacrum ignorat, huic nulla coelestium virtutum introductio patere potest, nulla spiritalis operatio succedere.
english_gloss: It is now time for us to turn to higher matters and to that portion of magic which teaches us to be skilled in and to know the laws of religions, and how we ought to attain truth through divine religion, and how we can abstract the mind and soul from earthly and corporeal things and convert ourselves to the lofty divine things. For one who lacks the mystery of the celestial and divine, and is ignorant of the sacred name of God, to him no introduction of celestial virtues can lie open, no spiritual operation can succeed.

vocabulary.definition: to be skilled in, expert in, practiced
to attain, obtain, achieve
to abstract, draw away, detach
lofty things, sublime things, heights
to succeed, follow after, come about

source_notes: Book III's opening claim — that without religious knowledge and knowledge of the divine name, no magical operation can succeed — makes religious piety the necessary foundation of ceremonial magic. This distinguishes Agrippa's system from diabolism (which requires rejection of God) and from mere naturalism (which ignores the divine). Magic is a form of prayer and contemplation.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Nominibus Divinis Hebraicis — Hebrew Divine Names
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xi
latin_text: Hebraeorum magistri docent quod Deus decem nominibus insigniri solet apud Hebraeos. Primum et principalissimum nomen eius est Ehieh, quod proprie esse et existentiam sonat nec ulli nisi ipsi Deo tribuendum est. Secundum Iod, quasi Sabaoth, hoc est exercituum. Tertium El, quod potentiam et firmitatem importat. Quartum Elohim, quod interpretatur Dei ac iudicum et angelorum commune nomen est. Quintum Elohim Gibor, hoc est Deus fortis vel potens. Sextum IHVH vel Tetragrammaton, nominum omnium sanctissimum et incomprehensibile, extra quod nullum legitimum nomen Dei esse arbitrantur.
english_gloss: The masters of the Hebrews teach that God is customarily distinguished by ten names among the Hebrews. The first and most principal of his names is Ehieh, which properly sounds being and existence and is to be attributed to no one but God himself. The second is Yod, as it were Sabaoth, that is of hosts. The third El, which imports power and firmness. The fourth Elohim, which is interpreted as the common name of God and judges and angels. The fifth Elohim Gibor, that is God strong or powerful. The sixth YHVH or Tetragrammaton, the most holy and incomprehensible of all names, beyond which they consider no legitimate name of God exists.

vocabulary.definition: Ehyeh (Hebrew: I AM), divine name of pure being
Sabaoth (Hebrew: hosts/armies), divine epithet
Gibbor (Hebrew: strong, mighty, hero)
incomprehensible, beyond grasp
the four-letter divine name (YHWH)

source_notes: Agrippa's ten divine Hebrew names (following Reuchlin's De Arte Cabalistica) map onto the ten Sefirot of Kabbalah. Each divine name corresponds to a Sefira, an angelic order, a celestial sphere, and a part of the human body — creating the Sefirotic 'ladder' central to Kabbalistic prayer and ceremonial magic.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Reuchlin, Johann. De Arte Cabalistica. Trans. Martin Goodman and Sarah Goodman. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1993.

title: De Tetragrammato — The Tetragrammaton
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xi
latin_text: Nomen Tetragrammaton IHVH, apud Hebraeos summae reverentiae et incomprehensibile, quod ab antiquis Hebraeis characteribus propriis scriptum, alii Iehova pronuntiant, alii Jao, alii aliis modis. Ex hoc nomine quatuor literarum plena significatio ponitur: Iod Patrem, prima He Matrem sive divinum intellectum, Vau Filium sive Verbum, ultima He feminam sive Spiritum Sanctum designat. Ex quo intelligimus mysterium Trinitatis in sacratissimo Dei nomine occultum, et hinc magorum artem nominis Dei scire hoc est principale et efficacissimum in magia ceremoniali fundamentum.
english_gloss: The name Tetragrammaton YHVH, which among the Hebrews is of the highest reverence and incomprehensible, written by the ancient Hebrews in their own characters, some pronounce Jehovah, others Jao, others in other ways. From this name of four letters the full significance is placed: Yod designates the Father, the first He the Mother or divine intellect, Vav the Son or Word, the final He the feminine or Holy Spirit. From which we understand the mystery of the Trinity hidden in the most sacred name of God, and hence knowing the art of the name of God is the chief and most efficacious foundation in ceremonial magic.

vocabulary.definition: Yod (י), first letter of the Tetragrammaton
Vav (ו), third letter of the Tetragrammaton
to designate, indicate, mark out
Trinity, the threefold divine nature
hidden, concealed, mysterious

source_notes: Agrippa's Trinitarian reading of the Tetragrammaton — following Reuchlin and Pico — maps the Hebrew four-letter divine name onto Father/Mother-Intellect/Son-Word/Holy Spirit. This Christianized Kabbalah was the central strategy of Renaissance Christian Kabbalists to convert Jewish mysticism into proof of Christian theology.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Septuaginta Duobus Nominibus Dei — The 72 Names of God
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xxv
latin_text: Ex tribus versiculis Exodi, scilicet decimooctavo, decimonono et vicesimo capitis quinti decimi, quorum unusquisque habet septuaginta et duas literas, Hebraei magistri septuaginta et duo Dei nomina eliciunt — quae vocant Schemhamphorasch, id est explicatum, id est nomen distinctum sive separatum. Ex his nominibus septuaginta et duo angeli denominantur, quorum singuli ternas literas ex nomine Dei participant. Magi autem ex his nominibus et characteres angelorum et imagines eliciunt, per quos angelos evocant, interrogant et ad desiderata opera cogunt.
english_gloss: From three verses of Exodus, namely the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth of chapter fifteen, each of which has seventy-two letters, the Hebrew masters elicit seventy-two names of God — which they call Schemhamphorasch, that is, 'explained,' that is, the name made distinct or separated. From these seventy-two names are denominated seventy-two angels, each of which participates in three letters from the name of God. The magi moreover extract from these names the characters and images of the angels, through which they evoke the angels, interrogate them, and compel them to desired works.

vocabulary.definition: the Explicit Name (Hebrew: Shem ha-Meforash), the 72-fold divine name
to elicit, draw out, extract
to participate in, share in
to be named, denominated, designated
to compel, force, drive together

source_notes: The Shem ha-Meforash (Explicit Name) methodology derives from Kabbalistic biblical exegesis: Exodus 14:19-21 has three verses each of exactly 72 letters; reading them boustrophedon (right-left, left-right, right-left) produces 72 three-letter combinations, each a divine name, each governing an angel. Agrippa follows Reuchlin and Lull. The 72 angels correspond to the 72 divisions of the zodiac.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Ordine Angelorum — The Orders of Angels
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xvi
latin_text: Deus ipse omnibus rebus influit primo et proxime, deinde per angelos novem ordinibus dispositos: Seraphim, Cherubim, Throni, Dominationes, Potestates, Virtutes, Principatus, Archangeli, Angeli. Per hos ergo gradus omnes coelestis gratiae dona in nos devolvuntur: per Seraphim caritas, per Cherubim intellectus, per Throni stabilitas, per Dominationes magnificentia, per Virtutes fortitudo, per Potestates ordinata dispositio, per Principatus zelus divini honoris, per Archangelos revelatio mysteriorum, per Angelos custodia et gubernatio singulorum.
english_gloss: God himself flows into all things first and most directly, then through angels arranged in nine orders: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Powers, Virtues, Principalities, Archangels, Angels. Through these degrees therefore all gifts of celestial grace devolve upon us: through the Seraphim charity, through the Cherubim understanding, through the Thrones stability, through the Dominions magnificence, through the Virtues fortitude, through the Powers ordered disposition, through the Principalities zeal for divine honor, through the Archangels revelation of mysteries, through the Angels the custody and governance of individuals.

vocabulary.definition: to devolve, flow down, cascade
Seraphim (Hebrew: burning ones), highest angelic order
Cherubim (Hebrew: living ones), second angelic order
governance, steering, direction
of individuals, of each one separately

source_notes: The nine angelic orders follow Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite's Celestial Hierarchy, systematized by Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I q.108). Agrippa assigns a specific grace to each order, making the angelic hierarchy a ladder of spiritual attainment for the magician who wishes to invoke each level's corresponding gift.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. The Celestial Hierarchy. Trans. Colm Luibheid. New York: Paulist Press, 1987.

title: De Lingua Angelorum — The Language of Angels
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xxiii
latin_text: Angeli inter se et nobiscum collocuntur non voce sonora sed per intellectuales impressiones et illustrationes, vel per species in imaginationem nostram infusas. Locuntur autem et per voces, per somnia, per oracula, per visiones et per ecstases. Quam vocem Paulus vocat linguam angelorum, qua si loqui possit homo, vocat eam Apostolus vocem primam et altissimam, quam nemo hominum perfecte percipere valet nisi qui in spiritu rapiatur. Hebraei doctores dicunt hanc esse linguam sanctam, scilicet hebraicam, quae prima fuit et naturaliter ab Adamo usurpata.
english_gloss: Angels converse with each other and with us not through sonorous voice but through intellectual impressions and illuminations, or through species infused into our imagination. But they also speak through voices, through dreams, through oracles, through visions and through ecstasies. Which voice Paul calls the tongue of angels, by which if a man could speak, the Apostle calls it the first and highest voice, which no man can perfectly perceive unless he be caught up in the spirit. The Hebrew doctors say this is the holy tongue, namely Hebrew, which was first and was naturally used by Adam.

vocabulary.definition: impressions, imprintings, impacts
illuminations, enlightenings, clarifications
ecstasies, states of being outside oneself
to be caught up, seized, carried away
used, employed, appropriated, practiced

source_notes: Angelic communication theory synthesizes 1 Corinthians 13:1 ('tongue of angels') with Pseudo-Dionysian illumination theory and Kabbalistic doctrine of the primacy of Hebrew as God's creative language. The claim that Hebrew was Adam's natural language (and the original language of creation) is foundational to Renaissance Kabbalah and to Dee's Enochian angel-language system.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Characteribus per Revelationem Receptis — Characters Received Through Revelation
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xxx
latin_text: Sunt enim divinae omnipotentiae sacramenta atque vehicula, non ab hominibus, non etiam ab angelis, sed ab ipso summo Deo certo modo pro suorum characterum immobili numero et figura sempiterna stabilitate instituta, divinitatisque harmoniam spirantia divinaque assistentia consecrata: quare illa timent superi, tremunt inferi, colunt angeli, pavent cacodaemones et omnis reveretur creatura, omnis veneratur religio. Quorum religiosa observatio devotaque cum timore ac tremore invocatio virtutem nobis magnam praestant deificamque unionem atque etiam supra naturam mirabilium operum efficientiam.
english_gloss: For these are sacraments and vehicles of the divine omnipotence, established not by men, not even by angels, but by the most high God himself in a certain way with the immovable number and sempiternal stability of their characters, breathing the harmony of divinity and consecrated by divine assistance: therefore the supernal powers fear them, the infernal tremble, angels worship, evil spirits are terrified, and every creature reverences, every religion venerates them. Their religious observance and devoted invocation with fear and trembling bestow on us great virtue and deifying union and also the efficacy of marvelous works beyond nature.

vocabulary.definition: sacraments, sacred mysteries, solemn pledges
vehicles, carriers, conveyances
sempiternal, everlasting, eternal
evil spirits, malevolent demons
deifying, making divine, god-making

source_notes: The divinely-instituted characters — sacred figures that cause universal fear/reverence across all ontological levels — are the theoretical apex of Agrippa's magical system. They transcend human invention, being established by God with eternal stability. The 'deifying union' (unio deifica) they enable is the highest goal of Book III: theosis through magical practice.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Vinculis Spirituum — On the Binding of Spirits
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xxxiii
latin_text: Vinculum quod in nobis spiritum ligat est propria mens nostra, quia ab ea extenduntur omnes virtutes spirituales. Spiritus ergo ligantur per nomina divina, per sacra signa, per sanctas deprecationes, per suffumigationes et per loca et tempora propria, per nomina spirituum superiorum eis dominantium et per virtutes aliorum spirituum. Quod si spiritus per haec onmia non obedierit, opus est exorcismi virtute ad eum coercendum, quam virtutem Christus dedit apostolis et per eos servis suis fidelibus.
english_gloss: The bond that binds the spirit in us is our own mind, for from it all spiritual virtues are extended. Spirits are therefore bound through divine names, through sacred signs, through holy prayers, through fumigations and through proper places and times, through the names of higher spirits dominating them, and through the virtues of other spirits. But if the spirit does not obey through all of these, it is necessary to use the virtue of exorcism to coerce it, which virtue Christ gave to the apostles and through them to his faithful servants.

vocabulary.definition: bond, chain, binding, constraint
to be bound, tied, restrained
prayers, entreaties, supplications
to coerce, restrain, confine
exorcism, adjuration, expulsion of spirits

source_notes: The taxonomy of spirit-binding — divine names, signs, prayers, fumigations, places/times, higher spirits' names, exorcism — is Agrippa's synthesis of the Solomonic and Scholastic traditions.
