The final recourse to exorcism (Christ's gift to the apostles) places ceremonial magic within orthodox Christian practice, making the magician a latter-day apostle.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Furore Prophetico — On Prophetic Frenzy
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xlvi
latin_text: Furor propheticus supra omnem philosophiam positus est, maxima donum a Deo collatum, nec arte nec studio, nec voluntate humana acquiritur, sed sola divina gratia conceditur. Hic mentes nonnunquam quibusdam usurpat qui nec ad id dispositi nec parati erant: unde aliquando in prophetarum libris legimus pueros, quosdam etiam agrestes et idiotas prophetas fuisse. Haec gratia etiam in somno et in valetudine et in furentibus interdum locum habet, ut non hominum sed Dei opus esse videatur.
english_gloss: Prophetic frenzy is placed above all philosophy, the greatest gift conferred by God; it is acquired neither by art nor by study, nor by human will, but is conceded by divine grace alone. This sometimes seizes the minds of those who were neither disposed nor prepared for it: hence we sometimes read in the books of the prophets that boys, and even rustics and idiots, were prophets. This grace also sometimes has its place in sleep and in illness and in the frenzied, so that it appears to be the work not of men but of God.

vocabulary.definition: prophetic, of prophecy, inspired
to seize, take possession of, employ
rustics, countryfolk, rural people
idiots, common people, the uneducated
to be conceded, granted, allowed

source_notes: Prophetic frenzy (furor propheticus) is for Agrippa the highest and most authentic form of magical inspiration, precisely because it cannot be produced by technique — it is pure divine gift. The examples of boys and idiots prophesying proves that this grace bypasses human merit and preparation. Agrippa follows Iamblichus's De Mysteriis III on genuine vs. imitative prophecy.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Gradibus Animarum — The Grades of Souls
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xliv
latin_text: Anima nostra quatuor habet potentias, videlicet mentem, rationem, imaginationem et sensum. Has potentias quatuor mundi complent: mens intelligibilis, ratio coelestis, imaginatio astralis, sensus elementalis. Per has quatuor virtutes anima in quatuor mundi statos sese diffundit: per mentem in mundum intelligibilem, per rationem in mundum coelestis, per imaginationem in mundum astral, per sensum in mundum elementalem. Per quos gradus anima nostra ascendere potest ad primam causam, quae Deus est, et descendere in ultima, quae materia elementalis.
english_gloss: Our soul has four powers: mind, reason, imagination, and sense. These four powers the four worlds fill: mind with the intelligible, reason with the celestial, imagination with the astral, sense with the elemental. Through these four virtues the soul diffuses itself into the four states of the world: through mind into the intelligible world, through reason into the celestial world, through imagination into the astral world, through sense into the elemental world. Through these degrees our soul can ascend to the first cause, which is God, and descend to the last things, which is elemental matter.

vocabulary.definition: powers, faculties, capabilities
imagination, image-making, phantasy
intelligible, knowable by intellect alone
to diffuse, spread out, pour through
astral, stellar, of the stars

source_notes: The fourfold soul-world correspondence is Agrippa's key to magical ascent: by activating each faculty (mind, reason, imagination, sense) with its appropriate world, the magician's soul can traverse all four cosmological levels and reach the first cause. This is the practical upshot of all three books: the magician who knows natural, celestial, and divine magic can ascend the full hierarchy.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Incantamentis et Carminibus — On Incantations and Charms
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xlviii
latin_text: Carmina et incantamenta non solum ad eos qui ea pronunciant, sed etiam ad alios longe distantes extenduntur, per spiritum quidem mundi et per spiritus viventes in aere in quos animus vehementi affectu prolatum verbum imprimit et qui inde tanquam instrumenta ad ea quae vult efficienda utuntur. Ecclesia quoque primitiva utebatur sacris quibusdam incantamentis contra morbos et tempestates, quae omnia sub veneratione alicuius numinis vel pronunciando orantes vel aliquando scripta appensa sive alligata deferentes saepe miranda efficiebant.
english_gloss: Charms and incantations extend not only to those who pronounce them but also to others far distant, through the spirit of the world indeed and through the living spirits in the air into which the soul, through the word spoken with vehement emotion, imprints itself, and which spirits then are used as instruments to bring about what it wills. The primitive Church also used certain sacred incantations against diseases and storms, which all — either pronouncing them while praying under the veneration of some deity, or sometimes carrying them written and hung or bound — often accomplished wonderful things.

vocabulary.definition: incantations, spells, magical formulas
vehement, intense, forceful
to imprint, stamp, impress upon
instruments, tools, means
hung, suspended, attached

source_notes: Agrippa legitimizes incantation by citing the primitive Church's use of sacred charms against disease and storms. This historical argument — that early Christians practiced incantatory healing — defuses the charge that verbal magic is inherently pagan. The aerial spirit mechanism (words imprint on the spiritus mundi) provides the natural-philosophical explanation.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Generibus Daemonum — Types of Demons
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xvii
latin_text: Daemones mali tria sunt genera: primum eorum qui in aetheris regionibus morantur et ex alto insidiantur, tentant et turbant cunctos homines; secundum qui terras et aquas et aera medium incolunt et praefecti sunt bellis, pestibus et aliis malis; tertium qui apud nos versantur, quos Latini lares, lemures et larvae, Graeci vero eidola et idola appellant.
english_gloss: There are three kinds of evil demons: first those who dwell in the ethereal regions and lie in ambush from on high, tempting and disturbing all men; second those who inhabit the earth and waters and middle air and are set over wars, plagues, and other evils; third those who dwell among us, whom the Latins call lares, lemures, and larvae, but the Greeks eidola and idola.

vocabulary.definition: ether, the upper atmosphere, the heavens
to lie in ambush, to lurk, to plot against
lemures, Roman spirits of the restless dead
larvae, masks; Roman malevolent spirits
eidola, images, spectral apparitions (Greek)

source_notes: Agrippa's tripartite demon taxonomy synthesizes Apuleius (aerial demons), the church fathers (earthly demons), and Roman folk religion (domestic spirits). The three-tier spatial hierarchy mirrors the three-world cosmology: ethereal, aerial/terrestrial, and chthonic demons correspond to intellectual, celestial, and elemental realms.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Genio Proprio — On One's Personal Genius
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xxi
latin_text: Unusquisque nostrum habet genium sive angelum custodem a Deo attributum, qui mentem nostram ad recta incitat et ab errore deducit. Hunc genius noster magis audit cum animus noster, ab omnibus rebus terrenis abstractus, sese in se colligit et divinis se rebus occupat et orationi contemplationique vacat.
english_gloss: Each of us has a genius or guardian angel assigned by God, who incites our mind to right things and leads it away from error. Our genius hears us more when our soul, abstracted from all earthly things, gathers itself into itself and occupies itself with divine things and is free for prayer and contemplation.

vocabulary.definition: genius, guardian spirit, personal divine attendant
guardian, keeper, protector
to incite, urge, stimulate, inspire
to lead away from, guide away
contemplation, meditation, spiritual vision

source_notes: The personal genius or guardian angel doctrine synthesizes Roman genius tradition with Platonic daimon (Socrates' daimonion in the Apology) and Christian guardian angel theology. Agrippa's key point — that the genius speaks more clearly when the mind is free from sensory distraction — makes contemplative prayer the preparatory state for angelic communication.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Animis Beatorum — Souls of the Blessed
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xlv
latin_text: Animae beatae post obitum divinis honoribus dignantur et pro diis coluntur: sic apostoli et martyres et confessores et virgines Christianis in honore sunt. Sed et heroum animae, quae inter nos et deos mediae dicuntur a Platonicis, a magia invocari solent ad praedicendum futura et ad multa alia opera efficienda, tanquam mediae inter nos et divinum.
english_gloss: The souls of the blessed after death are deemed worthy of divine honors and are worshipped as gods: so the apostles and martyrs and confessors and virgins are held in honor by Christians. But also the souls of heroes, which the Platonists say are intermediate between us and the gods, are usually invoked by magic to predict future things and to accomplish many other works, as intermediaries between us and the divine.

vocabulary.definition: blessed, happy, fortunate, divinely favored
death, departure, decease
confessors, those who profess the faith without martyrdom
heroes (Greek: demi-gods), semi-divine souls
intermediate, middle, mediating

source_notes: Agrippa equates the Christian saints with Platonic heroes — intermediate divine beings between gods and mortals (Symposium 202e-203a). This bold syncretism legitimizes necromantic invocation of the dead by equating it with Christian saint-veneration. The heroes/saints function as magical intermediaries between human practitioners and the divine.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Ascensu Animae — The Ascent of the Soul
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter lxi
latin_text: Mens igitur humana, dum a rebus sensibilibus abstracta est et in se collecta puraque et clara, per gradus virtutum ad rerum intelligentiam ac divinum contemplationem conscitur ascendere. Et qui ad hunc gradum pervenit, ea quae sunt supra nos intuetur et facit et dictat et etiam futura praenoscit, prophetans non tanquam homo sed tanquam deus.
english_gloss: The human mind therefore, when it has been abstracted from sensible things and gathered into itself and is pure and clear, is known to ascend through degrees of virtues to the understanding of things and to divine contemplation. And one who has reached this degree beholds and does and dictates the things that are above us, and also foreknows future things, prophesying not as a man but as a god.

vocabulary.definition: abstracted, drawn away, separated
to know together, to be recognized, to ascend (here)
to behold, gaze upon, contemplate
to foreknow, know in advance
prophesying, speaking with divine inspiration

source_notes: The soul's ascent to divine contemplation is the teleological culmination of De Occulta Philosophia: the magician who has mastered natural, celestial, and divine magic and purified his soul can prophesy 'not as a man but as a god' (non tanquam homo sed tanquam deus). This deification language recalls Ficino's Theologia Platonica and Pico's Oration.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Religione et Superstitione — Religion vs Superstition
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter iv
latin_text: Superstitio itaque, licet a vera religione aliena sit, non tamen tota aut omnis reprobata est, quoniam in multis etiam toleratur et a religionis antistitibus observatur. Dico autem superstitionem eam maxime quae est similitudo quaedam religionis: quatenus imitatur quicquid in religione est ex miraculis, ex sacramentis, ex ritibus, ex observationibus et caeteris ceremonialibus, quae vera religio habet.
english_gloss: Superstition therefore, although alien from true religion, is not entirely or wholly reproved, since in many things it is tolerated and even observed by religious officiants. I speak of that superstition especially which is a certain likeness of religion: insofar as it imitates whatever religion has from miracles, from sacraments, from rites, from observations and other ceremonies which true religion possesses.

vocabulary.definition: superstition, excessive or false religious practice
reproved, condemned, rejected
officiants, high-priests, religious guardians
other, the rest, remaining
ceremonial, of ceremonies, ritual

source_notes: Agrippa's nuanced distinction between religion and superstition — acknowledging that superstition imitates religion and is even tolerated by religious officials — creates a large gray zone in which ceremonial magic can operate. The tolerance of 'superstition' by the church itself (for folk devotions, relic cults, etc.) undermines a sharp sacred/magical boundary.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Modo Invocandi Deos et Spiritus — Procedure for Invoking Gods and Spirits
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter xxxvi
latin_text: Orando, consecrando, sacrificando, invocando, virtutes spirituales atque coelestes attrahere et rebus tuis quibus velis imprimere omneque scientiae magicalis opus ea ipsa vivificare. Quisquis autem praeter autoritatem officii, absque sanctitatis et doctrinae merito, praeter naturae educationisque dignitatem aliquid in magicis operari praesumpserit, sine fructu laborabit ac se, simul et credentes sibi, decipiet.
english_gloss: By praying, consecrating, sacrificing, invoking, to attract spiritual and celestial virtues and imprint them on what you will and vivify every work of magical knowledge with that same. But whoever has presumed to operate in magic beyond the authority of office, without the merit of holiness and learning, beyond the dignity of nature and education, will labor without fruit and will deceive both himself and those who believe in him.

vocabulary.definition: consecrating, dedicating, making sacred
sacrificing, offering sacrifice
to vivify, give life to, animate
to presume, undertake without authorization
merit, desert, worth, qualification

source_notes: The invocation procedure — pray, consecrate, sacrifice, invoke — is presented as requiring triple authorization: ecclesiastical (office), personal (sanctity/learning), and natural (born under proper stars/education). This triple qualification distinguishes the legitimate Magus from the charlatan. The warning against unauthorized magic is both ethical and practical.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: De Suffumigationibus ad Spiritus — Suffumigations for Spirits
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter lxii
latin_text: Ad bonos spiritus evocandos suffumigationes ex rebus odoriferis et mundis et sanctis adhibendae sunt, quae ex gummi nobili et aromatibus conficiuntur, ut thus, myrrha, crocus et similia. Ad malos vero et noxios spiritus constringendos, foetida et graveolentia adhibenda, ut sulphur, asphaltum, lacrima abiegna, et his similia. Quia sicut animae ad sua symbola respondent, sic et spiritus ad sua symbola conveniunt.
english_gloss: For evoking good spirits, fumigations from fragrant and pure and holy things are to be used, which are made from noble gum and aromatics, such as frankincense, myrrh, saffron, and similar. But for binding evil and harmful spirits, fetid and ill-smelling things are to be applied, such as sulphur, asphalt, fir resin, and the like. Because just as souls respond to their symbols, so spirits gather to their symbols.

vocabulary.definition: fragrant, scent-bearing, aromatic
gum, resin, adhesive substance
fetid, foul-smelling, stinking
ill-smelling, heavy-scented (of foul odors)
symbols, corresponding signs, tokens

source_notes: The distinction between pure/fragrant fumigations for good spirits and fetid/sulfurous ones for evil spirits follows the sympathetic principle: like attracts like. Good spirits are attracted by noble aromatics (frankincense, myrrh) because these are the earthly analogs of their celestial purity; demons are attracted to sulfur because of their chthonic nature.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.

title: Conclusio Operis — Conclusion of the Work
author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
work: De Occulta Philosophia, Book III, Chapter lxv
latin_text: Haec igitur est Occulta Philosophia sive Magia: triplici partita, physica, mathematica, theologica, quae plenissimam omnium rerum cognitionem parit et in eis mirabilia efficit. Et hoc est quod philosophi summi vocant artem regiam et summae artis originem et magnum naturae miraculum et terrenorum angelum et omnium arcanum arcanum.
english_gloss: This therefore is the Occult Philosophy or Magic: divided into three, physical, mathematical, theological, which produces the fullest knowledge of all things and works marvels in them. And this is what the greatest philosophers call the royal art, and the origin of the supreme art, and the great miracle of nature, and the earthly angel, and the secret of all secrets.

vocabulary.definition: the fullest, most complete, most total
to produce, give birth to, bring forth
royal, kingly, befitting a king
miracle, wonder, marvelous thing
secret, mystery, hidden thing

source_notes: The closing definition of Occult Philosophy — as the royal art that is simultaneously natural, mathematical, and theological — is Agrippa's final synthesis. The accumulated epithets ('great miracle of nature,' 'earthly angel,' 'secret of all secrets') represent a crescendo of Hermetic and Platonic panegyric. The three-book structure has made the case that magic is legitimate philosophy.
bibliography: Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius. De Occulta Philosophia Libri Tres. Ed. Vittoria Perrone Compagni. Leiden: Brill, 1992.
Lehrich, Christopher I. The Language of Demons and Angels: Cornelius Agrippa's Occult Philosophy. Leiden: Brill, 2003.
